Important examples / cases

Penn / Save the Children identifiable-victim experiment (Intro). Students gave 2.83 to Rokia, 1.16 to “millions hungry”; warning students about the bias halved donation to Rokia rather than raising it for the millions. The book’s framing exhibit for “stop debating the wrong scale.”
Pak Solhin (Bandung casual laborer) (ch. 2). Believed himself to be in a nutrition-poverty trap; authors read his case as a labor-market and depression-induced collapse, not a literal calorie trap. Iconic instance of the inverted-L-not-S adult-nutrition story.
Oucha Mbarbk (rural Morocco) (ch. 2). Owns TV, parabolic antenna, DVD player despite reporting hunger. “Television is more important than food.” Boredom is a real consumption category; the poor optimize for present pleasantness against pessimistic horizons.
Cohen-Dupas TAMTAM bed-net experiment (Kenya, ch. 3). Demand collapses with price but conditional usage is 60-90% regardless of price paid. Refutes Easterly’s free-means-worthless claim with RCT data.
Seva Mandir 2-lb-of-dal incentive for immunization (Udaipur, ch. 3). Full immunization 6% → 38% with a small immediate reward; the canonical present-bias-correcting nudge.
Pratham ASER survey (India, ch. 4). 700,000 children, 600 districts. 35% can’t read a first-grade paragraph; 30% can’t do basic division; the empirical anchor of the learning-crisis literature.
Israel Operation Solomon airlift (1991, ch. 4). 15,000 Ethiopian Jewish children with barely-literate parents reached 65% twelfth-grade-no-repeat (vs 74% Russian-emigrant peers with 11.5-year-educated parents). The “schools can compensate for severe family disadvantage” demonstration.
Bogotá CCT lottery (ch. 4). Within-family resource-concentration on the lottery-winning child harms the loser-sibling more than household income gains help.
Kenya Duflo-Dupas-Kremer triple RCT (ch. 5). ABCD curriculum null, “sugar daddies” info works, uniforms work, ABCD cancels uniforms. The cleanest information-vs-preference-vs-structural-incentive comparison in the book.
Matlab Bangladesh family-planning RCT (ch. 5). 141 villages, 1977-1996. Reduced fertility 1.2 children/woman, no significant per-child human-capital effect. Refutes Becker.
Udry Nigerian informal-loan diary (ch. 6). 2.5 active credit-relationships per household; loan terms adjust to shocks; health shocks systematically uninsured.
SKS Microfinance health insurance pilot (Andhra Pradesh, 2007, ch. 6). Mandatory → loan renewals dropped 60%→50%; ¼ found pre-payment loophole; voluntary → adverse selection killed it; ICICI Lombard pulled out. The textbook case of micro-insurance design failure.
Banerjee-Duflo-Glennerster-Kinnan Hyderabad Spandana RCT (2007-09, ch. 7). 104 neighborhoods, 52 randomly assigned. Modest positive — more new businesses (5%→7%), more durables, no transformation; cited as the paper that downgraded microcredit’s expectations.
Krishna District (AP) microfinance crisis (2005, repeated 2010, ch. 7). Belief-contagion-driven mass-default that took years to recover. Demonstrates fragility of MFI equilibrium.
Sri Lanka de Mel-McKenzie-Woodruff cash-grant lottery (ch. 9). 250 grants returned 60%/year on average; 500 grants returned no more in absolute terms — the headline marginal-vs-average evidence.
BRAC / Bandhan ultra-poor graduation program (Bangladesh, West Bengal, ch. 9). Asset-grant + consumption-stipend + literacy + savings + hand-holding produces durable improvements; the model that works where pure microcredit doesn’t.
Atkin Mexican maquiladora child-height study (ch. 9). Children of maquila-town mothers significantly taller, gap closing the entire poor-Mexican-to-American difference. Stability matters more than income alone.
Reinikka-Svensson Uganda school-funding leakage (1996, ch. 10). 13% of central funds reaching schools → newspaper-publication intervention → 80% reaching by 2001. Information disclosure as a corruption fix.
Olken Indonesia KDP audit RCT (ch. 10). Random audit threats cut theft of wages and materials by ⅓; auditors didn’t need to be especially honest.
Brazil electronic voting (ch. 10). Picture-confirmation interface reduces invalid votes 11%; newly-enfranchised voters poorer, less educated; elected politicians more likely to invest in public health; reduction in low-birth-weight babies.
Chattopadhyay-Duflo West Bengal panchayat-reservation (ch. 10). Random reservation of ⅓ pradhan positions for women → women-led GPs invest more in women-preferred infrastructure; village prejudice falls; aspirations for daughters rise.
Wantchekon Benin presidential-campaign experiment (ch. 10). Same candidate, clientelist-vs-unity speech in random villages: 80% vs 70% support. Ethnic voting is a heuristic in the absence of information.
Banerjee-Green-Pande UP “don’t vote on caste” street-play (ch. 10). Caste voting 25%→18% from a single NGO information campaign.

Critiques and limitations

The “sweeping” they reject is also a sweeping. The book’s anti-grand-theory stance is itself a grand thesis (the 5 lessons + 3 principles claim universal applicability). When does not having a grand theory actually constitute a grand theory? Critics including Pritchett, Deaton, and (in the same period) Ravallion have argued that the RCT program privileges what is measurable over what is important (governance, structural transformation, macroeconomic stability), and that the J-PAL canon’s headline interventions (deworming, dal-for-immunization, Pratham summer camps) are individually low-cost but together don’t add up to anything comparable to the take-off observed in Korea or Vietnam. Banerjee-Duflo’s later Good Economics for Hard Times partially concedes this.
External validity is repeatedly assumed but rarely proven. A Kenya bed-net result is generalized to “the poor” (a 3-billion-person population). The book is alert to this and mentions replication, but the structural-economic-and-cultural variation across the 18-country dataset is much larger than the variation across replication sites. The “deworming → 20% lifetime earnings” result depends on a 2004 Miguel-Kremer paper that has been the subject of extensive replication-and-debate.
The marginal-vs-average return distinction works elegantly for the OP-curve story but obscures heterogeneity. Some “small businesses” really are nascent QR-curve firms (Xu Aihua); some really are subsistence-OP. Lumping them produces averages that drive policy in either direction. Better disaggregation would help.
The good-job thesis is in tension with the book’s own micro-experimentalism. Industrial policy / labor-market regulation / urban-housing investment are precisely the macro institutional levers that the book is otherwise epistemically humble about. The conclusion-page prescription (loan guarantees to medium firms; Korean industrial policy; Chinese state-asset hand-overs) sits awkwardly with the methodological caution elsewhere.
Behavioral mechanisms are sometimes invoked too loosely. Time-inconsistency, present-bias, stress-cortisol-cognition coupling, aspiration failure, stereotype threat — these are real but the book does not always carefully distinguish which mechanism applies in which case. A sceptical reader can construct alternative explanations for many of the book’s headline results (e.g., “free-means-worthless” might be irrelevant for nets but real for, say, school vouchers; the book never tests).
Limited engagement with the political economy of the donor side. The book takes the existence of well-meaning aid-and-development professionals largely as given and asks how to make their work better. Thoughtful critics (Sachs himself; the post-development scholars; in different ways Naomi Klein) ask whether the development apparatus is structurally incapable of not producing the three I’s. The book’s “reform-from-within” stance is more confident than this question warrants.
The microcredit conclusion is now contested even in the J-PAL canon. Subsequent work (Bandhan-style graduation programs, mobile-money-driven savings products like M-PESA, ROSCA digitization) has produced larger transformative results than 2010 microcredit RCTs. The book under-weights digital-finance possibilities.
The book is light on geopolitical and ecological context. Climate change, weaponized interdependence, pandemic preparedness, AI-driven labor displacement — all are absent or treated only at the margin. A 2026-revision would have to extend significantly. (Banerjee-Duflo’s Good Economics for Hard Times and post-COVID essays partially compensate.)
The “patient empirical accumulation” thesis assumes time the world may not have. If climate or geopolitical shocks compress the timeline for poverty exit, the book’s “we can wait another 50 years” framing is ethically and operationally inadequate.
The 18-country dataset privileges what is surveyable. Refugees, undocumented migrants, conflict-zone populations, urban shadow economies are systematically under-represented. A major slice of the world’s poor is invisible in the book’s empirics.

Links to other books

Methodological cousin to Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited — Stiglitz’s first-person institutionalist critique of IMF/World Bank technocratic failure complements Banerjee-Duflo’s micro-empirical critique of NGO/policy delivery. Both insist institutional structure shapes outcomes regardless of stated intentions. Stiglitz on capital-account-liberalization-as-the-single-most-important-cause-of-the-East-Asia-crisis is a macro parallel to Banerjee-Duflo’s micro claim that informal-insurance failure is the single most important driver of poor risk-aversion. Reading them together: Stiglitz explains why macro reforms imposed by Washington fail; Banerjee-Duflo show what kinds of reform actually work at the micro level given the macro environment.
Methodological contrast with Gary Goertz and James Mahoney - A Tale of Two Cultures — Goertz-Mahoney articulate the qualitative / set-theoretic / case-study tradition (necessary and sufficient conditions, process tracing, within-case analysis); Banerjee-Duflo are the canonical exponents of the experimental / variable-effects-large-N tradition. The two cultures debate is literally the methodological frame for understanding Poor Economics against an alternative empirical paradigm. Goertz-Mahoney would say that some of Banerjee-Duflo’s headline causal claims (deworming → 20% lifetime earnings) are statistical-effect estimates that miss the configurational causal structure (which combinations of conditions produce the outcome). Banerjee-Duflo would say Goertz-Mahoney’s case-comparisons are unreplicable and unfalsifiable. Read both together as the cleanest available statement of the methodological choice in social-science empirical research.
Information-vs-preference contrast to Bryan Caplan - The Myth of the Rational Voter — Caplan models voters as having systematically biased preferences (anti-foreign, anti-market, make-work, pessimistic) over policy; Banerjee-Duflo model voters as having information deficits and weak preferences over candidates that flip easily under information shocks. The Banerjee-Green-Pande “don’t vote on caste” street-play (ch. 10) is operationally a refutation of the strong-preference Caplan claim: caste voting is a heuristic, not a deep preference, in low-information environments. Reading them together: Caplan diagnoses why even informed voters might support bad policy; Banerjee-Duflo diagnose why even ill-informed voters might support good politicians given low-cost information access. The Caplan and Banerjee-Duflo prescriptions diverge sharply (Caplan: less democracy; Banerjee-Duflo: better information delivery to existing democracy) but the empirical disagreement is sharper than either author allows.
Behavioral-mechanism antecedent in Daniel C. Dennett - I’ve Been Thinking — Dennett’s intentional-stance + heterophenomenology framing supplies the philosophical scaffolding for “treat the poor as rational agents pursuing legible goals under their constraints” — the methodological commitment that distinguishes Poor Economics from older paternalist development literature.
Risk-and-fragility complement to Taleb — Taleb’s fragility concept describes systems whose downside outweighs upside in tail events; the Banerjee-Duflo cortisol-cognition mechanism is a behavioral instantiation: poor people are fragile in Taleb’s sense, and their adaptive coping (diversification across activities, refusal to specialize) is precisely what Taleb would call antifragile under risk constraint. The two literatures rarely converse but the structural fit is strong.
State-theory frame in Acharya and Lee - The Cartel System of States — Acharya-Lee on the territorial state system as a cartel; Banerjee-Duflo’s ch. 10 on micro-institutional reform within “bad” macro-states. Acharya-Lee predict that bad macro-institutions are self-enforcing (cartel logic); Banerjee-Duflo show that this leaves enormous room for reform inside the cartel-stabilized state, a less pessimistic reading.
Complements Angela Huyue Zhang - High Wire — Zhang on Chinese technocratic regulatory failure; Banerjee-Duflo’s three-Is diagnosis applied to Chinese tech regulation would say SAMR/CAC failures are mostly inertia and ignorance, not deep oligarchic capture. Reading the two together: Zhang gives the institutional ecology, Banerjee-Duflo give the design-detail toolkit.
Complements Authoritarian Commons - Neighborhood Democratization in Urban China — Qiao on bounded democratic micro-governance under authoritarian regime; Banerjee-Duflo ch. 10 on micro-rule reform compounds even under bad regimes. Qiao’s three stability conditions for the authoritarian commons map onto Banerjee-Duflo’s “small revolutions inside bad regimes” thesis. Both are arguing against the institutional-pessimism reading of authoritarian governance.
Industrial-policy parallel to Chris Miller - Chip War — Miller documents how good jobs at scale (semiconductor employment in Taiwan, South Korea, the US Sun Belt) drove durable middle-class formation; Banerjee-Duflo’s good-job thesis (ch. 9) is the development-economics version of the same observation. The Atkin maquiladora result and Miller’s TSMC employment story are different facets of the same structural-transformation argument.
Methodological complement to Karl Popper - The Logic of Scientific Discovery — Popper’s falsificationism formalized; Banerjee-Duflo’s RCT program is the operational-empirical face of falsificationism applied to social policy. Each RCT is, in Popperian terms, a high-information experimental falsification test of a specific causal claim. The book’s anti-grand-theory stance is an explicit Popperian rebuke of social-science theories that don’t expose themselves to refutation.

Open questions

Does the J-PAL program scale to economy-wide outcomes? The Pritchett-Banerjee debate. Single-RCT effects are real but their aggregation into national-development outcomes is not obvious. The book promises “small changes compound” but doesn’t model the compounding.
Is the good-job thesis correct in the post-AI-automation era? Atkin’s maquiladora result, Foster-Rosenzweig’s rural-factory-employment story, the Udaipur zinc-factory village all assume jobs at scale are creatable. If labor demand collapses (AI, robotics, post-industrial gig economy), the structural exit may close.
Does the book’s “small priming nudges” framework generalize to high-stakes / distrust-laden domains? The home-visit-raises-insurance-uptake-4× result works for marginal goods. Whether it works for vaccine-skeptical populations, AI-uncertain populations, religious-conservative populations is unclear.
What is the right replication-validity threshold? When a 2004 Kenya deworming RCT is generalized to global policy, how confident should we be? The 2015-2020 replication-crisis discussion in social psychology has barely touched J-PAL; it should.
Does the framework survive climate-shock? Many of the cases (rain-fed agriculture, weather-indexed insurance, microclimate diversification) assume relatively stable climatic baselines. Aggregate variance is rising.
Is the moral-obligation reading of informal insurance correct? The chapter argues for it from suggestive cases. Direct empirical tests (e.g., variation in religion-mediated norms) are sparse. If the reciprocity-game reading is correct, then formal insurance design should target reciprocity-substitutes; if moral-obligation, it should target solidarity-substitutes. The two prescribe different products.
Why does microcredit not graduate clients? The chapter notes Spandana average loans grow from 7000 to 10000 rupees in 3 years; 30 years of Grameen produced no graduation. Is this structural (zero-default culture incompatible with risk-taking) or contingent (a design choice that newer fintech products like Tala / Branch can address)?

Research uses

Yang’s blockchain-regulation research: the book’s three-I’s diagnosis (ignorance, ideology, inertia) translates directly to crypto-regulator behavior. The Banerjee-Duflo prescription of audit + information disclosure + default-design maps onto post-FTX disclosure regimes and stablecoin transparency requirements. Microcredit’s Krishna-District belief-contagion crisis is operationally identical to crypto-bank-runs (Terra/Luna May 2022, FTX November 2022); the book’s diagnosis of social-equilibrium fragility under information-shock is the canonical reference. The chapter on micro-insurance failure reads almost identically to crypto-insurance and DeFi-protocol-design challenges.
AI policy and cross-border data flows: the supply-vs-demand wallah debate (Sachs / Easterly / J-PAL) maps onto AI-policy debates (regulate-pre-deployment / market-handles-it / RCT-test-specific-interventions). The “information campaigns succeed under three conditions” portable claim is directly applicable to AI-public-communication design. The book’s stress-cortisol-cognition mechanism predicts that low-income users of AI tools will exhibit different decision-patterns than high-income users — relevant for product design and policy targeting.
Comparative policy analysis (China-tech-policy): the book’s “small revolutions inside bad regimes” thesis applies directly to Chinese SAMR / CAC / PBOC reform research. Banerjee-Duflo’s Chattopadhyay-Duflo panchayat-reservation result and Olken Indonesia audit result are the canonical micro-institutional-reform-within-authoritarian-regime references.
Personal-development / behavioral-design: the time-inconsistency / commitment-device / default-option toolkit is portable to first-person design questions (savings, exercise, learning habits, deep-work scheduling). The “saving brick-by-brick” insight that visible, illiquid, autoreinvested savings dominate cash savings under temptation is a personal-finance principle. The “expectations are self-fulfilling” finding has direct implications for setting personal aspirational goals.
Lobbying-network / institutional-research (with In Song Kim): the book’s case-by-case demonstration that political-economy outcomes are determined by micro-rules of engagement (who is invited, who speaks, who tabulates) is the right frame for lobbying-network analysis: lobbying-effect at the micro-rule level often dominates at-the-policy level. The Brazil electronic-voting result (interface change → enfranchisement → policy shift → infant outcomes) is a textbook case of micro-rule-determined macro-outcomes.
Education research and equality of opportunity: the illusory S-shape of parental expectations (ch. 4) is the most portable single mechanism in the book. It applies to college-major-choice patterns in middle-income families, to immigrant-family child-investment patterns, to first-generation-college-student behavior. The Bogotá CCT-lottery within-family resource-displacement result is the cleanest single-paper demonstration.

What I would miss if I only read this note
The book’s distinctive texture lives in the field-vignettes — Pak Solhin and his fishing rod in Bandung, Oucha Mbarbk and his television in rural Morocco, Ibu Tina and her stacks of unsellable shorts, Pak Sudarno’s nine children, Ben Sedan’s olive trees, the woman in Hyderabad selling dosas next to three other women selling dosas. These are not decoration. The book’s argumentative structure depends on the cumulative force of the reader being shown actual lives in their actual specificity, and then on Banerjee-Duflo’s restraint in not generalizing prematurely — they let the reader infer “Pak Solhin’s depression is doing more work than his calorie deficit” before saying so explicitly. The note compresses these into bullet points; the texture is irreducibly first-person observational. Reading the cases gives a trained intuition for which behavioral mechanism is operative in a new context, in a way that a list of mechanisms cannot.
The note also compresses Banerjee-Duflo’s distinctive voice — the dry acknowledgment that the dosa-seller, when invited to merge with two competitors, would politely decline; the affectionate-but-clear-eyed treatment of Padmaja Reddy and Fouad Abdelmoumni and Joe Madiath as fellow professionals doing imperfect work in good faith; the small joke about Nachiket Mor’s “cattle don’t have fingers” Aadhaar quip. The voice is part of the argument: the book is making a tonal claim that patient practitioners doing the actual work matter more than sweeping intellectuals and the prose enacts that claim. This is irreducible to a derivative note.
The book also compresses, more than the note can, the cumulative force of repeated mechanism exposure. By the third or fourth time you encounter the time-inconsistency mechanism (immunization in ch. 3, contraception in ch. 5, insurance in ch. 6, savings in ch. 8), you have absorbed it the way one absorbs an idiom — not as a labeled concept but as a way of seeing. The chapter-by-chapter table in this note flags the recurrences; reading the book, you internalize the pattern. Same for the S-shape vs inverted-L diagnostic, which becomes second nature by ch. 5 and structurally informs how you read chs. 6-10. The note compresses a 250-page sustained training of pattern-recognition into a list of patterns, which is not the same thing as having the recognition.
Finally, the note compresses the anger — quietly present in the Sachs / Easterly framing, more visible in the SKS Microfinance / Krishna District / Andhra Pradesh microcredit-crisis chapter, sharpest in the chapter on government-school nurses who run into elite-bias against their own community’s children. Poor Economics is restrained in tone but it is not neutral. Banerjee and Duflo are professionals committed to the work whose colleagues’ bad faith and laziness produce the failures the book documents, and the prose has the controlled urgency of professionals trying to fix what their guild has gotten wrong. None of this carries through into a derivative note. The book is best read once for the ideas and a second time for the voice and the cumulative anger; the note can substitute for neither.

Acharya and Lee - The Cartel System of States

Read chapter-by-chapter → Deep dive of The Cartel System of States — An Economic Theory of International Politics (7 chapters)

One-sentence thesis
The modern territorial state system is best understood as an economic cartel — a self-enforcing, geographically segmented oligopoly in which states (the suppliers) collude to not compete for the same citizens (the consumers) in the market for governance, with the consequence that mutual recognition rather than institutional efficiency defines what counts as a state, that border stability emerges from cartel-maintenance dynamics rather than international law as such, that wars are essentially price-war episodes after which cooperation rapidly resumes, and that the system has proven surprisingly robust to the three threats — interstate conflict, opportunistic entry by would-be states, and the rise of mass democracy — that ought naively to have unraveled it.
Why this book matters
A 2024 Oxford monograph that supplies what international-relations theory has lacked: a single self-enforcing mechanism that explains both the origin and the persistence of the territorial state system, and that does so by importing industrial-organisation tools (Bertrand competition, repeated-game cartel theory, entry deterrence, brand loyalty) into the classical IR vocabulary. It is more rigorous than Spruyt’s institutional-selection account, more parsimonious than the Westphalian-norms ideational accounts, and more politically grounded than realist offense-defense balance, because it locates the system’s stability in the specific political-economy interest of the rulers being governed against — namely, citizens.
For Yang’s research uses, the book sits at an exceptionally productive position: cartel theory is portable to any sovereignty-recognition question (Taiwan, Palestine, Somaliland, the digital-yuan/cryptocurrency boundary, the EU as quasi-state), to any tax-competition question (corporate inversion, OECD/G20 minimum-tax negotiations, BEPS), and to any state-recognition question in IR scholarship. The framing is also a clean complement to Angela Huyue Zhang - High Wire (which tells the inside-China regulatory dynamics story) and to Meg E. Rithmire - Land Bargains and Chinese Capitalism / Meg Rithmire - Precarious Ties (which tell the subnational-China story); Acharya-Lee supplies the international-system context within which Chinese state-building must operate. The timing is especially useful: published just before the post-2022 Ukraine and post-2023 AI/IP-rivalry periods raised exactly the kind of abstract-governance-market questions the framework is designed to handle (ch. 7).
The book also offers the unusual combination of formal-theoretic rigour (the spatial Bertrand model in ch. 2 is fully specified) and dense historical case work (Anglo-Scottish border 1500–1640; Spanish fueros; French intendent fiscal data; Atacama Desert; Pakistan-Afghan Durand Line). For Yang’s qualitative-IR work and for evaluating other people’s claims about state-system change, this is the right primary reference for the next several years.
Core argument

The market-for-governance abstraction. States supply a bundle of services (protection, dispute resolution, infrastructure, education, R&D, regulation) and citizens pay taxes for them; both supply and demand exist, so a “market for governance” exists in the loose-but-precise sense relevant to industrial organisation (ch. 1; ch. 2). The market has the potential to be competitive — a citizen near the border between two providers can in principle play the rulers off each other, extracting concessions in the form of lower taxes or greater autonomy. The classic illustration is the British Raj’s North-West Frontier, where competition with the Afghan ruler depressed taxes to the point of subsidy of local khans (ch. 1).
The spatial structure of cost and value. The cost of providing governance rises with distance from a ruler’s administrative core (Boulding’s “loss of strength gradient”); the value extractable per citizen is bounded by v — the point at which marginal taxation triggers revolt, exit, or tax avoidance (the “reservation price”). The geography of the model places ruler A and ruler B at endpoints of a line; their cost curves c_A, c_B rise with distance; profit per location is v − c(loc) where positive (ch. 2). Where two rulers’ positive-profit zones overlap, they are potential competitors — and the losses from such competition (L_A, L_B) are what they want to avoid.
The cartel agreement. The cooperative solution is for the rulers to set a boundary Y (where c_A = c_B, the joint-profit-maximising point) and agree not to compete across it. Each becomes a local monopolist over their share of the market and extracts the full rent v from their core. This is self-enforcing in repeated interaction via trigger strategies (cheating today triggers competitive future, more costly than the gain from cheating). Sustainability requires the discount factor to exceed both L_A/(L_A+L_B) and L_B/(L_A+L_B) — the cartel works when symmetric losses-from-competition are at stake (ch. 2).
The historical origin of the cartel in early-modern Europe. In the Middle Ages, low v and steep c curves left a large buffer zone between rulers’ practical reach. Universal claims (papacy, Holy Roman Empire, Austriae est imperare orbi universo) were costless because non-enforceable. The Commercial Revolution raised v; the Military Revolution + bureaucratic state-building lowered c. As cost curves flattened and value rose, the buffer zone shrank and the contested zone [X, Z] widened. This generated real losses-from-competition for the first time and motivated the sovereignty agreements that became the cartel — first bilaterally (the Anglo-Scottish 1552 demarcation; Treaty of the Pyrenees 1659; Westphalia 1648), then via the multilateral Congress of Vienna (1815) and the Berlin Conference (1884–85) (ch. 3).
Global expansion through colonial conquest and coerced opening. By 1900 the cartel had spread worldwide, mostly via European colonisation (Berlin Conference partition of Africa = pure cartel exercise, “straight lines reflecting limited awareness of local geographical and political realities”), with the few non-colonised East Asian polities forced into the cartel via the Treaty of Nanking (1842), Tientsin (1858), Kanagawa (1853), Kanghwa (1876). The expansion is geographically near-complete (only 1.6% of land contested today, per ch. 1) but functionally uneven: the Pakistan-Afghanistan Durand Line is an active competitive failure of the cartel; many African borders are stable precisely because they cross unprofitable terrain that no state cares to govern (ch. 4).
Conflict as cartel revelation, not cartel collapse. When relative governance costs shift asymmetrically (e.g., c_B drops while c_A is unchanged), the joint-profit-max boundary moves. War serves as a credible signalling mechanism — only a state whose costs have actually dropped will bear the cost of war over the disputed territory (ch. 5, Atacama Desert as canonical illustration). After the war the cartel reconstitutes quickly: Denmark accepts loss of Malmö; Spain accepts loss of Portugal; Mexico accepts loss of Texas/California; Germany accepts loss of Sudetenland and Silesia (ch. 5). Wars are price-war episodes within an equilibrium of long-term cooperation.
Entry deterrence as the canonical cartel function. The same logic that makes economic cartels suppress new entrants makes the state cartel suppress secession movements. Recognition is collectively withheld even when the entrant is institutionally capable (Confederacy 1861–65; Biafra 1967–70; Republic of the Rif 1921–26; Somaliland today). Recognition is extended when great-power interests align (Belgium 1830 — Britain wanted a buffer; decolonisation 1945–90 — US/USSR lacked colonial empires and benefited from smaller successor states). The model’s coordination problem (ch. 5, Fig. 9) is exactly the function international institutions like the UN and OAU have come to perform.
Democracy is not a threat to the cartel — it is a re-instantiation. A naive prediction has democratic citizens demanding open competition and lower monopoly tax. But the redistributive median-voter analysis shows that in a democracy that redistributes the cartel rent, the median voter in the core area prefers the cartel + redistribution over open competition (ch. 5, Fig. 10). The cartel survives democratisation because the identity of the “ruler” shifts from autocrat to pivotal voter / dominant lobby / large donor — but the cartel-versus-citizen logic remains. Empirically: Catalonia pays 27% of Spanish taxes and 20% of taxes today; Spain has used force to prevent independence (2017 referendum repression). The US fought a civil war to preserve territorial integrity; democracies are if anything more hostile to secession than autocracies (because democracies fight wars more successfully, democratic peace reduces interstate revision, and democratic accountability raises domestic costs of concession).
Nationalism is the cartel’s stabiliser. Investments in national identity create a discontinuous jump in governance cost at the border — own population is cheaper to govern, foreign population is harder. This makes the joint-profit-max boundary insensitive to small administrative-capacity shifts: borders persist even when the rival state has caught up technologically (ch. 6, Fig. 12). The Nepal-vs-Sikkim paired case is the cleanest illustration: Sikkim (no national-identity investment) was annexed by India in 1975; Nepal (with century-long national-identity investment via Gorkhapatra 1901, Radio Nepal 1951, standardised Nepali curriculum) was not, despite the “Indira doctrine” of Himalayan suzerainty.
International institutions as cartel headquarters. The UN is “the headquarters of the cartel” — membership is sufficient and almost necessary for international recognition; only 4 UN members are contested by >1 other member (Israel, Palestine, North Korea, China) and only 3 non-members are recognised by >1 member (Taiwan, Western Sahara, Kosovo) (ch. 6). The UNSC’s response asymmetry — rapid mobilisation against Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait in 1991 (35-nation coalition); no mobilisation against Russian Crimea takeover — reveals that UN action tracks cartel-leader interest, not abstract norm violation, exactly as the model predicts.
Globalisation transforms but does not abolish the cartel. The market-for-governance has shifted from physical territory to abstract policy space (trade, capital, IP, immigration, regulatory regimes). Apple’s “double Irish” / Jersey BEPS arrangements moved profits without moving production; OECD estimates 2015 tax-competition cost at $240B/year (ch. 7). The cartel’s response is managed trade (Stiglitz 2002 quoted: a real free-trade agreement would be “a few pages”; the TPP ran 6,000+ pages) and coordinated tax-floors (the 2021 OECD/G20 BEPS framework’s 15% minimum corporate tax, agreed by 136/140 members). The cartel adapts; it does not dissolve.
Forward-looking implications. Four 21st-century challenges: (i) immigration differentials driven by governance-quality differentials; (ii) failed states generating cross-border externalities the cartel cannot easily resolve (Afghanistan, Somalia, Syria, Venezuela); (iii) power shifts between US and China, especially over intellectual property — the asset class developed countries depend on as they shift to knowledge economies (ch. 7); (iv) new modes of conflict — economic warfare (Russia-Ukraine sanctions; “akin to a declaration of war” per Putin), cyber-warfare, IP theft. These are not refutations of cartel theory; they are the current operating challenges of a cartel that has migrated from territorial to abstract space.

Argument map
The reasoning runs from a core abstraction (the market for governance) through a self-enforcement mechanism (the cartel agreement) to a structural prediction (mutual recognition replacing institutional efficiency as the criterion of statehood), and then applies the framework historically (origin in Europe; spread by colonisation), to threats (conflict, entry, democracy), to stabilisers (nationalism, international institutions), and finally to the contemporary abstract-market transformation (globalisation, IP, China rise).
COST × VALUE GEOGRAPHY    EARLY-MODERN GROWTH
(c_A, c_B, v)         ─┐   (rising v + falling c)
                       │           │
                       ▼           ▼
       MARKET FOR GOVERNANCE     BUFFER ZONE
       (Bertrand competition)    SHRINKS
       (losses L_A, L_B)         (X moves west; Z moves east)
                       │           │
                       └───────────┴──> INCENTIVE TO COLLUDE
                                          │
                                          ▼
                                 CARTEL AGREEMENT (boundary Y)
                                 self-enforcing via trigger strategy
                                          │
                                          ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┐
        │                                 │                                 │
   3 THREATS                        2 STABILISERS                  TRANSFORMATION
   (ch. 5)                          (ch. 6)                        (ch. 7)
        │                                 │                                 │
   ─ Conflict (Atacama)            ─ Nationalism (Nepal/Sikkim)     ─ Abstract market
   ─ Entry (Belgium, Somaliland,   ─ International institutions      ─ Managed trade
     Confederacy, Rif)               (UN, OAU, EU as cartel HQ)      ─ IP, BEPS, US-China
   ─ Democracy (Catalonia)                                            ─ Failed states
                                                                      ─ Cyber/economic war
        │                                 │                                 │
        └─────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │
                                          ▼
                              CARTEL PERSISTS, MIGRATES,
                              REGULATES THE ABSTRACT MARKET

The diagram reads top-down. The model’s primitives — cost geography and bounded value — combine with the early-modern transformation to generate the cartel agreement. The cartel is then tested by three threats, supported by two stabilisers, and currently being transformed by the shift from territorial to abstract governance markets. Each downward arrow corresponds to a chapter-level argumentative move in the book.
Key concepts

Cartel of States — the central framing: states as a self-enforcing oligopoly of governance providers (newly created concept note).
Market for Governance — the supply-side abstraction Acharya-Lee build the model on (newly created concept note).
Skin in the Game — Taleb’s framework illuminates who actually pays when the cartel breaks: powerful mobile-capital holders extract concessions; immobile ordinary citizens absorb the monopoly tax. The cartel is a precise instance of asymmetric skin-in-the-game distribution.
Black Swan — entry events into the cartel (Belgium 1830; USSR dissolution; Eritrean/East Timorese independence) are rare, hard to forecast, and dominate the long-run shape of state count over time. The volatility-fragility logic of cartel dynamics shares structure with Taleb’s framing.
Heterarchy — modern governance markets exhibit lateral, multi-tier authority (national, EU, WTO, OECD, treaty-based) that resembles the heterarchical structure McCulloch named, not a clean strict-hierarchy.
Antifragility — the cartel exhibits a kind of antifragility: shocks (wars, secession movements, democratic transitions) have repeatedly strengthened it rather than weakened it, by triggering institutional adaptations (UN, OAU, managed trade).

Best chapters/pages to actually read

Ch. 1 (Introduction) — sets up the cartel framing through the Neche/Gretna and Point Roberts illustrations. Read first; the rest of the book applies the framing developed here. The Krasner (1993) quotation on “extruding out of universal alternatives to the sovereign state” anchors the historical claim, and the foreshadowing of chs. 5–7 is unusually direct for an academic introduction.
Ch. 2 (The Cartel Model) — the formal-theoretic chapter. The spatial Bertrand model, the trigger-strategy condition δ > L_A/(L_A+L_B), the discussion of independent vs interdependent cooperation in the three-state case (Belgium 1914 as illustration), and the comparison with rival theories (Westphalia hypothesis, Jervis offense-defense balance, Spruyt institutional selection, Alesina-Spolaore voting model). This is the chapter that makes the book novel; without it the book would be a competent IR essay.
Ch. 3 (The Cartel Emerges) — the historical-origin chapter. The Anglo-Scottish border (1500–1640) walk-through is the densest case. The quantitative French intendent fiscal data (Fig. 7, Mallet 1789 / Bonney 1999) showing 12.05× revenue growth in border provinces vs 3.81× in non-border provinces is the cleanest empirical anchor for the model’s prediction.
Ch. 5 (Challenges to the Cartel) — handles the three threats (conflict, entry, democracy) with one model extension each. The Atacama Desert case for conflict, the Rif/Somaliland/Belgium triplet for entry, the Catalonia case for democratic survival. The Fig. 10 redistributive-vs-competitive policy analysis is the key formal move.
Ch. 6 (Resilience of the Cartel) — Nepal vs Sikkim is the best-paired case study in the book. Read this section even if skimming the rest of the chapter. The UN-as-cartel-headquarters analysis (Iraq-Kuwait vs Crimea response asymmetry) is the cleanest prediction-test.
Ch. 7 (The Cartel Today) — most relevant for current research. The managed-trade analysis, the BEPS / Apple-Ireland material, the US-China IP / power-shift section, and the closing thought experiment about a single world government as logical-coherence test of the theory. Skip the section on emigration if you’ve read Stiglitz-on-globalisation already.
Skip: ch. 4’s Africa and Durand Line cases are well-written but theoretically secondary if you’ve internalised chs. 2–3. Save them for a second read or use them as worked examples.

Chapter-by-chapter distillation





















































#TitleSummaryLink1IntroductionBorder discontinuity puzzle (Neche/Gretna, Point Roberts) motivates the market-for-governance framing. The cartel theory introduced; foreshadows the three threats (chs. 5) and two stabilisers (ch. 6) and the modern abstract-market challenges (ch. 7).ch.12The Cartel ModelThe spatial Bertrand model with two rulers A, B and bounded value v; trigger-strategy self-enforcement; generalisations to two dimensions, non-uniform distribution, non-contiguous territory; three-state case (independent vs interdependent cooperation, Belgium 1914 illustration); critique of Westphalia hypothesis, Jervis, Spruyt, Alesina-Spolaore.ch.23The Cartel EmergesEarly-modern European transformation: Commercial Revolution + Military Revolution = rising v + falling c. Buffer zone shrinks; cartel agreement becomes profitable. Anglo-Scottish, Spanish fueros, Swedish Livland reduktion, French intendent cases. Vienna Congress as multilateral inflection.ch.34The Cartel Takes OverSpread of cartel beyond Europe via colonisation (Berlin Conference) and coerced opening (Tientsin, Nanking, Kanagawa). Conflict: war as revelation mechanism; Atacama case. Entry: collective-action problem of deterrence; Rif, Somaliland, Belgium triplet. Important examples / cases

Anglo-Scottish border (ch. 3) — the densest case study. 1552 five-man commission demarcates Scot’s Dyke; March Law jury composition with Scottish/English balance; “law books of the border” periodically synchronised; 16th-century English diplomats’ explicit elite-vs-borderer framing (“the less privy the Borderers be made to the division hereof, the more likely it is that the thing will take place”). Demonstrates all three steps of cartel emergence — mutual recognition, cooperative demarcation, cooperative enforcement.
French intendent fiscal data (ch. 3, Fig. 7) — Mallet 1789 / Bonney 1999. 1600–1695 nominal revenue growth: 3.81× non-border provinces, 6.20× formerly-border-now-interior, 12.05× border provinces. The cleanest quantitative anchor in the book.
Atacama Desert (ch. 5) — Saltpeter War 1879–82. Three claimants (Chile/Peru/Bolivia); no conflict 1820s–1860s when desert worthless; nitrate boom raises v; Chile’s superior army wins, consolidates 1884/1903. Bolivian renegotiation attempt unanimously dismissed by ICJ in 2018 — cartel stability ratified judicially long after.
Republic of the Rif vs Belgium 1830 (ch. 5) — paired case for entry deterrence. Rif had institutional substance (currency, army, schools); Belgium did not. Rif crushed by joint Franco-Spanish action (¼ million troops, poison gas). Belgium recognised because Britain wanted a French buffer. Recognition tracks great-power interest, not entrant capability.
Nepal vs Sikkim (ch. 6) — paired case for nationalism. Sikkim absorbed 1975 (“referendum” with 99.55% allegedly favouring incorporation). Nepal not absorbed despite “Indira doctrine,” because Nepal had inculcated national identity via Gorkhapatra (1901), Radio Nepal (1951), standardised curriculum (1950s), UN membership (1955). Bollywood-actor-disparagement riots in 1999/2000 demonstrate the cost-to-India of any annexation attempt would be prohibitive.
Apple-Ireland BEPS (ch. 7) — the canonical contemporary example. “Double Irish” and “Green Jersey” arrangements moved profits to low-tax Ireland; a single 300B IP transfer raised Irish GDP by 26.3% in one quarter. OECD 2015 estimate: 240B/year tax-competition loss. 60 Fortune 500 firms paid no tax on $79B profit.
Pakistan-Afghan Durand Line / FATA (ch. 4) — clearest case of competitive cartel failure. NWFP 1932 expenditure 36M rupees, revenue 8M; Central Provinces 7× population but 3× cost. FATA: 600 arms factories (2017); free electricity; no taxes; Frontier Crimes Regulation in force until 2018. Both Pakistan and Afghanistan compete for Pashtun loyalty exactly as medieval English/Scottish states competed for surnames.
UN response asymmetry: Iraq-Kuwait vs Russia-Crimea (ch. 6) — Iraq invasion of Kuwait condemned by UNSC in 4 days; sanctions imposed; force authorised in 3 months; 35-nation coalition led by US drove Iraq out. Russian Crimea annexation 2014: no comparable response, because Russia is a permanent UNSC member. Cartel theory predicts this exactly: enforcement tracks cartel-leader interest, not norm violation.

Critiques and limitations

Falsifiability concerns. The cartel model with cost-curve geometry, value-bound v, and trigger-strategy enforcement has many degrees of freedom. The book successfully post-hoc rationalises observed outcomes (border stability, failed-state recognition, war-followed-by-cooperation) but predictions are scarce; few cases would clearly refute the framework. The historical-origin claim (the system originated as a cartel) is more falsifiable than the operating-as-if claim, but the book’s strongest evidence is for the latter. A skeptic could read the book as a clever description-with-vocabulary rather than a positive theory; this is a real weakness for a framework that explicitly claims to compete with realism, institutionalism, and constructivism on theoretical grounds.
Identification weakness in the historical chapters. The French intendent fiscal data (Fig. 7) is striking, but the inferred mechanism (border treaties → fiscal capture from elites) competes with confounders (military pressure, dynastic centralisation, secular bureaucratic professionalisation, the Sun King’s personal ambition). Without a control group or counterfactual identification, the cartel-mechanism interpretation is one among several. Acharya-Lee acknowledge this implicitly through their notes on alternative explanations but don’t address it head-on. A natural-experiment design (varying treaty timing across paired regions) would strengthen the empirical claim materially.
The “ruler” elision. The model’s central actor — the “ruler” — is treated as a unitary profit-maximising agent, then in ch. 5 reinterpreted as the median voter or pivotal lobby in democracies. This rescues the framework but at the cost of changing the actor’s identity mid-argument. A more disciplined treatment would specify when the median-voter assumption is empirically supported (when redistribution is actually balanced-budget, when periphery vs core voters can be cleanly identified) and when it is not. Caplan’s Bryan Caplan - The Myth of the Rational Voter is the natural companion here: rational ignorance plus systemic biases mean the median voter often does not recognise the cartel-rent-redistribution bargain, raising doubt about the chapter’s predicted equilibrium.
Underweighting non-cartel governance forms. The framework treats non-state governance (Mafia, insurgent groups, merchant associations, Migdal-style local elites) as orthogonal to the main argument (footnote at ch. 2). But in many cases — drug-trafficking corridors, platform governance, Web3 / decentralised-finance jurisdictions, gig-economy labour relations — these alternative providers are exactly the “competitors” whose suppression is the cartel’s raison d’être. A more integrated treatment would help; in particular, Web3 / DAO governance is a non-territorial entrant whose suppression by the cartel (China’s mining ban; US securities enforcement against decentralised exchanges; EU’s MiCA framework) is precisely what cartel theory predicts but the book never analyses directly.
The IP / power-shift section is thin. Ch. 7’s discussion of US-China IP rivalry is the weakest section of the book, mostly because of citation availability at writing time. Krugman’s 1979 North-South product cycle is invoked, but the framework doesn’t integrate cleanly with cartel theory — IP is a non-rival good with strong returns to imitation, which differs from territorial governance in ways the cartel model doesn’t fully accommodate. The Acharya-Lee analysis of why China would refuse to accept US IP norms is correct as far as it goes, but it under-models the bargaining dynamics: Chinese acceptance of IP norms is partial and conditional, exchanged for market access and technology-transfer concessions, in ways the simple cartel-vs-entrant framing doesn’t fully capture.
No engagement with public-choice / regulatory-capture literature. Bryan Caplan’s Bryan Caplan - The Myth of the Rational Voter, Mancur Olson’s collective-action work, and the rent-seeking literature would all be productive complements; the cartel-vs-citizens framing has obvious affinity with public-choice traditions but the book under-engages them. Olson’s The Rise and Decline of Nations (1982) anticipates much of the cartel-collective-action mechanism the book develops; the absence of citation is striking.
Scope limitation — the abstract-market transformation may exceed the framework. Acharya-Lee note that as governance migrates from territory to mobile capital + IP + human capital, the original spatial Bertrand model loses its primary intuition (geography). They handle this by reinterpreting the line segment as policy space, but this is a strained reinterpretation: in policy space there is no “loss of strength gradient” with distance. The framework may need substantial modification to cover the next 30 years — perhaps a multi-dimensional discrete-policy-space model, perhaps a hybrid spatial-network model. The book gestures at this but does not deliver the formal extension.
Authorial voice is muted. Compared to Stiglitz, Zhang, or Rithmire, the prose is dry-academic. The case material is rich but the reader has to do interpretive work to feel the force of the argument. This is not a critique of accuracy, just of pedagogy: the book under-leverages its own findings rhetorically. A more polemical revised edition (in the spirit of Stiglitz’s Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited) could reach a much wider audience without sacrificing the formal-theoretic contribution; this is a missed opportunity given the importance of the framework.
Limited treatment of the EU as quasi-cartel-member. The book closes ch. 7 with a brief discussion of the EU as “alternative blueprint” but does not formally extend cartel theory to handle quasi-state entities. The EU’s customs union, Schengen area, monetary union, and emerging fiscal capacity are exactly the kind of intra-cartel-coordination the framework should illuminate, but Acharya-Lee leave this for future work. For Yang’s policy interests, this is the most consequential under-development of the framework.

Links to other books

State-cartel context for Angela Huyue Zhang - High Wire — Zhang focuses on the internal dynamics of Chinese tech regulation; Acharya-Lee supplies the external context (the international cartel within which Chinese state-building must operate). Reading Zhang’s analysis of the post-2022 Chinese rebalancing toward technological self-sufficiency through the cartel lens — China asserting cartel-leader status in the digital governance market — sharpens both books. Direct cross-reference exists: Zhang’s note explicitly cites Acharya and Lee - The Cartel System of States.
Subnational complement to Meg E. Rithmire - Land Bargains and Chinese Capitalism and Meg Rithmire - Precarious Ties — Rithmire on city-level land bargains and firm-state precarious ties supplies the vertical bottom of Chinese political economy; Zhang on national regulatory architecture supplies the middle; Acharya-Lee on international cartel supplies the top. The three together give the full vertical of how Chinese statehood actually operates, from real-estate developers to UNSC posture.
Methodological and ideological complement to Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited — Stiglitz argues globalisation has been managed badly by IMF/World Bank technocrats with weak feedback; Acharya-Lee argues the same outcome — managed trade rather than free trade — is the predicted equilibrium of the cartel framework. The two books reach the same descriptive conclusion via different theoretical routes; reading them together gives both a normative and a positive account of why the world economy looks as it does. Acharya-Lee directly quote Stiglitz on “managed trade” and the TPP’s 6,000-page length (ch. 7).
Public-choice foundation from Bryan Caplan - The Myth of the Rational Voter — Caplan establishes that median-voter outcomes can systematically diverge from welfare-maximisation. Acharya-Lee’s ch. 5 democratic-political-economy extension assumes balanced-budget redistribution and median-voter pivot; Caplan’s framework would deepen the analysis of when these assumptions hold and when they don’t.
Methodological cousin to Gary Goertz and James Mahoney - A Tale of Two Cultures — Acharya-Lee combine formal-theoretic modelling (ch. 2’s Bertrand competition) with within-case process-tracing (ch. 3’s Anglo-Scottish, ch. 5’s Atacama, ch. 6’s Nepal-Sikkim). Goertz-Mahoney describe exactly this two-cultures hybrid as the most productive form of contemporary IR/comparative-politics research. Acharya-Lee is a worked exhibit of what high-quality combined-methods political economy looks like.
Geopolitical context for Chris Miller - Chip War — Miller documents the US-China semiconductor rivalry; Acharya-Lee supplies the cartel-theoretic grammar for understanding why the US is willing to bear the costs of export controls (it is reasserting cartel-leader prerogatives over the IP-sub-market) and why China is willing to bear the costs of self-sufficiency drives (it is positioning to enter the cartel as a co-leader rather than fringe member). The two books together explain the IP/semiconductor-policy dimension of the abstract governance market.
Implicit Talebian framing — Acharya-Lee’s framework invokes Black Swan structurally without naming Taleb: cartel entry events (Belgium 1830; USSR dissolution; Eritrea/East Timor) are rare, hard-to-predict, and dominate the long-run shape of state count over time. The framework’s treatment of war as revelation mechanism shares structure with Antifragility: shocks have repeatedly strengthened the cartel by triggering institutional adaptations (League of Nations, UN, OAU, OECD). Reading Nassim Nicholas Taleb - Incerto alongside makes both deeper.

Open questions

Will the cartel survive the migration from territorial to abstract governance markets? Acharya-Lee answer “yes, by adaptation” — but the original spatial-Bertrand model relied on the loss-of-strength gradient, which has no clear analogue in IP / capital / cyber space. A 2030+ revision of the framework may need substantially different formal foundations. The most likely route is multi-dimensional policy-space competition, but this loses the geometric clarity of the original spatial model.
Is managed trade a stable cartel equilibrium or a transitional regime? The 2021 OECD/G20 BEPS framework is an unprecedented case of cartel-leaders coordinating against capital mobility. Whether this kind of coordination will hold or fracture (under nationalist populist pressure, US-China rivalry, AI-policy divergence) is empirically open and central for predicting the 2030–2040 governance-market structure.
How does AI-governance map onto the cartel framework? AI compute infrastructure is geographically concentrated (Taiwan, US, S Korea, Netherlands per Chris Miller - Chip War) but AI capabilities are non-rival once trained. The cartel logic applies cleanly to compute (export controls = cartel-leader move) but breaks for capabilities. A formal extension that treats training-stage IP and inference-stage services differently would be valuable.
What does opportunistic entry by a non-state network look like in this framework? The Islamic State explicitly rejected the sovereignty norm; cryptocurrency networks implicitly do. The framework treats these as coordination failures in entry deterrence, but a positive theory of non-state network entry would help interpret blockchain regulation, DAO governance, and platform-state competition.
How does the framework handle the EU? Acharya-Lee close ch. 7 with the EU as “alternative blueprint” — quasi-state without statehood. Whether the EU stays in this transitional position, evolves into a proper cartel member (federal Europe), or fragments back to nation-states is a live empirical question the book leaves open. The Brexit datum is informative: the cartel’s pull is strong enough that exit costs remain large even when domestic politics favour exit.
Can democratic citizens learn to want cartel-breaking? The redistributive median-voter argument predicts citizens prefer cartel + redistribution. But this assumes citizens accurately perceive the bargain. If the welfare cost of cartel monopoly becomes legible (post-pandemic immigration debates, post-tech-platform regulatory awareness), democratic preferences could shift. This is the long-run political question hidden inside the framework.
Does the framework predict regulatory convergence or divergence on climate? Climate is a negative externality the cartel must coordinate over (per ch. 7’s closing thought experiment). The Paris-Kyoto-Copenhagen sequence shows partial coordination; the question is whether the cartel can sustain action without the kind of distinct-territorial-rents that motivated earlier cooperation. The framework predicts cartel coordination occurs only when cartel-leader interests align — and on climate, alignment is partial and contested.
What is the framework’s prediction for cartel-internal dispute mechanisms? The book mentions ICJ, WTO dispute resolution, the OECD’s coordinating role — but the cartel’s internal-dispute infrastructure is treated as exogenous. Whether the cartel’s internal disputes (e.g., US-China trade-war-via-WTO-blocking-of-appellate-body) are themselves cartel-defection events or cartel-strengthening rituals is a question the framework leaves open.

Research uses

Yang’s blockchain-regulation work: cartel theory supplies the right vocabulary for analysing why states have responded to cryptocurrency the way they have. DCEP (digital yuan) and central-bank digital currencies are cartel-defensive innovations — preserving the territorial monopoly over the medium of governance payment. Private cryptocurrencies (Bitcoin, Ethereum stablecoins) are opportunistic entrants that the cartel must either co-opt (regulated stablecoins, bank-issued tokens) or suppress (China’s 2017/2021 mining bans). The cartel framework predicts that cross-border CBDC interoperability protocols (mBridge, Project Agorá) will be governed by cartel-leader interests — China, US, EU, BIS — rather than by efficiency criteria. Useful explanatory frame, especially for the question of why crypto regulation has converged on similar features (stablecoin reserve requirements, exchange licensing, tax disclosure, anti-money-laundering) across otherwise very different jurisdictions: the cartel coordination mechanism is doing real work even where the political-ideological framings differ.
China-policy thinking: the framework is portable to Taiwan recognition (cartel maintenance — UN refusal to admit Taiwan is exactly the entry-deterrence prediction), South China Sea claims (cartel asymmetric-cost-shift dynamics), Belt and Road (China asserting cartel-co-leader position), AIIB/parallel-institution moves (institutional bid for cartel-co-leadership). Useful for evaluating Chinese state-action without lapsing into either alarm or apology — Chinese behaviour is intelligible as cartel-position-seeking by an emerging great power, neither uniquely revisionist nor purely defensive. The framework also illuminates why China invests heavily in nationalism (ch. 6’s mechanism — discontinuous cost jumps at borders) and why the post-2022 technological-self-sufficiency vector is exactly what cartel theory predicts an emerging-power-IP-importer would do.
Lobbying-network research with In Song Kim: the cartel framework reframes lobbying as the intra-cartel-member mechanism by which citizens (workers, farmers, capital holders) compete to shape the cartel-leader’s posture in international negotiations. Yang’s existing horizontal lobbying-network models could be extended to vertical cartel-cross-tier dynamics — modelling how domestic lobbying coalitions translate into international-cartel positions on trade, IP, immigration, environmental policy. Empirically: the persistence of farm subsidies in developed countries (despite their welfare cost and trade-distortion effects) is a clean test case for the framework — these subsidies persist because farm interests are decisive in cartel-leader politics, not because of efficiency.
AI-policy comparative analysis: each major AI jurisdiction (US sectoral + judicial, EU AI Act, China cyber-administration model, UK light-touch) reflects a different cartel-leader posture. The framework supplies the right unit of analysis: not “what AI rules does each country have” but “how does each country position relative to cartel-leader prerogatives over the AI-compute and AI-capabilities markets.” This is a more analytically tractable comparative frame than rights-based or risk-based taxonomies. The framework also predicts that AI-policy convergence will track cartel-leader coordination cycles — heavy convergence when US-China-EU interests align, divergence when they don’t.
Goldman quant work / macro views: managed-trade equilibrium has direct implications for cross-border tax-avoidance trades, BEPS-driven corporate restructuring, and tax-haven-jurisdiction macro positioning. The framework supplies a structural account of why these arbitrages persist (cartel adaptation, not regulatory failure) and when they should compress (when cartel-leader coordination tightens, as in the 2021 OECD agreement). Useful for relative-value trades on Ireland-vs-Cayman / Bermuda-vs-Jersey corporate-domicile spreads, for sovereign-CDS pricing on weak-cartel-member states, and for currency basis-swap analysis where capital-control regimes vary by cartel position.
Self-defence against secondary literature: Acharya-Lee is now the right benchmark for evaluating IR / comparative-politics journalism and policy commentary on state-system change. Pieces that don’t engage cartel logic (defaulting to Westphalian-norms or realist-balance-of-power framings) are operating with a partial frame. Useful self-discipline — the frame applies to coverage of UNGA votes, ICJ cases, sanctions regimes, BRICS-expansion politics, post-Brexit EU-UK relations, all the way to corporate-tax journalism.
Methodological example for combined-methods research: Acharya-Lee is one of the cleanest worked examples of formal model + within-case process tracing in contemporary political science. For Yang’s qualitative-IR work and any plan to combine modelling with case studies, the book is an explicit template — the model in ch. 2 is fully specified; the case studies in chs. 3–5 illustrate the model’s mechanism rather than re-deriving it. This division of labour between model and case is more disciplined than typical IR work and worth emulating.

What I would miss if I only read this note
The case-study density. Acharya-Lee’s argumentative force comes from the cumulative weight of historically specific cases: the 1518 Scottish privy council quotation about the Armstrongs being “in the Debatable landis, and agreit [in agreement] with Ingland”; the 1551 council minutes about “the great and heavy crimes committed upon our sovereign lady’s poor lieges by thieves”; the equivalente tax in Bourbon Valencia explicitly designed to equalise burdens with Castile; the 84% / 1.25% noble-vs-crown land split in pre-reduktion Livland; the Chilean state’s mining-tax negotiation with Bolivia in 1874 followed by Bolivia’s 10-cent-tax breach in 1878 that triggered war; Senators Schumer and Casey’s 2012 Ex-PATRIOT Act proposing 30% capital-gains tax on US citizenship-renouncers; the 1779 France–Austrian Netherlands border treaty mentioning a specific ditch separating two villages; the Phoebus/Great Lightbulb cartel granting GE “North America, Cuba, and the West Indies” while the French Compagnie General received “France, Greece, and joint rights in Bulgaria, Romania, Yugoslavia, and Turkey.” These cases do work on the reader that aggregated bullets cannot — they show, repeatedly, that the framework’s predicted mechanism actually operated in archival reality, and that the rulers and diplomats involved were aware of it.
The note also compresses the formal apparatus of ch. 2 — the Bertrand competition, the discount-factor condition (the literal δ > L_A/(L_A+L_B) and δ > L_B/(L_A+L_B) derivation), the multiple-equilibria structure of the three-state game, the geometric construction of Y and the loss-from-competition shaded areas, the Fig. 4-vs-Fig. 5 contrast that powers the historical-origin chapter. Re-deriving the model for oneself, even on a napkin, is the only way to develop the trained intuition for what the framework predicts in a new case (e.g., when applied to AI-compute or cryptocurrency or platform-governance). The compressed bullet-list version of the model loses this trainability — the reader who hasn’t sat with the figures cannot easily extend the framework to novel domains.
Equally, the note compresses Acharya-Lee’s explicit critique of rival theories. The book’s section-by-section dismantling of the Westphalia hypothesis (Ruggie, Philpott, Nexon, Osiander), the Jervis offense-defense balance, Spruyt’s institutional selection, and the Alesina-Spolaore voting-derived borders is itself a useful introduction to the contemporary theory of the state system. Without engaging the comparative critique, the positive contribution of cartel theory is harder to see clearly — what makes the cartel framework new is precisely what it absorbs from each rival theory while supplying the missing self-enforcement mechanism. The book functions as a structured tour of the field; the note can only point back to it.
Finally, the note compresses the quantitative figures — the French intendent fiscal data (Fig. 7), the treaty-mentions-of-borders running average (Fig. 6), the diplomatic-equality-by-dyad time series (Bayer 2006), the agriculture-vs-services-vs-manufacturing US GDP shares (Fig. 13), the net-migration-vs-governance-quality scatter (Fig. 14), the post-1850 number-of-states trajectory (Fig. 11). For a reader trying to internalise the framework as a working analytical tool rather than a remembered set of bullet-points, the empirical anchors matter. Specific numbers stay with the reader in ways that the verbal summary does not — “12.05× revenue growth in border provinces” is more memorable than “border provinces grew faster than non-border ones.”

01_Books/Adnan-Aziz---Elements-of-Progra.title: Elements of Programming Interviews
01_Books/Adnan-Aziz---Elements-of-Progra.content:
Adnan Aziz - Elements of Programming Interviews
One-sentence thesis
Aziz, Lee and Prakash argue that algorithmic-interview competence is a recognition reflex trained by drilling problems organized around a small, named set of patterns (data-structure, algorithm-design, abstract-analysis, system-design) — not a body of memorized solutions — and they back the claim with a 17-chapter problem catalog whose internal structure forces the reader to encounter each pattern five to twenty times in different costumes until the underlying invariant becomes visible at first glance.
Why this book matters
EPI is the harder sibling of McDowell’s Cracking and the difference matters: McDowell teaches how to interview (behavioral, soft skills, the 150-problem starter set with prose preambles), while Aziz teaches how to recognize the pattern under the costume (300+ problems with terse statements, hint-only Part III, and a Part IV that walks the brute-force-to-optimum derivation explicitly). For candidates targeting the algorithmic bar at Google, Meta, Jane Street, Citadel, or research-engineer roles, the McDowell-only path tops out around mid-level competence; the EPI path is what produces senior-level recognition speed. The two books are complements, not substitutes — McDowell first to internalize the interview as an event, EPI second to internalize the pattern catalog as a working vocabulary.
The book also matters as a taxonomy artifact. Chapter 4’s four pattern tables — data-structure, algorithm-design, abstract-analysis, system-design — are the cleanest taxonomy of algorithmic problem types in the interview-prep literature. A reader who masters those four tables has a search index against which any new problem statement can be queried: “which entry in Table 4.1 names the right structure? which entry in Table 4.2 names the right technique? which entry in Table 4.3 names the right analytical move?” That habit transfers directly to production work — code review, design review, and on-call debugging all benefit from “name the pattern first, derive the solution second.”
The third reason EPI matters is the variants discipline. Each solution in Part IV ends with 2–5 variants (“what if duplicates are allowed? what if the array is rotated? what if k is unbounded?”) that force the reader to re-derive the invariant under perturbed preconditions. This is exactly the Dijkstra-style derivation applied at interview scale, and it is the reason EPI graduates outperform LeetCode-grinding peers under stress: their preparation builds the derivation reflex, not just the recall reflex.
Core argument
Aziz’s argument is structurally simple and pedagogically aggressive. The book stakes five claims and demonstrates each with hundreds of pages of problem-solution evidence:

Patterns over problems. Interview problems look different but reduce to a small set of named patterns. Chapter 4’s four tables enumerate them: data structures (primitive, array, string, list, stack/queue, tree, heap, hash, BST), algorithm techniques (sort, recursion, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, greedy, invariants), abstract analyses (concrete examples, case analysis, iterative refinement, reduction, graph modeling), and system design moves (caching, parallelism, indexing, randomization). Mastery of the patterns is mastery of the problems.
Recognition is a muscle. Pattern recognition is not innate; it is built by encountering each pattern five to twenty times in different problem costumes. Part II’s 17 chapters are designed so that every chapter re-uses every previously-introduced pattern under a new data-structure constraint. By chapter 18 (greedy + invariants), the reader has seen invariants in chapters 4, 6, 8, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17 — and the recognition reflex is built by sheer repetition under varied costumes.
Brute force first, then refine. Every Part IV solution starts with the brute-force algorithm, names its complexity, then walks through the optimization derivation step by step. This is the iterative refinement abstract-analysis pattern made into a book-wide pedagogical convention. The reader who reads only the optimum solution learns the algorithm but loses the derivation path that produced it; the reader who attempts the brute force first, then reads the refinement, builds the path-finding reflex.
Hints are pattern-naming, not solving. Part III gives one-line hints, deliberately calibrated to name the pattern without giving the answer (“find an invariant,” “use a sweep,” “sort first”). The hint should reduce the search space by naming which pattern-table entry applies, leaving the reader to do the derivation. This three-stage scaffolding — problem in Part II, pattern-name in Part III, derivation in Part IV — is the book’s pedagogical engine.
Variants force re-derivation. Each Part IV solution closes with 2–5 perturbed-precondition variants. The variants ensure that the reader cannot pass by memorizing the headline solution; the derivation must survive perturbation, which means the reader must have understood the invariant, not just the code. This is the closest the interview-prep literature comes to [[Edsger W. Dijkstra - A Discipline of Programming|Dijkstra’s wp(S, R) derivations]] applied to whiteboard-scale problems.

The cumulative claim: an EPI graduate has recognition reflexes, not memorized solutions. When a Citadel quant-engineer interviewer presents a never-before-seen problem (“given a stream of stock-quote ticks, design a data structure that supports update(symbol, price) in O(log n) and top_k_by_volatility(k) in O(k log n)…”), the EPI graduate’s first move is not to search memory for “have I seen this exact problem?” but to query the pattern tables: “this is a streaming + top-k pattern, so heap + augmented-BST or Bloom-filter + sorted-set; the volatility metric implies a rolling-window invariant, which means we need Amortized Analysis for the update path.” That query loop is the deliverable.
Argument map
EPI’s pedagogical scaffolding flows top-down from the meta-claim (recognition is the deliverable) through the four pattern tables (the recognition vocabulary) into the three-stage drill (problem → hint → solution) that builds the reflex.
Algorithmic interview = recognition under time pressure
  └── recognition is a muscle, not a memory
        └── built by drilling 300+ problems organized by pattern (Part II)
              └── patterns enumerated in 4 tables (ch. 4)
                    ├── data structures (Table 4.1)
                    ├── algorithm techniques (Table 4.2)
                    ├── abstract analyses (Table 4.3)
                    └── system design (Table 4.5)
              └── each pattern re-encountered in many costumes (chs. 5–21)
        └── three-stage scaffolding (Parts II / III / IV)
              ├── Part II: terse problem statements
              ├── Part III: pattern-naming hints (one line each)
              └── Part IV: brute-force → refine → variants
                    └── variants force re-derivation under perturbation
        └── result: candidate sees pattern at first glance
              └── transfers to production code review, design, on-call

Key concepts

Algorithmic Pattern Recognition — the central pedagogical claim of the book; the four pattern tables are its operational form.
Time-Space Complexity Trade-off — every Part IV solution presents at least two algorithms with different (time, space) profiles and asks the reader to choose; the parity worked example moves O(n) → O(s) → O(1)-with-table.
Asymptotic Analysis — the lingua franca for comparing brute-force and optimum solutions; chapter 4’s complexity primer is the prerequisite for every Part IV refinement step.
Amortized Analysis — used in chapter 6 (dynamic-array doubling) and chapter 11 (heap operations), and in many Part IV variants where a single expensive operation is followed by many cheap ones.
Abstract Data Type — chapter 4’s data-structure pattern table is implicitly an ADT taxonomy; the heap-as-priority-queue and BST-as-sorted-map mappings are the load-bearing examples.
Invariant-preserving local repair — the cross-chapter discipline that ties together chapter 18 (greedy + invariants) with the rotations of chapter 15 (BSTs) and the sift operations of chapter 11 (heaps).
Brute-force-first iterative refinement — chapter 4’s abstract-analysis pattern, used as the structural template for every Part IV solution.

Best chapters/pages to actually read
The book is too long for a linear read; it is reference + drill material. Read in this order:

Chapter 4 (Problem Solving Patterns) — the load-bearing chapter. Read it twice. After the second read, all four pattern tables (4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.5) should be loaded into working memory. Without this, Part II is opaque; with it, Part II becomes a guided drill.
Chapters 1–3 (lifecycle, candidate playbook, interviewer playbook) — read once, before the first interview. The interviewer-playbook chapter (ch. 3) is the highest-leverage chapter for candidates because it explains what signal interviewers are calibrating against. Specifically, ch. 3’s “no single point of failure / multiple solutions / multi-area coverage” criteria for problem selection tell the candidate which kind of dialogue to expect.
Chapter 6 (Arrays) — start here for Part II. Five problems including Dutch national flag (problem 6.1) and max-difference (problem 6.2) cover invariants, two-pointer technique, and amortized resizing. The single highest-yield chapter per page.
Chapter 11 (Heaps) — the highest-yield chapter for systems-engineering candidates. The k-merge sorted streams problem and online-median problem are production algorithms that appear in stream processors, log aggregators, and quant-research signal pipelines.
Chapter 12 (Searching) — binary search and its variants. The first/last-occurrence variant and the search-rotated-array variant are the two most asked binary-search interview problems in the FAANG / quant ecosystem; mastering them is high-yield.
Chapter 17 (Dynamic Programming) — the chapter most candidates fail. Score-combinations, Levenshtein, knapsack, longest-non-decreasing-subsequence are the four canonical DP problems; if these four are reflexive, ~80% of DP interview problems become tractable.
Chapter 18 (Greedy + Invariants) — the chapter whose pattern recurs most across other chapters. The 2-sum / 3-sum and longest-contiguous-sequence problems exemplify the invariant-propagation discipline that ties the book’s pedagogy together.
Chapter 21 (Design Problems) — system-design questions for senior candidates. TinyURL, online advertising, distributed throttling. Pair with John Ousterhout - A Philosophy of Software Design for the API-design dimension that EPI’s design problems touch but do not deeply develop.

Skip-and-return strategy: chapters 7 (strings), 8 (linked lists), 9 (stacks/queues) are necessary but boring — the problems are mostly index-juggling drills. Do them when stamina allows. Chapter 20 (parallel computing) is shallow relative to a real systems text and can be deferred unless the target role explicitly tests concurrency.

21 (distributed throttling)Senior / staff-level interview
Important examples / cases
The parity problem (5.1) is the book’s signature worked example because it traverses three points on the Time-Space Complexity Trade-off curve in a single page: O(n) brute-force bit-iteration → O(s) using x & (x-1) to clear lowest set bit → O(1) per query with a 65,536-entry precomputed lookup table.
