magnesium block of NMDA; reversal potentials and conductance multiplication.Why a synapse is a time-varying conductance, not a number.(no chapter summary file in vault)14Extracellular Field RecordingsVolume conduction, current source density, EEG/LFP origins.How macroscopic electrical recordings relate to the underlying cellular currents.(no chapter summary file in vault)15Cellular Neurophysiology of Learning and MemoryLTP and LTD induction protocols, NMDA-receptor dependence, AMPA receptor trafficking, spine-shape plasticity, metaplasticity.The most plausible cellular substrate for memory; still partial.(no chapter summary file in vault)ABasic Electricity and Electrical CircuitsOhm’s law, Kirchhoff’s laws, RC circuits; recap.Bridge for biology students.(no chapter summary file in vault)BOptical MethodsVoltage-sensitive dyes, Ca²⁺ imaging.Complementary techniques to patch clamp.(no chapter summary file in vault)C–DHomework solutionsWorked problems for every chapter.Use them; the book is half-empty without these.(no chapter summary file in vault)
Important examples / cases
Classic preparations — the squid giant axon lineage (Loligo and Sepia, originally exploited by Hodgkin, Huxley, and Katz at Plymouth in the 1940s–50s) — anchor the historical narrative tying graphs to experimental ethos repeated in modern slice physiology. The squid axon’s exceptional diameter (up to 1 mm) is what made early voltage-clamp possible; the same conceptual lineage runs through the frog neuromuscular junction (Katz’s quantal analysis) and into mammalian brain slice work that dominates the modern field. Hippocampal slice recordings inherit the same ethos even where geometry breaks the spherical-soma approximation near branch points; mapping textbook cartoons onto actual rigs shows where simplified compartment models mis-track timing. Pharmacological channel-block vignettes (TTX for Na⁺, TEA for K⁺, conotoxins for Ca²⁺, AP5 for NMDA) pair well with updated ion-channel reviews when subtype names have shifted since the 1990s tables printed here. The textbook’s worked example of the giant axon’s space and time constants — explicitly numerical — is the right warm-up for any reader who wants to develop biophysical intuition rather than verbal fluency.
A second class of canonical cases is the frog neuromuscular junction, where the quantal hypothesis was first established. The book’s treatment of miniature endplate potentials (MEPPs) and their Poisson statistics is the clearest cellular-level argument anywhere that synaptic transmission is irreducibly probabilistic. Any modern paper invoking “synaptic noise” traces back through this preparation.
Critiques and limitations
Publication predates the optogenetics explosion, the connectomics revolution, and single-cell transcriptomics, so molecular identities appear schematic relative to 2026 atlases — Kv channel subtypes, GABA receptor diversity, and inhibitory interneuron taxonomy have all expanded substantially. Mathematical density intimidates verbal philosophers dipping casually; companion tutorials are advised for readers without ODE comfort. Species emphasis skews toward rodent-friendly preparations (squid axon, frog NMJ, hippocampal slice), so when citing primates, inference demands caution. Mitochondrial metabolism and glia interactions are underrepresented relative to contemporary consensus that metabolic budgeting and astrocytic signaling materially constrain computation — readers should pair this textbook with Nick Lane - Power Sex Suicide and Nick Lane - The Vital Question for the bioenergetic angle. Connectomics hype occasionally tempts readers to dismiss cable theory as obsolete — mistaken; compartment models remain operational tools despite richer connectivity graphs. Print quality affects grayscale reproduction of traces; readers relying only on scans should verify calibration bars against primary sources when feasible. The book also predates the modern dynamical-systems-of-neurophysiology literature (Izhikevich, Rinzel, Ermentrout’s bifurcation analyses), so although HH is treated rigorously, the reader does not get the bifurcation-theoretic vocabulary that explains why certain channel cocktails produce bursting, plateau potentials, or resonance. Finally, the cellular-to-behavioral chapter (15) is honest about being incomplete — the LTP-as-memory inference was already contested in 1995 and remains so — but a 2026 reader will want supplementary material on engram cells, optogenetic memory manipulation, and the modern critique of synaptic-weight memory storage.
Links to other books

Grounds idealizations in Warren S. McCulloch - Embodiments of Mind — Pitts–McCulloch logic abstracts away continuous dynamics this textbook restores. The all-or-none assumption (All-or-None Activity) is shown to be a population-level approximation over stochastic gating; the Logical Calculus of Neural Activity survives as a useful idealization but not as a literal description of cells.
Formal-machine bridge Marvin Lee Minsky - Computation Finite and Infinite Machines — Minsky’s finite-state machine view of neurons is the formal counterpart to what Johnston–Wu derive at the biophysical level; the books are complementary halves of the same picture.
Critique of the perceptron abstraction Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert - Perceptrons — Minsky and Papert argued the perceptron is computationally limited; Johnston–Wu show the perceptron is also biologically impoverished. Both critiques target the same simplification from different directions.
Modern AI counterpart Simon Prince - Understanding Deep Learning — Prince’s deep-learning units are scalar-weighted sums plus nonlinearities; reading Johnston–Wu first is the cleanest way to see what is omitted, and where the omission is or is not consequential for a given task.
Evolutionary framing Max Bennett - A Brief History of Intelligence — Bennett’s macro breakthrough stories acquire cellular instrumentation literacy by referencing ion-channel expansions and synaptic innovations whose physics are derived here.
Cell-biology context Bruce Alberts - Molecular Biology of the Cell — Alberts treats the cell membrane, ion pumps, and receptor signaling in general; Johnston–Wu specialize that machinery to neurons. Read Alberts ch. 11–12 alongside Johnston–Wu ch. 2.
Organism-scale context Neil Campbell - Biology Seventh Edition — Campbell’s nervous-system chapters give the systems-level scaffold (sensory, motor, autonomic) into which Johnston–Wu’s cellular detail fits.
Bioenergetic constraint Nick Lane - Power Sex Suicide, Nick Lane - The Vital Question — Lane’s case that mitochondrial bioenergetics constrain biological complexity sharpens Johnston–Wu’s implicit point that maintaining ionic gradients (the ATP cost of the Na/K-ATPase) is the metabolic load that bounds neural computation.
Physics adjacency Carlo Rovelli - Helgoland — Rovelli’s relational view of physical systems offers a philosophical frame for thinking about why the membrane potential is meaningful only in relation to the rest of the circuit, much as quantum states are relational rather than absolute.

Open questions
How much detail must AI-alignment discourse import from dendritic computation versus safely coarse-grain — unresolved interdisciplinary negotiation, with current evidence suggesting active dendrites can implement small multilayer networks per cell. Where should introductory courses spend scarce weeks: classical cable theory or modern optogenetic perturbation readouts — departments disagree given finite semesters. To what extent does spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) generalize beyond the cortical and hippocampal preparations where it was characterized — open question with a steadily expanding answer. How well do compartment-model simulations actually predict the response of a real neuron to a novel current injection — practical accuracy is good but not surprise-free. Whether memory is encoded in synaptic weights, in cell-intrinsic excitability, in network architecture, or in some combination — the field’s central unresolved cellular question. Whether the metabolic cost of maintaining ionic gradients is a hard constraint on cortical scaling (a Lane-style argument) or a soft engineering parameter — biology would lean toward the former, computer science toward the latter.
Pedagogy note
Pair each equation block with a tiny simulation reproducing one figure; the mismatch between code output and print teaches debugging habits that summaries cannot instill. During remote teaching, screen-share parameter sweeps — slide maximal conductances while voltage traces evolve — so learners feel causality as continuous dynamics rather than frozen panels. Short prediction prompts (“Will the overshoot grow if τ_h steepens?”) before revealing the run sharpen retention compared with passive reading. The textbook’s homework problems with full solutions in appendix D are unusually generous for a graduate text — exploit this; do not skip them on the false belief that working through worked solutions is “passive.” The cleanest teaching pattern is: state the equation, show the figure, run the simulation, vary one parameter, predict and verify, then narrate.
Research uses

Neuro–AI criticism — grounding metaphors before declaring artificial neurons brain-like operationally; naming the specific abstraction being made and what it discards.
Quantitative neuroscience preparation — prerequisite stepping stone toward dynamical-systems seminars and any modern theoretical-neuroscience course (Dayan & Abbott, Gerstner et al.) which assumes this material.
Clinical translation guardrails — clarifies mechanism vocabulary when evaluating pharmacological interventions marketed vaguely; “channel modulator” is a class, not a mechanism.
Teaching labs — scaffold for designing exercises exporting MATLAB/Python/NEURON simulations reinforcing differential equation intuition.
Grant appendix drafting — supplies precise ion-channel and synaptic vocabulary for biophysical experiment proposals when reviewers push back on hand-wavy ML analogies.
Ethics and welfare reviews — nociception pathways described at cellular resolution can inform careful wording; clinical judgment remains paramount.
Reading classical electrophysiology papers — Hodgkin–Huxley 1952, Katz 1969, Bliss & Lømo 1973, Hubel & Wiesel cellular recordings, Hodgkin & Katz 1949 — all become legible after this textbook in a way they are not before.
Building biologically-plausible learning rules — STDP, BCM, three-factor rules all start from the cellular machinery this book describes; without it, the rules are formal toys.

What I would miss if I only read this note
Equation-driven exercises — numeric intuition decays without pencil time — plus curated figures showing raw noisy traces rather than cartoon spikes. The textbook’s homework problems ramp difficulty in a way summaries cannot compress, and the appendix D worked solutions encode pedagogical choices a note cannot replicate. Office-hour metaphors instructors invent on the spot (leaky barrel for capacitance, bowling-ball ions for inertia, traffic-light NMDA for coincidence detection) often stick longer than formal notation alone; none of that interpersonal choreography survives here. Dimensional-analysis drills that train habit checking milliseconds versus milliseconds-squared, or millivolts versus volts, save careers from order-of-magnitude disasters — summaries rarely replicate that friction. Margin annotations classmates scribble (“exam spotlight”) encode cohort folklore absent from any note. Finally, the textbook’s integration of classic preparations (squid axon lineage, frog NMJ) with homework bridges historical ethos and modern modeling — losing the lab narrative severs motivation some learners need to tolerate differential equations emotionally. Most importantly, a note cannot substitute for the moment when, reading chapter 6 carefully, the reader realises that the action potential is predicted rather than described by the HH equations — that biology contains lawful, quantitative regularities derivable from first principles. That experience is the actual purpose of the book, and the note can only point at it.

01_Books/Daron-Acemoglu---Microeconomics.title: Microeconomics
01_Books/Daron-Acemoglu---Microeconomics.content:
Daron Acemoglu - Microeconomics
One-sentence thesis
A modern principles-of-microeconomics textbook organised around three unifying themes — optimization, equilibrium, empiricism — that argues introductory students should learn behavioral deviations, field-experimental evidence, game-theoretic strategic interaction, and information-economics market failures as core machinery rather than as honors-track appendices, on the wager that contemporary undergraduates will follow markets in their own lives (Uber surge pricing, eBay auctions, Airbnb listings, Coronavirus externalities) more readily than they will follow Marshallian price-quantity diagrams shorn of empirical anchor.
Why this book matters
This is the Third Edition (Pearson, 2022) of the Acemoglu-Laibson-List principles textbook, with eighteen main chapters plus three web chapters (financial decision-making; life/health/environment; political economy). It is the book a 2024–2026 undergraduate is most likely to meet in a competitive U.S. micro principles course, and the most authoritative “principles” alternative to the older market leaders — Mankiw’s Principles of Economics, Krugman-Wells, and Bernanke-Frank. It distinguishes itself by integrating rather than segregating three frontier research traditions: Acemoglu (institutional / political-economy / labor-economics rigor; MIT Institute Professor; John Bates Clark Medal 2005), Laibson (behavioral economics / hyperbolic discounting / household finance; Harvard chair), and List (field experiments; UChicago, formerly White House CEA 2002–2003; Arrow Prize 2008). The integration is doctrinal, not cosmetic — present bias appears alongside time discounting in Chapter 15 rather than in a “behavioral aside” sidebar; field experiments anchor the empirical claims at the start of nearly every chapter (“Evidence-Based Economics” openers).
For a research-oriented reader (quant-finance interview prep, AI-policy analysis, blockchain regulation, China political-economy modelling, lobbying-network research), this textbook serves three functions distinct from a graduate text like Mas-Colell/Whinston/Green or Varian Intermediate Microeconomics: it provides (i) a shared dialect for discussing micro-foundations with non-economist collaborators (data scientists, lawyers, policy analysts), (ii) a quick refresher map between standard diagrams and modern empirical citations, and (iii) a baseline curriculum-shape against which to detect what newer pedagogy (open-access OER, modular pods, Mankiw’s much narrower behavioral coverage) treats as core vs optional. The 2022 timing also matters: Chapters 1, 4, and 9 explicitly fold the COVID-19 health-vs-output trade-off, the April 2020 negative oil-price episode, and externality-driven vaccination policy into the standard examples — making the text a snapshot of how the principles canon absorbed the pandemic.
Core argument
The argument is pedagogical (what to teach undergraduates) rather than research-frontier (what to discover next). It proceeds:


Three unifying principles ground the entire curriculum (Preface; Chapter 1.2–1.5). Optimization (people try to choose the best feasible option, even when they fail), Equilibrium (systems sit where everyone is simultaneously trying to optimise), Empiricism (data are used to test the first two). The authors reject the idea that introductory micro is a series of “theoretical assertions with little empirical basis” (Preface, p. xx) — this is a methodological commitment, not just a stylistic one.


Optimization absorbs behavioral psychology by treating rational choice as a limiting case, not a literal description (Chapter 1.3, Chapter 3, Chapter 5). Cost-benefit analysis, marginal analysis, and budget-constraint geometry are taught as both descriptive and prescriptive tools. Choice-and-Consequence sidebars throughout (e.g. ch. 3 “Do People Actually Choose the Best Feasible Option?”, p. 46) explicitly admit deviations. Behavioral material is integrated rather than apologised for.


Demand and supply meet field-experimental data immediately (Chapter 4–5). The first detailed empirical example is gasoline-price elasticity (ch. 4.2), followed by the smoking-quit-for-$100 field experiment (ch. 5, pp. 99–101). The pedagogical wager is that students will internalise elasticity faster from a smoking-cessation RCT than from a textbook calculus exercise.


The Invisible Hand is presented with both its power and its failure modes side-by-side (Chapter 7, Chapter 9). Chapter 7 develops Pareto efficiency, social surplus, deadweight loss, and the Adam Smith / Hayek allocation argument (ch. 7.4, “FEMA and Walmart After Katrina”, “Command and Control at Kmart” — pp. 171, 173). Chapter 9 then immediately introduces externalities, public goods, common-pool resources, and the Coase Theorem (ch. 9.2, p. 218). The juxtaposition is the textbook’s central rhetorical move: the invisible hand is real and the failures of the invisible hand are real and the second-best policy choices among interventions are the substance of public economics.


Policy intervention is taught as constrained optimization with side-effects, not as panacea or villain (Chapter 10). Government Failures (10.3) — direct costs of bureaucracy, corruption, underground economy, regulatory capture — get equal billing with Market Failures. The “Equity Versus Efficiency” trade-off (10.4) and “Consumer Sovereignty and Paternalism” debate (10.5) are taught as live policy disputes, not as settled doctrine.


Strategic interaction is integrated, not bolted on (Chapters 12–14). Monopoly (ch. 12) leads into Game Theory (ch. 13: simultaneous-move games, Nash equilibrium, prisoners’ dilemma; backward induction in extensive-form games — ch. 13.5, p. 338), which then drives Oligopoly and Monopolistic Competition (ch. 14). The pedagogical claim is that you cannot understand modern industrial organisation (or, by extension, antitrust litigation, platform competition, or auction-design problems) without strategic-interaction tools.


Information economics is core curriculum (Chapter 16). Asymmetric information, adverse selection (used-car/Akerlof lemons exposition, ch. 16.1, pp. 396–397; health insurance, p. 397), signaling (Spence credentialing argument, ch. 16.1, p. 398), moral hazard (ch. 16.2), efficiency wages, and “skin in the game” insurance design (ch. 16.2, p. 404) — all treated as foundational rather than advanced.


Auctions, bargaining, and social economics extend the toolbox to the cases students actually encounter (Chapters 17–18). English/Dutch/first-price/second-price auctions and the Revenue Equivalence Theorem (ch. 17.1, p. 421) are taught because eBay exists; ultimatum games, charity, fairness, trust, revenge, peer effects, and herding (ch. 18) are taught because dictator-game and field-experiment evidence shows people care about these things in ways the older textbook canon largely ignored.


The cumulative argument is curricular, not predictive. A student who completes the eighteen chapters has a vocabulary in which to discuss any micro policy controversy — minimum wage, carbon tax, antitrust, platform regulation, two-sided markets, vaccine externalities, charity-tax-deduction design — without having to outsource the analytical work to specialists. The textbook’s real claim is that this vocabulary should be the modal undergraduate’s, not the honors student’s.


Argument map
The textbook’s pedagogical sequence runs principles → individual choice → markets → market failures → strategic interaction → information & contracts → social/behavioral extensions. Web chapters (financial decision-making; life/health/environment; political economy) extend each branch. The three unifying themes (optimization / equilibrium / empiricism) thread vertically through every chapter.
                THREE PRINCIPLES (Ch. 1)
   Optimization ──── Equilibrium ──── Empiricism
        │                │                │
        ▼                ▼                ▼
    Demand/Supply (Ch. 2-4)  ──→  Marshallian engine
        │
        ▼
PART II Foundations of Microeconomics (Ch. 5-11)
  Consumer (5) → Seller (6) → Perfect Competition / Invisible Hand (7)
                                   │
                                   ▼
                  Trade / Comparative Advantage (8)
                                   │
                                   ▼
        Market Failures: Externalities & Public Goods (9)
                                   │
                                   ▼
        Government in the Economy: Tax & Regulation (10)
                                   │
                                   ▼
                Markets for Factors (Labor, Capital, Land) (11)
                                   │
                                   ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┐
        ▼                                                 ▼
PART III Market Structure                  PART IV Toolbox Extensions
   Monopoly (12)                              Time & Risk (15)
       │                                          │
       ▼                                          ▼
   Game Theory (13)                          Information Economics (16)
       │                              (asymmetric info / adverse selection
       ▼                                / signaling / moral hazard)
   Oligopoly &                                   │
   Monopolistic Competition (14)                 ▼
                                              Auctions & Bargaining (17)
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
                                              Social Economics (18)
                                            (charity, fairness, trust,
                                             revenge, peer effects)

The two visible vertical moves are: (a) the price-theory → strategic-interaction shift between Parts II–III, which is where game theory becomes load-bearing rather than ornamental; and (b) the certainty → time-and-uncertainty shift between Parts III–IV, which is where behavioral / field-experimental tools earn their integration into core micro.
Key concepts

Pareto Efficiency — Acemoglu et al’s framing in ch. 7.1 (pp. 154–156): “An outcome is Pareto efficient if no individual can be made better off without making someone else worse off”; perfect competitive equilibrium is shown to be Pareto efficient. The First Welfare Theorem in textbook form.
Game Theory Concepts — Nash equilibrium, prisoners’ dilemma, dominant strategies, extensive-form games, backward induction (ch. 13). Includes the “first-mover advantage, commitment, and vengeance” treatment (ch. 13.5, p. 339) that connects game theory to credible-threat reasoning.
Information Asymmetry — adverse selection, signaling, moral hazard, principal-agent problem (ch. 16). Akerlof “lemons” used-car exposition (ch. 16.1, p. 396) and Spence signaling (p. 398) presented as the canonical pair.
Market Failure — externalities (negative and positive), public goods (non-rival, non-excludable), common-pool resources (tragedy of the commons), Coase Theorem (ch. 9). Used as the structural complement to the Invisible Hand chapter.
Mechanism Design — auction theory (English / Dutch / first-price / second-price; Revenue Equivalence Theorem, ch. 17.1, p. 421); bargaining and the Coase Theorem revisited (ch. 17.2). Introduced as the applied face of game theory plus information economics.
Skin in the Game — Acemoglu et al import this Talebian phrase explicitly (ch. 16.2, p. 404) for insurance-market moral-hazard solutions (deductibles, copays). One of the few cases where vault-canonical-concept-name and textbook-section-name coincide verbatim.
Rational Irrationality — relevant as the contrast case: Caplan’s argument that voters are systematically irrational in low-cost domains sits next to Acemoglu et al’s Chapter 18 evidence that consumers and donors are also systematically non-self-interested in measurable ways.

Key arguments created from this book

Behavioral and field-experimental material belongs in core principles, not appendix track — operationalised in the textbook’s chapter integration; argument note candidate.
The Invisible Hand and its Failures are pedagogical twins — the ch. 7 / ch. 9 juxtaposition is itself a pedagogical claim, distinct from the deeper-curriculum claim of Mas-Colell.

Best chapters/pages to actually read
For a researcher returning to micro after time in adjacent fields (data science, ML, law, finance), the highest-leverage chapters are:

Chapter 1 (pp. 2–18) — the three-principle scaffold (optimization / equilibrium / empiricism) and the COVID-19 health-vs-output framing. ~16 pp; read in one sitting; sets the textbook’s epistemic stance for everything that follows.
Chapter 5 (pp. 90–119) — consumer optimisation and demand elasticities, with the “smoker quits for $100/month” field experiment (pp. 99–101) as the empirical anchor. The indifference-curve appendix (pp. 116–119) is optional; the main chapter alone trains the budget-constraint reflex.
Chapter 7 (pp. 152–180) — Perfect Competition and the Invisible Hand, including Pareto efficiency (pp. 154–156), deadweight loss (p. 165), and the “FEMA and Walmart after Katrina” / “Command and Control at Kmart” pair (pp. 171, 173). The single most important chapter for arguing for market mechanisms.
Chapter 9 (pp. 210–238) — Externalities and Public Goods, including the COVID vaccination externalities feature (p. 216), Coase Theorem (p. 218), command-and-control vs corrective taxes (pp. 220–224), and Tragedy of the Commons (p. 233). The single most important chapter for arguing against market mechanisms in specific failures. Read together with Chapter 7 — they are the textbook’s central diptych.
Chapter 13 (pp. 324–345) — Game Theory and Strategic Play. Nash equilibrium, prisoners’ dilemma, extensive-form games, backward induction, “first-mover advantage / commitment / vengeance” (p. 339). Highest-leverage chapter for finance, antitrust, platform-strategy, and any negotiation literacy.
Chapter 16 (pp. 394–410) — Economics of Information. Adverse selection (used cars and health insurance), signaling (Spence labor-market argument, p. 398), moral hazard, efficiency wages, “skin in the game” insurance design. Highest-leverage chapter for insurance, contract, and platform-design literacy.
Chapter 17 (pp. 412–431) — Auctions and Bargaining. Revenue Equivalence Theorem (p. 421), eBay sniping, ultimatum games, Coase-Theorem-revisited. The chapter that motivates mechanism design without using the phrase.
Skip on first pass: the indifference-curve appendices (Ch. 5 appendix, Ch. 6 appendix on different cost structures, Ch. 11 monopsony appendix) unless you’re preparing for a calculus-based exam. Web Chapter 1 (financial decision-making) is largely review for any reader with finance exposure.

Chapter-by-chapter distillation



















































































































#TitleSummary1Principles and Practice of EconomicsThree principles (optimization / equilibrium / empiricism); scope of economics; positive vs normative; trade-offs; opportunity cost; cost-benefit analysis. COVID-19 health-vs-output worked as the running example.2Economic Science: Data and ModelsScientific method; means vs medians; correlation vs causation; experimental and natural experiments. Appendix on charts/graphs.3Optimization: Trying to Do the Best You CanOptimization-in-levels vs marginal analysis; budget constraints; apartment-renting as canonical worked example. Choice-and-Consequence sidebar admits people don’t always optimise (p. 46).4Demand, Supply, and EquilibriumMarket demand/supply curves; willingness to pay / accept; equilibrium; price ceilings/floors. COVID stay-at-home gasoline demand and the April 2020 negative oil-price episode are featured.5Consumers and IncentivesBuyer’s problem; budget constraints with two goods; consumer surplus; demand elasticities (price, cross-price, income). Smoking-quits-for-$100 RCT is the empirical anchor. Indifference-curve appendix.6Sellers and IncentivesSeller’s problem; production functions; cost curves; supply curve derivation; producer surplus; short-run vs long-run; firm entry/exit; zero economic profit in long-run competitive equilibrium; Uber-driver entry as worked example.7Perfect Competition and the Invisible HandSocial surplus; Pareto efficiency; deadweight loss; allocation across industries; command-economy comparison (Kmart, FEMA-Walmart-after-Katrina). Important examples / cases

Smoking-quits-for-$100/month RCT (Chapter 5, pp. 99–101) — the Volpp et al. field experiment (paying smokers to quit) used to teach income-effect mechanics. The textbook’s most pedagogically successful integration of behavioral / experimental evidence into core consumer theory.
Negative oil prices, April 2020 (Chapter 4) — “Letting the Data Speak: The Day Oil Became Garbage” (p. 81). Used to teach equilibrium-price formation in genuinely degenerate cases. A 2022-edition novelty.
COVID-19 vaccination externalities (Chapter 9, p. 216) — Choice-and-Consequence sidebar argues a flu shot can have an external effect “as high as 1.5 infections” (p. 216). The empirical hook for positive-externality policy.
FEMA / Walmart / Hurricane Katrina (Chapter 7, p. 171) — Walmart’s just-in-time supply chain reaching disaster zones faster than FEMA, used to argue for the price-coordination mechanism. Pairs with “Command and Control at Kmart” (p. 173) on the costs of central planning.
Uber driver entry in long-run equilibrium (Chapter 6, p. 141) — base-fare increases and driver-entry response. Used to teach long-run zero-profit condition with current platform-economy data.
Akerlof used-car lemons + Spence labor-market signaling (Chapter 16) — the canonical Nobel-Prize-winning information-economics pair, presented as the unifying examples for hidden-characteristics / adverse-selection / signaling.
eBay sniping (Chapter 17) — last-second-bid experiment used to illustrate why bid timing matters even when Revenue Equivalence Theorem says the expected outcome should be invariant to auction format under standard assumptions.
Penalty-kick game theory (Chapter 13, p. 334) — soccer-penalty data used to test mixed-strategy Nash predictions empirically.
Microsoft antitrust case (Chapter 12, p. 316) — the canonical 1998–2001 monopoly / tying case, used to teach price-regulation and antitrust remedies.

Critiques and limitations
The textbook has the characteristic limitations of any market-leading principles text written for a multi-author committee, plus a few specific to its 2022 third-edition vintage:

The integration is real but uneven. Behavioral material is genuinely woven into Chapters 5, 15, 18 — but Chapters 6, 7, 11, 14 retain a fairly traditional rational-actor texture. A student reading sequentially encounters the vocabulary of behavioral economics while still being trained on the machinery of neoclassical optimisation. This may understate how much of standard textbook reasoning the field has revised since Kahneman.
Game theory is integrated but compressed. Chapter 13 covers Nash, dominant strategies, extensive-form games, and backward induction in ~20 pages — adequate for principles but inadequate for any reader who wants to apply game theory to actual policy or strategy work. Compare Mas-Colell-Whinston-Green’s hundreds of game-theory pages.
Mechanism design appears only implicitly. Auction theory (ch. 17) and signaling (ch. 16) are mechanism-design topics but never named as such. A student finishes the textbook without knowing the phrase “mechanism design” or recognising that the Vickrey second-price auction (covered in ch. 17.1, p. 419) was the inaugural Nobel-winning mechanism-design contribution.
Political economy and institutions are exiled to the optional web chapter. Acemoglu’s most-cited research (with Robinson on extractive vs inclusive institutions; on AI-and-labor with Restrepo) is in Web Chapter 3 rather than the main eighteen chapters. The main book treats government as a generic regulator with capacity-and-corruption issues, not as the contested institutional outcome of bargaining among agents — a striking choice given the lead author’s research identity.
Developing-economy material is sparse. Examples are predominantly U.S. (with some U.K., E.U.) — small open economies, informal-sector labor markets, agricultural-economics specifics, and migration are mostly absent or relegated to short examples. A non-U.S. student gets the standard implicit-U.S. reference frame.
The Coase Theorem is presented as a clean result without serious discussion of its zero-transaction-costs assumption (ch. 9.2, p. 218). Real-world Coasean bargaining failures (when should we not expect bargaining to internalise externalities?) are touched but not foregrounded.
No serious treatment of network effects, two-sided markets, platform economics. The 2022 economy is dominated by these phenomena; the textbook handles them only as scattered examples in oligopoly (ch. 14) and externality (ch. 9) chapters, never as a unified topic. A student reading Andrew Chen - The Cold Start Problem would find this a striking gap.
General equilibrium is gestured at but not developed. Chapter 7’s invisible-hand argument is partial-equilibrium plus a hand-wave at allocation across industries (ch. 7.3). The Arrow-Debreu existence machinery isn’t taught (appropriate for principles, but worth flagging for any reader expecting to find it).
Climate, AI, and digital-platform regulation age unevenly. A 2022 textbook can’t anticipate post-ChatGPT antitrust questions or 2024-vintage AI-labor displacement debates that Acemoglu himself has since written extensively about (Acemoglu-Restrepo 2018–2024 papers). Treat the textbook’s current-events examples as 2020–2021 snapshots, not standing analysis.
Single-author voice vs three-author committee. The textbook is editorially polished, but a careful reader can sometimes feel the seams between Acemoglu-style institutional framing, Laibson-style behavioral specificity, and List-style field-experimental hooks. This isn’t a criticism so much as a fact.

Links to other books


Methodological contrast with Bryan Caplan - The Myth of the Rational Voter — Caplan argues voters are systematically irrational because the cost of error is privately near-zero in the political market (rational irrationality). Acemoglu et al document individual-level deviations (present bias, preference reversals, fairness preferences) but still teach median-voter and rational-actor machinery for normative analysis. The contrast is clean: Caplan’s argument should make a careful reader of Acemoglu et al uncomfortable about the textbook’s relatively unproblematised political-economy stance in Web Chapter 3.


Foundational micro for Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited — Stiglitz’s IMF-conditionality critique is built on information-economics arguments (his Nobel work on asymmetric information, ch. 16 in this textbook). Reading the two together: Acemoglu et al supply the formal apparatus (adverse selection, moral hazard, signaling) that Stiglitz uses applied to country-level institutional failures.


Disagreement-by-emphasis with George Soros - The Alchemy of Finance — Soros’s reflexivity argument explicitly attacks the efficient-markets / rational-actor baseline that Acemoglu et al teach. Reading them together is productive: Acemoglu et al is the canonical baseline Soros’s Reflexivity is in dialogue with. Soros would say chapter 4’s clean equilibrium and chapter 7’s clean invisible hand miss the boom-bust feedback loop financial markets actually exhibit.


Methodological complement to Acharya and Lee - The Cartel System of States — Acharya-Lee model international politics as a state-cartel using formal political-economy tools that descend from the IO / oligopoly framework Acemoglu et al teach in chapters 12–14. The “state-cartel” is a Cournot oligopoly with countries as players. Reading both makes the cross-domain reuse of micro-machinery explicit.


Extends to platform economics in Andrew Chen - The Cold Start Problem — Chen’s network-effects framework is implicit in Acemoglu et al’s oligopoly (ch. 14) and externality (ch. 9) chapters but never named as such. Reading them together fills the textbook’s most striking topical gap; Chen’s “atomic network” / “hard side” framework slots naturally onto the textbook’s cost-curve and market-structure machinery.


Applied to capital allocation in Sebastian Mallaby - The Power Law — Mallaby’s venture-capital LP / GP incentive analysis is direct applied-micro using ch. 16’s principal-agent and signaling tools (LP-as-principal, GP-as-agent; track-record-as-signal; carry-as-skin-in-the-game). The textbook gives Mallaby’s vocabulary; Mallaby gives the textbook’s mechanism-design chapter its richest current case study.


Methodological contrast with Gary Goertz and James Mahoney - A Tale of Two Cultures — Acemoglu et al sit firmly in the quantitative-causal-inference tradition Goertz-Mahoney describe (set-theoretic vs probabilistic). Their Evidence-Based Economics features exemplify the quantitative-causal-effect approach. Reading the two together highlights what the principles textbook cannot do: within-case process-tracing of how a specific market or institution actually functions — exactly Goertz-Mahoney’s qualitative complement.


China-applied in Angela Huyue Zhang - High Wire and Meg E. Rithmire - Land Bargains and Chinese Capitalism — Zhang’s dynamic-pyramid framework analyses Chinese tech regulation using IO / antitrust tools (ch. 12, ch. 14) plus information-economics (ch. 16). Rithmire’s land-bargain model is direct applied micro on land markets, property rights, and intergovernmental fiscal incentives. Both books assume the reader is fluent in the Acemoglu et al vocabulary.


Note on Acemoglu’s own other books: Why Nations Fail (Acemoglu-Robinson 2012), The Narrow Corridor (2019), Power and Progress (Acemoglu-Johnson 2023), and Introduction to Modern Economic Growth (the graduate-level companion) are all listed in the About-the-Authors section (p. vi). They are the political economy and growth counterparts to this micro principles text. None are currently in this vault — cross-link to them only after they are ingested.


Open questions

Where should mechanism-design sit in the principles canon? The textbook teaches its tools (auctions, signaling, principal-agent) without naming the field. Should principles students learn the term, or is it appropriately deferred to graduate work?
How much behavioral material should be load-bearing in core macro / micro? Acemoglu et al integrate it; Mankiw foregrounds rational choice; the field has not converged. A 2030-edition will still be answering this.
Will the multi-author committee format survive open-access modular pods? Pearson-Big-Three economics-textbook publishing has high margins and high switching costs; OER alternatives (CORE Econ, OpenStax) compete on price. Whether the integration the textbook accomplishes is replicable in a modular form is a live publishing-economics question.
What is the right relationship between principles micro and the political-economy / institutional-economics tradition Acemoglu personally exemplifies? Web Chapter 3 hints at integration; the main eighteen chapters resist it. A future edition could foreground rather than exile this material.
Should the Coase Theorem still be presented as a clean result? Empirical work on Coasean bargaining (high transaction-cost domains; behavioral deviations from rational bargaining) has accumulated. The textbook’s clean presentation may understate failure modes.

Research uses
This textbook serves five distinct research-prep functions for a reader with my (Yang’s) profile:

Goldman quant-finance interview prep. Chapters 5, 6, 7, 13, 15, 16 cover the micro fundamentals interview material: utility maximisation, cost curves, demand/supply, Nash equilibrium, present/future value, adverse selection. Useful as a structured refresher map; pair with Sebastian Mallaby - The Power Law for applied capital-allocation cases.
Blockchain-regulation research. Chapters 9 (externalities; Coase), 16 (asymmetric information; signaling), and 17 (auction / mechanism design) supply the analytical vocabulary for crypto-market failures (front-running, MEV, rug-pulls), token-distribution mechanism design (Dutch auctions, second-price), and stablecoin regulation (information-asymmetry / moral-hazard interpretations of run risk).
AI-policy analysis. The textbook’s main chapters predate Acemoglu’s recent AI-and-labor work (Acemoglu-Restrepo 2018–2024 papers; Acemoglu-Johnson Power and Progress 2023). Useful as foundation; supplement with Acemoglu’s research papers for the AI-displacement / task-automation modelling that the textbook does not yet contain.
China political-economy modelling. Use ch. 13 game theory and ch. 16 information economics as the formal apparatus; pair with Angela Huyue Zhang - High Wire and Meg E. Rithmire - Land Bargains and Chinese Capitalism for the institutional-economics applications. The textbook gives the toolkit; the China-PE books supply the cases.
Lobbying-network research with In Song Kim. Chapter 14 (oligopoly with differentiated products), Chapter 17 (bargaining), and Chapter 9 (public goods, free rider) supply the formal apparatus for industry-coalition / firm-government bargaining models. Chapter 18’s herding and peer effects translate naturally to political-coalition dynamics.

What I would miss if I only read this note
A textbook is largely diagrams, worked examples, and exercises, not propositions — and this note can replicate none of these. Specifically, I would miss: (a) the cumulative reps from end-of-chapter problems that build automatic reflexes for budget-constraint geometry, marginal-cost reasoning, Nash-equilibrium identification, and present-value calculation — fluency that note-reading alone does not produce; (b) the visual pedagogy of the textbook’s exhibits — the 4×4 game-theory payoff matrices, the indifference-curve / budget-line tangencies, the cost-curve U-shapes, the deadweight-loss triangles — which are how the field actually communicates and which note prose flattens; (c) the Evidence-Based Economics opening-question / closing-answer arc per chapter that grounds abstract concepts in named field-experimental results (the smoking-RCT, the broadband-and-inequality study, the Goldin-Rouse-Bertrand-Mullainathan discrimination work cited in ch. 11); (d) the Letting the Data Speak / Choice & Consequence / Letting the Podcast Speak pedagogical sidebars, which are dozens of distinct mini-cases that don’t get chapter-level summaries but cumulatively train the “stories about markets” muscle that distinguishes economists from adjacent quantitative analysts; (e) the MyLab Economics digital problem-set environment with adaptive-difficulty practice that the print/PDF reader doesn’t have access to but which the textbook’s pedagogy is designed around; (f) the Glossary (pp. 463+) and Index (pp. 473+) entries, which are themselves a curated map of which terms the field considers core; (g) the footnote-and-source-trail to the field-experimental literature that lets a curious reader go from the textbook example to the source paper to the replication / meta-analysis literature; (h) the authorial voice, particularly Laibson’s tendency to slip in retirement-savings examples and List’s tendency to slip in field-experimental “how I designed this” notes — small voice-of-a-practitioner moments that humanise the propositions and that bare summary erases entirely.

01_Books/David-D.-Burns---Feeling-Good.title: Feeling Good — The New Mood Therapy
01_Books/David-D.-Burns---Feeling-Good.content:
David D. Burns - Feeling Good
One-sentence thesis
Depression and most non-bipolar mood pain are maintained (not necessarily originated) by ten nameable cognitive distortions — repeatable bugs in the automatic thoughts that intervene between event and feeling — and a small set of paper-and-pencil disputation drills (the Daily Mood Log, the Triple-Column Technique, the Vertical-Arrow Method, the Antiprocrastination Sheet) reliably reduce the painful feelings these distortions produce; the book operationalizes Aaron Beck’s clinical paradigm into a self-help workflow that randomized trials have shown can match short-course antidepressants and twelve-week cognitive psychotherapy on the BDI and HRSD scales (ch. Introduction; Scogin & Jamison bibliotherapy studies). It is the prerequisite manual before David D. Burns - Feeling Great swaps out symptom-removal framing for resistance-and-empathy framing.
Why this book matters
This is the single most circulated cognitive-behavioral self-help book of the late twentieth century — Scogin and colleagues at Alabama (1990, 1995, 1997) showed in randomized trials that bibliotherapy with this volume alone produces depression-score drops comparable to professional CBT and to antidepressant medication, with a three-year non-relapse rate above 70% (introduction, revised edition). For interdisciplinary readers it does three things no other vault book does: (1) it gives a portable taxonomy of reasoning errors — all-or-nothing, overgeneralization, mental filter, disqualifying the positive, mind-reading, fortune-telling, magnification/minimization, emotional reasoning, should-statements, labeling, personalization — that translates into other rationality literatures including Bryan Caplan - The Myth of the Rational Voter (where the same errors appear as voter “rational irrationality”) and the bias literature inside Daniel C. Dennett - Brainstorms; (2) it provides the clinical proof case that treating beliefs can move both behavior and brain metabolism (Baxter et al. UCLA PET-scan replication on OCD, ch. 18), which is the empirical bridge between cognitive science and clinical psychiatry; (3) it pairs structurally with Pete Walker - Complex PTSD as the “first manual to try” when origin is appraisal-driven, before pivoting to trauma-stabilization framing when distortion-naming feels like blame. Historically, it matters as the proof that manualized introspection scales — that printed exercises can deliver clinically meaningful mood improvement without a therapist in the room — a precedent for every later structured-journaling app and self-help SaaS.
Core argument
Burns argues, against both psychoanalytic (“internalized anger”) and pure-biochemical (“serotonin deficit”) accounts of depression, that the proximate cause of every painful feeling is an antecedent thought, and that most of those antecedent thoughts are systematically distorted. The argument has six steps:


Cognitive primacy (ch. 1, 3). Between any external event E and any felt mood M, there interposes a cognition C — a perception, an interpretation, a self-statement — without which the mood does not arise. Burns illustrates this with the radio-tuning metaphor: the signal is not blown out, the dial is mistuned. Same event, different C, different M. This is empirically what cognitive therapists demonstrate session-by-session: when a patient reframes C, M shifts within minutes, not months.


Negative thoughts are usually distorted, not realistic. When a mood is depressed, the cognition C is almost never a calibrated read of E; it is filtered through one or more of the ten distortions. Burns is firm: this is not “positive thinking.” Realistic thoughts that happen to be negative produce sadness; distorted thoughts produce depression. The distinction is empirical (ch. 3 list; ch. 9 sadness vs. depression).


The distortions form a closed taxonomy with operational tests. All-or-nothing thinking is the dichotomization test (“would I describe a partly clean floor as ‘dirty’?”). Overgeneralization is the one-instance-becomes-rule test (the Svengali metaphor: every card turns into the Jack of Spades). Mental filter is the exclusively-negative-attention test (“did I miss the 83/100 because I focused on the 17?”). Mind-reading and fortune-telling are unjustified inference tests. Emotional reasoning is the feeling-as-evidence test (“I feel guilty therefore I must be guilty”). Should-statements are the self-imposed obligation test that produces guilt and resentment (Ellis’s “musturbation”). The list is finite, named, and testable.


Disputation by writing beats disputation by thinking. The treatment payload is the Daily Mood Log (or Triple-Column Technique): in column 1 record the automatic thought verbatim; in column 2 label which distortion(s) it instantiates; in column 3 write a believable rational response that you would defend in court. Writing matters because depressed cognition is too fast and too biased to dispute in real time. The vertical-arrow method (ch. 10) extends this: ask “if that were true, why would it upset me?” recursively until the silent assumption under the surface thought surfaces — usually a worth-equation like “my value equals my approval rating” or “my worth equals my achievements.”


Behavior is also a belief test. The Antiprocrastination Sheet (ch. 5) treats activities as behavioral experiments: predicted satisfaction vs. actual satisfaction, predicted difficulty vs. actual difficulty. Depressed predictions are systematically wrong in the pessimistic direction; running the experiment forces a calibration update. This is why Burns rejects the “lazy / passive-aggressive / self-rewarded” theories of do-nothingism (ch. 5): the patient lacks not motive but a corrected predictive model.


Outcome data legitimize bibliotherapy. Scogin/Jamison/Floyd/Smith (1990–97) ran the Immediate vs. Delayed Bibliotherapy trial with eighty patients meeting DSM major-depressive criteria. After four weeks, 70% of the Immediate group no longer met criteria; only 3% of the Delayed group recovered. After both groups read the book, 75% and 73% respectively had remitted, and at three-year follow-up roughly 70% remained off treatment with mean BDI below 10 (introduction, ch. Introduction notes). Baxter et al.’s PET-scan study (ch. 18) further showed that successful CBT and successful antidepressant treatment of OCD produced similar reductions in right-caudate metabolic activity — first evidence that talking therapy and pills can converge at the level of brain physiology.


The conclusion: depression is a maintenance disorder of belief that responds, often within weeks, to disciplined writing exercises that convert distorted automatic thoughts into balanced rational responses, supplemented by behavioral experiments. Severity matters — severe or suicidal cases need clinical oversight (ch. 2 BDC scoring rules; ch. 15 suicidal triage) — but the active ingredient is portable.
Argument map
Event ──> automatic thought ──> distortion(s) ──> mood plunge
                  │                                   │
                  ▼                                   ▼
         Daily Mood Log              behavior change ──> contradicting evidence
                  │                                   │
                  ▼                                   │
        balanced rational response <──────────────────┘
                  │
                  ▼
        vertical-arrow ──> silent assumption ──> worth-equation revision
                  │
                  ▼
              relapse prevention

The two operative loops are: (a) the inner loop (catch thought → label distortion → write rebuttal → mood relief, minutes-to-hours), and (b) the outer loop (vertical-arrow on chronic patterns → expose silent assumption → re-engineer worth-equation, weeks-to-months). The book’s effectiveness depends on running the inner loop frequently enough that the outer loop has data.
Key concepts

Cognitive Distortion — Burns’s namesake taxonomy of ten reasoning errors; the most portable export of the book and the fulcrum on which all the worksheets pivot.
Critical Rationalism — Burns’s disputation method is functionally Popperian: treat the automatic thought as a conjecture and try hard to refute it on paper rather than defend or believe it.
Falsifiability — the Triple-Column Technique requires that a rational response be evidence-bearing and believable, i.e. exposable to refutation by future experience.
Theory of Mind — mind-reading and personalization distortions are failures of calibrated theory-of-mind under depressed load: attributing intentions to others without checking.
Reflexivity — the believe-it-because-it-feels-true loop (emotional reasoning) is the clinical cousin of Soros’s reflexivity: belief alters the belief-formation environment, which then validates the belief.
Experimental Epistemology — behavioral experiments and the Antiprocrastination Sheet treat one’s own beliefs as testable claims, the introspective version of the McCulloch program.

Key arguments created from this book

Emotions are configurations of cognitive control, not rival faculties — Burns’s cognition-creates-mood claim sits inside this argument as the strongest empirical case; depression is the demonstration that mood is parasitic on appraisal.

Best chapters/pages to actually read

Ch. 3 “Understanding Your Moods” (the ten-distortions list) — the densest twenty pages in the book; rewrite each distortion’s defining example in your own nouns or you have not read it. Skip and the rest of the book is just worksheets without diagnostic vocabulary.
Ch. 4 “Start by Building Self-Esteem” — contains the Eric-the-law-student dialogue, the cleanest demonstration of the vertical-arrow technique applied to the worth-equation layer. This is also where Burns articulates why agreeing with the patient’s self-condemnation (the Freud move) is iatrogenic.
Ch. 5 “Do-Nothingism: How to Beat It” — the Lethargy Cycle diagram and the Antiprocrastination Sheet. Read this before anything later because most readers’ first failure mode is “I read the book and didn’t do the exercises”; ch. 5 is the chapter that anticipates that failure mode.
Ch. 7 “Feeling Angry?” — best treatment of should-statements in the book; Albert Ellis’s “musturbation” framing makes the cost of one type of distortion legible.
Ch. 10 “The Cause of It All” (vertical-arrow technique) — the most underrated chapter; the technique generalizes far beyond depression and is a portable interview-yourself protocol for any value-laden upset.
Ch. 14 “Dare to Be Average” — the perfectionism chapter; contains the Antiperfectionism Sheet (recorded satisfaction vs. recorded perfection-rating) which is the cleanest single experiment in the book.
Ch. 15 “The Ultimate Victory” — Holly’s role-played courtroom dialogue is the canonical demonstration of disputation under suicidal load. Read once even if not currently suicidal; it is the protocol you should know in case a friend ever needs it.
Ch. 18 “The Mind-Body Problem” — the Baxter PET-scan replication summary; this is the empirical paragraph to cite when someone says “talking therapy is just placebo.”

Skim the rest at first pass; the ten-distortions chapter and ch. 5 (do-nothingism) are non-negotiable, and budget six to eight weeks of daily logs if you actually want skill change rather than reading-pleasure. Highlighting without writing is the dominant failure mode.
Chapter-by-chapter distillation









































































































































#TitleSummarySourceIntroIntroduction (1999 rev.)Bibliotherapy outcome data: Scogin/Jamison RCT and 3-year follow-up; Baxter PET findings; positions cognitive therapy as DSM-grade treatment, not pop psychology.ch. Introduction1A Breakthrough in the Treatment of Mood DisordersHistory: Beck and Ellis 1950s-60s; Penn comparative trial of CBT vs. Tofranil; CBT matches or beats imipramine on twelve-week outcome.ch. 12How to Diagnose Your MoodsBurns Depression Checklist (BDC), 25 items 0–4; ranges 0–5 normal, 6–10 normal-but-unhappy, 11–25 mild, 26–50 moderate, 51–75 severe, 76–100 extreme; items 23–25 screen suicidal urges.ch. 23Understanding Your MoodsThe ten distortions chapter. Every later technique presupposes this taxonomy.ch. 34Start by Building Self-EsteemEric dialogue; vertical-arrow precursor; demolition of the Freudian “patient is right about being worthless” stance.ch. 45Do-NothingismLethargy Cycle; Antiprocrastination Sheet; rejection of the lazy/payoff/passive-aggressive theories.ch. 56Verbal JudoTalking back to criticism without escalation.ch. 67Feeling Angry?Irritability Quotient inventory; cognitive theory of anger; should-statement deconstruction.ch. 78Ways of Defeating GuiltGuilt-versus-remorse distinction; should-statement role.ch. 89Sadness Is Not DepressionDistinction between realistic-and-painful (sadness) and distorted-and-painful (depression).ch. 910The Cause of It AllVertical-arrow (downward-arrow) technique to expose silent assumptions.ch. 1011The Approval AddictionWorth-equation: approval as worth; cognitive deconstruction.ch. 1112The Love AddictionWorth-equation: love as worth.ch. 1213Your Work Is Not Your WorthWorth-equation: achievement as worth.ch. 1314Dare to Be AverageAntiperfectionism Sheet; perfection vs. satisfaction empirical decoupling; jogging anecdote.ch. 1415The Ultimate VictorySuicidal triage protocol; Holly courtroom role-play; hopelessness as symptom not fact.ch. 1516How I Practice What I PreachBurns’s own use of the techniques.ch. 1617The Search for “Black Bile”History of biological theories of depression.ch. 1718The Mind-Body ProblemBaxter PET-scan study; convergence of CBT and SSRI brain effects; integrated model.ch. 1819Antidepressant DrugsPharmacology survey for the lay reader.ch. 1920Consumer’s Guide to AntidepressantsPractical guidance on starting, titrating, switching.ch. 20
Important examples / cases

Eric, the law student (ch. 4) — vertical-arrow worked end-to-end: “if I make a fool of myself … then I’d be worthless”; reveals the silent assumption that approval is worth.
Patient A, the woman who feels better doing anything but worse lying in bed (ch. 5) — the cleanest empirical demonstration that activity, even trivial activity, beats do-nothingism on mood.
Patient B, the physician who threatens suicide if pushed to do homework (ch. 5) — the case that anchors the resistance is informational lesson Burns later expands into David D. Burns - Feeling Great.
The salesman with bird dung on his window (ch. 3) — the canonical overgeneralization example: a single event becomes a lifetime rule (“the birds always crap on me”).
The college student with 83/100 who concludes she will flunk out (ch. 3) — the canonical mental filter example.
The hospitalized woman who disqualifies all evidence of being liked (ch. 3) — the most extreme disqualifying-the-positive case in the book; instructive because it shows how the distortion can survive overwhelming counter-evidence.
The compulsive-slowness lawyer who shaves his head over hairline-perfectionism (ch. 14) — the upper limit of perfectionism-driven dysfunction; argues that perfectionism is fear-driven, not standards-driven.
Holly’s courtroom role-play (ch. 15) — Burns plays defense attorney to her self-prosecution; the protocol is “make the prosecutor argue the case against you so the absurdity of the indictment becomes visible.”

Critiques and limitations
The book has at least seven legitimate critiques. First, the self-help format provides no individualized risk triage; severe, psychotic, suicidal, or bipolar presentations need clinical oversight, and Burns says so but burying the warning inside ch. 2 means readers in crisis may not reach it. Second, the cultural framing is Western-individualist: somatic, communal, and spiritual idioms of distress (which dominate non-WEIRD populations) are thinly covered, and corporate-wellness deployments often strip the ethics layer leaving a blame-the-victim residue (corporate posters listing “your distortions” without therapist support). Third, the ten categories overlap — mind-reading often is overgeneralization; magnification often is mental filter — and clinicians and students reasonably argue the taxonomy is brittle. Fourth, the trauma-first critique (compatible with Pete Walker - Complex PTSD) is real: when origin is C-PTSD, naming distortions before stabilizing the nervous system can reinforce the I’m-defective loop the survivor entered therapy with. Fifth, Burns’s optimism about self-directed change underplays structural constraints — housing instability, abusive partners, racialized labor markets — which alter the feasibility curve of “just do the worksheets.” Sixth, the book predates the third-wave acceptance-and-commitment-therapy literature (Hayes, Linehan); some of what Burns calls “balanced thoughts” Hayes would call defusion-via-disputation, and ACT data suggest acceptance can succeed where disputation stalls. Seventh, by 2026 the bibliotherapy outcome data are old: Scogin’s eighty-patient samples were small, heterogeneous depression cohorts, and replication outside Alabama/Tuskegee remains thin; the headline “as good as drugs” claim should be re-stated as “in two small RCTs, comparable to short-course treatment in mild-to-moderate depression.”
A subtler limit: Burns’s case selection is biased toward eventual success. The reader sees Eric, Holly, the law student, the perfectionist physician — patients who responded. Treatment-resistant cases are mentioned but not foregrounded. The honest base rate of “tried the book, didn’t help” is invisible. David D. Burns - Feeling Great partially addresses this by foregrounding resistance as the next-layer object of treatment.
Links to other books

Direct sequel / methodological refinement — David D. Burns - Feeling Great: same paradigm, but symptom-removal framing replaced by positive-reframing-of-resistance framing; Burns retracts the assumption that all distortions should be disputed and adds an empathy-and-paradox layer.
Trauma-informed contrast — Pete Walker - Complex PTSD: agreement that thoughts amplify suffering, disagreement that thought-disputation is the right first move when origin is repeated childhood trauma. Walker’s stabilization-before-cognition sequencing is the explicit complement to Burns’s “start with the log.”
Cognitive-theory parent — Daniel C. Dennett - Brainstorms: shared concept of the mind as a system of belief-fixation modules; Burns is the clinical instantiation of Dennett’s general thesis that mood and reasoning are coupled.
Rational-irrationality cousin — Bryan Caplan - The Myth of the Rational Voter: same family of reasoning errors (especially mental filter, emotional reasoning, overgeneralization) appears in voter cognition; Caplan and Burns disagree on whether the errors are cheap to correct (Burns: yes, with worksheets; Caplan: no, voters lack the skin-in-the-game).
Common-knowledge contrast — Steven Pinker - When Everyone Knows That Everyone Knows: Pinker formalizes how social inference can rationally cascade; Burns’s mind-reading distortion is what happens when the same inference machinery runs without common knowledge — the depressed reader infers others’ contempt without check.
Methodological alignment — Karl Popper - The Logic of Scientific Discovery: Burns’s Triple-Column Technique is operationally Popperian — write the conjecture (automatic thought), specify what would refute it (rational response with evidence), prefer the better-corroborated alternative; the discipline is try to refute, not try to defend.
Multi-agent metaphor mirror — Marvin Minsky - The Society of Mind: distortions read as buggy critic-agents inside the mind; the worksheet is debugging-by-introspection.
Contemplative-pacing contrast — Thich Nhat Hanh - Peace Is Every Step: shared diagnosis (suffering is mediated by mind), divergent prescription (mindful noticing without disputation vs. structured cognitive debate). Useful when readers find Burns’s disputation aggressive.

Open questions

When does thought-recording become rumination? Daily Mood Log discipline can mutate into obsessive distortion-spotting; the book offers no stop-rule. Recent work on rumination (Susan Nolen-Hoeksema) suggests this is a real risk.
Can the worksheets be translated outside Anglophone psychology? “Should-statements” and “personalization” rest on linguistic structures that do not translate cleanly into Mandarin, Japanese, or Bantu-language idioms of distress; cross-cultural validation remains thin.
What is the active ingredient of bibliotherapy — the content, the writing-discipline, or just the externalization? Scogin’s RCT cannot dissociate them. If externalization is the active ingredient, any well-designed self-help workbook should match.
Where does CBT interface ethically with disability and toxic-positivity critiques? Burns insists balanced thoughts must be believable, not denial — but corporate adopters routinely flatten the distinction.
How should clinicians sequence medication titration with thought-records? Burns is permissive but unspecific; subsequent Beck-tradition work has tried to formalize this and remains unsettled.
At what level of depression severity does bibliotherapy alone become unethical? Scogin enrolled DSM major-depressive cases up to BDI ~30; behavior in the BDI 50+ range is undocumented.

Research uses
For an interdisciplinary research user, the book serves five distinct purposes. (1) Therapist training and chatbot prototyping: the worksheet structure is small enough to encode as an LLM-mediated dialogue; the open question is whether prompt-engineered disputation matches written disputation, since externalization-on-paper may be the actual mechanism. (2) Teaching applied epistemology: the ten distortions are an excellent introductory rationality curriculum because every category has a one-paragraph clinical example; pairing them with Bryan Caplan - The Myth of the Rational Voter’s rational-irrationality framing converts the list from self-help into political-economy pedagogy. (3) Medical residency: quick distortion-naming gives anxious-patient clinicians a humane bridge between informal counseling and full psychotherapy referral, especially in primary care where session length is fifteen minutes. (4) Quantitative lifelogging research: Daily Mood Logs are structured enough to feed into mood-volatility predictors, and a small literature has studied this; instrument designers should cite responsibly and document lay-adaptation drift. (5) Philosophy of psychiatry: Burns gives the cleanest clinical case study for the Dennett-style claim that mental states are functional rather than substance-defined — the same neurochemistry produces different moods conditional on appraisal, which is a working laboratory for the Brainstorms thesis. Occupational health psychologists adapting brief interventions for shift workers have remixed distortion vocabulary into ninety-second huddles; efficacy varies but the structure provides scaffolding inside chronically understaffed wards. High-school counselors selectively excerpt the taxonomy to normalize anxious cognition during exams without pathologizing ordinary stress. The unifying methodological note: every research adaptation must preserve the escalation pathway — bibliotherapy is not a substitute for clinical contact when suicidality, psychosis, or mania appear.
What I would miss if I only read this note
I would miss worksheet granularity — the printed checkbox prompts that force specificity at a level summaries skip. I would miss the tonal gentleness — Burns’s mid-paragraph dad-jokes that lower shame spikes during a miserable read; without that texture, the worksheets become another perfectionism arena. I would miss the gradual skill ramp the chapters embed — early wins (cleaning a desk; baking a pie) precede harder exposures (calling the friend who didn’t return your call), and the sequencing matters because behavioral confidence is the prerequisite for cognitive confidence. I would miss the embodied realization that balanced thoughts sound boring yet soothe physiology: in summary form, “I made a mistake but I’m not a failure” reads bland; in a depressed reader’s actual handwriting at 11 p.m. it lowers heart rate. I would miss the permission slips Burns embeds casually — explicit lowering of performance standards during recovery without a shame spiral — which are easy to mistranslate into hustle-culture optimism. I would miss the layout pleasures — the cartoons, the Burns Depression Checklist’s visual format, the Antiperfectionism Sheet’s column ruling — which the plaintext vault cannot mirror. I would miss the rolling repetition — the ten distortions reappear in every later chapter applied to a different domain (anger, guilt, perfectionism, suicidality), and that repetition is what installs the taxonomy as automatic vocabulary; reading them once in a summary leaves them inert. Above all, I would miss the discipline of writing the log — the act, not the description of the act, is the treatment; a note about CBT does not treat depression any more than a recipe feeds a hungry person.

01_Books/David-D.-Burns---Feeling-Great.title: Feeling Great — The Revolutionary New Treatment for Depression and Anxiety
01_Books/David-D.-Burns---Feeling-Great.content:
David D. Burns - Feeling Great
One-sentence thesis
Burns’s 2020 sequel reframes the 35% of David D. Burns - Feeling Good readers who didn’t recover as victims of an under-theorized force—resistance, properly understood as the patient’s own loyalty to what depression/anxiety/addiction silently buys them—and packages forty years of clinic correction into TEAM-CBT (Testing, Empathy, Assessment-of-resistance, Methods), a phased protocol that treats positive reframing of the symptom’s function as the precondition without which classical Cognitive Distortion dispute slides off the patient like rain off glass.
Why this book matters
Readers plateauing on classic thought records discover plausible reasons: unconscious loyalty to depression-as-shield, anxiety-as-alert-system, anger-as-boundary-enforcer, addiction-as-greatest-pleasure. Naming resistance as intelligence rather than character flaw restores dignity often stripped when clinicians imply failures of effort. The TEAM frame parallels relational ethics highlighted in Alain de Botton - The Course of Love (skills precede vibes) and trauma honoring in Pete Walker - Complex PTSD (safety precedes confrontation). For researchers studying psychotherapy adherence, Burns reframes dropout as misaligned alliance rather than patient laziness — a measurable shift since session-by-session symptom tracking falsifies clinician intuition cheaply. Burns’s claim that the 35% non-responder rate is largely an agenda-setting problem rather than a technique problem is empirically testable and aligns the book with Karl Popper - The Logic of Scientific Discovery’s spirit even where its statistical reporting falls short of academic norms. Primary care physicians receiving brief therapy cross-training might grasp why homework non-compliance signals empathic misses earlier — not motivational deficits — possibly altering referral conversations compassionately.
Core argument
Burns’s central diagnostic claim is that the 35% of Feeling Good readers and the bulk of long-term therapy stuck-cases share a common architecture: they have mixed feelings about recovery itself, and traditional CBT skips straight to method without making those mixed feelings conscious. The book operationalizes this in five stacked moves:

Distinguish outcome resistance from process resistance. Outcome resistance = “I’m not sure I want recovery”; process resistance = “I want recovery but won’t pay the price (homework, exposure, dropping the blame frame).” Burns’s “resistance table” cross-tabs these against four targets — depression, anxiety, relationship problems, habits/addictions — yielding eight distinct stuck patterns each with named entry points (ch. 3). This typology is the book’s most portable contribution.
Test every session, both ends. Burns’s brief mood/anxiety/anger/relationship/temptation/happiness scales (ch. 1, 28) sit between symptom checklists and full DSM diagnostics. Their function is falsifying therapist self-flattery: the chart, not the narrative, decides whether last week’s “great session” actually moved the symptoms. This is mid-Popperian falsificationism with a clipboard, and it explicitly separates Burns from charisma-driven schools.
Empathy without rescue. The E in TEAM is not “warm rapport” but a disciplined refusal to help during the listening phase. The therapist asks the patient to grade the empathy itself (“How accurate did I get your inner world?”) before any intervention. Burns reports that premature reassurance is the modal therapist failure and that patients can usually name it on a 0–5 scale.
Positive reframing of the symptom. Before disputing distortions, ask: what does this depression say about you that is awesome? Biyu’s depression at Harvard reveals high standards, family loyalty, integrity (ch. 3); Maria’s postpartum despair reflects fierce maternal commitment (ch. 2). Naming these protective functions melts the patient’s secret loyalty to the symptom. Only then does method-phase Socratic dispute land.
Methods as a deep, not wide, toolkit. Burns retains the ten-distortion taxonomy of David D. Burns - Feeling Good (chs. 12–22) — all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization, mental filtering, discounting the positive, jumping to conclusions (mind-reading and fortune-telling), magnification/minimization, emotional reasoning, should statements, labeling, self/other-blame — but argues their effectiveness is bounded by phases 1–4. The “double-standard technique” (would you say this to a beloved friend?) and the externalization-of-voices method appear as canonical examples (intro; ch. 22).

The closing Four Great Deaths of the Self chapters (chs. 23–27) extrapolate philosophically: depression recovery is the death of the inferior self; anger recovery the death of the superior self; addiction recovery the death of the self that needs the substance; anxiety recovery the death of the self that needs guarantees. This is Burns’s most explicit borrow from contemplative traditions and is where the book intersects Thich Nhat Hanh - Peace Is Every Step and (more loosely) Buddhist no-self doctrine, though Burns frames it pragmatically rather than metaphysically. The measurement emphasis quietly fights therapist grandiosity: symptom graphs humble charismatic interpretations when narratives seduce oversimplification. Cases illustrate abrupt breakthroughs after reframes land emotionally not logically, with Burns documenting workshop pedagogy showing therapists their own blind spots — intellectual grasp minus embodied empathy fails cases previously labeled resistant.
Argument map
The book reasons in a single forty-year arc: the Feeling Good bibliotherapy trials worked for roughly two thirds of moderately depressed readers within four weeks, leaving a stubborn third whose stuckness Burns spent decades trying to model. The dream-table episode (ch. 3) crystallized resistance into an eight-cell typology cross-tabbing outcome resistance versus process resistance against the four targets depression, anxiety, relationship problems, and habits/addictions. The TEAM protocol then enforces a sequential pipeline whose ordering is load-bearing: Testing falsifies therapist intuition session-by-session; Empathy is graded by the patient (0–5) rather than self-assessed by the therapist; Assessment of resistance surfaces protective symptom benefits via tools like the magic-button test and positive reframing; only afterward do classical CBT Methods dispute the inherited ten-distortion list. The pipeline closes with the Four Great Deaths of the self chapters, which generalize the resistance frame philosophically: each recovery is the death of an attachment to a self-image (inferior self, superior self, substance-needing self, certainty-needing self).
Feeling Good 4-week recovery rate ≈ 65%
        │
        ▼
Why does the other 35% fail?  ← Burns's working puzzle, 1980-2020
        │
        ▼
Hypothesis: resistance is real but mis-modeled
        │
        ▼
T  Testing  ─────► falsify therapist intuition session-by-session
E  Empathy  ─────► graded by patient, not therapist
A  Assessment of Resistance ─────► outcome × process × four targets
M  Methods (CBT classics) ─────► only after A unblocks
        │
        ▼
"Sudden change" cases (5-min to multi-session)
        │
        ▼
Four Great Deaths of Self  → depression / anger / anxiety / addiction

Premature methods stage yields pseudo-compliance — the dominant failure mode the sequel was written to fix. Burns’s argument is that the order T→E→A→M is not negotiable: any therapist who skips A in the name of efficiency converges on the Feeling Good 35% non-responder rate by construction.
Key concepts

TEAM-CBT — phased alliance-aware protocol; Testing→Empathy→Assessment-of-resistance→Methods (intro, ch. 2).
Outcome vs process resistance — eight-cell typology across four targets (ch. 3).
Positive reframing — validating symptom survival logic before dispute (chs. 3–9, 22).
Magic button test — would you press a button that erased the symptom instantly? (ch. 3) — surfaces hidden objections.
Acceptance paradox — reduced struggle intensity paradoxically lowers impairment (chs. 23–27).
Externalization of voices — having the patient verbally embody the negative thought so the therapist can dispute the role, not the person (chs. 4–9).

Chapter-by-chapter distillation























































SectionChaptersFocusFront-matterIntro, 1, 2TEAM origin story; baseline scales; CliffsNotes synthesisI. Stuckness theory3Resistance table; outcome × process × four targetsI. Live cases4–9Karen, Melanie, Mark, Marilyn (stage-4 lung cancer), Sara (germ phobia) — full session arcsI. Method bridge10–11Daily Mood Journal (“Daily MoJo”); structured escape planII. Crush distortions12–22One distortion per chapter, each followed by exercisesIII. Four Great Deaths23–27Inferior self, superior self, “let’s be specific” flaw audit, Grateful-Dead acceptanceIV. Relapse prevention28–29Re-test scales; build a relapse plan before relapseV. Research update30–31Mark Noble’s neuroplasticity bridge; etiology speculationVI. Resources32–33Free tools; “Fifty Ways to Untwist Your Thinking” (master technique list)
Annotate margins noting which TEAM letter dominates each paragraph when studying — students surprised by uneven emphasis discover prior holistic-gloss readings remained superficial. Mark Noble’s chapter (30) is the only neuroscience chapter and is explicitly speculative; treat it as analogy rather than evidence.
Important examples / cases
Burns’s verbatim transcripts matter pedagogically — students see pauses, laughter, therapist missteps corrected — unlike polished textbook monologues. The Frank-the-carpenter vignette in the introduction (Burns runs the “double-standard technique” on a depressed contractor in five minutes at the front door) is the book’s compressed thesis. Biyu (Harvard freshman, ch. 3) demonstrates the magic-button refusal pattern that exposes outcome resistance. Nadine (the suicidal physician whose brother died, ch. 22) shows Socratic dismantling of self-blame across five sessions.
