synergy decomposition; cash vs stock payment; takeover defenses; Grossman-Hart 1980 free-rider problem.29Corporate GovernanceAgency conflicts; board structure; equity-based compensation; SOX 2002 / Dodd-Frank 2010; international governance variation.30Risk ManagementWhen hedging adds value (distress, tax convexity, internal-funds preservation); insurance pricing; futures / options / swaps; Metallgesellschaft case.31International Corporate FinanceForeign-currency vs domestic-currency NPV equivalence; covered interest parity F = S(1+r_d)/(1+r_f); segmented vs integrated markets; country risk.
Important examples / cases

HomeNet running example (Chs. 8, 18, 19) — fictitious Cisco home-networking project used to teach FCF construction, NPV with leverage, and end-to-end DCF modelling. The textbook’s most extended applied example.
Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Tesla beta data (Ch. 10, Table 10.6) — 2017–2022 betas computed from weekly returns; Walmart 0.41, Coca-Cola 0.83, Microsoft 0.93, Apple 1.06, AMD / Tesla / Avis substantially above 1. The empirical anchor for the systematic-risk discussion.
Anheuser-Busch / InBev acquisition (Ch. 28 opening) — 2008 $70-per-share-cash deal used to motivate M&A valuation mechanics.
Ideko target case study (Ch. 19) — full PE-buyout-style DCF, including beta unlever / relever, terminal-value handling, exit-multiple sensitivity, equity-IRR computation. The chapter mimics the work product of a private-equity associate.
Argentina 2001 sovereign default (Ch. 6) — used to teach the gap between yield-to-maturity and expected return when default probability is non-zero.
Walmart vs Hormel beta contrast (Ch. 10) — non-cyclical packaged-food beta 0.16 vs Walmart superstore 0.41; teaches that beta reflects business-cycle sensitivity.
Myron Scholes interview (Ch. 21) — Scholes’ own retrospective on the Black-Scholes derivation, the journal-rejection history, and the 2007–2009-crisis criticism. Pairs naturally with Roger Lowenstein - When Genius Failed as the LTCM-failure case study.
Google 2004 Dutch-auction IPO (Ch. 23) — used to contrast book-building vs auction IPO mechanisms and to discuss whether ≈15% first-day-underpricing can be reduced by mechanism design.
Sarbanes-Oxley 2002 / Dodd-Frank 2010 regulatory case (Ch. 29) — used to teach how governance rules become costly responses to scandal-revealed agency-cost realisations.

Critiques and limitations
The textbook has the characteristic limitations of any market-leading MBA-grade corporate-finance textbook in its 6th edition (2023 vintage), plus a few specific to its theory-first authorial perspective:

CAPM is taught as if it were correct, then the problems are flagged in Ch. 13. A student reading sequentially internalises CAPM-as-the-discount-rate before being told it has known empirical failures (size, value, momentum, post-earnings-announcement drift). The Ch. 13 caveats do not affect Chs. 12, 18, 19, 22 calculations, which all silently assume CAPM. A more honest pedagogy might foreground multifactor models earlier; the textbook’s choice tracks practitioner reality (CAPM is still what most CFOs use) but understates the empirical case for alternatives.
Behavioral finance is appendix-like. Ch. 13’s behavioral content — disposition effect, overconfidence, herding, limits to arbitrage — is presented as exception material, not as theory. A student who reads only Chs. 1–12 and 14–22 finishes the book without much exposure to the post-1990s behavioral revolution. Compare Daron Acemoglu - Microeconomics’s deeper integration of behavioral material.
Black-Scholes is taught with constant-volatility / no-jump / lognormal-returns assumptions barely flagged. Ch. 21 mentions these are simplifications but does not develop volatility smiles, stochastic volatility (Heston), jump diffusion (Merton 1976), or local-volatility models — all of which are in active practitioner use post-1987-crash. The 2007-2009-crisis Scholes-interview gestures at this but the chapter’s worked examples are all constant-vol Black-Scholes. A reader encountering Roger Lowenstein - When Genius Failed’s LTCM case learns why this matters in a way the textbook does not foreground.
Agency theory is compressed and U.S.-specific. Ch. 16’s treatment of agency costs is consistent but does not develop the full Tirole / Holmström-Tirole / Aghion-Bolton machinery, and Ch. 29’s governance examples are predominantly U.S. (with brief gestures at Continental-European stakeholder models, German two-tier boards, Japanese keiretsu). A reader studying Angela Huyue Zhang - High Wire or Meg E. Rithmire - Land Bargains and Chinese Capitalism needs to import most China-specific governance / capital-structure content from elsewhere.
The role of intermediaries is under-developed. Banks, broker-dealers, insurance companies, money-market funds, exchanges, clearing houses — the institutional plumbing that the 2008 GFC stressed — appear only in scattered examples. The book’s frictionless-markets default downplays the welfare-economic significance of intermediation, and the post-GFC literature (Gorton, Adrian, Brunnermeier, Pedersen) is barely cited.
No serious treatment of dynamic security design or contracting. Despite DeMarzo’s research being on dynamic security design, the textbook stays at the static / single-period / two-period level. Readers wanting Tirole’s Theory of Corporate Finance depth must go to a separate graduate text.
Information-economics treatment is shallow relative to its importance. Pecking order (Myers-Majluf) and free-cash-flow problem (Jensen) appear in Ch. 16 but are not rigorously derived; the asymmetric-information apparatus from Daron Acemoglu - Microeconomics Ch. 16 is assumed but not redeveloped. A student finishing the textbook can apply pecking-order intuition but cannot prove it.
Network effects, two-sided markets, and platform-economy capital structures are absent. The 2023 economy is dominated by intangible-heavy, platform-driven firms whose capital-structure logic differs from the textbook’s manufacturing-/retail-vintage examples. A reader of Andrew Chen - The Cold Start Problem would find this striking.
Crypto and digital-asset finance are essentially absent. The 6th edition was published before mainstream adoption of stablecoin, DeFi, and tokenised-asset instruments. A 2030 edition will need a major addition; a reader with interest in blockchain-financial-economics must supplement extensively.
AI / labor / automation interactions with capital-budgeting and capital-structure are absent. The Acemoglu-Restrepo-Johnson 2018-2024 literature on AI and labor displacement is not cited; no Ch. 8 example treats AI capex differently from manufacturing capex; no Ch. 16 example treats high-skill-labor-replacement risk as a distress factor. A student studying Sebastian Mallaby - The Infinity Machine alongside this textbook must impute these connections.
The textbook is U.S.-centric in its tax-code, governance, and currency examples. The Global Edition retrofits non-U.S. case studies but the structural treatment (e.g. Ch. 15’s interest-tax-shield calculations, Ch. 23’s IPO mechanics, Ch. 29’s SOX compliance) remains U.S.-anchored. A non-U.S. CFO must mentally re-translate.
Two-author voice but largely seamless. Unlike a multi-author committee textbook (compare Daron Acemoglu - Microeconomics), Berk-DeMarzo’s joint voice is unified; there is no observable seam between Berk’s asset-pricing-equilibrium framing and DeMarzo’s contracting-and-capital-structure framing. This is editorially admirable but means the reader does not see the disagreements between asset-pricing and corporate-finance theory traditions that exist in the research literature.

Links to other books


Foundational microeconomic prerequisite: Daron Acemoglu - Microeconomics — Acemoglu et al supply the price-theory, mean-variance utility, and information-economics machinery (adverse selection, moral hazard, signalling, principal-agent) that Berk-DeMarzo’s Chs. 11, 13, 16 take as given. Reading them sequentially: Acemoglu Ch. 16 develops adverse selection / signalling / moral hazard rigorously; Berk-DeMarzo Ch. 16 applies the same apparatus to capital-structure choices without re-deriving it. The pairing is the canonical price-theory + corporate-finance diptych in U.S. business-school instruction.


Empirical-philosophy contrast with George Soros - The Alchemy of Finance — Soros’s reflexivity argument explicitly attacks the rational-actor / efficient-markets / no-arbitrage baseline that Berk-DeMarzo treat as foundational. Reading them together is productive: Berk-DeMarzo is the canonical mainstream against which Soros’s Reflexivity is in dialogue. Soros would say that boom-bust feedback loops in capital markets — the kind he profited from — make the textbook’s clean Ch. 14 MM analysis miss the dynamics that actually produce the financial-crisis episodes Ch. 16 / Ch. 23 / Ch. 30 cite as cautionary tales.


LTCM as Black-Scholes-Merton failure case in Roger Lowenstein - When Genius Failed — Lowenstein’s narrative of Long-Term Capital Management’s 1998 collapse is the single most important real-world case study of the Ch. 21 framework breaking under stress (LTCM’s principals included Robert Merton and Myron Scholes themselves). The Berk-DeMarzo textbook teaches Black-Scholes as a clean replication argument; Lowenstein documents the constant-volatility / no-jump / liquidity-frictionless assumptions failing simultaneously in August-September 1998. Read together, the pair gives both the formal apparatus and the cautionary case.


Venture-capital / private-equity application in Sebastian Mallaby - The Power Law — Mallaby’s history of venture capital is direct applied corporate finance using Ch. 16’s principal-agent and signalling tools (LP-as-principal, GP-as-agent; track-record-as-signal; carry-as-skin-in-the-game), Ch. 21’s option machinery (VC investments are call options on follow-on rounds), and Ch. 23’s IPO mechanics (the exit channel for VC-backed firms). Berk-DeMarzo gives Mallaby’s vocabulary; Mallaby gives Berk-DeMarzo’s institutional-finance chapters their richest current case studies.


Chip-industry capital-budgeting / capex application in Chris Miller - Chip War — Miller’s history of the semiconductor industry is a sustained applied case for the textbook’s capital-budgeting (Ch. 8), real-options (Ch. 22), and risk-management (Ch. 30) machinery: TSMC’s fab-construction decisions are real-options problems with timing flexibility; foundry-vs-IDM strategic choices are corporate-structure questions; export-control geopolitical risk is a Ch. 30 / Ch. 31 cross-currency / country-risk problem. The textbook gives the toolkit; Miller gives the running case.


Information-economics application in Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited — Stiglitz’s IMF-conditionality critique builds on his Nobel-winning information-economics work, the same apparatus that underlies Berk-DeMarzo Ch. 16. Reading the two together: Berk-DeMarzo supplies the formal tools (asymmetric information, adverse selection, moral hazard); Stiglitz applies them at country-level institutional scale (capital-account-liberalisation as adverse-selection trap; conditionality as principal-agent contracting failure).


Methodological complement in Abhijit V. Banerjee - Poor Economics — Banerjee and Duflo’s RCT-driven development-economics methodology is the empirical counterpart to Berk-DeMarzo’s theory-driven corporate-finance methodology. Both belong to the post-1990s social-science empirical-revolution but operate in different domains. Reading both helps a researcher see what RCT-style identification would look like applied to corporate-finance questions (microfinance loan structure, capital-structure-experiment in small firms) — work that Banerjee and his Poverty Action Lab collaborators have actually done.


Capital-structure / capex applied to platforms in Andrew Chen - The Cold Start Problem — Chen’s network-effects framework is implicit in Berk-DeMarzo’s discussions of platform IPO timing (Ch. 23) and risk-management for two-sided-market firms (Ch. 30) but never named as such. Reading both fills the textbook’s most striking topical gap; Chen’s “atomic network” / “hard side” framework slots onto Ch. 8 capex-decision frameworks in a way that distinguishes platform-firm capital-budgeting from manufacturing-firm capital-budgeting.


Note on companion / related textbooks not currently in this vault: Brealey-Myers-Allen Principles of Corporate Finance (12e), Ross-Westerfield-Jaffe Corporate Finance (13e), Tirole The Theory of Corporate Finance (graduate-level theoretical companion), Cochrane Asset Pricing (graduate asset-pricing companion), Hull Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives (graduate derivatives companion), Damodaran Investment Valuation (practitioner-focused companion), and Berk-DeMarzo’s own Fundamentals of Corporate Finance (the lighter undergraduate twin). Cross-link to them only after they are ingested.


Open questions

Is no-arbitrage really the right organising principle for corporate finance, or is it a Berk-DeMarzo authorial idiosyncrasy? Brealey-Myers-Allen organise around NPV-then-CAPM-then-MM as separable modules; Berk-DeMarzo’s chain is more elegant but more rigid. Whether this difference matters pedagogically (vs cosmetically) is an open question.
How should a 2030 edition incorporate stochastic volatility, jumps, and crypto-asset pricing? The 6th edition’s Black-Scholes treatment is constant-vol; future editions need to either acknowledge the empirical failures in body text or add a chapter on volatility-smile pricing.
Does the WACC / APV / FTE equivalence hold under more exotic leverage policies? The textbook’s equivalence proof assumes either (i) constant target leverage (WACC) or (ii) predetermined debt schedule (APV) or (iii) flow-to-equity discounting at r_E (FTE). Real-world dynamic capital-structure policies (Hennessy-Whited, DeMarzo-Sannikov dynamic-trade-off) require modifications.
Should the textbook foreground the limits-to-arbitrage literature (Shleifer-Vishny, Gromb-Vayanos, Brunnermeier-Pedersen)? Currently this material is squeezed into Ch. 13 caveats. Given that the entire textbook builds on no-arbitrage, the failure of arbitrage in stress periods deserves more than a footnote.
What is the right relationship between corporate finance and labor economics, AI economics, and climate economics? Acemoglu’s recent research argues these are deeply linked; Berk-DeMarzo treat them as exogenous. A future edition could integrate; current edition does not.

Research uses
This textbook serves five distinct research-prep functions for a reader with my (Yang’s) profile:


Quant-finance / investment-banking interview prep. Chs. 3, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 21 cover the corporate-finance fundamentals that appear in interview question banks: NPV / IRR mechanics, DCF construction, CAPM beta and cost of capital, MM propositions, WACC / APV / FTE distinctions, Black-Scholes inputs and Greeks. Useful as a structured interview-prep map; pair with Sebastian Mallaby - The Power Law for VC-style case studies and Roger Lowenstein - When Genius Failed for derivatives-failure cases.


Blockchain-economics and regulatory research. Ch. 14’s MM machinery applied to stablecoin reserve structure (debt-vs-equity-like claims on a reserve pool), Ch. 16’s information-asymmetry / agency-cost framework applied to DeFi protocol governance (token-as-equity, validator-as-agent), Ch. 21’s option-pricing applied to perpetual futures and structured DeFi products, and Ch. 28’s M&A / Ch. 30’s risk-management applied to crypto-asset-treasury management at corporates. The textbook supplies the analytical vocabulary; the crypto-specific institutional features are an extension.


AI-policy and platform-economics research. Ch. 8’s capex frameworks adapted for AI compute investment, Ch. 22’s real-options machinery applied to model-training-then-deploy decisions, Ch. 30’s risk-management framework adapted for catastrophic-AI-risk hedging (where standard derivatives don’t exist). Pair with Sebastian Mallaby - The Infinity Machine for the AI-firm-history case, Andrew Chen - The Cold Start Problem for platform-economics extension.


China political-economy modelling. Ch. 16’s agency-cost machinery applied to state-owned-enterprise capital-structure (multiple principals: party-state, controlling shareholder, public investors), Ch. 23’s IPO mechanics adapted to the Hong Kong / Shanghai / Shenzhen exchanges, Ch. 31’s international corporate finance applied to RMB-USD covered-interest-parity arbitrage and capital-control-driven segmentation. Pair with Angela Huyue Zhang - High Wire (regulatory-state interaction with corporate finance) and Meg E. Rithmire - Land Bargains and Chinese Capitalism (land-finance / local-government-debt as a corporate-finance problem).


Lobbying-network / corporate-political-strategy research. Ch. 28’s M&A material on antitrust review (Microsoft, AT&T, Pfizer-Wyeth cases) and Ch. 29’s regulatory-regime material (SOX, Dodd-Frank, post-FTX legislative responses) are direct corporate-political-strategy content. Cross-link to In Song Kim’s lobbying-network research on industry-coalition formation around regulatory change, with the textbook supplying the firm-level cost-benefit-of-political-action analytical apparatus.


What I would miss if I only read this note
A graduate-grade corporate-finance textbook is largely worked examples, end-of-chapter problems, and Excel-based modelling, not propositions — and this note can replicate none of these. Specifically, I would miss: (a) the cumulative reps from end-of-chapter problems that build automatic reflexes for NPV calculation under non-trivial cash-flow patterns, IRR pitfalls in mutually exclusive projects, beta unlevering / relevering algebra, MM-Proposition-II equity-cost adjustments, WACC / APV / FTE consistency-checks, binomial-tree backward-induction, and Black-Scholes input-sensitivity — fluency that note-reading alone does not produce; (b) the Ideko case-study spreadsheet build (Ch. 19) that turns the abstract Parts 1–5 machinery into an actual deliverable PE-style DCF model with sensitivity tables, exit-multiple analysis, and equity-IRR computation — this is what private-equity associates, investment-banking analysts, and corporate-development professionals actually build, and the textbook’s pedagogy is engineered around the student building it themselves; (c) the MyLab Finance adaptive-difficulty problem-set environment, which is how the print/PDF reader actually internalises the formulas — the textbook expects the student to use this; (d) the CFO and practitioner interview boxes scattered throughout (David Viniar at Goldman on bank-treasury risk; Sidney Hindle of Hindle Power on emerging-market investing; Myron Scholes’ own retrospective in Ch. 21 on the Black-Scholes derivation and the 2007–2009-crisis criticism) — these are voice-of-practitioner moments that humanise the propositions and that bare summary erases entirely; (e) the diagrams and visual pedagogy — efficient-frontier curves with the tangency portfolio at T, capital-market-line and security-market-line graphs, NPV-profile and IRR-where-NPV-crosses-zero charts, Black-Scholes N(d_1) shaded normal-distribution illustrations, binomial-tree branching diagrams, MM-Proposition-II linear plot of r_E vs D/E, tradeoff-theory V_L curve with tax-shield-rising / distress-cost-falling crossover — which is how the field actually communicates and which note prose flattens; (f) the glossary ([source extract], ~120K chars) with its hundreds of canonical term definitions, which is itself a curated map of the field’s vocabulary; (g) the footnote-and-source-trail to the original research-frontier papers (Modigliani-Miller 1958, Black-Scholes 1973, Merton 1973-1974, Myers-Majluf 1984, Jensen 1986, Fama-French 1992, Cox-Ross-Rubinstein 1979) that lets a curious reader go from textbook example to source paper to current research literature; (h) the Sixth Edition Global content — additional non-U.S. case studies (LVMH, Samsung, Vale, ICBC), OECD-equivalent cross-references for U.S. tax numbers, multi-currency end-of-chapter problems — that the U.S.-edition-only summary would miss; and (i) the detailed contents ([source extract], ~43K chars) of every section heading and sub-heading across 31 chapters, which is a finer-grained map than the chapter-by-chapter table above and which lets a reader looking for a specific topic (e.g. “rights offerings vs cash offerings”, “Black-Scholes with continuous dividends”, “covered interest rate parity”) jump directly to the relevant pages.

Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

Read chapter-by-chapter → Deep dive of Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited — Anti-Globalization in the Era of Trump (13 chapters)

One-sentence thesis
The IMF/World Bank “Washington Consensus” of the 1990s — capital-account liberalization, rapid privatization, fiscal-austerity-in-crisis, and trade liberalization without sequencing — was predictably and predictedly the wrong policy package for developing countries (East Asia 1997-98, Russia post-1991, Argentina-Latin America), produced predictable distributional and macroeconomic disasters, and the same market-fundamentalist failure mode has now (2017 Revisited edition) come home to roost in advanced countries as the New Discontents — Trump, Brexit, Le Pen, the populist anti-globalization wave — which Stiglitz argues are the political consequences of two decades of globalization mismanaged for corporate and financial-sector interests rather than for ordinary citizens, advanced or developing.
Why this book matters
The single most influential insider critique of late-twentieth-century international economic institutions, written by a Nobel-laureate (and former Clinton CEA chair, then chief economist of the World Bank 1997-2000) who watched the Asian-crisis bailouts, the Russian transition, and the Latin American IMF programs from inside the building. The original Globalization and Its Discontents (2002) was a global bestseller (>1 million copies, 40 translations — Afterword) that the IMF’s then-chief-economist Ken Rogoff publicly attacked, an attack that Stiglitz reads in the 2017 Afterword as confirming the book’s reach. The 2017 Revisited edition adds ~250 pages: a four-chapter Part I (“Globalization’s New Discontents”) that re-applies Stiglitz’s framework to advanced-country populist backlash post-2008, and a long Afterword tracing the policy battles since 2002.
For Yang’s purposes the book is the canonical primary source for three live questions: (a) why China and other emerging markets rationally reject capital-account liberalization and IMF-style conditionality (directly relevant to blockchain regulation, China-tech-policy work, AI cross-border data-flow regimes); (b) how international institutions become structurally captured by sector-specific elite interests and what that implies for any new global rules-of-the-game (relevant to lobbying-network research and to AI governance design); (c) the political-economy mechanisms through which mismanaged globalization generates anti-globalization populism (Trump, Brexit, the “New Discontents”) and why protectionist responses make things worse rather than better. Compared to alternatives — Rodrik’s more academic Globalization Paradox, Krueger’s pro-IMF defenses, Easterly’s market-skeptic but anti-aid critique — Stiglitz is uniquely valuable for combining first-person institutional access with a Nobel-grade theoretical frame (imperfect-information economics, Theory of the Second Best). The 2017 timing matters: the Revisited edition was written as Trump’s first months unfolded and reads with unusual urgency, reflecting Stiglitz’s view that the populist wave is the predictable political consequence of failures he had documented fifteen years earlier.
Core argument

Two-and-a-half centuries of trade theory promised globalization would benefit all countries. Adam Smith and David Ricardo argued specialization and exchange raise aggregate income everywhere; Paul Samuelson (Stiglitz’s thesis advisor) showed that with full employment and lump-sum compensation transfers, trade liberalization unambiguously raises national income (ch. 1). Stiglitz takes this as the baseline pro-globalization case, then attacks each premise in turn.
The economics literature also contained clear warnings, which were ignored. Stolper-Samuelson predicts unskilled-worker wages in advanced countries will fall under trade liberalization unless offset by redistribution; with imperfect information and incomplete risk markets (Stiglitz’s own theoretical work), the standard efficiency conclusion fails (ch. 1, Afterword “New Theories for a New World”). The fault was not “economic science” — it was politicians and economists-as-cheerleaders telling “white lies” (e.g., “trade creates jobs”; ch. 1) and ignoring the distributional warnings.
The Washington Consensus is the operational form of the failure. Coined for the 1980s convergence between 15th Street (US Treasury) and 19th Street (IMF) in DC, it bundled privatization, deregulation/liberalization, trade openness, and fiscal austerity (Introduction; ch. 5; ch. 7). The package was originally a response to Latin American problems (hyperinflation, runaway deficits) but was generalized as one-size-fits-all to economies with utterly different structural problems (ch. 5; ch. 7).
Capital-account liberalization is the most damaging single element. Stiglitz states bluntly: “I believe that capital account liberalization was the single most important factor leading to the crisis” — referring to East Asia 1997-98 (ch. 8). Free flows of short-term hot money fuel asset bubbles on the way in and force devaluations and bank failures on the way out; capital flows are pro-cyclical (out during recessions when most needed; ch. 8). The IMF pushed liberalization at the very moment (October 1997 Hong Kong meetings) when its own member countries’ finance ministers were begging for the right to impose capital controls (ch. 8).
Crisis-response austerity is Hooverite. Standard macroeconomics since Keynes prescribes counter-cyclical fiscal expansion in recessions; the IMF in East Asia demanded fiscal contraction, high interest rates, and balanced budgets (ch. 8). The IMF later admitted the fiscal stance was “excessively austere” (ch. 8). Stiglitz coins the term beggar-thyself policies (ch. 8): even worse than Depression-era beggar-thy-neighbor tariffs because the contraction was inflicted on the country itself to rebuild reserves and repay foreign creditors — and the contagion effect on neighbors was identical.
The Russian “shock therapy” failure was structurally analogous. Rapid liberalization + rapid privatization + premature opening of capital account, in the absence of legal-regulatory infrastructure, produced not a market economy but asset-stripping crony capitalism (ch. 9). Russian GDP fell 45% from 1990-1998, deeper than the WWII contraction (ch. 9). The IMF approved an 11.2B loan in July 1998 as part of a 22.6B multilateral package; the package collapsed within three weeks (ch. 9). Stiglitz documents how oligarchs and Western banks used the IMF tranche to wire dollars out of the country to Cyprus and Switzerland before the inevitable devaluation (ch. 9). The contrast with China — which sequenced liberalization slowly, kept capital controls, retained state-led industrial policy — is the empirical refutation of shock therapy.
The institutions are structurally biased toward financial-sector interests. Stiglitz’s governance critique: the IMF is run by finance ministers and central bank governors who are professionally and personally tied to the financial community (Robert Rubin Goldman→Treasury→Citigroup, Stan Fischer IMF→Citigroup; ch. 5). The US has the only single-country veto. Decisions are taken behind closed doors. The result is “taxation without representation” for developing-country citizens whose lives are reshaped (ch. 5). The Asian Monetary Fund (Japan offered $100B in 1997 to compete with IMF) was killed by the US precisely because Treasury did not want regulatory competition (ch. 8, Afterword).
The 2017 update — New Discontents: same failure, advanced-country variant. Trump, Brexit, Le Pen, Wilders are the political consequence of the same institutional structure inflicting wage stagnation and inequality on US/UK/EU workers (Introduction; chs. 1-3). Mechanism: globalization-driven outsourcing weakens worker bargaining power (ch. 1); short-term capital flows force short-termism on firms (ch. 2); investment agreements (ISDS, NAFTA Ch.11, TPP) give foreign corporations rights exceeding those of domestic firms — the Philip Morris vs. Uruguay smoking-regulation case is the canonical exhibit (ch. 2); tax-base erosion via fiscal paradises (Apple’s 0.005% Irish rate; ch. 2) means governments lose the fiscal capacity needed to compensate losers; intellectual-property regimes embedded in trade agreements (TRIPS, TPP) raise drug prices and serve large incumbents (ch. 2); CEO-shareholder governance reform shifts corporate income from wages to executive compensation (ch. 4).
Trump’s New Protectionism will fail. History has moved on (manufacturing employment is declining globally regardless of trade policy; ch. 3); the trade deficit is determined by macroeconomic savings-investment balance, not trade policy (ch. 1, ch. 3); a 45% tariff against China just shifts imports to Vietnam and Bangladesh while raising prices for the Walmart shoppers Trump claims to represent (ch. 3); reciprocal tariffs would produce a trade war whose first-round losers are Trump’s own Rust Belt voters (ch. 3). The “America First” stance also accelerates US loss of soft power and the inevitable shift toward a multipolar world order (Introduction; ch. 4; Afterword).
Reform agenda — managed globalization with inclusive growth. Stiglitz’s third-way prescription: (a) capital controls under defined conditions plus financial-transactions taxes (Tobin-style); (b) sequenced liberalization with institutional infrastructure first; (c) sovereign-debt restructuring mechanisms; (d) a global-reserve system to replace the dollar-Treasury anchor (China, Russia, France supported a UN study of this; the US blocked it — Introduction); (e) global tax cooperation against fiscal paradises; (f) more-democratic IMF governance; (g) progressive taxation, strengthened collective bargaining, and labor-friendly macroeconomic policy domestically. The model: Scandinavian social protection without protectionism (Introduction; ch. 4). Stiglitz’s positive contribution to a new framework is the Stockholm Consensus — ten development-policy principles he and four other former World Bank chief economists signed onto (Afterword).

Argument map
The book’s reasoning runs from theory + warnings → Washington Consensus as institutional vehicle → case-study failures (East Asia, Russia, Latin America, Africa) → 2017 update: same mechanism in advanced countries → Trump’s protectionism is the wrong response → managed-globalization alternative. The structural move is: the failure is institutional, not technological; therefore the fix is institutional rebuilding, not retreat.
