Best chapters/pages to actually read
If you read three chapters, take 3, 15, and 26. If you have time for five, add 8 and 18.


Chapter 3 (the first morning at Zanmi Lasante) is the densest single chapter on what PIH actually does at the clinical level: courtyard rounds, the gangrene case, the comma, the Pott’s-disease woman bent at 90°, the sorcery consult, Ti Ofa and the indinavir bottle. Read first if you want to understand why Farmer’s day is built the way it is. Pairs with the operations of Zanmi Lasante’s TB and AIDS programs in chapters 4 and 24.


Chapter 8 (Léogâne + arrival in Cange + the founding moment) is the chapter to read for the moral architecture’s origin. The young pregnant woman in the malaria coma needing a transfusion she cannot afford. The sister’s tout moun se moun. Farmer’s decision on the road back to the central plateau: “I’m going to build my own fucking hospital. And there’ll be none of that there, thank you.” This is the chapter the rest of the book derives from.


Chapter 15 (the ten Carabayllanos and the amplification diagnosis) is the technical and analytical center of the book. The patients are seen one after another on a wooden bench at the El Progreso clinic; their records show they had completed DOTS strictly under direct observation, then been retreated under the WHO formula derived from 20-year-old African trial assumptions — and emerged with four- and five-drug resistance. The diagnostic insight (the WHO retreatment regimen amplifies resistance in patients who were already mono- or two-drug-resistant) is the technical claim that overturned global TB doctrine. The chapter pairs with chapter 16 (the Chicago speech that publicized it) and chapter 18 (the Boston meeting where DOTS-plus was conceded by WHO).


Chapter 18 (DOTS-plus and the Goldfarb confrontation) is the chapter to read for the cost-effectiveness debate at its sharpest. Goldfarb’s $6M arithmetic — 5,000 inmates DOTS or 500 MDR — is the strongest version of the utilitarian argument PIH faces. Kim’s Margaret Mead reply is the strongest non-strategic version of PIH’s answer. Together with chapter 19 (the price-driving-down strategy as a way to dissolve the trade-off), this is the policy fight in two acts.


Chapter 26 (the hike to Casse, “the long defeat”) is the chapter to read for the book’s ethical position at its fullest. Farmer’s monologue on the trail — about the boy John, the cost of a doctor’s salary, common cause with the losers, every patient as a sign — is the most-quoted passage of the book and the position the rest of his career operationalizes. Pair with chapter 25 (the John story it is responding to) for the full force.


Chapter 5 (the childhood) if you want to understand why Farmer is built for this work. The Blue Bird Inn bus, the Lady Gin boat, the Warden, the cockroaches in the bilge, the part-time Hogan’s Drugstore job, the Tolkien-at-11 reading list. After this chapter, the four-hour nights and the dentist-chair-as-improvement-over-other-places-he-has-slept stop seeming like asceticism and start seeming like baseline.


Chapter 12 (junta years; The Uses of Haiti) if you want the political-economy claim at its angriest. Useful to read against Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited and against Acharya and Lee - The Cartel System of States — Farmer’s view from Cange of how American policy serves Haitian dictators is the high-resolution local version of those macro arguments.


Chapter 25 (the boy John) if you want the hardest case for the method. A maximum-effort, maximum-cost, maximum-failure case. Read first if you want to know what objection chapter 26 is actually answering.

What I would miss if I only read this note
I would miss the texture of how Farmer talks. The comma placeholder for “asshole” directed only at third parties comfortable with the global distribution of money and medicine. “It’s anatomy and pus. It’s always anatomy and pus.” The Haitian e-mail Kidder gets at Miami after a 36-hour absence: “We miss you as the dry, cracked earth misses the rain.” Kidder’s gloss: “Haitians, man. They’re totally over the top. My kind of people.” The escalator scene in Miami: “The more ruffles, the more stumbles.” These are doing analytical work a summary cannot replace; they substantiate Kidder’s claim that Farmer’s voice is funny in a way the policy moments alone cannot show.
I would miss the texture of Kidder’s own slow conversion. Chapter 1 ends with Kidder calling Farmer “disturbing” and pulling away; chapter 26 ends with Kidder accepting Farmer as both his guide and his doctor for the day, sharing a candy bar under Orion’s belt at the end of an 11-hour hike. The arc is not Farmer changing — Farmer barely changes — but Kidder’s posture toward the comma relaxing. The book is doing something unusual: a journalist’s slow surrender of standard cost-effectiveness skepticism, rendered honestly enough that a reader still skeptical (as I partly remain) can map their own position onto Kidder’s per-chapter shifts.
I would miss the moments where the book lets Farmer be unsure or guilty. The eclamptic-mother case at Zanmi Lasante a month after Catherine was born, where the stillborn baby’s death sends Farmer outside to weep and then to the realization “I thought I was the king of empathy for these poor kids, but if I was the king of empathy, why this big shift because of my daughter?” The Paris kitchen scene where Didi drops something and Farmer covers his mouth with both hands. The Catherine-versus-kwashiorkor-child photograph he carries — one stuffed-animals daughter, one starving patient. Without these, Farmer flattens into a saint Kidder explicitly refused to render him as.
I would miss the period detail. The François Duvalier Airport. Madame Max Adolphe (former warden of Fort Dimanche, “Buchenwald,” now national chief of tontons macoutes). The 1986 kouri in Port-au-Prince when Ophelia and Paul opened their car doors to wounded demonstrators. The 1990 election rumour-cycle when the new Aristide government had not yet been couped. The 1991 cabbie at Logan: “Dr. Polo, there’s trouble down there.” The smell of burning tires that became Ophelia’s permanent association with Haitian political violence. The book is the closest thing the post-2003 reader has to a primary text on the late-Duvalier and post-Duvalier years from inside a Haitian peasants’ clinic.
Finally I would miss the institutional-archaeology specifics. The MacArthur grant (220,000, 1993) entirely donated to PIH's Institute for Health and Social Justice. The 1987 founding (1M Tom White seed). The first Brigham pharmacy “borrow” of 92,000 in second-line drugs ("Robin Hood attitude"). The 45M Gates grant of July 2000 and its near-identical match to Jim Kim’s ask. The Lima airport ritual (“Paul Farmer, TB Commissioner” suitcase labels). The Cange staff (200 community health workers, 12 nurses, 12 doctors) by 2002. These are the operational artifacts; they are what someone trying to build a PIH-like organization (the position the book is implicitly recruiting for) would want to know.
Important examples


The 1988 noncompliance study (ch. 4). The two-arm comparative study Farmer ran out of his Cange wheelchair after his shattered leg. 48% cure (medicine only) vs. 100% cure (medicine + monthly cash + community health workers). Operationalized as permanent program. Twelve years of zero deaths.


The Léogâne transfusion failure (ch. 8). Pregnant young woman in malaria coma; sister cannot afford both blood and transport; Farmer scrapes $15; she and the unborn baby die. Sister’s tout moun se moun. The founding moment of Farmer’s hospital ambition.


The Péligre Dam (ch. 4). Brown & Root of Texas, U.S. Export-Import Bank, 1956. Drowned the central-plateau farmland; produced the squatter settlement Farmer would later build Zanmi Lasante into. The structural-cause case study Farmer cites in every speech.


Father Jack’s death (ch. 14). Beloved Roxbury / Carabayllo priest, no prior TB treatment, treated at the Brigham, dies a month into therapy of five-drug-resistant TB he contracted in Carabayllo. The diagnostic event that pulled PIH into MDR.


The ten Carabayllanos (ch. 15). Suitcase labeled “Paul Farmer, TB Commissioner.” All ten resistant to four or five first-line drugs. Diagnostic claim: WHO retreatment had amplified their resistance, not the other way around.


The Chicago speech (ch. 16). Farmer’s “myths and mystifications about MDR-TB” talk at the International Union Against Tuberculosis. Ken Castro calls it “provocative.” Farmer turns back: “Why do you qualify my talk as provocative? I just said we should treat sick people.”


The Green Light Committee (ch. 19). Kim’s institutional invention to make low second-line drug prices conditional on a sound underlying DOTS program. By 2000: capreomycin 98 cents/vial (-97%), a four-drug-resistant case treatable for 1,500 (down from 15,000).


Christian’s recovery (ch. 17). Three-year-old at the Children’s Hospital in Lima, 22 pounds, dying of MDR. Farmer’s empiric regimen — high-dose ethambutol + four second-line drugs including a fluoroquinolone, against received pediatric “wisdom” derived from immature beagle pups. Two years later Christian runs across the corridor toward Farmer.


The Peruvian doctor’s daughter (ch. 17). Same day as Christian. The TB doctor’s own daughter is on the WHO retreatment regimen despite a Mass State Lab culture showing total resistance. The father had known for months but couldn’t risk his job. Farmer plays a “charade” of fresh diagnosis to give the assembled doctors face-saving cover for the second-line switch.


The boy John (ch. 25). Maximum-effort, maximum-cost, maximum-failure case. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma diagnosed late; medevacked to Mass General at ~$20,000; dies. The case the chapter-26 “long defeat” speech is answering.


The hike to Morne Michel (ch. 4) and the hike to Casse (ch. 26). Two “scattershot” 5- and 11-hour walks into the central plateau to find a single noncompliant TB patient and visit a single recovered scrofula patient’s family. “The objective is to inculcate in the doctors and nurses the spirit to dedicate themselves to the patients.” The book’s recurring proof that Farmer’s method does not scale through efficiency but through fidelity at the unit-of-one level.


The clock at Cange (ch. 26 / Afterword). In 2002, twenty years after Brown & Root drowned the farmland of Cange’s water refugees, the petition Ti Fifi helped draft wins electricity from the Péligre dam to Cange for a few hours a day. Closing the loop the book opened in chapter 4.


Critiques and limitations


Single-protagonist sample size. Kidder is candid that Farmer is sui generis (chapter 24’s wall sign is essentially the disclaimer), but the book remains one extended portrait of one charismatic clinician. The PIH operation as documented here would not exist without (a) Tom White’s substantial fortune (he funded the seed and underwrote the gap years), (b) Père Lafontant’s pre-existing community-organizing infrastructure in Cange, (c) Ophelia Dahl’s financial discipline, (d) Jim Kim’s policy-shop aptitude. Replication outside that specific four-cornered scaffolding is the empirical question the book mostly defers. PIH’s later expansion to Rwanda, Lesotho, Sierra Leone (post-publication) is the partial answer; whether the model works without a Farmer-like central figure is still unclear.


Romance vs. reportage tension. Kidder is sympathetic in ways that occasionally read as romance — the Tolkien-at-11 reading lists, the “fuckin’ saint” janitor moment, the “luminescent smile.” Some single-source anecdotes are reported as the team told them (the Aristide friendship, the smuggled $10,000 to the underground resistance, the various close-call confrontations). A skeptical reader needs to remember that this is authorized-portrait genre with the access trades that genre always involves.


The cost-effectiveness debate is not actually settled in the book. Farmer’s strategic answer (close the price gap so the trade-off vanishes) and his non-strategic answer (“the long defeat”) are different positions. The strategic answer was vindicated by Kim’s price-reduction work, but the strategic answer only works in cases where prices can be driven down 90-95% — i.e., where patents have expired and generic manufacturers exist. For genuinely expensive interventions where the price reflects real R&D costs (the John case is a counterexample: Mass General provided the cancer treatment for free, but generalized application of that protocol would not be cheap), the long-defeat answer is the only answer, and it carries a different cognitive load than the price-reduction answer. The book elides this distinction.


Triage-by-neglect critique not engaged on its strongest version. The argument Farmer faces is not “your hospital is too expensive” but “your hospital crowds out other interventions that would save more lives.” Goldfarb articulates this in chapter 18; PIH’s price-reduction strategy answers part of it; but the book never formally addresses the steady-state version where every dollar spent on a maximum-effort case is a dollar not spent on a high-volume cheaper intervention. Abhijit V. Banerjee - Poor Economics and Esther Duflo’s RCT framework is the empirical shape this critique now takes; reading the two books against each other is the productive way to inhabit this gap.


Liberation theology as spec. The book treats preferential option for the poor as a self-implementing ethical specification, but liberation theology’s actual history is contested (Vatican intervention against it in the 1980s; Romero’s assassination by U.S.-aligned death squads; the politics of the church of the poor vs. the institutional Catholic hierarchy). Farmer’s reading is unusually operational; whether the spec ports to non-Christian or non-Latin-American settings is an open question, especially in his later Russian and African work.


Workplace cost framed individually. Farmer’s four-hour nights, two million miles, hepatitis A from a ceviche he ate while overworked, daughter and wife in Paris: Kidder notices but does not theorize. The PIH-as-organization question of how to retain talent without burning it out — Ophelia’s “normalize the experience” effort in chapter 24 — is gestured at but not engaged. Read alongside Pete Walker - Complex PTSD for nervous-system vocabulary the global-health culture in 2000 lacked, and against the engineering-crunch literature Tracy Kidder - The Soul of a New Machine is the source text for.


The political-economy critique of aid is partial. Farmer is unsparing about U.S. policy toward Haiti, the Duvaliers, the IMF/World Bank conditionalities, the structural-adjustment framing, and the U.S. Army occupation. But PIH’s own funding picture (Tom White’s privately accumulated construction-company fortune; the Gates Foundation’s $45M; Soros’s contingent grants; the World Bank loans Farmer ends up shaping) is not held to the same critical standard. The book does not engage what it would mean if PIH’s model can only scale through philanthropic capital sourced from the same political-economic system it is critiquing — a tension Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited makes explicit at the IMF/World Bank scale.


Gender and labor. The PIH-er staff is described as “majority female” and “rather good-looking” (Ophelia’s word, ch. 25); much of the unglamorous coordination work falls to Ophelia, Ti Fifi, Mamito Lafontant, Carole Smarth, Serena Koenig, Sonya Shin, Jen Furin, Meche Becerra. Kidder notices the pattern but doesn’t theorize the gender economy of PIH’s labor structure. A modern reader will want to read against contemporary scholarship on global-health labor (and against the engineering-crunch parallel in Tracy Kidder - The Soul of a New Machine where the labor pattern is similarly noticed but not interrogated).


What I would track / open questions

Whether the PIH model survives Farmer’s death (Farmer died February 2022; this is post-publication and tagged (secondary, not verified in this vault), but the question this book opens is the literal answer to chapter 24’s wall sign).
Whether the second-line drug price reduction strategy generalizes to the genuinely-novel-IP case (CAR-T, mRNA cancer vaccines, Lecanemab-class neurodegeneratives). PIH’s victory is partly a pharmaceutical-economics victory contingent on patent expiry.
Whether the long defeat posture — common cause with the losers — is psychologically sustainable for staff who do not share Farmer’s specific trait distribution. Kim’s “If Paul is the model, we’re fucked” is the diagnostic; the answer is not in the book.
Whether the Cuba-Council-of-State pipeline (two Cange students per year to medical school in Cuba, 500 Cuban doctors in Haiti) survives U.S.-Cuba political cycles.
Whether the distal intervention framework (cure the disease, then change the conditions that produced it) is replicable at national scale. The Afterword’s Lascahobas success is the encouraging case; the failed expansion of National Highway 3 is the discouraging case. Surface to the vault Open Questions dashboard.

Research uses


Global health policy. This is the book’s primary research use. The MDR-TB doctrinal turn (1996-2002) is documented here at scene-level granularity that scholarly histories of WHO seldom achieve. The Green Light Committee, the IDA / Doctors Without Borders / generic-manufacturers play, the WHO essential-drugs-list lobbying, the Gates grant mechanics — these are operational artifacts a contemporary global-health policy researcher will not find better-documented in any single source. Pair with the Afterword’s June 2002 timestamp for closure.


Development-aid theory. The book is the strongest single-source critique of cost-effectiveness analysis as a gatekeeping discipline. Its position is not that cost-effectiveness is wrong but that it is selectively applied — “MDR treatment is cost-effective in a place like New York, but not in a place like Peru.” Read against Abhijit V. Banerjee - Poor Economics for the RCT empiricism that grew up partly in response to this debate, and against Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited for the macro structural-adjustment critique Farmer’s micro version aligns with.


Liberation theology as operational specification. Farmer’s Duke-era reading of the Latin American bishops is operationalized over twenty years into a working model. For anyone interested in how a moral-philosophical position translates into an enforceable organizational specification, this is the canonical case study. The preferential option for the poor concept ports surprisingly well to non-Catholic global-health practice; the long defeat and accompaniment concepts (the latter not heavily emphasized in this book but central to Farmer’s later work) are part of the same operational vocabulary.


Engineering-management parallels. PIH’s “we’ll figure out the means after we make the assertion” strategy (Kim’s $45M Gates ask; the Carabayllo “let’s try ten patients first” gambit) is operationally similar to the Tracy Kidder - The Soul of a New Machine signing-up mechanism — a deliberate over-commitment that creates the conditions for its own fulfillment. The buffer-manager pattern (West absorbing politics so engineers could believe Eagle was theirs) reappears in Farmer’s relationship to Père Lafontant and to the larger PIH organization. Reading the two Kidder books together is the highest-yield Kidder-on-Kidder pairing in this vault.


Anthropology of global health. Farmer’s AIDS and Accusation and Infections and Inequalities are the scholarly companions to this popular text. The “geography of blame” frame — TB and AIDS scapegoating mapped onto pre-existing racial and economic hierarchies — is portable to current pandemic discourse. Useful for syllabus reading on medical anthropology alongside Arthur Kleinman’s work (Kleinman protected Farmer at Harvard during medical school, ch. 11).


Personal-decision use. The book is unusually directive in its ethical demand. Its question — “are you incapable of complexity?” — is the question Farmer faces Kidder with, and through Kidder faces every reader with. The book functions as an enforced re-evaluation of how one’s own time, money, and attention are allocated. Whether one accepts Farmer’s specific resolution or not, the question itself is the artifact. A useful pairing is the Tracy Kidder - The Soul of a New Machine question of what trades engineers are making with their lives — Farmer’s answer to that question is the most extreme version this vault contains.


Biographical method. Kidder’s authorial discipline — never letting Farmer’s voice collapse into a single attitude, refusing the great-man frame, letting Goldfarb’s strongest objection stand without rebuttal, embedding the wall-sign disclaimer in chapter 24 — is a model for any writer engaging a charismatic subject. Useful as a counter-template to Walter Isaacson - Elon Musk’s explicit acceptance of the great-man framing.


Key concepts

Preferential option for the poor — the Latin American bishops’ 1968 declaration that the church has a duty to favor the impoverished; Farmer’s organizational specification; see Preferential Option for the Poor.
Long defeat — Farmer’s name for the stance of “common cause with the losers” — fighting on regardless of winning. From Tolkien (the “long defeat” of the Eldar against Morgoth in The Lord of the Rings); Farmer’s framing in chapter 26; see Long Defeat (Tolkien-Farmer).
Pragmatic solidarity — the early-PIH coinage for sending resources down “the steep gradient of inequality” rather than waiting for revolution or sustainability; rejection of “appropriate technology” as “good things for rich people and shit for the poor”; see Pragmatic Solidarity.
The great epi divide — Farmer’s coinage for the partition of humanity between populations who die in their seventies of aging diseases and those who die ten to forty years earlier of preventable illness. Runs through countries and through cities (Mission Hill > Cuba; Harlem > Bangladesh).
Amplification — Farmer’s chosen term for what the WHO retreatment regimen does to mono- or two-drug-resistant TB patients (selecting for further resistance). Chosen over “recruitment of further resistance” because it sounds worse.
Distal intervention — the PIH method of curing the disease first, then changing the conditions that produced the disease (Alcante’s family at Casse: TB cure first, then concrete floor + metal roof + tuition + nutrition).
Comma — Farmer’s verbal placeholder for “asshole,” directed only at third parties comfortable with the global distribution of money and medicine.
AMC — area of moral clarity. PIH internal coinage for situations where the right thing to do is plain, even if doing it is hard.
WL — white liberal. Farmer’s term for sympathetic but underwilling-to-sacrifice would-be allies.
Bwat — Creole for “box.” Farmer’s checkbox notation on his daily yellow-legal-pad task lists.
Tout moun se moun — “We are all human beings.” The Léogâne sister’s repeated phrase that became Farmer’s answer to the question of whether being an American is a sufficient identity.

Links to other books


Sibling Kidder voice and method — Tracy Kidder - The Soul of a New Machine — same author, same long-form embedded technique, same authorial discipline of letting the protagonist’s voice be funny and idiosyncratic without flattening into caricature. The two books read together are an exhibit in how Kidder uses one organizational unit (one team in one basement for one year; one clinic in one mountainside for eighteen years) to extract a generalizable structural argument. Both books also share a labor-cost subtext Kidder notices but does not theorize.


Singular-figure biography contrast — Walter Isaacson - Elon Musk — Isaacson centers the visionary and accepts the great-man frame; Kidder centers the team and the institutional infrastructure (Tom White, Lafontant, Ophelia, Kim) and refuses the frame Farmer is otherwise built for. The PIH wall sign with the hidden punchline (“If Paul is the model, we’re fucked”) is Kidder’s explicit epistemic warning against the Isaacson reading. Useful contrast for thinking about authorial responsibility when reporting on a still-active charismatic subject.


Development aid and structural adjustment critique — Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited — Farmer’s micro-scale view from Cange (the Péligre Dam, the Creole-pig eradication, the IMF conditionalities reaching down to peasant farmers) is the high-resolution local complement to Stiglitz’s IMF/World Bank-scale critique. The 1956 Brown & Root dam project is the kind of intervention Stiglitz’s framework predicts will produce the effects Farmer documents.


Cost-effectiveness counterpoint — Abhijit V. Banerjee - Poor Economics — the RCT-empirical position that grew up partly in response to debates Farmer was central to. Banerjee/Duflo’s evidence on cash transfers, deworming, education, and microcredit interventions is partly an attempt to put a rigorous empirical floor under the debate Farmer and Goldfarb argue out in chapter 18. Reading the two together — Farmer’s “common cause with the losers” against Banerjee’s “what does the evidence actually show works per dollar?” — is the highest-yield development-economics pairing in this vault.


State-failure context for Haiti — Acharya and Lee - The Cartel System of States — Acharya/Lee’s framework predicts the kind of state-formation pathology Haiti exemplifies (centralized predation, weak service provision, persistent inequality). Farmer’s documentary work on the U.S. occupation, the Duvaliers, the post-1991 junta, and the post-2000 Aristide period is the on-the-ground counterpart to that structural argument.


Network and geography of disease — Andrew Chen - The Cold Start Problem — the atomic network / hard side framing Chen uses for platform dynamics has a public-health analogue: Farmer’s familias tebeceanas (TB families) and the prison/shelter network dynamics where MDR concentrates are the same kind of concentrated-node problem. Useful contrast between the two.


Authoritarian capitalism / state autonomy — Angela Huyue Zhang - High Wire / Meg E. Rithmire - Land Bargains and Chinese Capitalism — the Cuban medical infrastructure Farmer admires (chapter 21) is one of the cleanest examples of Authoritarian Capitalism Variants producing a public-good outcome (universal healthcare, doctors per capita 2x U.S.) Stiglitz’s framework alone underpredicts. Farmer’s argument — “they were talking about managing wealth; he was talking about managing poverty” — is the reframe.


Crunch / human-cost — Pete Walker - Complex PTSD — Farmer’s four-hour nights, his reckless ignoring of his own hepatitis A symptoms, his “I’ve never known despair and I don’t think I ever will,” the PIH-er burnout pattern Ophelia tries to “normalize” out of in chapter 24 — all gesture at nervous-system consequences the global-health culture in 2000 lacked vocabulary for. Walker’s framework supplies the vocabulary.


The lean iteration counterpoint — Eric Ries - The Lean Startup — PIH’s “let’s try ten patients first” Carabayllo gambit (chapter 16) is structurally similar to Ries’s MVP: small-N pilot before scale-up. But the Carabayllo “iteration” runs on two-year drug courses and lives, not on weekly software releases; the cost of being wrong is different in kind. The contrast clarifies what Lean Startup methodology can and cannot port to.


Founder-network / institutional infrastructure — Reid Hoffman - The Start-Up of You / Andrew Chen - The Cold Start Problem — PIH’s network of allies (Howard Hiatt at the Brigham, William Foege at Gates, George Soros, Hillary Clinton, Eli Lilly’s board, Doctors Without Borders, IDA) is the institutional substrate that made the Carabayllo demonstration scale globally. Hoffman’s permanent beta and Chen’s hard side are useful concepts for reading PIH’s organizational growth pattern.

Tracy Kidder - The Soul of a New Machine
One-sentence thesis
A 32-bit minicomputer (Data General’s Eagle, later the Eclipse MV/8000) was built in roughly a year, by a sealed-off team of about thirty engineers — half of them new graduates — through a recurring set of management moves (signing-up, mushroom management, pinball, flying-upside-down, trust as the late-stage substitute for control), and the resulting computer “is no canard” but a working artifact whose best parts of itself live in the engineers — which is what Kidder means by the soul of a new machine and what Ruskin meant by free labor freely given (ch. 15).
Why this book matters
Kidder won the 1982 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction and the National Book Award for this account of Data General’s Eclipse Group debugging the Eagle prototype between 1978 and 1980 (secondary, not verified in this vault — but the book itself is clearly contemporaneous reporting from inside the basement of Building 14A/B in Westborough, Massachusetts). It is the canonical popular-press portrait of the late-1970s minicomputer-era engineering culture, the literary template Schreier, Isaacson, and the entire “engineers building hard things” genre have been working in for forty years, and a remarkably durable management text in disguise: the book’s organizing concepts (signing-up, mushroom management, pinball, the wars, flying upside down, trust, the kludge) are still cited in startup and engineering-management literature in the 2020s without their origins always being attributed.
What makes the book uniquely useful for a wiki built around what to read deeply is its level of zoom: Kidder rides along with one project, in one basement, for one cycle, and the prose can therefore drop down to the level of a single eight-cent NAND gate (ch. 12) without losing track of the corporate politics one floor up (ch. 14, ch. 15) or the home-life burnout patterns at the lab benches (ch. 11, ch. 13). It is one of the few books in this vault where the unit of analysis stays consistent through both the technical layer (microcode → assembly → gates) and the human layer (recruiting → signing-up → burnout → dispersal). For comparison: Walter Isaacson - Elon Musk is biography centered on the visionary; Jason Schreier - Blood Sweat and Pixels is anthology across ten case studies; Chris Miller - Chip War is geopolitics across decades. Kidder is one project, one team, one year — and the unity is what gives the book its leverage.
Core argument
The book is narrative reporting, not a thesis-driven argument, but Kidder is plainly making a case. The cumulative claim, decomposed:


The Eagle was not commissioned by the company; it was willed into existence by the team and West. Data General had bet on the Fountainhead Project (FHP) in North Carolina to deliver the company’s 32-bit supermini. The Eclipse Group was nominally supposed to extend the 16-bit Eclipse line. West, Wallach, and Alsing engineered Eagle from the leftover materials of EGO (the previously cancelled “kill North Carolina” project, ch. 2), pitching it externally as low-key “insurance” against FHP slipping while internally proselytizing it as “the answer to VAX” (ch. 2, ch. 6). De Castro’s contribution was a single constraint — “no mode bit” — which West later glosses as a succinct description of the perfect machine (ch. 15). Without West’s PR campaign, the architectural specification (Wallach’s 200-page seven-revision spec, ch. 4), and the simulator (Firth’s Trixie-hosted paper Eagle, ch. 8), the project would not have happened.


The team was selected on a deliberate filter: technical fire-in-the-eyes plus willingness to sign up, with grades as a screen for endurance. Alsing’s interview script (ch. 3) is an engineered ritual where the recruit must say things like “I want to do a big machine” with sufficient conviction that Alsing decides he means it; the bad-news disclosure (“a bunch of cynics and egotists, hard to keep up with, very long hours”) functions to load the recruit into a contract he cannot retroactively repudiate. Inspiration: Seymour Cray’s videotape claim that he hires inexperienced engineers because “they do not usually know what’s supposed to be impossible” (ch. 3). One candidate is rejected for listing “family life” as his main avocation. By the project’s start the team is ~12 veterans plus ~12 kids, divided into Hardy Boys (hardware, under Rasala) and Microkids (microcode, under Alsing).


The signing-up mechanism is itself the productive unit of the book’s management theory. Kidder repeatedly returns to the moment in which a recruit transitions from being told to do something to volunteering to do it (ch. 3, ch. 6). Carman: “you have to go through the sign-up. To be sure you’re not conning anybody.” The signing-up reframes overtime, weekend work, and physical exhaustion as the volunteer’s commitment, not the manager’s coercion. Operationally it’s also Tom Sawyer’s fence (ch. 3) — the manager makes the work look like a privilege so the engineers paint it themselves. This is the part of the book that is most cited in management literature, often without attribution to Kidder.


Architectural and tooling decisions made early under enormous time pressure dominated downstream timelines. Wallach’s “golden moment” — folding ring number into the first three bits of the 32-bit address so segment number = ring number = security level (ch. 4) — was the architectural innovation; it was found in a few days, while two years of his prior work on FHP were lost when that project went south. Firth’s simulator (ch. 8) was the second pivotal tooling choice: Alsing extracted it via a rigged friendly competition between Peck (six weeks, used briefly) and Firth (2.5 months full version + two months refinement); without it, microcode debugging would have queued behind hardware debugging on shared prototypes and the project would have run multiple years longer. The PAL-chip gamble (ch. 6, ch. 14, ch. 15) — sole-sourcing brand-new programmable array logic chips when conventional wisdom required at least two suppliers — could have killed the project when the supplier nearly went bankrupt; it survived only because Data General resolved supply through other channels and the announcement was delayed to spring 1980.


Debugging is where craft replaces architecture. Chapter 12 (the missing NAND gate) is the most procedurally precise lab description in the popular-engineering canon. The bug was a “time bomb” — a Sys-Cache-to-IP invalidation that the IP failed to obey, leaving stale instructions in the I-cache that fired wrong many cycles later. The fix was one extra NAND gate (eight cents wholesale) that delayed a competing signal; Holberger named the new signal “NOT YET.” The chapter’s craft observations — Veres’s morning-shower forward-search reframe, time-in-a-computer as something Rasala can see “wide” at the analyzer, the surgery analogy with stripped-wire fragments dropping into the back of a board — are why this section is excerpted in engineering textbooks. By the late chapters (ch. 15) the Hardy Boys can “feel what was wrong with their machine” — Holberger fixes a residual bug by adding one wire, unable to explain why it works.


Kidder’s argument about West runs on two layers, the second of which is the book’s actual contribution. Layer one: West built a good machine in the commercial sense — Eagle was ~10% faster than VAX at single-precision Whetstones, two prototypes shippable, ~10% of all new Data General orders by early 1981, the company’s product line rejuvenated. Layer two (ch. 14): West’s real function was to absorb all complaints, refuse all upward-flowing criticism of his team, and let the recruits believe Eagle was their machine. Alsing’s reconstruction: “When this is all over, there are gonna be thirty inventors of the Eagle machine. Tom’s letting them believe that they invented it. It’s cheaper than money.” Rosemarie Seale’s reconstruction (ch. 14): “He set himself out there as the bad guy… for people to grow up they need someone to lay their problems on. ‘You’re the daddy.‘” This is Kidder’s claim about why skilled adults work overtime without overtime pay — they were given enough freedom to invent inside a sealed bubble that hid the politics from them, while a manager at the perimeter ate the politics on their behalf.


The reward system was pinball, and it was a partial lie. West coined the term (ch. 14): “You win one game, you get to play another. You win with this machine, you get to build the next.” The team understood this implicit promise as the real compensation — much more so than stock options (which were strongly suggested but never explicitly promised, and which Holberger’s burned paycheck-stub scene in ch. 14 establishes were dwarfed by the technicians’ overtime pay). The book ends with the contradiction of pinball: in fall 1980 the Eclipse Group was disbanded, dispersed across the company and across the country; many didn’t get to play another game with the same team. West stayed (ch. 16): “Yeah, it’s all blown apart, but the ethic’s still in place. In some sense spreading that around may be beneficial.” In the epilogue: “It was a summer romance. But that’s all right.”


Kidder’s literary frame is Ruskin’s Nature of Gothic (ch. 15). Ruskin distinguished work fragmented into trivial tasks fit only for slave labor (industrial age) from work in which whole craft was demanded of free labor, freely given (medieval cathedrals). Kidder is explicit: “That’s what West and his team of engineers were looking for, I think.” The soul in the title is Ruskin’s soul — the part of the worker that is in the work because the work allowed enough latitude for it to be there. Guyer (ch. 15): “Ninety-eight percent of the thrill comes from knowing that the thing you designed works, and works almost the way you expected it would. If that happens, part of you is in that machine.”

Best chapters/pages to actually read
If you only have time for three chapters, take 2, 12, and 14. They give you, in order, the political setup that makes Eagle possible, the craft moment that makes Eagle work, and the human cost that makes Eagle expensive. If you have time for five, add 3 (signing-up) and 15 (the Ruskin frame).


Chapter 2 (The Wars) is the cleanest setup-of-stakes chapter in the book: EGO/FHP/Eagle politics, West’s clandestine VAX inspection, the constraint inheritance (“no mode bit”) from de Castro, and West’s two-faced positioning of Eagle as both insurance and answer-to-VAX. Read first if you want to understand how an internal R&D project survives when the company has officially bet on a different one.


Chapter 12 (The Case of the Missing NAND Gate) is the chapter to read for craft. A multi-day debugging case at the level of single signals between IP, Sys Cache, and Main Memory. Veres’s forward-search reframe (in the shower), Holberger naming the fix signal “NOT YET,” and the eight-cent NAND gate as the entire repair. Best chapter in the book on the asymmetry between finding a bug and fixing one. Pairs with the live-game-coordination patterns in Jason Schreier - Blood Sweat and Pixels (Diablo III’s Reaper of Souls late pivot is a similar synchronized-cut structure).


Chapter 14 (The Last Crunch) is the chapter where the human cost becomes most explicit. The carpenters arriving mid-final-push and tearing down the cubicle walls, the new sized-by-seniority cubicles “carved out in steel partitions,” Holberger’s burned paycheck stub, Rasala melting a chip socket with the heat gun and being teased back to life, and the first failed Adventure attempt followed by Carman literally shaking the ALU board to find the last flakey. Read this if you want a sober counterweight to the romance the book otherwise leans into.


Chapter 3 (Building a Team) is the most-cited single chapter in management literature. Alsing’s recruiting interview is reproduced in many books; the rejection of the candidate who listed “family life” as his avocation; the basement physical layout as a deliberate insecurity-generating device; Cray’s “they don’t know what’s impossible.” Read this if you want the source material for what later books (Schreier, Isaacson, Hoffman) reuse.


Chapter 15 (Canards) is Kidder’s interpretive payoff. The Ruskin / Gothic-cathedral frame; the team’s debate over who built Eagle; Guyer’s articulation that “98 percent of the thrill comes from knowing that the thing you designed works, and works almost the way you expected it would. If that happens, part of you is in that machine.” Read this if you want the book’s thesis stated rather than dramatized.


Chapter 9 (A Workshop) is the secondary character-study chapter. West’s restored 1780 farmhouse, the basement workshop with every tool labeled and put away, the Magic Marker board at work that says “Not Everything Worth Doing Is Worth Doing Well” while at home everything is done well. Read for the contradiction at the center of the book’s protagonist: an obsessive craftsman managing a deliberately quick-and-dirty engineering effort.


Chapter 11 (Shorter Than a Season) if you want the burnout case study. Josh Rosen’s trajectory from Special Systems “star” to the engineer leaving a note on the terminal saying he’s going to a Vermont commune and “will deal with no unit of time shorter than a season.” Pairs with Pete Walker - Complex PTSD for nervous-system vocabulary the engineering culture lacks.


Chapter 13 (Going to the Fair) if you want Kidder’s social-effects framing. Useful for what it doesn’t claim — revolution is the wrong word; computers extend executives’ reach without redistributing power; ~40% of commercial applications turn out uneconomical (cited but not sourced). Tom West’s bulldozer line.


The book’s edition pagination is unstable across reprints; chapter titles are the navigational key. The page_refs_reliable flag is set to false because the EPUB extraction here lacks page mapping.
What I would miss if I only read this note
I would miss the texture — the Microlounge dialogue (“Maybe the electrons aren’t in the computer at all. They just turn on the lights”), Rasala’s son saying “I hope your machine breaks, Daddy” (ch. 7), Rosemarie’s furtive grin at Alsing while nodding toward West’s office door (“It’s like one of those terrible movies. I just have to see how it comes out”) (ch. 3), the bus driver yelling “Keep it down back there!” on the NCC trip (ch. 13), West’s wife’s “Tom likes to do things ‘right’ — and I mean quotes around ‘right’” (ch. 9). These are doing analytical work that a summary cannot replace: they substantiate Kidder’s claim that Eagle was built by people who could be teased and who teased each other, and that the workplace was, in spite of the hours, funny.
I would also miss the texture of West’s evasiveness. The ghost-story laugh in the prologue, the way he reads notes upside down across his desk and then smiles to admit he can (“In business, you learn to read memos upside down” — ch. 16), the narrow tidy windowless office with one stack of papers edges-squared, the seven weeks behind a closed door designing the IOP after being told he couldn’t run the team. Kidder is making a quiet argument that West is unknowable — the recruits don’t know him, even Alsing only sees flashes of the old folksinger — and that this opacity is how he buffers the team. A summary loses the slow accumulation of that argument.
Finally I would miss the period detail the book is now valuable for: 1979-era 220-nanosecond clock cycles, 32-bit machines being a new product category, “knockoff companies” called “third-party peripheral manufacturers,” IBM’s three-year back-orders on the 4300 line, RCA and Xerox each losing about $1B trying to compete with IBM, the NCC fair as the central industry event, “knock-off” as a verb. These are not arguments — they are the substrate against which the book’s claims about engineering culture have to be evaluated.
Important examples

The clandestine VAX inspection (ch. 2). West walks into a customer’s machine room, opens a VAX cabinet still being installed by a DEC technician, counts chips and types. ~22,500 BOM (DEC was selling for >100K). The point is not industrial espionage — the literature was public — but West needing to touch the machine. “In some engineers, however, reading does not constitute knowing. For them, touch is the first of the senses.”
Wallach’s golden moment (ch. 4). Eight rings = eight segments = first three address bits. A few days of work after years of design machines that never shipped. “Where did that come from?”
The simulator (ch. 8). Firth’s paper Eagle in Trixie. The rigged competition with Peck. Without it, microcode debugging would have queued behind hardware debugging.
The missing NAND gate (ch. 12). Eight cents wholesale. Holberger names the new signal “NOT YET” in the spirit of Eclipse Group naming.
The melted chip socket (ch. 14). Rasala’s heat-gun mistake reanimates the team after the August slump.
Carman shakes the ALU board (ch. 14). The VP literally shakes the board on its extender; Gallifrey fails on the spot. They replace all sockets in the center of the ALU; the last flakey is gone.
The clock-on-a-cart (ch. 16). Alsing carrying West’s office clock to West’s new upstairs office; getting lost; sitting around the cart in a windowless room. “Going back downstairs Alsing had the feeling he had just attended a funeral.”
“Business Development” (epilogue). West, asked his title at the announcement event door, says “Business Development.” The reporter doesn’t realize he was the project lead. Alsing pulls the reporter aside to correct the record.

Critiques and limitations

Single-project sample size. The book describes one project at one company in one year. Kidder’s generalizations about engineering culture (signing-up, mushroom management, pinball) are drawn from an N of one. The book would have been stronger with a comparison case — even a brief one to FHP / North Carolina, which Kidder treats almost entirely from West’s perspective. Readers should be wary of importing the book’s organizing concepts into other contexts wholesale.
Access asymmetry. Kidder was inside the Eclipse Group basement, not in de Castro’s office, not in North Carolina, not on the FHP team. De Castro is interviewed but only briefly; FHP engineers are not. The result is that the book takes the Eclipse Group’s framing of the politics largely at face value. The brief encounter with de Castro (ch. 15) is more equivocal than the team’s caricature suggests — “I think that if you try to foster that attitude, you will be unsuccessful” is a real management theory, not just laconic Captain-talk.
Workplace harm framed individually. Like later books in the engineering-narrative tradition (Jason Schreier - Blood Sweat and Pixels especially), Kidder humanizes individual decision-makers in ways that can underplay structural exploitation. Hour-norms set by exempt-employee classification; overtime denied to engineers but paid to technicians (ch. 14); the carpenters timed to disrupt the final push; the cubicles sized by seniority “carved out in steel partitions.” The book notices these but does not theorize them. A modern reader needs supplementary labor-history vocabulary (game-worker organizing post-2018 is the rough analogue).
Period of business model. Eagle was a minicomputer in a market of three years’ lead times and discrete product cycles. Software was something you shipped on floppy disks. The cycle Kidder describes (1-year project, 2-year product life of the previous Eclipse, fixed competitor like VAX) does not generalize cleanly to web/SaaS/live-service contexts where the launched product is the first day of an ongoing operation. Read the book for what the engineers cared about and how they organized themselves; do not read it for cycle-time generalizations.
Romance vs. reportage. Kidder is sympathetic to the team and to West in ways that occasionally read as romance (the closing folk-song image; the Ruskin frame). Some details are reported as the team told them (the Keronix arson rumor; the de Castro Fudgsicle scene). Readers should treat single-source anecdotes as such.
Gender. The team is overwhelmingly male; Betty Shanahan is “the team’s lone female engineer” (ch. 3) and Rosemarie Seale is the secretary-emotional-anchor. Kidder notices but does not interrogate. Read against contemporary scholarship on gender in 1970s-80s computing if you want a fuller picture.
Reproducibility. West’s central question to himself in ch. 14 — “Wasn’t that obvious? You could never reproduce a project such as this one, even if you wanted to.” — followed by his own answer (“Yeah, you can repeat it”) — is the book’s most-cited line that is also most likely to be wrong. The Eclipse Group did not reproduce; it dispersed. Whether the ethic (West’s word, ch. 16) reproduces is unanswered.

What I would miss / further what I want to track

The dispersal arc. Wallach later co-founded Convex Computer (secondary, not verified in this vault). Alsing went to California. Rasala followed. West stayed at Data General into a marketing role with Asia-Pacific responsibilities, then eventually left. The book ends in fall 1980 / spring 1981; everything I want to know about whether pinball did reproduce happens after the last page.
The financial epilogue. Data General’s ~1981 disappointing earnings (ch. 16) presaged a long decline; the company was acquired by EMC in 1999 (secondary, not verified in this vault). The MV/8000 was the high point; the Eclipse line itself was a multi-year run.
The legal epilogue. Several Wallach-era patents were filed. Whose names ended up on which patent claim, and how the meetings (epilogue) reconciled, is a thread Kidder leaves dangling.

Research uses

Engineering management. This is the book’s primary research use. The named mechanisms — signing-up, mushroom management, flying upside down, trust as the late-stage replacement for control, pinball as the real reward, the buffer-manager — are operational concepts that can be tested against a contemporary engineering team. Especially useful for thinking about what kinds of projects benefit from sealing the team off vs. integrating it tightly with the rest of the company.
Recruitment design. Alsing’s interview script is a classroom artifact for thinking about how high-commitment hiring rituals work and how they fail (the candidate who lists family life). Read alongside Reid Hoffman - The Start-Up of You for the founder-network framing and against modern critiques of “mission-driven” hiring rhetoric.
Software-process thinking. The simulator chapter (ch. 8) is unusually clean as a case study in tooling investment as a multiplier. The Peck-vs-Firth rigged competition is also a small classic of incentive design.
History of computing. The book is contemporaneous primary-press reporting on the late minicomputer era, useful for syllabus reading on the period between the IBM mainframe age and the personal-computer revolution, alongside more recent accounts like Chris Miller - Chip War for the broader semiconductor trajectory. The 32-bit supermini moment (DEC VAX 11/780, Eagle / Eclipse MV/8000, others) is the architectural transition that made Unix-on-supermini and then the workstation era possible.
Labor history. Read against later game-industry crunch literature (Jason Schreier - Blood Sweat and Pixels) and pre-tech-union organizing literature for how exempt-employee classification, deniable overtime obligations, and “you signed up” rhetoric prefigure contemporary tech-labor discourse.
Literary nonfiction craft. Kidder is an exemplar of the long-form-immersion form. Useful as a model for any writer who wants to spend a year inside an engineering team and produce a book; the prologue’s storm-on-the-sloop opening is one of the most-imitated set pieces in the form.
Personal-decision use. The book is also a personal artifact for engineers who want to think about what trades they are making. Rosen’s commune note, Holberger’s burned paycheck stub, Wallach’s “I’m a fighter” framing, West’s own postpartum wake-up at 3 AM — these are not management theory, they are case material for an engineering career.

Key concepts

Signing-up — the implicit overtime contract a recruit accepts by joining; the productive unit of the team’s labor; see Signing Up (Soul of a New Machine).
Mushroom management — “put ‘em in the dark, feed ‘em shit, and watch ‘em grow”; the deliberate withholding of corporate context from recruits to keep them focused on the work; see Mushroom Management.
Pinball — the implicit reward of getting to play another game (build the next machine) if you win this one; West’s coinage; partly a lie in retrospect since the team disbanded; see Pinball Reward Structure.
Flying upside down — West’s metaphor for the Eagle project’s risk profile (sole-source PALs, kids fresh out of school, year-long schedule); see Flying Upside Down.
The kludge — the local idiom for an inelegant computer design; “a wart on a wart on a wart”; the most disdainful term in the engineer’s vocabulary; the constraint that Eagle’s Eclipse compatibility forced on Wallach.
Trust as a late-stage management substitute for control — West’s word in ch. 7; the move he had to make when he discovered he could not himself debug Eagle.
The buffer manager — Alsing and Rosemarie’s reconstruction of West’s job: absorb politics, refuse upward criticism of the team, let recruits believe Eagle is theirs, accept that you will be misperceived as cold and absent.
The wars — the team’s idiom for internal company politics over which design becomes the company’s next product (FHP vs EGO, Eagle vs FHP). Cold Start Theory’s adversarial cluster dynamics extend the same pattern at company-vs-company scale.
Fly upside down / golden moment / canard / no muss no fuss — the Eclipse Group’s small dialect, evidence Kidder gathers in ch. 2 and ch. 7 that a sealed engineering team develops its own argot as a marker of in-group commitment.

Links to other books

Engineering-narrative complement to Jason Schreier - Blood Sweat and Pixels — Kidder is one project, one year, one team; Schreier is ten case studies across a decade. The mechanisms generalize: scope-pressure (Schreier ch. 1, Kidder ch. 2), late-stage synchronized cuts (Diablo III’s Reaper of Souls, Eagle’s “no, the schedule is real”), engine misfit (Frostbite/Dragon Age, Eclipse-instruction-set/Eagle), and crunch as a scheduling technology rather than emergency response. Kidder is the source text these later books are working in.
Founder-narrative contrast with Walter Isaacson - Elon Musk — Isaacson centers the visionary; Kidder centers the team and the manager who buffers the team. The Kidder reading of the Tesla production line would emphasize the line workers and the mid-level production managers, not Musk.
Hardware/industrial history adjacent to Chris Miller - Chip War — Miller covers the semiconductor industry over decades at geopolitical scale; Kidder covers one rung up the stack (chip → board → CPU → minicomputer) at one project. The PAL-chip sole-source crisis (Kidder ch. 6, ch. 14) is the small-scale instance of the supply-chain-fragility theme Miller develops.
Crunch / human-cost adjacent to Pete Walker - Complex PTSD — Rosen’s burnout (ch. 11), Rasala’s “long-term tiredness,” Holberger’s “burn-out city” (ch. 14), and West’s “I wake up at 3 AM, sweating, worried” (ch. 16) all point to nervous-system consequences that Kidder gestures at but does not clinicalize. The vocabulary Walker provides is exactly what the engineering culture in 1979 lacked.
Lean iteration counterpoint to Eric Ries - The Lean Startup — Ries emphasizes Build-Measure-Learn at the level of customer-validated learning. Kidder’s Eagle is the opposite case: a year of design and debugging behind a sealed door before the first customer sees the machine, justified by the fact that you can’t iterate a CPU after silicon is laid down. The two books are useful read against each other for thinking about which kinds of artifacts admit which kinds of iteration.
Talent / deliberate-practice adjacent to Geoff Colvin - Talent Is Overrated — Wallach’s spec rewritten seven times; Alsing’s teaching-by-rigged-competition; the Hardy Boys’ eventual ability to “feel what was wrong with their machine” (ch. 15). Kidder is showing deliberate practice happening in industrial conditions, not training conditions.
Network / cold-start adjacent to Andrew Chen - The Cold Start Problem — DG’s NCC booth set higher than IBM’s, the “Hertz-Avis” advertising strategy against DEC, Wallach’s tour of pin-compatible memory makers and OEMs in ch. 13 — a snapshot of a tightly networked industry where small startups feed off the giants.
Founder-stake / skin-in-the-game counterpoint to Reid Hoffman - The Start-Up of You — the engineers had no equity stake to speak of; the implicit reward (pinball) was non-financial. Useful for thinking about what non-equity commitment mechanisms can substitute for skin in the game in highly skilled creative work.
Authoritarian-capitalism comparison to Angela Huyue Zhang - High Wire / Meg E. Rithmire - Land Bargains and Chinese Capitalism — the Eclipse Group’s sealed-bubble dynamic, in which the team is allowed to invent precisely because it is buffered from the larger institution, has surprising parallels to Authoritarian Commons dynamics where local autonomy is allowed inside a larger framework that can withdraw it at any moment. The fall-1980 disbanding of the Eclipse Group is the moment the larger institution withdrew the autonomy.
