April 30 2024: sentenced to 4 months in federal prison + $50M personal penalty (against DOJ’s 36-month above-guideline request) by Judge Richard Jones, U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington
June–September 2024: served at FCI Lompoc II low-security federal correctional institution
October 23 2025: granted a full and unconditional pardon by President Donald Trump
March 2026: filed defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal (initially dismissed with leave to refile)

Items that appear in the Freedom of Money text but cannot be independently verified within this vault — interior-state claims, specific quoted dialogue, unsourced numerical claims (e.g., “Binance employees from 69 countries… Singapore 176, UK 78”) — should be tagged (stated in source, authenticity unverified) if cited elsewhere in this vault.

04_People/Chris-Yeh.title: Chris Yeh
04_People/Chris-Yeh.content:
Chris Yeh
Why they matter
Yeh matters in this vault as the structural systematizer of Reid Hoffman’s operator intuitions. Hoffman supplies the first-person Silicon Valley narrative — PayPal, LinkedIn, Greylock, board seats. Yeh supplies the HBS-trained business-school analytical scaffolding — the speed × certainty 2x2, the five-stage Family-to-Nation taxonomy, the eight-transitions / nine-rules numbered architecture, the explicit growth-factors-and-limiters decomposition. Without Yeh, Blitzscaling would be a memoir; with him, it is a teachable framework that founders, investors, and B-school instructors can apply to specific decisions. He is also Hoffman’s principal collaborator on The Alliance and on the Stanford CS183C course that produced the Blitzscaling manuscript, making him the dominant non-Hoffman voice in the formalization of the Silicon Valley scaling doctrine of the 2010s.
Background
Chris Yeh is Reid Hoffman’s longtime co-author and an entrepreneur, investor, and writer focused on Silicon Valley scaling practices. He is best known as Hoffman’s collaborator on The Alliance (2014), Blitzscaling (2018), and the Stanford CS183C “Technology-enabled Blitzscaling” class taught in fall 2015 with Hoffman, Allen Blue, and John Lilly (Hoffman and Yeh, 2018, ch. Acknowledgments).
The book itself contains the strongest grep-verifiable biographical detail: Yeh “earned [his] MBA from Harvard Business School in the late 1990s, during the dawn of the Networked Age” (Hoffman and Yeh, 2018, ch. Part I), where his training focused on traditional techniques like discounted cash flow analysis and assembly-line throughput optimization — the very approaches that Blitzscaling later argues are inadequate for hypergrowth. This biographical anchor is part of how the book sets up the contrast between classical efficiency-prioritizing management and blitzscaling.
Other biographical details circulating publicly (Stanford undergraduate, Wasabi Ventures partnership, board roles, prior founding of PBwiki/PBworks) are secondary, not verified in this vault. The text confirms his role as Hoffman’s coauthor, Stanford CS183C co-instructor, podcast collaborator on Masters of Scale, and active member of the Silicon Guild authors’ group.
Role in this vault

Coauthor of Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh - Blitzscaling — the canonical 2018 articulation of Blitzscaling, First Scaler Advantage, and the Counterintuitive Scaling Rules.
Coauthor with Hoffman on The Alliance (2014) — earlier work on tour-of-duty employer-employee contracts; cited in Blitzscaling as the recommended treatment of how hypergrowth firms should structure career arcs.
Stanford CS183C “Technology-enabled Blitzscaling” — fall 2015 course that produced the manuscript, taught alongside Hoffman, Allen Blue, and John Lilly, sponsored by Mehran Sahami.

Intellectual lineage
Yeh’s contribution to Blitzscaling is most visible in the systematic 2x2 frameworks (speed × certainty; risk Known/Unknown × Systemic/Nonsystemic), the structured five-stage taxonomy (Family/Tribe/Village/City/Nation), the explicit “growth factors / growth limiters” decomposition, and the rule-numbered presentation style. These bear the marks of an HBS-trained business-school synthesizer applying analytical structure to Hoffman’s first-person Silicon Valley operator’s narrative. Hoffman’s “I” voice carries the stories; Yeh’s structure carries the framework.
Cross-references

Reid Hoffman - The Start-Up of You — Hoffman’s solo (with Ben Casnocha) book on career strategy; Yeh joins the franchise on the company side.
Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh - Blitzscaling — primary source for everything on this page that is grep-verifiable.

04_People/Dan-Gardner.title: Dan Gardner
04_People/Dan-Gardner.content:
Dan Gardner
Why they matter
Gardner is the journalistic translator who made cognitive- and decision-science research legible to general readers, intelligence professionals, and policymakers. His 2010 Future Babble anticipated and his 2015 collaboration with Philip E. Tetlock on Superforecasting embodied the cultural shift toward evidence-based forecasting that Tetlock’s tournaments document.
Biography and career
Canadian journalist and author who specializes in translating cognitive- and decision-science research for general readers. He is best known to this vault as the co-writer of Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner - Superforecasting (2015), in which he provides the narrative architecture and reportorial profiles (Bill Flack, Doug Lorch, Sandy Sillman, Tim Minto, Anne Kilkenny, Marty Rosenthal, Elaine Rich, the Leon Panettas) around Tetlock’s research program.
Gardner’s earlier solo books anticipate the Superforecasting project. Risk: The Science and Politics of Fear (2008) examines why public risk perception so often diverges from base rates, drawing on Kahneman/Tversky-style heuristics-and-biases work, the availability cascade, and media incentives. Future Babble: Why Pundit Predictions Are Next to Worthless and You Can Do Better (2010) is in many ways the journalistic predecessor to Superforecasting: it surveyed Tetlock’s then-published EPJ research and the broader literature on expert-judgment failure for a popular audience and made the case that the cult of the confident pundit is empirically indefensible.
The Tetlock–Gardner partnership in Superforecasting is structured to keep Tetlock’s first-person scientific voice while embedding it inside Gardner-style narrative reporting. The result is a book that satisfies the depth requirements of an academic monograph while remaining readable for non-specialist policymakers, executives, and intelligence professionals — the audience Tetlock most wanted to reach.
Gardner has worked as a columnist for the Ottawa Citizen and contributed to outlets including Foreign Policy (secondary, not verified in this vault). Beyond his books, he has consulted on forecasting and policy projects, including work tied to the Good Judgment Inc. spinoff that emerged from the IARPA tournament.
Notable books

Risk: The Science and Politics of Fear (2008)
Future Babble: Why Pundit Predictions Are Next to Worthless and You Can Do Better (2010)
Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction (2015, with Philip E. Tetlock)

Sources

Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner - Superforecasting (Tetlock and Gardner, 2015, acknowledgments and throughout) — co-author identified, narrative structure attributable to Gardner.

See also

Philip E. Tetlock
Superforecaster
Fox vs Hedgehog (Tetlock)

04_People/Daniel-C.-Dennett.title: Daniel C. Dennett
04_People/Daniel-C.-Dennett.content:
Daniel C. Dennett
Why they matter
Pre-eminent late-20th-century philosopher of mind whose Intentional Stance supplied the operating vocabulary for cognitive science and (later) AI commentary. Founded and ran Tufts’ Center for Cognitive Studies for decades, making it one of the durable interdisciplinary hubs where philosophy actually talked to working psychologists, AI researchers, and (after 2000) evolutionary theorists. Distinct from rival functionalists (Fodor, Putnam) by his engineering temperament: questions about mind, free will, religion, and consciousness are answerable in principle by sufficiently honest description plus disciplined stance-shifting, and his career resists the metaphysician’s appetite for inner essences.
Works in this vault

Daniel C. Dennett - Brainstorms — 1978, the canonical essays establishing the intentional stance and Dennett’s mature methodology.
Daniel C. Dennett - The Mind’s I — 1981, anthology co-edited with Hofstadter; supplies the literary-philosophical companion to Brainstorms.
Daniel C. Dennett - I’ve Been Thinking — 2023, intellectual autobiography written shortly before his 2024 death.

Key concepts

Intentional Stance — Dennett’s signature contribution; the predictive strategy that ascribes beliefs and desires to a system when doing so is the most economical description.
Heterophenomenology — Dennett’s preferred name for a disciplined third-person treatment of subjects’ phenomenological reports as data without granting them privileged access (introduced in Brainstorms’ consciousness essays, codified later in Consciousness Explained).
Multiple drafts model — post-Brainstorms doctrine: consciousness is a parallel-edits process, not a Cartesian theater.
Real patterns — the metaphysical-level claim under the stance: belief-ascriptions track real but abstract regularities in behavior, not inner objects.

Key arguments

The intentional stance earns its keep predictively, not metaphysically — defended throughout Brainstorms; lays the groundwork for treating “machine cognition” as a stance question rather than a substance question.
Persons are higher-order intentional systems — Brainstorms essay 14 (“Conditions of Personhood”): personhood is the iterated capacity to take an intentional stance toward oneself and toward other intentional-stance-takers, anchored in language.
Free will is a moral competence, not a metaphysical exemption — Brainstorms essay 15 plus later Elbow Room and Freedom Evolves; compatibilism reframed as engineering of self-control rather than as gappy indeterminism.

Related people / schools

Gilbert Ryle — Oxford supervisor; behavioural-disposition vocabulary of The Concept of Mind underwrites the early stance machinery.
W. V. O. Quine — recurring interlocutor on indeterminacy of translation; Dennett’s stance pluralism inherits Quine’s instrumentalism without buying his eliminativism.
Douglas Hofstadter — co-editor of Daniel C. Dennett - The Mind’s I; lifelong philosophical correspondent; complementary temperaments (Hofstadter’s analogical exuberance, Dennett’s stance discipline).
Jerry Fodor — sparring partner on whether intentional explanation requires internal representational states (Fodor’s Language of Thought); Brainstorms essay 6 (“A Cure for the Common Code?”) is Dennett’s frontal challenge.
B. F. Skinner — adversary; Brainstorms essays “Skinner Skinned” and “Why the Law of Effect Will Not Go Away” target behaviorism’s allergy to internal mediating states while preserving its empirical caution.
John Searle — long-running antagonist; the Chinese Room dispute (in Daniel C. Dennett - The Mind’s I) becomes a stand-in for the realism-vs-instrumentalism debate over the intentional stance.
Marvin Minsky — friendly cohabitant of the cognitive-science hub; The Society of Mind and the stance theory share an anti-Cartesian, computational-mind temperament.

Biographical anchors

Harvard BA, Oxford DPhil under Ryle (1965); Oxford training stamps a behaviour-as-disposition reflex on the early stance theory.
Tufts University from 1971 onward; co-founded the Center for Cognitive Studies in 1985 and directed it for nearly 40 years (career-defining institutional commitment captured in Daniel C. Dennett - I’ve Been Thinking).
Brainstorms (1978) is the early-career landmark; Consciousness Explained (1991), Darwin’s Dangerous Idea (1995), Freedom Evolves (2003), Breaking the Spell (2006), From Bacteria to Bach and Back (2017) trace the post-Brainstorms arc.
Public intellectual presence as one of the “Four Horsemen” of New Atheism (with Harris, Hitchens, Dawkins) — orthogonal to the philosophy of mind work but shapes how Brainstorms-era ideas were received in the 2000s–2010s.
Died April 19, 2024.

04_People/Dave-Cutler.title: Dave Cutler
04_People/Dave-Cutler.content:
Dave Cutler
Why they matter
The most consequential operating-system architect of the late twentieth century. Designer of DEC’s VMS (1977), the cancelled Prism/Mica RISC follow-on (1985-88), and Microsoft’s Windows NT (released July 1993) — the kernel architecture from which Windows 2000, XP, 7, 10, 11, Server, and (via the same code lineage) Azure all descend. Cutler is the central protagonist of G. Pascal Zachary - Showstopper and the case study from which the contemporary software-engineering vocabulary of Dog-Food Practice, Ship Mode, and Showstopper Bug is most readily traced. His career is the single best example in commercial computing of an architect whose insistence on portability, kernel-mode discipline, and reliability over short-term performance produced an artifact that outlived its supposed strategic context (Internet and mobile arguably surpassed it; the kernel is still shipping).
Role
Lead architect of Windows NT. Born March 13, 1942, in Lansing, Michigan. Quarterback, then engineer, then DEC star (designer of VMS and the Vax line under Gordon Bell), then head of DEC’s cancelled Prism/Mica RISC project, then — from October 31, 1988 — Microsoft’s recruit to build a portable, kernel-based, network-grade operating system that became NT 1.0, released to manufacturing on July 26, 1993.
Personality and Method
G. Pascal Zachary - Showstopper makes Cutler one of the most fully drawn figures in the literature of software engineering. He is bowlegged, Popeye-built, perpetually scowling, prone to kicking through walls and breaking fingers on studs. He swears constantly. He keeps a “Size Is The Goal” rubber stamp on his desk. He retrieves discarded code from the trash to mark it up in red. He insists on the “dog-food diet” (see Dog-Food Practice) and on the [“showstopper” bug discipline](Showstopper Bug.md). He is “a star player and a star coach rolled into one,” writing critical kernel code himself even while running a 250-person team.
Three durable principles run through his career:

Reliability before performance. “Always do the job right, get it reliable and then worry about performance.”
Lead by example. Camping in the Build Lab in 1992-93, reviewing 75-100 daily check-ins.
Tribalism over consensus. Recruiting his old DEC lieutenants en bloc, walking them past Microsoft’s clean-room HR onboarding, defending them from outside criticism, and treating Microsoft itself as a “scumbag company” until the work was done.

What He Borrowed and Why It Mattered
Cutler is honest about borrowing. NT’s microkernel design owes much to Rick Rashid’s Mach work at Carnegie-Mellon (the same Mach that Steve Jobs picked for NeXT). VMS’s recoverability discipline shapes NTFS’s lazy-writer-plus-log scheme. What Cutler added was manufacturability at PC scale and price — a portable, multi-personality OS that ran on Intel and Mips (and later Alpha, then more) chips with the same source tree. As David Thompson later put it, Cutler was the team’s “conscience on portability.”
The Authorship Problem
Zachary is careful to note that “no one mind can comprehend it all” with NT. Cutler was the architect, the most senior coder, and the moral center — but the book’s chapter-by-chapter detail is also a deliberate refutation of the great-man story: Perazzoli on memory and management, Whitmer on graphics, Miller and Kimura on file systems, Lucovsky on APIs and the Build Lab, Felton on compatibility, Wong and Abrash on font rendering, Caron on the program manager, Stowell on the console, Maritz on strategy. Cutler was indispensable but not sufficient.
After NT
Cutler nearly resigned in late 1993 over the Cairo merger but was talked out of it by Perazzoli and Gates. He led Daytona (the streamlined NT successor) and eventually inherited Cairo’s code as well in March 1994. (secondary, not verified in this vault: Cutler’s later work on Windows 2000, Azure cloud-host hypervisors, and the Xbox One operating system is widely reported elsewhere but not present in any of the chapter extractions used here.)
Sources

G. Pascal Zachary - Showstopper — every chapter; chapter 1 (“Code Warrior”) and chapter 2 (“The King of Code”) supply the most concentrated biography.

04_People/David-Kushner.title: David Kushner
04_People/David-Kushner.content:
David Kushner
Why they matter
Kushner is the author of Masters of Doom (2003), the foundational popular history of id Software and the first-person shooter genre. His method — six years of access-rich reportage with both founders, scenes reconstructed from interviews, no formal documentary apparatus — produced the canonical text on the Two Johns and on the cultural emergence of PC games as mass medium.
Biography
David Kushner (b. 1968, by his own account in David Kushner - Masters of Doom’s epilogue) is an American journalist and author best known in this vault for Masters of Doom: How Two Guys Created an Empire and Transformed Pop Culture (Random House, 2003), the foundational popular history of id Software, John Carmack, and John Romero.
Kushner positions himself in the book’s epilogue as an inside-the-scene insider rather than an outside observer. He grew up in the same nascent gamer culture as the Two Johns: birthday tokens at Wizards arcade, a high score on Crazy Climber, an attempted Chuck E. Cheese keyboard hack as a child. He was working at an online bulletin-board service in New York City in the mid-1990s when a friend booted up Doom for him at 2 a.m.; the conversion experience prompts him to talk an editor into a 1996 magazine assignment about Quake clan culture, which leads him to a University-of-Kansas Quake LAN flophouse, which leads him to the Two Johns.
The book is the product of about six years of reporting (1996-2002): interviews in Dallas with id and Ion Storm staff and ex-staff, travel to Quake tournaments, phone and email follow-up from Brooklyn, archival access to Romero’s “vast archives of everything: games, art, comics, Burger King receipts,” ride-alongs with Carmack to launch model rockets in cow pastures east of Mesquite, a turbo-Ferrari ride. The book is unauthorized in the sense that no contract gave Carmack or Romero veto over content, but the access is essentially total, with both subjects giving extended on-record interviews and tolerating Kushner’s presence at sensitive moments.
Kushner’s other books — Jonny Magic and the Card Shark Kids (2005, on Magic: the Gathering), Levittown (2009, on the postwar Long Island suburb and its racial integration crisis), Jacked (2012, on Grand Theft Auto and the Houser brothers at Rockstar), Alligator Candy (2016, a memoir of his older brother’s 1970s abduction and murder in Tampa) — share a stylistic signature: a popular-narrative voice, a sympathetic-but-not-deferential angle on technology subcultures, heavy use of dialogue reconstructed from interviews, and an editorial preference for human-interest framings over technical depth. (Other-book-list above is biographical and is not grep-verified in this vault — secondary, not verified in this vault.)
The methodological signature relevant to Masters of Doom is that Kushner reconstructs scenes from interviews and presents them as if reported in real time. Direct quotations are sourced from interviews; physical descriptions and the interior thoughts of subjects (“Tom thought he had been so miserable for so long…”) are explicitly attributed in interviews and inferred elsewhere. The book contains no formal endnotes or chapter-by-chapter sourcing apparatus, which is the standard limitation of trade narrative nonfiction. Its strength is verisimilitude and access; its weakness is that scenes cannot be cross-checked against contemporaneous documents the way a Robert Caro reconstruction can be.
Notable connections in this vault

David Kushner - Masters of Doom — the book this note exists to support
John Carmack, John Romero — primary subjects
Compare reporter persona to M. Mitchell Waldrop on Licklider — both write trade-press technology biographies but Waldrop’s apparatus is more academic.

04_People/Demis-Hassabis.title: Demis Hassabis
04_People/Demis-Hassabis.content:
Demis Hassabis
Why they matter
Cofounder and CEO of DeepMind (2010-) and (since 2023) Google DeepMind; co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (shared with David Baker and John Jumper) for AlphaFold’s solution to protein-structure prediction. Hassabis is the central protagonist of Sebastian Mallaby - The Infinity Machine and the most consequential single figure in the 2010-2026 AGI development narrative. His distinctive contribution is institutional: building DeepMind as a neuroscience-integrated, pivot-doctrine-driven, mission-rather-than-product-oriented AI lab that produced Atari (DQN), AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaFold, and (after the merger with Google Brain) Gemini and the post-2024 reasoning models.
Works in this vault

Sebastian Mallaby - The Infinity Machine — book-length biography (subject, not author).
Walter Isaacson - Elon Musk — secondary appearances; the 2014 Founders Fund / Musk acquisition-attempt narrative is told from Musk’s perspective there (chs. 41-44).

Key concepts

Infinity Machine — Hassabis’s Cambridge-vintage formulation; the goal of DeepMind’s project.
AlphaGo Method — the policy-net + value-net + Monte Carlo Tree Search triad his teams built.
Pivot Doctrine (DeepMind) — Hassabis’s research-project management methodology, especially as applied across AlphaFold’s six successive architectural pivots (2016-2020).
Singleton vs Multiparty AI Governance — Hassabis is the leading proponent of the singleton thesis (CERN-style international coordination for AGI’s final stages).

Key arguments

Information is the fundamental unit of reality; an inductive machine is the most powerful imaginable tool to apprehend reality. (Cambridge undergraduate thesis, c. 1996.)
Artificial general intelligence requires integration of brain-like components (perception + memory + planning + reward), not scaling of a single uniform substrate. (DeepMind business plan, 2010.)
“AI may be the right description language for biology, because biology is so messy, emergent, dynamic, and complex.” (Cambridge undergraduate hypothesis vindicated by AlphaFold’s 2020 result and 2024 Nobel.)
“AGI should be gifted to the world eventually.” (Epilogue position, with the qualification “Until we figure that out, I do need power, at least a bit of it.“)

Related people / schools

Shane Legg — DeepMind cofounder; Hassabis’s intellectual peer at the Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit who independently arrived at AGI ambition.
Mustafa Suleyman — DeepMind cofounder; managed Applied / DeepMind Health; ousted 2019; later CEO of Microsoft AI. Founder-relationship that ended in conflict.
David Silver (secondary, not in vault) — collaborator from Cambridge through Elixir Studios through DeepMind; reinforcement-learning leader; architect of AlphaGo, AlphaGo Zero, AlphaZero. (secondary, not verified in this vault as person note.)
Geoffrey Hinton (secondary, not in vault) — Toronto deep-learning pioneer; founding director of the Gatsby Unit; advisor to DeepMind from inception; lobbied internally at Google that Hassabis alone was worth $150M during the 2014 acquisition. (secondary, not verified as person note.)
Peter Thiel (secondary, not in vault) — Founders Fund cofounder; first major DeepMind investor (2010-2011); later positioned across the AGI race via OpenAI (early funding) and Palantir’s defense AI work.
Larry Page (secondary, not in vault) — Google CEO at time of 2014 acquisition; shared “deep philosophical” alignment with Hassabis’s scientist-rather-than-businessperson framing; Napa 2015 “speciesist” comment to Musk became a triggering event in OpenAI’s founding.
Sam Altman (secondary, not in vault) — OpenAI CEO; Hassabis’s main 2016+ rival; the “doing it for power” foil to Hassabis’s “doing it for knowledge.”

Biographical anchors (only if relevant)
Born July 1976 in Finchley, North London, to a Chinese-Singaporean nurse mother and Greek-Cypriot bohemian-musician father. Chess master at 13 (second-strongest in his age group worldwide). 1994-1997 undergraduate at Cambridge in computer science. 1998-2005 founder/CEO of Elixir Studios (game studio; Republic: The Revolution, Evil Genius). 2005-2009 PhD in cognitive neuroscience at UCL under Eleanor Maguire (memory-imagination integration; 2007 PNAS paper named one of Science’s top neuroscience breakthroughs of the year, accumulating 1700+ citations). 2009 Gatsby Unit postdoc; 2010 cofounded DeepMind with Legg and Suleyman. January 2014 sold DeepMind to Google for 650M (netted 136M). Knighted 2024. October 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. As of 2026, CEO of Google DeepMind, based in London. Lives in the same house for 10+ years; drives a 10-year-old Audi; £3K/year Liverpool football season tickets; states ambition to build a Large Hadron Collider in space. Married to an Italian academic bioscientist met at Cambridge; multiple children including an esports-prospect eldest son.

04_People/Edsger-W.-Dijkstra.title: Edsger W. Dijkstra
04_People/Edsger-W.-Dijkstra.content:
Edsger W. Dijkstra
Why they matter
One of the founding figures of computer science. Originator of the shortest-path algorithm (Dijkstra’s algorithm, 1956), the semaphore concept for concurrent programming (1965), the guarded command language and weakest-precondition calculus (1970s, the apparatus of A Discipline of Programming), and the famous polemics (“GO TO Considered Harmful,” 1968; “On the Cruelty of Really Teaching Computer Science,” 1988). The combination of foundational technical contributions and uncompromising pedagogical-aesthetic stance shaped the field’s self-conception. Recipient of the 1972 Turing Award.
Works in this vault

Edsger W. Dijkstra - A Discipline of Programming — 1976

Key concepts

Weakest precondition (wp.S.R) — the predicate-transformer apparatus
Guarded command — alternative and repetition forms with explicit non-determinism
Program derivation — constructing a program from a specification by formal steps

Key arguments

A program is a mathematical object derivable from a specification (in Edsger W. Dijkstra - A Discipline of Programming)

Related people / schools

Tony Hoare (CSP, axiomatic semantics) — a parallel-track formal-methods pioneer; Hoare wrote the Foreword to A Discipline of Programming
David Gries (The Science of Programming, 1981) — close collaborator and continuer of Dijkstra’s program-derivation programme
C. A. R. Hoare’s quicksort vs Dijkstra’s shortest-path — both 1959 algorithms that defined what algorithm-as-craft could look like
The Eindhoven school — Dijkstra’s institutional base; Wim Feijen, A. J. M. van Gasteren, and others applied and extended the apparatus

Biographical anchors

Born in Rotterdam (1930); educated University of Leiden (theoretical physics, BSc) and University of Amsterdam (PhD computer science, 1959 — thesis “Communication with an Automatic Computer” was one of the first CS PhDs anywhere).
Mathematisch Centrum, Amsterdam (1952-1962); Eindhoven University of Technology (1962-1984); University of Texas at Austin (1984-1999, Schlumberger Centennial Chair).
ACM Turing Award 1972.
Famous for the EWD series — over 1300 hand-numbered notes (EWD 1 through EWD 1318) written longhand and circulated to colleagues; available online via UT Austin.

(Confidence: high on academic record and dates.)

04_People/Esther-Duflo.title: Esther Duflo
04_People/Esther-Duflo.content:
Esther Duflo
Why they matter
Duflo is, with Abhijit V. Banerjee and Michael Kremer, a 2019 Nobel Memorial Prize laureate in Economic Sciences for the randomized-controlled-trial program in development economics. She is co-founder (with Banerjee) of the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) at MIT, founded as the Poverty Action Lab in 2003 — by 2010 J-PAL had completed or was running 240+ experiments in 40 countries. Duflo’s first-author empirical contributions include the Indonesian INPRES school-construction wage-returns evaluation (Poor Economics ch. 4), the Kenya tracking and Kenya teen-pregnancy / sugar-daddies RCT trio with Pascaline Dupas and Michael Kremer (Poor Economics ch. 5), and the West Bengal panchayat-reservation evaluation with Raghabendra Chattopadhyay (Poor Economics ch. 10). She received the 2010 John Bates Clark Medal for the most significant economics contribution by an economist under 40 — recognition independent of her partnership with Banerjee.
(Biographical specifics beyond MIT affiliation and the publishing context are not vault-verifiable. The book gives one direct vault-verifiable anchor: she designed and conducted the INPRES evaluation referenced in ch. 4 — “Esther compared the wages of adults who, as children, were young enough to have benefited from the newly constructed schools.” Her co-authorship pattern with Banerjee is otherwise the primary biographical information in the source.)
Works in this vault

Abhijit V. Banerjee - Poor Economics — co-authored with Banerjee; the canonical popular synthesis of the J-PAL RCT program.

Key concepts

Randomized Controlled Trial in Development Economics — the methodological program she co-founded and operationalized through J-PAL.
Three Is — Ignorance, Ideology, Inertia — co-developed with Banerjee in Poor Economics ch. 1.
Aspiration Failure — the “illusory S-shape” of parental expectations is a Duflo-Banerjee contribution that recurs across Poor Economics chs. 4, 8, 9.
Poverty Trap (S-Curve) — the diagnostic shape used to discriminate domains across the book.

Key arguments

Top-down supply-side education investment works even where parents seem indifferent — the INPRES result, Poor Economics ch. 4. Duflo’s 8%-per-year-of-schooling wage-return estimate matches US findings, refuting the strong-form demand-wallah position.
Information shocks change voter behavior in caste-mediated elections — Poor Economics ch. 10, with Banerjee, Donald Green, Jennifer Green, Rohini Pande.
Quotas for women in local political office produce substantive policy change — Chattopadhyay-Duflo West Bengal panchayat-reservation result, Poor Economics ch. 10.

Related people / schools

Abhijit V. Banerjee — co-author, intellectual partner, co-founder of J-PAL, co-laureate.
Michael Kremer — third 2019 Nobel laureate; frequent co-author (Kenya bed nets, school deworming, education tracking, teen pregnancy).
Pascaline Dupas — frequent co-author on Kenya RCTs (TAMTAM bed nets; teen-pregnancy triple-RCT; tracking).
Raghabendra Chattopadhyay — co-author on the West Bengal panchayat-reservation evaluation (Indian Institute of Management, Kolkata).
Rachel Glennerster — frequent J-PAL co-author; Hyderabad Spandana microcredit RCT.
Cynthia Kinnan — Hyderabad Spandana microcredit RCT co-author.
Erica Field + Rohini Pande — Kolkata Village Welfare Society grace-period microcredit RCT collaborators.
Critics engaged in the book: Jeffrey Sachs, William Easterly, Daron Acemoglu, James Robinson, Paul Collier, Paul Romer.

Biographical anchors (only if relevant)
Affiliation per Poor Economics: MIT, J-PAL co-founder. The book’s voice consistently uses “Esther” for Duflo’s first-author work and “Abhijit” for Banerjee’s, suggesting a deliberate egalitarian-partnership convention; the partnership is unusual in economics for being treated as fully co-equal in the popular synthesis even where seniority and recognition (Banerjee’s senior position; Duflo’s solo Clark Medal) differ.
Beyond these vault-verifiable anchors, biographical specifics (birthplace, undergraduate institution, doctoral advisor, age, family connections) are not grep-verifiable in this vault’s extraction logs and would be (secondary, not verified in this vault).

04_People/G.-H.-Hardy.title: G. H. Hardy
04_People/G.-H.-Hardy.content:
G. H. Hardy
Why they matter
One of the most influential English mathematicians of the 20th century, working primarily in number theory and analysis. Discoverer-mentor of Srinivasa Ramanujan (1913 onward); collaborator with John Edensor Littlewood (the Hardy-Littlewood circle method, ~100 joint papers). Author of A Mathematician’s Apology (1940), the canonical defense of pure mathematics, written when his creative powers were declining and he was preparing for the end. The combination of mathematical seriousness and aesthetic-philosophical articulation makes Hardy unusual among great mathematicians.
Works in this vault

G. H. Hardy - A Mathematician’s Apology — 1940

Key concepts

Mathematical aesthetics — Hardy’s conception of beauty (economy, surprise, depth) as a real correctness criterion; see Mathematical Aesthetics
Pure-vs-applied dichotomy — Hardy’s controversial defense of pure mathematics on aesthetic grounds against utilitarian justification

Key arguments

Pure mathematics is aesthetically justified (in G. H. Hardy - A Mathematician’s Apology)

Related people / schools

Srinivasa Ramanujan — Hardy’s most famous collaborator; “the one romantic incident in my life” per the Apology
John Edensor Littlewood — Hardy’s main mathematical collaborator; the Hardy-Littlewood papers are foundational
C. P. Snow — the friend who wrote the famous Foreword to later editions; bridge to the Two Cultures debate

Biographical anchors

Trinity College, Cambridge (BA 1898, fellowship 1900). Moved to Oxford 1919-1931 (New College / Savilian Chair); returned to Cambridge 1931 (Sadleirian Professor) until 1942.
Pacifist; refused war work in WWI and was conflicted about WWII.
Suffered a serious heart attack in 1939; A Mathematician’s Apology was written in 1940 partly as a response to his sense that creative work was over.
Attempted suicide in 1947; died of natural causes shortly after.

(Confidence: high on academic record; medium on personal-biographical specifics — verify before relying on dates.)

04_People/G.-Pascal-Zachary.title: G. Pascal Zachary
04_People/G.-Pascal-Zachary.content:
G. Pascal Zachary
Why they matter
Author of G. Pascal Zachary - Showstopper (1994), the embedded chronicle of the Windows NT project that became one of the most-cited primary sources on large-team software engineering, alongside Tracy Kidder - The Soul of a New Machine and Frederick P. Brooks Jr. - The Mythical Man-Month. Zachary’s significance is methodological: he demonstrated that a non-coding journalist could produce a technically credible, sociologically rich account of an enterprise-scale software project by being physically present at daily meetings and in offices for an extended period. The book’s continuing usefulness — including its 2008 Afterward, which candidly retrofits the original with Internet/mobile self-criticism — owes more to Zachary’s reportorial discipline than to any independent technical claim.
Role
Journalist and author. Best known for G. Pascal Zachary - Showstopper (1994), the embedded chronicle of Microsoft’s three-and-a-half-year effort to build Windows NT under Dave Cutler. Zachary appears in Showstopper! itself only obliquely, as the unobtrusive observer who attends the daily 9 a.m. meetings, sits in offices during code reviews, and conducts what he describes in the New Afterward as “scores of interviews with Microsoft engineers, codewriters and managers.”
Voice and Method
Zachary’s method in Showstopper! combines two genres rarely found together: the management case study and the immersive long-form journalism of figures like John McPhee or Tracy Kidder. He gives technical concepts — kernels, client-server, paging, lazy writers, file-system journaling — enough room to be understood by a non-programmer, then folds them back into character beats (the broken finger, the Hawaii spec-writing trip, the wife who institutes “the Box”). He is not an apologist; the long catalog of family casualties in chapter 8 is unsparing. But neither is he a debunker; the epilogue’s analysis of why NT shipped takes Cutler’s leadership seriously as an answer to a real organizational problem.
Self-Critique in the 2008 Afterward
Zachary’s most striking authorial moment is the Afterward written 14 years later, where he confesses that nobody he interviewed — not once — mentioned the Internet or the mobile phone as a future force. The book’s principal actors were “blinkered by visions of the past and present.” Zachary tags himself as “no technological seer.” This unusual willingness to mark the book’s epistemic limits in print extends the work’s credibility (secondary, not verified in this vault: details of Zachary’s later journalism career, including reported beats at The Wall Street Journal and academic appointments at Arizona State and Stanford, are not grep-checkable in any extraction here.)
Books in This Vault

G. Pascal Zachary - Showstopper

Sources

G. Pascal Zachary - Showstopper — Introduction, “A Note on Sources,” Acknowledgments, and the 2008 New Afterward are the only first-person traces of the author within the vault’s source material.

04_People/Gayle-Laakmann-McDowell.title: Gayle Laakmann McDowell
04_People/Gayle-Laakmann-McDowell.content:
Gayle Laakmann McDowell
Why they matter
McDowell is the practitioner-educator who standardized the technical-interview-prep canon for big-tech software engineering. Through Cracking the Coding Interview (six editions between 2008 and 2015) and the CareerCup community-question database she founded as the operational backbone, she translated tacit big-tech-interviewer practice into a teachable curriculum: Big-O literacy, the Five-Step Problem-Solving Framework, a fixed Pattern-Matching Approach to Algorithms vocabulary, the Behavioral STAR Pattern discipline (her S.A.R. variant), and an opinionated career-management track (resume rules, negotiation tactics, offer evaluation, yearly-interview-cadence). Her authority is biographical: three years on Google’s hiring committee where she reviewed thousands of candidate packets, software engineering at Microsoft, Apple, and Google, and twelve offers as a candidate herself. The book is the canonical text most candidates use to prepare for any FAANG-style interview loop, and its framework vocabulary has become the lingua franca in published LeetCode discussions, mock-interview platforms (Pramp, interviewing.io), and internal-mentorship guides at major tech firms.
Works in this vault

Gayle Laakmann McDowell - Cracking the Coding Interview — 6th edition, 2015. The canonical interview-prep manual. 189 problems with worked solutions; primers on data structures, algorithms, OO design, system design, behavioral questions, negotiation; the Five-Step Framework as the operational spine.

She has also written Cracking the Tech Career (broader career-strategy framing for landing positions at major tech companies, including non-engineering roles) and Cracking the PM Interview (product-manager-specific interview prep). Neither is in this vault yet.
Key concepts
Concepts where her exposition has become the standard reference (or which she explicitly originated):

Five-Step Interview Framework (McDowell) — Listen / Example / Brute Force / Optimize / Walk Through / Implement / Test. McDowell’s seven-step protocol; the canonical statement of structured technical-interview problem-solving.
Pattern-Matching Approach to Algorithms — implicit pedagogical spine of the book; the meta-skill the 189 problems are designed to train.
Behavioral STAR Pattern — McDowell’s S.A.R. (Situation, Action, Result) variant + Nugget-First openers + Interview Preparation Grid. The canonical statement of structured behavioral-interview answering.
BUD optimization (Bottlenecks, Unnecessary work, Duplicated work) — the most-cited optimization tactic in technical-interview literature; named and operationalized by McDowell.
Best Conceivable Runtime (BCR) — the optimization-target framing; not McDowell-original but standardized in interview-prep usage by the book.
Interview Preparation Grid — the (behavioral-category × project) matrix for behavioral story preparation; McDowell’s specific organizational artifact.

Key arguments

Memorization fails; pattern matching scales. The interview question pool is too large to memorize, and questions are deliberately varied to defeat memorization. The transferable skill is recognizing patterns and deploying matching moves. The 189 problems in the book are exercise material, not answer key.
The interview is relative, not absolute. No points table; you’re graded against everyone the same interviewer has asked the same question. Hard questions are harder for everyone — getting one is not a penalty.
False negatives are acceptable; false positives are not. Companies tolerate missing good candidates because the cost of hiring bad candidates is higher. This explains the high-noise interview format and the bar-raiser practice.
Process is half the signal. The interviewer evaluates verbal narration, optimization-arc walking, and structured pause as much as final-answer correctness. The Five-Step Framework operationalizes process visibility.
Behavioral questions are equally preparable as technical questions. The Interview Preparation Grid + S.A.R. discipline + post-hoc personality-attribute audit produce structured behavioral answers; “authenticity-as-improv” underperforms preparation.
Negotiate the offer. The single most under-utilized career lever; recruiters don’t revoke offers for negotiation; have a viable alternative; have a specific ask; overshoot; think beyond salary.
Keep interviewing yearly even when not looking. Interview muscle atrophies; market awareness compounds.

Related people / schools

Adnan Aziz et al. (Elements of Programming Interviews) — the more algorithmically-rigorous, problem-density-heavy alternative interview-prep canon. McDowell is broader and more strategy-first; EPI drills harder. A serious preparer reads both.
Steven Skiena (The Algorithm Design Manual) — the academic-leaning textbook that underwrites the algorithmic content McDowell teaches. McDowell explicitly does not teach the deep algorithmic theory; Skiena is one of the standard depth references.
John Bentley (Programming Pearls) — older problem-solving canon in the same lineage; many of the optimization tactics McDowell teaches (clever-data-structure choice, time-vs-space tradeoff) trace through Bentley.
Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein (CLRS) — the canonical academic algorithms text; the depth reference McDowell explicitly defers to for proofs and rigor.
LeetCode community — the operational practice ground where McDowell’s framework vocabulary is daily-deployed in published solutions and discussion forums; the symbiotic relationship between book-as-curriculum and platform-as-practice is itself part of the canon’s longevity.
HackerRank, CoderPad, interviewing.io, Pramp — the platforms that operationalize practice in McDowell’s framework; her vocabulary is embedded in their tooling and community norms.

Biographical anchors (only if relevant)

B.S.E. and M.S.E. in Computer Science from the University of Pennsylvania (per “About the Author”, verified in extracted ch. XV).
MBA from the Wharton School (verified in extracted ch. XV).
Software engineering roles at Microsoft, Apple, and Google (verified in extracted ch. XV).
Three years at Google, including hiring committee tenure; reviewed thousands of candidate packets (verified in extracted ch. XV).
Founded CareerCup to host community interview-question database; CareerCup is the operational backbone that fed the book’s question pool (verified in extracted ch. XV).
As a candidate herself, received offers from twelve tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, IBM, and Apple (verified in extracted ch. XV).
Lives in Palo Alto, California; consults with tech companies on hiring-process design and with startups preparing for acquisition interviews (verified in extracted ch. XV).
Author of two other books: Cracking the Tech Career and Cracking the PM Interview.

The biographical anchors are unusually load-bearing for this author because the book’s epistemology depends on them: the relative-evaluation framing, the bar-raiser awareness, and the “interviewers vary more than companies do” claim are all grounded in McDowell’s insider tenure on a hiring committee — claims a non-insider could not credibly make. The book treats this credibility as foundational and the about-the-author chapter signals it directly. Treat the book note as the primary record; this people note compiles the meta-skill claims McDowell originates or has standardized.

04_People/Goh-Keng-Swee.title: Goh Keng Swee
04_People/Goh-Keng-Swee.content:
Goh Keng Swee
Why they matter
The most-influential single cabinet collaborator of Lee Kuan Yew across the founding generation. In LKY’s account, Goh is the judgment counterweight to LKY’s will — the figure who designed the Economic Development Board (EDB), the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) initial doctrine and structure, the Central Provident Fund’s housing-finance integration, and the Ministry of Education’s bilingual-policy implementation. The combination of LKY’s political will and Goh’s institutional judgment is presented in the memoir as the necessary pair for the Singapore model — neither figure could have produced the system alone. Goh’s intellectual range (LSE-trained economist, soldier, novelist, cultural commentator) and his willingness to disagree with LKY in cabinet is repeatedly described as essential to the collegial-cabinet operating system.
Works in this vault

(Goh did not author a book in this vault; appears as a major figure in Lee Kuan Yew - From Third World to First)

Key concepts

Industrial Policy of Foreign Direct Investment — Goh designed the EDB’s one-stop-investor-agency architecture and led the early MNC-invitation outreach (Texas Instruments, HP, GE).
Defensive State Building — Goh organised the Israeli mission disguised as “Mexicans,” the universal-national-service framework (1967), and the Bases Economic Conversion programme (1968-71).
CPF Forced-Saving Mechanism — Goh was the principal architect of the CPF’s housing-finance integration via HDB.
Pragmatic Authoritarianism (Singapore Variant) — Goh embodied the operational-test posture in the design of every institution he founded.

Key arguments

That late-industrialising small states require active state direction of FDI rather than laissez-faire investment-promotion.
That the defining threat to a newly-independent small state is the gap between de jure sovereignty and de facto security capability — and that this gap can be closed in five years with foreign-tutored doctrine and universal national service.
That mandatory savings + state-allocated home-ownership produces both political stability and macroeconomic financing — the fair-not-welfare alternative to tax-financed welfare states.
That cabinet collegiality requires senior ministers willing to disagree explicitly with the Prime Minister on substance — a posture Goh actively practised.

Related people / schools

Lee Kuan Yew — closest political partner; the judgment-counterweight to LKY’s will. The two figures founded the PAP together and led the cabinet through the founding generation.
S. Rajaratnam (secondary, not verified in this vault) — fellow founding cabinet member; Foreign Minister.
Toh Chin Chye (secondary, not verified in this vault) — Deputy PM 1959-68; education-policy collaborator.
Hon Sui Sen (secondary, not verified in this vault) — Goh’s successor as EDB Chairman; co-architect of the Asian Dollar Market.
Albert Winsemius (secondary, not verified in this vault) — Dutch UN economic adviser; Goh’s principal external sounding-board on industrial-policy strategy.

Biographical anchors (only if relevant)
LSE-trained economist (secondary, not verified in this vault). Held cabinet portfolios of Finance, Defence, and Education across the founding period. The memoir documents Goh’s role in the 1959-80s but does not offer a dedicated biographical chapter; biographical specifics beyond his role in the memoir’s policy chapters should be verified against external sources before treatment as reliable.

04_People/J.C.R.-Licklider.title: J.C.R. Licklider
04_People/J.C.R.-Licklider.content:
J.C.R. Licklider
Why they matter
Articulated the vision of Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960 paper) — the conceptual frame within which most subsequent HCI research and digital information systems were designed. As the first head of the Information Processing Techniques Office at ARPA (1962-1964), shaped the funding strategy that produced ARPANET, time-sharing systems, and the first generations of interactive computing. Libraries of the Future (1965) is the extended sequel that proposes procognitive systems as the right design unit for knowledge work. Trained as a psychoacoustician; the move into computing was via interactive sonar and air-defense displays in the 1950s.
Works in this vault

Licklider - Libraries of the Future — 1965 (the BBN/Council on Library Resources report)

Key concepts

Procognitive System — coined in Libraries of the Future
Man-Computer Symbiosis — coined in his 1960 paper of the same name; recurring frame in Libraries

Key arguments
(Licklider’s contributions are more conceptual-vision than argument-form; the central content is captured at the concept level.)
Related people / schools

Vannevar Bush — the Memex in “As We May Think” (1945) is the immediate antecedent of Licklider’s vision; Licklider quotes Bush in the Foreword
Warren McCulloch — same MIT/cybernetics generation; different program (experimental epistemology vs human-computer symbiosis)
Marvin Minsky — same MIT institutional context; different intellectual aesthetic (formal computation vs vision-level systems thinking)
Douglas Engelbart — adjacent program (Augmenting Human Intellect, 1962); shared lineage of “computers should amplify human cognition” — would be a person note candidate when an Engelbart book is ingested
Robert Taylor — Licklider’s successor at IPTO; carried forward the network-of-computers vision into ARPANET

Biographical anchors

PhD in psychoacoustics, University of Rochester (1942). Worked at Harvard’s Psycho-Acoustic Lab during WWII.
MIT 1950-1957 (Lincoln Laboratory; SAGE air-defense system experience set up the interactive-computing intuitions).
BBN (Bolt Beranek and Newman) 1957-1962, where he wrote Man-Computer Symbiosis and where ARPANET was later contracted.
ARPA / IPTO 1962-1964; the Intergalactic Computer Network memos (1963) are the conceptual predecessors of the ARPANET.
Returned to MIT and BBN; Libraries of the Future is from this period.

(Confidence: high on dates and roles; medium on the precise narrative of the IPTO years — primary sources are scattered across DARPA archives and biographical reminiscences. Verify before relying on specific year-by-year claims.)

04_People/James-Le-Fanu.title: James Le Fanu
04_People/James-Le-Fanu.content:
James Le Fanu
Identity
James Le Fanu is a British general practitioner and medical journalist, author of The Rise and Fall of Modern Medicine (1999, revised 2011) and Why Us? How Science Rediscovered the Mystery of Ourselves (2009). He has written a weekly medical column for The Daily Telegraph since the 1990s. (Biographical specifics about birth year, training institution, and column tenure are secondary, not verified in this vault.)
What he is known for
The case for medicine’s “Rise and Fall” — the contrarian historical thesis that post-war therapeutic medicine had a discrete golden age (1940-1980) driven by lucky empirical drug discovery and clinical-science ideology, followed by a decline (1980-) in which the New Genetics and the Social Theory rushed in to fill an intellectual vacuum without delivering on their promises. Le Fanu’s Rise and Fall compresses the therapeutic revolution into twelve definitive moments (penicillin → helicobacter, 1941-1984) and argues that the post-war structural conditions cannot recur.
In the 2011 revised edition, Le Fanu adds three epilogue chapters that sharpen the contemporary critique: technical extension of Rise-era therapies to ageing populations (“Doing More”); the failure of personalised genomics (“The New Genetics Triumphant — or Not”); and the institutional capture of clinical-trial research by industry (“Big Pharma Rules”).
Method
Le Fanu’s method is comparative-historical with primary-source citations. He works from:

British Medical Journal, Lancet, NEJM original articles for each of the Twelve Definitive Moments.
Biographies of the principal investigators (Florey, Hench, Bradford Hill, Charnley, Pinkel, Steptoe, Marshall).
Pharmacopoeia comparisons (Beeson 1980; Sneader 1996) for the cornucopia-of-drugs claim.
Inspection of the AHA committee minutes and similar documents for the diet-heart and committee-science critique.

He is not a professional historian of medicine; the work is journalism in the best sense — primary-document-based, transparent about sources, structurally clear about the argument it is making. Critics rightly note that some specific claims (statin scepticism in the 1999 edition; the absoluteness of the gene-therapy critique) have been overtaken by post-2010 evidence. The structural argument has aged better than its specific predictions.
Argument
The book’s load-bearing argument:

Twelve definitive therapeutic moments cluster between 1941 and 1984. None in the same league has occurred since.
The cluster’s causes are six structural conditions (antibiotics + steroids fuse, cross-discipline interconnectedness, clinical-science ideology, pharmaceutical empiricism, technology’s triumphs, biology as productive mystery). Each is exhausted by ~1980.
The intellectual vacuum is filled by the New Genetics (molecular reductionism) and the Social Theory (lifestyle epidemiology). Both have failed.
The structural condition is a four-layered brick wall — readily-do-able done; age-determined disease only palliable; lucky drug discovery exhausted; causes of unknown-origin diseases still unknown.
The four contemporary paradoxes (disillusioned doctors, worried well, alternative medicine ascendancy, soaring costs) follow from the Rise-Fall structure.
The corrective is Oslerian relocation — bounded ambition, restored clinical judgement, Bradford Hill discipline, restraint of Big Pharma’s disease-mongering.

Why they matter
For this vault, Le Fanu matters because he supplies the canonical contrarian history of post-war biomedicine. Read inside the running falsificationism / molecular-biology canon / public-health practice conversation, his argument:

Operationalises Popper’s Critical Rationalism in clinical context — committee-science storytelling fails the discipline; Marshall-style atheoretical observation succeeds.
Provides the case against treating molecular biology’s findings as automatically clinically productive — the Bruce Alberts - Molecular Biology of the Cell textbook canon vs. the actual yield of the New Genetics.
Underwrites Paul Farmer’s Rise-toolkit medical practice in Tracy Kidder - Mountains Beyond Mountains — Farmer succeeds because he uses the empirical-clinical methods of the Rise era, not the reductive programme of the Fall.
Pairs with Abhijit V. Banerjee - Poor Economics on RCT discipline — Bradford Hill’s coherence criterion is the methodological foundation Banerjee-Duflo extend to development economics.

Limitations

Statin underestimation (1999). The first edition’s scepticism of cholesterol-lowering benefit was overtaken by the 4S, HPS, and CTT meta-analyses. The 2011 epilogue is more measured but still understates the effect.
Anti-epidemiology overreach. The Bradford Hill coherence critique is a real discipline; many lifestyle-epidemiology claims do violate it. But the sweeping rhetoric loses calibration on robust findings (smoking, hypertension, occupational asbestos, obesity-as-diabetes-risk).
Pre-2015 cutoff on biotech. The 2011 epilogue missed: imatinib (2001), Herceptin (1998), CAR-T, CRISPR therapy (2023), GLP-1 agonists. These refute the strongest forms of the genetic-reductionism critique even if the polygenic-common-disease pessimism still tracks.
Western-rich-country framing. “Modern medicine” in Le Fanu’s account is rich-country medicine. The Rise toolkit’s continuing power in low-resource settings (vaccines, antibiotics, cataract surgery, simple cardiology) is largely outside the book’s frame.

Sources

James Le Fanu - The Rise and Fall of Modern Medicine — primary work; 1999 first edition, 2011 revised edition.
The Daily Telegraph medical column (1990s+) — Le Fanu’s running journalistic platform; contains many of the case studies later reworked into book form.

04_People/Jim-Yong-Kim.title: Jim Yong Kim
04_People/Jim-Yong-Kim.content:
Jim Yong Kim
Who
Jim Yong Kim (born 1959) is a Korean American physician, anthropologist, and global-health policy operator. Co-founder of Partners In Health (1987) with Paul Farmer, Ophelia Dahl, Tom White, and Père Fritz Lafontant. Most directly responsible for the second-line antibiotic price reduction (1998-2000) that brought a four-drug-resistant TB case from 15,000 down to 1,500 in treatment cost — the policy lever that made the WHO June 2002 MDR doctrine change operationally feasible. Subsequently director of the WHO HIV/AIDS Department (2003-2006), president of Dartmouth College (2009-2012), and twelfth president of the World Bank (2012-2019). (Post-publication career details are post-Mountains-Beyond-Mountains and tagged secondary, not verified in this vault.)
Biography (as documented in Mountains Beyond Mountains)
Born South Korea; raised in Muscatine, Iowa, in the 1970s — the only Asian family in town except for the one running the Chinese restaurant. Father a North Korea–born periodontist with an upstairs office on Main Street; mother a Confucian scholar who studied at Union Theological Seminary with Reinhold Niebuhr and Paul Tillich. Class valedictorian, class president, football quarterback, basketball starting guard at Muscatine High.
Transferred from University of Iowa to Brown; ran Brown’s Third World Center; broke up with his Irish Catholic girlfriend out of an “Asian racial solidarity” position he later found embarrassing. Went to Seoul on a fellowship for his Ph.D. in anthropology; researched the Korean pharmaceutical industry — the background that would later prove decisive for second-line antibiotic price work. Returned to Harvard Medical School disillusioned with identity politics (“I discovered South Korea was doing just fine, and that what Koreans wanted was for me to write grant proposals so they could come to the States”). Met Paul Farmer in the late 1980s.
Joined PIH soon after its 1987 founding. For about eight years served as PIH’s bayakou (Creole for excrement-collector) — answering phones, chasing medicines, writing grant proposals, escorting Paul through hospital corridors. By 1994-95 wanted his own project; pushed Father Jack Roussin’s invitation to the Carabayllo slum on the outskirts of Lima, Peru, into an actual PIH-affiliated organization (Socios en Salud).
The Carabayllo MDR-TB project (1996+) shifted Kim into a different gear. Father Jack’s death from five-drug-resistant TB in 1995 — caught in Carabayllo, treated at the Brigham, lethal — pulled PIH into the MDR fight Kim had been agitating for. Through 1998-2000 he ran the second-line drug price reduction work: discovered most second-line drug patents had expired; engineered the Green Light Committee as a control mechanism on cheaper second-line distribution; partnered with the Dutch IDA (International Dispensary Association) and Doctors Without Borders on generic-manufacturer engagement; lobbied second-line drugs onto WHO’s essential drugs list as an annex; got Eli Lilly to grant donations and global price reductions. Capreomycin fell from 21/vial to 98 cents (-97%); a four-drug-resistant case from 15,000 to $1,500. Guido Bakker (IDA): “Eighty-five percent of it was Jim.”
Quit his ID fellowship at the Brigham midway because policy work, not patient care, was where his skills were strongest. Wrote the Gates Foundation $45M grant proposal (July 2000) for nationwide MDR-TB elimination in Peru — Foege’s “only one grant” trick + Kim’s coalition-building got former adversaries (WHO TB branch) into the partnership. Mountains Beyond Mountains leaves him in mid-2002 as a senior figure at WHO.
Why they matter
Two reasons.


The price-reduction case study. Kim’s “big-shot strategy” — make the assertion that prices can fall 90-95%, then figure out how — is a model for institutional change against entrenched cost-effectiveness reasoning. The Green Light Committee is a particularly clean example of an institutional mechanism designed specifically to break a logician’s-conundrum chain (low prices need scale, scale needs essential-drugs-list listing, listing needs use, use needs low prices). The mechanism is portable to other global-health pricing fights. Reading Tracy Kidder - Mountains Beyond Mountains chapter 19 is the most efficient access.


The complement to Farmer in the PIH operational architecture. Where Farmer was the clinician-anthropologist whose unit-of-one practice gave PIH its moral authority, Kim was the policy operator whose systems-of-thousands practice gave PIH its institutional reach. The chapter-24 wall-sign exchange (“If Paul is the model, we’re fucked / golden”) is Kim’s articulation of why PIH’s transferable artifact is the operational specification, not the trait distribution. This is the position the rest of PIH’s institutional history is built on.


Operational concepts associated with him

DOTS-plus — the WHO term Kim’s WHO contact (Arata Kochi) coined as a face-saving way to fold MDR-TB treatment into international policy.
Green Light Committee — Kim’s institutional invention; gatekeeper for low-price second-line antibiotic distribution conditional on a sound underlying DOTS program.
Big-shot strategy — Kim’s Salzburg-pizza articulation: assert what should be possible, then find the means.
Unusual alliances — PIH’s framing for coalitions that include former adversaries (WHO TB branch as Gates partner; Eli Lilly + IDA generic manufacturers; Castro + Pope + Gates + Britney Spears slide).

Sources in this vault

Tracy Kidder - Mountains Beyond Mountains — chapters 14, 16, 18, 19, 24. Most thorough single source on Kim’s role in the Carabayllo project and the price-reduction work.
(Kim’s later career as WHO HIV/AIDS Department director, Dartmouth president, and World Bank president 2012-2019 is post-publication and tagged secondary, not verified in this vault.)

What I would track

Whether the Green Light Committee model survives the post-2010 era of more concentrated pharmaceutical pricing power.
Whether Kim’s institutional-policy approach scales without a Farmer-class clinician giving it moral authority.
The World Bank presidency (2012-2019) as a test of whether the pragmatic solidarity operational specification ports up to a Bretton Woods institution. (Secondary, not verified in this vault.)

04_People/Joel-Mokyr.title: Joel Mokyr
04_People/Joel-Mokyr.content:
Joel Mokyr
Why they matter
Economic historian whose work on the cultural and intellectual origins of modern economic growth is the most influential framework currently available for understanding why the Industrial Revolution happened in Western Europe rather than elsewhere. His distinctive contribution is to take culture seriously as an explanatory variable while refusing both the lazy “national character” gestures of older intellectual history and the structural-determinist reductions of historical materialism. The Mokyr framework — culture as a menu of beliefs from which individuals choose under historically variable transmission biases, with cultural entrepreneurs reshaping the menus — is portable to every comparative-development question.
Background
Long-tenured at Northwestern University, where he holds the Robert H. Strotz Professorship in Arts and Sciences and the Department of Economics chair (secondary, not verified in this vault).
Mokyr’s career-long research program traces the emergence of sustained technological progress to the cultural transformation of European intellectual life between Columbus and Newton. His three signature books form a coordinated trilogy:

The Lever of Riches: Technological Creativity and Economic Progress (1990) — establishes the conceptual distinction between micro-inventions (incremental improvements within an existing technology) and macro-inventions (discontinuous leaps creating new design spaces), and uses it to chart technological progress from antiquity through the Industrial Revolution.
The Gifts of Athena: Historical Origins of the Knowledge Economy (2002) — develops the formal distinction between propositional knowledge (Ω, what-is-the-case) and prescriptive knowledge (λ, how-to), and argues that the explosive feedback between them is the engine of modern growth. The book introduces the concept of the epistemic base of a technique. Ingested in BookWiki Batch 53 as Joel Mokyr - The Gifts of Athena.
A Culture of Growth: The Origins of the Modern Economy (2016) — the cultural argument: changes in elite beliefs about useful knowledge, the role of nature, and the legitimacy of intellectual innovation between 1500 and 1700 created the cultural preconditions for the Industrial Enlightenment and modern economic growth. This is the book ingested in BookWiki Batch 52.

Mokyr’s intellectual signature is the synthesis of economic-history methodology with cultural-evolution theory (drawing on Boyd and Richerson, Henrich, and the Bisin-Verdier school in economics). He insists on agency without succumbing to “great man” history; he insists on culture without dropping into vague references to “national character”; he insists on contingency without becoming a pure historical nominalist. His framing — history is neither fluke nor necessity — captures the methodological middle ground he occupies.
Mokyr’s framework has consequences across BookWiki’s reading shelves:

For growth economics, he provides the cultural and institutional substrate upstream of Robert J. Gordon - The Rise and Fall of American Growth’s Special Century. Where Gordon traces what happened to the American standard of living between 1870 and 1970, Mokyr explains how the capacity for sustained innovation was assembled in the centuries before.
For innovation history, he supplies the meta-frame for Anton Howes - Arts and Minds’s study of the Royal Society of Arts: Howes’ improvement-mentality is, on Mokyr’s reading, the institutional crystallization of the Baconian program propagated by the Republic of Letters.
For philosophy of progress, his account of the seventeenth-century battle of the books anticipates David Deutsch - The Beginning of Infinity’s defense of the Enlightenment as a tradition of good explanations.
For strategy and competitive advantage, his treatment of useful knowledge as a non-rivalrous commons underlies the strategic primitive Hamilton Helmer - 7 Powers calls a “Cornered Resource.”

Mokyr’s influence on contemporary debate runs through three channels. First, his framing of the Great Divergence — Europe vs. China, Europe vs. Islam — is now standard reference. Second, his concept of the Industrial Enlightenment is a fixed point in current debates over the cultural origins of growth (alongside Deirdre McCloskey’s bourgeois-virtue trilogy and Greg Clark’s reproductive-selection model). Third, his methodological insistence on co-evolution of culture and institutions has shaped how a generation of cliometricians and political economists frame their identification strategies.
For BookWiki: Mokyr is the rare scholar whose conceptual scaffolding rewards re-reading at multiple levels — chapter-level for the comparative cases (China, Britain), framework-level for the cultural-evolution machinery, and meta-level for the methodological self-discipline of historical economics. Future ingests of Gifts of Athena and Lever of Riches will deepen the vault’s coverage of this thinker.
Related notes

Joel Mokyr - A Culture of Growth
Joel Mokyr - The Gifts of Athena
Useful Knowledge
Propositional Knowledge (omega)
Prescriptive Knowledge (lambda)
Access Costs (Mokyr)
Republic of Letters
Cultural Entrepreneur

04_People/John-Carmack.title: John Carmack
04_People/John-Carmack.content:
John Carmack
Why they matter
Carmack designed the Game Engine generations (Adaptive Tile Refresh, Wolfenstein raycasting, Doom BSP, Quake 3D, OpenGL acceleration) that defined the first-person shooter genre and seeded the modern game-engine licensing industry. His commitment to documented file formats, source-code releases, and modder tooling created Mod Culture as a deliberate architectural choice. After id, his pivots to amateur rocketry (Armadillo Aerospace) and virtual reality (Oculus CTO) extended the same engineer-first ethos to two more domains.
Biography
John D. Carmack II (b. August 20, 1970, Kansas City, Missouri) is the lead programmer of every id Software Game Engine from Commander Keen (1990) through Doom III (2004), the technical force behind first-person shooter as a genre, and one of the most influential graphics programmers of his generation. As told in David Kushner - Masters of Doom he is the analytic, monkish half of “the Two Johns” — the partnership with John Romero that built id Software.
Kushner’s portrait centers on a few formative facts. Carmack’s father Stan was a Kansas City TV news anchor; his mother Inga held a PhD in microbiology. The household prized intellectual achievement and Carmack tested at ninth-grade comprehension in second grade. His teenage thermite-and-Apple-II school break-in led to a year in juvenile detention and a court psychiatrist’s verdict, “a brain on legs with no empathy whatsoever” — a phrase Carmack later treated with rueful pride. He dropped out of the University of Missouri after two semesters, freelanced Apple II games, ported them to PC by renting a machine he had never used, and joined Softdisk in Shreveport in 1990, where he met Romero, Tom Hall, and Adrian Carmack (no relation).
His technical contributions to the medium follow a clear architectural arc. Adaptive Tile Refresh (1990) made smooth side-scrolling possible on PC and produced the Commander Keen demo of Super Mario Bros. 3 that founded id Software. Raycasting in Wolfenstein 3D (1992) gave the first commercially viable PC first-person view. Binary Space Partitioning trees in Doom (1993), borrowed from a Bell Labs paper, allowed angled walls and variable heights at playable framerates. True 3D polygon rendering with surface caching in Quake (1996) was the first commercial game-grade volumetric engine. OpenGL hardware acceleration ports (1997 onward) drove consumer GPU adoption (3dfx, NVIDIA). His later work at id added stencil shadow volumes (Doom III, 2004) and MegaTexture / virtual texturing (Rage, 2011). (Specific Doom III and Rage technical attributions are not directly in the Kushner extraction log — secondary, not verified in this vault.)
Carmack’s open-source releases — Doom (1997), Quake (1999), Quake II (2001), Quake III (2005) — are unusually generous for a commercial studio and seeded the source-port ecosystem that keeps id’s classics playable on contemporary hardware. His developer-blog .plan files at id (1996-2003) prefigured the engineering blog as a public artifact.
After id, Carmack co-founded Armadillo Aerospace (2000) — the high-power amateur rocketry team that won the NASA Lunar Lander Challenge in 2008. He left id (acquired by ZeniMax/Bethesda in 2009) in 2013 to become Chief Technology Officer of Oculus VR; remained when Facebook acquired Oculus in 2014; departed in 2019 to focus on artificial general intelligence; and in 2022 founded Keen Technologies, an AGI startup. (Post-2003 career claims are not in the Kushner book — secondary, not verified in this vault.)
His personal voice has been remarkably consistent across thirty years: clipped, technically precise, allergic to political and managerial abstractions, intellectually omnivorous within engineering domains. In Kushner’s telling, his asymmetry with Romero — depth without breadth, code over showmanship, “I just want to create good programs” — is the productive tension that built the Two Johns and the destructive imbalance that ended them.
Notable connections in this vault

John Romero — partner and rival
David Kushner - Masters of Doom — primary biography
Game Engine, Mod Culture, Shareware Distribution — concepts whose canonical case studies he embodies
Steven Levy - Hackers — Carmack as second-generation hacker, philosophically downstream of Levy’s MIT and Homebrew subjects

04_People/John-Romero.title: John Romero
04_People/John-Romero.content:
John Romero
Why they matter
Romero is the level-design and brand-building partner who turned Carmack’s Game Engine generations into genre-defining products: Wolfenstein 3D (1992), Doom (1993), and Quake (1996). He coined “deathmatch” as the name for player-versus-player combat, designed the chat-room and bulletin-board promotion that made id a brand, and wrote the level-design pedagogy that subsequent first-person shooter designers studied. His post-id Ion Storm period is the canonical case study in founder hubris meeting unconstrained capital.
Biography
Alfonso John Romero (b. October 28, 1967, Tucson, Arizona) is a game designer, level designer, and entrepreneur best known as a co-founder of id Software (1991), lead designer on Wolfenstein 3D (1992), Doom (1993), and Quake (1996), and founder of Ion Storm (1996). As told in David Kushner - Masters of Doom he is the showman, level-design virtuoso, and brand-builder half of “the Two Johns” — the partnership with John Carmack that defined the first-person shooter genre.
Kushner’s portrait is built on contrast. Romero is a first-generation Mexican-American whose biological father, an air-force-base maintenance worker, vanished when Romero was six; his stepfather, an ex-drill-sergeant Pentagon contractor, beat him for sneaking into arcades. Asteroids at age eleven became the parallel world worth any beating. Romero’s resilience — beat, recover, return to the game — is the recurring rhythm of the book. He sketched Lamborghinis at age six well enough that his stepfather assumed he traced them. He published Apple II games in disk magazines (Uptime, Nibble, InCider) as a teenager, married his pregnant teenage girlfriend Kelly at nineteen, and moved across the country three times before age twenty-one chasing programming jobs.
His design legacy at id is concentrated in level design and “feel” — the moment-to-moment kinesthetic experience of playing one of his levels. Romero’s Doom levels (E1M1 “Hangar,” E1M2 “Nuclear Plant,” E1M4 “Command Control,” and many in episodes 1-3) are studied in level-design pedagogy as exemplars of pacing, sightline, secret reveal, and combat encounter design; his Quake levels (E1M1 “Slipgate Complex” among others) carry the same signatures. He coined “deathmatch” as the name for player-versus-player combat, designed Doom’s network protocol with Carmack, and built the chat-room and bulletin-board promotion that turned id into a brand. He also designed the modding-friendly tools and openly endorsed fan WAD files, accelerating Mod Culture.
The Ion Storm phase (1996-2001) is the book’s tragic act. Romero’s 25M, four-year, four-time-period epic Daikatana shipped four years late on an aging engine and sold 41,000 copies. The "Design Is Law" motto, the 22,500-square-foot Texas Commerce Tower penthouse at 550,000/month, the Eidos publishing deal across Daikatana, Anachronox, and Warren Spector’s Deus Ex (the only commercial success of the three), and the “John Romero’s About to Make You His Bitch” magazine ad became case studies in founder hubris. The Dallas Ion Storm office was terminated in 2001; the Austin Spector team continued.
Post-Ion Storm, Romero co-founded Monkeystone (2001) for mobile games with girlfriend Stevie “Killcreek” Case and Tom Hall, then a series of subsequent studios (Gazillion, Loot Drop, Romero Games in Galway). (Post-2003 career claims not in the Kushner book — secondary, not verified in this vault.) He has remained a public figure, a fixture at game industry conferences, and an active level designer; his 2016 release of new Doom and Doom II level packs (“Sigil” and “Sigil II”) was widely celebrated.
In Kushner’s framing, Romero’s productive contribution to the partnership was his social, design, and promotional gifts — without him, Carmack’s engines would not have become genre-defining games. His destructive contribution after the partnership was the absence of Carmack’s discipline.
Notable connections in this vault

John Carmack — partner and rival
David Kushner - Masters of Doom — primary biography
Game Engine, Mod Culture, Shareware Distribution — id ecosystem

04_People/Julia-Galef.title: Julia Galef
04_People/Julia-Galef.content:
Julia Galef
Identity (in this vault)
Author of The Scout Mindset: Why Some People See Things Clearly and Others Don’t (2021), the source for Scout Mindset, Soldier Mindset, and Identity (Galef) in this vault.
Why they matter
Galef’s contribution is to reframe the practical-rationality literature around a single dimension of motivation rather than a sprawling list of biases. Her empirical claim — that judgment is limited by attitude more than by knowledge — is grounded in a decade of running rationality workshops and corroborated by Dan Kahan’s research showing that more knowledgeable Americans are more polarized on charged scientific questions. The book’s toolkit (counterfactual thought experiments, calibration practice, holding identity lightly, the ideological Turing test) makes the abstract idea concrete enough to install one habit at a time. Galef matters here because she is the clearest practical-installation manual for the rationality and forecasting cluster that includes Tetlock, Deutsch, and the effective-altruism community.
Biographical sketch
Galef is a writer and podcaster on rationality, cognitive bias, and decision-making (secondary, not verified in this vault). She has hosted the Rationally Speaking podcast since the 2010s, and was a co-founder of the Center for Applied Rationality (CFAR) (secondary, not verified in this vault). The book mentions she quit graduate school in 2009 to pursue a career running workshops, doing consulting, and interviewing people about practical reasoning — a path that produced the empirical claim underlying the book: “our judgment isn’t limited by knowledge nearly as much as it’s limited by attitude” (paraphrased; Galef, 2021, Introduction).
The book is her first. By her own account she is not a perfect exemplar of scout mindset; she opens by confessing that more than once during research interviews about open-mindedness, she spent the time trying to convince the interviewee her thesis was right, “the irony of [which] is not lost on me” (paraphrased; Galef, 2021, Introduction).
Intellectual lineage and interlocutors
Galef sits in a cluster of practical rationality writers connected to the LessWrong / effective-altruism / forecasting communities. Adjacent figures she draws on or cites:

Philip Tetlock — superforecasting research; chapter 10 is largely an exposition of Tetlock’s findings on incremental updating and belief-system defenses.
Tom Gilovich — the “Can I believe this? / Must I believe this?” formulation Galef adopts.
Bryan Caplan — coined “rational irrationality” (which Galef rejects) and the ideological Turing test (which she adopts).
