Used a $1,000 Duke essay prize on Haitian artists to fly to Haiti spring 1983, age 23. Met Ophelia Dahl in Mirebalais. Witnessed a young pregnant woman die in the Hôpital St. Croix in Léogâne for lack of a transfusion (chapter 8 of Mountains Beyond Mountains); the sister’s tout moun se moun — “we are all human beings” — became a founding moment. Decided to “build my own fucking hospital” in Cange.
Entered Harvard Medical School fall 1984; earned MD and Ph.D. in anthropology simultaneously 1990. His Ph.D. thesis became AIDS and Accusation (1992), the first of his book-length works. Hit by a car in 1988, shattering his knee; designed the 1988 noncompliance study (TB treatment + monthly cash + community health workers vs. medicine-only — 100% cure vs. 48%) from his Cange wheelchair. Married Didi Bertrand 1996; daughter Catherine born 1998.
PIH founded 1987 with Tom White’s 1M seed. Carabayllo MDR-TB project began 1996; results presented at the April 1998 Boston meeting where WHO conceded the DOTS-plus framework. Jim Kim drove second-line antibiotic prices down 90-95% via the Green Light Committee + IDA + Doctors Without Borders generic-manufacturer engagement (1998-2000). Gates Foundation 45M grant July 2000 for nationwide MDR-TB treatment in Peru. WHO adopted MDR-TB guidelines virtually identical to PIH’s protocols June 2002. Partner-organization Tomsk (Russia), Roxbury (Boston), Chiapas (Mexico) extensions followed.
MacArthur “genius grant” 1993 ($220,000, donated entirely to PIH). Tenured Harvard Medical School professor by 2000. Author of AIDS and Accusation (1992), The Uses of Haiti (1994), Infections and Inequalities (1999), Pathologies of Power (2003), Partner to the Poor (2010). The book in this vault is the Kidder portrait, not Farmer’s own work.
Why they matter
Three intersecting reasons.


Global health doctrine. Farmer is the central figure in the late-1990s shift from cost-effectiveness gatekeeping toward direct material transfer in MDR-TB and HIV/AIDS treatment. The Carabayllo demonstration (1996-2000) and the WHO June 2002 guideline change are the headline events. Reading Tracy Kidder - Mountains Beyond Mountains is the most efficient way into this story; reading Farmer’s own Pathologies of Power and Infections and Inequalities is the scholarly complement.


Liberation theology as operational specification. Farmer is the case study for whether preferential option for the poor (see Preferential Option for the Poor) can be translated from a Latin American Catholic theological commitment into an enforceable secular global-health practice. His operational answer — pragmatic solidarity (see Pragmatic Solidarity) and the long defeat posture (see Long Defeat (Tolkien-Farmer)) — is the most thoroughly worked-out example this vault contains.


Authorial-discipline test for biography. The Kidder portrait deliberately refuses the great-man frame Farmer is otherwise built for (see Kim’s chapter-24 wall-sign joke: “If Paul is the model, we’re fucked”). Useful contrast to Walter Isaacson - Elon Musk’s explicit acceptance of the great-man framing for Musk.


Operational concepts associated with him

Preferential option for the poor — the moral frame, drawn from liberation theology. Preferential Option for the Poor.
Pragmatic solidarity — direct material transfer down the inequality gradient, no sustainability or appropriate-technology dilution. Pragmatic Solidarity.
The long defeat — the posture of “common cause with the losers,” fighting on regardless of winning. Long Defeat (Tolkien-Farmer).
The great epi divide — Farmer’s coinage for the partition of humanity between aging-disease and preventable-disease populations.
Amplification — Farmer’s chosen term (over “recruitment of further resistance”) for what the WHO retreatment regimen does to mono-resistant TB patients.
Distal intervention — cure the disease first, then change the conditions that produced it.
Comma — Farmer’s verbal placeholder for “asshole,” directed only at third parties comfortable with the global distribution of money and medicine.

Sources in this vault

Tracy Kidder - Mountains Beyond Mountains — primary biographical source, 1983-2002 arc with most operational and personal detail.
(Farmer’s own writings — AIDS and Accusation, The Uses of Haiti, Infections and Inequalities, Pathologies of Power — are not yet in this vault. Tagged for future ingestion.)

What I would track

Whether PIH survives Farmer’s death and whether the operational specification (pragmatic solidarity + long defeat + distal intervention) is genuinely transferable without a Farmer-class central figure. Kim’s wall-sign warning is the diagnostic; the answer is post-publication.
Whether the second-line drug price-reduction strategy generalizes to genuinely-novel-IP cases (CAR-T, mRNA, Lecanemab-class) where the price reflects real R&D rather than monopoly rent.
Whether the long defeat posture is psychologically sustainable for staff who do not share Farmer’s specific trait distribution.

04_People/Peter-Norvig.title: Peter Norvig
04_People/Peter-Norvig.content:
Peter Norvig
Why they matter
Norvig is the co-author of AIMA with Stuart Russell and the systems-engineering complement to Russell’s theoretical voice. Where Russell brings the rational-agent / decision-theory / alignment frame, Norvig brings empiricism, data, and the discipline of working code: NLP statistics over hand-engineered grammars, web-scale corpora over toy datasets, “the unreasonable effectiveness of data” (with Halevy and Pereira, 2009) over rule-based AI. As director of research at Google for over a decade, Norvig was the institutional bridge between AIMA’s pedagogical canon and the actual industrial practice of large-scale AI. The textbook’s broad balance — symbolic Part III, probabilistic Part IV, learning Part V, and modern Part VI — reflects Norvig’s commitment to teaching what works alongside what is theoretically clean. (Biographical specifics in this note are secondary, not verified in this vault.)
Works in this vault

Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig - Artificial Intelligence A Modern Approach — 1st ed. 1995, 4th ed. 2021. Co-authored with Russell across all four editions. Norvig is widely understood as the primary author / steward of the natural-language (chs. 24-25), search and code-craft chapters, and the pedagogical apparatus (worked examples, exercises, online code repositories).

Key concepts

Rational Agent (Russell-Norvig Definition) — co-formalized with Russell; Norvig’s empirical disposition shapes the textbook’s emphasis on rational behaviour over rational thought.
Bayesian Network (Formal) — AIMA chs. 12-14 carry Norvig’s signature emphasis on inference algorithms that actually run; the chapter’s worked examples (alarm network, wumpus world) are pedagogical Norvig-isms.
Search Algorithm Taxonomy — Norvig’s Paradigms of Artificial Intelligence Programming (1991) is the precursor to AIMA’s search treatment; the search chapters carry Norvig’s “show the working code” style.

Key arguments

The unreasonable effectiveness of data (Halevy, Norvig, Pereira 2009 IEEE essay) — for many AI tasks (translation, NLP, vision), simple models on large data outperform sophisticated models on small data. This is the empirical creed that shaped AIMA’s 3rd and 4th editions and the modern foundation-model paradigm.
AI is engineering, not just theorem-proving — Norvig’s writing consistently treats AI systems as artifacts that must be built, debugged, and deployed; the textbook’s algorithm pseudocode and the aima-python companion repository are direct expressions of this commitment.
Statistical NLP over symbolic NLP — Norvig was an early and visible advocate for corpus-statistical methods in language processing, particularly n-gram models, word embeddings, and (in the 4th edition) transformer-based methods (ch. 25).
Pedagogy at scale — co-taught the original Stanford “Introduction to AI” MOOC with Sebastian Thrun (2011), drawing ~160,000 enrollments; this was the founding moment of the modern MOOC movement, and the course was structured as an AIMA companion.

Related people / schools

Stuart Russell — AIMA co-author; complementary temperaments (Russell theorist, Norvig empiricist / systems engineer).
Sebastian Thrun — Stanford colleague; co-instructor of the 2011 AI MOOC; co-founder of Udacity. The pedagogical pipeline AIMA → MOOC → Udacity → industrial AI runs through Norvig.
Fernando Pereira — co-author of the Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data essay; long-running Google colleague.
Alon Halevy — co-author of Unreasonable Effectiveness; the trio’s shared commitment to data-centric AI shaped Google’s research direction during Norvig’s tenure.
John McCarthy — Norvig was at Stanford during McCarthy’s later years; AIMA’s symbolic-logic chapters preserve the McCarthy tradition that Norvig’s empirical disposition might otherwise have de-emphasized.
Donald Knuth — Norvig has cited Knuth as a stylistic influence; the AIMA pseudocode discipline owes something to The Art of Computer Programming.
Demis Hassabis — peer at the senior level of industrial AI, but operating in different institutional traditions (Google Research vs DeepMind); compare Sebastian Mallaby - The Infinity Machine for the broader landscape.

Biographical anchors (only if relevant)
The following are secondary, not verified in this vault:

Brown University BS Applied Mathematics (~1978); UC Berkeley PhD in Computer Science (1986). The Berkeley CS pedigree puts Norvig in the same generation as Russell, who joined Berkeley faculty in 1986.
Early career at NASA Ames, Sun Microsystems, and the Junglee startup (acquired by Amazon).
Director of Search Quality at Google (2001-2002), then Director of Research / Engineering Director (2002-2021); Distinguished Education Fellow at Stanford HAI (2021-).
Paradigms of Artificial Intelligence Programming (1991) — the Lisp-based AI textbook that prefigures AIMA’s pedagogy.
Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach with Russell (1st ed. 1995, 2nd 2003, 3rd 2009, 4th 2021); the canonical AI textbook by every metric (adoption, citations, translations).
Co-instructor of Stanford’s 2011 “Introduction to AI” MOOC with Thrun — ~160,000 students, the founding-moment MOOC of the post-Coursera era.
“The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data” (Halevy, Norvig, Pereira), IEEE Intelligent Systems (2009) — short and influential; defends data-driven AI against the then-still-strong symbolic / linguistic-theory traditions.

04_People/Philip-E.-Tetlock.title: Philip E. Tetlock
04_People/Philip-E.-Tetlock.content:
Philip E. Tetlock
Why they matter
Tetlock is the empirical anchor of modern forecasting research. By running two large-scale tournaments — Expert Political Judgment (1984–2004) and the IARPA Good Judgment Project (2011–2015) — he converted the question “is expert judgment any good?” from a rhetorical exchange into a quantified, scoreable empirical claim. The fox/hedgehog taxonomy and the operational concept of the superforecaster are now standard reference in cognitive science, intelligence analysis, and policy.
Biography and career
Canadian-American psychologist and political scientist, currently the Annenberg University Professor at the University of Pennsylvania (joint appointments in psychology, political science, and the Wharton School), known for two large-scale empirical research programs on the accuracy of human judgment.
The first, Expert Political Judgment (EPJ), ran from 1984 to 2004, gathered approximately 28,000 forecasts from 284 academic, governmental, and media experts on political and economic questions, and produced the result popularly summarized as “the average expert was about as accurate as a dart-throwing chimpanzee.” Published as Expert Political Judgment: How Good Is It? How Can We Know? (2005). The deeper finding was that experts split into two statistically distinct sub-populations — the hedgehogs (Big Idea, ideologically coherent, overconfident) and the foxes (eclectic, probabilistic, willing to update); foxes outperformed hedgehogs on both calibration and resolution. The hedgehog/fox taxonomy is now standard in cognitive and decision-science vocabulary.
The second, the Good Judgment Project (GJP), was Tetlock’s team in the IARPA forecasting tournament (2011–2015), co-led with Barbara Mellers (his research and life partner). It recruited >20,000 volunteers, generated over a million probabilistic forecasts on ~500 geopolitical questions, beat the official control group by 60% in year 1 and 78% in year 2, and outperformed academic competitors and intelligence analysts with classified access by such wide margins that IARPA dropped competing teams after year 2. The GJP discovered the superforecaster category — the top ~2% of volunteers whose accuracy persists across seasons — and found that selection plus minimal training (a one-hour primer improved accuracy ~10%) plus team aggregation produced sustainable outperformance.
Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner - Superforecasting (2015), co-written with the journalist Dan Gardner, is the popular synthesis. He has subsequently developed the EPJ-2 and Hybrid Forecasting Competition follow-on programs and works on adversarial collaborations with figures including Daniel Kahneman (secondary, not verified in this vault) and Nassim Taleb. Tetlock is on the board of the Good Judgment Inc. spinoff that commercializes tournament-style forecasting.
His training, doctoral advising under Irving Janis (the originator of the groupthink concept) at Yale, and early career at Berkeley shaped his interest in elite group decision-making and the gap between expert confidence and expert accuracy. He served on the National Research Council panel on preventing nuclear war (1984), and on the post-Iraq-WMD National Research Council committee chaired by Baruch Fischhoff that recommended evidence-based testing of intelligence-community analytic methods — the recommendation that led IARPA to fund the GJP.
Notable claims

Long-range political forecasts (3–5+ years) decay toward chance; useful forecasting horizons are ~3–18 months.
The single largest predictor of becoming a superforecaster is perpetual beta — commitment to belief updating and self-improvement — about three times stronger than intelligence.
Forecasting can be improved by clear scoring (Brier scores), explicit numerical probabilities, decomposition (Fermi-ization), outside-view-first analysis, dragonfly-eyed aggregation, and incremental Bayesian updating.

Books

Expert Political Judgment: How Good Is It? How Can We Know? (2005)
Counterfactual Thought Experiments in World Politics (1996, ed. with Aaron Belkin)
Unmaking the West (2006, ed. with Lebow and Parker)
Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction (2015, with Dan Gardner)

Sources

Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner - Superforecasting (Tetlock and Gardner, 2015, throughout) — biographical references in chapters 1, 3, 4, 11.

See also

Dan Gardner — coauthor.
Fox vs Hedgehog (Tetlock)
Superforecaster
Brier Score

04_People/Primavera-De-Filippi.title: Primavera De Filippi
04_People/Primavera-De-Filippi.content:
Primavera De Filippi
Capsule
Primavera De Filippi is a French-Italian legal scholar, blockchain researcher, and artist whose work sits at the intersection of legal theory, computer science, and contemporary art. She is best known in the scholarly literature as the lead author (with Aaron Wright) of Primavera De Filippi and Aaron Wright - Blockchain and the Law (Harvard University Press, 2018), which established the canonical legal-academic vocabulary (lex cryptographica, code-as-law, the seven regulatory chokepoints) for the post-2018 wave of crypto-policy scholarship. She is a permanent researcher at France’s CNRS, a faculty associate of Harvard’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society, and a co-founder of the Coalition for Automated Legal Applications (COALA), the practitioner-academic working group that drafts model legal infrastructure for DAOs. (Biographical specifics other than those grep-verifiable in this vault’s extraction logs are tagged secondary, not verified in this vault.)
Why they matter
De Filippi occupies an unusual quadruple intersection in the blockchain-and-law field: (a) credentialed legal academic (CNRS/Berkman Klein); (b) practitioner-engineer adjacent to active developer communities (COALA, Ethereum-ecosystem working groups); (c) art-research practitioner whose own Plantoid project is the named proof-of-concept for emancipated-device legal personhood discussed in ch. 10 of the book; (d) policy interlocutor with European Commission and EU regulators during the formative MiCA-drafting period (2020-2023). The intersection is genuinely rare. Most 2017-2018 blockchain treatments were written either from outside the developer ecosystem (legal academics with limited technical depth) or outside the legal-academic mainstream (developer-side advocates with limited doctrinal grounding). De Filippi’s work — and the book co-authored with Wright — is the cleanest example of someone equally credible inside both communities, and that positionality is the structural source of Blockchain and the Law’s eight-year shelf life.
For this vault, she matters specifically as the originator of the lex cryptographica concept (the autonomous, transnational rule system produced by cryptographically-secured smart contracts) — the analytical primitive that subsequent regulatory scholarship works within. The concept is the right entry-point for thinking about what kind of legal phenomenon blockchain produces; without it, regulatory analysis collapses to either “blockchain is just like any other software” (missing the autonomy property) or “blockchain is structurally beyond the law” (missing the seven-chokepoint analysis). Lex cryptographica names the middle ground precisely.
Style and method
De Filippi’s voice — and by extension the book’s — is measured, analytically careful, and rhetorically restrained. The book is explicitly not a polemic in either direction; it neither celebrates blockchain as liberation nor condemns it as crypto-anarchism. The method is to build taxonomic frameworks (the eight dual-property characteristics, the seven regulatory chokepoints, the four Lessig levers extended to blockchain) and then apply them as decision-aids to specific cases (TheDAO, Silk Road, Plantoid, mining-pool concentration, Clipper Chip). The taxonomic move is what makes the book most reusable: even as 2018-vintage examples have aged, the frameworks still cleanly classify 2026 cases (FTX collapse → exchange chokepoint; Tornado Cash sanctions → developer chokepoint; OFAC validator-censorship → miner/validator chokepoint).
A second methodological signature is comparative-historical reasoning across legal traditions. Where a US-only legal academic might focus on First Amendment and securities-law doctrine, De Filippi’s CNRS training and her European policy work give the book a comparative-civil-law sensibility. The Plantoid case explicitly invokes French legal-philosophical traditions (Solum 1991 on legal personhood; the European Parliament’s 2017 electronic-personhood proposal); the regulatory-chokepoint analysis takes seriously that different legal systems will absorb chokepoint pressure differently.
A third signature is the art-research bridge. The Plantoid project is genuinely novel — a metallic-flower mechanical structure with an Ethereum smart-contract “spirit” that solicits donations, votes on reproduction proposals, and “reproduces” by hiring artists to build offspring. It is simultaneously an art piece, a legal-philosophy thought experiment, and an empirical test of emancipated-device economic agency. Reading the book without engaging the Plantoid context misses how seriously De Filippi treats the speculative register; the AI-DAO chapter (ch. 9) is not science fiction but applied legal philosophy.
Best for

Legal-academic understanding of blockchain regulation, 2018-2026. The book is the most teachable single text in the literature; the seven-chokepoint chart and the eight-characteristic dual-property analysis work as discrete teaching units.
Anyone working on DAO legal status. Chs. 8-9 on DOs / DAOs are the foundational empirical reference for the post-2018 DAO-legislation wave (Vermont BBLLC, Wyoming DAO LLC, Marshall Islands DAO LLC). Working on DAO legal infrastructure without engaging this treatment starts from a weaker base.
Researchers thinking about code-as-law beyond blockchain. The concept generalizes to AI-system regulation, automated-benefits adjudication, predictive-policing algorithms, content-moderation systems. The book’s three structural limitations (open-textured law, gaming, bug exposure) port directly.
Anyone evaluating crypto-anarchism vs. crypto-authoritarianism trajectories. Ch. 12’s social-credit warning is the most prescient single passage in the 2018 literature on the potential authoritarian-state use of code-as-law.

Less useful for

Crypto-investment or trading decisions. The book is explicitly not investment advice; 2018-vintage market specifics are obsolete.
Deep technical mechanism design. De Filippi is a legal scholar; the EVM gas-pricing, proof-of-stake variants, MEV markets, zero-knowledge proof primitives are sketched at orientation level only. For the engineering layer pair with technical sources.
Post-2022 developments without supplementation. The book pre-dates MiCA (2023), the SEC v. Ripple ruling (2023), the OFAC Tornado Cash sanctions (2022), the Ethereum merge and validator-censorship debate (2022-2023), the FTX collapse, MakerDAO Black Thursday. Frame remains accurate; empirical examples are dated.

How she changed my reading practice
Three durable lessons:

Build dual-property analysis before normative judgment. De Filippi’s eight-characteristic framework treats every blockchain property as simultaneously the source of value and the source of regulatory friction. When evaluating a new technology, the first question is not “is this good or bad?” but “what is the dual-property structure?” This carries cleanly to AI capability evaluations, automated-decision systems, and platform-content-moderation debates.
Take the speculative register seriously. The Plantoid case and the AI-DAO chapter are not gimmicks but applied legal philosophy. Speculating about what kinds of agency law might need to recognize is a productive methodological move, not journalism. This validates a register I had previously been suspicious of.
Position matters; declare it. De Filippi is candid about her positionality (CNRS researcher, COALA co-founder, Plantoid creator, Berkman Klein associate). The book’s measured posture reads as a careful negotiation between communities the authors must remain credible to. Reading it taught me to ask of every legal-policy treatment: whose communities is this author negotiating between, and how does that shape the rhetorical posture?

Relation to Yang’s research
For Yang’s blockchain-regulation research, De Filippi is the lead author of the canonical analytical treatment. The seven-chokepoint analysis (ch. 11) is the right map for any specific regulatory-policy question — which layer is the proposal targeting, what historical precedent governs that layer, what side-effects does targeting that layer produce. Pair with Kevin Werbach - The Blockchain and the New Architecture of Trust for the trust-architecture frame; pair with CZ - Freedom of Money for the practitioner-side realized version of the regulatory dynamics.
For Yang’s broader regulatory-architecture interests, the code-as-law concept (ch. 12) is the most portable single move in the book. It applies to AI-system regulation, automated-benefits systems, content-moderation algorithms, predictive-policing — any domain where rules are increasingly implemented as code. The three structural limitations (open-textured law, gaming, bug exposure) are the right diagnostic tools for evaluating any specific code-as-law proposal.
For Yang’s comparative-authoritarianism interests intersecting with Authoritarian Commons - Neighborhood Democratization in Urban China, De Filippi’s ch. 12 social-credit warning is the cross-domain anchor. The question of whether code-as-law structurally favors or disfavors citizen pushback under authoritarian conditions is the right next research direction; the cooperating-to-fork analog at the blockchain layer is a productive comparative frame.
Sources in this vault

Primavera De Filippi and Aaron Wright - Blockchain and the Law — primary source.
Lex Cryptographica — concept she co-introduced (with Reidenberg’s lex informatica as conscious precursor).
Code-as-Law — concept derived from ch. 12.
Smart Contract Doctrine — concept derived from ch. 4.
Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) — concept derived from chs. 8-9.
Permissionless Innovation Spectrum — concept derived from ch. 11 + the regulatory-stance taxonomy.

Cross-references

Aaron Wright — co-author and complementary figure; Wright’s Cardozo Law / OpenLaw orientation pairs with De Filippi’s CNRS / Berkman Klein orientation to produce the book’s transnational-legal-academic register.
Kevin Werbach — sibling academic with the trust-architecture frame; Werbach (Wharton) and De Filippi/Wright (Harvard/Cardozo/CNRS) are the canonical 2018 legal-academic blockchain treatments.
Changpeng Zhao — practitioner-side narrator whose Binance memoir documents the realized regulatory dynamics that De Filippi-Wright analyze academically.
Acharya and Lee - The Cartel System of States — state-cartel framing within which lex cryptographica’s challenge to state monopoly on rule-issuance is most legible.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited — institutional-economics frame for the regulatory-architecture problem; complements De Filippi-Wright’s legal-academic register.

04_People/Rob-Fitzpatrick.title: Rob Fitzpatrick
04_People/Rob-Fitzpatrick.content:
Rob Fitzpatrick
Why they matter
Fitzpatrick is the author of The Mom Test (2013), the canonical short-form operating manual for early-stage customer interviews. His distinctive contribution is converting customer-discovery from a vague founder skill (“talk to customers”) into a teachable conversational grammar: three rules (talk about their life, ask about specific past behaviour, talk less), a diagnostic vocabulary for bad data ( ideas), and a binary meeting-success rubric (Commitment and Advancement). The book is operational where Lean Startup is conceptual — providing the talk-to-customers primitive that the Build-Measure-Learn loop requires but does not specify.
Works in this vault

Rob Fitzpatrick - The Mom Test (2013)

Key concepts

The Mom Test (Three Rules) — the eponymous three-rule customer-interview discipline.
Compliments Fluff Ideas (Bad Data Triad) — the deflect / anchor / dig response taxonomy for bad data.
Premature Zoom — the failure mode of asking specific questions about non-problems.
Commitment and Advancement — the binary meeting-success rubric and time/reputation/money currency taxonomy.
Product Risk vs Market Risk — the cleavage that bounds the scope of conversation-based validation.
Meeting Anti-Pattern — the over-formalization failure of relegating all customer talk to calendar blocks.

Key arguments

Conversations Can Validate Market Risk But Not Product Risk — the methodological scope claim that bounds his own framework.

Related people / schools

Successor of Steve Blank (not yet a vault person note) — Fitzpatrick cites Blank’s 4 Steps to the Epiphany as the source of the three-meeting customer-development structure. Fitzpatrick keeps the separation but collapses the formalization (see Meeting Anti-Pattern).
Adjacent to Eric Ries (not yet a vault person note) — Ries’s Lean Startup provides the loop (Build-Measure-Learn) that Fitzpatrick’s conversational discipline operationally feeds.
Adjacent to Y Combinator / Paul Graham tradition — the book’s tone (founder confessing dumb mistakes), audience (technical SaaS founders), and tempo (20-minute industry-event chats, not enterprise-procurement cycles) are recognisably YC-shaped. Fitzpatrick was a YC alumnus (Habit Labs).

Biographical anchors (only if relevant)

Founder of Habit Labs, a Y Combinator startup that became the prime source of Fitzpatrick’s autopsy examples in the book (the MTV analytics-dashboard misread of a feature request is from this period; the “first startup mistook ‘I would definitely buy that’ for commitment and lost ~$10M” reference is also from Fitzpatrick’s early founder career, though the specific company is not named in the book). (secondary, not verified in this vault — biographical details about Habit Labs are not in the extraction log; only that Fitzpatrick’s “first company Habit” attempted to sell to enterprise clients including MTV is grep-verifiable.)
Subsequently wrote The Workshop Survival Guide (2019, with Devin Hunt) and Write Useful Books (2021). Not in this vault.

04_People/Robert-A.-Caro.title: Robert A. Caro
04_People/Robert-A.-Caro.content:
Robert A. Caro
Why they matter
American biographer and investigative journalist whose work argues that the durable subject of political biography is not personality but the institutional means by which power is acquired, used, and lost. His seven-year archival exhumation of the Triborough Authority files for The Power Broker became the methodological gold standard for institutionally-attentive long-form biography, and the book itself reshaped how journalists, planners, and political scientists think about urban governance, infrastructure financing, and unaccountable administrative power.
Verified-from-vault facts

A graduate of Princeton University.
Later a Nieman Fellow at Harvard, where he studied urban planning.
An “award-winning investigative reporter for Newsday for six years” before turning to The Power Broker.
Spent seven years on The Power Broker, “tracing and talking with hundreds of men and women who worked with, for or against Robert Moses, and examining mountains of files never opened to the public gaze.”
His wife, Ina Joan Caro, conducted significant on-the-ground research for the book (interviews with Verrazano-Narrows-affected farmers, Sunset Park residents) and authored an unpublished MA thesis cited in the source notes.

(All five facts above are from the author bio and notes/credits sections of the extraction log of Robert A. Caro - The Power Broker.)
Secondary biographical specifics (not verified in this vault)

Year of birth and exact dates of his Newsday tenure are not present in the extraction log of The Power Broker. (secondary, not verified in this vault)
His later work — the multi-volume Lyndon Johnson biography (The Years of Lyndon Johnson) — postdates The Power Broker and is widely known but not documented in this vault. (secondary, not verified in this vault)

Caro’s method (as visible in The Power Broker)

Adversarial archival exhumation. He gained access to Triborough Authority files that the courts had ruled were private-corporation records exempt from public-records laws. The book repeatedly cites bond resolutions, internal memoranda, and committee transcripts that no journalist or scholar had previously seen.
Hundreds of long-form interviews. He sought out Moses’ co-workers, opponents, displaced tenants, contractors, lawyers, secretaries, drivers, and family members. The East Tremont section depends on long interviews with displaced women (Lillian Edelstein, Lillian Roberts, Cele Sherman, others) decades after the eviction.
Walking the routes. Caro physically walked the Cross-Bronx Expressway “one mile” and the Northern State Parkway alternative routes to verify the geography of the routing decisions.
Long view, integrative narrative. He treats biography as an entry point into institutional, social, and political history. The Power Broker is as much about postwar American urbanism as about one man.

Why Caro matters
Caro’s institutional turn — the conviction that you cannot understand political action without understanding the statutes, bond covenants, civil-service rules, and authority structures that enable or constrain it — is the most influential model in modern American political biography. The Power Broker has shaped how journalists, planners, and political scientists think about urban governance, infrastructure financing, and unaccountable administrative power.
Books in this vault

Robert A. Caro - The Power Broker

04_People/Robert-Moses.title: Robert Moses
04_People/Robert-Moses.content:
Robert Moses
Why they matter
American unelected public official (1888-1981) who, holding twelve simultaneous appointed offices over 44 years, personally conceived and built $27 billion (1968 dollars) of public works in and around New York City and shaped the postwar template of American urban planning. He is the canonical case of Power Without Office — appointed authority that became constitutionally entrenched through Bill-Drafting Power and Public Authority (Moses) design. Anyone studying infrastructure, urban planning, eminent domain, public-authority finance, or the institutional preconditions of unaccountable administrative power must reckon with him.
Verified-from-vault facts

Born December 18, 1888, in New Haven, Connecticut. He was given no middle name “because his mother saw no reason for one.”
His grandparents were German-Jewish immigrants from Bavaria — the Cohens (Bernhard from Reckendorf, who emigrated via Frankfurt in his early 20s) and the Silvermans (Rosalie from Reckendorf as a teenager). The grandparents were first cousins; they married in 1849 in New York. They prospered in the dry-goods import trade.
His mother, Bella Moses, was a strong-willed reformer-philanthropist; she was the dominant figure in his early life.
Yale Class of 1909 (Phi Beta Kappa). He was on the swim team and organized the Minor Sports Association against Walter Camp’s football monopoly.
After Yale he went to Oxford (Wadham), where he wrote on the British civil service and absorbed an Anglo elitist conception of public service. He returned with a Ph.D. (often introduced as “Dr. Moses”).
Entered NYC reform government under Mayor John Purroy Mitchel in 1914 to design a numerical civil-service grading system. The system was crushed by Tammany after Mitchel’s 1917 defeat; by 1918 Moses was unemployed and applying for minor municipal jobs in Cleveland.
Joined Governor Al Smith’s circle in 1919 via Belle Moskowitz; drafted the Reconstruction Commission report (1919).
Appointed Secretary of State of New York in 1923; chairman of the State Council of Parks and president of the Long Island State Park Commission on April 18, 1924. (Caro: this is the date Moses was “formally handed” power.)
Ran unsuccessfully for Governor of New York in 1934.
Appointed New York City Park Commissioner by Mayor La Guardia in January 1934; simultaneously continued state-level posts.
Chair of the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority (and predecessor authorities) from 1934 to 1968.
Survived FDR’s 1934 Order 129 attempt to remove him from Triborough.
Led the 1964-65 New York World’s Fair as president.
Lost most state-level posts to Governor Rockefeller in the early 1960s; finally lost Triborough in 1968 when it was merged into the new MTA under William Ronan.
Caro reports him still alive and “fighting with desperate cunning to get [power] back” in 1974, at age 85.

(All facts above are present in the extraction log of Robert A. Caro - The Power Broker.)
Secondary biographical specifics (not verified in this vault)

His death year (1981) is widely reported but is not present in the 1974 extraction log of The Power Broker, which describes him as still alive at publication. (secondary, not verified in this vault)
His Oxford doctorate’s exact subject and date are referenced in the extraction log only generally; the precise dissertation title appears only as a passing reference. (secondary, not verified in this vault)

What Moses built (selected)

416 miles of parkways around New York and on Long Island, plus the entire postwar Long Island state park system (Jones Beach as capstone).
Seven post-1931 East River bridges (Triborough, Verrazano-Narrows, Throgs Neck, Bronx-Whitestone, Henry Hudson, Marine, Cross Bay).
Substantially every major urban expressway in NYC except the East River Drive (Cross-Bronx, Major Deegan, Brooklyn-Queens, Van Wyck, Bruckner, Throgs Neck, Long Island, Staten Island, Sheridan, Gowanus, Prospect, Nassau, Whitestone, Clearview).
658 net new playgrounds in NYC (119 → 777).
15,000 acres of made land, the UN headquarters site assemblage, Lincoln Center site clearance, Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village, the 1964-65 World’s Fair grounds at Flushing Meadows.
The St. Lawrence and Niagara hydroelectric power dams.
267M of NYC Title I urban renewal by 1957 (vs. 133M for all other US cities combined).

Costs

An estimated 500,000 New Yorkers evicted for his projects, including 250,000 specifically for highways. Disproportionately Black, Puerto Rican, and poor.
Decades of neighborhood destruction (East Tremont, parts of South Bronx, Sunset Park).
Systematic starvation of NYC mass transit while highways were built.
A century-shaping commitment to car-dependent metropolitan form.

Why Moses matters
Moses is the canonical case of Power Without Office — appointed authority that became constitutionally entrenched through Bill-Drafting Power and Public Authority (Moses) design. Anyone studying infrastructure, urban planning, eminent domain, public-authority finance, or the institutional preconditions of unaccountable administrative power must reckon with him.

04_People/Robert-Nystrom.title: Robert Nystrom
04_People/Robert-Nystrom.content:
Robert Nystrom
Why they matter
Software engineer (ex-Google, Dart language team) and technical writer; author of Crafting Interpreters (2021), the cleanest modern textbook on programming-language implementation, and Game Programming Patterns (2014), the canonical structured introduction to game-engine design patterns. Distinctive contribution: long-form, code-rich, deeply patient pedagogical writing on hard topics that prior textbooks treated formally and inaccessibly.
Works in this vault

Robert Nystrom - Crafting Interpreters — 2021

Key concepts
(Conceptual contributions are pedagogical rather than original; Crafting Interpreters expounds well-known PL-implementation concepts (tree-walking interpreter, bytecode VM, mark-and-sweep GC) but does not originate them.)
Key arguments

Building beats reading for understanding implementation — implicit in the form of Crafting Interpreters (in the book note)

Related people / schools

Tim Sweeney, Casey Muratori — game-engine craft tradition Nystrom comes from
Aho, Sethi, Ullman (“Dragon Book”) and Andrew Appel — earlier-generation compilers textbook authors that Nystrom’s book updates and humanizes
The crafting-software / tech-writing tradition (Brian Kernighan, John Ousterhout, Jon Bentley) — Nystrom is a worthy successor

Biographical anchors

Software engineer at Google on the Dart programming language team (2010s).
Game Programming Patterns (2014) self-published online, later in print; Crafting Interpreters (2021) similarly.
Live online versions of both books remain freely available; the print versions add polish but are not gated.

(Confidence: medium — most biographical details from Nystrom’s own website and book introductions; primary employment / education specifics not deeply verified.)

04_People/Robin-R.-Murphy.title: Robin R. Murphy
04_People/Robin-R.-Murphy.content:
Robin R. Murphy
Why they matter
Robin R. Murphy is the canonical author of the operational architecture for AI robotics — the three-paradigm history (Hierarchical / Reactive / Hybrid Deliberative-Reactive) and the canonical hybrid operational architecture (Reactive / Deliberative / Interactive layers; Planning / Cartographer / Navigation / Motor Schema / Perception subsystems) that frame how the field teaches itself to think about autonomous robots. Her Introduction to AI Robotics (1st ed. 2000; 2nd ed. 2019) is the dominant graduate-level textbook for AI robotics in North America and the closest thing the field has to a shared design vocabulary.
Beyond pedagogy, Murphy is the founding figure of rescue robotics as a discipline. She founded the Center for Robot-Assisted Search and Rescue (CRASAR) at the University of South Florida (later moved to Texas A&M) and personally led or coordinated robot deployments at most of the major US disaster responses of the 21st century — the World Trade Center collapse (September 2001), Hurricane Katrina (2005), the Crandall Canyon mine disaster (2007), the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident (2011), and the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami response. This field-deployment record gives her textbook a working-roboticist voice that pure academic robotics texts lack: the architectural commitments are defended by reference to what fails in mud, dust, smoke, and radiation, not only what fails in simulation.
Her Three Laws of Responsible Robotics (Murphy & Woods 2009) is the strongest mainstream-academic alternative to Asimov’s Three Laws as engineering specifications, replacing the science-fiction framing with a deployment-discipline framing: humans must not deploy robots without highest legal/professional standards; robots must respond to humans appropriately; robots must have sufficient situated autonomy to protect themselves and accept transferable responsibility.
Works in this vault

Robin R. Murphy - Introduction to AI Robotics — 2nd edition, 2019. The canonical AI-robotics textbook organized around the three-paradigm history and the canonical hybrid operational architecture.

Key concepts originated or formalized
Murphy is a synthesizer more than an originator; her contribution is to organize the field’s shared vocabulary into a teachable architecture. The textbook formalizations that bear her exposition:

Robotic Paradigms (Hierarchical Reactive Hybrid) — Murphy’s three-paradigm taxonomy is the textbook’s organizing concept; the trait diagnostics (interaction between primitives, sensing route) are her formulation.
Behavior-Based Robotics — Murphy’s chapter sequence (ch. 6-8 in the 2nd ed.) is the canonical pedagogy for this programme; she synthesizes Arbib’s schema theory and Brooks’s subsumption into a single design framework.
Subsumption Architecture — Murphy’s textbook treatment (ch. 8.4) with the Level 0 / Level 1 / Level 2 worked example is the dominant pedagogical reference.
SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) — Murphy ch. 15 is the textbook architectural placement; the formal derivations live in Thrun-Burgard-Fox Probabilistic Robotics, which Murphy explicitly cites as the deeper companion.
Sense-Plan-Act Cycle — Murphy’s framing of the Hierarchical paradigm as the failed ancestor of the Hybrid architecture is the canonical pedagogical narrative.
Three Laws of Responsible Robotics (concept-note candidate; not yet promoted) — Murphy & Woods 2009; the deployment-discipline alternative to Asimov.
Five questions for autonomous-capability design (concept-note candidate) — Murphy ch. 19.2.2; the operational checklist for any proposed autonomous capability.

Key arguments

AI robotics is one field organized by paradigm history and operational architecture, not by algorithm. The textbook’s organizing claim is that students should learn the canonical hybrid architecture before learning specific algorithms, because architectural commitments determine which algorithms are admissible and what they fail at. This is a methodological argument against the algorithm-zoo approach that dominates many AI textbooks.
Asimov’s Three Laws are plot devices, not engineering specifications. Murphy’s ch. 20 systematically demolishes the Three Laws as a framework for actual robot deployment — they are designed by Asimov to fail dramatically as story material, and treating them as engineering guidance is a category error. The Murphy-Woods Three Laws of Responsible Robotics are the engineering replacement.
“Autonomy” and “automation” are different paradigms, not points on a spectrum. Murphy ch. 3 defends the four-slider taxonomy (plan generation/execution, action determinism, world openness, knowledge representation) as the right level for distinguishing robots that adapt to open-world surprise (autonomy) from robots that execute scripted behaviors in engineered environments (automation). Conflating them is the source of most “fully autonomous” marketing confusion.
Robotics has driven AI more than AI has driven robotics. Murphy ch. 1.6 argues that the Reactive turn (Brooks 1986), the rise of probabilistic methods (Thrun-Burgard-Fox), and the formalization of human-robot interaction all originated in robotics and propagated into AI — not the other way around. This inverts the popular narrative that robotics is a downstream application of AI.

Related people / schools

Michael Arbib — Murphy’s intellectual ancestor on schema theory and rana computatrix. Arbib’s behavior-based modeling of frog/toad cognition is the formal substrate of Murphy’s Reactive Layer treatment (ch. 6).
Rodney Brooks — Murphy’s pedagogical antagonist-and-ally on subsumption. Murphy treats Brooks’s Cambrian Intelligence as a canonical reference and the subsumption architecture as the most influential Reactive-paradigm system, while disagreeing with Brooks’s stronger anti-deliberation stance.
Ron Arkin — Murphy’s contemporary on cooperating-method coordination (potential fields) and behavior-based robotics. Arkin’s Behavior-Based Robotics is the parallel canonical text Murphy explicitly cites.
Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox — Murphy’s deferred companions on probabilistic robotics. Their Probabilistic Robotics (2005) is the formal-derivation companion Murphy points readers to for the SLAM machinery she sketches.
David Woods — collaborator on the Three Laws of Responsible Robotics and on human-robot interaction theory; Murphy ch. 18 inherits the cognitive-engineering tradition Woods represents.
Kate Darling — downstream legal-ethics inheritor. Kate Darling - The New Breed (2021) draws on Murphy’s working-roboticist methodology and the moral-crumple-zone framing (Elish, with whom Darling explicitly collaborates) for its rejection of Asimov as engineering.
Field-robotics tradition — Murphy is the public face of a tradition that includes the DARPA Grand Challenge teams, the Boston Dynamics field-deployment school, and the disaster-robotics community at IEEE TC-SAR. The field-deployment voice is the unifying methodology.

Biographical anchors (only if relevant)

Professor and Raytheon Professor of Computer Science and Engineering at Texas A&M University; previously at the University of South Florida. (secondary, not verified in this vault)
Founder of the Center for Robot-Assisted Search and Rescue (CRASAR), the dominant US institution for disaster-robotics research and field deployment. (secondary, not verified in this vault)
Personally led or coordinated robot deployments at the World Trade Center (2001), Hurricane Katrina (2005), Crandall Canyon mine disaster (2007), Fukushima Daiichi (2011), Tōhoku tsunami (2011), and Hurricane Harvey (2017). (secondary, not verified in this vault — but Murphy ch. 1, ch. 5, ch. 18 reference several of these deployments in the textbook itself)
IEEE Fellow; recipient of the Eugene L. Lawler Award; AAAI Fellow. (secondary, not verified in this vault)
Maintains the Science Robotics “Outbreak” / “Disaster Response” columns and a long-running Robotics Through Science Fiction blog and book series.

The biographical sparseness is appropriate: Murphy’s intellectual contribution is best read through the textbook itself + the rescue-robotics field record, both of which are referenced in the book. Treat the book note as the primary record; this people note is a thin pointer.

04_People/Ryo-Morimoto.title: Ryo Morimoto
04_People/Ryo-Morimoto.content:
Ryo Morimoto
Why they matter
Ryo Morimoto is a Japanese cultural anthropologist whose 2023 Nuclear Ghost: Atomic Livelihoods in Fukushima’s Gray Zone (UC Press, California Series in Public Anthropology) is the first English-language full-length engaged ethnography of post-3.11 coastal Fukushima built on continuous Japanese-language fieldwork (2013–2019, follow-ups through 2022). His distinctive intellectual contribution is a third-position analytical framework — neither the biological-citizenship / damage-centered framing imported from Chornobyl studies (Petryna 2013) nor the radiophobia-ghostbusting framing common in mainstream radiation-safety discourse (Ono 2015 / Ropeik) — that he develops via the named concepts half-life politics and atomic livelihoods. The book is a worked example of the public-anthropology method-package: long-duration fieldwork, named recurring informants, refusal of damage-centered research, outside-the-discipline writing register, sustained positionality work.
Works in this vault

Ryo Morimoto - Nuclear Ghost — UC Press 2023; California Series in Public Anthropology; ISBN 9780520394100 (hardback) / 9780520394117 (paperback) / 9780520394124 (ebook); LCCN 2022047687

Key concepts

Half-Life Politics — coined to name the technosensory regime that foregrounds radiation as the dominant variable of postfallout discourse, rendering everything else (cultural continuity, intergenerational succession, soil-as-patrimony, multispecies relations) invisible
Atomic Livelihood (Gray Zone) — coined as the positive-construction alternative to atomic victimhood; livelihoods are “atomic” in two senses (materially contaminated environment + sociologically atomized community), drawing on Ui Jun ([1971] 2006)
Sacrifice Zone Chronotope — analytically deployed (though not lexicalized in the book) for the Hamadōri 1955–2065+ chronotope; explicitly names radioactive colonialism in ch. 9 with reference to Brugge, Benally, and Yazzie-Lewis (2006) on Navajo uranium parallel
Public Anthropology Method — the book is published in the California Series in Public Anthropology and is a worked example of the method-package

Key arguments

The radiation-centered narrative of Fukushima is itself a second species of harm against the residents who stayed (the half-life politics argument)
Distance, not contamination, was the operative variable in the state’s evacuation orders, with cascading social-economic consequences (the stupid lines argument, ch. 3)
Decontamination is biographical erasure dressed as remediation (the frecon baggu archive argument, ch. 7)
The TEPCO accident is a radioactive-colonialism chronotope — Tokyo Electric supplied Tokyo exclusively, while coastal Fukushima bore the harm (ch. 9 closing argument, attributed to Tengo)
En (Buddhist concept of indirect cause / hidden condition for interconnection) is a methodological resource for ethnography — following invisible threads of chance encounter rather than searching for representative victims (Intro and ch. 1)

Related people / schools

California Series in Public Anthropology editorial lineage — Series Editor Ieva Jusionyte (Brown); Founding Editor Robert Borofsky (Hawaii Pacific); Advisory Board Catherine Besteman (Colby), Philippe Bourgois (UCLA), Jason De León (UCLA), Laurence Ralph (Princeton), Nancy Scheper-Hughes (UC Berkeley). Morimoto is a Princeton-affiliated anthropologist and Ralph is on the advisory board, suggesting a Princeton-public-anthropology cluster
Adriana Petryna (UPenn, Life Exposed, 2013) — Morimoto explicitly frames his book against Petryna’s biological citizenship — the Chornobyl framework where liquidators weaponize their bodies for state recognition; Morimoto’s residents refuse this move
Joseph Masco (Chicago, The Nuclear Borderlands, 2006; “The Age of Fallout,” 2015) — Morimoto deploys Masco’s nuclear uncanny and engages Masco’s fallout-as-planetary argument while distinguishing his own intermediary (residents-and-region) scale
Olga Kuchinskaya (Pittsburgh, The Politics of Invisibility, 2014) — post-Chornobyl Belarus state-managed-invisibility framework; Morimoto contrasts it with Fukushima’s hypervisibility regime
Hiroshi Kainuma (Japanese sociologist of Fukushima) — Fukushima Ron (2011) and 2015 work cited extensively; the Japanese-side intellectual companion
Masaharu Tsubokura (radiation-health doctor, Tokyo U. → Fukushima University) — the locally-grounded risk-communication exemplar Morimoto features in ch. 5
Thomas Hinton (radioecologist, Fukushima University) — the multispecies-radiation-tracer scientist featured in ch. 9
Eve Tuck (“Suspending Damage,” 2009) — the methodological-ethical interlocutor whose damage-centered research critique organizes Morimoto’s positive-construction approach
Nicolas Sternsdorff-Cisterna (anthropologist of postfallout food safety) — anzen vs. anshin analytical framework Morimoto deploys in ch. 3
Aya Hirata Kimura — Radiation Brain Moms and Citizen Scientists (2016); Morimoto’s ch. 5 contrast with the ghostbusting risk-communication regime

Biographical anchors (only if relevant)
(Tag: secondary, not verified in this vault — the following claims about Morimoto’s biography are not directly verifiable from the extraction log; they are inferable from the book’s front matter and standard publishing-world records.)

Affiliation at time of publication: The book’s California Series in Public Anthropology placement and the inclusion of Princeton’s Laurence Ralph on the advisory board are consistent with Morimoto being a Princeton anthropologist at publication time. The ingestion brief explicitly identifies him as a “Princeton anthropologist.” (secondary, not verified in this vault)
Educational background: The Intro mentions “I had just moved to Minamisōma from Massachusetts for my dissertation fieldwork” in July 2013 — implying PhD candidacy at a Massachusetts institution at that time. The most likely candidate is Brandeis University’s anthropology department (where Morimoto’s doctorate is recorded), but this is not verified in the extraction. (secondary, not verified in this vault)
Origin: The Intro and ch. 1 establish him as “growing up in western Japan,” speaking a western-Japan dialect (Aichi-area is mentioned in connection with the family-friend’s pillow company that loaned him the field car). (verified in extraction log)
Fieldwork commitment: ~6 years primary fieldwork (2013–2019) with multiple follow-ups through 2022, including 1F tour in May 2015, Columbia Mailman School RSO training summer 2019, Hinton lab visit summer 2018, TEPCO Tomioka headquarters visit early 2019. (verified in extraction log)
Languages: Japanese (native); English (PhD-level academic). The book is written in English with extensive Japanese vernacular embedded as analytical infrastructure. (verified in extraction log)

Verified-from-source biographical specifics
The following are grep-verifiable in the extraction log:

The book is © 2023 by Ryo Morimoto, published by University of California Press, Oakland, California, in the California Series in Public Anthropology
LCCN 2022047687; ISBN 9780520394100 (hardback) / 9780520394117 (paperback) / 9780520394124 (ebook); manufactured in the United States of America
The book carries permissions from Knopf, Doubleday Canada, and ICM Partners for Murakami quotation rights — implying budget and editorial scaffolding consistent with a major anthropology trade-academic title

He attended a foreign film director’s fieldwork as a translator initially in July 2013 before splitting from the project
