06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: MEGA — Make Economics Great Again
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.1 — MEGA: Make Economics Great Again
Framing chapter. Polarization is exploding (US split-ticket voting at record low; 81% of partisans hold negative view of out-party; views cluster in “bunches of grapes”). Yet on the major economic questions — immigration, trade, taxes, role of government — public views are based on personal-values affirmation rather than evidence and have hardened into tribal markers.
Trust deficit. Only 25% of Americans trust economists in their own field of expertise (politicians 5%, nurses 84%, weather forecasters 50%). On ten IGM-Booth survey items, the academic-economist consensus and public opinion diverge sharply: 100% of Booth panel disagreed that steel/aluminum tariffs improve welfare; only 37% of public agreed. Telling respondents what experts think does not move opinion (NAFTA case: 51% pro vs 46% pro depending on whether expert view was disclosed first — small).
Why the gap. Three causes: (1) the visible “TV economists” are firm spokespersons with predictable market-optimism slant, looking like academics in suit and tie but uncoupled from the evidence; (2) academic economists rarely explain reasoning in public — careful nuance gets edited out of TV interviews — leaving the loudest voices to dominate; (3) economists are fallible (IMF growth-forecast error 2.8 pp over two-year horizons in 2000–2014, no better than guessing 4% — economics is more like medicine or plumbing than physics, “intuition grounded in science, guesswork aided by experience, plus trial and error”).
Authors’ positioning. Anti-grand-theory, anti-pat-answer. The valuable thing economists offer is not the conclusion but the path — what facts were known, how they were interpreted, what deductive steps were taken, where uncertainty remains. Best economics is “frequently the least strident.”
Methodological commitment for the book. Reject narrow GDP/income notions of well-being. Restore “deep human desire for dignity and human contact” to the center. The book will tackle: immigration, trade, growth, inequality, climate, automation, government, social policy. The reader is not asked to agree but to “adopt a little bit of our methods” and engage seriously across the divide.
Anchor RCT/dataset. The authors’ own 2018 ten-thousand-person US survey, paralleling IGM Booth questions; referenced throughout the book to compare expert vs public opinion.
Key contrast with Poor Economics (predecessor). Poor Economics applied the RCT/empirical-mechanism toolkit to poor-world problems (food, health, education, fertility, credit, savings, business, politics). Good Economics applies the same toolkit to rich-world problems where the popular intuitions are equally wrong. Same epistemic program, new continent.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: From the Mouth of the Shark
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.2 — From the Mouth of the Shark (Migration)
Headline. The “napkin economics” of immigration — labor supply curve shifts right, wages must fall — is wrong on both ends. (a) Even very large refugee/migrant influxes do not depress native wages or employment. (b) The far bigger anomaly is how few people migrate even when wage gaps are huge. The labor market is not a watermelon market.
Scale of the perceived problem vs reality. International migrants are 3% of world population — same in 1960, 1990, 2017. EU non-EU intake is ~0.1–0.5% of population/year. 2018 EU asylum applications: 638k, 38% granted = ~1 in 2,500 EU residents. Italian survey: actual immigrant share 10%, perceived 26%. Le Pen’s claims (99% adult-male, 95% on welfare) — actual 58% adult-male, 55% in labor force.
Information vs preference. Two RCTs: when respondents are told the true numbers, they update factual beliefs but not policy views. Le Pen voters exposed to fact-checks did not move. Simply thinking about migration makes people more parochial.
The supply-demand framework fails on the wage side. Five mechanisms refute it:

Demand-side offset. Migrants spend money locally, shifting labor demand right. Czech-commuter case (workers crossed border to Germany, spent earnings at home in Czech Republic): native employment fell — confirming the no-spending-no-offset prediction.
Mechanization deferral. Cheap migrant labor delays labor-saving tech. 1964 bracero expulsion from California: tomato-harvester adoption went 0%→100% in three years; in Ohio (no braceros) no change. Wages didn’t rise after expulsion. California temporarily abandoned asparagus, lettuce, celery.
Task reorganization & complementarity. Migrants take communication-light tasks; natives upgrade to communication-heavy ones. Danish refugee-dispersal data: natives in high-migrant areas upgraded from manual to non-manual jobs.
Migrants do jobs natives won’t. Lawn-mowing, eldercare, fruit-picking. Skilled women’s labor-force participation rises with migrant supply (cheaper childcare).
Efficiency wages. Stiglitz: firms pay above market to make firing-as-punishment credible. Wage band is therefore narrow — natives are protected by incumbency. Hiring is not like buying watermelons; firms screen heavily, demand references, hate intra-firm wage inequality. Czech case: natives’ “job losses” were lower-gains, not actual displacements.

Skilled migration is the more mixed case. Fewer of the protective frictions apply (efficiency-wage rents are smaller, formal credentials substitute for personal trust). One foreign nurse displaces 1–2 native nurses in US data. Trump-favored “skilled migration” hurts native skilled workers even as low-skilled migration does not.
Why so few migrate. This is the deeper puzzle.

Wage gaps are huge. Visa lottery winners from Tonga to NZ: 3× income increase within one year. Indian H1-B winners: 6× their stay-home peers. Yet hundreds of millions of poor stay put.
Forced-mobility natural experiments. Westman Islands (Iceland) 1973 lava: those whose homes were destroyed (random) saw $3,000+ higher annual income decades later, mainly because the young got out of fishing into college/other careers. Finland post-WWII: 11% of population forced to relocate, ended up richer than rest of country 25 years later. Pure inertia keeps people from moving even when moving pays.
Bangladesh seasonal-migration RCT (Mushfiq Mobarak et al.): Information alone had zero effect; 11.50 (one bus fare + 2 days food) caused 22% to migrate; migrants made 105 average, sent home $66, raised family calorie consumption ~50%. Half didn’t repeat migration the following year. Information is not the binding constraint.
Nepal study (Maheshwor Shrestha): Migrants overestimated mortality by ~10×; correcting that estimate increased migration. Information about wages reduced it (migrants had been overestimating earnings 25%).

Why people stay. Connections (jobs found through co-ethnics — Munshi Mexico-US drought instrument; refugee-resettlement-with-co-ethnics replication). Comfort and informal-insurance networks (you may have a network at the destination but a deeper one at home). Akerlof-style market unraveling for the unconnected (employers suspicious of anyone without referrals; lemons-market logic). Family ties and Lewis (1954) free-rider problem (going gives the family $100 extra but you don’t benefit personally → you stay). Loss aversion (Kahneman-Tversky): active-choice failures hurt more than passive failures. Risk vs Knightian uncertainty: migration is uncertain (unknown unknowns), and people avoid uncertainty more than they avoid risk. Self-image protection: would-be migrants who stay can always tell themselves they would have succeeded.
The “American restlessness” myth is dying. US internal migration: 7%/year moving counties in 1950s; <4% in 2018. Rich states no longer attract more population (since ~1990). Low-skilled workers actually moving inward (away from coasts). Reason: housing costs eat the wage premium for low-skilled — janitor in NYC vs Deep South: nominal +32%, real -6% after rent. Lawyer: nominal +45%, real +37%. Low-skilled stay in cheap inland places.
Comeback Cities don’t comeback. Rise of the Rest fund tour ($150M, Bezos-Schmidt-backed) — Akron, Detroit, South Bend. Chicken-and-egg: young educated workers won’t move without amenities; amenities can’t open without enough workers. Industry clustering compounds the problem.
Implication for policy. Real migration crisis is not “too much” but too little — both internally and across borders. Fix barriers: streamline process, communicate honestly about costs/benefits, ease remittances, subsidize migration insurance against failure (in Bangladesh case, insurance against failure was as effective as paying for the bus ticket), provide childcare assistance, housing subsidies. Make integration easy. Identity-politics backlash to migration is real and predictable — happens in every wave (US 1924 National Origins Act repeated each generation). The right response is not to stop migration but to invest in the public goods that allow integration.
Cross-references inside the book. The “stickiness” of labor markets revealed in this chapter is the master concept that drives chapters 3 (trade), 5 (growth), 7 (automation), and 9 (cash and care).

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: The Pains from Trade
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.3 — The Pains from Trade
Headline. Three claims, each at odds with textbook trade economics:

Aggregate gains from trade for a large economy like the US are small (Costinot & Rodríguez-Clare estimate ~2.5% of GDP — one year of decent growth could pay for full autarky in perpetuity).
The Stolper-Samuelson prediction that trade raises wages of the abundant factor (low-skilled labor in poor countries) repeatedly fails. After 1985–2000 liberalizations in Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, India, Argentina, Chile — inequality went up everywhere.
The losers from trade are concentrated geographically and don’t get compensated, producing irreversible local destruction.

Public vs expert. 100% of IGM Booth panel disagreed that steel/aluminum tariffs help; only 37% of public agreed. 65% of public thinks low-skilled workers are hurt by trade with China; only 21% think they are helped. Comparative advantage is the example Samuelson gave Ulam of “a non-trivial true social-science proposition” — but the public never bought it.
Topalova’s heretical paper. Petia Topalova (MIT PhD student) used the 1991 Indian liberalization as a within-country natural experiment. Different districts had different tariff exposure depending on industry mix. Result: districts more exposed to tariff cuts had slower poverty reduction and slower decline in child labor. Stolper-Samuelson predicted the opposite. Paper was rejected by top journals; she went to the IMF (more open-minded than the academy). Eventually replicated in Colombia, Brazil, the US — all show the same pattern.
Why Stolper-Samuelson fails. Resources are sticky. Workers don’t move; capital is locked in declining firms (banks evergreen loans rather than face defaults); even within multi-product firms, declining product lines aren’t shut down (Topalova found minimal “creative destruction”). When trade shock arrives, instead of reallocation, wages drift down and everyone hangs on. The Stolper-Samuelson model assumes frictionless mobility; reality is the opposite.
Why poor exporters can’t break in. Reputation is everything. International buyers (Amazon, brand retailers) can’t afford defects. The price of production is 10–15% of retail; cutting production cost 50% saves only 7.5% — not enough to overcome a quality-uncertainty discount. ATA-Egypt carpet program: took 5 years to land first significant order, even with US NGO + Italian designer + dedicated intermediary. Hamis Carpets (the intermediary) had to absorb buyer-side disputes (the tea-acid antiquing case). For an Egyptian T-shirt maker to undercut China by $4/hour requires Amazon to gamble its reputation — they won’t. Industrial clusters (Tirupur knitwear, Zhili children’s wear) emerge as the solution: a known intermediary plus shared cluster reputation.
The China shock (Autor-Dorn-Hanson). US commuting zones exposed to Chinese import competition saw large concentrated losses: manufacturing employment fell, total employment fell more (clustering downward spiral — laid-off workers spend less, local businesses close, housing values drop, neighborhood deteriorates, no new firms come). Young men less likely to graduate college, fewer marriages, more out-of-wedlock births, “deaths of despair” rise. Workers did not move to other regions. Replicated in Spain, Norway, Germany.
Government response. Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) was the official compensation mechanism — and it works (workers approved by lenient caseworkers earned 50k more over 10 years, full ROI on retraining). But it was tiny: only 23¢ of the 58 in extra transfers per affected adult came from TAA; disability insurance ate most of it (one-tenth of trade-displaced workers went on disability — a one-way street out of the labor force). Obamacare denial in red trade-affected states made it worse: disability claims rose 1% in non-expansion states, fell 3% in expansion states. The economist consensus that “we can compensate the losers” was a fantasy in the actual political economy.
Trade war doesn’t help. Trump’s 2018 steel/aluminum tariffs save some steel jobs but create new losers in agriculture (China retaliated on 128 mostly-agricultural products; US ag exports to China are 16% of total ag exports; ~1M US jobs depend on ag exports, mostly in nonfarm sector). The transition costs are real and they hit different counties this time.
Smaller countries need trade more. US gains from trade are 2.5% of GDP because 8% of consumption is imports. Belgium’s import share is 30%+. For small/poor countries (Africa, SE Asia, southeastern Europe), trade matters far more — but they face the biggest reputation barriers. National integration via railroad delivers comparable productivity gains: 19th-century Indian rail expansion → 16% faster ag productivity growth in connected districts; US rail → 64% land-value gain.
Policy prescription. Expand TAA (GI-bill style): full tuition, 36-month stipend, place-based supplements. Subsidize firms in trade-affected regions to retain older workers (55-62) until social security age (Summers-Glaeser-style payroll-tax cut). Make it explicit that the tax base benefits all of trade and should pay for the losers. Don’t waste money on tariffs.
Cross-chapter resonances. The “sticky economy” master concept from ch.2 applies again. The local-destruction story prefigures ch.7 (automation), where “deaths of despair” originally documented in trade-affected counties become the central phenomenon of the inequality chapter.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: Likes, Wants, and Needs
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.4 — Likes, Wants, and Needs
Headline. Becker-Stigler’s “De Gustibus Non Est Disputandum” doctrine — that preferences are stable, coherent, and not to be questioned by economists — is wrong about racism, peer effects, identity, and most of what drives political polarization. Preferences are radically context-dependent. And yet this is liberating, because it means preferences can be changed by altering context — without coercion or propaganda.
The Becker-Stigler hope refuted. Bigoted bakers should go bankrupt because of lost business. They don’t, because (a) like-minded customers reward them, and (b) preferences are themselves shaped by community membership. Bigotry can be good business and good politics.
Standard preferences can rationalize fads (Banerjee 1992, herd behavior). People may rationally join the crowd on the train platform if they suspect others have private information. One artificial up-vote on a comment website (random-assignment RCT) raises top-grade probability significantly months later — the cascade compounds. So fads do not refute standard preferences.
Norms can be sustained without true preferences (folk theorem). Caste discrimination, racial discrimination, and small-community cooperation (Ostrom Swiss-cheese alpine commons, Kenya/Sri Lanka fisheries) all work via the same logic: norm-violators excluded, exclusion-violators excluded, etc. Pretty much any norm — including bad ones — can be self-enforcing. The film Samskara iconic case: Brahmin who slept with a low-caste prostitute; no one will cremate him for fear of pollution; body rots in public. Caste-panchayat enforcing tradition over law (the 14-yr-old rape victim beaten for going to police).
Statistical discrimination can produce racism without preference. “Ban-the-box” study: when employers can’t see felony status on application, they statistically discriminate against black applicants (assuming higher prior conviction rate). Pre-BTB white-vs-black callback gap was 7%; post-BTB it became 43%. The well-intentioned reform made things worse. Trust-game experiment with Ashkenazi senders sending less to Eastern Jewish receivers — but Eastern Jews returned money at exactly the same rate as Ashkenazis. The stereotype was unfair, and even Eastern senders had absorbed it.
Self-fulfilling prophecies & stereotype threat. Steele’s classic experiment: black students score lower when test framed as IQ test; white students score worse when told the experiment is about Asian math superiority. Princeton golf experiment: same students; race primed → black score worse on “general sports performance”; “natural athletic ability” framing → black score better; “sports intelligence” framing → white score better. Everyone has bought the stereotypes. In a French grocery, biased supervisors managed minority cashiers less well (didn’t visit cashier stations); minority productivity suffered, “confirming” the prejudice. Bangladesh women managers: technically as good as men but workers didn’t listen → lines underperformed → confirming bias.
Acting white norm. L.A. Hispanic high schoolers offered free SAT prep: take-up was 11pp lower when the choice would be made public — for non-honors students. They feared “acting white.” Asian students don’t have this norm. History selects which norms get sustained.
Coherent arbitrariness (Ariely-Loewenstein-Prelec, Kahneman-Thaler endowment). Mug/pen endowment: WTA 2-3× WTP. Trackball/wine bid manipulated by writing-down-of-SSN-last-two-digits as anchor: SSN >80 bid 200-350% more than SSN <20. People don’t have absolute valuations. Robbers Cave (Sherif): randomly divided 11-12-yr-olds → animosity emerged → joint task → animosity dissolved. Rwanda Belgian-fabricated Hutu-Tutsi distinction → 1994 genocide. Preferences are partly invented and partly malleable.
Self-reinforcing segregation. Schelling tipping points (Card: most US cities tip at 5–15% black share). Homophily means even mild own-group preference + crowded out-group → near-total separation. US cross-racial marriage 50 years after Loving v. Virginia: 1 in 6 newlyweds. India 74% endogamy. Mostly because finding similar-to-self is easier within-group.
Echo chambers. Twitter politically-engaged users: 84% of conservative followers are conservative; 69% of liberal followers are liberal. 92% of liberal messages from liberal sources, 93% of conservative from conservative. Even on non-political topics. Gentzkow-Shapiro: party-affiliation prediction from a single sentence of congressional speech rose from 55% (1873-early-1990s) to 83% (2007-09). Newt Gingrich’s 1994 takeover and the rise of political consultants is a turning point.
Are echo chambers from the internet? Mixed evidence. Gentzkow-Shapiro 2009 isolation index for online news (7.5pp) is lower than offline news. Polarization is rising even among 65+ (least online) and rose less among 18-39 (most online). Cable TV (Fox shifted right since 2004) plays a key role. Korean online experiment: users who chose their news sources moderated more than users force-fed random sources — because they understood and discounted bias. The internet’s filter-bubble automatic customization is the real problem.
Motivated beliefs (Bénabou-Tirole). We don’t reason from neutral premises. We protect a self-image (intelligent, kind, etc.). We rationalize prejudice in the language of “objective fact.” Calling people “racist” or “deplorable” assaults that self-image and entrenches the position. Calling racists “fine people” lets them feel better about themselves and doubles down (Trump strategy, “morally reprehensible but effective”).
Wilson on inner-city ghettos applies to white Rust Belt. When the social problems described for black inner cities in 1997 (joblessness, family dissolution, social disorder) describe Vance’s white Appalachia in 2017, the white community’s self-image-defense response is to ratchet up the caricature of the other — single-mother-on-welfare becomes single-mother-gang-member.
Operationally tractable interventions.

Contact hypothesis (Allport 1954, 27-RCT review): contact reduces prejudice if status is equal, goals shared, cooperation real, authorities support it. Random college roommate with minority-race student: white more likely to support affirmative action and continue mixed friendships in year 2.
Delhi private-school RP (rich+poor reservation policy): kids who ran the relay-race-with-playdate exercise selected better runners regardless of caste only if exposed to mixed schools. Familiarity dissolved the playdate-aversion.
UP cricket league RCT: mixed-caste teams produced more cross-caste friendships AFTER. But teams that competed against other-caste opponents made less progress. Competition undermines contact. France 1998/2018 World Cup soccer was the cooperative-shared-purpose case.
Schelling-aware housing: Singapore’s per-block ethnic quotas; Paris housing projects integrated into fancy neighborhoods. Boston busing was unpopular but METCO program (busing minority kids to majority schools) worked, no harm to majority kids.

The four operational implications. (1) Calling people racists deepens racism. (2) Voters don’t have absolute racial preferences — Mayawati 2007 UP shift to broad-poor-coalition; deep-red Medicaid-expansion ballot wins in Utah/Nebraska/Idaho. (3) Bigoted voting is often indifference to the political system: simple street-theater messaging (“don’t vote on caste”) moved 10% of UP voters away from caste-party preferences. (4) Best route to combatting prejudice is to give citizens a reason to engage with policy substance — restore public conversation credibility.
Bridge to next chapters. Subsequent chapters examine substance — growth, inequality, climate, automation, government — that an engaged citizenry would need to reason about. The endorsement here is that public conversation can be restored if the substance is delivered with humility and structural respect for ordinary people’s dignity.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: The End of Growth?
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.5 — The End of Growth?
Headline. Economists know much less about growth than the policy debate pretends. The 1820–1970 sustained-growth period was historically anomalous; the post-1970 slowdown may be a return to normal. Patient policies focused on the well-being of the worst-off (health, education, courts, infrastructure) deliver more measurable welfare gains than chasing the elusive 0.3 pp acceleration in TFP growth — and they can spell the difference between a country being ready to ride the next growth wave when it comes and missing it entirely.
The Trente Glorieuses. US per-capita GDP growth 1.76%/yr 1870–1929; 2.5%/yr 1950–1973. France 4× per-capita GDP gain in one generation. Driven mostly by total factor productivity (TFP) — Solow’s “measure of our ignorance” — not capital accumulation per se. Then OPEC 1973 → stagflation → permanent slowdown (post-1973 TFP at 1/3 the prior pace).
Gordon vs Mokyr. Robert Gordon: today’s innovations are not as transformative as electricity and internal combustion; “spot the robot” — hotel clerks, cleaners still human. Predicts 0.8%/yr growth for next 25 years. Joel Mokyr: globalized science, lasers, 3D printing, brain aging being slowed will deliver new growth. Their disagreement reveals: economists have no good predictive theory of growth.
Solow’s exogenous-growth model. Diminishing returns to capital → richer economies grow more slowly. Convergence: poor countries should catch up. But empirically, 1960 GDP and subsequent growth rate are barely correlated. Solow’s escape: convergence holds for “otherwise identical” countries. TFP improvements are exogenous and cross-country similar at the frontier — so balanced-growth rates equalize.
Lucas-Romer endogenous growth & the TFP puzzle. If India differed from US only by capital scarcity, the marginal return on capital in India would have to be 58× US — but capital doesn’t flow there in those volumes (sticky economy, contra Lucas’s frictionless assumption). So intrinsic productivity (TFP) must be lower in India. Romer: spillovers/network effects mean ideas in some places generate more ideas → poverty traps in idea-spillover terms. This justifies industrial policy targeting clusters.
Acemoglu-Johnson-Robinson institutionalism. Settler colony / non-settler colony division based on European mortality → different institutions → different long-run growth (1995 colony GDP per capita differential explained largely by 18th-century settler mortality). “Institutions matter” is robust enough to be the most-cited result in growth empirics.
But misallocation matters more than aggregate scarcity. Hsieh-Klenow: misallocation of capital across firms in India and China leaves enormous TFP on the table — if they reallocated capital like the US, TFP would jump 30-60%. The reason China grew so fast 1979-2010 is partly that pre-1979 misallocation was so severe; the gains from re-allocating dwarfed Solovian capital deepening. Same for India post-1991.
Self-inflicted misallocation in developing-country labor markets. Government jobs pay 2× private-sector wage in poor countries → masses of young people queue (28M Indian applications for 90k railway jobs). Some Ghanaian graduates wait years for the right job; meanwhile, others creatively become DJs at funerals or nut farmers. Some labor market regulations entrench formal-informal duality. Cutting government wages or capping age-eligibility for civil-service exams could free up vast productive labor.
Convergence is not automatic. Japan: predicted by Vogel (1979) to overtake the US. Stopped growing in 1980. Aging population + low immigration; needed TFP miracle that didn’t come. China: aging, slowdown probable, may take 35+ years to reach US per-capita GDP at 5% Chinese vs 1.5% US growth (optimistic). Middle-income trap: of 101 middle-income economies in 1960, only 13 reached high-income by 2008.
India’s manufacturing miracle is mysterious but probably finite. Post-2002 sharp acceleration in plant-level technology upgrading. Likely driven by generational shift (foreign-educated children inheriting parental businesses) and accumulated profits enabling scale-up. As the worst-managed firms shed and remaining firms approach the frontier, the misallocation-elimination gain shrinks. India will plateau, perhaps lower than China’s plateau.
Trickle-down doesn’t trickle. Reagan-Thatcher tax cuts didn’t accelerate growth in US/UK. The instinct that “we have to be business-friendly to preserve growth” cost the bottom 99% in both economies in the 1980s onward, with no growth payoff. IMF since 2017 includes inequality in country-team analysis (a major institutional shift).
The pivot. GDP is a means, not an end. Sri Lanka and Guatemala have similar GDP per capita; Sri Lanka’s maternal/infant/child mortality is comparable to the US, Guatemala’s much higher. Targeted health interventions (the malaria-net case — 75% drop in malaria deaths 2005–2016 with 582M nets distributed in 2014–16, mostly free) deliver verifiable welfare gains without a known recipe for growth. The book’s prescription: stop chasing the growth mirage; invest in human capital and institutional quality. If/when growth comes, citizens will be ready to climb on.
Bridge. Climate (ch.6), automation (ch.7), inequality (ch.7’s second half) all assume a slow-or-no-growth backdrop. The book’s policy program is built for that world.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: In Hot Water
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.6 — In Hot Water (Climate)
Headline. Climate change is massively inequitable: rich countries (and rich consumers worldwide) are responsible for most emissions, while poor countries bear most of the cost. Within-country, the rich pollute many times more than the poor. The “free lunch” of energy efficiency is largely a mirage; meaningful action requires both technology and consumption change. Carbon taxes are right, but only if structured to be revenue-neutral and explicitly redistributive.
The 50-10 rule. 10% of the world’s population (highest emitters) cause ~50% of CO₂ emissions; the bottom 50% (lowest emitters) cause ~10%. North American per-capita CO₂e: 22.5 tons; Western European 13.1; Chinese 6; South Asian 2.2. The richest Indians and Chinese are already in the global top-10% of polluters. The poorest 7% of Indians emit 0.15 tons.
Heat damage is concentrated in poor countries. Per-degree-Celsius year-on-year rise: -1.4% per-capita income, but only in poor countries. India productivity in garment factories: -2% per °C above 27-28°C. Mortality impact of extra hot day in India is 25× that in the US. Cold-country impact: vineyards in Moselle Valley benefit. The world’s poor near the equator suffer the hardest hits.
Air conditioning paradox. US has 87% household AC (2011); India 5%. AC saves lives (US mortality from heat fell 6× from 1920s-1930s to today, mostly from AC). But standard ACs use HFC refrigerants — much more potent greenhouse gases than CO₂. Kigali 2016 amendment: rich-country phase-out 2019; China 2024; India + small group 2028 — buying time but locking in a decade of cheap dirty AC adoption in India. India argues “save lives today, fix climate later”; the “later” may not come.
Energy efficiency gap may not exist. McKinsey 2009 said efficiency investments would yield $1.2T in net savings; IEA said efficiency could deliver 49% of needed cuts. Reality from RCTs:

Greenstone Michigan WAP study (~7,500 households): only 6% take-up despite aggressive promotion; energy savings 1/3 of engineer estimates; not because of rebound effect (no temperature increase).
Gujarat firm energy-audit RCT: audits + free consultancy → firms produced more (rebound effect) → no net energy reduction.

Economists usually want carbon taxes (Nordhaus 2018 Nobel). But preferences for environmental action are themselves shaped by context, not from-the-sky. Default-option experiment in Sacramento: when peak-pricing was made the default, 90% stayed in vs 20% choosing it actively. People can’t articulate their environmental preferences, so the default-design lever matters. Energy use is a habit (Paris green building, sweater-in-office). Once habit changes, taxes don’t hurt much.
Pollution kills now, not just in 2070. China north-of-Huai-River subsidized coal heat → 5.5-year life expectancy gap, 3.7B life-years lost equivalent. Indian cities top the global pollution list; Delhi air in Nov 2017 reached 48× WHO limit. 9M premature deaths from air pollution globally (Lancet 2015), 2.5M in India alone. So “develop now, clean up later” is killing people now.
Delhi’s pollution sources: stubble burning in Punjab/Haryana; construction dust; vehicle exhaust; trash burning; cooking fires. Solution menu: subsidize farm-residue management (~Rs 20B = $14/Delhi resident); ban open fires; modern trash collection; ban old/diesel cars; congestion pricing; better public transit; enforce industrial standards; upgrade thermal plants. None is out of reach. Demand for cleaner stoves is shockingly low — even free distribution unused — apparently because households don’t connect indoor air pollution to health outcomes.
Yellow Vests problem. Climate policy must not be a tax on the working class to assuage rich-Parisian guilt. Macron’s 2018 carbon-tax-without-redistribution framing failed. The right design: explicit revenue-neutral carbon tax (carbon revenue → flat lump-sum to all, larger as share of low-income consumption → poor come out ahead, incentive to reduce emissions preserved). Announce in advance to allow habit adjustment.
Green New Deal evaluation. Right instinct — link climate action with redistribution and public-investment job creation. Useful counter to the carbon-tax-as-elite-imposition narrative. But: economic literacy required to defend carbon tax even within left-wing programs; just-transition policies (rich countries paying poor countries to leapfrog to clean tech) should be central.
Cross-references. Sticky economy from chs.2-3 means displaced coal workers won’t smoothly become solar engineers; same TAA-style support needed. Habit formation from ch.4 (preferences are context-dependent) is the basis for default-design and tax-announcement strategies. Inequality from ch.7 is the political constraint on credible climate policy.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: Player Piano
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.7 — Player Piano (Automation, Inequality, Despair)
Headline. Two related stories. (1) AI/robots will likely worsen the displacement of routine and middle-skill workers; current US tax code subsidizes excessive automation; the Luddites were less wrong than economists assumed. (2) The Reagan-Thatcher trickle-down experiment after 1980 produced an explosion in inequality without producing the promised growth, hollowed out the middle class, and produced “deaths of despair” that now define the white American working-class crisis.
The automation evidence.

Acemoglu-Restrepo: one extra robot per commuting zone reduces employment by 6.2 workers and depresses wages. Effects strong for non-college workers in routine manual jobs. No offsetting employment gains in any other group. Looks like the China-shock pattern from ch.3.
Luddite reality check: real blue-collar wages in Britain fell almost 50% between 1755 and 1802 during the height of industrial mechanization; recovered to 1755 levels only in 1820 (65 years later). The “long run is fine” defense is a euphemism for “two generations of misery.”
Currently: typists displaced; bookkeepers displaced; mid-skill clerical jobs hollowed; Annie Duflo’s AI assistant Fin replacing human assistants; AI legal/financial paralegals coming. McKinsey: 45% of US jobs automatable; OECD: 46% in 35 OECD countries.
IGM Booth panel split 28-20-24 (agree-disagree-uncertain) on whether AI will substantially raise long-term unemployment. Rare uncertainty.

Excessive automation: tax-code distortion. US tax code:

Payroll taxes on labor; no equivalent on capital.
Accelerated depreciation for capital expenditures.
Interest-deduction for capital financing.
This biases firms toward “so-so automation” — robots just productive enough to displace workers but not productive enough to raise total productivity. Most R&D resources go to labor-displacing rather than labor-augmenting innovation. Acemoglu-Restrepo: the worst case is so-so automation that displaces without efficiency gain. South Korea 2017 robot tax (cut subsidies + outsourcing tax) is the only existing policy response. EU rejected one. Bill Gates supports.

Trickle-down failed. US top marginal tax rate: >90% (1951-1963), Reagan cut to <30%, never substantially recovered. UK: 83% (1978) → 60% (1979) → 40% (~ever since). Result: growth didn’t accelerate; wages stagnated for the bottom; top-1% share of national income reverted to 1928 (Roaring Twenties) levels by 2017 in the US. Top-1% wealth share: 22% (1980) → 39% (2014). Continental Europe: very different — inequality stayed compressed after WWII, with one Sweden upswing exception. Pre-tax and post-tax inequality track each other in the US — the change is about pre-tax compensation, not just tax policy.
The 1980 turning point is policy-driven, not just structural. Reagan-Thatcher coincided with computerization, China/India opening, globalization. But:

Skill-biased tech change should produce a continuous wage-distribution widening; instead, the wages between 100k-200k grew only slightly, while >$500k incomes exploded. Tech change alone doesn’t explain the very-top-end concentration.
Why didn’t continental Europe see the same widening? Tech change reached them too. Difference is institutional/policy.
Saez-Diamond-Piketty optimal-tax research: top marginal income tax rate should be 70% or more; revenue would not decline because the rich don’t actually stop working (Switzerland tax-holiday natural experiment proves this for the broad population).

Why the rich don’t stop working. Switzerland 1999-2001 transition from arrears-based to pay-as-you-earn taxes created tax holiday years for income earned 1997-98. Workers knew taxes due would be zero. Effect on labor supply: zero — none on hours, none on participation. Globally consistent finding: high taxes don’t kill labor supply.
Wealth tax could raise real revenue. Saez-Zucman: 2% wealth tax on >50M plus 3% on >1B affects 75k Americans, raises $2.75T over 10 years (1% of GDP). Combined with Zucman’s anti-evasion proposals (global financial registry, multinational profit allocation by sales, regulating tax-haven enablers) — politically tractable revenue.
Inequality + low mobility = despair. Americans believe in mobility (12% of bottom-quintile children reach top quintile in popular belief; 7.8% in reality, lower than European average ~11%). When the dream confronts reality, two reactions:

Despair (Case-Deaton): white middle-aged less-educated mortality rising; deaths from drugs, alcohol, suicide; life expectancy declining 2015-2017. Specific to US whites without college; black mortality kept falling. Each cohort entering the labor market after the late 1970s did worse than predecessor (in marriage, employment, social ties, mental health).
Anger (Autor-Dorn-Hanson): trade-shock counties replaced moderate politicians with extremists; supports Trump-style scapegoating of immigrants and trade. Conservative wins lead to lower social spending → exacerbates the original problem.

Norway tax-porn experiment. Tax records went online in 2001. Increased awareness of one’s relative position: poor became sadder, rich happier. We are all in some version of this experiment via social media. Bling/platinum-card consumption signals status; the urge weakens after a self-affirmation exercise.
Implication. The simple narrative — “automation is the new threat” — is partly a deflection. The same political choices that produced 40 years of growing inequality can also produce the right responses to the next wave: progressive taxation including wealth tax; revenue-neutral carbon tax; serious safety net; place-based industrial policy; social policy that respects dignity (ch.9). The inequality crisis has been visible since 1980; we don’t need AI to start fixing it.
Cross-chapter resonances. Sticky-economy and place-based-loss themes from chs.2-3 reappear here. The political-economy constraints articulated in ch.4 (echo chambers, motivated beliefs, loss aversion) explain why the policy response has been so feeble. The cash-and-care reforms in ch.9 are the proposed solution.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: Legit.gov
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.8 — Legit.gov (Government Capacity)
Headline. Wealth and income tax reform alone cannot finance the social policies needed; broader taxes on the merely-rich and the middle class are required. The political obstacle is the eroding legitimacy of government — citizens’ belief that the state is corrupt, incompetent, and not on their side. This belief is partly true, partly self-fulfilling, and substantially the result of decades of economist-amplified anti-state rhetoric. Restoring legitimacy is the precondition for everything else.
Tax reform alone doesn’t add up. US total tax revenue: 27% of GDP (2017), tied with South Korea, near OECD bottom. Denmark 46%, France 46%, Sweden 44%. Even raising income tax rates to Danish levels would reduce top incomes (companies stop paying astronomical salaries) without raising much revenue. Saez-Zucman 2% wealth tax plus 3% billionaire tax: $2.75T over 10 years, 1% of GDP. Necessary but not sufficient. Real fiscal expansion requires the average earner to pay more — politically forbidden in current US discourse.
Taxes don’t kill labor supply (Switzerland holiday natural experiment, again). People believe their neighbors will stop working if taxed (only 35% of survey respondents believe an average middle-class person would work as much under higher taxes), even though they themselves wouldn’t (72% say they would not stop). The “lazy American” trope is unfounded but politically powerful.
Distrust of government. Pew 2015: only 23% of Americans trust the government always or most of the time. 59% have negative opinion. 32% would prefer tax cuts on the rich to higher taxes for redistribution. This is the legacy of Reagan’s “government is the problem” framing.
Punjab water-electricity case (Manpreet Singh Badal). Free farm electricity is exhausting the water table. Economically optimal fix: lump-sum payment to farmers, then charge for electricity → preserves welfare while incentivizing conservation. Tried 2010: farmers didn’t trust the government would actually pay; rejected the policy; Badal lost his job. Revived 2018 with reverse order — give cash up front, then deduct electricity charges. Even so, farmer associations remain suspicious. Distrust is a binding constraint.
Privatization is not a panacea. Private schools in India: cheaper but children randomly assigned to them have no better test scores than public-school peers. Liberian school-to-NGO/for-profit transfer (2016): mixed results, only Bridge Academy did better, but only by spending more and capping class size. France: private placement services for long-term unemployed perform worse than public ones.
Corruption obsession misdiagnoses the problem. Corruption is often the inevitable cost of doing things the market would not do (tax collection, school admissions, pollution fines). Privatizing tax collection (historic “tax farming”) corrupted the system worse. The 2019 Stanford/Yale admissions scandal: when society pushes back against pure market price-discovery, side doors emerge. The point is not that corruption doesn’t matter, but that the obsession with anti-corruption transparency creates its own pathologies.
Italian Consip case. Italy created Consip — a centralized procurement office for government departments after corruption scandals. Departments could buy from Consip or independently. They mostly chose Consip, even though independent purchase was usually cheaper. The benefit of Consip: insulation from corruption accusations. Net: Consip cost the government more.
Economists’ anti-government rhetoric is damaging. Bumbling/corrupt-government caricature deters talented young Americans from public service (Esther: “neither of us has ever had an undergraduate … tell us they were headed to a career in government”). India dice-roll experiment (replicating Swiss bankers): students intending government careers cheat more than students going elsewhere. Replicated in Denmark: government-bound students cheat less. Government legitimacy and integrity are partly self-reinforcing.
Pakistan procurement-flexibility RCT. Hospital and school procurement officers given small discretionary cash budgets did better: lower prices, more savings. Constraint without trust ≠ better government.
Federal Acquisition Regulation: 1,800 pages. No major US tech firm bid on the Obamacare computer-system contract — the paperwork barrier was prohibitive. USAID contracting is dominated by “Beltway bandits” who specialize in the paperwork, not the work.
Latin America counter-example. 2000s Latin America saw real inequality reduction. Conditional cash transfer programs (Mexico’s Progresa/Oportunidades/Prospera) used the quid-pro-quo framing — transfers tied to school attendance and health checks — to win bipartisan support, even from the right. RCTs validated child welfare gains. Successive governments rebadged but didn’t cut. By 2019 Mexico’s left government is replacing CCT with unconditional transfer (RCT-validated path).
Tax design lessons from Latin America. When Mexico’s CCT-design philosophy spread (with RCT data attached), the public conversation about redistribution shifted across the developing world. India’s 2019 elections: both major parties had cash-transfer programs as central platform — historic first. Careful program design + experimental validation can break political stalemates.
Implication. Restoring government legitimacy is the central political problem of our time — “much greater than space travel, perhaps even than curing cancer.” Requires (1) economists stop the anti-government snicker; (2) attract talent into public service via prestige and adequate authority; (3) design programs that visibly serve citizens rather than chase the suspicion of fraud; (4) experimentally validate before scaling; (5) make tax progressivity explicit and tie revenue visibly to outcomes (revenue-neutral carbon tax, etc.).
Cross-chapter. This chapter sets up ch.9 — once we accept that government must do more, the next question is how social policy should be designed to preserve dignity and legitimacy.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: Cash and Care
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.9 — Cash and Care (Social Policy)
Headline. Universal Basic Income is too expensive to be truly universal; conditional cash transfers (CCTs) work but cost a lot in conditionality compliance and exclude the most vulnerable; pure unconditional cash works but doesn’t restore dignity. The real design challenge is cash plus respect — programs whose architecture treats the poor as agents, supports their plans seriously, and prioritizes integration over policing. The “graduation” model (BRAC/Bandhan-style) and the Sénart “young creators” model show what this looks like.
Universal Basic Income. Friedman’s NIT, Yang’s 1,000/month proposal, Hamon (France), Hillary Clinton, India's 2019 election proposals, Switzerland 2016 referendum (lost 75-25). Logic: hands-off respect for poor people's autonomy. Cost: 1,000/month per US adult = $3.9T/yr — bigger than the entire federal budget, would need Denmark-level taxes plus elimination of all existing welfare. Not universal in practice — would need to phase out at higher incomes, reintroducing targeting.
The conditionality cost. Mexico CCT (Progresa): 10% of every 100 pesos transferred goes to admin overhead. 34% of admin to identifying beneficiaries; 25% to verifying conditions. Heavy on staff time, light on transfers.
Vulnerable people get excluded by complexity.

Morocco water-connection program (Esther): “Veolia bus” had no one on it; signup required city-hall bureaucracy. Field-officer document-pickup intervention: 7× signup increase.
Delhi widow pension: $85 PPP/month, eligible women 2/3 not enrolled. Information alone didn’t help; help with the application form mattered; physical accompaniment to the office mattered most. Even with full help, take-up only 26% (women had given up on the government delivering).
US SNAP elderly outreach: 6% baseline take-up; information → 11%; assistance → 18%.
Stigma: SNAP labeled “Golden State Advantage Card” got more take-up than identical “food stamps” program.
Morocco Tayssir CCT: families with most-at-risk children opted out because they feared failure to meet attendance conditions would shame them. Unconditional transfer presented as “help to educate your kids” worked better.

Fear of cash misuse is empirically baseless.

119 developing countries have unconditional cash assistance; 52 have CCTs; ~1B participants. RCTs across the spectrum.
Cash recipients spend more on food (often raise share of expenditure on food).
No increase in tobacco/alcohol spending.
No effect of giving cash to men vs women in terms of “vice” spending. (Authors still favor giving to women — restores intra-household power balance.)
No reduction in labor supply. (NIT experiments New Jersey/Pennsylvania 1968-72 had small effects but sample-design flaws; consensus is that effect is small or zero.) Reagan-era warnings about welfare “creating dependency” not supported by data: Heather Ross’s $5M experiment thesis settled this empirically.
Ghana bag-making + asset-transfer RCT (Banerjee-Karlan-Osei-Udry): asset recipients produced more bags, especially of complex designs, despite extra workload of tending the asset. Most plausible: cash relieves cognitive bandwidth → people work better, not less.

Dignity is the missing variable.

Asaf-ud-Daula’s Bada Imambara (Lucknow, 1784): elites whose homes were destroyed at night so they could “rebuild” by day to earn famine-relief wages. Dignity preservation is ancient.
Shaw’s Alfred Doolittle: “I’m one of the undeserving poor. I’m always up against middle-class morality.”
Reagan’s “welfare queen” framing → 1996 PRWORA → TANF replaces AFDC + work requirements. Macron 2018 leaked tape repeating “make the poor more responsible” 6 times in a few minutes.
India ration shop preference over cash: 2/3 of households prefer food, often citing protection-from-temptation (cash is too easy to spend on bad things). The preference partly reflects internalized stigma.
Chantal (TAE employee, France): disabled couple with disabled children; asked for home assistance; given foster-care placement instead, lost custody for 10 years over a “temporary” intervention. Same callous pattern: Swiss farm-placement of poor children until 1980s; Canadian indigenous-school assimilation. “Discrimination is in effect a form of racism against the poor.”

The graduation model works (BRAC/Bandhan/CGAP). Asset transfer + 18-month consumption stipend + literacy training + savings + health support + hand-holding. RCTs across 7 countries (BRAC India, Pakistan, Ghana, Honduras, Peru, Ethiopia, Yemen): substantial and durable impact. India 10-year follow-up: beneficiaries have more consumption, more assets, healthier, happier — graduated from “outliers” to “normal poor.” Cash alone in long-run follow-ups doesn’t have this durable effect.
Sénart “young creators” program (RCT-tested). Disadvantaged French youth offered help in starting their own businesses. Caseworkers spend an hour+ per first interview taking the proposed project seriously. Outcome: more employment, higher earnings, but less self-employment — because the project is the entry point for restoring confidence, not the destination. Effect strongest for most-disadvantaged. Compared with a competing “select-the-most-promising” program: zero effect.
Becoming a Man (Chicago South Side). Cognitive-behavioral therapy for at-risk teen boys teaching them to gauge whether violence is warranted in this specific situation, rather than telling them “violence is wrong.” Reduced arrests by 1/3; violent-crime arrests by 1/2; raised graduation rates ~15%. Same dignity-respecting design philosophy.
ATD Fourth World Montessori schools. Emergency-housing-project schools as well-resourced as elite Paris private Montessori. Same underlying principle.
Implication. Social policy must (a) treat the poor as agents with plans, not as objects of intervention; (b) provide cash as a baseline because it works and the poor know what to do with it; (c) invest in respect-preserving program design (low conditionality, no humiliating application processes, no stigma branding); (d) for those at the bottom, layer asset-plus-coaching on top of cash, validated experimentally; (e) experimentally validate before scaling. Hope, not surveillance, is the fuel that makes people climb. “Defining people by their problems is turning circumstance into essence.”
Cross-references. Builds on ch.4 (preferences and dignity), ch.7 (inequality and despair as the targets of social policy), ch.8 (government legitimacy as the precondition). The book’s culminating prescription: a humane, experimentally-grounded social state that earns its legitimacy by visibly working.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: Conclusion — Good and Bad Economics
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch.10 — Conclusion: Good and Bad Economics
The book’s coda. All economies are sticky. The textbook story of frictionless reallocation — workers move, capital flows, prices clear — fails empirically across migration, trade, automation, and growth. Stickiness explains why the gains from globalization concentrated in some places and the pains in others; why there is so little catch-up among displaced workers; why local destruction outlives any policy response by years.
Good and bad economics.

Good: Reinikka-Svensson information disclosure on Ugandan school grants; insecticide-treated bednet free distribution (after RCT settled the price debate); HIV antiretrovirals to drive testing; Progresa CCT and its cousins; J-PAL micro-evidence on what actually works.
Bad: Trickle-down tax cuts (Reagan-Thatcher and imitators); the “free trade is unambiguously good” sales pitch that ignored local destruction; “government is the problem” framing that delegitimized public action; the “growth-at-any-cost” obsession that delayed climate action and drowned out distributional questions.

Keynes’s epigraph applied. “Practical men who believe themselves quite exempt from any intellectual influence are usually the slaves of some defunct economist.” Bad economics has captured policy. Good economics is no panacea but is a precondition for sane policy.
The four-I diagnosis (extending Poor Economics’s “three I’s”). Ignorance, intuitions, ideology, inertia. Together they produce plausible-looking answers that betray us. The only defence: vigilance, skepticism of “obvious” claims, patience with complexity, honesty about uncertainty.
Closing line. “Economics is too important to be left to economists.” The call to action is for the engaged citizen who is willing to read carefully, weigh evidence, resist tribal certainty. The book has aimed to provide a starter kit.
Bridge to Poor Economics. Where Poor Economics (2011) was the methodological-foundation document for the RCT revolution applied to poor-world problems, Good Economics for Hard Times (2019) is the popular-public-economics application of the same toolkit to rich-world problems. The thesis arc — patient empirical reconstruction beats grand theory — is identical. The continents and the policies differ. Together they form the canonical statement of the J-PAL school’s worldview.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: Abhijit V Banerjee Good Economics For Hard Times — Chapter Deep Dives
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Abhijit V Banerjee Good Economics For Hard Times — Chapter Deep Dives
10 chapters

Ch.1 — MEGA — Make Economics Great Again
Polarization is exploding (US split-ticket voting at record low; 81% of partisans hold negative view of out-party; views cluster in “bunches of grapes”).
Ch.2 — From the Mouth of the Shark
The “napkin economics” of immigration — labor supply curve shifts right, wages must fall — is wrong on both ends.
Ch.3 — The Pains from Trade
Three claims, each at odds with textbook trade economics: 1. Aggregate gains from trade for a large economy like the US are small (Costinot & Rodríguez-Clare estimate ~2.5% of GDP — one year of decent growth could pay for full autarky in p…
Ch.4 — Likes, Wants, and Needs
Becker-Stigler’s “De Gustibus Non Est Disputandum” doctrine — that preferences are stable, coherent, and not to be questioned by economists — is wrong about racism, peer effects, identity, and most of what drives political polarization.
Ch.5 — The End of Growth?
Economists know much less about growth than the policy debate pretends.
Ch.6 — In Hot Water
Climate change is massively inequitable: rich countries (and rich consumers worldwide) are responsible for most emissions, while poor countries bear most of the cost.
Ch.7 — Player Piano
Two related stories. (1) AI/robots will likely worsen the displacement of routine and middle-skill workers; current US tax code subsidizes excessive automation; the Luddites were less wrong than economists assumed.
Ch.8 — Legit.gov
Wealth and income tax reform alone cannot finance the social policies needed; broader taxes on the merely-rich and the middle class are required.
Ch.9 — Cash and Care
Universal Basic Income is too expensive to be truly universal; conditional cash transfers (CCTs) work but cost a lot in conditionality compliance and exclude the most vulnerable; pure unconditional cash works but doesn’t restore dignity.
Ch.10 — Conclusion — Good and Bad Economics
All economies are sticky. The textbook story of frictionless reallocation — workers move, capital flows, prices clear — fails empirically across migration, trade, automation, and growth.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: Think Again, Again
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch. 1 — Think Again, Again
Frame
Banerjee and Duflo open with the identifiable-victim effect (Save the Children flyer experiment: students gave 2.83 for one Malian girl Rokia vs 1.16 for “millions hungry”; warning students about the bias halved the donation to Rokia rather than raising it for everyone) to motivate the book’s whole approach: stop debating “is poverty too big to solve” and start naming concrete sub-problems with concrete answers. The polarized macro debate between Jeffrey Sachs (poverty traps exist; one big aid push escapes them; The End of Poverty argues 195B/year 2005-2025 ends global poverty) and William Easterly / Dambisa Moyo (no traps; aid corrupts; markets and freedom suffice; *White Man's Burden*, *Dead Aid*) cannot be resolved at the country-level cross-section because counterfactuals are unobserved. Aid is also a small fraction of anti-poverty spending (5.7% of African government budgets in 2003; India spent 31B PPP just on primary education that year and receives essentially zero aid).
The poverty-trap diagnostic
The chapter’s core formal device is the S-shape vs inverted-L comparison:

S-shape (Sachs world). Income tomorrow vs income today curve is flat at low income, rises sharply, then flattens. Below the threshold, you’re below the 45° line: tomorrow < today, you spiral down to a low fixed point N. Above, you spiral up. → Poverty trap exists; a one-time push past the threshold permanently lifts the household.
Inverted-L (Easterly world). Curve rises steeply at low income then flattens. Always above 45° at low end → no trap; one-time gifts give a temporary boost only.

The empirical work in the rest of the book is asking, domain by domain (food, health, education, fertility, savings, business), which curve is the right one here? The answer is usually inverted-L for the variable everyone debates and S-shaped somewhere unexpected nearby (e.g. childhood nutrition, business technology choice). This is the structural payoff of replacing macro debate with micro evidence.
The bed-net case as method-template
The Sachs-vs-Easterly free-vs-priced bed-net dispute is the canonical tractable instance: do people use free nets, do they pay for the next one, do free nets crowd out private sellers? Pascaline Dupas’s Kenyan RCT (later replicated in Uganda, Madagascar) randomly assigned subsidy levels; ch. 3 will report findings. The lesson is methodological: randomize assignment to comparable groups, run the experiment, accumulate replications across contexts.
J-PAL and the new approach
Authors founded the Poverty Action Lab (later Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, J-PAL) at MIT in 2003 to industrialize this approach. By 2010: 240+ experiments in 40 countries. The book is built on these RCTs plus qualitative fieldwork across an 18-country dataset of households living on <99 cents/person/day.
Three I’s and the depth-over-breadth thesis
Closing thesis the book argues throughout: most policy failure is not grand-conspiracy elite capture but the three I’s — ideology, ignorance, inertia — on the part of experts, aid workers, local policy makers. The corollary is hopeful: small details fixed in the right places can compound into a real exit from poverty. This is not the sweeping-answer style of either Sachs or Easterly; it is patient empirical accumulation.
Why this chapter is high-leverage

States the entire book’s methodological identity in 30 pages.
The S-shape / inverted-L diagram is reused across all 9 substantive chapters.
The Sachs/Easterly framing recurs in chs. 2 (food), 3 (health), 4 (education), 5 (family), 7 (credit), 10 (politics).
The “three I’s” frame is the book’s takeaway prescription.

Compression check
Source ~9000 words → summary ~600 words. ~15:1 compression.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: A Billion Hungry People?
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch. 2 — A Billion Hungry People?
Standard view & its ground
The UN’s first Millennium Development Goal pairs poverty with hunger; many countries’ poverty lines are calorie-budget anchors; food subsidies are massive (Egypt: $3.8B = 2% of GDP in 2008-09; India’s PDS loses >½ of wheat and >⅓ of rice to spoilage and theft). The intuitive story: poor people eat too little → they’re weak → they earn too little to eat enough → poverty trap (formalized by Leibenstein, Mirrlees in the 1958-1976 literature).
Empirical surprise: poor people don’t behave as if starving
Across the 18-country dataset:

Food is 36-79% of consumption (rural extremely-poor) and 53-74% (urban) — substantial but not maximal.
In Udaipur, the typical poor household could spend 30% more on food if it cut alcohol/tobacco/festivals; it doesn’t.
Income elasticity of calories ~0.67 in 1983 Maharashtra (poorest to richest very poor), so a 1% income gain raises calorie spending only 0.67% — and even that goes mostly to better-tasting not more calories (millets are cheapest per calorie; ⅔ of grain spending was on rice/wheat at twice the calorie cost).
Jensen and Miller’s “flight to quality”: subsidizing rice or wheat noodles in two Chinese regions led to less consumption of the staple and more shrimp/meat — total calories did not rise (and may have fallen).
Deaton and Drèze: Indian per-capita calorie consumption is declining over 25 years despite rising real incomes and falling food prices. ~75% of Indians now consume below the official “minimum” calorie line.
Self-reported “enough food” rose from 17% to 2% reporting not having enough between 1983 and 2004.
Strauss’s Sierra Leone study: 10% calorie increase → at most 4% productivity rise; the curve is inverted-L, not S-shape, in that domain.

Conclusion: there is no nutrition-based poverty trap for adults in most contexts today. Pak Solhin (Bandung casual laborer) thought he was in one; reading is that his job vanished, his age locked him out of construction apprenticeships, and depression compounded the loss — the bind is structural-labor-market and psychological, not literal-calorie.
Where the trap does live: in utero and early childhood

Barker hypothesis (BMJ 1995): in-utero conditions affect lifetime outcomes. Tanzania iodine capsules to mothers → ½ year more schooling for the in-utero cohort (~7.5% gain in Central/Southern Africa total educational attainment if universal).
Anne Case and Chris Paxson: height-earnings correlation is fully mediated by IQ; both reflect childhood nutrition.
Kenya deworming: 2 years of school deworming pills → 20% higher adult earnings (~3,269 PPP lifetime gain per child at 1.36/year program cost — see ch. 1 epigraph).
WISE iron supplementation (Indonesia): 7/year fortified fish sauce → 46 PPP/year self-employment income gain.
Half of Indian under-5 children are stunted; ¼ severely so. Indian women among shortest globally; only Eritrea worse. China has 386 Olympic medals over 8 games (avg 48); India 0.92 over 22 (below Trinidad-and-Tobago at 0.93 with 1/1000 the population) — childhood nutrition leaves marks visible at population scale.

Why don’t the poor eat better?

Information: micronutrients are not directly observable; one anemic Indonesian’s $40 yearly gain is invisible against weekly income noise. Employer pays piece rate, not calorie sensitivity.
Resistance to outside diet advice: 1966-67 Bengal — chief minister suggesting less rice was greeted with vegetable-garlands of protest.
Temptation/quality preference: Orwell on white-bread-and-margarine British workers; Oucha Mbarbk in rural Morocco — owns a TV, parabolic antenna, DVD player despite hunger (“television is more important than food”). Festival spending in Udaipur (no TV): 14% of budget; in Nicaragua (radio penetration): essentially zero. Boredom is a real constraint.
Pessimism about radical change: poor families behave as if no expenditure is large enough to permanently change life trajectory, so they prefer making the present pleasant. This is the aspiration-failure mechanism that recurs across the book.

Policy implication
Stop assuming “more cheap grain” suffices. Direct micronutrient interventions targeting pregnant mothers and young children — fortified flour, iodized salt, deworming pills, conditional cash transfer with nutritional supplements (Mexico, Colombia, Kenya) — have outsized social returns. PROGRESA-style CCTs and Micronutrient Initiative / HarvestPlus orange-flesh sweet potato (Uganda, Mozambique) instantiate this. American/EU food-aid policy is mistargeted by the calorie-quantity frame.
Why this chapter matters
Templates the book’s signature move: take a sweeping macro claim (“a billion hungry people”), break it into three precise sub-claims (do they eat enough? if not, are they trying to? if not, why?), use RCT/survey evidence to refute the simple S-shape story for adults, then locate the real S-shape in childhood nutrition where most policy ignores it.
Compression
Source ~25k words → summary ~750 words. ~33:1 compression.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: Low-Hanging Fruit for Better (Global) Health?
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch. 3 — Low-Hanging Fruit for Better (Global) Health?
The puzzle
Cheap, evidence-backed health technologies — chlorine bleach for water, ORS (sugar+salt+water) for diarrhea-dehydration, ITNs for malaria, deworming pills, basic immunization, exclusive breastfeeding, iodized salt, iron-fortified flour — exist and could save the bulk of the 9 million annual under-5 deaths. But uptake is dismally low: in Zambia, 98% of households know Chlorin treats water but only 10% use it ($0.18/month); in India, only ⅓ of under-5 diarrhea cases get ORS; <40% of world infants are exclusively breastfed; basic immunization rates in rural Udaipur are 5% before intervention.
The Sachs frame
Health-poverty trap: malaria-prevalent countries are 1/3 the per-capita income of malaria-free ones; sick adults are unproductive → countries can’t afford eradication → stuck. Eradication push pays for itself many times over (Bleakley/Lucas: malaria eradication in US South 1951 and Latin America → 50% lifetime income gain for malaria-free cohorts; smaller but positive in India, Paraguay, Sri Lanka). Bed-net cost-benefit: 14 net, 5-year life, 30% reduction in infection probability × 50% earnings effect × 590 Kenyan adult income = $295 expected gain → dominates dramatically.
Why isn’t the market plucking the fruit?

Government supply-side dysfunction. World Bank Absenteeism Survey (2002-03, 6 countries): 35% nurse absenteeism on average (43% in India). Udaipur: 56% of health-post visits found facility closed. Das & Hammer “3-3-3 rule” for Delhi private/public clinic visits: 3 minutes, 3 questions, 3 medicines, often injectable steroids+antibiotics. ⅔ of unqualified urban “doctors” had no medical degree.
Demand-side puzzle. Even when nurses are present (Seva Mandir intervention raised from 40% to >60% attendance), patient flow does not increase. Even when free monthly immunization camps run with clockwork regularity in Udaipur, only 6% → 17% full-immunization conversion.
Cure-not-prevention bias. Udaipur poor saw a doctor every 2 months on average; <¼ of visits to public facility, >½ to private (often unqualified), remainder to bhopas (traditional exorcists). Spending was on antibiotic shots and saline drips, not on cheap prevention.

Mechanisms (this chapter’s theoretical contribution)
“Free means worthless”? — refuted
Cohen-Dupas TAMTAM bed-net experiment in Kenya: demand collapses as price rises (almost everyone takes free; near-zero at PSI’s $0.75 price). But conditional on receiving a net at any subsidized level, 60-90% of households used it, with no usage difference by price paid. The Easterly “subsidies-as-wedding-veils” anecdote does not survive RCT replication. Subsidy is fine; the failure mode is somewhere else.
Faith and theory
Patients lack the high-school biology that would let them reject “medicine must enter the bloodstream” → they prefer injectables → they are over-medicated in unsterile conditions → drug-resistant bacterial strains and steroid-induced premature aging. Self-limiting illnesses (most outpatient visits) feed spurious causal attribution to whatever was prescribed. Immunization, which prevents events that may not have happened anyway, is structurally unteachable from individual experience.
Hope and the placebo function of healthcare
A Bengali doctor: the poor cannot afford treatment for chronic disease (chest pain, blood in urine), so they show up only for self-limiting conditions to receive any treatment that signals doing-something. This explains the bhopa/healer/preacher market — symptoms come and go, attribution is generous, hope is the consumed good.
Time inconsistency / nudge
Seva Mandir + the authors’ RCT: offering 2 lbs of dal (~$1.83 PPP) per immunization shot raised full-immunization rates from 6% to 38% — a 6× jump from a small immediate reward. Stainless-steel-plate completion bonus did less. Mechanism: the cost (couple of hours, mild post-shot fever) is immediate, the benefit (avoided measles) is future and probabilistic. Standard hyperbolic-discounting present-bias means a tiny immediate offset can flip the decision. Distributing dal also lowered cost-per-immunization because fixed-cost nurse time was used more efficiently.
”Don’t bribe people for what’s good for them” — argued against
Both right (markets-only) and left (paternalism-of-information) traditions oppose incentives. Authors disagree on two grounds: (a) “beliefs” the poor hold are mostly weak (the dal experiment shows: evil-eye fear isn’t strong enough to refuse 40 rupees), and (b) action does not follow intention without scaffolding. Apply Thaler-Sunstein Nudge: defaults, small immediate incentives, friction-reduction (Kremer’s free chlorine dispenser at the village well — turn-the-knob auto-dose; cheapest known intervention against diarrhea per RCT). The authors’ Seva Mandir iron-fortified-flour program failed because the default flipped: millers had no incentive to fortify unless asked, and the small “ask” cost killed adoption.
Policy implication

For prevention with positive externalities (immunization, sanitation, nets), subsidies should sometimes be greater than 100% — pay people to consume.
Default-design matters as much as price: piped chlorinated water > chlorine bottles, regardless of household income.
Government should NOT primarily run delivery (absenteeism / 3-3-3 problem) but should regulate, fund, and audit local NGOs / private providers.

Why this chapter is high-leverage
It introduces three behavioral mechanisms (faith-as-hope, time-inconsistency, default-as-equilibrium) that recur in chs. 4 (education uptake), 5 (contraception), 6 (insurance), 8 (savings). It also demonstrates the RCT-as-mechanism-discrimination method: the price-sensitivity-vs-usage decoupling refutes Easterly directly with empirical evidence.
Compression
Source ~25k words → summary ~800 words. ~31:1 compression.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.title: Top of the Class
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/abhiji.content:
Ch. 4 — Top of the Class
The puzzle
Schools are built and largely free; enrolment is high (sub-Saharan primary 54% → 70% from 1999-2006; South Asia 75% → 88%; even among the extremely poor, primary enrolment >80% in half the 18-country dataset). But absenteeism is 14-50%. Pratham’s ASER survey (700,000 children, 600 Indian districts): 35% of 7-14-year-olds can’t read a first-grade paragraph; only 30% can do basic division. Replicated in Kenya (Uwezo), Pakistan (LEAPS, 80% of 3rd-graders can’t read 1st-grade text). World Bank Absenteeism Survey (2002-03): teachers in Bangladesh, Ecuador, India, Indonesia, Peru, Uganda miss 1 day in 5; 50% of Indian public-school teachers not teaching when they should be.
The supply-vs-demand wallah debate

Supply wallahs (Sachs, UN MDG framers): the problem is access; build schools, hire teachers, mandate attendance, offer Conditional Cash Transfers.
Demand wallahs (Easterly): the problem is returns to education; if jobs require skill, parents will demand school; supply will follow. Public over-supply is wasted.

The CCT case (PROGRESA → OPORTUNIDADES)
Santiago Levy’s 1997 Mexican PROGRESA — payments conditional on school attendance + preventive health — was rolled out as RCT to lock in political durability. Secondary enrolment 67% → 75% (girls), 73% → 77% (boys). Survived three administrations because the data were randomized and persuasive. Spread to Latin America, Bloomberg-NYC. But: Malawi and Morocco RCTs found unconditional cash transfers had nearly identical effects to conditional. Implication: the binding constraint is parental income, not parental incentive. Liquidity matters because borrowing against a 10-year-old’s future earnings is impossible.
Top-down works

Indonesia INPRES (Suharto, post-1973 oil shock): top-down school-building rule (priority to under-schooled districts). Duflo’s evaluation: each extra year of primary schooling raised wages 8% — same as US returns.
Taiwan 1968 9-year compulsory schooling: large effects on schooling, employment, and child mortality.
Compulsory schooling in Malawi/Kenya (via free uniforms): reduced teen pregnancy.

So both supply and demand matter; the polarized debate is wrong; the real question is what determines learning given enrolment.
Why schools fail to teach (this chapter’s theoretical contribution)
Private schools beat public, but not by much
Private schools have lower absenteeism (8 percentage points) and higher test scores (15 percentage points reading at 5th grade). LEAPS Pakistan: private 3rd-graders 1.5 years ahead in English, 2.5 in math. But:

Pratham’s Balsakhi program (a young woman with 10 years of schooling + 1 week’s training, working with the bottom 20 children) generated test-score gains 2× the private-school effect at a fraction of the cost.
A Pratham summer camp run by the same government teachers produced large gains. Same teachers, different mandate.

The curse of expectations / illusory S-shape
Parent collages (Seva Mandir): children’s futures are pictured as gold jewelry and cars — mediated by a government job. Madagascar parents: 70% expect a secondary-school graduate to get a government job (actual rate: 33%). Parents perceive returns as convex — primary 6%/year, junior high 12%, senior secondary 20%. Reality is roughly linear. Believing the curve is S-shaped means: invest everything in one promising child, write off the rest.
Bogotá CCT lottery (winners get monthly transfer, losers don’t): in two-child families with one winner, the loser child was less likely to be enrolled than children of double-loser families — even with positive household income shock. Resource-concentration on the chosen winner.
This manufactures a poverty trap where none exists. Education has near-linear returns, but parents’ belief in S-shape leads them to behave as if there were one.
Stereotype threat / elite-bias schools
Steele’s stereotype threat replicated for caste in Uttar Pradesh: low-caste children solving mazes performed identically to high-caste — until names (revealing caste) were collected first. Then performance dropped sharply. Teachers (including same-caste teachers) graded the same exams worse when names were visible.
Curricula and exams are designed for the elite minority who will pass the public secondary exam; the bottom 80% are written off. Calcutta and Kenyan primary schools explicitly expel low-performers to maintain pass-rate statistics. India’s 6.6 lb. limit on first-grader textbook bags is a symptom of the elite-bias bloat. Pratham summer camps work because the mandate flips: every child masters the basics.
Reengineering

Focus on basic skills + commitment that every child can master them (Pratham; KIPP/Harlem Children’s Zone “no excuses” charters; Boston charter studies show 40% of citywide white-black math gap closable).
Tracking by initial level (Duflo-Dupas-Kremer Kenya): teachers can target instruction; gains persist.
Cheap, well-trained semi-volunteers can teach basics; intensive teacher training is not necessary.
Information shock to parents: a Madagascar program that simply told parents the actual income returns to a year of schooling raised test scores at near-zero cost — the cheapest known education intervention evaluated to date. Parents whose initial estimates were too low gained twice as much.
Computer-assisted learning (Banerjee-Cole-Duflo-Linden Vadodara math game, 2 hours/week) — gains as large as much more expensive interventions, partly because each child sets their own pace, partly because it bypasses teacher elite-bias.
Israeli Ethiopian-Jewish Operation Solomon (1991) airlift: children of barely-literate parents reached 65% twelfth-grade-without-repeat completion vs 74% for Russian-emigrant children of 11.5-year-educated parents — schools can compensate for severe family-background disadvantage.

Why this chapter is high-leverage
It establishes the book’s most consequential single concept — the illusory S-shape generated by parental expectations that produces a real poverty trap from a non-existent one. This shape-of-belief mechanism applies in chs. 5 (fertility / one-talented-child), 8 (savings / pessimism), 9 (entrepreneurship / quality-quantity).
