06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: The Machine Learning Landscape
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 1 — The Machine Learning Landscape
Formal spine

Definition (operational): A computer program learns from experience E with respect to task T and performance measure P if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with E (Mitchell-style framing imported by Géron).
Taxonomy axes (orthogonal, can be combined):

Supervision: supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, self-supervised, reinforcement.
Online vs batch: streaming partial-fit vs full retrain.
Instance-based vs model-based: memorize-and-retrieve vs estimate parameters of a function family h_\theta.


Worked formal example — life-satisfaction model:
\text{life\_satisfaction} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 \cdot \text{GDP\_per\_capita}
Géron uses this trivial linear model as the standing example for what training means: pick \theta_0, \theta_1 so the model fits.

Core challenges (the chapter’s load-bearing list)

Insufficient training data.
Nonrepresentative training data (sampling bias, sampling noise).
Poor-quality data.
Irrelevant features.
Overfitting (high variance, model fits noise).
Underfitting (high bias, model too simple).

The bias/variance vocabulary is introduced informally here and made formal in ch. 4.
Testing-and-validating discipline
Splits are not optional:

Train / validation / test partition.
Train-dev set when train and production distributions differ — distinguishes overfitting from data mismatch.
No-free-lunch: hyperparameter tuning on the test set inflates the apparent score and degrades generalization.

Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
It establishes the vocabulary every later chapter assumes (supervision, generalization, hyperparameter, regularization). The single most important conceptual move: separating model parameters (learned by the algorithm) from hyperparameters (chosen by the engineer) — a distinction the book uses to organize all of Part I.
Cross-references in the book

Ridge / lasso / bias–variance trade-off get formal treatment in ch. 4.
The instance-based / model-based split prefigures the SVM (ch. 5), decision tree (ch. 6), and k-means (ch. 9) chapters.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: End-to-End Machine Learning Project
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 2 — End-to-End Machine Learning Project
Formal spine

Performance measure for regression — Root Mean Square Error (Equation 2-1):
\mathrm{RMSE}(X, h) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left(h(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\right)^2}
Mean Absolute Error (Equation 2-2) — robust to outliers, used when heavy-tailed errors are expected:
\mathrm{MAE}(X, h) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left|h(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\right|
RMSE corresponds to the \ell_2 norm; MAE to the \ell_1 norm. Higher norms penalize large errors more, but are less robust to outliers — the same \ell_p trade-off that returns in ch. 4 with ridge vs lasso regularization.

The 8-step ML project checklist (Géron’s structuring move)

Frame the problem. Decide supervised/unsupervised, batch/online, performance measure.
Get the data — and immediately hold out a test set with stratified sampling.
Explore (visualize, look for correlations, hunt for combinations of attributes).
Prepare data: clean (impute), encode categoricals, scale numerics.
Shortlist promising models, evaluate via cross-validation.
Fine-tune (grid search, randomized search, ensemble methods).
Present and interpret.
Launch, monitor, retrain.

The checklist is so central that Géron reproduces it as Appendix A.
Pipeline as the central abstraction
Scikit-Learn’s Pipeline([(name, transformer), ...]) chains fit_transform calls, ending with a final estimator. Two reasons it carries weight:

Leak-prevention: fitting (e.g., StandardScaler) must happen on the training set only; the same fitted transformer is then transform-applied to validation and test. A pipeline mechanizes this.
Hyperparameter scoping: GridSearchCV over a pipeline lets the search range over preprocessing choices and model hyperparameters jointly.

ColumnTransformer extends this pattern by routing different column subsets through different sub-pipelines (numeric vs categorical), then horizontally stacking outputs. This is the cleanest formal handle in scikit-learn for “the engineering layer” between raw data and a model.
Stratified vs random test split
Stratified sampling on the strata of an important variable (here, income category) avoids sampling bias when categories are unevenly distributed. Géron demonstrates that a naive train_test_split on the housing dataset produces a test set whose income distribution diverges from the population — invalidating later cross-validation comparisons.
Cross-validation as the standard scoring loop
K-fold CV: split the training set into K folds; for each fold, train on the other K-1 and score on the held-out fold; report mean and standard deviation. Géron’s running California-housing example uses K = 10. The standard deviation is as informative as the mean — it tells you when one model’s apparent advantage is within noise.
Fine-tuning: grid vs random search

GridSearchCV: exhaustively enumerates a hyperparameter grid. Cost grows multiplicatively in the number of axes.
RandomizedSearchCV: samples from distributions over each hyperparameter for a fixed budget. Bergstra & Bengio (2012, cited by Géron) showed random search dominates grid search when only a few hyperparameters matter, because random sampling explores each axis at more distinct values.

Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
It is the canonical “how a serious project is structured” walkthrough. Every later chapter assumes the reader has internalized the pipeline / cross-validation / grid-search loop demonstrated here.
Cross-references in the book

Linear regression formalism is deferred to ch. 4.
Ensemble methods (RandomForestRegressor) are introduced informally here, formalized in ch. 7.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Classification
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 3 — Classification
Formal spine
For a binary classifier with confusion-matrix counts TP, TN, FP, FN:

Precision (Equation 3-1):
\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}
Recall / sensitivity / true positive rate (Equation 3-2):
\text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}
F1 score (Equation 3-3) — harmonic mean:
F_1 = \frac{2}{\frac{1}{\text{precision}} + \frac{1}{\text{recall}}} = \frac{TP}{TP + \frac{FN + FP}{2}}
ROC curve: plot of TPR vs FPR (FPR = FP/(FP+TN)) over decision-threshold sweep. The area under the curve (AUC) is a threshold-free summary; perfect classifier has AUC = 1.

The precision/recall trade-off
Every classifier with a real-valued decision function has a threshold; sweeping it generates the precision/recall curve. Raising the threshold increases precision but lowers recall. There is no choice that dominates; the application’s cost structure picks the operating point. Géron’s rule of thumb: for very imbalanced classes, prefer the precision/recall curve to the ROC curve, because ROC’s TPR/FPR can flatter a classifier when negatives vastly outnumber positives.
Multiclass strategies

One-versus-rest (OvR / OvA): train K binary classifiers, predict class with highest score.
One-versus-one (OvO): train K(K-1)/2 pairwise classifiers; vote.

Some algorithms (Random Forest, naive Bayes, softmax) handle multiclass natively. SVMs scale poorly with training set size, so OvO (smaller training sets per pairwise model) wins for SVMs; logistic regression and most others use OvR.
Multilabel and multioutput

Multilabel: each instance assigned multiple binary labels (e.g., “face is large” AND “face is smiling”).
Multioutput: outputs are themselves vectors over a label set (e.g., per-pixel denoising — one categorical output per pixel).

Error analysis discipline
The chapter’s most-skipped-most-important section. After training, plot the normalized confusion matrix and look at the rows/columns where errors concentrate. Géron’s MNIST example reveals that 8/5 confusion is a stable failure mode — pointing to specific feature engineering (e.g., closed-loop counts) rather than blind hyperparameter tuning.
Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
It locks the loss-vs-metric distinction in: cross-entropy / log-loss is the training objective; precision, recall, F1, AUC are the evaluation objectives. Mismatch between them is the root cause of most production-model surprises.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Training Models
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 4 — Training Models
This is the formally densest chapter in Part I. It establishes the optimization vocabulary for every later model.
Formal spine — linear regression

Hypothesis (Equation 4-1): \hat{y} = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \theta_n x_n.
Vectorized form (Equation 4-2): \hat{y} = h_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \theta^\top \mathbf{x} (with x_0 \equiv 1).
Cost (Equation 4-3): mean squared error
\mathrm{MSE}(X, h_\theta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left(\theta^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} - y^{(i)}\right)^2
Closed-form Normal equation (Equation 4-4):
\hat{\theta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y
Complexity O(n^{2.4})–O(n^3); SVD-based pseudoinverse \hat\theta = X^+ y is O(n^2) and works when X^\top X is singular.

Gradient descent — three flavors

Gradient vector (Equation 4-6):
\nabla_\theta \mathrm{MSE}(\theta) = \frac{2}{m} X^\top (X\theta - y)
Update rule (Equation 4-7):
\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} - \eta \, \nabla_\theta \mathrm{MSE}(\theta^{(t)})
Batch GD: full X at every step. Convex MSE ⇒ guaranteed convergence to global min if \eta small enough.
Stochastic GD: one random instance per step. Faster per-iter, noisier path; can escape local minima but oscillates around the optimum unless \eta is annealed (a learning schedule).
Mini-batch GD: batches of size b \in \{32, 64, 128, ...\}. Compromise; the actual workhorse in deep learning.

Géron’s intuition note on convexity: MSE for linear regression is convex with Lipschitz-continuous gradient, so the bowl has a unique minimum. Feature scaling (StandardScaler) reshapes an elongated bowl into a circular one — without it, GD zig-zags down a narrow valley.
Polynomial regression and the bias/variance trade-off

Add polynomial features x_1, x_2, x_1^2, x_1 x_2, x_2^2, ... then fit a linear model in the expanded feature space.
Bias/variance decomposition (the chapter’s theoretical landmark):
\mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(x) - y)^2] = \underbrace{(\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)] - f(x))^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{f}(x))}_{\text{variance}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}}
Géron states this verbally rather than as a display equation but the components — bias (wrong assumptions, underfit), variance (sensitivity to training set, overfit), irreducible noise — are the chapter’s vocabulary.

Regularized linear models — three penalty geometries

Ridge (\ell_2, Equation 4-8): J(\theta) = \mathrm{MSE}(\theta) + \frac{\alpha}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \theta_i^2.
Closed-form: \hat\theta = (X^\top X + \alpha A)^{-1} X^\top y with A the identity except A_{00} = 0 (bias term unregularized).
Lasso (\ell_1, Equation 4-10): J(\theta) = \mathrm{MSE}(\theta) + 2\alpha \sum_{i=1}^{n} |\theta_i|. Geometry of the \ell_1 ball forces some \theta_i to zero — automatic feature selection. Non-differentiable at zero; use a subgradient (Equation 4-11) with \mathrm{sign}(\theta_i) \in \{-1, 0, +1\}.
Elastic net (Equation 4-12): mix ratio r between \ell_1 and \ell_2. r=0 is ridge; r=1 is lasso.
Early stopping: stop when validation error stops improving — Hinton called it a “beautiful free lunch.”

Géron’s defaults (memorable practitioner heuristic): always have some regularization. Ridge by default. Switch to lasso/elastic-net when feature selection is desired. Elastic net beats lasso when features outnumber instances or are strongly correlated.
Logistic and softmax regression

Logistic prediction: \hat{p} = \sigma(\theta^\top \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\theta^\top \mathbf{x}}}.
Log-loss for one instance: -y \log(\hat p) - (1-y)\log(1 - \hat p). The cost is convex; no closed form, but gradient descent works.
Softmax (multinomial logit): \hat{p}_k = \frac{\exp(s_k(\mathbf{x}))}{\sum_j \exp(s_j(\mathbf{x}))} with s_k(\mathbf{x}) = \theta_k^\top \mathbf{x}. Trained via cross-entropy:
J(\Theta) = -\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{k=1}^{K} y_k^{(i)} \log\!\left(\hat{p}_k^{(i)}\right)

Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
Every Part-II deep learning chapter stands on three machineries from this chapter: (1) gradient descent, (2) cross-entropy as the canonical classification loss, (3) regularization via norms. Skipping ch. 4 to read transformers will produce someone who recognizes architecture diagrams without knowing why training succeeds or fails.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: SVMs, Decision Trees, and Ensemble Learning
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Chs. 5–7 — SVMs, Decision Trees, and Ensembles (combined)
These three chapters form the pre-deep-learning workhorse trilogy of scikit-learn. Combined here because they co-cite and co-evaluate.
Ch. 5 — Support Vector Machines
Formal spine

Linear SVM hard-margin (only when classes are linearly separable):
\min_{\mathbf{w}, b} \tfrac{1}{2} \|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad t^{(i)} (\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b) \geq 1 \;\; \forall i
with t^{(i)} \in \{-1, +1\}.
Soft-margin (slack variables \zeta^{(i)} \geq 0):
\min_{\mathbf{w}, b, \zeta} \tfrac{1}{2} \|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^{m} \zeta^{(i)} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad t^{(i)}(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b) \geq 1 - \zeta^{(i)}
C is the regularization strength: small C → wider margin, more violations; large C → narrow margin, fewer violations.

The kernel trick
The Lagrangian dual depends on inputs only through inner products \mathbf{x}^{(i) \top} \mathbf{x}^{(j)}. Replacing this product with a kernel K(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{x}^{(j)}) corresponds (Mercer-condition permitting) to an inner product in some higher-dimensional feature space, without ever computing the lifted features. Standard kernels:

Polynomial: K(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = (\gamma \mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{b} + r)^d.
Gaussian RBF: K(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \exp(-\gamma \|\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}\|^2).

Practitioner takeaways

LinearSVC for linear, large data; SVC with kernel='rbf' for nonlinear, moderate data.
SVMs scale poorly: training is roughly O(m^2)–O(m^3), so use OvO for multiclass and avoid for m > 10^5.

Ch. 6 — Decision Trees
CART training algorithm (formal)
CART is a greedy recursive splitting algorithm minimizing the Gini-impurity-weighted child loss:
J(k, t_k) = \frac{m_{\text{left}}}{m} G_{\text{left}} + \frac{m_{\text{right}}}{m} G_{\text{right}}
where G = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k^2 is the Gini impurity of a node, and (k, t_k) is the (feature, threshold) pair tested. Recurse on each child until depth/min-samples/impurity stopping criterion.
Entropy alternative: H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k. Géron’s empirical claim: Gini and entropy give similar trees in practice; Gini is slightly faster to compute. Use Gini by default.
Hyperparameters as regularization
max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, max_leaf_nodes, max_features — all reduce variance at the cost of bias. Trees are high-variance (small data perturbations swing splits) — which motivates ensembling them.
Sensitivity to axis orientation
CART splits are axis-aligned. A 45°-rotated decision boundary needs many splits to approximate. Standardizing or using PCA to align axes with variance helps.
Ch. 7 — Ensemble Learning
Voting classifier
Combine K heterogeneous classifiers:

Hard voting: majority vote.
Soft voting: average predicted probabilities (requires probabilistic outputs). Soft voting usually beats hard.

Bagging and pasting
Train K models on bootstrap-sampled (bagging, with replacement) or uniform-sampled (pasting, without replacement) subsets of the training set. Aggregation reduces variance without inflating bias. Out-of-bag (OOB) score: each training example is held out by ~37% of bagged models, providing free validation.
Random Forest
A bagged ensemble of decision trees with additional randomness: at each split, only a random subset of features (size \sqrt{n} default) is considered. Decorrelating trees further reduces variance. Feature importance is read off as the (depth-weighted, normalized) Gini reduction attributable to each feature averaged across trees.
Boosting

AdaBoost — sequentially train weak learners; up-weight examples the previous learner mis-classified. Final classifier weighted by per-learner accuracy.
Gradient Boosting — sequentially fit each new tree to the residuals (negative gradient of the loss) of the running prediction. With squared-error loss this is literally fitting residuals; for log-loss / other losses it is fitting the negative gradient. The single most accurate off-the-shelf classical-ML method on tabular data.
HistGradientBoosting (HistGradientBoostingClassifier) — bins continuous features into discrete buckets, accelerating training by 10–100×; the scikit-learn answer to LightGBM / XGBoost.

Stacking
Train a meta-learner (e.g., logistic regression) on the predictions of base learners. Use out-of-fold predictions to avoid the meta-learner overfitting to base-learner training noise.
Why these chapters matter in the book’s arc
For tabular data, gradient-boosted trees frequently beat deep nets — and Géron is one of few textbook authors who states this plainly. Understanding why (axis-aligned splits compose cheaply; tree-ensembles capture interactions without manual feature engineering) is essential before flipping to Part II’s neural network chapters.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Dimensionality Reduction and Unsupervised Learning
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Chs. 8–9 — Dimensionality Reduction and Unsupervised Learning
Ch. 8 — Dimensionality Reduction
The curse of dimensionality (formal intuition)
In high-dimensional space, training instances are mostly far apart and near hypercube edges. A unit-cube point’s expected distance to the nearest neighbor is \approx 0.66 in 1D, \approx 1.42 in 2D, but \approx 408 in 1,000,000D. Models extrapolate, do not interpolate, when dimensions are high — bias dominates variance.
Principal Component Analysis

Center X. The principal axes are the right singular vectors of X = U \Sigma V^\top; the variance along axis k is \sigma_k^2 / m.
Project X onto the first d principal components: X_{d\text{-proj}} = X V_d, where V_d is the matrix of the first d columns of V.
The explained variance ratio of component k is \sigma_k^2 / \sum_j \sigma_j^2; choose d as the smallest value with cumulative ratio above (e.g.) 0.95.
Randomized PCA (O(m d^2 + d^3), Halko–Martinsson–Tropp) and Incremental PCA (mini-batch fit, suitable when data exceeds memory) are scikit-learn’s scalable variants.

Random Projection (Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma)
For m instances in \mathbb{R}^n, a random projection into \mathbb{R}^d with d = O(\log(m) / \epsilon^2) preserves pairwise distances within factor 1 \pm \epsilon with high probability. Embarrassingly cheap; surprisingly competitive baseline before fancier methods.
Manifold methods

Locally Linear Embedding (LLE): each point reconstructed as a weighted sum of its k neighbors; preserve those weights when embedding to lower-d.
t-SNE / UMAP (mentioned briefly): visualization-only; preserve local structure at the cost of global geometry. Distances on a t-SNE plot do not correspond to distances in the original space.

Ch. 9 — Unsupervised Learning Techniques
k-means
Lloyd’s algorithm:

Initialize K centroids (random or k-means++: pick centroids one at a time biased away from existing ones).
Assign each instance to the closest centroid.
Update each centroid to the mean of its assigned instances.
Repeat until centroids stop moving.

Lloyd’s algorithm is guaranteed to converge but to a local optimum dependent on initialization. MiniBatchKMeans for large datasets; n_init=10 to retry.
Selecting K

Inertia plot (within-cluster sum of squared distances): elbow heuristic.
Silhouette coefficient s = (b - a) / \max(a, b) where a is the mean intra-cluster distance and b the mean nearest-cluster distance; s \in [-1, 1], higher = better-separated.
Silhouette diagram: per-instance coefficients sorted by cluster — reveals cluster size imbalance and mis-assignment.

DBSCAN
Density-based: a core point has at least min_samples neighbors within radius eps. Clusters are connected components of core-point reachability. Does not require choosing K; instead requires the radius parameter. Robust to non-convex clusters; identifies outliers as noise points. Predicts on new instances only via a separately-fit classifier (KNeighborsClassifier on the labeled training set is the standard recipe).
Gaussian Mixture Models
Soft clustering via a generative model: each instance drawn from one of K Gaussian components with weights \pi_k, means \mu_k, covariances \Sigma_k. Fit by Expectation-Maximization:

E-step: for each instance, posterior probability of each component.
M-step: update \pi_k, \mu_k, \Sigma_k as the posterior-weighted statistics.

Selecting K for GMMs: minimize Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) or Akaike (AIC). The Bayesian GMM automates this by placing a Dirichlet-process prior over component weights — unused components shrink toward zero.
Anomaly detection via density

Threshold the GMM density: instances below the p-th percentile are flagged.
Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, Local Outlier Factor: alternative recipes when density estimation is hard.

Why these chapters matter in the book’s arc
They close Part I’s classical-ML sweep. The autoencoder chapter (ch. 17) reframes PCA as a 1-layer linear autoencoder with tied weights — the bridge between classical dimensionality reduction and deep representation learning.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 10 — Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks with Keras
The first chapter of Part II. The book pivots from scikit-learn to Keras/TensorFlow. The conceptual move that the chapter makes — and that organizes everything that follows — is treating an MLP as the composition of a linear layer with a nonlinearity, repeated.
Formal spine

Threshold logic unit (TLU / artificial neuron): h_w(\mathbf{x}) = \phi(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b) for some activation \phi.
Dense (fully connected) layer: stacks L TLUs in parallel:
h_W(\mathbf{X}) = \phi(\mathbf{X} W + \mathbf{b})
with W \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{in}} \times n_{\text{out}}}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{out}}}.
Multilayer Perceptron (MLP): L stacked dense layers; the deep network is the composition. Without nonlinear \phi between layers, the entire stack collapses to a single linear map — Géron makes this point with the toy f(g(x)) = 10x + 1 derivation.

The XOR moment
Single-layer perceptrons cannot learn XOR (Minsky-Papert 1969). Two-layer MLP with three TLUs can; the chapter walks through the construction. Géron uses this as the historical motivation for backpropagation: training an MLP requires a way to assign credit backward through the hidden layers.
Backpropagation (the chapter’s main result)
The algorithm Linnainmaa published in 1970 (his thesis) and Rumelhart-Hinton-Williams popularized in 1986. Géron’s six-step paraphrase:

Forward pass: feed a mini-batch through the network, caching every intermediate activation.
Compute output error using the loss function.
Apply chain rule to compute partial derivatives of loss w.r.t. each output-layer parameter.
Recurse backward layer by layer using the chain rule to compute gradients w.r.t. every weight and bias.
Take a gradient descent step on every parameter.
Repeat for the next mini-batch; one full pass over the training set is an epoch.

Reverse-mode autodiff (the abstract algorithm; Appendix B in the book) is the engine. Backpropagation = reverse-mode autodiff applied to the neural-network computational graph + gradient descent.
Activation functions






























ActivationFormulaWhySigmoid\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})Smooth probability-like output, but saturates → vanishing gradientstanh\tanh(z) = 2\sigma(2z)-1Zero-centered output; faster early convergence than sigmoidReLU\max(0, z)Cheap, no saturation for z>0, the modern default; “dying ReLU” issue handled in ch. 11Softmax\hat p_k = e^{s_k}/\sum_j e^{s_j}Multiclass output layer
Géron’s note: biology used sigmoid; engineering uses ReLU; the biological analogy was misleading.
Symmetry breaking via random initialization
If all weights are initialized to the same value, all neurons in a layer compute identical functions and backprop updates them identically — a layer of H neurons reduces to one. Random initialization (Glorot/He, formalized in ch. 11) is required, not optional.
The three Keras APIs
Géron’s central pedagogical structure:

Sequential API — tf.keras.Sequential([Dense(...), Dense(...)]). Linear stack of layers; covers ~80% of practical models.
Functional API — graph-of-layers; needed for multi-input, multi-output, residual, or wide-and-deep architectures.
Subclassing API — write a Model subclass with arbitrary call(self, inputs) Python; needed for dynamic models, e.g., conditional control flow per instance.

Trade-off: subclassing trades static-graph optimizations and easy serialization for full Python flexibility. Use the highest-level API that does the job.
Hyperparameter tuning for neural nets
The chapter introduces (and ch. 11 elaborates) the layered hyperparameter hierarchy: learning rate > batch size > optimizer choice > number of layers > neurons per layer > activation function > initialization. Géron’s heuristic: tune learning rate first (it dominates), then optimizer, then architecture.
Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
It is the threshold between Part I (classical ML in scikit-learn) and Part II (deep learning in Keras). Every Part-II chapter assumes the dense-layer + ReLU + Adam + cross-entropy primitive established here.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Training Deep Neural Networks
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 11 — Training Deep Neural Networks
The chapter that makes deep learning work. Géron’s framing: the classical 1990s impasse — “deep” was bad — wasn’t a fundamental limit but a stack of solvable engineering problems (initialization, activation, optimizer, regularization). This chapter walks through the modern stack of fixes.
The vanishing/exploding gradients problem
Gradients computed by backprop multiply layer-wise Jacobians. With sigmoid activations and naive variance-matching initialization, gradients shrink (\to 0) or explode (\to \infty) as depth grows. Two interventions:
Glorot (Xavier) and He initialization
Goal: keep activation variance and gradient variance roughly constant across layers. With fan-in n_{\text{in}} and fan-out n_{\text{out}}:

Glorot uniform: W \sim \mathcal{U}\left(-\sqrt{6/(n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}})},\, \sqrt{6/(n_{\text{in}}+n_{\text{out}})}\right). Use with tanh, sigmoid, softmax.
He uniform/normal: W \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, 2/n_{\text{in}}). Use with ReLU and variants.
LeCun: W \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, 1/n_{\text{in}}). Use with SELU.

Géron’s sticky takeaway: initialization is not a detail; it is the foundation. Bad init can make a network un-trainable regardless of optimizer choice.
Better activation functions

Leaky ReLU: \max(\alpha z, z) with \alpha = 0.01 — fixes “dying ReLU.”
ELU: z if z > 0, \alpha(e^z - 1) otherwise — smoother, mean-near-zero.
SELU: scaled ELU; with LeCun init, batches stay self-normalizing layer-by-layer.
GELU: z \cdot \Phi(z) — the Transformer-era default, especially for NLP.
Swish: z \cdot \sigma(z).
Mish: z \cdot \tanh(\mathrm{softplus}(z)).

Batch Normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy 2015)
For each mini-batch, normalize each pre-activation feature to zero mean and unit variance, then apply a learned affine transform:
\hat z = \gamma \cdot \frac{z - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta
\gamma, \beta are learned per-channel; \mu_B, \sigma_B are running averages tracked at training time and frozen at inference. Effects: reduces internal covariate shift, allows higher learning rates, partially regularizes (mini-batch noise acts like dropout).
Gradient clipping
Cap the gradient \ell_2-norm to a threshold to prevent occasional exploding-gradient steps from destroying the model. Standard for RNNs.
Reusing pretrained layers (transfer learning)
The chapter’s most-cited section. Standard recipe:

Load a pretrained model on a related task (e.g., ImageNet-trained ResNet for a vision task).
Drop the top (output) layers; keep the lower (feature-extraction) layers.
Add new top layers tailored to the target task.
Freeze all reused layers (layer.trainable = False); train only the new top.
After a few epochs, unfreeze the upper-most reused layers and continue training with a much smaller learning rate to fine-tune.

Géron’s honest aside: transfer learning works well for deep convolutional models (lower layers learn generic edge/texture detectors) and poorly for small dense networks (specific patterns don’t transfer). The chapter’s pedagogical “I cheated” disclosure — confessing he tried many random seeds until transfer learning showed a clean win — is one of the book’s strongest epistemic moments. Most papers do this; few authors admit it.
Variants when no pretrained model exists

Unsupervised pretraining: train an autoencoder or GAN on the unlabeled data, reuse its lower layers as initialization for the supervised task. The 2006 Hinton revival recipe.
Pretraining on an auxiliary task: train on a related task with abundant labels. Self-supervised learning (e.g., masked-word prediction in NLP) is the modern realization.

Faster optimizers
Five canonical optimizers:

Momentum (Polyak 1964): \mathbf{m} \leftarrow \beta \mathbf{m} + \eta \nabla J(\theta), \theta \leftarrow \theta - \mathbf{m}. \beta = 0.9 standard.
Nesterov accelerated gradient: evaluate gradient at \theta - \beta \mathbf{m} (look-ahead).
AdaGrad: per-parameter learning rate scaled by inverse of accumulated squared gradient. Decays too fast for deep nets.
RMSProp: AdaGrad with exponentially-decaying gradient-squared accumulator.
Adam (Kingma & Ba 2014): momentum + RMSProp combined. The de facto default.
AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient step, fixing a known Adam misbehavior — the right modern default.

Learning rate scheduling
Power scheduling, exponential, piecewise constant, performance-based, 1cycle (Smith). The 1cycle schedule (rise then fall once) often beats fixed-rate Adam by a noticeable margin.
Regularization in deep nets

\ell_2 weight decay (a.k.a. ridge): default in AdamW.
Dropout (Srivastava 2014): randomly zero out a fraction p of activations in each forward pass at training time; rescale by 1/(1-p) at inference. Forces the network to not rely on any single neuron. p \in [0.1, 0.5] typical; lower values for big networks.
Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout: keep dropout on at inference, average predictions over many forward passes — cheap Bayesian uncertainty estimate.
Max-norm: constrain each weight vector to \|w\|_2 \leq r after each update.

The chapter’s “summary and practical guidelines” table
Géron ends the chapter with a now-famous (in DL pedagogy) recipe table: kernel init = He; activation = ReLU/Swish/Mish; normalization = batch norm / layer norm; regularization = early stopping + L2 + dropout; optimizer = Nadam or AdamW; LR schedule = performance-based or 1cycle. This is the practitioner’s distilled cheat sheet.
Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
It is the chapter that converts “I can write a Keras model” into “I can train a Keras model that converges.” Without ch. 11, ch. 14’s CNNs and ch. 16’s transformers would feel like architectural recipes whose hyperparameters appear by magic.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Custom Models, Training, and Data Pipelines with TensorFlow
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Chs. 12–13 — Custom Models, Training, and Data Pipelines
Ch. 12 — Custom Models and Training with TensorFlow
The chapter where Keras’s “high-level API” abstractions are peeled back to the underlying TensorFlow tensor operations.
TensorFlow as accelerated NumPy

tf.Tensor: n-dimensional array on CPU/GPU; immutable.
tf.Variable: mutable wrapper for trainable parameters.
Most NumPy functions have TensorFlow analogs; @ works as matrix multiplication; broadcasting follows NumPy semantics.
Type strictness: TensorFlow does not implicitly cast between dtypes (unlike NumPy). Mismatched-dtype additions raise.

Custom components

Custom loss: any function L(y, \hat{y}) that returns a scalar tensor. For losses with hyperparameters, subclass tf.keras.losses.Loss so get_config() serializes the hyperparameters.
Custom layer: subclass tf.keras.layers.Layer; implement build(input_shape) (where you create weights), call(inputs) (forward), and optionally compute_output_shape.
Custom model: subclass tf.keras.Model; same as a custom layer, except that it has a fit() method.
Custom training loop:
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    y_pred = model(X_batch, training=True)
    loss = loss_fn(y_batch, y_pred)
gradients = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)
optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(gradients, model.trainable_variables))
This is what fit() does internally; writing it explicitly is required when training requires arbitrary control flow (GANs alternating discriminator/generator updates, RL with experience replay, multi-task losses with adaptive weights).

tf.function and AutoGraph
@tf.function traces a Python function into a TensorFlow graph. The traced graph is cached per-input-signature and runs without Python overhead — typically 5–10× faster on small ops, more on GPU. Quirks worth respecting:

Python-side print and counters fire only during tracing (the first call).
Use tf.print for runtime printing.
Loops with Python control flow are unrolled (slow); tf.range/tf.while_loop get compiled.

Ch. 13 — Loading and Preprocessing Data with TensorFlow
tf.data API
The standard way to feed large datasets to TensorFlow models. Datasets are lazy, streamable iterables of tensors.

Chaining transformations: .map(parse_fn), .filter(predicate), .batch(32), .shuffle(buffer_size=10000), .repeat(num_epochs).
Interleave: read in parallel from multiple files, alternating examples across them — necessary for randomization across sharded datasets.
Prefetch: dataset.prefetch(1) overlaps GPU computation of step N with CPU preparation of step N+1. The single biggest input-pipeline speedup.

TFRecord format
Protobuf-serialized binary records. The canonical format for very large datasets: compact, streamable, gzip-compressible. The Example and SequenceExample protobufs cover most cases.
Keras preprocessing layers
The 2.x-era simplification: preprocessing is done inside the model so deployment ships one artifact. Built-in layers:

Normalization — per-feature standardization with adapt()-learned mean/std.
Discretization — bucketize.
CategoryEncoding — one-hot or multi-hot.
StringLookup / IntegerLookup — vocabulary mapping.
Hashing — feature hashing for very-high-cardinality categoricals.
Embedding — learned dense vectors for categorical features (the foundation of NLP and recommender models).
Image preprocessing: Resizing, Rescaling, RandomFlip, RandomRotation, RandomCrop.

Géron’s important practical note: data augmentation layers (RandomFlip, RandomRotation) are active only when training=True. At inference time they pass inputs through unchanged.
TensorFlow Datasets (TFDS)
A registry of curated datasets (MNIST, ImageNet, IMDB, …) with versioned splits. tfds.load("imdb_reviews", split="train") returns a ready tf.data.Dataset.
Why these chapters matter in the book’s arc
They are the plumbing layer. Anyone wanting to (1) modify the training loop for non-standard objectives, (2) feed multi-TB datasets without OOM, or (3) ship a self-contained inference graph needs the abstractions established here. Skipping them produces ML engineers who can prototype but cannot productionize.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 14 — Deep Computer Vision Using Convolutional Neural Networks
Formal spine
The convolutional layer
Replace the dense layer’s all-to-all connectivity with local, weight-shared connectivity. For a feature map at output spatial position (i, j) and output channel k:
z_{i, j, k} = b_k + \sum_{u=0}^{f_h - 1} \sum_{v=0}^{f_w - 1} \sum_{c=0}^{f_{n'} - 1} x_{i \cdot s_h + u,\, j \cdot s_w + v,\, c} \cdot w_{u, v, c, k}
with f_h \times f_w the receptive field, s_h, s_w stride, f_{n'} the input depth, and w the (shared) filter weights. The number of parameters per filter is f_h f_w f_{n'} + 1 — independent of input image size.
Two architectural priors

Translation equivariance: a feature anywhere in the image is detected by the same filter — a CNN doesn’t relearn “edge” for every spatial position.
Locality: the receptive field is small; long-range dependencies are built up by stacking layers (each layer’s effective receptive field grows).

Pooling layers
Down-sampling without learnable parameters:

Max pooling: f \times f window, output is the max. Translation-invariant within the window; injects a small invariance to local distortion.
Average pooling: replaced by max pooling in most modern architectures.
Global average pooling: per-channel mean over the entire spatial map; collapses to one value per channel. Used as the final layer before the classifier in modern CNNs (replaces flatten+dense, fewer parameters).

CNN architectures (chronological)













































YearArchitectureKey innovation1998LeNet-5 (LeCun)First successful conv net (handwritten digits)2012AlexNet (Krizhevsky-Sutskever-Hinton)ImageNet breakthrough; ReLU, dropout, GPU training2014VGGNetStacked 3 \times 3 convs; uniform deep design2014GoogLeNet / InceptionInception module (parallel filter sizes); 1 \times 1 convs as channel-wise projections2015ResNet (He et al.)Residual connections h(x) = f(x) + x; trains 152-layer nets2016XceptionDepthwise separable convolutions (factorize spatial and channel mixing)2017SENetSqueeze-and-excitation: per-channel attention re-weighting
ResNet’s residual connection (the chapter’s load-bearing result)
Instead of h(x) = f(x), learn h(x) = x + f(x). The network only has to learn the residual f(x) = h(x) - x. Two consequences:

Identity is the default; layers that don’t help converge to small f rather than degrading the signal.
The gradient flows directly through the skip connection — addressing vanishing gradients in very deep nets.

Géron’s note: ResNet’s success is the empirical answer to the “depth is hard” problem. Modern transformer blocks (ch. 16) inherit residual connections directly from ResNet.
Choosing an architecture (Géron’s practitioner heuristic)

























ConstraintPickDefaultResNet-50 or EfficientNetCompute-constrained / mobileMobileNet, EfficientNet-LiteHighest accuracy regardless of computeNASNet, EfficientNet-L2Custom / interpretableInception, Xception
Object detection

Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN): replace dense layers with 1 \times 1 convs so the network outputs a spatial map of class predictions; same model works for any input size.
YOLO (You Only Look Once, Redmon 2015 onward): single-pass detection; predicts bounding-box coordinates and class probabilities for a grid of anchor cells. Real-time speed is the main argument for YOLO.
Mean Average Precision (mAP): the standard metric. For each class, compute precision/recall at varying confidence thresholds; the area under the precision/recall curve is AP; average over classes.

Semantic segmentation
Per-pixel classification. The standard architecture is an encoder-decoder (e.g., U-Net) with skip connections from encoder layers to decoder layers — preserves high-frequency boundary information that pooling would destroy.
Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
Vision was the breakthrough domain for deep learning (AlexNet 2012). The chapter establishes the architectural-prior vocabulary (translation equivariance, locality, weight sharing) that recurs in every subsequent chapter. The transfer-learning recipe from ch. 11 is reapplied here with concrete pretrained ImageNet models.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Sequences, NLP, and the Transformer Architecture
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Chs. 15–16 — Sequences, NLP, and the Transformer
Ch. 15 — Processing Sequences Using RNNs and CNNs
Recurrent layer (formal)
A simple RNN cell at time step t:
\mathbf{h}_t = \phi\!\left(W_x \mathbf{x}_t + W_h \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{b}\right), \quad \mathbf{y}_t = W_y \mathbf{h}_t
The same parameters W_x, W_h, W_y are reused at every step — parameter sharing across time.
Backpropagation through time (BPTT)
Unroll the network over the sequence length T, then backprop through the unrolled graph. Two pathologies:

Vanishing gradients: products of Jacobians shrink → long-range dependencies un-learnable.
Exploding gradients: gradients grow without bound → use gradient clipping.

Gated cells (the cure for vanishing gradients)

LSTM (Hochreiter-Schmidhuber 1997): cell state \mathbf{c}_t flows nearly linearly; three gates — forget, input, output — control read/write/erase. Cell state acts as long-term memory; hidden state as short-term.
GRU (Cho et al. 2014): simpler — two gates (update, reset). Comparable performance to LSTM on most tasks; fewer parameters.

Time series forecasting

ARMA / ARIMA as classical baselines. Géron explicitly recommends not skipping these; deep models often need to beat a well-tuned ARIMA, not the other way around.
Sequence-to-sequence forecasting: predict h steps ahead by training the model to produce all h outputs at once, rather than autoregressively.

Ch. 16 — Natural Language Processing with RNNs and Attention
Char-RNN and stateful RNNs
Generate Shakespeare-style text by training a character-level LSTM. Stateful: preserve hidden state across batches when consecutive batches contain consecutive subsequences. Demonstrates the language model objective: predict the next token given history.
Embeddings and pretrained language model components
Word embeddings as dense vectors that map similar tokens to nearby points. Pretrained components (Word2Vec, GloVe historically; modern BERT-derived encoders) replace random initialization for the embedding layer.
Encoder-decoder architecture for translation
A two-stage model:

Encoder RNN reads source sentence, produces a context vector (final hidden state).
Decoder RNN generates the target sentence one token at a time, conditioned on the context.

The bottleneck problem and attention
A single context vector cannot summarize a long sentence. Attention (Bahdanau 2014; Luong 2015) lets the decoder look back at every encoder hidden state at each output step, weighted by a learned alignment score. The “context” becomes a weighted sum recomputed per decoder step.
The transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017) — the chapter’s centerpiece
Pure attention; no recurrence. Drops the entire RNN apparatus.
Scaled dot-product attention (Equation 16-3)
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_{\text{keys}}}}\right) V
with shapes:

Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{queries}} \times d_{\text{keys}}} — queries (one row per query position).
K \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{keys}} \times d_{\text{keys}}} — keys.
V \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{keys}} \times d_{\text{values}}} — values.
Q K^\top has shape [n_{\text{queries}}, n_{\text{keys}}] — the similarity score matrix.
After softmax (row-wise), each row sums to 1; output has shape [n_{\text{queries}}, d_{\text{values}}].

The 1/\sqrt{d_{\text{keys}}} scaling prevents the softmax from saturating when d_{\text{keys}} is large.
Multi-head attention
Run h parallel attention layers, each with its own linear projections of Q, K, V into smaller subspaces. Concatenate outputs and project back. Géron’s intuition: each head can specialize in querying a different feature of the input (one head focuses on syntactic role, another on coreference, etc.).
Self-attention vs cross-attention

Self-attention: Q, K, V all derived from the same input — the encoder/decoder uses this to relate every position to every other position in its own input.
Cross-attention: Q from decoder, K, V from encoder — the decoder consulting the encoded source.

Positional encoding
Since attention is permutation-equivariant, it has no notion of order. Inject sinusoidal (or learned) positional embeddings:
PE_{p, 2i} = \sin(p / 10000^{2i/d}), \quad PE_{p, 2i+1} = \cos(p / 10000^{2i/d})
Added (not concatenated) to the token embedding.
Transformer block (encoder)
x → MultiHeadAttention(self) → +residual → LayerNorm
  → FeedForward (2-layer MLP)  → +residual → LayerNorm

Stack N such blocks (typically 6 for the original; 12+ for BERT-base; 96+ for GPT-3).
Avalanche of transformer models
Géron taxonomizes:

Encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa): pretrained via masked language modeling; downstream classifiers fine-tuned on top.
Decoder-only (GPT family): pretrained via next-token prediction; few-shot via in-context learning.
Encoder-decoder (T5, BART): pretrained via span-masking + reconstruction; flexible for any seq2seq task.

Vision Transformers (ViT)
Treat image patches as tokens. A 224 \times 224 image cut into 16 \times 16 patches becomes a 196-token sequence; feed through a transformer encoder; global average + classification head. Competitive with CNNs at sufficient scale.
Hugging Face Transformers library
Géron’s note: don’t reimplement — use from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel. The library is the de facto registry of pretrained transformer weights.
Why these chapters matter in the book’s arc
Together they cover the single most important architectural development in ML between 2017 and the book’s 2022 cutoff. Chapter 16 is mandatory reading for anyone doing modern NLP, multimodal, or even vision (ViT) work. The scaled-dot-product equation is the conceptual hinge that everything contemporary turns on.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Autoencoders, GANs, and Diffusion Models
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 17 — Autoencoders, GANs, and Diffusion Models
The chapter unifies generative modeling under the lens of what objective is being optimized.
Autoencoders
Formal structure
An autoencoder is a pair (encoder f, decoder g) trained to reconstruct its input:
\min_{f, g} \; \mathbb{E}_x \|x - g(f(x))\|^2
If f is linear, g is linear, and the bottleneck dimension is d, the optimal weights span the same subspace as the top-d principal components — autoencoders generalize PCA.
Variants

Stacked autoencoder: multiple encoder/decoder layers; pretrain layer-wise (greedy) or end-to-end.
Tied weights: decoder weights = encoder weights transposed; halves parameter count.
Denoising autoencoder (Vincent et al. 2008): corrupt the input (x \to \tilde x), train g(f(\tilde x)) \approx x. Forces robust representations.
Sparse autoencoder: add an \ell_1 or KL-divergence penalty on the bottleneck activations to enforce that few neurons fire per input.
Convolutional autoencoder: encoder is a CNN; decoder uses transposed convolutions. Standard for image data.

Variational Autoencoder (VAE) — Kingma & Welling 2013
Probabilistic autoencoder with a stochastic bottleneck. The encoder outputs a Gaussian distribution q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(\mathbf{x}), \sigma_\phi^2(\mathbf{x})); the decoder p_\theta(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z}) reconstructs from a sample.
Training objective is the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO):
\mathcal{L}(\phi, \theta; \mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{z})] - D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) \| p(\mathbf{z}))
First term is reconstruction quality; second term regularizes the latent distribution toward a unit-Gaussian prior p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(0, I). The reparameterization trick — sample \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), then \mathbf{z} = \mu + \sigma \cdot \epsilon — makes the objective differentiable through the sampling step.
VAEs generate by sampling \mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and running the decoder.
Generative Adversarial Networks (Goodfellow et al. 2014)
Two-player minimax game
\min_G \max_D \;\; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]

Generator G: maps noise \mathbf{z} to fake samples.
Discriminator D: distinguishes real from fake; outputs probability of “real.”
Trained alternately: D on the current G, then G to fool the current D.

The difficulties of training GANs (the chapter’s load-bearing section)

Mode collapse: G produces only a few of the modes of p_{\text{data}}.
Non-convergent oscillation: D and G never settle.
Vanishing gradients for G: when D is too good, \log(1-D(G(z))) saturates. Use the alternative loss -\log D(G(z)).

GAN variants

Deep Convolutional GAN (DCGAN) — Radford 2015: architectural recipe for stable training (batch norm, strided convs, LeakyReLU, no fully-connected layers).
Progressive Growing of GANs — Karras 2017: train at low resolution first; gradually add layers and increase resolution.
StyleGAN — Karras 2018: separates “style” (per-layer modulation from learned mapping network) from “noise” (per-pixel stochasticity); enables stunning controllable face generation.

Diffusion Models (the 2020-onward dominant paradigm)
Forward process
Iteratively add Gaussian noise to a sample over T steps:
q(\mathbf{x}_t | \mathbf{x}_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_t; \sqrt{1 - \beta_t} \mathbf{x}_{t-1}, \beta_t I)
After T steps, \mathbf{x}_T is approximately pure Gaussian noise.
Reverse process
Train a neural net \epsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) to predict the noise added at step t. Generate by sampling \mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and iteratively denoising via the predicted noise. Training objective (Ho et al. 2020):
\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0, \epsilon}\!\left[\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)\|^2\right]
where \mathbf{x}_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf{x}_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\epsilon with \bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s=1}^{t}(1 - \beta_s).
Why diffusion won

Stable training (no minimax game).
Better sample diversity than GANs.
Trades training simplicity for inference cost: generation requires T (often 50–1000) sequential denoising steps. Recent work (DDIM, distillation) reduces this dramatically.

The unifying lens
Géron’s pedagogical move: organize generative models by training objective, not by sample modality.





























FamilyObjectiveAutoencoderReconstruction errorVAEELBO (reconstruction − KL to prior)GANMinimax adversarial gameNormalizing flow (mentioned, not deep)Exact log-likelihood via change-of-variablesDiffusionNoise-prediction MSE
This taxonomy is the same one Prince’s Understanding Deep Learning uses, and is now standard.
Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
This is the chapter that prepares the reader for image-generation policy debates (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E), GAN-based deepfakes, and self-supervised pretraining recipes. The VAE-ELBO derivation also rehearses the variational-inference pattern that recurs in modern reinforcement learning.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Reinforcement Learning
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 18 — Reinforcement Learning
Formal spine
The setting
An agent interacts with an environment over discrete time steps. At each step t:

Agent observes state s_t.
Selects action a_t via policy \pi(a | s).
Environment returns reward r_{t+1} and new state s_{t+1}.

Goal: maximize expected discounted return:
G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}
with discount factor \gamma \in [0, 1).
Markov Decision Process (MDP)
Five-tuple (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, T, R, \gamma):

T(s, a, s') = P(s' | s, a) — transition probability.
R(s, a, s') — reward function.

The Markov property: s_{t+1} depends only on s_t, a_t, not on history.
Bellman optimality equations
V^*(s) = \max_a \sum_{s'} T(s, a, s') \left[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V^*(s') \right]
Q^*(s, a) = \sum_{s'} T(s, a, s') \left[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') \right]
When T and R are known, value iteration and policy iteration solve these via dynamic programming. RL is what we do when they are not known.
Policy gradients
Parameterize the policy \pi_\theta(a | s) as a neural network. Optimize \theta via the policy-gradient theorem:
\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\!\left[ \sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t | s_t) \cdot G_t \right]
Training recipe (REINFORCE):

Run a few episodes with current \pi_\theta, recording (s_t, a_t, r_t).
Compute discounted returns G_t for each step.
Standardize returns to reduce variance (subtract baseline).
For each (s_t, a_t), take a gradient step in the direction \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t | s_t) \cdot G_t.

The credit assignment problem: at the end of an episode, which action caused the reward? Returns G_t are noisy estimators; baselines and bootstrapping (TD methods) reduce variance at the cost of bias.
Q-learning
Off-policy, value-based. Maintain Q(s, a); update via:
Q(s, a) \leftarrow (1 - \alpha) Q(s, a) + \alpha \left[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') \right]
Convergence to Q^* guaranteed under tabular settings if every (s, a) visited infinitely often and \alpha decays appropriately.
Exploration policies

\epsilon-greedy: with probability \epsilon random action, else greedy.
Softmax: action probabilities proportional to \exp(Q(s, a) / \tau).
Upper confidence bound (UCB): bonus for under-visited actions.

Deep Q-Learning (DQN, Mnih et al. 2015)
Approximate Q(s, a) \approx Q_\theta(s, a) with a neural net. Two stabilizing tricks needed for it to work:

Experience replay: store transitions (s, a, r, s') in a buffer; sample mini-batches uniformly. Decorrelates training data.
Fixed Q-value targets (target network): use a stale copy Q_{\theta^-} to compute TD targets; sync \theta^- \leftarrow \theta every N steps. Prevents the target moving with the prediction.

DQN’s loss:
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s, a, r, s')}\!\left[ \left( r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q_{\theta^-}(s', a') - Q_\theta(s, a) \right)^2 \right]
DQN variants

Double DQN (van Hasselt 2015): \max_{a'} uses \theta (online) for action selection but \theta^- (target) for value evaluation. Reduces overestimation bias.
Prioritized experience replay: sample transitions in proportion to TD-error magnitude.
Dueling DQN: factor Q(s, a) = V(s) + A(s, a) — separate state-value and action-advantage heads.

Overview of popular RL families
Géron’s compact taxonomy:

























FamilyExamplesValue-basedQ-learning, DQN familyPolicy-basedREINFORCE, TRPO, PPOActor-criticA2C, A3C, DDPG, SACModel-basedDyna-Q, MuZero
PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization, Schulman 2017) is named as the modern default for continuous-control tasks; SAC (Soft Actor-Critic, Haarnoja 2018) for sample-efficient continuous control.
Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
RL is the bridge between supervised learning (predict y from x) and decision-making (choose a to maximize reward). The framework is necessary to understand RLHF (the alignment of language models via human-feedback rewards), AlphaGo/AlphaZero, and contemporary game-playing agents. Géron’s explicit acknowledgment that RL “is the most challenging branch of ML” is appropriate — the chapter is honest about why getting these algorithms to work in practice is harder than the math suggests.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.title: Training and Deploying TensorFlow Models at Scale
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/aureli.content:
Ch. 19 — Training and Deploying TensorFlow Models at Scale
The book’s most-different chapter: where every previous chapter trains a model on one machine, this chapter is about shipping models and parallelizing training. The chapter is unusually time-bound — the cloud APIs and TPU specifics will age — but its conceptual taxonomy of parallelism is durable.
Serving a TensorFlow model
Saved model format
The portable artifact: model.save("path/") produces a directory containing the computation graph, weights, and signatures (named input/output tensor specs). Multiple version numbers can coexist; serving infrastructure picks the latest by default.
TensorFlow Serving
A C++ server that hosts SavedModel artifacts and exposes:

gRPC API: low-latency, binary; preferred for high-throughput.
REST API: simpler; HTTP+JSON.

Configurable for dynamic batching (collect simultaneous requests and batch them), versioning, and A/B traffic split.
Vertex AI / managed inference
Google’s hosted alternative; abstracts the server. Géron walks through both real-time prediction and batch prediction (large prediction job over a dataset stored on Cloud Storage).
Mobile and embedded deployment
TensorFlow Lite: convert SavedModel to a .tflite flat buffer, optionally quantized (float32 → int8). Quantization typically reduces size by 4× and latency by 2–3× at modest accuracy cost. TensorFlow.js runs models in the browser via WebGL or WASM.
GPU computation
Memory management
The default TensorFlow behavior is to allocate all GPU memory at startup. Two options to avoid this:

tf.config.set_logical_device_configuration(...) — pre-allocate a fixed amount.
tf.config.experimental.set_memory_growth(gpu, True) — grow on demand.

Device placement
Operations run on whichever device hosts their inputs. Explicit placement via with tf.device('/GPU:0'): blocks. Mixing devices without good reason invites slow CPU↔GPU copies.
Training across multiple devices
Géron’s central distinction:
Model parallelism
Split a single model across devices. Each device hosts a slice of the model; activations flow between devices during the forward pass. Useful when a model doesn’t fit on one device; expensive due to device-to-device communication.
Data parallelism
Replicate the full model on each device; each device processes a different mini-batch slice. Two synchronization patterns:

Synchronous SGD with all-reduce: all replicas compute gradients; gradients are averaged (all-reduce) before the optimizer step. Equivalent to a K\times-larger batch.
Asynchronous SGD with parameter server: each worker reads parameters, computes gradients, and writes updates back independently. Faster wall-clock but suffers stale gradients; rarely used in modern practice.

Mirrored Strategy (tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy) is the standard data-parallel API; MultiWorkerMirroredStrategy extends it across machines; TPUStrategy for Google’s tensor-processing-unit accelerators.
Pipeline parallelism (briefly mentioned)
Split a deep model into sequential stages on different devices and pipeline mini-batches through them. Reduces idle time relative to naive model parallelism.
Hyperparameter tuning at scale
Vertex AI Hyperparameter Tuning (Bayesian optimization over a search space) and Keras Tuner (local). Géron recommends Hyperband — bandit-style early stopping that races configurations.
Why this chapter matters in the book’s arc
It is the chapter that converts “I trained a model on my laptop” into “I deployed a model that handles 10K requests/second” and “I trained a model on 64 GPUs.” Skipping it produces ML practitioners who cannot reason about cost, latency, or scale — three categories that dominate every real production deployment.
The taxonomy of data parallel vs model parallel vs pipeline parallel is the durable conceptual takeaway; specific cloud APIs will age but the parallelism patterns will not.
