06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_01_introduction
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
Introduction — The four-layered paradox
Le Fanu opens with a paradox: post-war medicine has been astonishingly successful — antibiotics, transplants, hip replacements, IVF, chemotherapy curing childhood leukaemia — yet four discontents have grown alongside that success.


Disillusioned doctors. Surveys show “regrets about chosen career” rising 14% (1966 cohort) → 26% (1976) → 44% (1981) → 58% (1986). By 1996 a quarter of UK medical graduates had no plans to work in the NHS.


The worried well. The proportion claiming to be “concerned about their health” rose from 1-in-10 to 1-in-2 over thirty years. This is medically inspired (“Healthism”): the simple “don’t smoke, eat sensibly” of 1965 has become an ever-widening menu of supposed dietary, environmental, and behavioural threats.


Soaring popularity of alternative medicine. In the US, visits to “unconventional therapy” providers (425M/yr) now exceed visits to primary care physicians (388M).


Spiralling health-care costs. UK NHS budget doubled from £23.5bn (1988) to £45bn (1998). The “more funding will fix it” assumption looks wrong.


These paradoxes, Le Fanu argues, are not coincidences but symptoms of a single phenomenon: medicine has had a Rise (1940s-1970s) and a Fall (1980s-present). The chronology of breakthroughs — clustered between 1941 and 1984 — itself reveals it. The “definitive moments” pantheon (sulphonamides, penicillin, cortisone, streptomycin, chlorpromazine, intensive care, open-heart surgery, hip replacement, transplantation, stroke prevention, paediatric oncology, IVF, helicobacter) is overwhelmingly pre-1980. The book’s task is to explain why post-war medicine succeeded, why innovation slowed, and why the false ideologies of the New Genetics and Social Theory rushed in to fill the resulting intellectual vacuum.
Methodological cue from Lewis Thomas (quoted): nineteenth-century medicine had jettisoned its therapeutic ritual (bleeding, purging) by 1830s. Diagnosis became central; treatment was almost empty (digoxin, aspirin, salvarsan, vitamins, thyroxine, insulin — that was it). The Rise will close that gap; the Fall reopens a different one.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_02_penicillin-1941
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM1 1941: Penicillin — the first definitive moment
The therapeutic revolution opens with Albert Alexander, a 43-year-old policeman who scratched his face on a rose bush, became septic, lost an eye, and on 12 February 1941 received the world’s first systematic injections of penicillin from Charles Fletcher in Oxford. Five days of striking improvement; then the supply ran out; he died a month later.
Le Fanu’s argument is that penicillin’s discovery was not a triumph of scientific reasoning but a chain of staggering accidents:

The mould wafted. Fleming’s contaminating Penicillium notatum (1928) was a rare strain that drifted up from a fungus expert’s lab below — not a typical mould.
The bench, not the incubator. Fleming uncharacteristically left the petri dish out before holiday.
The nine cool days. London’s exceptionally cool late-July 1928 favoured penicillium growth; the subsequent warm period favoured staphylococcus growth. Reverse the temperatures and there is no halo.
The reproducibility puzzle. Ronald Hare (1964) showed Fleming’s observation was unreproducible under standard incubator conditions — confirming the climatic accident.
Fleming gave up. He did no clinical follow-through, believing such naturally occurring chemicals would be too toxic.
Florey rediscovered. Florey + Chain (Oxford, biochemist + microbiologist) succeeded where Fleming failed — Chain’s biochemistry could go beyond observation to mechanism.
Florey’s wartime gamble. With Britain expecting German invasion in 1940, Florey converted his Oxford pathology department into a penicillin factory using bedpans and milk jugs — “a triumph of will over reason.”

Florey’s Nobel speech codified the screening method that would generate streptomycin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, etc. — these become “a gift from nature.” Selman Waksman (streptomycin) eventually concluded antibiotics are not chemical-warfare weapons in soil ecology — they are a “purely fortuitous phenomenon.” Why a few microbes produce these complex molecules at all is, in Le Fanu’s recurring phrase, “the mystery of mysteries.”
Theme: empirical fortune drove the Rise, not deductive science from first principles.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_03_cortisone-1949
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM2 1949: Cortisone — empiricism’s second pillar
If antibiotics defeat external enemies (bacteria), cortisone mobilises the body’s own healing machinery. Philip Hench at the Mayo Clinic noted in 1928 that one rheumatoid-arthritis patient’s symptoms remitted during an attack of jaundice, and over years observed the same pattern in pregnancy. He hypothesised a “Substance X” — some endogenous hormone elevated in both states — and spent twenty years failing to find it (bile salts, liver extracts, transfused jaundiced blood: nothing).
The breakthrough came from a parallel and unrelated programme: Edward Kendall, also at Mayo, was characterising adrenal-cortex hormones (Compounds A, B, E, F). It took the wartime Luftwaffe rumour (German pilots boosted by adrenal-cortex extract supposedly flying at 40,000 ft) and the resulting US Air Force programme to push pharmaceutical synthesis far enough that, in 1948, Lewis Sarett at Merck produced enough Compound E to give Hench. On 21 September 1948 Mrs Gardner, a 29-year-old crippled by RA, received 100mg/day. Within four days she walked to town for three hours.
Two near-misses preserved the discovery: Hench’s “vastly excessive” 100 mg dose (a tenth as much would have shown nothing) and the crystal size in Merck’s preparation (which dissolved at the right rate). The 1949 film of “before/after” patients drew a standing ovation; the Nobel followed within twelve months.
The reductive lesson: cortisone failed as a chronic RA cure (side effects — moon face, ulcers, vertebral collapse) but proved a “panacea” for ~200 conditions with unknown causes (asthma, lupus, eczema, optic neuritis, polymyalgia, anaphylactic shock). Hench’s deeper finding: vast disease categories share uncontrolled inflammation as their pathological feature, not specific aetiology.
Le Fanu’s structural claim: cortisone allowed doctors to “pole-vault the hurdles of their own ignorance.” It is the second proof that the post-war Rise depended on empirical luck — endogenous chemistry whose mechanism was still not fully understood fifty years later.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_04_streptomycin-rct-smoking-1950
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM3 1950: Streptomycin, Smoking, and Sir Austin Bradford Hill
Two events of 1950 jointly anchor a paradigm shift: (a) the streptomycin + PAS combination achieving “marked improvement” in 80% of TB patients, and (b) Doll and Bradford Hill’s case-control study proving smoking causes lung cancer. The shift is from the germ-theory paradigm (find a cause, give a drug) to the social/epidemiological paradigm: identify risk factors in everyday life that explain non-infectious diseases.
The pivotal figure is Sir Austin Bradford Hill, Professor of Medical Statistics at the LSHTM. Personally lucky (himself a TB survivor since WWI), institutionally rooted in the Pearson–Galton British biostatistical lineage via his mentor Major Greenwood, he architected:


The 1946 streptomycin RCT. Britain had little dollar reserve, so streptomycin was scarce. Bradford Hill turned scarcity into ethical opportunity: a randomised trial was not just permissible but required given limited drug. The randomised controlled trial (RCT) entered medical practice as the standard for new drug evaluation. Thalidomide (1960) globalised the requirement.


The 1950 lung-cancer case-control study. Doll and Bradford Hill’s BMJ paper (30 September 1950) showed, with rigorous bias-control, that smokers of 25+ cigarettes/day faced a ~25-fold lung-cancer risk versus non-smokers. The American confirmation arrived almost simultaneously.


Le Fanu’s verdict is mixed. Bradford Hill’s work was foundational and largely correct: tobacco does cause lung cancer; RCTs are necessary; statistical inference can be a “new and genuine insight into the nature of disease.” But his legacy also contained a fatal seed. By making statistics “the sole arbiter of scientific truth,” he authorised the later Social Theory’s overreach — its claims that diet, environmental pollution, and lifestyle cause most non-infectious diseases. Bradford Hill himself insisted any statistical inference must be internally coherent: many lines of evidence pointing the same way. His successors abandoned this discipline.
The chapter introduces Le Fanu’s running tension: empiricism (the lucky-drug-discovery side of the Rise) vs. statistical mechanism (the case-control side that will, in misuse, drive the Fall).

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_05_chlorpromazine-polio-icu-1952
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM4 + DM5 1952: Chlorpromazine and the Copenhagen polio epidemic
1952a — Chlorpromazine. The first antipsychotic emerged from Henri Laborit’s clinical observation (Paris) that the antihistamine promethazine, given to surgical patients to prevent shock, induced a state he called “euphoric quietude.” This empirical clinical observation — not theory of schizophrenia — led the chemists at Rhône-Poulenc to synthesise variants. Chlorpromazine (1952) emptied asylums, made schizophrenia treatable, and triggered the psychopharmacological revolution. Le Fanu’s signature note: nobody knows why a histamine-blocker should affect dopamine in the brain in a way that controls psychosis. The map of mental illness “remains a blank.”
1952b — Copenhagen polio epidemic and the birth of intensive care. When polio paralysed respiratory muscles, the iron-lung was the only option, and overflow was lethal. Bjørn Ibsen, an anaesthetist, recognised that the curare-and-positive-pressure ventilation he used in surgery could be transferred to the polio ward — relays of medical students manually bagged patients around the clock. Mortality dropped from ~80% to ~25%. Modern intensive care medicine — mechanical ventilation, ICU staffing models, the very category “critically ill but recoverable” — was created in this Copenhagen wing.
These two 1952 moments share the structural pattern Le Fanu emphasises:

No mechanistic understanding required. Chlorpromazine works without a theory of schizophrenia; ICU works without a theory of polio (though the cause was known).
Cross-disciplinary borrowing. Surgery → psychiatry; surgery → polio ward.
Acute clinical observation by a non-eminent practitioner. Laborit was a surgeon, not a psychiatrist; Ibsen was an anaesthetist transplanting his own toolkit.

This is the kind of progress empirical clinical practice generates and Le Fanu argues that mechanistic-reductionist research programmes in the 1980s+ progressively crowded out.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_06_open-heart-surgery-1955
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM6 1955: Open-heart surgery — technology lit by the war
The “last frontier.” Until the 1950s the heart was technically off-limits — operations had to be done within the four-minute oxygen budget after circulatory arrest, ruling out repair of complex congenital defects or valves. Two enabling moves removed that constraint:


Wartime experience. Dwight Harken in 1944-45 removed bullets and shrapnel from soldiers’ hearts under D-Day battlefield conditions and demonstrated the heart could be entered surgically. This dissolved the surgical taboo.


The pump (cardiopulmonary bypass). John Gibbon (Philadelphia) developed the heart-lung machine over twenty years; first successful use 1953. Walt Lillehei in Minnesota briefly used “controlled cross-circulation” — a parent’s circulation as biological pump for a child’s open-heart repair — before mechanical bypass became reliable.


Open-heart surgery is the Le Fanu archetype of empirical-technical progress without deep mechanistic insight: surgeons learned, in operating-room iteration, what the heart could and could not tolerate. The Blalock–Taussig “blue baby” operation (1944, treating Fallot’s tetralogy) had shown a cyanotic newborn could be made pink; cardiac catheterisation (McMichael’s controversial technique, see ch. 12 of book Part I) made anatomical diagnosis possible; then bypass closed the loop.
The chapter is also Le Fanu’s argument for the war as accelerator: at least four definitive moments (penicillin scale-up, cortisone via the Luftwaffe rumour, ICU via curare anaesthesia experience, and open-heart surgery via Harken’s combat operations) emerged from wartime urgency that broke pre-war professional caution. Bush’s 1946 “Endless Frontier” essay made the policy case for state-funded research; the NIH and NCI rose on its momentum.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_07_hip-replacement-1961
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM7 1961: Charnley’s hip replacement — the squeak that started it
John Charnley, a Manchester orthopaedic surgeon, redesigned the artificial hip after a chance interaction with a patient whose Judet prosthesis squeaked so loudly his wife avoided being in the same room with him. The squeak vanished after some weeks; the obvious inference was that the hip had become smoother. Charnley drew the opposite conclusion: the squeak meant unacceptably high friction, and a low-friction prosthesis was needed.
This led to a multi-year iteration on materials: PTFE (Teflon) failed because wear debris triggered foreign-body reactions; high-density polyethylene worked. The cement (PMMA) anchoring the prosthesis to bone was a separate engineering breakthrough. The Charnley low-friction arthroplasty (1962-onwards) is the canonical chronic-degenerative-disease intervention: it does not address aetiology of arthritis but mechanically replaces a worn joint, restoring mobility for a decade or more.
Le Fanu’s structural point: hip replacement is the model of late-Rise medicine. Most disease burden in advanced countries is age-determined and chronic-degenerative (arthritis, cataracts, atherosclerosis); the “do-able” engineering response is more powerful than the elusive aetiological one. The chapter pre-figures Part IV’s argument that future medical progress lies in such mechanical / pharmacological palliation, not in unravelling cause.
By 2010 (the revised epilogue) the number of hip replacements in those over 80 had increased twelve-fold. The “biomedicalisation of ageing” is one of the few legitimate reasons the post-2000 medical enterprise expanded — extending an established Rise-era technology to a wider age range, not new science.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_08_kidney-transplant-1963
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM8 1963: Kidney transplantation — the immunology accident
Surgical transplantation was anatomically simple — vascular anastomosis was a known technique. The barrier was immunological rejection of foreign tissue. The first successful (identical-twin) kidney transplant was done by Joseph Murray in Boston in 1954: no rejection problem because the donor was genetically identical. The wider question — how to give organs to non-related recipients — required immunosuppression.
The breakthrough came from cancer chemotherapy research. George Hitchings and Gertrude Elion at Burroughs Wellcome were screening “false building-block” compounds (the same competitive-inhibition principle Donald Woods had derived from sulphonamides) targeting DNA synthesis to treat leukaemia. 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) was an anticancer drug; its derivative azathioprine (Imuran) suppressed the immune response.
In 1963 Roy Calne (Cambridge) and Murray (Boston) used azathioprine + steroids (cortisone again) to do non-twin kidney transplants. The combination cleared the immunological barrier without killing the recipient outright. Cyclosporine (1976, Borel/Sandoz) — discovered by screening soil fungi for antibiotic activity, an entirely different programme — replaced azathioprine as the dominant immunosuppressant by the 1980s.
Le Fanu’s structural point: transplantation rests on a stack of accidents — sulphonamides → competitive-inhibition principle → 6-MP → azathioprine → transplant tolerance — and on borrowing from cancer chemotherapy, antibiotic screening, and steroid pharmacology. None of these came from a “transplant immunology” research programme. Pre-1985, a working physician adept at borrowing across silos could move medicine forward; post-1985, the increasingly specialised molecular research enterprise lost that productive opportunism.
The chapter also contains the moral subtext of the early transplant era — desperate patients, high mortality, the “courage to fail” that Renée Fox documented. This is the world clinical science created and that Maurice Pappworth’s Human Guinea Pigs (1967) attacked.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_09_stroke-prevention-1964
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM9 1964: Prevention of strokes — the one true preventive triumph
Le Fanu’s Rise pantheon includes one preventive intervention: lowering blood pressure to prevent stroke. Hypertension as a stroke risk factor was known epidemiologically by mid-century, but no safe drug existed. The 1950s breakthrough was, again, sulphonamide-derived: the diuretics (chlorothiazide, hydrochlorothiazide) emerged from Carl Beyer’s chemical play on the sulphonamide molecule’s incidental fluid-loss side-effect. Bendrofluazide became the first safe widely-prescribable antihypertensive.
The Veterans Administration trial of 1964 (and follow-up VA trials through the 1970s) showed convincingly that lowering moderate-to-severe diastolic blood pressure prevented strokes. Stroke mortality fell sharply across Western populations from the late 1960s onwards. Le Fanu treats this as the model of legitimate preventive medicine: a measurable intermediate (BP), a safe drug, large effect size in RCTs, mortality falling.
He places this against the false preventive medicine of the 1980s+: dietary advice, cholesterol obsession, environmental scares. The honest preventive triumph requires (a) a measurable physiological variable, (b) a drug-and-trial-validated intervention, (c) a clear effect on hard endpoints. Most “Social Theory” public-health interventions lack one or more.
The chapter also opens onto the family of related cardiovascular drug classes — beta-blockers (Black, ICI, 1964), calcium-channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, statins (Endo, Akira, Sankyo, 1976; lovastatin commercialised 1987) — each a sulphonamide- or microbial-screening-style discovery whose efficacy had to be later confirmed by RCT. The stroke story is the crystalline case where empiricism, RCT, and preventive policy align.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_10_curing-childhood-cancer-1971
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM10 1971: Curing childhood cancer — combination chemotherapy and the Pinkel protocol
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) of childhood was uniformly fatal until ~1948. Sidney Farber (Boston) showed in 1947-48 that aminopterin — a folate antagonist designed by Yellapragada Subbarao using competitive-inhibition logic from sulphonamide work — produced temporary remissions. Methotrexate followed.
The accumulating arsenal — methotrexate, 6-MP (Hitchings/Elion), vincristine (1958, Eli Lilly, from periwinkle screening), prednisone (a cortisone derivative), L-asparaginase, cyclophosphamide, anthracyclines (from streptomycete soil screening) — gave the NCI groups (Frei, Freireich, Holland, DeVita) tools but no protocol. The breakthrough in 1971 was Donald Pinkel’s “Total Therapy” at St. Jude: aggressive multi-drug induction, CNS-directed prophylaxis (intrathecal methotrexate + cranial irradiation), maintenance, and consolidation. ~50% cure rate, where 0% had existed.
Le Fanu’s structural point: every drug in Pinkel’s regimen came from an unrelated serendipity — folate-antagonist work for nutrition, plant alkaloid screening for antimicrobials, soil microbe screening for antibiotics, adrenal hormone work for arthritis. Curing childhood leukaemia is the maximally interconnected case: four accidents and a courageous protocol.
The chapter’s “human cost” subtext (per Renée Fox’s Courage to Fail): early protocols were brutal — nausea, alopecia, infection deaths, late effects of cranial radiation. The clinical-science ideology that made it possible to keep going through high mortality during the experimentation phase is the same ideology Pappworth attacked. Both are needed; both have a shadow side.
Importantly, this is the last definitive moment whose mortality impact is clear and large for a non-age-determined disease. After 1971, oncology’s gains became marginal — many adult solid tumours respond modestly to chemotherapy at the cost of substantial toxicity. The Rise’s dose-response to chemotherapy investment is plateauing.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_11_ivf-1978
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM11 1978: The first test-tube baby — IVF and four-strand interconnectedness
Louise Brown’s birth on 25 July 1978 followed seven years of failure by Patrick Steptoe (gynaecologist, Oldham) and Robert Edwards (physiologist, Cambridge). The technical achievement required four independent research traditions to converge:

Embryology. Edwards had to overturn two textbook errors about human fertilisation (timing of egg maturation; capacitation requirements).
Endocrinology. Hormonal control of the female cycle, exogenous gonadotropin protocols, the LH surge.
Radioimmunoassay. Yalow & Berson’s 1959 technique — itself a Nobel-winning advance from diabetes research — let Edwards measure tiny hormone changes in patient blood.
Optics / laparoscopy. Steptoe’s laparoscope, derived from the Hopkins endoscope (1959), allowed minimally-invasive egg retrieval from the ovary.

The seven-year delay is itself a Le Fanu lesson. In 1971 Steptoe and Edwards had used a strategy they later abandoned in favour of “adding Primolut” to sustain the second half of the cycle. They were wrong; the original strategy had been right. They could not know this in real time. The point: “scientists never know why something is not working until they come across something that does.” Hindsight is unavailable in the moment.
Aftermath: 40,000 IVF pregnancies in the next two decades; extension to unexplained infertility, male infertility (ICSI), donor eggs. IVF is the late-Rise paradigm of interconnectedness — multiple Rise-era technologies (laparoscopy, RIA, gonadotropin pharmacology) chained together.
Le Fanu’s worry: post-1985, when the New Genetics absorbed most molecular-research funding, this kind of opportunistic cross-disciplinary integration became harder. Reductionism rewards single-discipline depth; clinical breakthroughs like IVF reward breadth and clinical-empirical opportunism.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_12_helicobacter-1984
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
DM12 1984: Helicobacter — the bacterium nobody saw
Barry Marshall, a 32-year-old Australian junior doctor at Royal Perth Hospital, swallowed in summer 1984 a cocktail containing helicobacter from a dyspeptic patient’s stomach. Within a week he had gastritis, putrid breath, vomiting; antibiotics resolved it within 24 hours. The self-experiment proved Robin Warren’s 1983 observation — “small curved bacilli” in stomach biopsies — was the actual cause of gastritis and peptic ulcer.
The pre-Marshall consensus: bacteria cannot survive gastric acid (which dissolves meat, burns concrete). Therefore peptic ulcer must come from “stress” or “personality.” The Wolf-Wolff “Tom” experiments (1940s, the man with a gastrostomy fistula whose mood-linked gastric secretions seemed to bear out psychosomatic theory) and the Franz Alexander Freudian theories of “infantile dependence” had become consensus. Rats, monkeys, and “executive monkey” experiments (cruel; later debunked methodologically) reinforced it. Cimetidine (1976, James Black, the H2-receptor antagonist) treated the symptom by suppressing acid, and seemed to confirm “excess acid” as cause — but ulcers recurred when treatment stopped.
Marshall’s path required:

Theoretical naïveté. He had no prior research training: “youth and inexperience” let him think “the unthinkable.”
An accidental clinical clue. A patient’s tetracycline-for-chest-infection coincidentally cleared the dyspepsia and the bacilli on follow-up gastroscopy.
Easter holiday culture extension. The 35th attempt at culture grew because the dish was incubated for 8 days (Easter break) instead of standard 48 hours. Helicobacter is slow-growing; standard protocol would never have isolated it.

A 1990 Lancet trial confirmed: antibiotics curing helicobacter eliminate ulcer recurrence; cimetidine alone does not. By the 2000s the standard treatment for peptic ulcer is a 7-14 day antibiotic course; ulcer surgery (vagotomy, gastrectomy) has nearly disappeared. Stomach cancer is implicated too.
Le Fanu’s argument: Helicobacter is the prophecy. Many “diseases of unknown cause” — multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, schizophrenia, Crohn’s, type 1 diabetes — show pattern-of-occurrence features that strongly suggest infectious or biological agents. The proper Part-IV future for medical research is not the New Genetics’ reductive obsession or the Social Theory’s lifestyle-blaming — it is more Marshalls: clinically rooted, atheoretical, willing to think the unthinkable, with PCR and other modern tools to find the agents.
The book’s pivot: definitive moments end with helicobacter. Everything in Parts III-IV asks why nothing has filled the slot since.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_13_part-i-rise-synthesis
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
Part I — The Rise: Big Bang, Clinical Science, Cornucopia, Technology, Mysteries
This part takes the twelve definitive moments and extracts six structural causes of the post-war therapeutic revolution. Le Fanu argues these conditions collectively explain why 1940-1980 was the Golden Age and why no later period can be expected to recur it.
1. Antibiotics + steroids = the fuse. Penicillin (DM1) and cortisone (DM2) were both endogenously-produced compounds whose discovery was unanticipated. Together they cleared two vast categories of disease (bacterial infection; uncontrolled inflammation), and made later definitive moments possible. Steroids enabled organ transplantation (anti-rejection) and Pinkel’s leukaemia regimen (immunosuppression). Antibiotics enabled transplantation (managing immunocompromised infection) and the entire surgical advance of the period.
2. Interconnectedness. No DM was self-contained. Sulphonamides (1933 Domagk) → competitive-inhibition principle → Hitchings/Elion → 6-MP, azathioprine (transplantation), allopurinol (gout), acyclovir (herpes), methotrexate (cancer). Laparoscopy (DM11) borrowed from endoscopy (DM4 sub-theme); IVF (DM11) used radioimmunoassay; chlorpromazine (DM4) came from antihistamine work; intensive care (DM5) from anaesthetic curare practice. Cross-discipline transfer was the dominant mode.
3. The clinical-science ideology (chapter “Clinical Science: A New Ideology for Medicine”). John McMichael at the Hammersmith Postgraduate Medical School (1935→) drove the shift from Lord Horder’s traditional bedside diagnostician to the Sir Thomas Lewis–style researcher who treats the patient as both clinical responsibility and experimental opportunity. McMichael’s heart-catheterisation studies (1943) crossed an ethical Rubicon — Lewis himself thought it improper. But the ideology of being willing to push intervention beyond the patient’s immediate benefit produced cardiac surgery, transplantation, and chemotherapy. Pappworth’s 1967 Human Guinea Pigs attacked the same ideology. Le Fanu treats this as a tension, not a verdict: the clinical-science ethic was necessary for the Rise and vulnerable to abuse.
4. The pharmaceutical revolution (chapter “A Cornucopia of New Drugs”). The 1930s doctor had ~12 proven drugs (digoxin, aspirin, salvarsan, insulin, thyroxine, morphine, etc.). By 1960 there were 2,000+. Beeson’s edits to Cecil’s Textbook of Medicine — first edition 1927 vs fourteenth 1960 — show only ~30 drugs from the first edition still in use; almost all 2000+ are new. The mechanism: a “lead” (chance observation) → chemists synthesise hundreds of variants → clinical screening. Crucially this method does not require understanding the cell. Cell biology was primitive through the 1960s. Drug discovery was empirical.
5. Technology’s triumphs. The pump, dialysis, endoscopy, intraocular lens implants (Ridley 1949), the Hopkins endoscope (1959), CT (Hounsfield 1973), MRI, Charnley’s hip — engineering progress, often by clinical practitioners moonlighting in workshops, producing physical solutions to disease. The Le Fanu point: these innovations did not require deeper biology either; they required mechanical understanding of organs and tools.
6. The mysteries of biology. Le Fanu’s running motif. Why do Penicillium moulds make penicillin? Why does chlorpromazine block dopamine? Why does cortisone control inflammation? Why is helicobacter unique among bacteria in tolerating gastric acid? The answers were not (and largely still are not) known. The Rise built on biological mystery rather than dispelling it. The Fall, Le Fanu will argue, was a category error — assuming biology had been (or was about to be) demystified by molecular biology.
These six conditions converged 1940-1980. They cannot be re-engineered. The Fall is, in part, the simple exhaustion of “what was do-able.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_14_part-ii-end-of-optimism
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
Part II — End of the Age of Optimism
By the late 1970s the four pillars of the Rise were each visibly faltering.
The Revolution Falters. The pace of definitive innovation slowed. The 1980s gave the world helicobacter (1984), HIV identification (1984), and triple therapy for AIDS (1996); the 1990s gave statins as preventive cardiology (lovastatin 1987 commercialised) and Viagra (1998). These are real but mostly extensions of Rise-era discoveries, not new categories.
The Dearth of New Drugs. Le Fanu’s most empirically anchored claim. The 1950-1975 period produced multiple genuinely new drug classes per year (antibiotics, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, calcium-channel blockers, antipsychotics, tricyclics, SSRIs in the late 80s, etc.). Post-1985, the pharmaceutical industry’s pipeline of new mechanisms runs dry. New drug approvals continue but are dominated by:

“Better mousetrap” me-too variants (next-generation statins, next-generation SSRIs);
Reformulations and combinations;
Biotech-produced versions of existing drugs (recombinant insulin, GH).

The Beeson/Sneader documentation through the 1990s shows the rate of first-in-class approvals collapsing. This is the empirical engine — chemistry’s lucky productive coincidence with biology — running out of unscreened compound space and unprobed targets.
Technology’s Failings. Le Fanu’s catalogue: foetal monitoring (introduced for cerebral palsy prevention; failed); excessive imaging (CT for every headache, endoscopy for every dyspepsia); cancer screening of marginal benefit (mammography overdiagnosis; PSA later); high-cost end-of-life ICU prolongation (the General Franco case study; ~25% of US health spending in last 6 months of life). Technology as such is not the problem; uncritical extension of technology to marginal uses is.
The Clinical Scientist as an Endangered Species. The McMichael-style clinically-grounded experimenter is replaced by the laboratory-only molecular biologist. Universities hire molecular geneticists, not clinical investigators. Funding chases “basic mechanism” research that no longer feeds back into therapeutic insight.
The intellectual vacuum left by these four failures is the conceptual space the Fall — the New Genetics and the Social Theory — rushes in to fill. Both promise something the Rise could not deliver: understanding the cause of disease. Both will fail.
Bradford Hill’s RCT, ironically, becomes the gatekeeper that makes the new failures auditable. Marcia Angell’s later critique of pharmaceutical-industry trial manipulation (Big Pharma chapter) shows the same toolkit being subverted from within.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_15_part-iii-fall-new-genetics
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
Part III ch. 1 — The Brave New World of the New Genetics
Le Fanu defines the New Genetics as the post-1972 program: recombinant DNA (Cohen-Boyer, 1973) → genetic engineering of biological products → genetic screening of foetuses → gene therapy → the Human Genome Project (begun 1990, completed 2001). It promises three deliverables, each of which Le Fanu argues has failed.
(i) Genetic engineering / biotechnology. The first commercial product was recombinant human insulin (Genentech, Boyer/Swanson, 1982). It works, but pork insulin had worked for sixty years and recombinant insulin’s incremental clinical benefit is small for most diabetics. Recombinant erythropoietin (EPO), growth hormone (GH), interferons, factor VIII — most either replace existing products or are of marginal therapeutic benefit. Le Fanu’s point: the technology is genuinely impressive, but it does not generate new disease categories curable; it makes existing protein drugs via a different process.
(ii) Genetic screening. ~4,000 single-gene disorders exist, almost all very rare. The major exceptions (Huntington’s, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia) can be tested for in foetuses. The aspiration was elimination by selective abortion. Reality: cystic fibrosis screening uptake low, gene-and-mutation heterogeneity huge (hundreds of CFTR mutations), and genetic testing for common adult disease (cancer, heart disease) reveals risks too modest and too multifactorial to act on. The “Case of the Missing Heritability” (post-2008 GWAS era; Le Fanu cites in revised epilogue): for diabetes, ~800 implicated genes, 780+ unknown. Polygenic risk is not actionable.
(iii) Gene therapy. The supreme aspiration: physically correct defective genes. Three decades on, gene therapy works in a handful of rare cases (severe combined immunodeficiency 1990s; inherited blindness; recent CAR-T for leukaemia and CRISPR-based sickle cell — much of this post-dates Le Fanu’s revised edition but his structural pessimism is by then well-established). For common diseases the approach simply does not work.
Le Fanu’s structural critique is in three parts:

Evolution selects against deleterious genes. Therefore monogenic diseases are rare and polygenic contributions to common disease are small. This is a thermodynamic-style upper bound on what genetic medicine can deliver.
Genes are vastly more complex than the central dogma allowed. Splicing, alternative reading frames, regulatory regions, epigenetics, RNA species (miRNAs), 3D chromatin organisation. The “DNA → RNA → protein” picture has been extended to a system whose interactome cannot be reduced to “the gene for X.”
Public belief outruns delivery. Daily newspaper headlines (“Gene Find Gives Insight into Brittle Bones”) create the impression of a moving frontier; “hope” and “prospect” appear in 90% of headlines, “cure” almost never. The intellectual prestige of molecular biology absorbs research funding without therapeutic return.

The chapter title — “Brave New World” — is double-edged. The reductionist promise was Aldous Huxley’s totalitarian fantasy of a genetically engineered humanity; the actual delivery has been ambiguous incremental tech without the dystopia or the cures.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_16_part-iii-fall-social-theory
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
Part III ch. 2 — Seduced by The Social Theory
The Social Theory: most common diseases (heart disease, stroke, most cancers) are caused by Western lifestyle — diet, alcohol, environmental pollution, sedentariness. Therefore most are preventable by behaviour change. Le Fanu argues this thesis is largely false, has profoundly distorted public-health policy, and has caused the “worried well” pathology of paradox 2.
The argument has five sub-sections in the book; the load-bearing claims:
(i) The McKeown thesis (Thomas McKeown, The Role of Medicine, 1976). McKeown showed Victorian-era infectious-disease mortality fell before effective medical interventions arrived; therefore (he claimed) the decline was due to nutrition, sanitation, and improved living standards. Le Fanu accepts McKeown’s historical observation but argues it was wrongly extrapolated to the post-1950 era of non-infectious chronic disease, where the supporting epidemiology is much weaker.
(ii) The rise and fall of heart disease. Heart disease mortality rose dramatically in the West 1920-1965, then fell sharply 1965-2000. The Social Theory claims dietary fat caused the rise; reduced fat consumption + statin use caused the fall. Le Fanu’s counter-argument:

Ancel Keys’ Seven Countries Study (1958) established the diet-heart hypothesis on flawed cherry-picked country selection (the 22-country dataset became 7);
The American Heart Association’s 1957 committee originally rejected the Keys thesis as not “internally coherent” in Bradford Hill’s sense; the 1961 reconstituted committee (with Keys and Stamler as members) reversed the verdict on no new evidence;
Saturated-fat reduction in the US population was minimal during the period heart-disease mortality fell;
The fall correlates better with smoking cessation, antihypertensive therapy (DM9), and emergency cardiac care than with dietary change;
Recent (post-2010) meta-analyses (PURE, etc.) have largely vindicated Le Fanu’s skepticism on saturated fat as a cardiac driver.

(iii) Beyond tobacco: Sir Richard Doll and the “causes of cancer.” Doll and Peto’s 1981 Causes of Cancer report attributed ~35% of cancers to diet, ~30% to tobacco. The diet figure was an interval estimate without primary evidence — Le Fanu calls it “a guess.” Yet by 1998 the UK Chief Medical Officer was advising the public that 3 lamb chops per day (or equivalent) increased cancer risk — Le Fanu’s signature example of medical advice “indistinguishable from quackery.”
(iv) Environmental alarums. Sellafield leukaemia cluster originally attributed to radioactive emissions (incompatible with measured doses by ~400-fold); Leo Kinlen’s population-mixing studies show a much better fit with infectious-cause hypothesis (rural construction workers introducing a virus to isolated populations). Pesticide and electromagnetic-field cancer scares similarly fail Bradford Hill’s coherence test.
(v) The end. The Social Theory survives because (a) it gives the public an action (“eat better”) and the politician a budget item (“health promotion”), (b) its statistical foundations are technical enough that few non-specialists can audit them, (c) media incentive structures favour scary findings, (d) committee science (the “expert committee” mechanism) launders weak evidence into policy.
Le Fanu’s positive proposal: Most chronic non-communicable disease is age-determined biology, not modifiable lifestyle. The honest preventive interventions are tobacco cessation, hypertension control, vaccination, and trauma reduction — not dietary moralising.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.title: ch_17_part-iv-causes-and-consequences
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:
Part IV — Learning from the past, looking to the future
Learning from the past. Le Fanu states the unifying claim: medicine’s Rise (~1940-1980) ran on lucky empiricism + cross-disciplinary opportunism + clinical-science ideology. By the late 1970s the four-layered “brick wall” stopped further progress:

The readily do-able has been done (transplants, cataracts, hips, immunisation against major communicable disease, antibiotics for major bacterial infections).
The chronic diseases of ageing can be ameliorated and palliated, not cured.
The bottom of the barrel of lucky drug discoveries has been scraped — the chemical compound space and microbial-screening yield are largely exhausted.
The causes of the common diseases of mid-life (multiple sclerosis, Crohn’s, schizophrenia, RA, type 1 diabetes) remain unknown.

The Fall is the set of “false strategies” attempting to break this wall:

Hammer away. Use existing technologies more aggressively (CT for headaches, chemotherapy for marginal-benefit cancers, ICU for the dying).
Pole-vault. Cancer screening, foetal monitoring — strategies whose theoretical logic seemed sound but whose impact on hard endpoints is small or negative.
Circumvent. The Social Theory: prevent disease by behaviour change. Doesn’t work for most non-infectious chronic disease.
Undermine. The New Genetics: hope that molecular reductionism will eventually demolish the wall. Hasn’t, and Le Fanu argues structurally cannot.

Looking to the future. The honest path:

Discard error. The Social Theory’s intellectual falsehoods need an independent inquiry akin to Harvey discarding pre-circulatory anatomy. The New Genetics’ pretensions need correction (it can produce useful biology; it cannot produce the medicine its advocates promised).
The “banyan tree” warning. “Under the banyan tree nothing grows”: genetics and epidemiology now cast such long shadows that no other research programmes can secure funding. Diversifying medical research back into clinical observation, infectious-cause hypothesis testing for “unknown” diseases, and Bjørn Ibsen-style cross-disciplinary borrowing.
Slay the dragon Progress. Le Fanu’s most contrarian move: medicine has wrongly identified itself with scientific progressivism. Its core methods — careful observation, distinguishing true from false, treating the patient — are continuous with Hippocrates and Osler. The “shock of the new” obsession (Richard Horton, Lancet editor, quoted) has displaced clinical wisdom and tacit judgement.
Restrain capitalism’s tail risk. The pharmaceutical industry’s structural need to innovate has, in the absence of new lucky discoveries, generated “better mousetraps” and “useless mousetraps” + clinical-trial manipulation. Marcia Angell’s testimony (Big Pharma chapter) describes how trials are now company-designed, company-analysed, company-published, with academic authors as nominal contributors.

Epilogue (revised edition, 2011). Ten years on:

“Doing more”: coronary angioplasty, keyhole surgery, surgery in 80+ year olds — extending Rise-era methods to wider populations. Real benefit, not new science.
“The New Genetics Triumphant — or Not”: Human Genome Project completed 2001, “missing heritability,” personalised genomics “no longer a foregone conclusion.”
“Big Pharma Rules”: revenues doubled 400bn→800bn; UK NHS budget tripled; “blockbusters falling off a cliff” as patents expire; switch to expensive specialty drugs ($20,000/course) for tens of thousands rather than cheap drugs for millions.

Final Osler quote (paraphrased by Le Fanu): the doctor’s work is to prevent disease, relieve suffering, heal the sick — same as in Ancient Greece, the methods continuous, the knowledge base expanded but the ethical posture stable. The Rise and Fall is one episode, glorious but bounded, in this long tradition.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/james-.content:

Ch.3 — DM2 1949: Cortisone — empiricism’s second pillar
If antibiotics defeat external enemies (bacteria), cortisone mobilises the body’s own healing machinery.
Ch.4 — DM3 1950: Streptomycin, Smoking, and Sir Austin Bradford Hill
Two events of 1950 jointly anchor a paradigm shift: (a) the streptomycin + PAS combination achieving “marked improvement” in 80% of TB patients, and (b) Doll and Bradford Hill’s case-control study proving smoking causes lung cancer.
Ch.5 — DM4 + DM5 1952: Chlorpromazine and the Copenhagen polio epidemic

John Charnley, a Manchester orthopaedic surgeon, redesigned the artificial hip after a chance interaction with a patient whose Judet prosthesis squeaked so loudly his wife avoided being in the same room with him.

Surgical transplantation was anatomically simple — vascular anastomosis was a known technique.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_00_preface_and_authors
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Front Matter — Preface, Authors, Pedagogical Architecture
About the authors. Jonathan Berk holds the A.P. Giannini Professor of Finance at Stanford GSB (formerly Berkeley Haas, formerly UBC). PhD in Finance from Yale. Pre-academic career as an associate at Goldman Sachs (the textbook’s only personal anecdote-source for sell-side practice). Best known for the Berk-Green model of mutual-fund flows and performance (JPE 2004), which argues that mutual-fund alpha disappears in equilibrium because investor capital chases skill until expected net alpha is zero — an EMH-consistent active-management equilibrium. Won the Stephen A. Ross Prize. Peter DeMarzo is the Mizuho Financial Group Professor of Finance, also at Stanford GSB. PhD from Stanford. Best known for foundational work on dynamic security design and contracting (DeMarzo-Sannikov 2006) and on financial-intermediary capital structure. Past president of the American Finance Association.
The author pairing is methodologically unified — both are theorists who treat arbitrage and equilibrium as the load-bearing concepts; the textbook reflects this in its insistence that the Law of One Price organises the entire curriculum (rather than introducing arbitrage as a Part-7 derivative-pricing tool, as some MBA texts do).
Pedagogical philosophy (Preface, Ch. 13 ch_13_preface).

One unifying principle. The Law of One Price (no-arbitrage) is the single conceptual axiom from which every quantitative result in the book is derived. Berk-DeMarzo are explicit about this: “we believe that the Law of One Price is the one unifying principle that underlies all of financial economics and links all of the ideas throughout this book.” Other textbooks (Brealey-Myers-Allen, Ross-Westerfield-Jaffe) treat NPV-then-CAPM-then-MM as separable modules; Berk-DeMarzo deliberately weave one chain.
NPV decision rule taught as theorem, not procedure. Ch. 3’s NPV rule is derived from value-additivity which in turn is derived from no-arbitrage. The student who finishes Ch. 3 has seen a complete argument; subsequent chapters add inputs (risk-adjusted rates in Part 4; tax-adjusted rates in Parts 5–6; option-replicated rates in Part 7), not new axioms.
Real-firm data and CFO interviews. Each chapter opens with current-events data (the book’s 6th edition adds 2017–2022 beta data, 2008–2020 yield curves, mid-2020s case studies on Tesla, Netflix, Apple, Amazon). Many chapters include CFO/practitioner interview boxes (David Viniar at Goldman, Sidney Hindle of Hindle Power, Myron Scholes himself in Ch. 21).
Common notation across chapters. A unified symbol table ([source extract]) introduces r, r_f, \beta, \sigma, V, E, D, \tau_C, \text{NPV}, \text{FCF}, \text{WACC} at the front, with overloading collisions (e.g. r_E for equity cost of capital and R_E for realised equity return) carefully signposted.
MyLab Finance integration. The textbook is engineered around an online problem-set environment with interactive examples. The print/PDF reader misses adaptive practice and live-data widgets that the textbook expects the student to use (the “Best chapters” list in the book note flags this gap).

Sixth edition (Global Edition) differences. The Global Edition (Pearson 2023) contains additional non-U.S. case studies (LVMH, Samsung, Vale, ICBC), retains U.S. tax-code numbers but cross-references to OECD-equivalent rates, and adds chapter problems with international currency conventions. Otherwise content tracks the U.S. 6th edition closely.
Reading prerequisites. The book presumes (a) algebra plus introductory calculus (derivatives, exponentials, logarithms — used in Ch. 21 Black-Scholes); (b) basic probability / statistics (variance, covariance, normal distribution); (c) accounting literacy at the level of a one-semester financial-accounting course (Ch. 2 reviews the four statements but does not teach accounting from scratch); (d) introductory microeconomics (utility, indifference curves, marginal analysis), supplied by Daron Acemoglu - Microeconomics.
Compression. Front matter ([source extract] through [source extract], ~30K chars excluding the detailed contents) → ~530 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_01_introduction
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 1 — Introduction (Chapters 1–3)
Formal spine. The textbook opens by defining the corporation as a legal person separable from its owners (Dartmouth College v. Woodward 1819 cited as the U.S. constitutional precedent), distinguishing the four firm types (sole proprietorship, partnership, LLC, corporation), and then laying down the single unifying axiom that organises everything that follows: the Law of One Price (no-arbitrage).
Formal statement (Ch. 3.4):
\text{If two assets generate identical future cash flows in every state, then they must trade at the same price in a competitive market.}
Equivalently, a portfolio that generates non-negative cash flows in every state and a strictly positive cash flow in some state must have a positive price; a portfolio that costs zero today and generates non-negative cash flows in every state with a strictly positive payoff in some state cannot exist (no-arbitrage). This is the textbook’s “one unifying principle that underlies all of financial economics” (preface, Ch. 1, Ch. 3).
The NPV decision rule is derived from no-arbitrage:
\text{NPV} = \text{PV}(\text{benefits}) - \text{PV}(\text{costs})
A project is value-creating iff \text{NPV} > 0; the Separation Principle then says financial decisions (financing, distribution policy) can be analysed independently of investment decisions whenever capital markets are competitive, because trading fairly priced securities has zero NPV.
Chapter 1 — The Corporation and Financial Markets. Sketches the agency structure (shareholders → board → CEO/CFO), the dual roles of financial managers (investment, financing, working-capital management), and the institutional plumbing of stock markets (NYSE specialists, Nasdaq dealer market, dark pools). Introduces the divergence between shareholder value maximisation (the textbook’s normative benchmark) and the broader stakeholder view (employees, suppliers, customers, society) that empirical corporate-governance debates orbit. Sole proprietorships are 72% of U.S. firms but 4% of revenue; corporations are 18% of firms and 82% of revenue. The 2008 GFC (Bear Stearns, Lehman, AIG, GM bailouts) is presented as a case in which the institutional rules themselves were renegotiated.
Chapter 2 — Financial Statement Analysis. Walks through the four accounting statements — balance sheet (assets = liabilities + equity), income statement (revenue → net income via COGS, SG&A, D&A, interest, taxes), statement of cash flows (operating + investing + financing), and statement of stockholders’ equity — and maps each to valuation-relevant inputs: book vs market value of equity, the market-to-book ratio (P/B), the price-earnings ratio (P/E), enterprise value (EV = market equity + net debt), and EBITDA. Introduces the DuPont decomposition of ROE into profit margin × asset turnover × leverage as a diagnostic. Closes with case studies of accounting failures (Enron mark-to-model abuse; WorldCom capitalising operating expenses; the Sarbanes-Oxley response) — important for the book’s later treatment of agency costs and information asymmetry.
Chapter 3 — Financial Decision Making and the Law of One Price. The book’s theoretical fulcrum. It presents the six-step decision framework (cost-benefit → market price as decision input → arbitrage → Law of One Price → no-arbitrage prices → Separation Principle), then derives the NPV rule as the operational form of value-additivity under no-arbitrage. The chapter explicitly states that “an arbitrage opportunity has positive NPV” and that competitive frictionless markets must be normal-form no-arbitrage (called “normal markets” in the book to avoid the stronger “complete markets” or “efficient markets” labels). Value-additivity — that the price of a portfolio equals the sum of prices of its components — is derived as a consequence: it is the formal structure that makes capital-budgeting tractable and that the Modigliani-Miller propositions (Part 5) and Black-Scholes formula (Part 7) will both invoke.
Why this Part matters. Berk-DeMarzo’s pedagogical wager is that one axiom — no-arbitrage / Law of One Price — generates almost every result in the rest of the textbook (NPV, bond pricing, stock valuation, CAPM under additional risk-averse-investor assumptions, MM I and II, the WACC formula, all option-pricing models, real-options valuation, the irrelevance of payout policy in perfect markets, capital-structure-irrelevance theorems). This is in deliberate contrast to textbooks that teach NPV as a procedure first and theory later. The chapter-3 proof structure (“if not no-arbitrage, then strictly positive arbitrage profit available; investors will trade until equilibrium prices restore no-arbitrage”) is the template the reader should expect to see re-applied in chapters 14, 15, 18, 21.
Notation introduced (carries through the book): r (interest rate), \text{NPV} (net present value), \text{PV} (present value), C_t (cash flow at date t), r_f (risk-free rate). Compression: ~317K raw → ~750 words ≥400:1 (formal-spine summary).

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_02_time_money_interest
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 2 — Time, Money, and Interest Rates (Chapters 4–6)
Formal spine. This Part operationalises the Law of One Price by giving the reader the time-value-of-money machinery that turns “present value of a stream of cash flows” from slogan into computable formula.
Chapter 4 — The Time Value of Money. The three rules of “time travel”:

It is only possible to compare or combine values at the same point in time.
To move a cash flow forward in time, multiply by (1+r) once per period:  \text{FV}_n = C \times (1+r)^n.
To move a cash flow backward in time, divide by (1+r) once per period:  \text{PV} = C_n / (1+r)^n.

For a stream \{C_0, C_1, \ldots, C_N\}:
\text{PV} = \sum_{t=0}^{N} \frac{C_t}{(1+r)^t}, \qquad \text{NPV} = \sum_{t=0}^{N} \frac{C_t}{(1+r)^t}.
Closed forms derived (Ch. 4.5–4.7):

Perpetuity: \text{PV} = C/r (constant cash flow forever, first paid at t=1).
Growing perpetuity (Gordon-form): \text{PV} = C/(r-g), requires g < r.
Annuity: \text{PV} = (C/r)\,[1 - 1/(1+r)^N].
Growing annuity: \text{PV} = \frac{C}{r-g}\bigl[1 - \bigl(\frac{1+g}{1+r}\bigr)^N\bigr].

Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is defined implicitly as the discount rate that makes \text{NPV} = 0 — the chapter sets up the rule but defers the multi-IRR pitfalls to Ch. 7. Worked examples include retirement saving, annuity-due conversions, and the geometric/arithmetic distinction.
Chapter 5 — Interest Rates. Distinguishes:

Effective Annual Rate (EAR) vs Annual Percentage Rate (APR): \text{EAR} = (1 + \text{APR}/k)^k - 1, where k is the number of compounding periods per year.
Real vs nominal interest rate (Fisher equation): 1 + r_{\text{nominal}} = (1 + r_{\text{real}})(1 + \pi), with the linear approximation r_{\text{real}} \approx r_{\text{nominal}} - \pi when both are small.
Term structure / yield curve: different r_n for different maturities n; PV of a stream uses the appropriate r_n per cash-flow date in principle.

Introduces the discount factor 1/(1+r_n)^n as the price of a 1 zero-coupon bond, the **opportunity cost of capital** as the rate the firm could earn on a market alternative of equivalent risk and maturity (the heart of capital-budgeting practice), and the **after-tax interest rate** r(1 - \tau)$ that becomes load-bearing in Part 5’s WACC and APV chapters.
Chapter 6 — Valuing Bonds. Defines a coupon bond’s price as the PV of its cash flows discounted at appropriate spot rates:
P = \sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{C}{(1+y_t)^t} + \frac{F}{(1+y_N)^N}
with C = coupon, F = face value, y_t = spot rate for maturity t. Yield to maturity (YTM) is the single rate y such that the bond’s market price equals the PV of its cash flows discounted at y. The chapter then proves three classical results:

Bond price moves inversely with yield (mathematical: derivative of PV w.r.t. yield is negative).
Bond price approaches face value as maturity approaches (pull-to-par).
Longer-maturity and lower-coupon bonds have higher duration and thus higher interest-rate risk.

Distinguishes Treasury (default-free) from corporate bonds, introduces credit spreads (yield in excess of risk-free benchmark) as compensation for default risk, and walks through a sovereign-default case (Argentina 2001) to motivate why “yield” and “expected return” diverge once default probability is non-zero. Replication argument for coupon bonds (a coupon bond is a portfolio of zero-coupon bonds) is the chapter’s invocation of the Law of One Price — value-additivity from Ch. 3 used in earnest.
Why this Part matters. Every later valuation in the book — DCF for stocks (Ch. 9), NPV for projects (Chs. 7–8), tax shield (Ch. 15), levered firm value (Ch. 18), option pricing (Chs. 21–22) — is just PV machinery from this Part with the cash-flow forecast and discount rate filled in differently. The reader who internalises the perpetuity, annuity, and growing-perpetuity closed forms can derive the Gordon Growth Model (Ch. 9), the value of an interest tax shield (Ch. 15), and the constant-WACC valuation formula (Ch. 18) in one or two algebraic steps each.
Notation: r, r_f, C_t, F, \text{PV}, \text{FV}, \text{NPV}, \text{IRR}, y (YTM), y_t (spot rate), \tau (corporate tax rate), \pi (inflation), EAR, APR. ~309K raw → ~700 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_03_valuing_projects_firms
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 3 — Valuing Projects and Firms (Chapters 7–9)
Formal spine. Translates NPV into the capital-budgeting and equity-valuation settings.
Chapter 7 — Investment Decision Rules. The textbook’s normative claim: NPV is the only decision rule that always gives the right answer; alternatives are useful as supplements but can be wrong. Formal results:

NPV rule. Accept iff \text{NPV}>0; for mutually exclusive projects, choose the one with highest NPV.
IRR rule. Accept iff \text{IRR} > r (the cost of capital). The chapter proves the IRR rule coincides with NPV when (a) cash flows have a single sign change (one outflow then inflows, or vice-versa) and (b) there is a single cost of capital. Pitfalls demonstrated by example: (i) borrowing-vs-investing reversal — when up-front cash inflows precede outflows, the IRR rule reverses; (ii) multiple IRRs — Descartes’ rule of signs implies up to as many IRRs as sign changes in the cash-flow stream; (iii) different scale or timing across mutually exclusive projects can make IRR rank wrong while NPV ranks right.
Payback period. Years until cumulative inflows recover the initial outlay. Easy but ignores time value of money and post-payback cash flows; routinely used as a rough screen.
Profitability index. \text{PI} = \text{NPV}/\text{Investment}. Useful when capital is rationed: rank projects by PI and accept top until budget exhausted.

The chapter ends with a survey result (Graham-Harvey 2001 cited): IRR is in practice the most-used rule among CFOs, but NPV is taught as the gold standard because it is the only rule that follows directly from value-additivity (Ch. 3) without auxiliary conditions.
Chapter 8 — Fundamentals of Capital Budgeting. Operationalises NPV by walking through the HomeNet running example (a fictitious Cisco home-networking project). The chapter’s substantive content:


Free cash flow (FCF) is the right object to discount, not accounting earnings. Define
\text{FCF}_t = (\text{Revenue}_t - \text{Costs}_t - \text{Depreciation}_t)(1-\tau) + \text{Depreciation}_t - \text{CapEx}_t - \Delta\text{NWC}_t.
The depreciation term is added back because it is a non-cash expense; CapEx and changes in net working capital (\Delta\text{NWC}) are subtracted because they are real cash outflows. The (1-\tau) on operating profit captures incremental corporate tax liability.


Use incremental, not total, cash flows. Sunk costs are excluded; opportunity costs are included; cannibalisation of existing-product cash flows is included as a negative incremental flow; salvage value at project end is included; allocated overhead is included only if it is genuinely incremental.


Sensitivity, scenario, and break-even analysis. Standard techniques to bound NPV uncertainty around point estimates of each input.


Real-options preview. Choices to delay, expand, or abandon are flagged here and developed in Ch. 22.


The book’s economic depreciation discussion makes the connection: tax depreciation (MACRS) generates a depreciation tax shield \tau \times D_t each year, which feeds directly into FCF and hence NPV.
Chapter 9 — Valuing Stocks. Applies PV to equity:


Dividend Discount Model (DDM). P_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \frac{D_t}{(1+r_E)^t} where r_E is the equity cost of capital. Three special cases:

Zero-growth (perpetuity): P_0 = D/r_E.
Constant-growth (Gordon Growth Model): P_0 = D_1/(r_E - g), g < r_E.
Two-stage / multi-stage DDM for high-growth firms transitioning to steady state.



Implied growth rate from retention. g = b \times \text{ROE}, where b = retention ratio and ROE = return on equity, links payout policy to growth and prepares for Ch. 17.


Total Payout and FCF Valuation Models. When firms repurchase shares as well as pay dividends, the total payout model discounts the firm’s total payout (dividends + repurchases) and divides by current shares outstanding. The discounted free-cash-flow model values the enterprise (i.e., the firm’s assets), discounting FCF at the WACC, then subtracts net debt to back out equity. Equation:
V_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \frac{\text{FCF}_t}{(1+r_{\text{wacc}})^t}; \quad E_0 = V_0 + \text{Cash}_0 - \text{Debt}_0.


Comparables / multiples valuation. P/E, EV/EBITDA, EV/Sales, P/B; pros (simple, market-anchored) and cons (only as good as the comparable set, can compound mispricing).


Information and stock prices. Foreshadows Ch. 13: if no investor has private information beyond the price, the price reflects only public information, and the typical investor cannot expect to profit from public-information-based trading. This is the Efficient Markets Hypothesis (EMH) in informational form that Berk-DeMarzo will develop quantitatively in Part 4.


Why this Part matters. This is where the book teaches the practitioner skill set: building a DCF model for a project (HomeNet) or a firm (the Kenneth Cole case study) using FCF projection, discount-rate selection, terminal-value handling, and multiples cross-checks. Subsequent Parts (4 risk-adjusted discount rates; 5 capital-structure-adjusted discount rates; 6 leveraged DCF) progressively refine the discount rate used in this Part’s NPV / DDM / FCF formulas.
Notation: FCF, \DeltaNWC, CapEx, D_t (dividend), r_E, r_D, r_{\text{wacc}}, PI, IRR, Gordon g. ~340K raw → ~870 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_04_risk_and_return
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 4 — Risk and Return (Chapters 10–13)
Formal spine. Builds the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) as the textbook’s primary tool for choosing the discount rate r_E that Part 3 left exogenous, then tests the model against empirical anomalies in Ch. 13.
Chapter 10 — Capital Markets and the Pricing of Risk. Empirical priming and decomposition.


Realised return on a stock from t-1 to t: R_t = (P_t - P_{t-1} + D_t)/P_{t-1}. Average annual returns 1926–2020 (Ibbotson/SBBI-style table): small stocks > large stocks > corporate bonds > Treasury bonds > T-bills > inflation, with volatility ranking the same direction. Risk and return are positively correlated in the cross-section of asset classes.


Variance and standard deviation: \text{Var}(R) = E[(R-\bar R)^2], \text{SD}(R) = \sqrt{\text{Var}(R)}. Cross-section evidence on individual stocks shows volatility is not monotonically related to expected return — the cross-section of individual-stock volatility says nothing useful about the cross-section of expected returns.


Diversification. Define a portfolio with weights \{x_i\}, \sum x_i = 1. Portfolio return: R_P = \sum_i x_i R_i. Portfolio variance for an equally-weighted portfolio of N stocks with average individual variance \bar\sigma^2 and average pairwise covariance \bar c:
\text{Var}(R_P) = \frac{1}{N}\bar\sigma^2 + \Bigl(1-\frac{1}{N}\Bigr)\bar c.
As N\to\infty, the first term vanishes and \text{Var}(R_P)\to\bar c. This proves idiosyncratic (firm-specific, diversifiable) risk vanishes in a large portfolio; only systematic (market-wide, non-diversifiable) risk remains.


Pricing implication. Investors holding diversified portfolios cannot demand a risk premium for diversifiable risk (they can eliminate it costlessly). Therefore a security’s risk premium depends only on its systematic risk, measured by beta with respect to the market portfolio:
\beta_i = \frac{\text{Cov}(R_i, R_{\text{Mkt}})}{\text{Var}(R_{\text{Mkt}})}.
Beta measures the percent change in a security’s return per 1% change in the market’s return. Average beta = 1; cyclical industries (autos, airlines, technology) have \beta>1; non-cyclical industries (utilities, packaged food, pharma) have \beta<1. Table 10.6 reports betas 2017–2022: Hormel 0.16, Walmart 0.41, Coca-Cola 0.83, Microsoft 0.93, Apple 1.06, Tesla and AMD substantially above 1.


Chapter 11 — Optimal Portfolio Choice and CAPM. Mean-variance optimisation.


Two-asset portfolio: E[R_P] = x_1 E[R_1] + x_2 E[R_2]; \text{Var}(R_P) = x_1^2 \sigma_1^2 + x_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2 x_1 x_2 \text{Cov}(R_1, R_2). Diversification benefit increases as correlation falls below 1.


Efficient frontier. Set of portfolios that minimise variance for each level of expected return.


Tangency portfolio with risk-free asset. Adding a risk-free asset with return r_f to the choice set gives the Capital Market Line (CML): a straight line from (0, r_f) to the tangency portfolio T. Investors hold combinations of r_f and T; under the CAPM assumptions (homogeneous expectations, frictionless markets, all investors choose mean-variance-optimal portfolios over the same horizon), the tangency portfolio equals the market portfolio.


CAPM equation (Eq. 11.22). Equilibrium expected return on any security:
E[R_i] = r_f + \beta_i\,(E[R_{\text{Mkt}}] - r_f).
The market risk premium E[R_{\text{Mkt}}] - r_f is rescaled by the security’s beta. The Security Market Line (SML) is the graph of this equation in (\beta, E[R]) space: every traded security plots on the SML in equilibrium.


Chapter 12 — Estimating the Cost of Capital. Practitioner conversion of the CAPM into a usable discount rate.

Risk-free rate. Use Treasury yields of maturity matching the project life.
Market risk premium. Historical average (≈ 5%–6% over 1926–2020) vs forward-looking implied premium from current market dividend yields and growth-rate forecasts.
Equity beta from regression. R_{i,t} - r_{f,t} = \alpha_i + \beta_i (R_{\text{Mkt},t} - r_{f,t}) + \varepsilon_{i,t} — OLS slope is the empirical beta. Standard errors and the difference between equity beta and asset (unlevered) beta are flagged.
Unlevering and relevering beta. Asset beta: \beta_U = (E\beta_E + D\beta_D)/(E+D); relever when leverage changes.
Cost of debt. YTM is biased upward as a measure of expected return because it ignores default. Use yield adjusted for expected default loss in CAPM-consistent estimates.
WACC formula. Combining the cost of equity (from CAPM) and the after-tax cost of debt:
r_{\text{wacc}} = \frac{E}{E+D}\,r_E + \frac{D}{E+D}\,r_D\,(1-\tau_C).
This is the discount rate used in the FCF valuation of a firm with constant target leverage (Part 6 makes the leverage-policy assumption explicit).

Chapter 13 — Investor Behavior and Capital Market Efficiency. The empirical referee:

Efficient Markets Hypothesis (EMH). Three forms: weak (past prices reflected), semi-strong (all public information reflected), strong (all information including private reflected). Berk-DeMarzo’s framing is informational/competitive: in equilibrium, a typical investor cannot profit from public information because rivals will trade until the alpha is gone.
CAPM tests. The CAPM beta is the only relevant risk factor under the model; empirically, size, value (book/market), and momentum generate persistent abnormal returns inconsistent with CAPM. The chapter introduces the Fama-French three-factor model (market, SMB, HML) and the Fama-French-Carhart four-factor model (adding momentum) as multifactor extensions.
Investor behavior anomalies. Disposition effect, overconfidence, herding, attention bias, sentiment effects. The chapter is unusually candid about the gap between CAPM-based capital-budgeting practice and the mixed empirical record.
Efficient-market caveat. Market prices reflect available information, but this does not mean prices are correct (Shleifer-Vishny limits to arbitrage). Berk-DeMarzo treat EMH as an equilibrium claim about expected returns net of risk premia, not a metaphysical claim.

Why this Part matters. This Part sets the discount rate used in every prior NPV calculation, and is the part of the book that maps most directly onto interview-style questions in equity research, investment banking, and any academic finance research role. The proof that diversifiable risk earns no premium — derived purely from the no-arbitrage / large-portfolio argument — is one of the most frequently re-derived results in finance.
Notation: R_i, \bar R, \sigma_i, \sigma_M, \beta_i, x_i, E[R_i], r_f, r_E, r_D, r_{\text{wacc}}, \tau_C, EMH, CML, SML. ~509K raw → ~1100 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_05_capital_structure
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 5 — Capital Structure (Chapters 14–17)
Formal spine. The Modigliani-Miller theorems and their progressive enrichment as frictions are introduced.
Chapter 14 — Capital Structure in a Perfect Market. The benchmark.
MM Proposition I (Ch. 14.2). Under three perfect-capital-market conditions — (1) investors and firms trade the same securities at competitive prices equal to PV of cash flows; (2) no taxes, transaction costs, or issuance costs; (3) financing decisions do not change the cash flows or reveal new information — the total value of a firm is independent of its capital structure:
V_L = V_U,
i.e. the market value of the levered firm V_L = E + D equals the market value of the otherwise-identical unlevered firm V_U. The proof is arbitrage via homemade leverage: any investor who prefers different leverage from the firm’s choice can borrow or lend on personal account at the same rate as the firm and replicate the alternative payoff. If V_L \ne V_U for two firms with identical assets, an arbitrageur shorts the overvalued firm, longs the undervalued firm plus a homemade-leverage adjustment, and earns a riskless profit until prices converge — a direct application of the Law of One Price (Ch. 3).
MM Proposition II (Ch. 14.3). The cost of equity for a levered firm rises linearly with the debt-equity ratio:
r_E = r_U + \frac{D}{E}\,(r_U - r_D),
where r_U is the unlevered cost of capital and r_D is the cost of debt. The intuition: debt financing concentrates cash-flow risk on the residual equity claim, so equity-holders demand a higher expected return as leverage rises. The pretax WACC (i.e. the cost of capital of the firm’s assets) is invariant to capital structure:
r_{\text{pretax-wacc}} = \frac{E}{E+D}\,r_E + \frac{D}{E+D}\,r_D = r_U.
This is the “leverage just rebalances the slices of a fixed pie” intuition. Beta version of MM II: \beta_U = \frac{E}{E+D}\beta_E + \frac{D}{E+D}\beta_D — the firm’s asset beta is a value-weighted average of equity and debt betas.
Chapter 15 — Debt and Taxes. First friction: corporate taxes.

Interest Tax Shield. Interest is deductible from taxable corporate income at marginal rate \tau_C. For a firm paying interest I_t in year t:
\text{Interest Tax Shield}_t = \tau_C \times I_t.
Levered firm value with permanent debt. PV of the tax shield is \tau_C \times D (treating the tax shield as a perpetuity at r_D on permanent debt D):
V_L = V_U + \tau_C\,D.
This is the MM with corporate taxes version of Proposition I. Implication: pure tax considerations push the firm toward 100% debt financing.
Personal taxes. Once we add personal taxes on interest income (rate \tau_i) and equity income (effective rate \tau_e blending dividend and capital-gains rates), the effective tax advantage of debt is \tau^* = 1 - \frac{(1-\tau_C)(1-\tau_e)}{1-\tau_i}, which can be substantially smaller than \tau_C alone — the Miller (1977) personal-tax offset.
WACC with taxes (the formula students memorise):
r_{\text{wacc}} = \frac{E}{E+D}\,r_E + \frac{D}{E+D}\,r_D\,(1-\tau_C),
strictly less than the unlevered r_U when there is debt, because debt’s tax shield reduces the firm’s effective cost of capital. Critical point flagged in Ch. 18: the WACC formula assumes the firm rebalances debt to a constant target debt-to-value ratio; if debt level is fixed instead (perpetual fixed face), use APV instead (Ch. 18).

Chapter 16 — Financial Distress, Managerial Incentives, and Information. The frictions that bound debt away from 100%.

Direct costs of bankruptcy (legal/administrative, ~3–4% of pre-distress firm value) and indirect costs (lost customers, suppliers, employees; fire-sale asset-liquidation discounts; managerial distraction).
Tradeoff theory of capital structure: the optimal D/V balances the marginal tax shield against the marginal expected-distress cost:
V_L = V_U + \tau_C\,D - \text{PV}(\text{distress costs}).
Agency costs of debt. Asset substitution / risk-shifting (high-leverage equity-holders prefer riskier projects because of their convex payoff); debt overhang (Myers 1977 — equity-holders reject positive-NPV projects whose value largely accrues to debt-holders); cashing-out / milking (extracting value from a near-bankrupt firm).
Agency costs of equity. Free-cash-flow problem (Jensen 1986) — managers of low-leverage firms with abundant FCF over-invest; debt’s commitment to cash payouts is a discipline device.
Information / signaling. Pecking order (Myers-Majluf 1984): firms prefer internal funds → debt → equity, because adverse selection makes equity issuance look like bad news. Capital-structure signaling: leverage announcements reveal management’s belief about firm prospects.
Synthesis. The optimal capital structure is firm-specific and depends on industry-level distress technology, tangibility of assets, growth prospects, profitability, and tax-shield value.

Chapter 17 — Payout Policy. The dividend-irrelevance corollary.

MM payout-irrelevance (in perfect markets). With no taxes, transaction costs, or information differences, the firm’s choice between paying dividends, repurchasing shares, or retaining cash for future payout cannot change firm value. Investors who want different cash-flow timing can rebalance personally.
Tax preference. Dividends are taxed at ordinary income (or preferential dividend rate); capital gains are tax-deferred and may receive preferential rates → tax preference for repurchases over dividends in U.S. tax regimes for most of the 20th century.
Clientele effects. Investors with different tax circumstances self-sort into stocks with payout policies that suit them; the marginal investor’s tax rate determines the equilibrium payout-policy effect.
Signaling and stickiness of dividends. Empirically, managers smooth dividends (Lintner 1956) and treat dividend cuts as last-resort signals; dividend-payment-history is a costly signal of stable cash flow.
Repurchases. Three forms: open-market, fixed-price tender offer, Dutch auction; all three implement payout but differ in signalling and tax timing.

Why this Part matters. This is the heart of corporate finance — how firms should finance themselves. The MM theorems establish the frictionless benchmark; the next three chapters identify the four families of frictions (taxes, distress costs, agency costs, information asymmetry) that drive observed capital structures away from that benchmark. The reader who internalises this Part can reason from first principles about LBO capital structure (high tax shield + disciplined FCF → high-leverage optimum), startup capital structure (high distress cost + intangible assets → equity-dominated), and bank capital structure (regulatory minimum + safety-net subsidy → distorted equilibrium).
Notation: V_L, V_U, E, D, r_E, r_D, r_U, r_{\text{wacc}}, \tau_C, \tau_i, \tau_e, \tau^*, I_t, \beta_E, \beta_D, \beta_U. ~498K raw → ~1050 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_06_advanced_valuation
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 6 — Advanced Valuation (Chapters 18–19)
Formal spine. Three internally consistent methods for valuing a levered investment, plus a synthesis case study.
Chapter 18 — Capital Budgeting and Valuation with Leverage. The book gives three alternative valuation methods that, when applied correctly to the same project, must give the same NPV by the Law of One Price.
(1) WACC method. Discount unlevered free cash flows at the after-tax WACC:
V_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \frac{\text{FCF}_t}{(1+r_{\text{wacc}})^t}, \quad r_{\text{wacc}} = \frac{E}{E+D}\,r_E + \frac{D}{E+D}\,r_D\,(1-\tau_C).
Assumption: the firm rebalances debt continuously to maintain a constant target debt-to-value ratio D/V. The WACC method is correct under this target-leverage policy.
(2) APV (Adjusted Present Value, Myers 1974, Ch. 18.3). Decompose firm value into the unlevered value plus the PV of the tax shield:
V^L_0 = V^U_0 + \text{PV}(\text{Interest Tax Shield}) = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \frac{\text{FCF}_t}{(1+r_U)^t} + \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \frac{\tau_C\,r_D\,D_{t-1}}{(1+r_{\text{TS}})^t}.
Discount the tax shield at r_D if debt level is predetermined (fixed face value), at r_U if debt is rebalanced to maintain target leverage. APV is more flexible than WACC because it can handle changing leverage, debt-financed acquisitions, and time-varying tax-shield risk.
(3) FTE (Flow-to-Equity, Ch. 18.4). Discount levered free cash flow to equity-holders (after interest and principal) at the cost of equity r_E:
E_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \frac{\text{FCFE}_t}{(1+r_E)^t}.
FCFE = FCF − after-tax interest − net debt repayment. FTE gives the equity value directly.
Equivalence. Berk-DeMarzo prove that under consistent leverage assumptions all three methods produce identical NPV — this is the leveraged-firm analog of Modigliani-Miller’s value-additivity, and again invokes the Law of One Price. The choice among methods is a practitioner one based on which leverage policy and which inputs are easiest to estimate.
Other Ch. 18 topics.
