Issuance costs (front-loaded fees on new debt or equity reduce realised proceeds and modify NPV); subsidised financing (project-specific concessional rates create subsidy NPV that adds to project NPV); personal taxes’ effect on the discount rate; computing project beta from comparables (industry asset-beta proxy then re-lever for the project’s leverage).
Chapter 19 — Valuation and Financial Modeling: A Case Study. End-to-end DCF model — by hand, in Excel, then with Monte Carlo / sensitivity:

Forecasting the income statement and balance sheet for the target firm (Ideko, the running case) under base, optimistic, and pessimistic scenarios.
Computing FCF from forecast earnings and balance-sheet changes.
Choosing the cost of capital: unlever industry comparables, average asset betas, relever to the target firm’s planned post-acquisition leverage.
Terminal value via constant-growth perpetuity (\text{TV}_T = \text{FCF}_{T+1}/(r_{\text{wacc}}-g)) or via exit multiple (e.g. EV/EBITDA at year T).
Sensitivity analysis on growth, margin, leverage, exit multiple — quantifying the range of NPV outcomes.
Output: equity value, IRR for the equity sponsor, exit-year debt/equity ratio.

The case study mirrors what private-equity associates and investment-banking analysts actually build; the book uses it to show how the abstract Parts 1–5 machinery composes into a deliverable model.
Why this Part matters. This Part is the interview-ready capstone: any private-equity, investment-banking, equity-research, or corporate-development role requires fluency in WACC vs APV vs FTE and in building a multi-year DCF with sensitivity. The conceptual point — that consistent leverage assumptions force the three methods to agree, and that violating any assumption breaks one method preferentially — is the most-frequently-violated point in practitioner practice and is the textbook’s most concrete contribution to correct leveraged valuation.
Notation: \text{FCF}, \text{FCFE}, V^U, V^L, r_U, r_E, r_D, r_{\text{wacc}}, r_{\text{TS}}, \tau_C, D_t, \text{TV}_T. ~258K raw → ~600 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_07_options
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 7 — Options (Chapters 20–22)
Formal spine. Black-Scholes and binomial option pricing, then real-options applications to corporate finance.
Chapter 20 — Financial Options. Definitions and structural results.

Call option: right (not obligation) to buy underlying at strike K on/before expiration T. Put option: right to sell at K. European = exercisable only at T; American = exercisable any time up to T.
Payoff at expiration: call = \max(S_T - K, 0); put = \max(K - S_T, 0).
Put-call parity (European, no dividends). For options with the same strike K and expiration T on the same non-dividend-paying stock:
C + \text{PV}(K) = P + S.
A long call plus a risk-free zero-coupon bond paying K at T has identical payoff to a long put plus the underlying stock. Proof: both portfolios have payoff \max(S_T, K) at expiration; by the Law of One Price (Ch. 3) their current prices must be equal. With dividends \text{Div} paid before expiration: C + \text{PV}(K) + \text{PV}(\text{Div}) = P + S.
Option-price bounds without a model. \max(S - \text{PV}(K), 0) \le C \le S; \max(\text{PV}(K) - S, 0) \le P \le \text{PV}(K); American calls on non-dividend-paying stocks always have the same value as European (early exercise is suboptimal); American puts can have positive early-exercise premium.

Chapter 21 — Option Valuation. Three pricing techniques, all derived from the Law of One Price.
(1) Binomial Option Pricing Model (Cox-Ross-Rubinstein 1979). In a single-period model, suppose the stock can move only to u\,S (up) or d\,S (down). Construct a replicating portfolio of \Delta shares of stock and B in risk-free bonds whose payoff matches the option’s payoff in both states:
\Delta\,u\,S + B(1+r_f) = C_u, \qquad \Delta\,d\,S + B(1+r_f) = C_d.
Solving:
\Delta = \frac{C_u - C_d}{(u-d)\,S}, \qquad B = \frac{u\,C_d - d\,C_u}{(u-d)(1+r_f)}.
By the Law of One Price, the option’s current price equals the cost of the replicating portfolio: C = \Delta\,S + B. Iterating backward through a multi-period binomial tree gives the price of any path-independent option, including American options (compare exercise vs continuation at each node).
(2) Black-Scholes Formula (Black-Scholes-Merton 1973). As the number of periods grows infinite (period length shrinks to zero) and the underlying becomes a continuous-time geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility \sigma, the binomial price converges to the Black-Scholes formula (Eq. 21.7) for a European call on a non-dividend-paying stock:
C = S\,N(d_1) - \text{PV}(K)\,N(d_2),
where \text{PV}(K) = K\,e^{-r_f\,T} is the PV of the strike at the continuously-compounded risk-free rate, N(\cdot) is the standard-normal cumulative distribution function, and
d_1 = \frac{\ln[S/\text{PV}(K)]}{\sigma\sqrt{T}} + \frac{\sigma\sqrt{T}}{2}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}.
The five inputs are S, K, T, r_f, \sigma. Crucially, the expected return on the stock does not appear — the formula does not require any view on the stock’s expected return. Berk-DeMarzo emphasise (citing the Scholes interview) that this is the key insight: by hedging away systematic risk via a replicating portfolio, the option’s price depends only on inputs that can be observed or estimated from market data.
For a European put: by put-call parity, P = \text{PV}(K)\,N(-d_2) - S\,N(-d_1). With dividends paid at constant yield q, replace S with S\,e^{-qT} throughout.
(3) Risk-neutral probabilities. Under the risk-neutral measure \mathbb{Q}, defined by setting the expected stock return equal to the risk-free rate, every asset’s price equals its risk-neutral expected discounted payoff:
C = e^{-r_f T}\,\mathbb{E}^\mathbb{Q}[\max(S_T - K, 0)].
In the binomial model, the risk-neutral up-probability is \rho = \frac{(1+r_f) - d}{u - d}. The risk-neutral approach is equivalent to the replicating-portfolio approach by construction; it is often computationally simpler.
Beta of an option. The option’s beta is the share-equivalent beta of its replicating portfolio: \beta_{\text{option}} = \frac{\Delta\,S}{\Delta\,S + B}\,\beta_S — call options have higher beta than the underlying stock (because B<0 for calls); put options have negative beta. Application: estimating the beta of risky debt by treating debt as a portfolio of risk-free debt minus a put on firm assets (Merton 1974 structural credit model).
Chapter 22 — Real Options. Applying option pricing to capital budgeting decisions.

Option to delay (timing option). When a project’s NPV is volatile and the investment is irreversible, waiting has positive value because the firm preserves the option to abandon if conditions deteriorate. Standard NPV undervalues such projects by ignoring the timing option.
Option to expand (growth option). A staged-investment project includes embedded calls on follow-on opportunities. R&D and venture-capital investments are largely valued for their growth options.
Option to abandon (put option on firm continuation). Salvage values represent puts on the project; ability to abandon caps downside.
Decision trees and binomial real-options valuation. The book illustrates with binomial trees (rather than Black-Scholes) because real-option payoffs are typically discrete and project-specific.

Why this Part matters. Black-Scholes-Merton is the textbook’s clearest demonstration that the Law of One Price applied with continuous-time replication can price an enormous family of derivative claims without any utility-theoretic input. The same machinery underlies every derivatives-pricing model in practitioner use, the structural credit-risk models (Merton 1974, KMV), the executive-compensation literature on stock options, and corporate-finance applications to capital structure (the equity of a leveraged firm is a call option on firm assets — Merton 1974). The 1997 Nobel Prize for Scholes and Merton (Black having died in 1995) is the canonical example of formal financial-economics theory altering practitioner reality. Limitations: constant volatility, no jumps, frictionless trading, lognormal returns — assumptions that fail in stress periods (e.g. LTCM 1998, GFC 2008) and that the LTCM case study in Roger Lowenstein - When Genius Failed dramatises.
Notation: S, K, T, r_f, \sigma, C, P, N(\cdot), d_1, d_2, \Delta, B, u, d, \rho, q. ~298K raw → ~880 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_08_long_term_financing
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 8 — Long-Term Financing (Chapters 23–25)
Formal spine. Institutional mechanics of equity, debt, and lease financing.
Chapter 23 — Raising Equity Capital. The lifecycle of a firm’s equity from sole-proprietorship founding to public listing.

Sources of private equity. Angel investors, venture-capital limited partnerships (institutional LPs commit capital; GPs invest and earn 2-and-20 typical fee structure, with “carry” = ≈20% of fund profits above a hurdle rate), private-equity buyout funds, sovereign-wealth funds, corporate venture arms.
Pre-money / post-money valuation. \text{Post-money} = \text{Pre-money} + \text{New Investment}. Each new round dilutes prior holders unless they participate pro-rata.
IPO mechanics. Best-efforts vs firm-commitment underwriting; book-building vs Dutch auction (Google 2004 cited); stages — file S-1, road show, price the offering, lock-up period, secondary-market trading. Empirically: first-day underpricing averages ≈15% (1990s ≈21%, 2000s lower), creating money-on-the-table for issuers; Berk-DeMarzo discuss the winner’s-curse and information-extraction explanations.
SEOs (seasoned equity offerings). Cash offerings vs rights issues; announcement effects — equity issuance announcements cause average price drops of 1.5–3% (consistent with Myers-Majluf 1984 adverse-selection signal).
Costs of public listing. Direct (underwriter spread ≈7% for IPOs in U.S., legal/accounting/printing); indirect (underpricing, regulatory burden); ongoing (Sarbanes-Oxley compliance, disclosure).

Chapter 24 — Debt Financing. Debt instruments and indenture structure.

Types of debt. Bank loans (term loans, revolvers, syndicated facilities); commercial paper (short-term, unsecured, large-corporate, money-market funded); corporate bonds (notes ≤ 10y, debentures > 10y, mortgage bonds, asset-backed); convertible bonds (debt + embedded equity option, valued via Ch. 21 techniques); sovereign and municipal debt.
Bond features. Coupon rate, maturity, call provisions (issuer option to retire early at predetermined price — a short put the bondholder writes), sinking-fund provisions, convertibility, put provisions.
Bond covenants. Affirmative (maintain financial ratios, deliver financials), negative (restrict dividends, additional borrowing, asset sales), event-driven (change-of-control puts). Covenants are contractual responses to the agency-cost-of-debt problems identified in Ch. 16.
Credit ratings. S&P (AAA → D), Moody’s (Aaa → C); investment-grade (BBB-/Baa3 and above) vs high-yield (“junk”). Yield = risk-free + credit spread; credit spreads widen sharply in recessions (Merton 1974 structural model and Black-Scholes-derived intuition).
Convertible bonds priced via Ch. 21 binomial tree on the underlying stock plus the bond’s coupon/principal claims — combining Parts 6 and 7.

Chapter 25 — Leasing. When and why firms lease rather than buy.

Operating lease vs capital (finance) lease. Accounting and tax distinctions affect the lease-vs-buy NPV calculation; ASC 842 / IFRS 16 reforms (2019) require most operating leases to be capitalised on-balance-sheet.
Lease-vs-buy NPV. Compare PV of after-tax lease payments (using r_D(1-\tau_C)) against PV of buying (purchase cost minus PV of depreciation tax shield minus PV of after-tax salvage value). The correct discount rate for after-tax lease payments is the after-tax cost of debt because lease obligations are debt-like fixed claims.
Why lease in real markets (frictions absent in MM-style perfect-markets analysis): differential tax brackets between lessor and lessee (low-tax-bracket firm leases from high-tax-bracket firm to share the depreciation tax shield), asset-specificity / agency considerations, off-balance-sheet financing (now reduced by ASC 842), and lessor specialisation in residual-value risk.

Why this Part matters. Where Parts 5–6 supplied the theory of capital structure, Part 8 supplies the institutional menu — the actual instruments, intermediaries, and rules a CFO chooses among. The reader who connects this Part to Part 5 sees that issuance costs (Ch. 23), call provisions (Ch. 24), and lease-vs-buy choices (Ch. 25) are all responses to the four families of capital-market frictions (taxes, distress, agency, information) — i.e. the menu makes sense only as the equilibrium artefact of the frictions Part 5 names.
Notation: Pre-money, post-money, dilution, IPO underpricing, S-1, SEO, covenant taxonomy. ~296K raw → ~530 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_09_short_term_financing
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 9 — Short-Term Financing (Chapters 26–27)
Formal spine. Working-capital optimisation and short-term cash management — how the firm finances its operating cycle.
Chapter 26 — Working Capital Management. The cash conversion cycle:
\text{CCC} = \text{Days Inventory} + \text{Days Receivables} - \text{Days Payables} = \text{DIO} + \text{DSO} - \text{DPO}
is the average number of days between cash outflow on inventory/payables and cash inflow from collections. A firm with \text{CCC}>0 has a funding gap it must finance with short-term debt or equity; a firm with \text{CCC}<0 (e.g. Amazon historically, supermarket chains) is financed by suppliers.

Receivables management. Credit-policy choice (which customers, what terms — e.g. “2/10, net 30” implying 2% discount for payment within 10 days else net at 30); aging schedules; collection vs default-loss tradeoff. The implicit cost of foregoing the 2/10 discount: (1.02041)^{18.25} - 1 \approx 44.6\% APR, so customers should typically take the discount.
Payables management. Stretching payables shrinks CCC but damages supplier relationships and may forfeit early-payment discounts; the value is \le the cost of equivalent short-term debt financing.
Inventory management. Carrying costs (storage, insurance, obsolescence) vs stockout costs; just-in-time vs safety stock; EOQ formula Q^* = \sqrt{2DS/H} with D = annual demand, S = order cost, H = holding cost per unit per year.
Cash management. Optimal cash balance trades off transaction cost of converting between cash and securities against opportunity cost of foregone interest (Baumol-Tobin / Miller-Orr models).

Chapter 27 — Short-Term Financial Planning. The 12-month rolling cash forecast.

Cash-budget construction. Project monthly receipts, disbursements, beginning/ending cash balance for each forecast month under base, optimistic, pessimistic scenarios.
Short-term financing choices. Bank lines of credit (committed vs uncommitted; revolving vs non-revolving); commercial paper (large public firms only; backed by line-of-credit commitment as fallback); accounts-receivable factoring (selling receivables to a factor at discount, transferring credit risk); inventory financing (warehouse receipts, floor planning); banker’s acceptances (international trade).
Matching principle. Permanent working-capital needs financed long-term; seasonal / cyclical needs financed short-term. Mismatching produces refinancing risk (e.g. Bear Stearns 2008: short-term repo financing of long-term illiquid assets).
Term-structure considerations. Short-term debt is typically cheaper than long-term, but exposes the firm to refinancing risk and rate-rise risk; CFO’s tradeoff is liquidity insurance vs cost.

Why this Part matters. Treasury and CFO offices spend most of their day-to-day attention on short-term financing — credit lines, cash forecasting, receivables aging, supplier-payment timing — yet the standard MBA finance curriculum subordinates this material to capital-structure theory. The book’s compact treatment is sufficient for any operating role; the 2008 short-term-funding crisis (Lehman, Bear Stearns, money-market-fund “breaking the buck”) is the salient example of how short-term-financing failure can take down systemically important institutions, making this Part more important post-GFC than its page-budget suggests.
Notation: CCC, DIO, DSO, DPO, EOQ, Q^*, line-of-credit, factoring. ~133K raw → ~370 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: ch_part_10_special_topics
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Part 10 — Special Topics (Chapters 28–31)
Formal spine. Mergers & Acquisitions, Corporate Governance, Risk Management, International Corporate Finance.
Chapter 28 — Mergers and Acquisitions. Markets for corporate control.

Stylised facts. M&A waves cluster (1960s conglomerate; 1980s LBO/hostile-takeover; 1990s strategic; 2000s leveraged-buyouts; 2010s tech consolidation). The textbook reports merger-wave statistics and largest historical deals.
Sources of synergy. Economies of scale or scope; vertical integration; expertise transfer; market-power gain (often blocked on antitrust grounds); efficiency gains from replacing under-performing management; tax shield expansion from increased leverage capacity; risk-reduction (questioned — shareholders can diversify themselves).
Valuation of merger gains. \Delta V = V_{T+A} - (V_T + V_A) = net synergy value. Premium paid: P_T - V_T \le \Delta V for shareholder-value-creating deals from acquirer perspective.
Method of payment. Cash (taxable to target shareholders, signals confidence); stock (non-taxable rollover; signals overvaluation per Myers-Majluf); mixed.
Takeover defenses. Poison pills (shareholder rights plans); staggered boards; supermajority voting; white-knight defenses; Pac-Man defense; golden parachutes. Each defense affects the bidding-game equilibrium and target-shareholder welfare.
Free-rider problem (Grossman-Hart 1980). A diffuse target shareholder optimally tenders only at full post-merger value, leaving no surplus for the bidder; this rationalises bidder toehold purchases and two-tier offers.

Chapter 29 — Corporate Governance. Mechanisms aligning manager and shareholder incentives.

Agency conflicts. Manager–shareholder, controlling–minority shareholder, debtholder–equityholder.
Board structure. Independent directors; audit/compensation/nominating committees; CEO-chairman separation.
Compensation design. Equity-based (options, restricted stock, performance shares); the textbook uses Black-Scholes (Ch. 21) to value executive options. Backdating scandals (2005–2007) discussed.
Regulatory regime. Sarbanes-Oxley 2002 (CEO/CFO certifications, internal-control reporting, audit-firm independence), Dodd-Frank 2010 (say-on-pay, clawbacks).
International governance differences. Anglo-American shareholder primacy vs Continental-European stakeholder model vs Japanese keiretsu / German two-tier-board system; family-controlled firms predominate outside the U.S./U.K.

Chapter 30 — Risk Management. When and how firms hedge.

MM under hedging. In perfect capital markets, hedging is irrelevant — investors can hedge their own portfolio exposures. Reasons hedging adds value: reducing expected distress costs (Ch. 16), preserving internal funds for positive-NPV investment when external finance is costly (pecking order / Myers-Majluf), tax-convexity benefits (when expected-tax-liability function is convex in pre-tax income, hedging that income reduces expected taxes), management-incentive considerations.
Insurance pricing. Premium = expected loss + administrative cost + cost of capital + adverse-selection premium + moral-hazard premium. Firms self-insure when transaction costs / informational frictions exceed actuarial benefits.
Commodity hedging via futures and forwards. Long hedge (buy futures to lock in input cost), short hedge (sell futures to lock in output price). Basis risk when the hedge instrument’s underlying differs from the firm’s exposure.
Interest-rate hedging. Rate swaps to convert floating-rate debt to fixed (or vice versa); duration matching for asset-liability management; the textbook discusses Metallgesellschaft (1993) as a cautionary case.
Currency hedging. FX forwards, options, swaps; transactional vs translational vs economic FX exposure.

Chapter 31 — International Corporate Finance. Multi-currency capital budgeting.

Internationally integrated capital markets. Under perfect-capital-markets assumption (Ch. 14, extended cross-currency), the value of a project is the same when computed in either currency. Two valuation methods:

Foreign currency NPV: project FCF in foreign currency, discounted at foreign-currency cost of capital, then converted at spot.
Domestic currency NPV: convert each foreign FCF to domestic via forward rates (covered interest parity), then discount at domestic cost of capital.


Covered interest rate parity. F = S \times \frac{1+r_d}{1+r_f} where S is spot, F is forward, r_d and r_f are domestic and foreign risk-free rates. Deviations are arbitrage opportunities.
Internationally segmented markets. When capital controls or differential taxation prevent integration, the WACC and discount rate must reflect the firm’s actual investor base — domestic-only investors price local-currency-denominated assets, requiring localised cost-of-capital estimation.
Country risk. Sovereign default risk, expropriation risk, exchange controls; built into cost-of-capital via country risk premium spreads or via explicit cash-flow scenario analysis.

Why this Part matters. Mergers and corporate governance are the applied face of agency-cost theory (Ch. 16); risk management is the applied face of capital-structure friction theory (Ch. 16, Ch. 18); international corporate finance is the multi-currency generalisation of every prior valuation result. The reader who has internalised Parts 1–7 can derive most of this Part as application; the reader who tries to learn corporate finance starting from Chapter 28 will lack the conceptual scaffolding the textbook builds across the prior 27 chapters.
Notation: \Delta V, premium, synergy, S, F, r_d, r_f (covered interest parity), basis risk, duration, convexity (taxes). ~397K raw → ~720 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.title: Jonathan Berk Corporate Finance — Chapter Deep Dives
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/jonath.content:
Jonathan Berk Corporate Finance — Chapter Deep Dives
11 chapters

Ch.0 — Front Matter — Preface, Authors, Pedagogical Architecture
Jonathan Berk holds the A.P. Giannini Professor of Finance at Stanford GSB (formerly Berkeley Haas, formerly UBC).
Ch. — Part 3 — Valuing Projects and Firms (Chapters 7–9)
Translates NPV into the capital-budgeting and equity-valuation settings.
Ch. — Part 5 — Capital Structure (Chapters 14–17)
The Modigliani-Miller theorems and their progressive enrichment as frictions are introduced.
Ch. — Part 1 — Introduction (Chapters 1–3)
The textbook opens by defining the corporation as a legal person separable from its owners (Dartmouth College v.
Ch. — Part 8 — Long-Term Financing (Chapters 23–25)
Institutional mechanics of equity, debt, and lease financing.
Ch. — Part 7 — Options (Chapters 20–22)
Black-Scholes and binomial option pricing, then real-options applications to corporate finance.
Ch. — Part 9 — Short-Term Financing (Chapters 26–27)
Working-capital optimisation and short-term cash management — how the firm finances its operating cycle.
Ch. — Part 2 — Time, Money, and Interest Rates (Chapters 4–6)
This Part operationalises the Law of One Price by giving the reader the time-value-of-money machinery that turns “present value of a stream of cash flows” from slogan into computable formula.
Ch. — Part 4 — Risk and Return (Chapters 10–13)
Builds the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) as the textbook’s primary tool for choosing the discount rate r_E that Part 3 left exogenous, then tests the model against empirical anomalies in Ch. 13.
Ch. — Part 10 — Special Topics (Chapters 28–31)
Mergers & Acquisitions, Corporate Governance, Risk Management, International Corporate Finance.
Ch. — Part 6 — Advanced Valuation (Chapters 18–19)
Three internally consistent methods for valuing a levered investment, plus a synthesis case study.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_01_failures
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 1 — The Failures of Globalization
The trade-policy core of the GAID Revisited additions. Stiglitz separates the case for globalization (Smith / Ricardo / Samuelson — overall national income rises with comparative-advantage trade) from the case-as-actually-implemented (politicians told the “white lie” that “trade creates jobs”; in fact trade-policy is jobs-neutral when monetary/fiscal policy work, but if they don’t work, trade policy can destroy more jobs than it creates).
Key analytical move: the trade balance is macroeconomic, not trade-policy-determined. Trade balance ≡ savings-investment balance. The US runs a trade deficit because it under-saves; tariffs against China don’t change the deficit, just shift it to Vietnam or Bangladesh. This is presented as elementary economics that Trump has not grasped.
Five mechanisms by which standard models fail:

Sometimes job destruction outpaces job creation (especially after 2008 with high unemployment).
Increased risk: globalization exposes firms and individuals to tail risks they cannot insure (oil price, exchange rate, German dependence on Russian gas as analytical exhibit).
Imperfect competition: Walmart, with market power, can drive small producers out across countries.
Dynamic comparative advantage: shifting production to China meant China learned and the US lost technological capacity (“learning by doing”; spillovers; clusters).
Exchange-rate effects: dollar overvaluation (driven by Reagan-era deficits + flight-to-safety) made US manufacturing uncompetitive regardless of any country’s “manipulation.”

Stolper-Samuelson: with free trade and well-functioning markets, unskilled workers across countries converge to the same wage; in advanced countries, this means unskilled wages fall. This was never highlighted by globalization advocates — willful deception, ignorance, or naive belief in trickle-down economics?
Bargaining power: corporations gained credible threat to relocate factories abroad → workers had to accept lower wages → unions weakened → political voice for labor shrank → vicious downward spiral.
Managed trade, not free trade: TPP ran 6,000+ pages. A true free-trade agreement would be a few pages. The complexity exists because trade agreements are special-interest accommodations, not free-trade implementations.
Technology vs. globalization: 65-80% of manufacturing job losses are from technology, not trade. But citizens can do something about trade (vote for protectionists), so they focus on trade. Thought experiment: with no tech change but full globalization, unskilled wages would still plummet — confirming the trade contribution is real even if not majority.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_02_dimensions
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 2 — The Multiple Dimensions of Globalization
Beyond trade in goods: globalization also encompasses cross-border investment, finance, ideas (intellectual property), and people. Stiglitz argues that each of these has been mismanaged in parallel ways — each shows the same pattern of corporate-driven rules, asymmetric distribution of gains, and underweighting of distributional consequences.
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI): in principle benign (firms with comparative advantage operate cross-border), but Trump’s threat-via-tweet to specific firms is a rule-of-law violation. Spillovers can justify FDI promotion in regions with high unemployment. But forcing US firms to invest domestically gives foreign firms an advantage and undermines US headquarters location.
Short-term capital flows: the central villain. Hot money enters during booms (appreciating exchange rate, hurting exporters), exits during stress (crashing exchange rate, triggering crisis). Cannot finance long-term factory investment. Externalities not priced — speculators bear no cost for crisis they trigger. The 1997-98 East Asia crisis is the empirical exhibit. Recipients are “almost guaranteed to be worse off.”
Short-termism: short-term capital flows induce CEO short-termism (compensation tied to current stock price → dividends and buybacks over investment). Macro consequence: slowing economic growth post-1980. Mismatch with actual long-term needs (long-term savings exist via pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, but intermediation is short-term-biased).
Investment agreements (ISDS): bilateral investment treaties and trade-agreement chapters give foreign firms the right to sue governments for regulations that reduce profits, in private arbitration where the firm appoints judges. Philip Morris vs. Uruguay (2010): tobacco-warning regulations triggered a $7M-cost arbitration; Uruguay won (helped by Bloomberg’s financing) but the chilling effect on regulation is the point. Canada lost multiple NAFTA Ch. 11 cases. Foreign firms thus get better property protection than domestic firms.
Fiscal paradises and tax competition: globalization enables corporate tax avoidance. Apple’s 0.005% Irish rate revealed in 2013 European hearings is the canonical exhibit. LuxLeaks (Ireland, Luxembourg) and Panama Papers exposed scope. Outcome: tax burden shifts to immobile factors (unskilled workers — who suffer triple from lower wages, higher relative tax, and loss of services as government revenue erodes).
Intellectual Property (TRIPS, TPP IP provisions): drafted by USTR in consultation with US drug and entertainment companies. Myriad Genetics BRCA breast-cancer-gene patent: blocked Yale’s free alternative test for years until ACLU-led suit reached Supreme Court (naturally existing genes cannot be patented). IP rules embedded in trade agreements give advanced-country governments enforcement teeth (trade sanctions). $20B+ flows annually from low/middle-income countries to US in IP royalties — comparable to total US development aid.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_03_new_protectionism
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 3 — The New Protectionism
Trump’s tariff agenda is the wrong response to the New Discontents — even from the perspective of those it claims to help.
Manufacturing won’t come back: global manufacturing employment is declining due to productivity growth exceeding demand growth, regardless of trade policy. Even if production returns to the US, it will use robots, not the displaced workers. Manufacturing is now 8% of US employment, services 80%. The fixation on manufacturing is “a country with a mind-set stuck in a world gone by” — coal mining now employs fewer than the solar industry.
Global power has dispersed: post-WWII unipolar moment is gone. China, India, the BRICS exceed advanced-country shares of historical norm. Returning to a world where the US writes globalization’s rules unilaterally is impossible. The “America First” stance accelerates the loss of US soft power.
Why Trump’s specific tools fail:

45% tariff on China would raise Walmart prices 45% on the first round; in the second round US imports shift to Vietnam, Bangladesh; no jobs return.
Macro identity binding: trade deficit = (savings - investment). Tariffs can shift bilateral imbalances but cannot change overall deficit. Trump’s tax cuts and infrastructure spending (reducing savings) will worsen the deficit.
Standards of living go down (importing from second-cheapest sources, not cheapest).
Triggers higher inflation → Fed raises rates → stronger dollar → wider trade deficit.
Rule-of-law violations (intimidating specific firms) damage US institutional credibility.

Trade war prospects: WTO dispute mechanism allows reciprocal duties; Smoot-Hawley 1930 is the warning. Even if Republican Congress restrains him, “Trump’s bark may be worse than his bite.”
Two centuries of historical anomaly: in 1820 China + India had 45% of global GDP; colonialism reduced that share to under 10% during the period when “the West began writing the rules of the game.” The current rebalancing is the inevitable correction of the anomaly, not a “rigging” of US trade deals.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_04_can_be_saved
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 4 — Can Globalization Be Saved? An Agenda for Equitable Globalization with Shared Prosperity
The prescriptive chapter. The right question is not whether to globalize but what rules govern globalization, set by whom, on whose behalf.
The underlying problem is global governance: interdependence without global government produces “global governance without global government.” Decision-making is dominated by finance ministries → multinationals’ interests → the rules are biased.
Ten principles of reformed globalization:

Globalization is a means to an end (higher living standards), not an end in itself.
Global rules are needed where there are cross-border externalities (focus there, not on regulatory harmonization).
Global action becomes more important as interdependence grows (climate, pandemics).
Governance matters: representativeness, legitimacy, transparency, accountability.
Government and civil society must both regulate globalization (private sector alone produces inequality, environmental degradation, instability).
Large economies (US, China, EU) must consider externalities they impose on small economies (US QE → emerging-market volatility).
One-size-fits-all doesn’t work; developing countries differ from developed.
Any rule change has winners and losers; assistance to losers is essential, not optional.
Social dimensions (cultural, public health) matter beyond pure economics.
Reforms must be evaluated using realistic models (with imperfect information, market failures), not idealized perfect-competition models.

Domestic agenda:

Reduce inequality in market income (curb monopoly power, strengthen unions, restore corporate-governance accountability).
Reform financial sector to lend to SMEs, not to extract via predatory practices.
Progressive taxation (capital taxed at same rate as labor); strengthen earned-income tax credit; close tax loopholes; ensure firms pay fair share.
Help economic restructuring (manufacturing → services transition).
Active macroeconomic policy aimed at full employment (the strongest anti-inequality tool).

Why Scandinavia is the operative model: small countries that had to be open; designed inclusive policies because they understood market forces produce winners and losers; achieved “social protection without protectionism.”
Why the politics is hard: existing political coalitions reflect existing distributive arrangements; the corporate-financial elite that benefited from current globalization will resist reform. The center-left was “cognitively captured by the arguments for benefits of globalization” and only gradually (Bernie Sanders 2016, eventually Hillary Clinton on TPP) is shifting.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_05_promise_global_institutions
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 5 — The Promise of Global Institutions
The institutional-history foundation chapter. Bretton Woods (July 1944): IMF (global stability) + World Bank (originally International Bank for Reconstruction and Development; “Development” added almost as an afterthought). Both founded on Keynesian premise that markets often fail and collective action at the global level is necessary. The proposed third Bretton Woods institution (international trade) only emerged as the WTO in 1995.
The 1980s ideological shift: under Reagan-Thatcher, the IMF and World Bank became “missionary institutions” pushing market-fundamentalist ideas onto developing countries. Inside the World Bank, an early-1980s purge: Ann Krueger replaced Hollis Chenery as chief economist. Chenery’s team focused on market failures and government’s role; Krueger’s frame was government-as-problem and free-markets-as-solution. Many first-rate economists left.
Mission drift / mission overreach: the IMF’s mandate was macroeconomic crisis response. Through structural-adjustment lending and conditionality, it took on “almost any structural issue” (financial markets, labor markets, trade policy, pension privatization). When the World Bank produced controversial recommendations, the IMF stepped into the vacuum.
Governance critique:

Heads of IMF (always European) and World Bank (always American) chosen behind closed doors.
IMF voting based on 1944 economic weights with minor adjustments; US has only single-country veto.
“Speaks for each country” matters: at the IMF, finance ministers and central bank governors speak — closely tied to the financial sector. Robert Rubin (Goldman → Treasury → Citigroup), Stan Fischer (IMF → Citigroup) are the canonical career paths.
WTO: trade ministers represent business interests; environmental and labor concerns are obstacles, not constituencies.
Decision-making behind closed doors with no developing-country veto = “taxation without representation.”

The Washington Consensus emerges: a “consensus between IMF, World Bank, and US Treasury about the ‘right’ policies for developing countries.” Originally a response to Latin American hyperinflation and budget deficits, generalized to a one-size-fits-all package.
Capital controls and sequencing: European countries banned free capital flows until the 1970s; the IMF demanded developing countries open immediately. The “small boats on rough seas” metaphor: liberalization without institutional infrastructure invites capsizing.
The fundamental indictment: by the late 1990s, “close to 100 countries had faced crises” (the Fund’s mission was preventing crises). “Every major emerging market that liberalized its capital market has had at least one crisis.” Yet the IMF kept pushing the same prescription.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_06_broken_promises
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 6 — Broken Promises
First-person reportage from Stiglitz’s first months at the World Bank (he started February 13, 1997). Compresses the contrast between the Bank’s culture (motto: “Our dream is a world without poverty”; staff in-country) and the IMF’s culture (5-star hotels, 3-week missions, Washington-dictated programs).
The Ethiopia case (March 1997): prime minister Meles Zenawi had won a 17-year guerrilla war and was rebuilding the country. Per capita income $110/year. Macroeconomic results outstanding: no inflation, prices falling, growth steady. Yet the IMF had suspended its lending program. Two disputes:

Whether foreign aid should be counted as budget revenue. The IMF said no (aid is “unstable”); Stiglitz had his staff verify that aid was more stable than tax revenues. The IMF position was “absurd implications” — implying no aid-receiving country could spend on what aid was given for.
Whether Ethiopia could prepay an existing US bank loan without IMF approval. The repayment made financial sense (Ethiopia paid more on the loan than it earned on its reserves), but the IMF objected to the procedure — Ethiopia had not asked permission. To the IMF this was “standard operating procedure”; to Ethiopia it was “a new form of colonialism.”

A third dispute: financial-market liberalization in Ethiopia. Ethiopia’s entire banking system was smaller than Bethesda, Maryland’s. The IMF wanted Ethiopia to open to foreign banks and split its largest domestic bank. Ethiopia knew Kenya had followed similar advice and suffered 14 banking failures in 1993-94. Ethiopia resisted; the IMF suspended its program.
Stiglitz’s “intellectual lobbying” restored Ethiopian World Bank lending; he coordinated with administration officials to put pressure on the IMF. Lessons drawn:

The IMF prioritizes process over substance.
The IMF treats itself as the “monopoly supplier of sound advice.”
Behind-closed-doors decision-making invites suspicion of power-politics motivations.
The IMF has limited country-specific knowledge but applies one-size-fits-all anyway.
Standard macroeconomic models (assuming full employment, no involuntary unemployment) are particularly inappropriate for developing countries.

The deeper indictment: when an IMF-friendly model says there’s no involuntary unemployment, observed unemployment must be greedy unions or politicians. Policy prescription: cut wages. This is a logically consistent position from a wrong model.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_07_freedom_to_choose
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 7 — Freedom to Choose?
The systematic case against Washington Consensus prescriptions, organized by pillar.
Privatization: in principle, governments should not run steel mills (with exceptions like Korean and Taiwanese state mills). But the IMF pushed speed over quality. Three failure modes:

Markets don’t immediately fill the gap. Morocco chicken-raising: government stopped distributing newborn chicks per IMF advice; private supplier appeared but wouldn’t guarantee survival rates; the women’s industry collapsed. Markets emerge slowly, often badly.
Privatization without regulation creates monopolies. Côte d’Ivoire telephone privatization: French firm got monopoly including new cellular services; raised prices so high students couldn’t afford internet.
“Briberization”: privatization without good governance becomes asset transfer to insiders. Russia’s loans-for-shares (1995-96) is the canonical case — oligarchs captured natural-resource assets at fractional prices.

The deeper insight: government activities often arise because markets failed (Fannie Mae for mortgages; social-security annuities). Eliminating the government provider does not summon a market.
Liberalization: trade liberalization is the most-supported pillar but requires sequencing. Job destruction outpaces creation in the short run, especially with high IMF-imposed interest rates; East Asian success was slow, sequenced trade opening with industrial policy and capital availability. China’s gradualism: dismantling trade barriers 20 years after starting reform, by which point growth was robust.
Hypocrisy: Western countries pushed liberalization on developing countries while keeping their own agricultural subsidies and textile barriers. Bolivia eradicated coca production but the US kept its sugar markets closed; one World Bank calculation showed Sub-Saharan Africa’s income fell 2% due to the Uruguay Round. Treaty of Tientsin (1858) is invoked as the historical precedent — “almost diabolical approach to a balance of trade.”
Capital-market liberalization: the worst pillar. Hot money cannot finance long-term investment; capital flows are pro-cyclical (out during recessions); developing countries must hold reserves equal to short-term foreign loans to manage risk → effectively borrowing at 18% from US banks while lending to US Treasury at 4%. China’s success without capital-account opening is the empirical refutation of the IMF’s “diversification” argument.
The 1999 Zhu Rongji visit: US Treasury insisted on faster Chinese financial-market liberalization despite State Department and USTR opposition. China couldn’t accept (East Asia 1997 was fresh); negotiations failed; reformers in China were temporarily discredited. Wall Street’s special interest in early access trumped both US national interest and global stability.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_08_east_asia_crisis
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 8 — The East Asia Crisis: How IMF Policies Brought the World to the Verge of a Global Meltdown
The empirical anchor of GAID. Thai baht collapse July 2, 1997 (down ~25% overnight from 25/$ rate), spread to Malaysia, Korea, Philippines, Indonesia. By 1998 Indonesian GDP fell 13.1%, Korean 6.7%, Thai 10.8%. Korean urban poverty tripled; Indonesian poverty doubled; tenfold unemployment increase in Indonesia.
Stiglitz’s central diagnosis: capital-account liberalization was “the single most important factor leading to the crisis.” The IMF and Treasury had pushed it on East Asia in the late 1980s and early 1990s despite the region having no need for additional capital (high savings rates).
Two crisis patterns:

Korea: solid 30-year track record (per-capita income up 8x); chaebol borrowed abroad under US pressure. Late 1997 Wall Street rumors → banks refused to roll over short-term debt → self-fulfilling crisis.
Thailand: speculative attack on the baht. Speculator borrows 24B baht, converts at 24/to1B; week later, exchange rate is 40/, 600M repays the loan, $400M is profit. Bank-run dynamics on currency.

IMF response: $95B bailouts (with G-7 contributions); conditions included higher interest rates, fiscal contraction, and “structural reforms” (some unrelated to crisis — abolishing Indonesia’s clove monopoly).
Why the response failed:

Misdiagnosis: IMF treated East Asia like Latin America (excess demand, fiscal profligacy, hyperinflation). East Asia had surpluses, low inflation, high corporate debt. The right response to insufficient demand is stimulus; the IMF prescribed contraction.
High interest rates with high corporate debt = mass bankruptcy.
Hooverite austerity: budget contraction during recession is what Hoover did 1930-32. Stanley Fischer (IMF Deputy Managing Director) defended balanced budgets in a 1997 Financial Times op-ed; Stiglitz objected on the same grounds the Council of Economic Advisers used against the US balanced-budget amendment.
Beggar-thyself policies: contraction inflicted on the country to rebuild reserves. Identical contagion effect on neighbors as classical beggar-thy-neighbor, but worse — the country also weakens itself.
Crisis management exacerbated capital flight: IMF criticism of country fundamentals made investors flee faster.

Asian Monetary Fund killed: Japan offered $100B in 1997 to help create an alternative regional fund. Korea and other crisis countries supported it. US Treasury and IMF blocked it (didn’t want regulatory competition; AMF would have been Japan- and China-led). Stiglitz: “still resented in Asia”; eventually morphed into the more modest Chiang Mai Initiative.
Korea’s earlier path: 1993 trade negotiations included pressure for financial-market liberalization. Stiglitz at CEA argued for prioritization: was forcing Korean liberalization in US national interest? Lawrence Summers at Treasury blocked the question. Robert Rubin’s NEC declined to take it to the president. Special-interest finance trumped national-interest analysis.
Malaysia exception: Mahathir imposed capital controls in 1998 against IMF advice. Malaysia’s downturn was “shorter and shallower than that of any of the other countries.” Empirical refutation of IMF orthodoxy.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_09_who_lost_russia
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 9 — Who Lost Russia?
The most damning narrative chapter. Russia’s transition from communism to a market economy was the second-largest economic experiment of the 20th century (after the 1917 Revolution itself). It failed catastrophically.
The numbers: Russian GDP fell 45% from 1990 to 1998 — a deeper contraction than the Soviet Union experienced 1940-46 in WWII (when industrial production fell 24%). Investment essentially stopped. Life expectancy fell 3+ years. Moldovan GDP fell 67%, Ukrainian by 67%. Most former-communist countries except Poland, Hungary, Slovenia, Slovakia had GDPs below 1989 levels a decade later.
Shock therapy vs. gradualism: the central debate. Shock-therapists (US Treasury, IMF) won. Gradualists (Stiglitz, others) warned that:

Privatizing without regulation → monopolies / asset stripping.
Liberalizing prices without distribution infrastructure → hyperinflation that wipes out savings.
Opening capital account before institutional infrastructure → flight of newly-privatized assets to Cypriot and Swiss accounts.

All three predictions were borne out.
The Chinese counterexample: gradualist sequencing produced double-digit growth and 800M people moving out of poverty. China’s 1990 GDP was 60% of Russia’s; by 2000 it was 60% larger.
Privatization as asset stripping: with high interest rates and minimal financial infrastructure, new owners couldn’t restructure productively. Rational response: sell the assets, wire the money out. The 1995-96 loans-for-shares scheme (organized by Anatoly Chubais — later hosted at Lawrence Summers’s home, signaling US support; ch. 10) was Russia’s defining act of looting.
The 1998 crisis: ruble had been overvalued (Russia flooded with imports, domestic production crushed). Oil prices fell 40% (early 1998) due to East Asia recession. Russian government had borrowed heavily; oligarchs had received state assets but paid little tax. By June 1998 ruble interest rates hit 60%, then 150%; dollar-denominated Russian debt yielded 50%.
The IMF rescue: 11.2B IMF loan on July 20, 1998 (part of 22.6B package). World Bank pressured to add 6B but compromised at 300M tranches. Stiglitz argued internally that Russia was either resource-rich enough to manage without help, or too corrupt to use it productively — either way, the case against more lending was strong.
Three weeks later: August 17, 1998, Russia announced unilateral suspension of payments and ruble devaluation. Money was already in Cypriot/Swiss accounts. Stiglitz: “When the IMF was confronted with the facts — the billions of dollars that it had given (loaned) Russia were showing up in Cypriot and Swiss bank accounts just days after the loan was made — it claimed that these weren’t their dollars.” (Some quipped the IMF should have wired the money directly to Switzerland.)
Global contagion: triggered Brazil currency crisis, Long Term Capital Management collapse (Fed-engineered private bailout), Latin American emerging-market shocks.
The silver lining: the devaluation finally allowed Russia’s import-competing sectors to grow. The first sustained Russian recovery began because the IMF rescue failed.
Underlying lesson: shock-therapists “studiously ignored the advice of Russian scholars… a simple reason: they believed that the market revolution which was about to occur made all of the knowledge available from these other disciplines irrelevant.” Market fundamentalism as a religion replacing Marxism as a religion.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_10_unfair_fair_trade
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 10 — Unfair Fair Trade Laws and Other Mischief
Politically-charged chapter on the IMF’s role as a “political institution” advancing US Treasury and Wall Street interests, illustrated through case studies.
Russia / political context: the 1998 bailout was “dictated by a concern to maintain Boris Yeltsin in power.” Treasury supported (or quietly tolerated) the loans-for-shares privatization corruption because it served the political goal of getting Yeltsin reelected. Strobe Talbott’s 1993 worry — “had there been too much shock and too little therapy?” — captured early administration unease that Treasury suppressed.
The Aluminum Cartel (1994): the cleanest illustration of how anti-trust principles are abandoned when convenient. Paul O’Neill (Alcoa CEO; later G.W. Bush Treasury Secretary) proposed a global aluminum cartel to raise prices after the 1994 price collapse. Alternative: file dumping charges against Russia (whose aluminum exports were below “fair market value” by US methodology, even though Russia was selling at international prices given its low electricity costs).
Stiglitz at the Council of Economic Advisers opposed the cartel. The Antitrust Division supported him. But:

The State Department supported the cartel (“State prized order above all else”).
Robert Rubin at the National Economic Council sided with State.
The cabinet approved it; Ann Bingaman (Antitrust) put the cabinet “on notice that there might have been a violation of the antitrust laws.”

The cartel worked for a while (raising prices). Stiglitz’s deeper critique: “we were trying to teach Russia about market economics. They learned a lesson, but it was the wrong lesson… the way to do well in market economics was to go to the government! We did not intend to teach crony-capitalism 101.”
USEC privatization (1990s): the United States Enrichment Corporation handled imports of Russian uranium from deactivated nuclear warheads (a “swords to plowshares” agreement). After privatization in 1998:

USEC had monopoly power that wouldn’t have passed antitrust scrutiny.
USEC had incentive to limit Russian uranium imports (to keep US prices up).
Stiglitz documented a secret USEC-Russian agreement: Russia offered to triple deliveries, USEC paid “hush money” to refuse and keep refusal secret.
Bipartisan congressional bills were introduced to renationalize.

The dumping-laws structural critique: US uses peculiar methodology to estimate “cost of production” for foreign producers — typically using Department of Commerce’s “BIA” (best information available), supplied by US firms seeking protection. Comparator countries are arbitrary (Poland’s golf carts compared to Canada’s). The system is “naked protectionism.”
Why this matters for the broader argument: the IMF and Treasury’s claim that they were applying neutral economic principles is contradicted by their political-economy decisions. The Treasury-Wall-Street pipeline (Rubin from Goldman → Treasury → Citigroup) and the State-Department-cartel-tolerance pattern reveal that “general interest” was operationally “specific-sector interest.”
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_13_way_ahead
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Ch. 13 — The Way Ahead
The 2002 prescriptive chapter. Globalization “is here to stay”; the question is how to manage it. Stiglitz’s two-part diagnosis of why the international institutions fail: interests (financial-sector capture) and ideology (market fundamentalism as quasi-religion).
The ideology side: market fundamentalism is a “lens” through which evidence that contradicts beliefs is dismissed. For believers, capital-market liberalization was obviously desirable; instability was an “adjustment cost” of transition. The IMF resisted modern economics’ insights about imperfect information and second-best because ideology supplied the answer ideology did not require.
The interests side: the case is strongest in ch. 12 (Stiglitz’s allegation that IMF behavior is best explained by treating the institution as if it were pursuing financial-sector interests rather than its stated mission). Bilateral trade agreements with ISDS provisions; WTO commercial-interest dominance; private arbitration with corporation-appointed judges; “chilling effect” on environmental regulation — these patterns are systematic, not accidental.
There is not just one market model: Japanese, German, Swedish, American versions differ markedly. Sweden combines markets with significantly larger government redistribution and produces equal or higher living standards. Asian models (China, Taiwan, Korea, Malaysia) differ from both. The IMF’s insistence on a single model is therefore not derived from economics but from ideology.
Adam Smith was more nuanced: “Smith was far more aware of the limitations of the market, including the threats posed by imperfections of competition, than those who claim to be his latter-day followers.” The market-fundamentalist invocation of Smith is selective.
Need for international public institutions: not abolition. The IMF “fills a role” — global crisis-response capacity is needed. But governance reform is essential:

Voice for emerging markets commensurate with economic weight.
Transparency in decision-making.
Diversity of perspectives at decision tables (not just finance ministries).

Reform agenda components:

Improved crisis response (not Hooverite austerity).
Sequenced liberalization with institutional capacity built first.
Sovereign-debt restructuring mechanisms.
Capital controls under defined conditions.
Tobin-style transaction taxes.
Global tax cooperation.
Stronger labor and environmental standards.

The institutional politics: changes in rhetoric (more poverty talk) aren’t sufficient if the underlying decision-making structures are unchanged. Some critics call for IMF abolition; Stiglitz disagrees: it would be recreated. Reform must be substantive.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_15_afterword
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Afterword to the 2017 Edition
Long (~250-page) afterword tracing globalization’s evolution from 2002 to 2017. Stiglitz reads the post-2002 trajectory as broadly vindicating GAID’s critique while acknowledging some institutional reform.
Reception of the 2002 GAID: bestseller (~1M copies, 40 official translations, two pirated editions). Ken Rogoff (then IMF Chief Economist) launched a vitriolic ad-hominem attack, accusing Stiglitz of “selling snake oil” by advocating capital controls. Within a few years the IMF itself adopted the same position. Stiglitz: the venom of the IMF response confirmed the book’s reach.
Theoretical foundations of GAID: Stiglitz’s imperfect-information research program (his shared 2001 Nobel work) showed that “even small amounts of information imperfection could have very large effects” — overturning the Adam-Smith-invisible-hand result. “Adam Smith’s invisible hand was invisible — it wasn’t there.” Whenever there is imperfect information or incomplete markets (always), markets are presumed inefficient and selective intervention can improve welfare. The Theory of the Second Best (Lipsey-Lancaster) shows that moving toward an idealized first-best market in the presence of other distortions can reduce welfare — direct refutation of “more liberalization is always better.”
The Stockholm Consensus (2016): a thirteen-economist alternative including four former World Bank chief economists (including Stiglitz). Ten principles: development must be inclusive, attentive to inequality, environmentally sustainable, properly balanced between market/state/civil society. One-size-fits-all rejected.
Battles over policy reviewed:

Capital controls: largely won. Even the IMF now accepts capital controls as legitimate macro-prudential tool.
Privatization: ongoing failures (UK railroads, Chile pension funds, Mexican roads — Mexico spent $8B renationalizing privatized highways).
Trade liberalization: vindicated. The New Discontents in advanced countries make the distributional critique abundantly clear.

The 2008 global financial crisis: did more to discredit Washington Consensus than anything Stiglitz could have written. Originated in the US (the supposed model country); financial-sector deregulation was the cause; spread globally because of cross-border capital flows. Post-crisis: US-China growth gap widened (12 pp in 2009); emerging-market share rose; dollar-system fragility exposed.
Institutional rebalancing:

G-20 replaces G-7 as key forum (China, India, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, etc.).
AIIB (Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank) created over US opposition.
BRICS Bank / NDB.
Chiang Mai Initiative — the modest version of the killed Asian Monetary Fund.
South-South trade agreements (Pacific Alliance: Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru).
Doha Development Round abandoned in 2015 (US refused to remove cotton subsidies).

Trump and the soft-power loss: Trump’s election accelerated US loss of soft power. Stiglitz: even the silver lining of multipolarity is real — concentration of power in one country left global outcomes too dependent on US politics.
Climate as the test of global governance: 2016 Paris Agreement entered into effect; Trump’s withdrawal announcement was rejected by other 194 signatories. Cities and states within US continued to comply. Demonstrates that global governance can hold even when one major country defects.
The institutional reform tally: IMF partially reformed (capital controls, fiscal stance); WTO prevented post-2008 beggar-thy-neighbor outbreak; new emerging-market institutions filled gaps; but elite-capture mechanism remains structurally similar.
The anti-globalization populist wave: Trump, Brexit, Le Pen, Wilders are the predicted political consequence of two decades of corporate-driven globalization in advanced countries. But the New Protectionism is the wrong response: tariffs cannot reverse the macroeconomic trade-balance identity, and protectionism within advanced countries does not address the actual causes of inequality.
The Stiglitz acknowledgments (close to the end): notable mention of the Institute for New Economic Thinking (INET, funded by George Soros), where Stiglitz headed the financial-contagion task force. Long list of co-thinkers — Dani Rodrik, Olivier Blanchard, Christine Lagarde, Justin Yifu Lin, Kaushik Basu. The institutional ecosystem of post-2002 critical international-economics scholarship is significantly Stiglitz-shaped.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.title: ch_19_intro
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
Introduction to Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited
Trump’s January 2017 inauguration “threw a hand grenade into the global economic order” (Stiglitz’s framing). The introduction’s purpose: re-frame the original 2002 GAID analysis (which focused on the developing-world discontents) for a 2017 world in which the advanced-country middle and working classes have joined the anti-globalization coalition — Trump in the US, Farage / Brexit in the UK, Le Pen in France, Wilders in the Netherlands, etc.
Stiglitz lists eight themes from GAID that proved equally applicable to advanced countries: globalization was oversold; benefits less than promised; large distributional consequences; institutional governance deficient; positions reflect special interests not general interest; positions reflect ideology as well as interests; globalization shifts power toward winners; globalization undermines fiscal capacity needed to compensate losers (e.g., race-to-bottom corporate tax rates, Apple’s 0.005% Irish rate).
Three key changes since 2002: (1) climate change has heightened North-South injustice (advanced countries emitted; developing countries bear costs); (2) East Asia post-1997 hoarded reserves (trillions of dollars in US T-bills) creating a perverse capital flow from poor to rich; (3) intellectual-property payments now flow systematically South-to-North; (4) East Asia’s manufacturing-export-led growth model may be reaching its end as global manufacturing employment shrinks.
Three forward paths: doubling-down on Washington Consensus (failed); New Protectionism (Trump’s tariffs — also will fail); fair globalization with shared prosperity (Stiglitz’s preferred path — borrows from Scandinavia, requires reform of both domestic and international rules).
Coins the framework “social protection without protectionism” as the prescriptive core. The introduction also contains the historical context: Cold War constraint on US power → end of Cold War → US-led globalization → 1999 Seattle protests → 9/11 → 2008 crisis → Trump.
Joseph E. Stiglitz - Globalization and Its Discontents Revisited

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/joseph.content:
