06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_01_intertemporal_trade_and_current_account
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 1 — Intertemporal Trade and the Current Account Balance
Formal spine. A two-period small open endowment economy (later extended to investment, two-region world, taxation, labor mobility) is the load-bearing scaffold for the entire textbook: every later chapter is some elaboration, generalization, or distortion of this object.
Notation and objects. i indexes individuals (later dropped via the representative-agent shortcut); c^i_t is consumption in period t; y^i_t is the period-t endowment; r is the world real interest rate (for borrowing or lending in period 1); \beta \in (0,1) is the subjective discount factor with \delta = (1-\beta)/\beta the corresponding rate of time preference; u(\cdot) is the period utility function with u'>0, u''<0 (and an Inada-style \lim_{c\to0}u'(c)=\infty to keep consumption interior); B_t is end-of-period t-1 holdings of net foreign assets carried into period t; CA_t = B_{t+1}-B_t is the period-t current account; K_t, I_t are capital stock and investment; G_t is government consumption; F(K) is a strictly concave neoclassical production function with F(0)=0.
Lifetime preferences and budget.
U^i_1 = u(c^i_1) + \beta u(c^i_2), \qquad c^i_1 + \frac{c^i_2}{1+r} = y^i_1 + \frac{y^i_2}{1+r}.
The intertemporal budget constraint restricts the present value of consumption to the present value of output (perishable; storage dominated by lending at r>0).
Intertemporal Euler equation (Result 1.1).
u'(c^i_1) = (1+r)\beta\,u'(c^i_2) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{u'(c^i_1)}{u'(c^i_2)} = \beta(1+r).
The marginal rate of substitution between today and tomorrow equals the relative price of date-1 consumption in terms of date-2 consumption. Special case \beta=1/(1+r): c_1=c_2 — the consumer wants a flat lifetime path (perfect consumption smoothing); each period’s consumption is \bar c = [(1+r)y_1+y_2]/(2+r).
Current-account identity (Result 1.2). With investment and government, period-t current account is
CA_t = B_{t+1}-B_t = Y_t + r_t B_t - C_t - G_t - I_t = S_t - I_t,
where S_t = Y_t + r_tB_t - C_t - G_t is national saving. The current account is fundamentally an intertemporal phenomenon — saving in excess of domestic capital formation flows into net foreign asset accumulation. Norway’s North Sea oil decade (1973–94) illustrates: huge deficits in the mid-1970s as energy-sector investment surged, then surpluses repaying the debt as oil revenues materialized.
Autarky interest rate and the comparative-advantage interpretation. The autarky interest rate r^A solves u'(Y_1)/[\beta u'(Y_2)] = 1+r^A. Trade pattern: if r^A > r the country borrows in period 1 (imports present consumption at the relatively cheap world price) and runs a current-account deficit; if r^A<r it lends. The greater the gap |r-r^A|, the larger the gains from trade. Welfare-wise, an unbalanced current account is not a pathology — autarky point A gives strictly less utility than the integrated point C on the indifference-curve diagram.
Temporary vs permanent shocks. With \beta=1/(1+r): a temporary output rise (only Y_1\uparrow) produces a current-account surplus (smoothing into the future); a permanent rise (Y_1 and Y_2 rise equally) leaves the current account unchanged. Future-dated shocks have the opposite-signed current-account effect of an equal-magnitude current shock. This template recurs in chapter 2’s many-period generalization.
Investment and the consumption-investment separation (Result 1.3). With the production function Y=F(K) and capital fully reversible (so p_K\equiv 1), the first-order condition for investment is
F'(K_2) = r,
i.e. the marginal product of capital equals the world interest rate. This separates investment from consumption preferences entirely: a less patient (lower \beta) country in a perfect world capital market does not invest less, because it can finance any positive-NPV project at r. The separation requires (i) a small open economy, (ii) a single tradable good, (iii) frictionless capital markets — all three are relaxed in subsequent chapters (nontradables in ch. 4, sovereign risk in ch. 6, large-country general equilibrium in ch. 3).
Two-region world economy and equilibrium r. With Home and Foreign endowments Y_1, Y_1^* and Y_2, Y_2^*, the world equilibrium real interest rate r^W clears the world saving = world investment market: S(r^W)+S^*(r^W) = I(r^W)+I^*(r^W). Application: the 1980s real-interest-rate puzzle — the chapter argues investment-productivity shifts (rather than saving shifts alone) help explain the persistence of high world real rates in that decade. Application: war and the current account — wars are quintessential temporary output reductions that draw down foreign assets / increase external debt (Britain in WWI, US Civil War borrowing).
Taxation and labor mobility. A tax on foreign borrowing introduces a wedge between domestic and world interest rates; at the optimal tariff a large country can extract terms-of-trade gains in present-value (a “Metzler tariff” applied to capital flows). International labor mobility is treated as an additional intertemporal-trade margin: workers can move physically in addition to (or instead of) capital flowing.
Why this chapter matters. Chapter 1 establishes the currency in which every later chapter trades: an Euler equation, an intertemporal budget constraint, a current-account identity, an autarky-vs-world-interest-rate comparison. The chapter’s polemical move is the assertion that “current-account deficits are bad” is incoherent without specifying the autarky alternative — sometimes a deficit is the welfare-maximizing response to opening capital markets.
Notation: c^i_t, y^i_t, U^i_1, \beta, r, u(\cdot), B_t, CA_t, K_t, I_t, F(\cdot), S_t, G_t, r^A, r^W. ~50K raw chars → ~1100 words (≈45:1 compression).

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_02_dynamics_small_open_economies
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 2 — Dynamics of Small Open Economies
Formal spine. Generalize the two-period model of Chapter 1 to an infinite horizon with both deterministic and stochastic income, retaining a representative consumer with intertemporally additive preferences.
Notation. \beta=1/(1+r) (the standard simplifying assumption that subjective and market discount factors coincide); C_t, Y_t, B_t, I_t, G_t as before; E_t\{\cdot\} is the date-t conditional expectation (under rational/perfect-foresight expectations); W_t is permanent income / annuity value of resources.
Lifetime utility (deterministic).
U_t = \sum_{s=t}^{\infty} \beta^{s-t} u(C_s).
Multi-period intertemporal budget constraint. Iterating the period-t flow constraint B_{t+1}=(1+r)B_t+Y_t-C_t-G_t-I_t forward and imposing the transversality condition (no-Ponzi) \lim_{T\to\infty}(1+r)^{-T}B_{T+1}=0:
\sum_{s=t}^{\infty}\frac{C_s+G_s+I_s}{(1+r)^{s-t}} = (1+r)B_t + \sum_{s=t}^{\infty}\frac{Y_s}{(1+r)^{s-t}}.
Present value of consumption-plus-investment-plus-government equals initial wealth plus present value of output. Speculative-bubble appendix (2B): transversality rules out asset-price bubbles in this model class; without it, B_t can grow without bound while still satisfying period-by-period flow constraints.
Permanent-income / consumption-smoothing result (Result 2.1). With \beta(1+r)=1 the Euler equation reduces to C_{t+1}=C_t, i.e. constant consumption. Combined with the intertemporal budget constraint, optimal consumption equals the annuity value of total wealth:
C_t = \frac{r}{1+r}\left[(1+r)B_t + \sum_{s=t}^{\infty}\frac{Y_s-G_s-I_s}{(1+r)^{s-t}}\right].
This is the open-economy analogue of Friedman’s permanent-income hypothesis.
Current-account-as-shock-absorber prediction. The PIH consumption rule implies
CA_t = (Y_t-\bar Y_t) - (I_t-\bar I_t) - (G_t-\bar G_t),
where overbars denote permanent-income annuity values. A country runs a current-account deficit when current output is below permanent, when current investment is above permanent, or when current government spending is above permanent. This testable implication anchors decades of empirical work (Sachs 1981; Campbell 1987; Ghosh 1995).
Application: When is a country bankrupt? The transversality condition is not a debt-to-GDP threshold; it is the requirement that the present-value of future trade surpluses suffices to service the debt. A country with high current debt but high prospective output growth is solvent; one with low debt but no prospect of repayment is not.
Stochastic current account (Result 2.2). With uncertainty, the Euler equation becomes
u'(C_t) = (1+r)\beta\,E_t\{u'(C_{t+1})\}.
Under quadratic utility (or equivalently a CEQ approximation): consumption is a martingale: E_t\{C_{t+1}\}=C_t, and innovations to consumption equal r/(1+r) times the innovation to permanent output. Deaton’s paradox: if output is well approximated by a unit-root process, then permanent output innovations are roughly equal to current output innovations, and consumption should be more volatile than output — yet measured aggregate consumption is less volatile. The model under-explains observed consumption smoothness.
Application: productivity shocks and the current account. A persistent (rho-near-unity) productivity shock raises permanent income by approximately the size of the current shock, so consumption rises one-for-one and the current-account effect is small. A purely transitory shock raises permanent income only marginally, so the current account moves nearly one-for-one with the output innovation. Glick-Rogoff (1995) test this prediction against G-7 data and find it broadly consistent.
Consumer durables (sec 2.4). Durable goods D_t enter as a separate stock; the budget constraint becomes B_{t+1}+D_{t+1} = (1+r)B_t+(1-\delta_D)D_t+Y_t-C_t-X_t where X_t is durable expenditure. Result: durable purchases behave like investment, not consumption — they should be highly volatile and respond to expected real interest rates. This rationalizes why measured “consumption” in national accounts is more volatile than the theory’s C would predict (durables are mis-classified).
Firms, labor, and investment (sec 2.5). With the firm choosing capital to maximize present discounted value, V_t = \sum_{s=t}^\infty(1+r)^{-(s-t)}[F(K_s,L_s)-w_sL_s-I_s], the optimal-investment condition is
F_K(K_{t+1},L_{t+1}) = r + \delta,
with adjustment-cost extensions \Phi(I,K) giving rise to Tobin’s q: q_t = 1+\Phi_I(I_t,K_t) and V_t/K_t = q_t marginal-equals-average q under linear homogeneity. Investment responds gradually to changes in expected marginal products, a feature the model needs to match the substantial gap between observed and frictionless investment volatility.
Continuous-time and detailed-example appendices (2A–2C). Trend productivity growth: with output growing at constant g, the steady-state relationship between debt and output is b/y = -\sum-type closed forms; saving and investment co-move with g. The supplements at end of book develop the dynamic-programming and difference-equation tools used throughout: Bellman equation V(B) = \max_C \{u(C) + \beta V(B')\} subject to B' = (1+r)B+Y-C, with envelope-condition derivative V'(B) = (1+r)u'(C).
Why this chapter matters. This is the chapter that turns the two-period toy model into a workhorse infinite-horizon model. After this chapter the reader has: (i) the no-Ponzi transversality condition that constrains long-run debt dynamics, (ii) the PIH-style consumption rule that delivers testable current-account predictions, (iii) the stochastic Euler equation that organizes empirical work on consumption-volatility puzzles, and (iv) the Tobin-q-style investment apparatus that handles capital-stock dynamics. Every later chapter assumes fluency with these.
Notation: C_t, Y_t, B_t, I_t, G_t, r, \beta, u(\cdot), E_t\{\cdot\}, W_t, \delta, F(\cdot), w_t, q_t, \Phi(\cdot). ~70K raw chars → ~1050 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_03_life_cycle_tax_policy_current_account
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 3 — The Life Cycle, Tax Policy, and the Current Account
Formal spine. Drop the representative-consumer simplification and replace it with overlapping generations (OLG) of finitely-lived agents. Generations differ in age, save for retirement, and do not internalize the welfare of yet-unborn cohorts — features that overturn Ricardian equivalence and reshape the dynamics of public debt.
Notation. Two-period lives (young Y, old O); c_t^Y, c_{t+1}^O are consumption when young (date t) and old (date t+1); w_t is the wage when young; r_t is the real return on savings between dates t-1 and t; N_t is the size of generation born at t with population growth rate n (N_t=(1+n)N_{t-1}); K_t, L_t, A_t are capital, labor, productivity in the production function Y_t=A_t F(K_t,L_t), often Cobb-Douglas Y_t=K_t^\alpha (A_tL_t)^{1-\alpha}; g is the labor-augmenting productivity growth rate.
Ricardian equivalence (Result 3.1, baseline absent OLG). With infinitely-lived representative agents, the timing of lump-sum taxes is irrelevant: a tax cut financed by debt is met by an equal increase in private saving (because the future tax liability is internalized), leaving consumption and the current account unchanged. Government budget deficits do not cause current-account deficits in the representative-agent benchmark.
OLG breaks Ricardian equivalence (Result 3.2). A young person saves s_t^Y = w_t - c_t^Y for retirement; the old consume their accumulated savings. Lump-sum taxes that shift the generational incidence of fiscal burden (cut taxes on the currently young, raise on the currently unborn) raise lifetime consumption of the young, lower national saving, and produce a current-account deficit. Public debt is a way of taxing future generations to benefit current ones.
Diamond (1965) closed-economy steady state. With Cobb-Douglas Y=K^\alpha(AL)^{1-\alpha}, log utility u(c)=\log c, and population growth n:
k^* = \frac{\beta(1-\alpha)}{(1+\beta)(1+n)}\,(k^*)^\alpha A,
solving for the steady-state capital-labor ratio. Dynamic inefficiency can arise: if r<n+g in steady state, the economy is over-accumulating capital and Pareto improvements via permanent debt issue are possible (Appendix 3A).
Open-economy OLG with capital mobility. With access to a perfect world capital market at given r, the marginal product of capital ties down k and hence w. Per-capita aggregate saving (with old having no labor income) is
s_t = \frac{N_t s_t^Y + N_{t-1}s_t^O}{N_t+N_{t-1}} = \left(\frac{1+n}{2+n}\right)s_t^Y - \left(\frac{1}{2+n}\right)s_{t-1}^Y.
A rise in population growth n raises the ratio of young savers to old dissavers, raising aggregate saving per capita. This generates the chapter’s life-cycle prediction that fast-growing populations should run current-account surpluses.
Application: How are saving and growth related? Cross-country and within-country evidence shows a strong positive saving-growth correlation (Modigliani 1970; Carroll-Weil 1994), but the direction of causation is contested: life-cycle theory predicts growth → saving (high growth lifts working-age incomes faster, increasing saving relative to dissaving by retirees), while traditional Solow-style theory predicts saving → growth (through capital deepening). The OLG framework here is consistent with the former interpretation but does not establish it uniquely.
Investment and growth in steady state (sec 3.4). With trend labor-augmenting productivity growth A_{t+1}=(1+g)^{1-\alpha}A_t, steady-state investment-to-output and saving-to-output ratios are
\frac{I}{Y} = (n+g+ng)\,\frac{K}{Y} = (n+g+ng)\,\frac{\alpha}{r}, \qquad \frac{S}{Y} = \frac{\beta(1-\alpha)}{1+\beta}.
Both n and g raise both saving and investment — the chapter’s resolution to the Feldstein-Horioka puzzle.
Application: Feldstein-Horioka (1980) saving-investment puzzle. Cross-country regressions of I/Y on S/Y for OECD samples deliver slope coefficients near 0.9 (1960–74) and 0.6 (1982–91), apparently rejecting the perfect-capital-mobility prediction that domestic saving should be uncorrelated with domestic investment. The chapter’s life-cycle interpretation: demographic and productivity factors that drive long-run investment also drive long-run saving, generating a spurious positive correlation. Taylor (1994) confirms that controlling for age structure and growth substantially weakens the F-H association.
Public debt and the world interest rate (sec 3.6). In an OLG world economy, public debt issued by large countries crowds out world capital and raises r^W. Application: world interest rates and government debt since 1970 — the secular rise in OECD debt-to-GDP ratios is associated with elevated real rates, broadly consistent with the model’s prediction.
Aggregate vs intergenerational gains from trade. Opening to trade benefits the country as a whole (Chapter 1’s gains-from-trade theorem extends), but the welfare effect on specific cohorts can be negative. Specifically, if integration raises domestic r above r^A: the currently old (who hold capital) gain K\,dr, while the currently young and all future generations lose r\,k\,dr/(1+r) in present-value income. Government tax-and-transfer can implement Pareto-improving redistribution (tax the windfall to the old; transfer to the young) — but absent this redistribution, integration may face political opposition from cohorts who lose, even though aggregate welfare rises.
Why this chapter matters. This chapter introduces the fiscal-policy and demographic apparatus that the rest of the book deploys: aging societies (Japan, Italy) and emerging-market demographic dividends (1990s East Asia) have first-order current-account implications that the representative-agent model of chapter 2 cannot capture. The chapter also delivers the cleanest argument for why government budget deficits can cause current-account deficits — only when they shift the intergenerational incidence of fiscal burden.
Notation: c^Y_t, c^O_{t+1}, w_t, r_t, N_t, n, K_t, L_t, A_t, F(\cdot), \alpha, g, s^Y, s^O, k^*, b, B/Y, I/Y, S/Y. ~80K raw chars → ~1100 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_04_real_exchange_rate_terms_of_trade
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 4 — The Real Exchange Rate and the Terms of Trade
Formal spine. Drop the single-good assumption of chapters 1–3 and introduce multiple consumption goods — most importantly traded vs nontraded — to study the determinants of relative prices, real exchange rates, and the terms of trade.
Notation. C_T, C_N are consumption of tradables and nontradables; p is the price of nontradables in terms of tradables; P is the consumer price index (often Cobb-Douglas P=p^{1-\gamma} with tradables as numeraire and weight 1-\gamma on nontradables); \mathcal{E} is the nominal exchange rate (price of foreign currency in home currency); \mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{E}P^*/P is the real exchange rate; A_T, A_N are sectoral total factor productivity; \mu_{LT}, \mu_{LN}, \mu_{KT}, \mu_{KN} are factor income shares (\mu_{Lj}+\mu_{Kj}=1); w is the wage, r the rental rate of capital.
International price levels and the real exchange rate. Empirically, price levels are higher in richer countries — the Penn World Table shows a strong positive correlation between PPP-adjusted per-capita income and the price level (Figure 4.1). Pure PPP, P=\mathcal{E}P^*, is empirically rejected even over decades; persistent deviations are the norm.
Zero-profit conditions in tradables and nontradables. With CRS production functions and competitive factor markets:
1 = c_T(w,r;A_T), \qquad p = c_N(w,r;A_N),
where c_T,c_N are unit-cost functions. The world interest rate r is given to a small open economy by world capital markets, so the tradables zero-profit condition pins down w(r;A_T), and the nontradables zero-profit condition then determines p(r;A_T,A_N) — independent of demand.
Balassa-Samuelson result (Result 4.1). Log-differentiating the zero-profit conditions (with hat-notation for percentage changes):
\hat p = \frac{\mu_{LN}}{\mu_{LT}}\,\hat A_T - \hat A_N.
Provided nontradables are labor-intensive relative to tradables (\mu_{LN}/\mu_{LT}>1), faster productivity growth in tradables than in nontradables raises the relative price of nontradables. Harrod-Balassa-Samuelson real-exchange-rate prediction: countries with relatively higher tradables-vs-nontradables productivity growth experience real-exchange-rate appreciation and have higher overall price levels.
The Stolper-Samuelson logic — a relative price change benefits the factor used intensively in the expanding industry — runs in reverse: a rise in r lowers p when nontradables are labor-intensive, because higher capital rentals shrink the wage and hence the cost of labor-intensive nontradables.
Application: services prices and Japan. Time-series evidence across industrial countries shows the “Baumol-Bowen effect” (a rising relative price of services) in nearly all OECD countries 1970–85, especially Japan whose tradables productivity surged post-war while services productivity lagged. Japan’s real exchange rate has approximately doubled relative to its trading partners over 1950–92 (Figure 4.5) — much of the move is the cumulative HBS effect.
Long-run GDP-GNP diagram and the Rybczynski line. With capital mobile internationally, the GDP line (locus of efficient (Y_T,Y_N) combinations) has slope steeper than -p in absolute value when nontradables are labor-intensive; expanding the capital-intensive tradables sector requires importing capital. The GNP line C_T+pC_N=wL+rQ (where Q=B+K is total wealth) is the steady-state consumption budget. Demand homotheticity gives a straight-line income-expansion path through the origin; equilibrium consumption (C_T,C_N) is at its intersection with the GNP line, while production (Y_T,Y_N) sits vertically above C on the GDP line. Trade balance equals horizontal distance Y_T-C_T.
Consumption-based price index and real consumption. With Cobb-Douglas preferences u(C_T,C_N) = C_T^\gamma C_N^{1-\gamma}, the cost-of-living index is P=\gamma^{-\gamma}(1-\gamma)^{-(1-\gamma)} p^{1-\gamma} (in tradables units). Real consumption C \equiv C_T^\gamma C_N^{1-\gamma} behaves analogously to the single-good C in chapter 2: dynamic Euler equations and intertemporal budget constraints carry over with the appropriate price-index reinterpretation.
Consumption dynamics, the price level, and the real interest rate (sec 4.4). The relevant consumption-based real interest rate for the Euler equation involves both the world interest rate r (in tradables) and the expected change in p:
\frac{u'(C_t)/P_t}{u'(C_{t+1})/P_{t+1}} = \beta(1+r)\frac{P_t}{P_{t+1}} = \beta(1+r_t^C),
so 1+r_t^C = (1+r)P_t/P_{t+1} — anticipated changes in the price of nontradables drive a wedge between the world interest rate (in tradables) and the real interest rate relevant for total-consumption smoothing. Implication: a country anticipating productivity catch-up (Japan post-1950, Korea post-1970) faces a higher effective real interest rate (its real exchange rate will appreciate, raising P over time), which works against borrowing to consume early.
Terms of trade in a dynamic Ricardian model (sec 4.5). Extending Dornbusch-Fischer-Samuelson 1977 to dynamics, with a continuum of goods indexed by comparative advantage and endogenous nontradability arising from international transport costs, the equilibrium share of goods that are nontradable depends on transport-cost technology, country sizes, and productivity profiles. Productivity shocks shift the cutoffs along the comparative-advantage continuum, creating endogenous terms-of-trade and trade-balance dynamics. Box 4.2: the transfer effect — international transfers (Marshall plan, German reparations, oil-revenue redistribution) change relative spending patterns and hence terms of trade; the original Keynes-Ohlin debate is resolved as an empirical question about marginal propensities to consume traded vs nontraded goods.
Why this chapter matters. Chapter 4 is where international macro stops being closed-economy macro with two countries and starts being genuinely international — relative prices of traded vs nontraded goods are first-order determinants of real exchange rates, and HBS is the textbook’s most empirically successful long-run real-exchange-rate prediction. The chapter also sets up the price-index machinery that chapters 8–10 deploy for monetary models.
Notation: C_T, C_N, p, P, P^*, \mathcal{E}, \mathcal{Q}, A_T, A_N, \mu_{LT}, \mu_{LN}, \mu_{KT}, \mu_{KN}, w, r, k_T, k_N, \gamma, Q, r^C. ~85K raw chars → ~1100 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_05_uncertainty_international_financial_markets
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 5 — Uncertainty and International Financial Markets
Formal spine. Replace deterministic foresight with state-contingent uncertainty and study the role of international trade in risky assets. The benchmark is complete Arrow-Debreu markets; the puzzles arise from comparing complete-markets predictions with observed international portfolios and consumption co-movements.
Notation. s\in\mathcal{S} indexes states of nature; \pi(s) is the probability of state s; c(s) is state-contingent consumption; p(s) is the date-t price of an Arrow-Debreu security paying one unit of consumption in state s at t+1; r is the riskless rate; R_i is the gross return on asset i; E_t\{\cdot\} and \text{Cov}_t(\cdot,\cdot) are conditional expectation and covariance.
Trade across random states (sec 5.1, complete-markets benchmark). In a complete-markets small-country case, the consumer maximizes
E_0\sum_{t=0}^\infty \beta^t u(c_t) = \sum_{t=0}^\infty\beta^t\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_t}\pi_t(s)u(c_t(s))
subject to the date-zero present-value budget constraint over all state paths. First-order condition (Result 5.1): the marginal utility of consumption is proportional across all agents and states up to a country-specific Lagrange multiplier:
u'(c_t^h(s)) = \lambda^h \cdot \frac{p(s,t)}{\beta^t \pi_t(s)},
so consumption growth rates are perfectly correlated across countries in a complete-markets world: \Delta\log c^{\text{Home}} = \Delta\log c^{\text{Foreign}} up to constants.
Asset-pricing equation (Result 5.2, Lucas 1978 / consumption-CAPM). For any traded asset with payoff X_{t+1} and price V_t:
V_t = E_t\left\{\beta\,\frac{u'(C_{t+1})}{u'(C_t)}\,X_{t+1}\right\}.
The pricing kernel M_{t+1}\equiv \beta u'(C_{t+1})/u'(C_t) encapsulates risk preferences. Equity-premium decomposition: E_t[R^e_{t+1}-R^f_{t+1}] = -\text{Cov}_t(M_{t+1},R^e_{t+1})/E_t[M_{t+1}] — assets whose returns are negatively correlated with marginal utility (high payoff in good states) earn positive risk premia.
International portfolio diversification (sec 5.3). With identical preferences and homogeneous beliefs, the two-fund separation theorem says every investor holds the same portfolio of risky assets — the world market portfolio — leveraged by personal risk-free borrowing/lending. Predicted holdings: US investors should hold ≈40–60% of their equity portfolio in non-US stocks (matching world market-cap weights). Observed holdings (1990s): US investors held ≈8–10% in foreign equity. The wedge is the home bias puzzle.
Application: home bias. Possible explanations: (i) hedging against home-good consumption (fails in homothetic-preference cases per French-Poterba 1991); (ii) information frictions; (iii) explicit/implicit barriers to foreign investment; (iv) labor-income hedging — domestic equities may be a hedge against domestic labor-income risk if the two are negatively correlated (Bottazzi-Pesenti-van Wincoop 1996 find OECD evidence consistent). Status: unresolved.
Equity premium puzzle (sec 5.4 application). Using historical US data (Mehra-Prescott 1985), the CCAPM Euler equation requires implausibly high risk aversion (\rho>30) to rationalize the observed ≈6% equity premium given consumption-growth volatility ≈3%. The puzzle is even more severe in long-run global data:
E[R^e-R^f] \approx \rho\,\text{Var}(\Delta\log C),
so to match a 6% premium with \text{Var}(\Delta\log C)\approx 0.001, we need \rho\approx 60. Resolutions discussed: Epstein-Zin recursive utility separates risk aversion from intertemporal substitution; rare disasters (Rietz, Barro) raise effective consumption-growth volatility; habit formation (Constantinides; Campbell-Cochrane) raises effective risk aversion in downturns; long-run risk (Bansal-Yaron) — but no consensus.
Role of nontradables (sec 5.5). If a portion of consumption is non-tradable, complete tradables-asset markets cannot achieve full risk sharing of total consumption. With log-Cobb-Douglas preferences over C_T and C_N, however, payoffs to nontradable equities are perfectly correlated with the world tradable mutual fund and trade in tradable equities suffices. Implication: the nontradable-goods explanation of home bias works only with non-Cobb-Douglas preferences and specific intratemporal-elasticity values.
Application: gains from international risk-sharing. Lucas (1987) showed the welfare cost of US consumption variability is small (≈0.3% of perpetual consumption with risk aversion \rho=10), suggesting modest gains from perfect international pooling. Caveats: (i) Lucas assumes random-walk-around-trend dynamics; permanent shocks make the cost much larger; (ii) developing countries have far higher consumption volatility than the US; (iii) idiosyncratic risks are uninsurable but raise the price of laying off insurable risks (Mankiw-Zeldes 1991). Cole-Obstfeld (1991) find gains ≈0.2% of GDP for OECD; van Wincoop (1994) finds ≈5.6% with Epstein-Zin preferences and a random walk in consumption — sensitivity to assumptions is high.
Model of intragenerational risk-sharing (sec 5.6). OLG generations cannot trade with the unborn, so even with complete markets within each cohort, intergenerational risk-sharing is incomplete. With log utility and Home output exactly half of world output:
\mu_t = \frac{1}{1+\beta}\left[\frac{y_t}{y_t+y_t^*} + \beta E_t\left\{\frac{y_{t+1}}{y_{t+1}+y_{t+1}^*}\right\}\right],
so the Home young consume share \mu_t of world output regardless of state realizations. Aggregate consumption ratios across countries can fluctuate even with intragenerational complete markets — a sharper test than aggregate-cohort-pooled tests.
Application: testing complete markets via consumption divergence. Deaton-Paxson (1994) cohort-survey data from US, UK, Taiwan show consumption inequality within age cohorts grows over the life cycle — incompatible with full intra-cohort consumption insurance. Domestic markets are themselves incomplete; international markets can be no more complete than domestic.
Why this chapter matters. Chapter 5 is the textbook’s single longest chapter and the one with the highest density of asset-pricing results, equity-premium variations, and home-bias data. It is the formal apparatus underlying any cross-country asset-pricing project — international CAPM, real-exchange-rate-risk premia, sovereign-bond pricing.
Notation: s, \pi(s), p(s), c(s), \beta, u(\cdot), \rho, R_i, M_{t+1}, R^e, R^f, C_T, C_N, \gamma, \mu_t, y_t, y_t^*. ~110K raw chars → ~1150 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_06_imperfections_capital_markets
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 6 — Imperfections in International Capital Markets
Formal spine. Drop the perfect-capital-market assumption and study the frictions that limit international borrowing — most importantly sovereign risk (the inability of creditors to enforce contracts against foreign governments) and asymmetric information (hidden actions and hidden types).
Notation. D = sovereign external debt; \sigma = penalty (output loss / exclusion) imposed in default; V^R, V^D = value functions for repayment vs default; q = probability of default in equilibrium; r^* = risk-free world rate; r = sovereign-debt yield; \theta = hidden type or hidden effort; \phi = recovery rate.
Sovereign risk (sec 6.1). With no third-party enforcement against foreign governments, the borrower’s repayment incentive must come from anticipated future loss of capital-market access (Eaton-Gersovitz 1981) or direct sanctions (trade embargoes; legal seizure of assets abroad — though Box 6.1 notes sovereign immunity makes the latter weak). Without a credible enforcement technology, no debt is sustainable and lending breaks down even when efficient.
Eaton-Gersovitz reputation model (Result 6.1). A sovereign repays as long as the value of continued capital-market access exceeds the static gain from default:
V^R(D) \geq V^D \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u(C^R) + \beta V^R(D') \geq u(C^D) + \beta V^D,
where V^D is the value of permanent autarky after default. Debt limit: the maximum sustainable debt D^{\max} is determined by the inequality binding; beyond D^{\max}, default becomes optimal.
Equilibrium debt pricing. With probability q of default and zero recovery in default:
1 + r^*= (1-q)(1+r) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad r = \frac{r^* + q}{1-q}.
Risk-neutral creditors break even by requiring a yield premium r-r^* that compensates for default risk. With risk-averse creditors or systemic correlation, additional premia apply. Bulow-Rogoff (1989) critique: if creditors’ threats are limited to denying future lending, and the sovereign can save abroad, reputation alone cannot sustain positive debt levels — direct sanctions or output costs of default must be operative.
Application: cost of exclusion from world insurance markets. Cole-Kehoe (1995) and others use calibrated models to estimate that the welfare cost of permanent exclusion from international financial markets is small for stable advanced economies (≈0.3–1% of permanent consumption) but potentially large for developing-country economies with high consumption volatility (5%+). Default-cost size matters: if costs are small, debt limits are tight and lending is correspondingly limited.
Application: prior defaults and borrowing terms. Empirical work (Eichengreen-Portes; Lindert-Morton; Reinhart-Rogoff later work) finds that countries that defaulted in the 1930s or 1980s pay modest yield premia on subsequent borrowing — the punishment is real but not unlimited. Repeat defaulters (Argentina) face larger premia than first-time defaulters.
Sovereign risk and investment (sec 6.2). When debt service is costly relative to default, the sovereign has incentives to under-invest (an investment that would otherwise be profitable is dominated by default if it raises the value of continued access only modestly). Conversely, debt overhang distorts incentives toward shorter-horizon consumption, undermining capital accumulation. The chapter formalizes these effects in a two-period model with endogenous investment I chosen before the default decision is made; equilibrium I is below the first-best level whenever default is possible in the bad state.
Application: debt buybacks. The Bulow-Rogoff (1988) “secondary-market buyback paradox”: when a sovereign repurchases its own debt at the secondary-market discount, the residual creditors’ claim per dollar of remaining debt rises (because the same expected output stream is divided across fewer claims), so the buyback price is bid up to a level at which the sovereign captures little of the gain. Empirical evidence: Bolivia’s 1988 buyback at 11¢/$1 shifted the residual price upward dramatically; the country captured less than half of the apparent surplus.
Risk-sharing with hidden information (sec 6.3). When the borrower observes its own income / type but the lender does not, full risk-sharing is unachievable: any contract must be incentive-compatible (IC) — the borrower must (weakly) prefer truthful reporting. The constrained-optimal contract trades off insurance against incentives:
\max_{\{c(\theta)\}} E[u(c(\theta))] \quad \text{s.t.} \quad u(c(\theta))-\theta\geq u(c(\theta'))-\theta\,\forall\theta,\theta',
with the standard revelation-principle apparatus. Result: consumption co-moves with reported income more than under full insurance — partial risk-sharing only.
Moral hazard in international lending (sec 6.4). When the borrower’s effort e affects the project’s success probability but is unobservable, the contract must give the borrower skin in the game — debt-like contracts emerge naturally. The moral-hazard distortion explains why sovereign borrowing is concentrated in non-state-contingent debt rather than equity-like contingent claims (which would give optimal risk-sharing if effort were observable).
Application: financing constraints and investment. Empirical evidence (Hoshi-Kashyap-Scharfstein on Japanese keiretsu firms; Calomiris-Hubbard on US firms; Borenstein-Pelaez and Galindo-Schiantarelli on developing-country firms) shows investment-cash-flow sensitivity is greater for firms with weaker access to external finance — direct evidence that capital-market imperfections limit investment.
Recontracting sovereign debt (sec 6A). Default is rarely a binary outcome; debt restructurings (Brady deals 1989–94; Russia 1998; Argentina 2001–05; Greece 2012) involve renegotiation under bargaining frictions. The chapter sketches a Rubinstein-Ståhl alternating-offers framework: the equilibrium recovery rate \phi depends on relative bargaining power, the threat point (full default vs continued service), and the size of deadweight losses from prolonged restructuring.
Why this chapter matters. Chapter 6 is the textbook’s foundational treatment of why international capital markets do not behave like the frictionless markets of chapter 5. It supplies the formal vocabulary for sovereign-debt crises, IMF-conditionality debates (a complement to Stiglitz’s institutional critique), and emerging-market borrowing-cost puzzles. The combination of sovereign-risk and hidden-information frictions explains the empirical pattern of small advanced-country / developing-country differences in cross-border capital flows that the perfect-markets benchmark of chapter 5 cannot.
Notation: D, \sigma, V^R, V^D, q, r^*, r, \theta, \phi, IC, e, \beta. ~80K raw chars → ~950 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_07_global_linkages_and_growth
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 7 — Global Linkages and Economic Growth
Formal spine. Open-economy generalization of the neoclassical growth model (Solow-Swan 1956; Cass-Koopmans-Ramsey 1965) and the endogenous-growth literature (Romer 1986; Lucas 1988; Aghion-Howitt 1992), with stress on intercountry comparisons and capital mobility.
Notation. K, L, A — capital, labor, productivity; k=K/(AL) — capital per effective worker; y=Y/(AL)=f(k) — output per effective worker; s — saving rate; n — population growth; g — productivity growth; \delta — depreciation; \alpha — capital share; r — world real interest rate.
Solow-Swan in continuous time. With Cobb-Douglas Y=K^\alpha(AL)^{1-\alpha} and exogenous saving rate s:
\dot k = sf(k) - (n+g+\delta)\,k,
with steady state
k^* = \left[\frac{s}{n+g+\delta}\right]^{1/(1-\alpha)}.
Steady-state output per effective worker: y^* = (s/(n+g+\delta))^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}. Long-run growth in output per worker equals g (the exogenous productivity-growth rate); s affects only the level of y, not its growth rate.
Application: capital-output ratios since WWII (Box 7.1). Capital-output ratios K/Y are roughly stationary across major economies post-1950 (consistent with steady-state Solow), but with substantial cross-country level variation traceable to differences in s, n, and (residually) A. Mankiw-Romer-Weil (1992) show that augmenting Solow with human capital improves the cross-country fit dramatically.
International convergence (sec 7.2). Absolute convergence: poor countries grow faster than rich ones unconditionally. Empirically false across all countries (Pritchett’s “Divergence, Big Time”). Conditional convergence: controlling for steady-state determinants (s, n, h human capital), poor countries do grow faster — Barro-Sala-i-Martin (1992) estimate convergence rates ≈2%/year. Open-economy interpretation: with capital mobility, r is given by world markets and ties down k instantly; convergence in output per worker should be near-immediate. Slow observed convergence is evidence against the perfect-capital-market benchmark and for frictions of chapter 6 type plus immobile factors (human capital, technology).
Application: Baumol-De Long-Romer convergence debate (1870–1979). Baumol (1986) reported strong convergence among 16 industrialized countries. De Long (1988) showed sample selection bias (countries chosen ex-post for being rich in 1979) inflates convergence; expanded sample shows much weaker convergence. The episode illustrates how growth-empirics conclusions are sample-sensitive.
Application: public-capital accumulation and convergence. Investment in public infrastructure (Aschauer 1989) may explain part of cross-country growth differences not captured by private-capital accumulation. Munnell (1990) and follow-up studies show large but contested elasticities of output to public capital.
Endogenous growth (sec 7.3). When the social return to capital does not diminish (because of externalities, knowledge spillovers, or human-capital accumulation), the saving rate can affect the long-run growth rate, not just the level.
AK model. With Y = AK (capital broadly construed to include human capital and knowledge) and constant returns to the reproducible factor:
g_K = sA - \delta - n,
so a permanent increase in s permanently raises growth. The model rationalizes the East Asian growth-miracle pattern of high-saving, high-growth.
Romer (1990) horizontal-innovation model. Knowledge is produced by R&D using existing knowledge as input; long-run growth g depends on the population engaged in R&D, the productivity of that R&D, and the size of the market (scale effects).
Application: capital deepening and East Asian growth. Young (1995) decomposition shows much of East Asian high growth (Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore) came from factor accumulation (rising K/L and labor-force participation) rather than TFP — consistent with neoclassical Solow predictions, contra strong-form endogenous growth. Krugman (1994) extrapolates: the East Asian “miracle” is a transitional phenomenon, not a permanent growth-rate divergence.
Stochastic neoclassical growth (sec 7.4). Brock-Mirman (1972) framework with productivity shocks A_t and a planner / representative-agent solving
\max E_0\sum_{t=0}^\infty\beta^t u(C_t) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad K_{t+1} = A_t F(K_t, L_t)+(1-\delta)K_t-C_t.
The first-order conditions yield a stochastic Euler equation analogous to chapter 2 but with capital as the savings vehicle. International business-cycle implications (Backus-Kehoe-Kydland 1992): the calibrated complete-markets two-country model predicts much higher international consumption correlation than output correlation, but the opposite is observed empirically. The “Backus-Kehoe-Kydland anomaly” is the international counterpart of the Mehra-Prescott equity-premium puzzle.
Continuous-time growth as a limit of discrete-time (Appendix 7A). The transition between discrete-period and continuous-time formulations is technical but standard; continuous time is cleaner for comparative-dynamic exercises (e.g. golden-rule capital stock f'(k_g)=n+g+\delta), discrete time is cleaner for stochastic computation.
Stochastic OLG growth (Appendix 7B). Combining chapter 3’s OLG with chapter 5’s uncertainty: aggregate consumption-output ratios fluctuate even with intra-cohort risk-pooling, because cohort-specific shocks are not insurable across generations.
Why this chapter matters. Chapter 7 places international macro inside the larger growth-economics literature: convergence, endogenous growth, and the stochastic-growth foundation for international real-business-cycle models. The chapter’s open-economy slant is distinctive — most growth textbooks treat the closed-economy case and treat openness as an afterthought. The empirical sections (Baumol-De Long debate, East Asian decomposition, Feldstein-Horioka revisited, public capital) are the textbook’s most direct engagement with development-economics questions.
Notation: K, L, A, k, y, s, n, g, \delta, \alpha, r, f(\cdot), F(\cdot), h, K/Y. ~95K raw chars → ~950 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_08_money_and_exchange_rates_flexible_prices
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 8 — Money and Exchange Rates under Flexible Prices
Formal spine. Introduce money into the open-economy framework, initially with fully flexible prices. Build up from the Cagan (1956) hyperinflation model to general-equilibrium models with money in the utility function, then to nominal-exchange-rate determination, target zones, and speculative attacks.
Notation. M_t — nominal money stock; P_t — domestic price level; \mathcal{E}_t — nominal exchange rate (price of foreign currency in home currency); i_t — nominal interest rate; r_t — real interest rate; \pi_t = \log(P_t/P_{t-1}) — inflation rate; m_t = \log M_t, p_t = \log P_t, e_t = \log\mathcal{E}_t — log variables; \eta — semi-elasticity of money demand to inflation; \mu — money-growth rate.
Cagan money-demand equation. In log-linear form, real money demand is
m_t - p_t = -\eta\,E_t\{\pi_{t+1}\} = -\eta\,E_t\{p_{t+1}-p_t\}.
Cagan price-level solution (no-bubbles). Solving forward under transversality:
p_t = \frac{1}{1+\eta}\sum_{s=0}^\infty\left(\frac{\eta}{1+\eta}\right)^s E_t\{m_{t+s}\}.
The price level is the discounted present value of expected future money supplies — the canonical “asset-pricing” representation of P as forward-looking. With bubbles: p_t + b_0\,((1+\eta)/\eta)^t for arbitrary b_0 — ruled out by transversality but instructive.
Seignorage and the inflation-Laffer curve. Real seignorage revenue is
\text{Seig}_t = \frac{M_t-M_{t-1}}{P_t},
and with steady money growth \mu and Cagan money demand M/P=(1+\mu)^{-\eta}:
\text{Seig}(\mu) = \frac{\mu}{1+\mu}\,(1+\mu)^{-\eta} = \mu(1+\mu)^{-\eta-1}.
Maximizing yields the revenue-maximizing money-growth rate \mu^* = 1/\eta. Box 8.1: measured seignorage 1990–94 was below 1% of GDP for most OECD economies but 3% for Sweden — a small but nontrivial fiscal source. Time-consistency problem (Calvo 1978): without commitment, the seignorage-maximizing rate is not credible — the public anticipates ex-post temptation to surprise-inflate.
PPP and uncovered interest parity (UIP) — building blocks for monetary exchange-rate models.
P_t = \mathcal{E}_t P_t^* \quad \Rightarrow \quad p_t = e_t + p_t^*
1+i_{t+1} = (1+i_{t+1}^*)\frac{E_t\mathcal{E}_{t+1}}{\mathcal{E}_t} \quad \Rightarrow \quad i_{t+1} \approx i_{t+1}^*+E_t e_{t+1}-e_t.
Monetary model of the exchange rate (Result 8.1). Combining Cagan money demand, PPP, and UIP yields
e_t = \frac{1}{1+\eta}\sum_{s=0}^\infty\left(\frac{\eta}{1+\eta}\right)^s E_t\{m_{t+s}-\phi y_{t+s}+\eta i^*_{t+s+1}-p^*_{t+s}\},
i.e. the exchange rate is a forward-looking asset price driven by expected future fundamentals (money supplies, real income, foreign interest rates, foreign price levels). Empirical performance: very weak as a short-run model — the chapter’s hint of the “exchange-rate disconnect puzzle” formalized in chapter 9.
Money-in-utility models with maximizing individuals (sec 8.3). Replace ad-hoc Cagan money demand with the utility specification u(C, M/P) (Sidrauski 1967; Brock 1974). First-order conditions:
u_C(C_t, M_t/P_t) = (1+r)\beta\,u_C(C_{t+1}, M_{t+1}/P_{t+1}),
\frac{u_{M/P}(C_t,M_t/P_t)}{u_C(C_t,M_t/P_t)} = \frac{i_{t+1}}{1+i_{t+1}}.
The marginal rate of substitution between real balances and consumption equals the user cost of money i/(1+i). This delivers a formally derived money-demand function with comparative-statics implications matching Cagan’s reduced form.
Cash-in-advance models (Appendix 8A, Lucas 1982). Alternative microfoundation: agents must hold money equal to their consumption purchases (P_t C_t \leq M_{t-1}). Yields similar money-demand and exchange-rate dynamics but cleaner welfare analysis and naturally embeds the demand for money in transactions technology.
Nominal exchange-rate regimes (sec 8.4). Fixed vs floating. Under fixed rates, the central bank intervenes in the FX market to maintain \mathcal{E}_t = \bar{\mathcal{E}}, surrendering control over M to the parity (the trilemma: a country cannot simultaneously have free capital mobility, fixed exchange rates, and independent monetary policy). Under floating rates, M is the policy instrument and \mathcal{E} adjusts.
Target zones (sec 8.5, Krugman 1991). A target-zone regime allows \mathcal{E} to fluctuate within a band [\underline{\mathcal{E}},\bar{\mathcal{E}}] enforced by intervention at the edges. Under credible bands, expectations of mean-reversion at the band edges generate the smooth-pasting / honeymoon prediction:
e_t = m_t - \eta\,E_t\dot{e}_t,
with the equilibrium e(m) function S-shaped (rather than 45-degree as under pure float), giving the central bank “free monetary independence” within the band.
Speculative attacks on a target zone (sec 8.6, Krugman 1979). When a fixed-rate regime is unsustainable (foreign-reserve depletion or fiscal-monetary inconsistency), the timing of the attack is determined by the no-arbitrage condition: speculators attack when the post-collapse shadow exchange rate \tilde{\mathcal{E}}_t equals the parity. Closed-form attack-time formula for the canonical model: T = (R_0-\bar R)/\mu where R_0 is initial reserves, \bar R is the post-attack stock, and \mu is the deficit-financed money-growth rate.
Stochastic global GE with nominal assets (sec 8.7). Two-country general-equilibrium extension with maximizing individuals, nominal bond holdings, and real-vs-nominal-asset distinctions; develops the framework that chapter 10 uses for the redux model.
Why this chapter matters. Chapter 8 is the textbook’s bridge between the real models of chapters 1–7 and the sticky-price models of chapters 9–10. The key conceptual move is treating the exchange rate as a forward-looking asset price (not a flow-equilibrium quantity), which the rest of the textbook builds on. The chapter also delivers the formal apparatus for currency-crisis analysis (target zones, speculative attacks) that became central to 1990s emerging-market policy debates.
Notation: M_t, P_t, \mathcal{E}_t, i_t, r_t, \pi_t, m_t, p_t, e_t, \eta, \mu, \phi, R, b_0, u(C, M/P), y, p^*. ~85K raw chars → ~1100 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_09_nominal_price_rigidities
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 9 — Nominal Price Rigidities: Empirical Facts and Basic Open-Economy Models
Formal spine. Add sticky nominal prices to the open-economy framework, motivated by direct empirical evidence on price-adjustment frequency. Develop the Mundell-Fleming-Dornbusch model in modern dress, then introduce monetary-policy credibility (Kydland-Prescott; Barro-Gordon) as the conceptual bridge to chapter 10’s two-country general-equilibrium model.
Notation. P, P^* — domestic / foreign price levels (often log p, p^*); \mathcal{E}, e — nominal exchange rate; M, m — money supply; Y, y — output; r, i — real / nominal interest rates; q = e+p^*-p — log real exchange rate.
Empirical motivation: nominal-price stickiness (sec 9.1). Microeconomic evidence on price-adjustment frequency (Bils-Klenow; Nakamura-Steinsson) shows the median price duration in the US is 4–11 months depending on sector, with substantial heterogeneity. Internationally traded goods exhibit substantial deviations from the law of one price — same physical good, same currency, sells at different prices in different countries (Engel 1993, Crucini-Telmer-Zachariadis). Real-exchange-rate persistence: PPP deviations have half-lives of 3–5 years across developed economies (Rogoff 1996 “PPP puzzle”). The puzzle is that nominal-price stickiness alone is hard to reconcile with such long half-lives.
Mundell-Fleming-Dornbusch model (sec 9.2). A small open economy with sticky goods prices and flexible asset prices. Three equilibrium relationships:
y = \bar y + \phi(e+p^*-p),  (Aggregate demand: net exports rise with the real exchange rate)
m - p = \alpha y - \beta i,  (LM curve: real money demand depends on income and the nominal interest rate)
i = i^* + E_t\{e_{t+1}\}-e_t.  (UIP)
Dornbusch (1976) overshooting. With prices sticky in the short run but converging to PPP in the long run, an unanticipated permanent monetary expansion produces:

Long-run: \bar p \uparrow  proportionally; \bar e\uparrow proportionally (PPP).
Short-run: p fixed; nominal interest rate i falls (LM curve, real money supply rises); UIP requires E_t\{e_{t+1}-e_t\}<0, i.e. expected appreciation; so e must overshoot its long-run value \bar e.

Closed-form overshooting magnitude:
e_0 - \bar e = -\frac{1}{\beta\theta}(p-\bar p),
where \theta is the price-adjustment speed; sluggish prices (\theta\to 0) produce arbitrarily large overshooting. This is the textbook’s most famous flexible-monetary / sticky-price prediction and the conceptual ancestor of every subsequent New Open-Economy Macro model.
Empirical evidence on sticky-price exchange-rate models (sec 9.3). Mark (1995) finds long-horizon (3-5 year) predictability of exchange rates from monetary fundamentals; Meese-Rogoff (1983) classic finding that random-walk forecasts of nominal exchange rates beat structural models at short horizons. Resolution: at short horizons, nominal-rate volatility exceeds fundamentals’ volatility, so noise dominates; at long horizons, the structural model has more bite. The “exchange-rate disconnect puzzle” (also “Meese-Rogoff puzzle”) remains unresolved.
Choice of exchange-rate regime (sec 9.4). Under nominal rigidities, fixed and floating regimes have different stabilization properties. Mundell (1963) classic result extended:

Real shocks (productivity, terms-of-trade shifts) are better absorbed under floating rates (the exchange rate adjusts to clear markets without requiring sticky-price changes).
Nominal/monetary shocks are better absorbed under fixed rates (a nominal shock is fully neutralized by reserves intervention with no real consequences).

This trade-off is the formal basis of optimal-currency-area theory (Mundell 1961; McKinnon 1963; Kenen 1969): countries with high labor mobility, similar shock structures, and fiscal-transfer mechanisms benefit most from fixed/common-currency regimes.
Models of monetary-policy credibility (sec 9.5, Kydland-Prescott / Barro-Gordon). A monetary authority with discretion has the period objective
\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\lambda(y-\tilde y)^2+\pi^2\right],
facing a Phillips curve y - \bar y = \alpha(\pi-E_{t-1}\pi) where \tilde y > \bar y (the policymaker wants output above the natural rate). Discretion equilibrium: \pi^D = \alpha\lambda(\tilde y-\bar y) > 0 — a positive inflation bias without commitment. Commitment equilibrium: \pi^C = 0. The gap is the welfare cost of discretion; the equilibrium illustrates the time-consistency problem central to monetary-policy design.
Application: central-bank independence and inflation. Cukierman (1992), Alesina-Summers (1993): cross-country regressions show negative correlation between central-bank independence and inflation rates. Independence is the institutional commitment device that approximates the commitment equilibrium. Caveat: cross-section endogeneity — countries with strong inflation-aversion preferences may both choose independent central banks and have low inflation for cultural reasons.
Application: openness and inflation (Romer 1993). Cross-country evidence: more open economies have lower inflation. Mechanism: in an open economy, the ex-post gain from a monetary surprise is smaller (because PPP and import-price pass-through limit the output gain), reducing the equilibrium inflation bias. Romer’s regression: \pi = a - b\,\text{(openness)} with b<0 robustly significant.
Reputation and trigger strategies. Repeated-game analysis (Barro-Gordon 1983b) shows that with infinite-horizon repetition and sufficiently low discount rates, the commitment equilibrium can be sustained as a subgame-perfect equilibrium via trigger-strategy reputation: the public expects \pi=0 as long as the policymaker has delivered \pi=0, and reverts to high-inflation expectations after any deviation. This is the formal basis of the empirical “credibility takes years to build, minutes to lose” intuition.
Why this chapter matters. Chapter 9 is the textbook’s first detailed treatment of why money is non-neutral in the short run (sticky prices) and why monetary-policy choices have real welfare consequences (regime choice, credibility). The Mundell-Fleming-Dornbusch model remains the workhorse of practical international-finance teaching and policy analysis, and the credibility apparatus underlies modern central-banking institutional design (inflation targeting, central-bank independence, the ECB’s mandate). Chapter 10 then provides the microfounded general-equilibrium update.
Notation: P, P^*, \mathcal{E}, e, M, m, Y, y, r, i, q, \phi, \alpha, \beta, \theta, \mathcal{L}, \pi, \tilde y, \bar y. ~75K raw chars → ~1050 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.title: ch_10_redux_two_country_general_equilibrium
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Chapter 10 — Sticky-Price Models of Output, the Exchange Rate, and the Current Account (the “Redux” Model)
Formal spine. The textbook’s capstone — a microfounded two-country general-equilibrium sticky-price model that updates the Mundell-Fleming-Dornbusch framework with optimizing households, monopolistically-competitive firms, intertemporal budget constraints, and explicit welfare analysis. This is the Obstfeld-Rogoff (1995, 1996) “redux” model that founded the New Open-Economy Macroeconomics literature.
Notation. n — country size (Home share of world population, 1-n Foreign); z\in[0,1] — index of differentiated goods; \theta — elasticity of substitution between varieties (monopolistic-competition markup is \theta/(\theta-1)); C, C^* — Home and Foreign consumption indices over the continuum of varieties; p(z), p^*(z) — local-currency prices; \mathcal{E}, e — nominal exchange rate (log); P, P^* — consumer-price indices; M, M^* — money supplies; B — net foreign assets in real terms; \delta — interest-elasticity of money demand; \kappa — disutility-of-work parameter.
Demand and price indices. With CES preferences over varieties:
C = \left[\int_0^1 c(z)^{(\theta-1)/\theta}\,dz\right]^{\theta/(\theta-1)}, \qquad P = \left[\int_0^1 p(z)^{1-\theta}\,dz\right]^{1/(1-\theta)}.
Demand for individual variety z: c(z)=(p(z)/P)^{-\theta}C. Law of one price at the variety level: p(z)=\mathcal{E}p^*(z), so PPP holds at the aggregate price-index level under the chapter’s symmetric-preferences assumption.
Household problem. A representative Home household maximizes
U_t = \sum_{s=t}^\infty\beta^{s-t}\left[\log C_s + \chi\log\frac{M_s}{P_s} - \frac{\kappa}{2}y_s(z)^2\right]
subject to a flow budget constraint that combines bond holdings, money balances, and labor income from producing variety z (each household is also a monopoly producer of one variety).
Steady-state monopoly distortion. With flexible prices, monopolists set p(z)/P = \theta/(\theta-1)\cdot\kappa\,y(z)\,C — a constant markup over marginal cost. The implied steady-state output is
y_0 = \sqrt{\frac{\theta-1}{\theta\kappa}},
below the social optimum because of the markup. Monetary expansion that raises output toward the efficient level can be welfare-improving — the chapter’s central novel result.
Sticky prices: short-run vs long-run dynamics. Prices are preset one period in advance (p_0(z) fixed, p_1(z) flexible). An unanticipated permanent money shock has the following short-run effects (redux closed-form — log-linear approximation):

World consumption response: \hat c^W = \hat m^W (proportional to weighted world money shock m^W = nm + (1-n)m^*).
World real interest rate: \hat r = -\hat m^W/\eta (temporary monetary expansion lowers world real rate).
Exchange-rate response: \hat e = \hat m - \hat m^* in the long run (monetary neutrality), but with overshooting in the short run when the country experiencing the shock holds prices fixed.
Current-account response: asymmetric — the country whose money expands (Home) experiences a current-account surplus / deficit depending on parameter configurations; the chapter develops the closed-form \hat{CA} = (1-n)\,\delta(\hat m - \hat m^*)/[\delta(1+\theta)+2\theta].

Key welfare result (Result 10.1 — symmetric monopoly distortion only). Under the assumption that monopoly is the only distortion in the economy:
dU^R = \frac{\hat m^W}{\theta}.
The change in (the real component of) Home utility is proportional to the shock to world money, regardless of its origin. Foreign money expansion benefits Home as much as Home money expansion benefits Home. Intuition: in initial equilibrium, all monopolists set relative prices optimally, so small relative-price changes induced by exchange rates have only second-order welfare effects; the only first-order effect is the boost to global aggregate demand that mitigates the monopoly distortion. Implication: “beggar-thy-neighbor” is a misnomer in this benchmark — monetary policy spillovers are positive, not negative.
Caveat: distorting income taxes (sec 10.1.9). With a labor income tax \tau_L (introducing a second distortion alongside monopoly), the welfare result changes:
dU^R = \frac{(1-n)\hat m^*}{\theta} \cdot\left[1 - \frac{\tau_L(\theta-1)^2}{\delta(1+\theta)+2}\right].
For \theta close to 1 (heavy monopoly distortion), Foreign monetary expansion still benefits Home. For \theta large (more competitive economy, dominant tax distortion), Foreign expansion can lower Home welfare — the beggar-thy-neighbor mechanism re-emerges. Lesson: welfare conclusions about monetary spillovers are sensitive to which distortion dominates empirically.
Imperfect competition with preset nontraded goods prices (sec 10.2 — Dornbusch overshooting revisited). Replace traded-good monopoly with monopoly in nontradables. With \varepsilon\neq 1 in the money-demand specification (general isoelastic real-balance utility), the model can exhibit Dornbusch-style exchange-rate overshooting. Closed-form short-run nominal-exchange-rate response:
\hat e = \frac{\beta+(1-\beta)\varepsilon}{\beta+(1-\beta)(1-\gamma+\gamma\varepsilon)}\,\hat m,
with overshooting \hat e>\hat m when \varepsilon>1 (high interest-elasticity of money demand) — i.e. the same mechanism that drives Dornbusch overshooting in chapter 9 reappears in the microfounded setting.
Government spending and productivity shocks (sec 10.3). Productivity shock A\uparrow in tradables: real exchange rate appreciates (Balassa-Samuelson channel from chapter 4); current-account surplus on impact (intertemporal-substitution motive); persistent terms-of-trade shift. Government-spending shocks crowd out private consumption with predictable Mundell-Fleming-style spillovers but with sharper welfare implications now that consumption enters utility additively.
Nominal wage rigidities (sec 10.4). Replacing sticky prices with sticky wages gives a different model: monopoly distortion now in labor-market markup rather than goods-market markup. Pass-through application: with sticky wages and producer-currency pricing, exchange-rate movements transmit to import prices fully; with sticky wages and local-currency pricing, exchange-rate movements affect domestic profit margins, not import prices — the chapter foreshadows the LCP / PCP debate that dominates 2000s open-macro literature.
Why this chapter matters. Chapter 10 is the textbook’s signature contribution and the reason graduate students still read this 1996 textbook in 2025. The redux model is the canonical template for every subsequent New Open-Economy Macroeconomics paper (Lane 2001 survey; Clarida-Gali-Gertler 2002; Galí-Monacelli 2005; Engel 2011); the closed-form welfare result is the cleanest known welfare-analysis-of-monetary-policy result in any open-economy setting; and the chapter’s careful enumeration of how welfare conclusions depend on which distortions are operative anticipates 30 years of monetary-policy-spillover debates (Cooper coordination, Fed-vs-ECB asymmetric monetary stimulus, BIS “international monetary system” critique).
Notation: n, z, \theta, C, C^*, p(z), \mathcal{E}, e, P, P^*, M, M^*, B, \delta, \kappa, \chi, \beta, y(z), \hat{}, m^W, c^W, r, \tau_L, \varepsilon, \gamma, A. ~95K raw chars → ~1200 words.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/mauric.content:
Maurice Obstfeld Foundations Of International Macroeconomics — Chapter Deep Dives
10 chapters

Ch.1 — Intertemporal Trade and the Current Account Balance
A two-period small open endowment economy (later extended to investment, two-region world, taxation, labor mobility) is the load-bearing scaffold for the entire textbook: every later chapter is some elaboration, generalization, or distorti…
Ch.2 — Dynamics of Small Open Economies
Generalize the two-period model of Chapter 1 to an infinite horizon with both deterministic and stochastic income, retaining a representative consumer with intertemporally additive preferences.

Drop the representative-consumer simplification and replace it with overlapping generations (OLG) of finitely-lived agents.

Drop the single-good assumption of chapters 1–3 and introduce multiple consumption goods — most importantly traded vs nontraded — to study the determinants of relative prices, real exchange rates, and the terms of trade.

Replace deterministic foresight with state-contingent uncertainty and study the role of international trade in risky assets.
