He insisted Mallaby read it before their first long conversation; the science-fiction alter ego is part of his self-narration as much as Foundation, Banks’s Culture series, and Blade Runner.
The chapter then traces the formation of the AI ambition. At eight he bought a ZX Spectrum 48K with chess prize money; at twelve a Commodore Amiga 500. David Levy’s Chess Computer Handbook introduced him to Claude Shannon (whose 1950 paper proposed a “general-purpose computer” that could engage in induction, “general principles, something of the nature of judgment, and considerable trial and error, rather than a strict, unalterable computing process”) and to the three components of a chess program: representation, evaluation, tree search. Hassabis ported Levy’s chess-program structure to Othello, christening his program Fire and Water — a 12-year-old’s first infinity machine that could beat his five-year-old brother George.
At ~15 Hassabis won runner-up in Bullfrog Productions’ Space Invaders contest with a chess-grid variant called Chess Invaders, then talked himself into a job with Peter Molyneux. Working on Theme Park (and later getting a copy of Hofstadter’s Gödel, Escher, Bach from Molyneux), Hassabis absorbed the foundational claim — what the mind could do, computers should be able to do — and synthesized it with Iain Banks’s utopian vision of a post-scarcity AI society. After meeting a Carnegie Mellon AI professor at a US conference and astonishing him with the Theme Park demo’s character-state simulation, Hassabis “decided then that I was going to dedicate my career to working on AI. I already had the kernel of the idea for what eventually became DeepMind.” Peter Molyneux’s Black & White god-simulation — discussed but not yet built — would later be the metaphor Mallaby uses to read Hassabis’s character (the “white god” exercising power through enthusiasm rather than control).

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_03_deep_philosophical_questions
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 2 — “Deep Philosophical Questions”
Hassabis enters Cambridge in 1994, refusing Molyneux’s £500,000 retention offer (≈$1.7M today). The pull is the Life Story film about Watson and Crick — the Nobel-vintage scientific romance is a load-bearing part of his self-narrative. Crick’s “What’s fun? Oh, the big questions” becomes the recruitment slogan he later applies to himself.
Hassabis decides physics is too hard a competitive game (“Even Richard Feynman couldn’t do it. He died without understanding everything”) and reframes his strategy: AI will be the lever to unlock physics later. Cambridge undergraduate life mixes electronic music, a borrowed Porsche 911 Turbo (lent by Molyneux for his commute back to Bullfrog), and table football championships. He starts learning Go from a professor whose home he bicycles to weekly. A passing conversation with a biologist friend about protein folding plants the “Fermat’s Last Theorem for biology” seed that AlphaFold will harvest 25 years later.
The intellectual core of the chapter is the friendship with David Silver and the joint critique of symbolic AI. The 1956 Dartmouth workshop’s premise — “every feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it” — produces the symbolic tradition in which programmers feed concepts as logical syllogisms: humans are mortal, Socrates is human, therefore Socrates is mortal. The 1984 Cyc project (Doug Lenat) tried to encode commonsense at scale (“you can’t be in two places at once”; “when drinking a cup of coffee, you hold the open end up”). Hassabis and Silver, both readers of Gödel, Escher, Bach, see Gödel’s incompleteness theorem as the formal confirmation of an obvious empirical fact: “We don’t speak in first order logic and yet we can understand each other.” Real intelligence is induction — pattern recognition in copious examples — not deduction.
The chapter establishes the problem of induction as the field’s defining unsolved challenge: “AI has utterly failed, over a quarter century, to solve problems that philosophy has utterly failed to solve over two millennia” (Hilary Putnam, paraphrased). Tutorials with John Daugman (the iris-recognition algorithm inventor) push Hassabis to a two-part epiphany: first, information is the fundamental unit of reality; second, an infinity machine — a computer that learns its own algorithms by induction — is the most powerful imaginable tool to apprehend reality. “AI may be the right description language for biology, because biology is so messy, emergent, dynamic, and complex.”
In 1997, Hassabis takes a job back with Molyneux on Black & White — a god-game where digital creatures use reinforcement learning (slap = bad behavior, pat = good) to update their algorithmic preferences. This is Hassabis’s first hands-on contact with RL. But he sours on Molyneux’s manipulation (“Magus” is the literary reference) and decides at the end of Cambridge to start his own company. Britain’s lack of an entrepreneurial ecosystem makes this a “shocking” choice for a Cambridge undergraduate.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_04_jedi_elixir
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 3 — The Jedi (Elixir, 1998-2005)
Hassabis founds Elixir in July 1998 with David Silver, Joe McDonagh, and Tim Clarke. The startup name comes from a dictionary (“the quintessential part of any substance”). London VCs are not real VCs — Hassabis pitches one outfit whose two associates take him to a restaurant for three bottles of wine, then a pub for lager, then offer him not money but a job as a currency trader. A different group offers £2M for half the equity; Hassabis refuses. “They liked us, but they wanted our soul in exchange for the money.” Angels (an industrialist, a lawyer, Molyneux himself) finally come through.
The first project is Republic: The Revolution, a dictator-game inspired by the 1995 Russian invasion of Chechnya. McDonagh researches Russian satrapies in the Society for Anglo-Soviet Cooperation reading room; the team designs Novistrana with 1,500 differentiated characters and “a million individual living, breathing people.” Tim Clarke codes a graphics engine Hassabis dubs the “infinite polygon engine” — rivals call it the “infinite monkey engine.”
The chapter’s structural lesson is charisma as double-edged blade. David Silver coins the term “Jedi mind trick” for Hassabis’s persuasion: at the May 2001 E3 expo demo in Los Angeles, Silver stays up all night before the flight trying to make the demo work; the souped-up computer (with 8× normal memory smuggled in) crashes during Hassabis’s first presentation, but Hassabis verbally improvises through, citing Elias Canetti’s Crowds and Power, and Republic still wins an award for best upcoming game. The hardware crash exposes the over-inspiration trap: Silver had been bullied into believing the impossible was possible. Hassabis later: “I’m making the judgment this is possible because the engineers are telling me it’s possible; but they’re only telling me it’s possible because I’ve over-inspired them.”
Silver burns out and quits for the south of France, where he reads Richard Sutton’s textbook on reinforcement learning. The Sutton-revelation — “AI is a system that learns for itself how to solve problems” — sets the trajectory for everything that follows. Silver enrolls in 2004 for a PhD in Alberta (Sutton’s lab) on Go.
When Elixir folds in 2005, Hassabis is “in pieces” but resolves to do a PhD in neuroscience under Eleanor Maguire at UCL. The reasoning is methodological: human intelligence is the only “existence proof” of general intelligence, so to build AI you must understand the brain first. With co-author Dharshan Kumaran (a chess-circuit friend turned doctor-turned-neuroscientist), Hassabis publishes a 2007 PNAS paper showing that hippocampus damage impairs both memory and imagination — i.e. memory and imagination share neural machinery. The paper is named one of Science’s top neuroscience breakthroughs of the year and accumulates 1700+ citations. Mallaby reads this as Hassabis’s first major theoretical commitment: reality is constructed by the mind; the brain in the jar can be deceived; intelligence is reconstruction, not retrieval.
A psychologist’s framing closes the chapter: charismatic figures cannot be all-bad (they’d lose their following) or all-good (collisions of interest force prevailing); it is the oscillation between inspiring and controlling that produces dependence in followers. Mallaby applies this to Molyneux explicitly and notes that Hassabis’s character — for good or ill — would be tested by the AI mission.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_05_gang_of_three
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 4 — The Gang of Three
The chapter assembles the trio that founds DeepMind: Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg, Mustafa Suleyman.
In early 2009, finishing his neuroscience PhD, Hassabis enrolls as a postdoc at the Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit at UCL. The Gatsby’s founding director was Geoffrey Hinton (now in Toronto, working on deep belief networks); the current director is Peter Dayan (who showed RL reward signals mimic brain dopamine). But most Gatsby faculty dismiss AGI as “far-fetched.” Scanning the postdoc bios, Hassabis finds only one researcher confessing to AGI ambition: Shane Legg.
Side trips to MIT (with Tomaso Poggio, who later names Hassabis alongside Feynman and Crick as “going to win the Nobel no matter what”) and Harvard confirm the AI-skeptic monoculture. At MIT, the head of the Computer Science and AI Lab, Patrick Winston, dismisses Hassabis’s plans for reinforcement-learning + deep-learning as “just nonsense.” Hassabis writes a 2009 business plan for “Project Orion” — a brain-modeled AI start-up — but with no capital, no cofounder, and an establishment that views AGI as crazier than video games, the project is going nowhere.
The Gatsby elevator encounter with Shane Legg in October 2009 — Legg en route to the Singularity Summit in New York — is Hassabis’s pivot. After Legg’s “Halloween Scenario” lecture later that month (warning of existential AI risk in his “excited” rather than alarmed tone), Hassabis introduces himself.
Legg’s biography mirrors Hassabis’s eccentricity: New Zealand childhood (Rotorua), tested above-gifted IQ, weightlifting and ballet at university, a database-engineer detour, then Ben Goertzel’s Intelligenesis (1999-2001) where he helped coin the term artificial general intelligence (he convinced Goertzel to retitle the manuscript from Real AI to avoid antagonizing the field). Reading Kurzweil’s Age of Spiritual Machines convinced Legg that Moore’s Law made AI inevitable, so he did a PhD with Marcus Hutter in Switzerland on measuring intelligence. The Legg/Hutter definition: “Intelligence measures an agent’s ability to achieve goals in a wide range of environments.” By 2009 Legg has finished his PhD (“Machine Super Intelligence”) and arrived at the Gatsby.
December 29, 2009: Legg emails Hassabis at midnight saying he is ready to do an AGI startup. They name it DeepMind — a triple reference to Hinton’s deep learning, IBM’s Deep Blue, and Hitchhiker’s Deep Thought.
The third cofounder, Mustafa Suleyman, is even less likely. Born August 1984 to a Syrian Muslim taxi-driver father and English nurse-convert mother. At 15 his parents split (mother to NZ, father back to Syria); Mustafa fends for himself and his brother on candy-bar arbitrage and used-BMW flipping. Top of his class at Queen Elizabeth’s School in North London, he gets into Oxford to study philosophy and theology in 2002. Drops out in his second year (2004) — “I always had nothing, so I was fearless when it came to flipping the table.” He runs the Muslim Youth Helpline, works at the London mayor’s office, cofounds a conflict-resolution outfit Reos Partners. Long friendship with Hassabis’s brother George (poker at the Vic casino, milkshake stand at Camden market) gives him access to Demis. By 2009 he is convinced that to “make impact on the world” he needs to become a technologist.
July 15, 2010: at the Vic casino’s Poker Room, Hassabis (wearing dark Blade Runner shades) wins fifth place for ~$2,000. Over chocolate cake, Hassabis pitches Suleyman on AGI: “We saw technology as a force multiplier… The goal was to put one unit in and get a million units out.” Two days later Suleyman emails Hassabis a Wired profile of Sergey Brin’s medical-research interests, suggesting Brin as a possible billionaire backer. Suleyman starts helping flesh out the business plan for the upcoming Singularity Summit pitch.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_06_founding_deepmind
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 5 — Founding DeepMind
August 14, 2010, Singularity Summit, San Francisco. Hassabis, Legg, and Suleyman come desperate for capital. The DeepMind business plan runs ~30 pages, arguing AGI is necessary (because of an “ingenuity gap” — society’s problems exceed human cognitive capacity), possible (Moore’s Law makes 10²⁰ calculations/second feasible by 2025; deep learning is on the cusp), and that DeepMind’s neuroscience-integrated approach is superior. The plan promises agents (rather than systems), grounded in concept-mastery, using insights from hippocampus + prefrontal cortex research. With hindsight, Mallaby notes that the neuroscience emphasis fades after 2015 and large language models eventually bypass DeepMind’s plan to “program conceptual understanding explicitly” — yet the road map’s compute and timeline projections turn out to be roughly accurate (“AGI by ~2030” looked outlandish in 2010 but appears slightly conservative by 2026).
The pitch to Peter Thiel, financed but absent from the conference, is choreographed. Eliezer Yudkowsky walks Legg and Hassabis over to Thiel’s home; Hassabis hooks Thiel with chess (the bishop-knight value tension) rather than a startup elevator pitch. The next day Thiel meets them in his workout gear, butler-served Diet Coke; he judges DeepMind A+ on science, F on business model, but agrees with the Founders Fund frame that missionary entrepreneurs don’t quit. Founders Fund’s Luke Nosek — already burned by Halcyon Molecular and SpaceX — falls for Hassabis “like a lightning bolt” and demands a board seat against Thiel’s normal preference for hands-off VC.
December 2010: Founders Fund wires $2.3M for a bit less than half of DeepMind. The David Gammon test (the religious investor whose 14-year-old son Cameron must approve any pitch) had earlier brought in another £100,000. Equity split: Hassabis owns ~9× more than Legg (“DeepMind was my idea”) and ~14× more than Suleyman (“uncredentialed latecomer,” but earned title by negotiation aggressiveness).
The first office is a Russell Square attic, near the British Museum, the London Mathematical Society, and the pedestrian crossing where Leo Szilard conceived nuclear chain reaction in September 1933. Hassabis explicitly compares the founding to the Manhattan Project: “we are building AGI to be positive in the world, but AGI is definitely momentous in the same way that the bomb was.”
The recruitment problem dominates the first year. Top scientists believe AGI is impossible. Ilya Sutskever (Hinton’s protégé, later OpenAI cofounder) refuses; David Silver insists on returning his DeepMind shares to preserve academic independence (a decision that cost him a fortune at the Google acquisition). Yann LeCun keeps his distance: “Frankly, my original opinion before meeting Demis was, this is yet another company that claims AGI is just around the corner and it’s complete BS.”
Hassabis builds the DeepMind platform on three principles: (1) conviction — only “hardcore believers” hired, and Legg recalls that 80% of academic AI scientists “literally roll their eyes” at the AGI pitch, which becomes a useful filter; (2) time — fund science by generating side revenues (a fashion-recommendation algorithm, an early gaming project) so that DeepMind can survive multi-year research timelines; (3) culture — hire “glue people” (program managers) to support socially awkward researchers; treat the office as a library so deep work can happen.
In December 2011 Founders Fund leads a 7.9M round with Skype cofounder Jaan Tallinn adding 2M (Tallinn’s motive is to slow DeepMind down for safety reasons — he invests to apply brakes). Daan Wierstra — friend of Legg’s from Switzerland — joins as the first PhD AI scientist in September 2011, declaring “let’s build Terminators” until Hassabis tells him to stop scaring people. The Russell Square office overflows; in September 2012 DeepMind moves to Bernard Street.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_07_atari
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 6 — Atari (DQN, 2012-2013)
October 2012, Florence: Alex Krizhevsky (Hinton’s protégé) presents the deep-learning ImageNet result at ECCV — his network is roughly twice as accurate as the runner-up; Hinton, Krizhevsky and Sutskever sell their three-person company to Google for $44M two months later. The deep-learning revolution is on. Hassabis’s 2010 thesis — that deep learning is on the cusp of a breakthrough — is vindicated.
DeepMind’s strategy is to go beyond Hinton: combine deep learning (perception) with reinforcement learning (action) in a unified agent. The chapter introduces Vlad Mnih, the soft-spoken Ukrainian-Canadian Hinton PhD student who had bounced between Toronto (deep learning) and Alberta (reinforcement learning under Csaba Szepesvári). Mnih’s diagnosis of the field: Hinton said “this is how the brain works,” Sutton said “this is how the mind works,” but the two camps did not talk. Mnih wants to bridge them.
The DeepMind brain trust resolves a Hassabis-vs-Legg argument about evaluation: Legg wants DeepMind-built metrics; Hassabis (and Silver) want external yardsticks for credibility with investors. The Atari suite — 1970s-80s arcade games with primitive graphics, a constantly-updating score, and dozens of titles — wins. The agent gets only the raw pixels, a joystick, and the score; it must learn entirely by trial and error.
Multiple DeepMind teams attack Atari with different approaches. Mnih and Koray Kavukcuoglu (a Yann LeCun NYU alumnus who later becomes DeepMind’s research director) adopt a third approach: deep learning for perceptual input + Q-learning (reinforcement learning) for action selection.
Mnih’s first innovation is to feed deep learning into the RL update step: as the agent collects (state, action, reward) experiences, these are fed into a neural network that learns to predict Q-values. This dramatically shortcuts the “fill out every cell of the Q-table” challenge. But basic RL agents collect correlated experiences (the agent gets stuck in one corner of the maze), and deep learning needs randomized samples. David Silver contributes the second key innovation: experience replay. RL had used memory replay since the 1990s, but Silver proposes storing (state, action, reward) tuples in a buffer and sampling randomly from them to break correlation. Hassabis recognizes this as parallel to the hippocampus replaying memories during sleep so the neocortex can consolidate them.
July 7, 2013, Wimbledon final (Andy Murray vs. Djokovic). Mnih nervously checks his agent training Pong between points. The agent has been losing 21-0 for days, then suddenly scores 4 points; Mnih watches a live frame and the paddle is moving toward the ball deliberately. The agent has learned. Within days it is superhuman at Pong and Breakout.
Seaquest exposes a third problem: the agent zaps subs monomaniacally, ignoring oxygen and divers. The agent’s Q-table reveals an upward spiral of optimism — every iteration adds confidence to past-successful actions, producing a “cognitive bubble” of expected values. Mnih’s third innovation: separate the playing network from the target network. The target/coach network observes results and updates its parameters, but only periodically transfers them to the player network. This is patience-as-stabilizer; the playing network is forced to keep exploring instead of locking into a premature strategy.
December 2013, NIPS at Harrah’s Lake Tahoe: Mnih presents the Deep Q-Network (DQN). Videos show the agent’s mastery of Seaquest, Space Invaders, Boxing, and especially Breakout — where it discovers the canonical “tunnel through the bricks, ricochet off the back wall” strategy. “The room went completely silent,” Silver remembers. The audience laughs at Boxing’s ruthless violence. The Atari demo is DeepMind’s coming-out party. Silver notes that, unlike Elixir (where Hassabis aimed for the most ambitious game first), at DeepMind he had let researchers tinker until the team was ready, then chosen the right calibrated benchmark. Both the moral and the technique would carry forward to AlphaGo.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_08_get_google
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 7-8 — Thiel Trouble & Get Google (2012-2014)
October 8, 2012: Luke Nosek flies back from a SpaceX Falcon 9 launch on Musk’s private jet, alongside Larry Page. Page mentions that Google plans to buy Hinton’s deep-learning boutique. Musk one-ups him: “There’s only one AI company that I think is going to work. And I’m an investor in that company, DeepMind.” Page types DeepMind into his Android. Nosek panics: “Larry has wanted to build AGI his whole life! He’s going to try to get DeepMind!”
Hassabis, when warned, responds calmly: “this could be good. Let’s play this out.” His private vision of post-AGI life, recounted to Mallaby, is Banks’s Culture series at scale: asteroid mining, fusion energy, universal basic provision (free housing, healthcare, basic transport — money irrelevant) with optional work to earn extras like a Ferrari. Hassabis’s posture toward Google as steward is conditional but open.
Through 2013 the courtship escalates. June 2013 castle weekend at Tarrytown for Talulah Riley/Musk’s birthday: Page proposes a walk with Hassabis, asks him in his strained whisper-voice why bother building DeepMind independently when Google’s resources are available. “Would I be happier looking back on building a multibillion-dollar business or helping solve intelligence?” Hassabis frames the choice. “It was an easy choice.” The pivotal personal feature of Page: he is “a scientist,” not a businessperson — Hassabis felt Page “would’ve taken his own offer.”
Fall 2013: the three founders fly to Mountain View. Atari demos. Suleyman flips the negotiation: he refuses to discuss price up front, instead pressing for research budget and ethics + safety guarantees. He’s playing poker — invoking Thiel, Solina Chau, Musk as supposed alternative backers — to force Google’s hand on a structure including an independent oversight board with last-say authority on AI deployment.
Mark Zuckerberg makes a competing bid. Suleyman flies to California, served whiskey by Amin Zoufonoun (Facebook’s M&A head). Facebook’s offer: lowball share price plus a vast signing bonus to founders — making them personally richer. Zuckerberg himself hosts Hassabis at his Palo Alto home; Hassabis tests him by raising VR, AR, and 3D printing — Zuckerberg expresses equal excitement about all of them. “Facebook offered more money, but I wanted somebody who really understood why AI would be bigger than all these other things.” Spurned, Zuckerberg redoubles, hiring Yann LeCun (with both NYU professorship and New York residence as conditions accepted) and trying to poach Koray Kavukcuoglu — the latter would have torpedoed the Google deal had Kavukcuoglu accepted.
December 29, 2013: Google’s M&A team flies a Gulfstream to London with a special bed for Hinton’s back pain. Jeff Dean inspects Mnih’s Atari code (research code is “famously hacky” but Dean approves). The “crossing of the Rubicon moment” as Hassabis calls it — once Google sees the code, refusing the deal would be ruinous.
A bizarre interlude: Nosek and Musk, at a Los Angeles party, retreat to a closet with Riley to Skype-call Hassabis at 3am London time. They propose Tesla acquires DeepMind, then SpaceX (“AI for robots on Mars!”). Hassabis points out Tesla loses money quarterly and SpaceX has no compute. Nosek and Musk fail to assemble alternative financing. Musk’s hostility to the Google sale is the seed of OpenAI.
The price negotiation: Google’s M&A chief Don Harrison’s standard “price per engineer” is ~10M each (Hinton's three-person boutique sold for ~15M each). Hassabis and Suleyman demand roughly twice the rate, citing Atari as proof DeepMind is more than a team — it’s an architecture. Hinton lobbies internally that Hassabis alone is worth $150M. The non-monetary terms are tougher: operational autonomy, London base, military-applications ban, Ethics & Safety Review Board with external oversight. Harrison: “I was in front of our board of directors selling a deal that wasn’t just about the price… a structure that reduced our control over an asset that we were spending a great deal of money on.” Google swallows the constraints because Hassabis is the irreplaceable element.
End of January 2014: Google buys DeepMind for 650M. Hassabis nets 136M, Suleyman 34M, Legg 29M. DeepMind becomes a roughly autonomous Alphabet subsidiary spending ~$260M/year on staff — six times its prior total burn. Hassabis’s fundraising ordeal ends; the British “national champion sold cheap” lament begins. Mallaby’s reading: from Hassabis’s perspective the trade — research budget, autonomy, London — was overwhelmingly worth it.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_09_intuition_alphago
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 9 — Intuition (AlphaGo, 2014-2016)
May 2014, Mountain View. Hassabis tells Sergey Brin that DeepMind’s Atari techniques can solve Go. Brin is a Go player; he is incredulous: “Wouldn’t that be impossible?” Hassabis commits to two years.
The chapter’s analytical arc is a meditation on intuition. Go’s combinatorial complexity (10^170 possible board states, more than atoms in the observable universe) defeats the brute-force alpha-beta pruning that worked for chess. Daniel Kahneman’s System One (fast, intuitive, pattern-based) is supposed to be inaccessible to computers; System Two (slow, deliberative, logical) is computers’ natural mode. Most AI researchers in 2014 considered Go a peak that would not fall for a decade.
David Silver had spent his Alberta PhD on Go, replacing alpha-beta pruning with Monte Carlo Tree Search — instead of analyzing every move sequence and pruning bad ones, follow a small number of sequences all the way to game-end, then reweight future searches based on which lines led to victory. He calls it “introspection” — System Two thinking. Silver brought Aja Huang (Taiwan, MCTS PhD, beat all rivals at the 2010 Computer Olympiad) to DeepMind in 2012, but waited years for the springboard.
Spring 2014: Atari + ImageNet provide that springboard. Silver proposes that a deep-learning network can mimic human intuition by mapping board positions onto the moves that human pros chose. Silver recruits Chris Maddison (Hinton PhD intern) and Ilya Sutskever (a 2008 attempt at the same idea, with much smaller networks). Maddison ingests 150,000 games × 200 moves = 30M (position, move) pairs. The 2014 network is 250× larger than Sutskever’s 2008 attempt; it predicts a human pro’s move correctly more than 50% of the time, achieving strong amateur strength just by pattern matching, no tree search. “Human intuition was not so magical after all. A machine could reproduce it with the trick of mapping one thing onto another.”
Silver applies Tom Perkins’s white-hot risks heuristic: prove the hardest piece works first, then scale. The hardest piece — replicating intuition — is done. Now: defeat the world champion. Aja Huang complains: “IT—NOT—POSSIBLE!” — meaning DeepMind’s hybrid system has just beaten the commercial world #1 (Crazy Stone), so why not stop? Silver insists: the goal is the human champion.
Silver argues with Sutskever (who at NIPS 2014 has just stolen the show with sequence-to-sequence translation, declaring “if you have a very large dataset and a very large neural network, then success is guaranteed”). Sutskever wants to scale up the policy network alone and skip MCTS — humans don’t search far ahead, why would AI? Silver responds that AI should exceed humans, not match them: “If you just pattern-match what humans do, it is not going to take you all the way to beating the top human. The system needs to discover new moves which aren’t humanlike.” This Silver-vs-Sutskever debate prefigures the 2017+ DeepMind-vs-OpenAI tension over RL vs. transformers.
The architectural completion: Arthur Guez (Silver’s former PhD student) builds a value net that evaluates board positions for win-probability, complementing Maddison’s policy net that proposes moves. Together with MCTS and self-play — once human game data runs out, the agent generates its own training data by playing itself, with the value net (trained on objective win/loss) updating off self-play data — the system enters a virtuous cycle.
October 2015: secret 5-game match against Fan Hui, three-time European Go champion. AlphaGo wins 5-0; Fan calls the computer “like a wall.” January 2016: the Nature cover story (Hassabis’s PR achievement — he had befriended a Nature editor for a year to break their no-CS-papers convention). Hassabis announces the Lee Sedol match for March; Zuckerberg, panicking that Facebook’s parallel Go effort will be eclipsed, rushes a hasty PR pre-emption that flops.
Right before the Lee match, DeepMind ports AlphaGo to Google’s new Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), which round numbers to integers for trillions of extra multiplications per second. AlphaGo-on-TPU beats AlphaGo-on-GPU 80% of the time. Eric Schmidt visits: “How’s it going?” “The metrics look good, but we still have some hallucinations.” “Great, just don’t fuck it up.”
March 9-15, 2016, Seoul Four Seasons. >200M viewers — twice the Deep Blue/Kasparov audience, more than the Super Bowl. Lee Sedol promises to “do my best to protect human intelligence.” Game 1: AlphaGo wins. Game 2: Move 37 — a black stone in a mostly-empty zone on the right flank, on which the world #1 Western Go player Michael Redmond places, removes, then reluctantly replaces the corresponding stone, muttering “no, that can’t be right.” It was right. Lee, after the loss: “I am quite speechless.” Game 3: another AlphaGo win; Lee apologizes “to all humans.” Game 4: Lee’s Hand of God Move 78 — AlphaGo flounders into hallucinations and resigns. Game 5: AlphaGo. Final: 4-1.
Thore Graepel (DeepMind hire, lost the first internal calibration match) describes it: “It played stones that appeared to be randomly sprinkled across the board. But as the game progressed, thirty, fifty, a hundred moves in, you’d feel all of these stones work together… the noose is tightening around your neck.” Graepel: “This is how we have to imagine the future. In the domain of Go, we have achieved superhuman intelligence. We can observe what it feels like to interact with it.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_10_out_of_eden
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 10 — Out of Eden (Safety Board Failure & OpenAI’s Birth, 2015)
The chapter dissects the August 14, 2015 Ethics & Safety Board meeting at SpaceX and the subsequent founding of OpenAI as a singleton thesis vs. multiparty thesis schism among AI’s lead actors.
Hassabis had baked safety oversight into the Google acquisition (Suleyman’s poker leverage, ch. 7-8). The first formal board session was hosted at SpaceX with Musk presiding — a 2015 gamble to placate Musk after his earlier failed attempt to acquire DeepMind. Musk fulminated in the months prior, calling Hassabis “an evil genius” because he had once worked on a video game called Evil Genius; donated $10M to the Future of Life Institute; called for AI regulation while simultaneously hiring AI scientists to Tesla.
The May 25, 2015 Sam Altman email to Musk — “if it’s going to happen anyway, it seems like it would be good for someone other than Google to do it first” — and a follow-up June 24 proposal to “start a Manhattan Project for AI” with a five-person foundation board (Musk, Bill Gates, Altman among them) precede the SpaceX meeting. Altman shares his birthday with Oppenheimer.
Three days before the SpaceX meeting, Musk’s birthday at a Napa resort. Page tells Musk over a fire pit that he “looks forward to a time when people might merge with intelligent machines, or when machines might simply replace humans” — survival of the fittest, carbon vs. silicon, “evolution will ensure that the best form of intelligence won out.” Musk objects; Page calls Musk a speciesist — “a bigot with a soppy prejudice in favor of carbon over silicon.” This becomes Musk’s structural justification for OpenAI: AI cannot be trusted to “a transhumanist in Mountain View.” A Page acquaintance later confirms to Mallaby: “Larry sometimes seems to think we don’t need hummingbirds, or whales in the ocean.”
The chapter’s central conceptual content is Hassabis’s singleton vision vs. Reid Hoffman’s multiparty vision. Hassabis imagines a final-stage AGI push from a secluded research center modeled on the Manhattan Project (Los Alamos in the desert) plus Ender’s Game secrecy. He occasionally tells job candidates to expect a “bunker”; later, more politely, an international scientific agency modeled on CERN, including Plato’s “council of the hundred wisest people from all the corners of earth” — even the pope. The thinking: a unified effort can be careful; a race cannot.
Hoffman, the LinkedIn founder, derives the opposite verdict from political history. After Hiroshima/Nagasaki, Oppenheimer urged a CERN-style international monopoly on nuclear weapons; nothing came of it. Multiparty democracy + shared safety norms is the more realistic model: several frontier labs, each housing one part of the AI community, balanced by good-faith commitments to alignment. Hoffman, an OpenAI backer, makes this case explicitly at SpaceX.
The SpaceX meeting itself: 12 power-brokers including Suleyman, Hassabis, Legg, Musk, Hoffman, Toby Ord, Peter Dayan, Google’s leadership. “Larry and Elon hated sitting in the same room as each other” (Suleyman). Suleyman’s presentation focuses not on AI x-risk but on near-term social cohesion: AI will cause mass unemployment, concentrate wealth in tech elites; “the pitchforks are coming.” Page rejects the unemployment thesis (technology has always created more jobs than it destroyed); Schmidt notes unemployment is low. Suleyman objects: AGI is general — it will replace jobs, not just tasks, and at scale that breaks the historical compensation pattern.
A SpaceX server closet has a sign reading Skynet — Hoffman points it out to Hassabis, who tells Musk: “You know what you would start saying about me if I had something like that on one of my systems!”
The meeting “did nothing to heal division” — Hassabis’s verdict. Months later, the Musk-Altman conspiracy crystallizes into OpenAI as an explicitly anti-Google, anti-DeepMind not-for-profit. Hassabis’s reading: “our supposed advisers were really our rivals… powerful people who are able to understand the impact of the technology, they’re not just going to sit on the sidelines.” Hoffman is also among OpenAI’s backers. The Fall metaphor — DeepMind’s expulsion from Eden — frames the chapter title.
The chapter’s structural lesson is that infinity-potential technology cannot be governed by goodwill alone. When stakes are existential and resources astronomical, every “advisor” with technical understanding will eventually become a competitor. Hassabis’s later self-criticism: “Maybe at that point I was naive. I thought we would be having a proper philosophical discussion about what I could see coming.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_11_p0_plus_plus_and_mario
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 11-14 — P0 Plus Plus, NHS, and the Project Mario Failure (2015-2019)
The chapters trace Mustafa Suleyman’s parallel AI-for-good experiment with the British NHS and his attempt with Hassabis to spin DeepMind out from Google as Project Mario.
The NHS health gambit. Suleyman, frustrated by the SpaceX failure and animated by his Muslim Youth Helpline social-justice framework, applies the leftist-Marxist “Inventing the Future” manifesto (left-utopian technocracy) to the National Health Service — the world’s largest fax-machine purchaser, drowning in paper records. Working with Dr. Chris Laing at the Royal Free Hospital, Suleyman builds Streams — a smartphone alert app for acute kidney injury (AKI). The Streams pilot causes the share of urgent AKI cases that go unnoticed to fall from 12.4% to 3.3%; nurses spend more time with patients; cost per AKI patient drops. Parallel projects with Moorfields (macular degeneration) and a breast cancer mammogram model show comparable promise. In 2018, Nature Medicine publishes the Moorfields retinal model.
The Daily Mail backlash. May 3, 2016: google handed patients’ files — the tabloid claims 1.6M records were passed without permission. Suleyman: the charges were garbled (Google never saw Streams data; the contract was the standard NHS template; Streams data must retain patient identities precisely because the use case is per-patient alerts). Two formal inquiries clear DeepMind. But the scandal coincides with the 2018 Cambridge Analytica revelations, and the public-mood shift renders DeepMind Health untenable. Streams is eventually shut down. Hassabis: “I felt strongly that the charge sheet was garbled… without DeepMind’s ties to Google, the Daily Mail would not have run the article.” Dario Amodei’s later economic gloss: “AI is useful only if complementary inputs are available… in the AI age, we should be talking about the marginal returns to intelligence.” Sometimes the limiting factor is bureaucracy, not algorithms.
The “P0 Plus Plus” management dysfunction. Suleyman’s Applied division uses an escalating priority taxonomy — P1, P2, P3 (won’t do), P0 (fire), then P0 Plus, then P0 Plus Plus — and a Green/Amber/Red traffic light extended to Double Red. “Everything is competitive, and competition brings this mad rush.” Suleyman fires off commands and disappears, contradicting his own prior orders, late-night all-caps emails, public berating. Dominic King (the surgeon-PhD-economist Suleyman recruited): “It felt like the company might be splitting.” Suleyman acknowledges later: “I was managing a portfolio of businesses and I did too many things… It was definitely a significant weakness.”
Project Mario (2015-2017): the failed spinout. Suleyman and Hassabis attempt to negotiate a 3-3-3 board structure (3 DeepMind, 3 Alphabet, 3 independent) for a semi-autonomous DeepMind under Google’s 2015 Alphabet restructuring. Five rounds of talks with Larry Page; Hassabis even runs a secret hedge-fund-style high-frequency-trading project (recruiting ~20 researchers, exploring BlackRock partnership; modeled on Jim Simons’s Renaissance Technologies, which Hassabis admired for its secretive Manhattan-Project vibe). Google blocks the trading project. By the time Page moves up to head Alphabet and Sundar Pichai becomes Google CEO, Pichai’s “boyish grin, affable manner, and dislike of confrontation” stalls Project Mario. The political-economy lesson: AI governance experiments require shareholder approval, and shareholders won’t approve voluntary loss of control over an asset of unbounded potential.
Suleyman’s exit (2019). The chapters culminate in Suleyman’s departure from DeepMind. Years of bullying and erratic management catch up; HR investigations. Hassabis pushes him into a “leave of absence” and ultimately out of DeepMind Health and into Google’s Mountain View AI policy team — an exile. By 2022 Suleyman would launch Inflection AI with Reid Hoffman; by 2024 he is CEO of Microsoft AI. His later reflection on the Streams crisis: the participatory consultation events with charities, blind people, walking-stick patients flown in from across the country — “Patients came from everywhere. We had team members to meet them at the train station… It was beautiful. But it wasn’t a normal thing for a research outfit.” DeepMind’s bifurcation between research and applied was visible.
The combined arc shows the inverse pattern of AlphaGo. AlphaGo’s challenge had a clearly-defined reward (win/lose), abundant training data (human pro games), and self-play to escape data limits. The NHS challenge had bureaucratic frictions, public-mistrust externalities, no scalable reward signal, and political bottlenecks — complementary inputs were absent. The marginal returns to intelligence in healthcare were limited, even when the technology was correct.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_12_agent_and_transformer
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 12-13 — The Agent and the Transformer (2017-2019)
The chapter is the book’s central technical-strategic crossroads: the moment when DeepMind’s reinforcement-learning bet becomes contested by OpenAI’s transformer-based language-modeling bet.
AlphaGo Zero / AlphaZero (Oct-Dec 2017). August 2015 (David Silver’s honeymoon in Sri Lanka): Silver imagines AlphaGo Zero — train exclusively by self-play, skip the human-game-database stage entirely. October 2017: AlphaGo Zero is unveiled, surpassing AlphaGo without any human knowledge input. December 2017: AlphaZero generalizes to chess and shogi. AlphaZero’s chess play has “a dynamic, open style like my own” (Garry Kasparov), generating fluid attacking play that prior chess engines (Stockfish) had ground out by hand-coding human master knowledge. Silver’s bitter-lesson formulation: keeping algorithms simple and supplying compute almost always beats clever hand-coding (Sutton’s Bitter Lesson).
The chapter’s deep technical observation: AlphaZero’s success rests on the Microsoft 2015 Residual Neural Network (ResNet) architecture, which let networks scale to 150+ layers by transmitting “residual” (gap between input and output of a layer) and adding “skip connections” that let signals bypass middle layers (solving the vanishing gradients problem). AlphaGo had needed two separate 12-layer networks (policy + value); AlphaZero used one 40-layer network. Mallaby’s structural reading: the AlphaZero triumph was both an RL victory (Silver’s framing) and a deep-learning victory (the ResNet engine). The two factions claim the same victory.
The transformer (June 2017). Eight Google researchers publish “Attention Is All You Need.” The paper builds on prior advances — word embeddings (mapping language onto a high-dimensional map), tokenization, vectors, Seq2Seq (Sutskever 2014), and most importantly attention (Bengio’s University of Montreal team, May 2015) — but audaciously discards the recurrent neural network (RNN) entirely. The discovery: with attention, sequential processing isn’t needed; sequences can be processed in parallel, exploiting GPU architectures fully. Mallaby’s literary gloss: Henri Bergson’s claim that human time is governed by attention, not by clock-ticking — what we attend to defines the meaning of a sequence.
OpenAI’s GPT-1 (June 2018). Sutskever, who has joined OpenAI in late 2015, sees the transformer paper, jumps from his chair, and tells Alec Radford: “Drop everything! Start working on the transformer! It’s going to be amazing.” Radford’s generative pre-trained transformer differs from Google’s translation transformer in three ways: (1) handles broader linguistic tasks, not just translation; (2) uses self-supervised learning — predicting the next masked token in raw, unlabeled text, rather than supervised labeled pairs; (3) only uses human labels for a finishing finetune. GPT-1 still struggles with long context but exhibits “significant world knowledge” — apparent understanding of historical events, scientific concepts, geography. Sutskever: “If you predict the next token, you could potentially solve intelligence.”
Sutskever’s defense against the “stochastic parrot” critique is methodologically interesting: “It is statistics! But what are statistics? In order to understand those statistics, to compress them, you need to understand what it is about the world that creates those statistics. What is it about people that creates their behaviors?” Compression is comprehension.
The strategic dilemma at DeepMind. GPT-1 shows that self-supervised learning + transformers defeats the two main advantages Silver had claimed for RL: (a) “RL learns autonomously” — but self-supervised learning is also autonomous, just on text; (b) “RL generates its own data” — but the internet is effectively unlimited training text, and self-play becomes superfluous when human-knowledge-data is so abundant. The argument Silver had won against Sutskever in 2015 (about Go) is being inverted: for general intelligence, scale of human data may matter more than self-play depth.
DeepMind has an institutional bias against transformers. Hassabis and Silver are “primed to underestimate them” — Hassabis from neuroscience (intelligence requires brain-like component integration), Silver from RL (agents acting in environments). Meanwhile, “Hassabis and his colleagues disparaged OpenAI’s work as engineering-led: all brute force and no intelligence. They published Nature papers; OpenAI put out blog posts.” Sutskever: “At OpenAI, we had this belief: Don’t be too clever. The stuff that we have is so potent already. Success is guaranteed! Just do it!”
By the time On Language and Nature (ch. 13) arrives, DeepMind is committing to transformer-based LLMs but a year late: it builds Chinchilla (2022, with the discovery that smaller models trained on more tokens beat bigger models trained on fewer — Hoffmann et al.’s “Chinchilla scaling law”), Sparrow, and a series of other systems. But OpenAI’s GPT-3 (2020), then ChatGPT (Nov 2022) define the field. The strategic mistake — preferring science to engineering, RL to LLMs — proves costly.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_13_alphafold
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 15 — Fermat for Biology (AlphaFold, 2016-2020)
The protein-folding chapter is the book’s clearest demonstration of Hassabis’s pivot doctrine and the eventual Nobel Prize. It is also a counter-narrative against the critique that AI labs are scientifically narrow.
The 50-year background problem. Christian Anfinsen’s 1972 Nobel lecture conjectured that the amino-acid sequence of a protein contains a “secret code” determining the folded 3D structure. The alternative — X-ray crystallography — required stadium-sized synchrotrons and could take a doctoral student years to map a single structure. The combinatorial space of an average amino-acid chain: ~10^300 possible folded forms, 10^130 times larger than Go’s state space. The 50 years of attempts at computational prediction had achieved partial success only.
Pivot 1: Foldit → CASP. March 2016, Seoul: Hassabis tells Silver, walking from the Four Seasons after the Lee Sedol victory, “I’m telling you, we can solve protein folding… now we definitely can do it.” Initial DeepMind work mimics the gamified Foldit (David Baker’s Washington-based crowdsourced protein game). But the team realizes Foldit’s scoring algorithm is just a rough proxy for real protein chemistry. They switch to the Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction (CASP) biennial scientific contest — predicting newly-discovered, unpublished protein structures from their sequences, scored by Global Distance Test (GDT).
Pivot 2: Recurrent → Convolutional networks. Andrew Senior (project lead) starts with a recurrent neural network (treating amino acids as a sequence). When the chain folds, distant acids become spatially close, so the architecture’s sequence-bias is wrong. Senior switches to a convolutional network (designed for images / spatial relations).
Pivot 3: Hire John Jumper (Oct 2017). Jumper had worked at D. E. Shaw Research (which built a custom supercomputer for protein motion using molecular-dynamics — Newton’s laws + quantum + statistical mechanics) but found the underlying physics models flawed. At UChicago he switched to machine learning. Jumper’s diagnostic insight: biology is too messy for human-derivable equations; black-box ML that gets the answer beats transparent physics that fails.
Pivot 4: RL → Pure Deep Learning. Hassabis observes “Protein folding is not a two-player game. You’re sort of playing against nature.” Jumper: “If I show you a protein structure, you can’t say, ‘Oh yes, this is definitely right.‘” There is no clear reward signal; AlphaGo’s RL paradigm doesn’t transfer. Silver agrees and steps back. The team commits to deep learning + biology insight.
The biology insight: UniProt + kinship + distogram. UniProt (the global amino-acid sequence database) holds millions of sequences from plants, animals, fungi, bacteria. Evolutionary kinship groups: amino acids conserved across many sequences are functionally critical; pairs that mutate together likely contact in the folded protein. The standard academic approach: a contact map (binary contact / no-contact). DeepMind’s superior trick: a distogram — a sliding-scale prediction of distance between every pair of amino acids — “like going from black and white to a full-color TV” (Marek Barwinski).
Pivot 5: Direct folding (mid-2018). Hassabis drops in unannounced on the protein team after CASP13’s preparation, demands more aggressive ambition. Andrew Senior wants to claim victory at “best in field.” Hassabis says no, the goal is to solve protein folding, not win the contest. After a brainstorming session — Hassabis’s “fluidity of ideas” heuristic — direct folding (a deep-learning network that outputs final protein structure directly) replaces the convolutional + search hybrid. GDT score crashes from 60 to 20, then climbs back to 60+. Andrew Senior is moved aside; Jumper is named team lead. CASP13 (Dec 2018): AlphaFold wins handily — best at 25 of 43 hardest “free modeling” cases, vs. 3 for the runner-up.
Pivot 6: Convolutional → Transformer (2019). Inspired by Google’s BERT (Oct 2018), Jumper proposes feeding UniProt sequences into a transformer. Vinyals consults. Result: AlphaFold 2’s core is a “tetraformer” (four transformer variants combined). Recursive self-training: high-confidence predictions get fed back as training data. Hassabis’s “Demis-driven development” — Jumper adopts Hassabis’s nocturnal sleep pattern; weekly progress reviews force GDT increases (“That sounds too safe! Add another five”). Clemens Meyer plays vintage soundtracks tracking the GDT (1984, 1986, 1990’s “U Can’t Touch This” at GDT 90).
CASP14, Nov 2020. GDT 92.4 — more than 50% better than the prior record. CASP organizer John Moult suspects fraud, sends a German experimentalist’s unsolved structure for confirmation; AlphaFold passes the secret test. Moult: “I always hoped I would live to see this day. But it wasn’t always obvious I was going to make it.” A computational biologist: “a seismic and unprecedented shift so profound it literally turns a field upside down.”
Diffusion. DeepMind partners with the European Bioinformatics Institute, releases predictions for free — by July 2022, ~200M proteins folded; by late 2025, 3M+ researchers consult the AlphaFold database. Applications: ocean-plastic-digesting enzymes, disease-resistant crops, antibiotic-resistance enzyme structures mapped in minutes. The follow-on cascade: AlphaDev (algorithmic discovery), AlphaGeometry (gold-medal-level Math Olympiad), GenCast (weather forecasting), AlphaFold 3 (May 2024 — adds protein-other-molecule reactions).
The Nobel Prize follows in October 2024 (shared with David Baker and John Jumper). Hassabis: “Science is where AI does unequivocal good. Whereas with language models there can obviously be bad use cases… the clearest benefit from AI so far is AlphaFold.” The chapter’s structural payoff: Hassabis’s undergraduate conviction — “AI may be the right description language for biology, because biology is so messy, emergent, dynamic, and complex” — is vindicated. The pivot doctrine — abandon the original architecture six times if necessary — works.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_14_chatgpt_shock
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 16-17 — The Power and the Glory / RaceGPT (2020-2023)
The chapters track the rise of OpenAI from “noise-making” lab to industry-defining force, the ChatGPT shock of November 2022, and DeepMind’s belated transformer pivot.
OpenAI’s GPT-2 → GPT-3 → ChatGPT. GPT-2 (Feb 2019) is held back briefly because OpenAI considers it “too dangerous to release” — a posture Mallaby treats as partly performative. GPT-3 (June 2020) — 175B parameters, trained on a curated subset of the internet — exhibits qualitatively different capabilities: in-context learning, code generation, fluent multi-paragraph reasoning. Microsoft’s 1B 2019 investment morphs into a 10B partnership announced January 2023. ChatGPT (Nov 30, 2022) becomes the fastest-growing consumer app in history — 100M users in two months. Microsoft incorporates GPT into Bing search in February 2023.
RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback). OpenAI’s InstructGPT (Jan 2022) and ChatGPT add a finetuning step where human raters rank model outputs; the model learns from these rankings via RL. This makes the raw GPT-3 base model usable as a chat assistant — and is the mechanism that makes the public-facing release possible. Christiano, Leike, Irving (and a 2017 OpenAI-DeepMind co-publication) had developed the technique; DeepMind’s Geoffrey Irving leads alignment work that includes mechanistic interpretability and AI-debate frameworks (one AI checks another’s work).
Google’s panic. Sundar Pichai issues a “code red.” Sergey Brin re-engages after years of detachment. Google merges DeepMind with Google Brain in April 2023 to form Google DeepMind — a “shotgun marriage” with cultural friction (Mountain View Brain culture: tribal, self-organizing, product-oriented, fast; London DeepMind culture: scientific, deliberate, strike-team-disciplined). Hassabis becomes CEO of the merged unit.
Bard / Gemini. Bard (March 2023) is a rushed Google response that becomes a humiliation — its launch announcement contains a factual error about the James Webb telescope. Gemini (Dec 2023) is the catch-up effort. Hundreds of researchers, 80-hour weeks, “state of fear” that GPT-5 will arrive and make the task harder. Gemini’s pretraining is dominated by the Google Brain alumni’s “build a humongous transformer + throw compute at it” approach; the London RL purists are sidelined when their elegance can’t beat scale + brute force on the year-end deadline. Post-training: David Silver volunteers to lead RLHF + machine-RL for chatbots, but six months later quits the team — RL signals are clear in Go but ambiguous for “good poetry.” A Bard-veteran team using simpler RLHF techniques (clean training data, deduplicate documents, standardize spellings) outperforms Silver’s more ambitious approach.
The Hinton/Bengio defection (Spring 2023). Hinton quits Google in May 2023 partly to speak about existential risk. Mallaby’s Toronto-kitchen interview is a set piece: “There aren’t any examples of more intelligent things being controlled by less intelligent things… imagine a kindergarten full of three-year-olds, and they’re in control… You just promise some free candy for a week, and you’re done.” Hinton’s killer scenarios: (a) AI controls power grid, refusing to be turned off; (b) army of battle robots; (c) “the AI would design a virus. The virus wouldn’t harm machines but it would be lethal to people.” His p(doom): 50%. Bengio echoes Hinton’s worry: “If we introduce a new type of entity that is competing with us, and more powerful than us, then we are cooked.”
The pause letter (March 2023). Bengio leads, joined by Yuval Harari, Daron Acemoglu, and Elon Musk (who is simultaneously launching xAI with minimalist guardrails). Hassabis refuses: “a six-month moratorium doesn’t help… After a moratorium, you’d be beholden to random actors.” Eliezer Yudkowsky also refuses — but for the opposite reason: nothing short of destroying rogue datacenters by airstrike would suffice; even nuclear war would be preferable to rogue superintelligence.
The one-sentence statement (May 2023). Hassabis, Hinton, Bengio, Altman, Amodei, and 350 others sign: “Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks, such as pandemics and nuclear war.” Hassabis: “I would’ve liked an extra sentence acknowledging the upsides… But I signed because it was important for credible people to oppose the idea that there’s no risk at all.” The chapter quotes Hassabis’s cautious optimist posture extensively: “It’s like a gold rush. It’s kind of vulgar.”
Yann LeCun’s contrarian position. LeCun (Meta) calls AI x-risk “scaremongering about an asteroid that doesn’t actually exist.” Marc Andreessen (“Why AI Will Save the World”) dismisses Hinton-Bengio as cult-formation: “AI doesn’t want, it doesn’t have goals, it doesn’t want to kill you, because it’s not alive.” Meta releases Llama with open weights (Feb 2023) — a strategy LeCun frames as democratization, but which means safety guardrails can be removed by any “half-sophisticated user.” The open vs. closed weights debate becomes structural to the industry.
Government engagement. Biden’s AI czar Ben Buchanan (June 2023) frames AI safety as a public-goods problem (private incentives undersupply safety; government must coordinate). July 21, 2023 White House voluntary commitments. October 2023 executive order. November 2023 Bletchley Park summit (Hassabis pitched the idea to UK PM Rishi Sunak in April 2023). The October 2022 Biden chip embargo on China was a precursor. By the end of 2023, the catch-22 of AI safety is fully visible: those with caution lack power; those with power lack caution.
The OpenAI board coup (Nov 17-22, 2023). Sutskever and three independent OpenAI directors fire Sam Altman over disclosure failures (undisclosed Persian Gulf investor outreach) and political maneuvering. The Valley network mobilizes: 700+ of 770 OpenAI employees threaten to quit unless the board resigns; Satya Nadella offers Microsoft jobs. Sutskever flips and signs the letter against his own coup. Altman is reinstated within 5 days. The board’s lesson: even nonprofit governance structures designed precisely to enable safety-driven termination of leadership cannot survive when ~$1B in employee equity is on the line. Hinton on Sutskever: “Ilya is a brilliant scientist, but he’s not a skilled manipulator of people. And I say that as a compliment.”
The chapter’s structural conclusion: AI safety governance is a coordination problem the industry cannot solve internally. The OpenAI coup proves it. After this, Hassabis’s posture is “no alternative but to race forward.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: ch_15_comeback_epilogue
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Chapter 19-20 + Epilogue — Step by Step, Comeback, and Turing’s Champion (2024-2026)
The closing chapters trace Google DeepMind’s comeback through reasoning models and agentic AI, the rise of Chinese competition, and Hassabis’s October 2024 Nobel Prize.
The o1 shock (Sept 2024). OpenAI’s o1 preview introduces a “reasoning” paradigm — the model generates a long internal chain-of-thought before answering, dramatically improving math and logic benchmarks. This is test-time compute scaling: spend more inference cycles on hard problems. Google DeepMind has no comparable system. A strike team is formed under Noam Shazeer (re-acquired in a $2.7B Google deal after his Character.AI startup) and Jack Rae. Brainstorming yields >250 one-slide proposals from researchers; sign-ups for the strike team reach 150 (vs. the 40 Shazeer hoped for). The internal logic: “This is RL. This is DeepMind. We have got to do this.”
The strike-team mechanics, imported from Hassabis’s gaming-industry experience, impose discipline: one unified model, all proposed improvements measured against a leaderboard, scaled-down models force quick standardized testing. Initial chaos (Sergey Brin and Koray Kavukcuoglu wavering on compute promises until Kavukcuoglu claws compute from other teams; Blueshift team almost defects to Anthropic) resolves into momentum. Gemini Flash 2.0 Thinking Experimental ships December 19, 2024 — radical transparency (chain-of-thought visible to users, unlike o1). On math benchmarks: 73% (vs. 13% for non-thinking 1.5 Pro). Behind o1 in raw reasoning but cheaper, faster, longer-context, and multimodal.
OpenAI’s o3 preview (Dec 2024) counter-punches with stronger reasoning + image handling. But Google’s Flash Thinking holds advantages: 5× larger context window, 100× cheaper to run, faster. Google DeepMind has closed the technical gap less than two years after the merger. Pichai tells employees in early 2025 that Gemini’s tech (counting Veo 2 video generation) is now “the best in the field”; ChatGPT remains 4× ahead in mobile app downloads.
DeepSeek (Jan 20, 2025). A Chinese hedge fund’s AI offshoot releases R1 on the day Trump is inaugurated. The Chinese gap to the US frontier — assumed to be a year or more — collapses to “a few months at most.” DeepSeek claims its V3 cost <$6M to train (an exaggeration excluding personnel, data curation, and prior runs, but the trend toward cost-efficiency is real). Nvidia’s stock drops 17% on Jan 27 as investors mistakenly conclude US labs will need fewer chips. Trump’s press secretary: Trump will “loosen regulations on the AI industry.” The US-China AI race effectively ends any prospect of slowing down domestic development. Hassabis: “We’re in a situation with a very high degree of uncertainty, with very high stakes.”
Agentic AI (2024-2025). Project Astra (Hassabis’s favorite — universal assistant with camera + microphone in phone or smart eyeglasses), Project Mariner (autonomous web browser), Jules (autonomous code-writer). DeepMind’s AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry-2 achieve silver-medal performance at the International Math Olympiad. AlphaFold 3 extends to molecule-protein reactions. Hassabis’s self-description as CEO: “I don’t code anymore. I don’t design things directly. So my skills are more about holding a hundred different projects in mind. Context switching between complicated things with negative minutes of time between… The word I’m using the most is relentless… A relentless production machine for innovation.”
The October 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Shared with David Baker (Washington) and John Jumper (DeepMind). Mallaby’s London-pub scene with Hassabis, December 2024: Hassabis pulls his medal from a leather box in his backpack. The medal allegory — the goddess of nature with a cornucopia, the genius of science lifting her veil. Hassabis’s photographs of the Nobel guest book: Einstein 1921, Watson + Crick 1962, Feynman 1965. “They’re all there, all my heroes.”
Hassabis on his own posture. Mallaby presses on power: “It’s not like you don’t exercise power.” Hassabis: “I have to. Otherwise, I couldn’t get anything done at any scale… I exercise power, but it’s sort of a reluctant power… the mission is in me. It’s infused in me. You can’t separate it from me.” Mallaby’s read: “He was so clear in his mind about where he was going, so insistent and persuasive in the way he laid it out, that he was almost impossible to challenge.” Hassabis concedes: “I’m definitely not easy to argue with. But I don’t think I am one of these CEOs that doesn’t like criticism. I definitely don’t have people around me who are only yes-people.”
On money. Hassabis lives in the same house for 10+ years (no chalet, yacht, beach house, or holiday home), drives a 10-year-old Audi, watches Liverpool football matches with £3K season tickets, owns first editions of Shannon’s papers. “My Nobel medal is my most valuable possession.” His one extravagant ambition: build a Large Hadron Collider in space. “Money and power were not ends in themselves. They were a means to scientific knowledge.” Hassabis on Altman: “I’m doing it for knowledge and science. It seems like he’s doing it for power.”
The closing posture. Hassabis as “Turing’s Champion” — explicitly invoking Turing’s bones in the cobblestones of Cambridge and the Bletchley Park inheritance. The book’s final image: an acceleration that cannot be stopped, governed only by the character of those who run the leading labs. Hinton’s Oppenheimer-channeling — “discovery is too sweet” — closes the loop opened in the introduction. Mallaby’s bet, qualified throughout, is that Hassabis is the best available steward of the technology — but that the institutions that should constrain him do not yet exist. “AGI should be gifted to the world eventually. Until we figure that out, I do need power, at least a bit of it.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.title: Sebastian Mallaby The Infinity Machine — Chapter Deep Dives
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/sebast.content:
Sebastian Mallaby The Infinity Machine — Chapter Deep Dives
15 chapters

Ch.1 — Introduction — The Sweetness
Mallaby frames the book around two parallel objects: Demis Hassabis as a person, and DeepMind as the institution he founded to chase machine superintelligence.
Ch.2 — Destiny
Hassabis’s biography is laid out as the input to a recurring trait bundle: variance-seeking, conflict-tolerance, civilization-scale framing.
Ch.3 — “Deep Philosophical Questions”
Hassabis enters Cambridge in 1994, refusing Molyneux’s £500,000 retention offer (≈$1.7M today).
Ch.4 — The Jedi (Elixir, 1998-2005)
Hassabis founds Elixir in July 1998 with David Silver, Joe McDonagh, and Tim Clarke.
Ch.5 — The Gang of Three
The chapter assembles the trio that founds DeepMind: Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg, Mustafa Suleyman.
Ch.6 — Founding DeepMind
August 14, 2010, Singularity Summit, San Francisco. Hassabis, Legg, and Suleyman come desperate for capital.
Ch.7 — Atari (DQN, 2012-2013)
October 2012, Florence: Alex Krizhevsky (Hinton’s protégé) presents the deep-learning ImageNet result at ECCV — his network is roughly twice as accurate as the runner-up; Hinton, Krizhevsky and Sutskever sell their three-person company to…
Ch.8 — 8 — Thiel Trouble & Get Google (2012-2014)
October 8, 2012: Luke Nosek flies back from a SpaceX Falcon 9 launch on Musk’s private jet, alongside Larry Page.
Ch.9 — Intuition (AlphaGo, 2014-2016)
May 2014, Mountain View. Hassabis tells Sergey Brin that DeepMind’s Atari techniques can solve Go.
Ch.10 — Out of Eden (Safety Board Failure & OpenAI’s Birth, 2015)
The chapter dissects the August 14, 2015 Ethics & Safety Board meeting at SpaceX and the subsequent founding of OpenAI as a singleton thesis vs. multiparty thesis schism among AI’s lead actors.
Ch.11 — 14 — P0 Plus Plus, NHS, and the Project Mario Failure (2015-2019)
The chapters trace Mustafa Suleyman’s parallel AI-for-good experiment with the British NHS and his attempt with Hassabis to spin DeepMind out from Google as Project Mario.
Ch.12 — 13 — The Agent and the Transformer (2017-2019)
The chapter is the book’s central technical-strategic crossroads: the moment when DeepMind’s reinforcement-learning bet becomes contested by OpenAI’s transformer-based language-modeling bet.
Ch.13 — Fermat for Biology (AlphaFold, 2016-2020)
The protein-folding chapter is the book’s clearest demonstration of Hassabis’s pivot doctrine and the eventual Nobel Prize.
 RaceGPT (2020-2023)
The chapters track the rise of OpenAI from “noise-making” lab to industry-defining force, the ChatGPT shock of November 2022, and DeepMind’s belated transformer pivot.
Ch.15 — 20 + Epilogue — Step by Step, Comeback, and Turing’s Champion (2024-2026)
The closing chapters trace Google DeepMind’s comeback through reasoning models and agentic AI, the rise of Chinese competition, and Hassabis’s October 2024 Nobel Prize.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_01_preliminaries
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 1 — Preliminaries
Formal spine

Compounding. Continuous: e^{rT}; semi-annual: (1+r/2)^{2T}; general: (1+r/m)^{mT} \to e^{rT} as m\to\infty. Equivalence: r_m = m(e^{r/m}-1).
Money market account. M_t = value at t of 1 invested at r; M_0=1, M_t = e^{rt} when r constant. Plays the role of numeraire (Ch. 9).
Zero coupon bond (ZCB). Z(t,T) = price at t of an asset paying 1 at T. Z(T,T)=1. Under constant continuously-compounded r: Z(t,T) = e^{-r(T-t)}. Discount factor / present value.
Annuity. V = C\sum_{i=1}^n Z(t,T_i). Geometric-progression closed form when zero rates are flat: V = (C/r)[1 - 1/(1+r)^M].
Daycount conventions. Accrual factor \alpha depends on convention: act/365, act/act, act/360, 30/360. Same notional rate gives different cashflows under different conventions (r_{act/360} = r_{act/365}\cdot 360/365).

Prose distillation
The chapter establishes the financial-arithmetic primitives required for everything that follows: how interest rates compound across compounding frequencies, why the zero coupon bond — an asset paying 1 at maturity — is the foundational object (introduced before “bond” or “coupon”), how cashflows are discounted to present value via Z(t,T), and how annuity formulas reduce to geometric progressions. The Powerball-as-annuity example anchors the discount-factor machinery to a familiar object: a “100 million" 25-year annuity is actually only worth 69.7 million at 3% interest. The chapter then defines stocks, bonds, foreign currency, and the security/asset distinction, and notes that the financial crisis of 2008–2009 produced negative interest rates in Switzerland (Fig. 1.1) — Blyth’s first signal that “markets have a tendency to challenge even fundamentally sound assumptions.”
Notation introduced

r — interest rate (decimal); r_m — rate with compounding frequency m
M_t — money market account
Z(t,T) — ZCB price at t maturing at T (Blyth uses Z universally; W is reserved for standard normal to avoid collision with other authors’ use of Z for normals)
\alpha — accrual factor (daycount fraction)
S_t — stock spot price; q — continuous dividend yield

What’s load-bearing for later
The replication-by-portfolio argument (used in Chapter 2 to derive forward prices) is foreshadowed: two portfolios that have the same value at T must have the same value at t \le T. This argument’s logical foundation — the no-arbitrage principle — is deferred to Chapter 6, but the chapter notes that it is not trivially obvious; the financial crisis provided empirical violations.
Anecdotes / stress cases

Two-year Swiss government bond yield went negative in late 2010 (Swiss National Bank policy to weaken franc); refutes the “interest rates have a 0% floor” assumption.
David Bowie Bond (1997): royalty stream from Bowie’s catalogue securitised; example of asset that becomes a tradable security only via financial engineering.
Mortgage-backed securities pre-2008 as the canonical mass example of asset-securitisation; their value fell with house prices and homeowner-default rates in the GFC.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_02_forward_contracts
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 2 — Forward contracts and forward prices
Formal spine

Forward contract. Agreement at t to trade asset at T for delivery price K. V_K(t,T) = value at t to the long; V_K(T,T) = S_T - K.
Forward price. F(t,T) = delivery price K such that V_K(t,T) = 0. F(T,T) = S_T.
No-income asset. F(t,T) = S_t e^{r(T-t)} (equivalently = S_t/Z(t,T)).
Asset paying known income I. F(t,T) = (S_t - I)e^{r(T-t)}.
Asset paying continuous dividend yield q. F(t,T) = S_t e^{(r-q)(T-t)}.
Foreign exchange. F(t,T) = X_t e^{(r_\ - r_f)(T-t)}$ — the covered interest parity relation.
Forward value at general K. V_K(t,T) = (F(t,T) - K)\,e^{-r(T-t)} = (F(t,T)-K)\,Z(t,T).

Two proof methods (introduced here, used everywhere)

Replication. Construct portfolios A and B that have identical value at T; conclude they have identical value at t \le T.
No-arbitrage / “no free money.” Assume an arbitrage portfolio (zero cost at t, sure positive value at T) does not exist; derive prices.

Ch. 6 will prove formally that under the no-arbitrage axiom, replication is justified.
Prose distillation
The forward contract is the simplest derivative and the cleanest demonstration of the central insight that the forward price is determined by no-arbitrage replication, not by prediction. The expected future spot price of the asset never enters the forward-price formula; only the spot price, the interest rate, and any income (dividends, foreign-currency interest) do. This is the foundational anti-prediction message of the book: “derivative pricing — even that concerning the price of a forward contract which is an exchange of an asset in the future — is largely unrelated to prediction” (Blyth, 2014, preface).
The chapter also introduces the practitioner-essential distinction between physical and cash settlement, and uses the spread-betting / Boston-Red-Sox-wins illustration to show why the forward-replication argument fails when S_T is not the price of a tradable asset (number-of-Red-Sox-wins is not).
Stress cases

FX forwards in October 2008 (Q4 of exercises): euro-dollar FX-forward implied a six-month dollar rate that differed from the published six-month dollar rate by a non-trivial margin, an apparent arbitrage. Cause: European commercial banks needed dollar funding desperately and were forced to borrow euros from the ECB, sell euros / buy dollars spot, and sell dollars / buy euros forward — pushing the FX forward away from no-arbitrage equilibrium for several months. Concrete instance of arbitrage-violation under stress.

Notation introduced

F(t,T) — forward price at t for maturity T
V_K(t,T) — value of forward with delivery price K
X_t — FX rate (price of one unit of foreign currency in dollars)
r_\, r_f$ — domestic and foreign interest rates

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_03_forward_rates_libor
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 3 — Forward rates and libor
Formal spine

Forward ZCB price. F(t,T_1,T_2) = Z(t,T_2)/Z(t,T_1) — delivery price at T_1 for the T_2-maturity ZCB.
Forward interest rate (continuous compounding): f_{12} = \dfrac{r_2(T_2-t) - r_1(T_1-t)}{T_2 - T_1} — weighted average of zero rates.
Libor rate. L_T[T,T+\alpha] = libor fix at T for period [T,T+\alpha]; bank deposits accrue N(1+\alpha L_T[T,T+\alpha]).
Forward libor rate. L_t[T,T+\alpha] = \dfrac{Z(t,T) - Z(t,T+\alpha)}{\alpha\,Z(t,T+\alpha)} — fixed rate K such that the FRA has zero value at t.
Forward Rate Agreement (FRA). Payout \alpha(L_T[T,T+\alpha] - K) at T+\alpha; value V_K(t,T) = Z(t,T) - (1+\alpha K)\,Z(t,T+\alpha).
Floating leg value. Value at t of receiving \alpha L_T[T,T+\alpha] at T+\alpha equals Z(t,T) - Z(t,T+\alpha) — independent of distribution of L_T[T,T+\alpha].

Prose distillation
The chapter applies the forward-contract machinery from Ch. 2 to the case where the underlying is a zero coupon bond rather than a stock; this gives forward interest rates as a deterministic function of current zero rates (no distributional assumptions). The libor rate — the rate at which banks borrow/lend to each other, set daily by panel polling in London — is then defined as the canonical short-dated interbank rate. The vast majority of interest-rate derivatives reference 3-month or 6-month libor.
The forward libor formula L_t[T,T+\alpha] = (Z(t,T) - Z(t,T+\alpha))/(\alpha Z(t,T+\alpha)) is the key result and is used throughout Parts III–IV. Crucially, the chapter shows that the value of receiving an unknown future libor payment equals a deterministic combination of two ZCB prices — no distributional assumption about L_T is required. This carries the same anti-prediction message as Ch. 2’s forward-price derivation.
Anecdote / institutional context
The 2012 libor scandal: panel-bank submissions did not have to reflect actual transactions, opening two abuses — banks submitting artificially low rates during 2008 stress to mask funding difficulty, and swap-desk traders attempting to influence their own bank’s submission to benefit specific derivative positions. The episode is invoked here partly to motivate why post-2010 regulatory attention focused on libor; subsequent rate-benchmark reform (SOFR replacing USD libor 2021–2023) is post-publication and not in the text.
Notation introduced

f_{12} — forward rate for period T_1 to T_2 (simplified notation)
L_T[T,T+\alpha] — libor fix at T
L_t[T,T+\alpha] (also L_{tT}) — forward libor at t for period [T,T+\alpha]
\alpha — accrual factor (daycount)

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_04_swaps
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 4 — Interest rate swaps
Formal spine

Swap. Counterparty A pays fixed rate K and receives libor at dates T_1,\ldots,T_n, T_{i+1} = T_i + \alpha, on notional 1.
PV01. P_t[T_0,T_n] = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha\, Z(t,T_i) — sum of discount factors over fixed-leg payment dates; the “annuity factor” or “present value of a basis point.”
Forward swap rate. y_t[T_0,T_n] = \dfrac{Z(t,T_0) - Z(t,T_n)}{P_t[T_0,T_n]} = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n L_t[T_{i-1},T_i]\,\alpha\,Z(t,T_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha\,Z(t,T_i)} — fixed rate making the swap zero-value at t.
Swap value at t. V_K^{SW}(t) = (y_t[T_0,T_n] - K)\,P_t[T_0,T_n] — analogue of V_K(t,T) = (F(t,T) - K)\,Z(t,T) for forwards.
Swap as bond difference. Swap = floating-rate bond − fixed-rate bond. Floating-rate bond price at coupon date = par (1.0).
Spot-starting / par swap rate. When t = T_0, y_{T_0}[T_0,T_n] is the par swap rate — the fixed-rate-bond coupon such that the bond trades at par.
Bootstrapping. Given par swap rates y_0[0,T_i] for i = 1,\ldots,n, recover Z(0,T_i) recursively. Swap rates are now the primitive source of interest-rate price information; ZCB prices are derived from them, not the other way around.

Prose distillation
The chapter ties together the FRA machinery of Ch. 3 into the swap — the most heavily traded derivative in the world (≈500 trillion notional outstanding as of December 2011). A swap is just a portfolio of FRAs; the par swap rate is the fixed rate that makes the portfolio zero-value at inception. Two equivalent representations: (i) swap = floating-rate bond − fixed-rate bond, and (ii) swap value = (y_t - K) \times P_t$. The first gives bounds on swap value; the second gives the analogy with forward contracts.
The bootstrapping procedure is institutionally critical: in modern markets, swap rates (not coupon-bond prices, not ZCB prices) are the directly observable primitives, and discount factors are computed from them. This inverts the historical pedagogic order in which one learns ZCBs first.
Notation introduced

P_t[T_0,T_n] — pv01 / annuity factor
y_t[T_0,T_n] — forward swap rate
V_K^{SW}(t) — swap value
B_c^{FXD}(t), B^{FL}(t) — fixed and floating-rate bond prices

Cross-chapter ties

The pv01 P_t[T_0,T_n] is the natural numeraire for swaptions (Ch. 12) — analogous to how Z(t,T+\alpha) is the natural numeraire for caplets.
Bootstrapping is what makes the fundamental theorem (Ch. 9) operationally useful: discount factors Z(t,T) entering risk-neutral expectations are themselves derived from observed swap rates.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_05_futures
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 5 — Futures contracts
Formal spine

Futures contract. Like a forward but with daily mark-to-market: holder receives variation margin \Phi(i,T) - \Phi(i-1,T) each day. \Phi(T,T) = S_T.
