Constant-rate result. If interest rates are constant, \Phi(t,T) = F(t,T) — futures price equals forward price.
Random-rate / convexity correction. \Phi(t,T) - F(t,T) is proportional to the covariance between S_T and the money-market account M_T. Positively correlated \Rightarrow \Phi > F.
Eurodollar futures. Settlement price \Phi(T,T) = 100(1 - L_T[T,T+\alpha]). Tick size \25per basis point on$1$M effective notional.
Eurodollar convexity correction. \big(1 - \Phi(t,T)/100\big) - L_t[T,T+\alpha] > 0 — futures-implied rate exceeds forward libor because the futures contract pays variation margin earlier when rates are low.

Prose distillation
Futures look like forwards but the daily mark-to-market introduces interest on variation margin, which means the futures price differs from the forward price whenever the underlying asset price and the money-market account are correlated. For interest-rate futures (Eurodollar, short sterling, Euribor), the underlying is an interest rate, which is mechanically positively correlated with the money-market account — so the convexity correction is non-zero and matters. As of July 2012 the December 2015 Eurodollar contract had a 3.5bp convexity correction vs the corresponding forward libor.
The chapter is explicit about why constant-volatility / constant-rate Black-Scholes-style derivations are inappropriate for interest-rate futures: “this is not a useful result for interest rate futures!” This signposts the deeper problem of pricing interest-rate derivatives, which is the content of Part IV.
Anecdote
Blyth recounts that early in his finance career he tried to convince his boss that the Eurodollar convexity correction should be zero — having a “proof” via the forward-price-equals-futures-price result. The proof depended on constant interest rates. Lesson encoded for the reader: assumptions that look innocuous can be load-bearing in unexpected places.
Notation introduced

\Phi(t,T) — futures price
“Eurodollar” / “short sterling” / “Euribor” — currency-specific futures on 3-month libor
IMM dates — third Wednesday of March/June/September/December

Why this matters for later chapters
Eurodollar futures have non-zero vega, even though forwards and FRAs do not — because the futures price depends on the distribution of the underlying libor rate via the convexity correction, which is proportional to its variance. This is the first contract in the book whose price depends on a distributional assumption; it foreshadows Ch. 7’s transition to options, where distributional assumptions become unavoidable.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_06_no_arbitrage
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 6 — No-arbitrage principle
Formal spine

No-arbitrage axiom. There exists no self-financing portfolio \Pi with: zero cost at t (\Pi_t = 0); \Pi_T \ge 0 for all states with probability 1; \Pi_T > 0 for at least one state with positive probability.
Monotonicity theorem. If two portfolios A and B satisfy A_T \ge B_T in all states (probability-1), then A_t \ge B_t for all t \le T.
Corollary (replication). If A_T = B_T in all states, then A_t = B_t for all t \le T. This justifies all the replication proofs of Chs. 1–5.
Equivalence. No-arbitrage \iff replication-pricing is well-defined.

Prose distillation
This is the chapter where the no-arbitrage axiom is formally stated and shown to be the foundation underlying every replication proof in the book so far. Without it, none of the forward-price formulas, FRA values, or swap-rate identities are well-defined; with it, they all follow as corollaries of the monotonicity theorem.
Blyth makes the axiom-of-choice analogy explicit: in pure mathematics, the axiom of choice underpins set theory and lets one prove ordering / well-ordering / extremum results that would otherwise be unreachable; in quantitative finance, the no-arbitrage assumption plays an exactly analogous role, allowing the establishment of bounds on and ordering of derivative prices. “Without the assumption, quantitative finance becomes far messier, and it becomes hard to order derivative prices.”
Empirical violation under stress
Figure 6.1 plots the yield differential between two US Treasury bonds with identical maturity date 15 August 2015 (the 10.625% and 4.25% coupons). Until late 2008 the differential was small (basis-point level), consistent with Z_1(t,T) = Z_2(t,T). During the financial crisis the yield differential blew out to ~80bp and remained wide for several months — an empirical violation of the no-arbitrage principle, normalised only after government policy responses in early 2009. Blyth cites Taliaferro and Blyth (2011) for further discussion.
Why this chapter is the conceptual centre
Every derivative-price relation in the book is, in the end, a consequence of the monotonicity theorem applied to a cleverly constructed portfolio. The chapter elevates this to a principle and gives the reader the conceptual scaffolding for all that follows:

Ch. 7 (option bounds): all from monotonicity applied to call/put payoffs.
Ch. 8 (binomial replication): no-arbitrage \iff unique risk-neutral probability p^* = (r-d)/(u-d) \in (0,1).
Ch. 9 (fundamental theorem): no-arbitrage \iff ratios-of-prices-to-numeraire are martingales.
Chs. 13, 14: no-arbitrage bounds on Bermudan / libor-in-arrears prices in the absence of pricing models.

Notation introduced

\Pi — portfolio
“monotonicity theorem” — author’s term for the result derived here

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_07_options
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 7 — Options
Formal spine

European call. Right to buy at strike K at exercise date T. Payout C_K(T,T) = (S_T - K)^+ = \max(S_T - K, 0).
European put. Right to sell at strike K at T. Payout P_K(T,T) = (K - S_T)^+.
American option. Exercisable at any t \le T.
Bermudan option. Exercisable at finite set T_0,\ldots,T_n \le T.
Put-call parity. C_K(t,T) - P_K(t,T) = V_K(t,T) = (F(t,T) - K)\,Z(t,T). Model-independent — derived from monotonicity theorem (Ch. 6).
Call-price bounds. \max\{0, S_t - K Z(t,T)\} \le C_K(t,T) \le S_t. Both bounds tight (Ch. 10).
American = European call on no-dividend stock. \widetilde C_K(t,T) = C_K(t,T). Intuition: never optimal to exercise early because intrinsic value S_t - K \le C_K(t,T) already.
Convexity in strike. C_K(t,T) is a convex function of K. Proof via call butterfly portfolio + monotonicity.
Lipschitz in strike. C_{K_2}(t,T) \le C_{K_1}(t,T) \le C_{K_2}(t,T) + Z(t,T)(K_2 - K_1) for K_1 < K_2.
Digital call. Payout \mathbb{1}\{S_T \ge K\}.
Naive valuation fails. Discounting the expected payout under any actual probability does not give the arbitrage-free price (worked example with three-state world: portfolio of long stock + short call + loan creates arbitrage).

Prose distillation
Options are the second key derivative class, after forwards. The chapter’s pedagogic move is to derive everything one can about option prices without a pricing model — purely via monotonicity-theorem arguments on cleverly constructed portfolios (call spreads, put spreads, butterflies). The result: a rich set of model-independent inequalities (put-call parity, monotonicity in strike, convexity in strike, Lipschitz continuity, American=European for non-dividend-paying call) that constrain any candidate option-pricing model.
The transition to risk-neutral pricing (Chs. 8–10) is motivated by the failure of naive present-value-of-expected-payoff valuation: the worked three-state example shows that simply discounting the expected option payoff gives an arbitrageable price. Replication (Ch. 8) is required to nail down the unique arbitrage-free price.
Why call butterflies matter
The convexity-of-call-prices-in-strike result, proved here via a butterfly portfolio that has non-negative payoff at maturity, is the same machinery that re-emerges in Ch. 11 to recover the risk-neutral probability density from observed call prices: f_{S_T|S_t}(x) = (1/Z(t,T))\,\partial^2 C_K/\partial K^2 |_{K=x}. The butterfly is a tradable approximation to the Dirac delta of risk-neutral measure.
Options on forwards (Ch. 7.7)
European call on a forward contract with delivery price K and same maturity T as the underlying = European call on the stock with strike K, since F(T,T) = S_T. Useful for Ch. 10’s incorporation of random interest rates into Black-Scholes (work directly with F(t,T), which is a martingale under the Z(t,T) numeraire).
Notation introduced

C_K(t,T), P_K(t,T) — European call / put prices
\widetilde C_K, \widetilde P_K — American versions
D_K — digital call price
C^{F_K}_{K^*} — call with strike K^* on forward with delivery price K

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_08_binomial_replication
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 8 — Replication and risk-neutrality on the binomial tree
Formal spine

Two-state world. Stock S_0; at T=1, S_1 = S_0(1+u) (up) or S_0(1+d) (down), d < u. Constant rate r.
Replicating portfolio. For derivative with payoffs D(\omega_A), D(\omega_B), find (\lambda, \mu) such that \lambda S_1(\omega_A) + \mu = D(\omega_A) and \lambda S_1(\omega_B) + \mu = D(\omega_B). Solution unique because two assets span two states.
Risk-neutral probability. p^* = (r-d)/(u-d). Under p^*: E^*(S_1 \mid S_0) = S_0(1+r).
No-arbitrage condition (binomial). No arbitrage \iff d < r < u \iff 0 < p^* < 1.
Risk-neutral pricing. D(0) = (1+r)^{-1} E^*(D(1)) — the discounted risk-neutral expectation is the unique arbitrage-free price (replication-price = expectation-price).
Multi-step binomial tree. Apply replication backwards from leaves to root; equivalently D(0) = (1+r)^{-n} E^*(D(n)) where S_n has binomial distribution under p^*.
Cox-Ross-Rubinstein formula. For European call: C = S_0\,B(n,a,m) - K(1+r)^{-n}\,B(n,p^*,m) where a = p^*(1+u)/(1+r) and B(n,p,k) = P(X \ge k), X \sim \text{binomial}(n,p).

Prose distillation
This is the chapter where the central insight of derivative pricing crystallises. Two complementary proofs, each running through the same simple two-state binomial example, converge on a single arbitrage-free price:


Replication argument. A unique linear combination of stock and bond reproduces the option’s payoff in both states; by monotonicity (Ch. 6), the option’s price equals the cost of this replicating portfolio. This is what no-arbitrage demands.


Risk-neutral pricing. Under the unique p^* such that the discounted stock is a fair game (E^*(S_1) = S_0(1+r)), the discounted expected option payoff equals the replication price. This shows the replication price is consistent with no-arbitrage — i.e., admits a probability measure that supports it.


The terminology “risk-neutral” captures that p^* depends only on u, d, r (the values the stock can take and the risk-free rate), not on the actual probability p of an up-move. This is why the option’s price never references the stock’s expected return.
Why this is “the most powerful result of the book”
Blyth’s preface explicitly anoints the binomial-tree fundamental theorem (formalised in Ch. 9) as “the most powerful result of the book.” Because:

It establishes that replication and risk-neutral pricing give the same answer, and that this answer is the only arbitrage-free price.
It generalises immediately: multiple time steps (Ch. 8.3), continuous-time limits (Ch. 10), more general numeraires (Ch. 9), interest-rate-derivative numeraires (Chs. 12–14).
It is a constructive proof: the replicating portfolio tells you exactly how to hedge the derivative.

Notation introduced

u, d — up / down multipliers
p^* — risk-neutral probability (with respect to money-market numeraire)
E^* — expectation under p^*
B(n,p,k) — binomial tail probability P(X \ge k)
CRR — Cox-Ross-Rubinstein

Cross-chapter ties

Ch. 9: extends to general numeraires; the fundamental theorem.
Ch. 10: continuous-time limit (\Delta T \to 0, N \to \infty) gives lognormal S_T and Black-Scholes formula.
Ch. 12: caplets are valued by choosing Z(t,T+\alpha) as numeraire — same structure, different numeraire.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_09_martingales_fundamental_theorem
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 9 — Martingales, numeraires and the fundamental theorem
Formal spine

Martingale. Sequence X_0, X_1, \ldots with E(|X_i|) < \infty and E(X_{n+1} \mid X_0, \ldots, X_n) = X_n. Equivalently for Markov processes: E(X_{n+1} \mid X_n) = X_n. Tower law: E(X_n \mid X_m) = X_m for m \le n.
Discounted stock is a martingale. On the binomial tree, under p^*: E^*(S_n/M_n \mid S_m) = S_m/M_m.
Discounted derivative price is a martingale. C_K(m,n)/M_m = E^*(C_K(n,n)/M_n \mid S_m).
Fundamental theorem of asset pricing (binomial). No arbitrage \iff there exists a risk-neutral probability \mathbb{P}^* such that ratios of asset prices to the money-market account M_t are martingales under \mathbb{P}^*.
General fundamental theorem (numeraire form). For any positive asset N_t, no arbitrage \iff there exists an equivalent probability measure \mathbb{Q}^* (same null sets as \mathbb{P}) such that D(t,T)/N_t is a \mathbb{Q}^*-martingale for every traded asset price D. Applied: D(t,T)/N_t = E^{\mathbb{Q}^*}(D(T,T)/N_T \mid \mathcal{F}_t).
Change of numeraire. Different choices of N_t give different risk-neutral measures \mathbb{Q}^*; the Radon-Nikodym derivative between two such measures is a ratio of numeraires (sketched, derived properly only via Ito in Ch. 16).

Prose distillation
The chapter unifies replication, risk-neutrality, and the probabilistic concept of a martingale into a single load-bearing theorem. The fundamental theorem of asset pricing (Harrison-Kreps 1979 in continuous time; here proved on the binomial tree) is the textbook’s deepest result: it asserts the equivalence between three things that previously looked separate —

No arbitrage (the axiom of Ch. 6)
Replication via portfolios of basic assets (the Ch. 8 method)
Existence of a risk-neutral measure under which discounted prices are martingales (a probability-theoretic statement)

The theorem is what justifies pricing any derivative as a discounted risk-neutral expected payoff: D(t,T) = N_t\, E^{\mathbb{Q}^*}(D(T,T)/N_T \mid \mathcal{F}_t), where N is any positive-asset numeraire and \mathbb{Q}^* is the corresponding risk-neutral measure.
Why numeraire choice matters
Different numeraires produce different risk-neutral measures, all of which give the same prices for any traded asset (this is the consistency requirement of the fundamental theorem). But for any specific derivative, one numeraire is computationally easiest:

Money-market account M_t — the textbook default; useful when r is constant.
ZCB Z(t,T) (forward measure) — makes F(t,T) = S_t/Z(t,T) a martingale; used in Ch. 10 for stock options under random interest rates and in Ch. 12 for caplets.
PV01 P_t[T_0,T_n] (swap measure / annuity measure) — makes the forward swap rate y_t[T_0,T_n] a martingale; used in Ch. 12 for swaptions.
Stock S_t — makes M_t/S_t and K/S_t tractable; used in Ch. 10 to derive Black-Scholes by splitting the call payout.

Numeraire change is the single most powerful technique in interest-rate derivative pricing, because the right numeraire turns a difficult expectation into a tractable one.
Notation introduced

\mathbb{P}^* / \mathbb{Q}^* — risk-neutral measures
E^* — expectation under \mathbb{P}^*
N_t — generic numeraire
“filtration” \mathcal{F}_t — information available at t (Blyth uses informal notation)

Practical computation
For a stock derivative with payoff g(S_T) at T, using the ZCB numeraire:
D(t,T) = Z(t,T)\int g(x)\, f(x)\, dx,
where f is the risk-neutral density of S_T \mid S_t under the forward measure. This is the integral that must be computed in Ch. 10 for the lognormal Black-Scholes case.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_10_black_scholes
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 10 — Continuous-time limit and Black-Scholes formula
Formal spine

Logarithmic returns. \lambda_n = \log(S_n/S_{n-1}), IID with E(\lambda_i) = \mu\Delta T, \text{Var}(\lambda_i) = \sigma^2 \Delta T. Two-point: \lambda_i = \mu\Delta T \pm \sigma\sqrt{\Delta T}.
Lognormal limit (real-world). As N \to \infty on the binomial tree with up/down probability 1/2: \log S_T = \log S_0 + \mu T + \sigma\sqrt T\,W with W \sim N(0,1). Hence S_T \sim \text{lognormal}.
Risk-neutral limit. p^* = (r\Delta T - d)/(u - d) = 1/2 + \tfrac12((r - \mu - \sigma^2/2)/\sigma)\sqrt{\Delta T} + O(\Delta T). Under p^* the limiting distribution is
\log S_T \mid S_t \sim N\!\left(\log S_t + (r - \tfrac12\sigma^2)(T - t),\ \sigma^2(T - t)\right).
The actual drift \mu does not appear.
Black-Scholes formula. C_K(t,T) = S_t\,\Phi(d_1) - K\,Z(t,T)\,\Phi(d_2), where
d_1 = \frac{\log(S_t/K) + (r + \tfrac12\sigma^2)(T-t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T-t}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T-t}.
Equivalent forward-form: C_K(t,T) = Z(t,T)(F(t,T)\Phi(d_1) - K\Phi(d_2)).
Put via parity. P_K(t,T) = Z(t,T)(K\Phi(-d_2) - F(t,T)\Phi(-d_1)).
Greeks (Black-Scholes).

Delta (call): \partial C/\partial S_t = \Phi(d_1) \in [0,1]. ATMF delta \approx \Phi(\sigma\sqrt{T-t}/2), near but not equal to 1/2.
Vega (call): \partial C/\partial \sigma = S_t\,\sqrt{T-t}\,\phi(d_1) > 0. Same vega for call and put of same strike (from put-call parity).


ATMF straddle approximation. C_F + P_F \approx S_t \sigma \sqrt{T-t}\,\sqrt{2/\pi}\,(1 - \sigma^2(T-t)/24 + \ldots) — the "\sigma\sqrt{T}\sqrt{2/\pi}" practitioner heuristic.
Random interest rates. Working with the forward price F(t,T) = S_t/Z(t,T) (a martingale under Z(t,T) numeraire) lets the same formula apply when interest rates are random; \sigma now denotes forward-price volatility.

Prose distillation
The chapter takes the binomial-tree limit (\Delta T \to 0, N \to \infty, mean and variance of Y_T = \log(S_T/S_0) held fixed) and applies the central limit theorem to obtain a lognormal limiting distribution for S_T. Under the risk-neutral probability the actual drift \mu is replaced by r - \tfrac12\sigma^2, and the discounted-expected-payoff calculation reduces to a single Gaussian tail integral — yielding the Black-Scholes formula.
This route — tree → lognormal → expected-value integral — is conceptually distinct from the original Black-Scholes (1973) PDE-derivation, which proceeds via Ito’s lemma and the Black-Scholes partial differential equation (sketched in Ch. 16). Both routes give the same formula. Blyth’s preference for the probabilistic route is “appealing to probabilists” and operationally simpler: no stochastic calculus, just CLT on the binomial.
Why “the most important tail integral in finance”
Blyth notes (Ch. 10.3, p. 97 of the original): “this is the most important tail integral in finance, and I believe everyone should do it at least once. Revisiting it every couple of years after starting work on Wall Street is also a good way of keeping technically fresh.” The integral is
C_K(t,T) = Z(t,T)\int_{\log K}^{\infty}(e^y - K)\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma\sqrt{T-t}}\,e^{-(y-\nu)^2/(2\sigma^2(T-t))}\,dy.
With \nu = \log S_t + (r - \tfrac12\sigma^2)(T-t). Splitting the integral into the e^y part and the K part gives the two \Phi(\cdot) terms, with a completing-the-square trick supplying the d_1/d_2 structure.
Limiting cases (worked)

S_t \to \infty: \Phi(d_1), \Phi(d_2) \to 1; C_K \to S_t - K e^{-r(T-t)}, the value of a long forward.
\sigma \to 0: stock becomes deterministic. C_K \to (S_t - K e^{-r(T-t)})^+ — option becomes either a forward or worthless.
\sigma \to \infty: \Phi(d_1) \to 1, \Phi(d_2) \to 0; C_K \to S_t — upper bound from Ch. 7 is tight.

Notation introduced

\Phi — standard-normal cumulative distribution function (Blyth uses unmarked Greek \Phi, sometimes written N(\cdot) in other texts)
\phi — standard-normal density
\sigma — volatility (lognormal); \psi — normal-model volatility; conversion: \psi \approx \sigma F(t,T)
\mu — actual drift; replaced by r - \tfrac12\sigma^2 under risk-neutral measure
delta, vega, “Greeks” (Greek letters parametrising sensitivities)

Anecdote
“Black died in 1995 — there was a sense of sadness and respect among options traders that day.” Scholes and Merton received the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for option pricing. The original 1973 derivation is significantly different from the probabilistic route taken here; Blyth flags Ch. 16 for the PDE route.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_11_option_probability_duality
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 11 — Option price and probability duality
Formal spine

Digital from limiting call spread. D_K(t,T) = -\partial C_K(t,T)/\partial K. Limit of \lambda (K, K+1/\lambda)-call spreads as \lambda \to \infty.
Risk-neutral CDF from call prices. \mathbb{P}^*(S_T \le K \mid S_t) = 1 + Z(t,T)^{-1}\,\partial C_K/\partial K.
Risk-neutral density from call prices. f_{S_T \mid S_t}(x) = Z(t,T)^{-1}\,\partial^2 C_K/\partial K^2\big|_{K=x}. Positivity follows from convexity of C_K in K (Ch. 7).
Butterfly and density. B_{K,\lambda}(t,T) \approx (1/\lambda)\,Z(t,T)\,f_{S_T \mid S_t}(K) — butterfly price ≈ probability density at center × half-width × discount factor.
Calls as a spanning set. Any twice-differentiable payoff g(S_T) can be replicated via g(0) ZCBs, g'(0) stocks, and \int_0^\infty C_K(t,T)\,g''(K)\,dK — Carr-Madan-style replication. Hence call prices for all strikes determine the price of any payoff g(S_T).
Implied volatility. \sigma_K is the volatility that, when entered into Black-Scholes, reproduces the observed market call price C_K^\text{mkt}(t,T). Bijection: \{\sigma_K : K > 0\} \leftrightarrow \{C_K : K > 0\} \leftrightarrow \text{risk-neutral distribution of } S_T.
Volatility skew / smile. Empirical \sigma_K is not constant in K. Not an inconsistency — it means the risk-neutral distribution is not lognormal.

Prose distillation
The chapter establishes one of the most elegant results in derivatives: the set of call prices for a given maturity T is in one-to-one correspondence with the risk-neutral distribution of S_T. Two directions:

Distribution → call prices via the fundamental theorem and discounted expected payoff (Ch. 9).
Call prices → distribution via the limiting butterfly = density argument: \partial^2 C_K/\partial K^2 = Z(t,T)\,f_{S_T}(K).

The duality has practitioner consequences. Trading a butterfly is essentially trading a specific risk-neutral probability: if a trader’s view of the actual probability of an event differs from the risk-neutral probability implied by butterfly prices, a directional trade emerges.
Forwards vs options dichotomy
Blyth highlights the appealing dichotomy:

Forwards are as far as one can go in derivative pricing without distributional assumptions (Chs. 2–5).
Calls at all strikes encode the entire risk-neutral distribution at T (Ch. 11).

But option prices for maturity T do not determine the path of S_t for t \le T. Even option prices for all K and all T^* \le T do not pin down the stochastic process for S_t in general; Dupire (1994) and Derman-Kani (1994) give conditions under which they do (the “local volatility” model recovers an effective \sigma(S,t) from a complete option-price surface).
Implied volatility — what it is and isn’t
The Black-Scholes formula is a one-to-one function from \sigma to C_K at each fixed K. Inverting numerically yields \sigma_K, the implied volatility — a re-coding of the option price. Different \sigma_K for different K does not mean the risk-neutral distribution is simultaneously lognormal with multiple variances; it means the risk-neutral distribution is not lognormal. Practitioners use the implied-volatility surface as the canonical way to quote and compare option prices, even when the underlying model is not Black-Scholes.
Notation introduced

D_K(t,T) — digital call price
B_{K,\lambda}(t,T) — call butterfly with center K and half-width 1/\lambda
\sigma_K — Black-Scholes-implied volatility for strike K
“volatility skew” — non-constancy of \sigma_K in K

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_12_caps_floors_swaptions
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 12 — Caps, floors and swaptions
Formal spine

Caplet. Call on libor: payout \alpha\,(L_T[T,T+\alpha] - K)^+ at T+\alpha.
Forward numeraire. N_t = Z(t, T+\alpha) — the ZCB with maturity matching the caplet’s payment date. Under the corresponding risk-neutral measure \mathbb{Q}^{T+\alpha}, the forward libor L_t[T,T+\alpha] = (Z(t,T) - Z(t,T+\alpha))/(\alpha Z(t,T+\alpha)) is itself a ratio of assets to numeraire — hence a martingale.
Black-76 formula (rigorous). Assume L_T \mid L_{tT} \sim \text{lognormal}(\log L_{tT} - \tfrac12\sigma^2(T-t), \sigma^2(T-t)) under the forward measure. Then
C_K^\text{cap}(t,T) = \alpha\,Z(t,T+\alpha)\,(L_{tT}\,\Phi(d_1) - K\,\Phi(d_2)),
d_1 = \frac{\log(L_{tT}/K) + \tfrac12\sigma^2(T-t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T-t}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T-t}.
Cap. Portfolio of consecutive caplets at T_0, T_1, \ldots, T_{n-1} with payments at T_1, \ldots, T_n. ”T_0 by T_n cap.”
Floorlet. Put on libor: \alpha(K - L_T)^+. Floor = portfolio of floorlets. Cap-floor straddle = cap + floor of same strike & dates.
Swap numeraire. N_t = P_t[T_0, T_n] = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha\,Z(t,T_i) — the swap’s pv01 / annuity factor. Under the corresponding measure (the swap measure or annuity measure), the forward swap rate y_t[T_0,T_n] is a martingale (it is a ratio of (Z(t,T_0) - Z(t,T_n)) to P_t).
Payer swaption. Option to pay fixed K, receive libor on [T, T_n]. Payout at exercise: (y_T[T,T_n] - K)^+\,P_T[T,T_n].
Black formula for swaptions. Assume y_T[T,T_n] \mid y_t \sim \text{lognormal}(\log y_t - \tfrac12\sigma^2(T-t), \sigma^2(T-t)) under the swap measure. Then
\Pi_K(t,T,T_n) = P_t[T,T_n]\,(y_t\,\Phi(d_1) - K\,\Phi(d_2)),
with d_1, d_2 as in Black-76 with y_t replacing L_{tT}.

Prose distillation
The chapter introduces the largest options market in the world — interest-rate options ($500 trillion+ in notional outstanding as of December 2011) — and shows how the Ch. 9 numeraire-change machinery makes their pricing tractable. The key trick: each interest-rate option has a natural numeraire under which the underlying rate (libor for caplets, swap rate for swaptions) is itself a martingale, and the discount factor / pv01 can be taken outside the expectation. With a lognormal assumption for the rate under the natural numeraire, one obtains a Black-76-style formula.
Why this took 20 years to make rigorous
Black (1976) proposed pricing caplets by treating Z(T,T+\alpha) as a constant outside the expectation — heuristically reasonable but logically suspect, since Z(T,T+\alpha) = 1/(1+\alpha L_T) is a function of the random libor. The cap market adopted the resulting Black-76 formula and traded with it for two decades before Miltersen-Sandmann-Sondermann (1997) and Brace-Gatarek-Musiela (1997) proved that the formula was internally consistent (no arbitrage) under a specific change of numeraire — the forward measure. The lesson, repeated throughout Blyth: the right numeraire turns a difficult conditional expectation into a calculable one and can rescue an otherwise inconsistent pricing convention.
Symbol Table summary (Ch. 12 condensed)















































ContractUnderlyingPayout at TNatural numeraireFRAL_T\alpha(L_T - K)\,Z(T,T+\alpha)(no option)CapletL_T (call)\alpha(L_T - K)^+\,Z(T,T+\alpha)Z(t,T+\alpha)FloorletL_T (put)\alpha(K - L_T)^+\,Z(T,T+\alpha)Z(t,T+\alpha)Capseries of L_{T_i} (calls)sumseries of Z(t, T_i+\alpha)Payer swaptiony_T[T,T_n] (call)(y_T - K)^+\,P_T[T,T_n]P_t[T,T_n]Receiver swaptiony_T[T,T_n] (put)(K - y_T)^+\,P_T[T,T_n]P_t[T,T_n]
Anecdote — the 11am cutoff
Throughout the 1990s, US dollar swaptions were exercised by voice: the option holder had to call the seller before 11:00am New York time. “Every options trader would have a visceral fear of forgetting to exercise, of looking at the clock and seeing 11:05am.” Now nearly all swaptions are auto-exercised — exercised whenever in the money at expiry.
Notation introduced

C_K^\text{cap}, C_K^\text{call} — caplet vs equity-call price (Blyth uses C_K(t,T) overloaded; uses superscript only when needed)
\Pi_K(t,T,T_n) — payer-swaption price
“Black-76” — Black’s 1976 model for forward / futures / interest-rate options
“BGM” / “LMM” — Brace-Gatarek-Musiela / Libor Market Model (Ch. 15)

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_13_bermudan_swaptions
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 13 — Cancellable swaps and Bermudan swaptions
Formal spine

Cancellable swap. Swap with right (for one counterparty) to cancel at exercise dates T_j, T_{j+1}, \ldots, T_{n-1}. European cancellable: single exercise date.
Callable bond. Fixed-rate bond that issuer can buy back at par at T_j. Issuer often hedges with a cancellable swap.
Bermudan swaption B_K(t, T_0, T_n). Right at each T_i, i = 0, \ldots, n-1, to enter into a swap from T_i to T_n paying fixed K vs libor. Many exercise dates, one option (exercising at T_i extinguishes future exercise rights).
Bermudan = European cancellable swap + underlying swap. Pay fixed on swap from T_0 to T_n + own Bermudan receiver swaption with first exercise T_j on swap to T_n.
No put-call parity for Bermudans. Unlike European or American on stock — because exercising the Bermudan payer extinguishes future options, while a Bermudan receiver retains them.

Arbitrage bounds (model-independent)
For B_K = Bermudan payer, \Pi_K(t, T_i, T_n) = European payer at T_i, C_K^\text{cap}(t, T_0, T_n) = T_0-by-T_n cap:

(a) C_K^\text{cap}(t, T_0, T_n) \ge B_K(t, T_0, T_n) \ge \max_{0 \le i \le n-1} \Pi_K(t, T_i, T_n)
(b) \sum_{0 \le i \le n-1} \Pi_K(t, T_i, T_n) \ge B_K(t, T_0, T_n)

Bermudan is “between” European and cap: cap pays at every exercise date that’s ITM, Bermudan only at one.
Exercise criteria (model-independent)
Three tiers of “do not exercise” rules:

Trivial. Do not exercise if y_{T_i}[T_i, T_n] < K.
European-bound rule. Do not exercise if (y_{T_i}[T_i,T_n] - K)\,P_{T_i}[T_i,T_n] \le \max_{i+1 \le j \le n-1}\Pi_K(T_i, T_j, T_n) — i.e., if the intrinsic value of exercising now is less than the value of the most-valuable remaining European swaption.
Intermediate-rate rule. Do not exercise if y_{T_i}[T_i, T_j] < K for any i+1 \le j \le n. Reason: a “shorter” swap exists with par rate below K, dominating immediate exercise.

The third criterion shows that Bermudan exercise depends not only on co-terminal (diagonal) swaption prices but also on intermediate par swap rates, which many production pricing models do not properly incorporate.
Prose distillation
Bermudan swaptions are Blyth’s “favourite interest rate option” — easy to define, but with subtle exercise dynamics that practitioners frequently misunderstand. The chapter develops a series of model-independent arbitrage bounds and exercise criteria that constrain any admissible pricing model. These bounds are derived purely by the standard “assume violated, construct arbitrage” technique inherited from Ch. 6.
The economic relevance is large: Bermudan callable bonds are popular issuance instruments (issuer wants the right to refinance if rates fall), and corporate issuers commonly hedge by entering into Bermudan cancellable swaps with banks. The cancellable-swap rate K^{**} (the fixed rate at which the cancellable swap has zero value) is therefore an actively traded quantity.
Stress-period anecdote
In 2009, in the aftermath of the Lehman bankruptcy, Bermudan receiver swaptions traded at higher prices than libor floors of the same strike and underlying dates — an explicit violation of the elementary arbitrage bound (a Bermudan swaption is dominated by the cap/floor of the same strike). The bound violation lasted only a few days but is documented in Blyth (2012). It is a parallel to the Ch. 6 Treasury-yield-divergence example: under stress, even arbitrage relations that practitioners had taken as foundational can break.
Cancellable-swap-rate orderings (selected)
For 5-year cancellable swaps:

K\{6\text{nc}2\,\text{Berm }q\} \ge K\{5\text{nc}2\,\text{Berm }q\} \ge K\{5\text{nc}2\,\text{Berm s/a}\} \ge K\{5\text{nc}3\,\text{Berm s/a}\} \ge K\{5\text{nc}3\,\text{Euro}\} \ge \text{5yr swap rate}

Intuition: more cancellation optionality \Rightarrow higher fixed rate. Establishable when one option set is a subset of another. Counterexamples exist when sets are not nested.
Notation introduced

B_K(t, T_0, T_n) — Bermudan payer swaption price
“T_n-non-call-T_j” / "T_n\text{nc}T_j" — T_n-year swap, non-callable for T_j years
“Berm s/a” / “Berm q” — Bermudan with semi-annual / quarterly exercises after non-call period
“5nc3 Euro” — 5-year, non-call-3-year, single (European) exercise

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_14_libor_in_arrears
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 14 — Libor-in-arrears and constant maturity swap contracts
Formal spine

Libor-in-arrears (LIA). Same as a standard libor payment \alpha L_T[T, T+\alpha], except paid at T instead of T+\alpha. The seemingly innocuous payment-date change introduces a convexity correction.
LIA forward rate. Define \widetilde L_t[T, T+\alpha] as the value of K such that the in-arrears FRA (paying \alpha(L_T - K) at T) has zero value at t. Then \widetilde L_t > L_t in general.
Convexity correction (lognormal forward libor under forward measure). \widetilde L_t[T,T+\alpha] - L_t[T,T+\alpha] \approx \alpha\,L_t^2\,(e^{\sigma^2(T-t)} - 1)/(1 + \alpha L_t) — increases with libor volatility, libor level, and time to expiry.
Mechanism. Paying at T instead of T+\alpha changes the natural numeraire from Z(t,T+\alpha) to Z(t,T). Under the new measure, the forward libor is no longer a martingale — it acquires a drift from the change-of-measure Radon-Nikodym derivative.
Constant maturity swap (CMS). A swap where one leg pays a long-dated par swap rate (e.g., 10-year swap rate) at short-dated frequency (e.g., quarterly), instead of paying libor. The CMS leg has a convexity correction analogous to LIA but built around swap rates rather than libor.

Prose distillation
This chapter is the textbook’s clearest demonstration that payment timing matters — and that the no-arbitrage / fundamental-theorem machinery handles it elegantly through the change-of-numeraire calculation. A trade structure that looks identical to a standard swap, with only the payment date moved by 3 or 6 months, can produce a non-trivial convexity correction running to many basis points on long-dated trades.
The chapter recounts “one of the great trades in derivatives history” (Ch. 14.3 — “classic libor-in-arrears trade”): early-1990s desks recognised that the LIA convexity correction was systematically mispriced and structured trades to exploit the correction. Once correctly priced, the spread closed — but the episode established the convexity correction as a first-class concept in interest-rate derivatives.
The CMS leg
A CMS leg pays \alpha\,y_{T_i}[T_i, T_i + N] at T_{i+1}, where N is a fixed long-dated swap tenor (e.g., 10 years), at quarterly or semi-annual frequency. Mismatch between the swap rate’s natural pv01-numeraire (Ch. 12) and the actual payment-date discount factor produces a convexity correction analogous to LIA. CMS rates traded actively in the 2000s; CMS spreads (e.g., 10y CMS − 2y CMS) became a popular curve-trade product.
Why this chapter matters pedagogically
It shows that all the convexity / quanto / timing corrections in interest-rate derivatives — which look like a forest of ad-hoc adjustments in practitioner texts — flow from a single source: the change of numeraire / Radon-Nikodym drift adjustment. Once one understands the change-of-numeraire formalism (Chs. 9, 16), every such correction is a calculation, not a special case.
Notation introduced

\widetilde L_t[T, T+\alpha] — libor-in-arrears forward rate (Blyth uses tilde-L)
“CMS” — constant maturity swap
“convexity correction” — generic term for the difference between an in-the-natural-numeraire forward and an in-the-wrong-numeraire forward

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_15_bgm_framework
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 15 — The Brace-Gatarek-Musiela framework
Formal spine

BGM / Libor Market Model (LMM). Models the entire forward libor curve \{L_t[T_i, T_{i+1}] : i = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1\} as a system of correlated lognormal processes. Brace-Gatarek-Musiela (1997).
Volatility surface. \sigma(t, T) over the triangle 0 \le t \le T: instantaneous volatility at t of the forward libor for the period beginning at T. Calibrated to observed cap and swaption prices.
Cap on L_T[T, T+\alpha]. Price depends on the integrated variance \int_0^T \sigma^2(s, T)\,ds — i.e., on a line through the volatility surface.
European swaption. Price depends on weighted variances of multiple forward libors over their respective lives — i.e., on a region of the volatility surface.
Bermudan swaption. Price depends on (i) the same swaption-relevant region and (ii) the correlations between forward libors, since the exercise decision depends on the relative position of multiple forward rates.
Reset cap, midcurve options, forward-volatility trades. Each picks out a specific subset of the BGM volatility surface; pricing is reduced to integration over that subset.

Prose distillation
The chapter introduces the modern industry-standard model for interest-rate derivatives — the BGM (Brace-Gatarek-Musiela) framework, also known as the Libor Market Model (LMM). The model’s distinctive feature is that it takes forward libor rates as the fundamental modelled processes, with each L_t[T_i, T_{i+1}] being lognormal under its own forward measure. This makes the Black-76 caplet formula (Ch. 12) automatic and lets prices for caps, swaptions, Bermudans, midcurve options, and exotic structures all be expressed as expectations over a unified BGM volatility surface.
Calibrating the BGM volatility surface to observed cap and swaption prices is the operational task of the modern interest-rate options desk; pricing exotic interest-rate derivatives reduces to (i) computing which subset of the surface the exotic depends on and (ii) Monte-Carlo or closed-form integration over that subset.
Why this chapter is “rough guide” material
Blyth treats BGM at a sketch level — the exposition is the surface and what depends on what, not the full mathematical machinery (which would require continuous-time stochastic calculus and a proper martingale-measure construction). For the full theory see Brigo and Mercurio (2006), Hull (10e), or Joshi (2008). The pedagogic point is to show the reader that all the discrete-time machinery developed in Parts II–IV does correspond to a unified continuous-time framework that practitioners actually use, and to give vocabulary for further reading.
Surface-region exercises (Ch. 15.2)
The exercises ask the reader to shade, on the triangular \sigma(t,T) surface, the region that determines the price at t = 0 of:

A 2y-into-5y European swaption (block on the surface)
A 2y-by-7y cap on 3-month libor (line)
A 2y-into-5y Bermudan swaption (block, and additionally correlations within block)
A “reset cap” with strike fixed at a future libor reset date (single point)
A forward-volatility trade (very specific localised region)

These exercises operationalise the BGM surface as a map of which interest-rate option prices look at which part of the volatility-of-the-forward-libor curve.
Notation introduced

\sigma(t, T) — BGM instantaneous-volatility surface
“BGM” / “LMM” — Brace-Gatarek-Musiela / Libor Market Model
“midcurve option” — option with exercise date T on a forward-starting product (FRA / swap) that begins at T^* > T
“reset cap” — cap whose strike equals a libor rate at a future reset date

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: ch_16_continuous_time
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Ch. 16 — Rough guide to continuous time
Formal spine

Brownian motion (Wiener process). Continuous-time limit of symmetric random walk. Properties: W_0 = 0; W_s - W_t \sim N(0, s-t) for t \le s; increments are independent. W_t is a martingale.
Stochastic differential equation (SDE). dS_t = \mu(S_t, t)\,dt + \sigma(S_t, t)\,dW_t. Discrete analogue: \Delta S_t = \mu \Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,W, W \sim N(0,1).
Geometric Brownian motion (GBM). dS_t = \mu S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t. Discrete: \Delta S_t/S_t = \mu \Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,W.
Ito’s lemma. For f(X_t, t) with dX_t = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t:
df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\,dt + \frac{\partial f}{\partial X_t}\,dX_t + \tfrac12\,\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial X_t^2}\,\sigma^2\,dt.
Mnemonic identities: dt^2 = 0, dt\,dW_t = 0, (dW_t)^2 = dt.
Black-Scholes PDE. Apply Ito’s lemma to the option price C(S_t, t), construct delta-hedged portfolio \Pi_t = C - (\partial C/\partial S_t)\,S_t, set d\Pi_t = r\Pi_t\,dt:
\frac{\partial C}{\partial t} + r S_t\,\frac{\partial C}{\partial S_t} - rC + \tfrac12\,\sigma^2 S_t^2\,\frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial S_t^2} = 0,
with boundary C(S_T, T) = (S_T - K)^+. Solution: the Black-Scholes formula of Ch. 10.
Change of numeraire (continuous time). For numeraire N_t, ratio S_t/N_t is a martingale under the corresponding measure. Computed by applying Ito’s lemma to the ratio and demanding the drift term vanish — gives the change in \mu required.
Black-Scholes via two numeraires. Split call payout (S_T - K)^+ = S_T \mathbb{1}\{S_T \ge K\} - K \mathbb{1}\{S_T \ge K\}. Price first term using stock numeraire (under which \mu = r + \sigma^2); price second term using money-market numeraire (\mu = r). Sum the two probabilities of exercise weighted by the relevant numeraire — recovers Black-Scholes formula without computing any tail integral.

Prose distillation
The concluding chapter sketches the continuous-time analogue of the discrete-time fundamental theorem (Ch. 9): the same numeraire / martingale / risk-neutral structure operates, but the algebra runs on Ito’s lemma rather than the binomial-tree backward induction. Three pedagogic moves:


Brownian motion as random-walk limit. The CLT-based construction of W_t from symmetric random walks parallels the CLT-based limit on the binomial tree from Ch. 10.


Ito’s lemma as the chain-rule for stochastic processes. The extra (1/2)(\partial^2 f / \partial X^2)\sigma^2\,dt term — absent in the deterministic chain rule — is what makes continuous-time finance non-trivial and is the source of the convexity / Jensen-inequality structure that appears throughout derivative pricing.


Black-Scholes derived three ways. (a) Probabilistically as the discounted lognormal expectation (Ch. 10). (b) Via the Black-Scholes PDE under delta hedging (this chapter). (c) Via change of numeraire and splitting the payout (this chapter). All three give the same formula; each illuminates a different facet of the result.


Why include this chapter
Blyth’s preface admits the chapter is a “rough guide”: the rigorous theory of continuous-time finance requires real stochastic calculus (Shreve 2004, Joshi 2008), measure-theoretic probability, and the proper construction of martingale measures via Girsanov’s theorem. But the discrete-time machinery developed in Chs. 1–15 is the conceptual core of the subject. The continuous-time apparatus is in many ways an alternative language for the same content, and the chapter shows the reader the bridge.
Girsanov / change-of-measure (sketched)
Although Blyth does not formally invoke Girsanov’s theorem, the change-of-numeraire calculations (e.g., S_t/M_t under stock-numeraire vs money-market-numeraire) are exactly Girsanov-style change-of-measure operations expressed concretely. The Radon-Nikodym derivative between two equivalent risk-neutral measures is a ratio of (numeraire growth processes) — implicit in every “the drift becomes r + \sigma^2 under the stock numeraire” step.
Notation introduced

W_t — standard Brownian motion (Blyth reserves W for this, since Z is taken by ZCB price)
dS_t, dW_t — SDE differential notation
“geometric Brownian motion” — multiplicative SDE
“Black-Scholes PDE” — partial differential equation for option price
“Girsanov” / “change of measure” — implicit; full machinery beyond scope

Closing line
“Combining our results for A and B we obtain — without calculating any tail integrals or solving partial differential equations — the Black-Scholes formula, which seems an apt place to end.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.title: Stephen Blyth An Introduction To Quantitative Finance — Chapter Deep Dives
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/stephe.content:
Stephen Blyth An Introduction To Quantitative Finance — Chapter Deep Dives
16 chapters

Ch.1 — Preliminaries

Compounding. Continuous: e^{rT}; semi-annual: (1+r/2)^{2T}; general: (1+r/m)^{mT} \to e^{rT} as m\to\infty.

Ch.2 — Forward contracts and forward prices

Forward contract. Agreement at t to trade asset at T for delivery price K. V_K(t,T) = value at t to the long; V_K(T,T) = S_T - K. - Forward price. F(t,T) = delivery price K such that V_K(t,T) = 0. F(T,T) = S_T. - No-i…

Ch.3 — Forward rates and libor

Forward ZCB price. F(t,T_1,T_2) = Z(t,T_2)/Z(t,T_1) — delivery price at T_1 for the T_2-maturity ZCB. - Forward interest rate (continuous compounding): f_{12} = \dfrac{r_2(T_2-t) - r_1(T_1-t)}{T_2 - T_1} — weighted average of zer…

Ch.4 — Interest rate swaps

Swap. Counterparty A pays fixed rate K and receives libor at dates T_1,\ldots,T_n, T_{i+1} = T_i + \alpha, on notional 1. - PV01. P_t[T_0,T_n] = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha\, Z(t,T_i) — sum of discount factors over fixed-leg payment da…

Ch.5 — Futures contracts

Futures contract. Like a forward but with daily mark-to-market: holder receives variation margin \Phi(i,T) - \Phi(i-1,T) each day. \Phi(T,T) = S_T. - Constant-rate result.

Ch.6 — No-arbitrage principle

No-arbitrage axiom. There exists no self-financing portfolio \Pi with: zero cost at t (\Pi_t = 0); \Pi_T \ge 0 for all states with probability 1; \Pi_T > 0 for at least one state with positive probability. - Monotonicity theore…

Ch.7 — Options

European call. Right to buy at strike K at exercise date T.

Ch.8 — Replication and risk-neutrality on the binomial tree

Two-state world. Stock S_0; at T=1, S_1 = S_0(1+u) (up) or S_0(1+d) (down), d < u.

Ch.9 — Martingales, numeraires and the fundamental theorem

Martingale. Sequence X_0, X_1, \ldots with E(|X_i|) < \infty and E(X_{n+1} \mid X_0, \ldots, X_n) = X_n.

Ch.10 — Continuous-time limit and Black-Scholes formula

Logarithmic returns. \lambda_n = \log(S_n/S_{n-1}), IID with E(\lambda_i) = \mu\Delta T, \text{Var}(\lambda_i) = \sigma^2 \Delta T.

Ch.11 — Option price and probability duality

Digital from limiting call spread. D_K(t,T) = -\partial C_K(t,T)/\partial K.

Ch.12 — Caps, floors and swaptions

Caplet. Call on libor: payout \alpha\,(L_T[T,T+\alpha] - K)^+ at T+\alpha. - Forward numeraire. N_t = Z(t, T+\alpha) — the ZCB with maturity matching the caplet’s payment date.

Ch.13 — Cancellable swaps and Bermudan swaptions

Cancellable swap. Swap with right (for one counterparty) to cancel at exercise dates T_j, T_{j+1}, \ldots, T_{n-1}.

Ch.14 — Libor-in-arrears and constant maturity swap contracts

Libor-in-arrears (LIA). Same as a standard libor payment \alpha L_T[T, T+\alpha], except paid at T instead of T+\alpha.

Ch.15 — The Brace-Gatarek-Musiela framework

BGM / Libor Market Model (LMM). Models the entire forward libor curve \{L_t[T_i, T_{i+1}] : i = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1\} as a system of correlated lognormal processes.

Ch.16 — Rough guide to continuous time

Brownian motion (Wiener process). Continuous-time limit of symmetric random walk.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: Afterlives of the Hacker Ethic
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Afterwords - Afterlives of the Hacker Ethic
Frame
The anniversary materials revisit the hacker ethic after the personal-computer industry, open source, the Web, and modern software culture have matured. Levy can now see which parts of the ethic persisted and which were absorbed by companies.
Core point
The ethic survives as a repertoire rather than a stable constitution. Access, sharing, anti-authority rhetoric, technical meritocracy, and computers-as-beauty all remain influential, but they are selectively invoked by institutions with different incentives.
Why it matters
The afterwords make the book useful for modern platform analysis. A company can invoke hacker openness while enclosing distribution. A community can invoke merit while missing exclusion. A tool can promise democratization while centralizing infrastructure.
Links
Primary book note: Steven Levy - Hackers

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: True Hackers at MIT
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Part I - MIT True Hackers
Frame
The first part builds the original hacker ethic out of MIT’s Tech Model Railroad Club, early computer access, Spacewar, Greenblatt, Gosper, and the AI Lab. Hacking begins as a style of direct encounter with complex systems: get access, understand the machine by changing it, value elegance, and judge people by the quality of their hacks.
Core point
The ethic is local before it is ideological. Access to machines is scarce, so access becomes a moral issue. Information circulates because the community improves code by sharing it. Authority is distrusted because bureaucracy blocks exploration. Computers are treated as media for beauty and play, not just calculation.
Why it matters
This part is the cultural counterpart to M. Mitchell Waldrop - The Dream Machine. Waldrop gives the institutional story of interactive computing; Levy gives the lived subculture that made interactivity feel like liberation.
Links
Primary book note: Steven Levy - Hackers

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: Hardware Hackers
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Part II - Hardware Hackers
Frame
The second part moves from institutional machines to personal computers. Homebrew Computer Club, Altair, Tiny BASIC, Lee Felsenstein, and Steve Wozniak transform the hacker ethic into a democratizing hardware movement.
Core point
The dream changes from “let hackers access institutional computers” to “put computers in everyone’s hands.” But the move into personal computing creates the software-property conflict. If software should be free because sharing improves the culture, how do programmers get paid when software becomes a product?
Why it matters
This part explains why personal computing inherits both open sharing and entrepreneurial enclosure. Woz embodies the elegant builder; Gates’s complaint about unpaid copying embodies the emerging software market.
Links
Primary book note: Steven Levy - Hackers

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: Game Hackers
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Part III - Game Hackers
Frame
The third part follows hacker creativity into commercial game software. Sierra/On-Line, Broderbund, Sirius, Atari-adjacent culture, and individual game programmers turn code into entertainment products.
Core point
Games preserve the aesthetic side of hacking: cleverness, immersion, surprise, and technical compression. But they also intensify the commercial side: secrecy, deadlines, royalties, distribution, corporate politics, and market competition. The hacker becomes a creative worker inside an industry.
Why it matters
This section prevents a pure-romance reading of the book. The hacker ethic can create markets that then reshape the ethic. That pattern repeats later in open source, Web platforms, app stores, and AI developer ecosystems.
Links
Primary book note: Steven Levy - Hackers

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: ch_00_preface
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Preface — How a Cognitive Scientist Came to Common Knowledge
Pinker frames the book as the mature continuation of The Stuff of Thought (2007). In that earlier book he had argued that people often don’t say what they mean in so many words but veil their intentions in innuendo and doublespeak, because “barefaced statements generate common knowledge but genteel euphemisms do not, and common knowledge is what ratifies or annuls social relationships.” The 2025 book expands that linguistic argument into a general framework: common knowledge explains fundamental features of societal organization (political power, financial markets), design specs of human nature (laughter, tears, blushing, eye contact), and countless curiosities of public and private life (bubbles, crashes, road rage, anonymous donations, long goodbyes, revolutions, social-media shaming, academic cancel culture).
Pinker’s billing is deliberately broad: “Common knowledge really is that powerful a concept. It is the mental feat that explains one of the hallmarks of the human condition: individual minds can coordinate their choices for mutual benefit, allowing our species to thrive in collectives ranging from couples to societies. Many of our harmonies and discords, I hope to show, fall out of our struggles to achieve, sustain, or prevent common knowledge.” The preface flags that the framework is Aumann 1976 and Lewis 1969 in origin, technical in math, but underused in popular discourse.
The preface acknowledges the research collaborators (Julian De Freitas, Peter DeScioli, Omar Sultan Haque, Moshe Hoffman, Yuhui Huang, James Lee, Miriam Lindner, Maxim Massenkoff, Jason Nemirow, Laura Niemi, Lawrence Ian Reed, Kyle Thomas, Dylan Tweed) whose work appears in chs. 4-7. It also names the formal-domain experts who advised Pinker: Scott Aaronson, Robert Aumann himself, Herbert Clark, Eric Maskin, Dov Samet. This is unusual for a popular book and reflects the technical density of the underlying framework.
The preface dedicates the book to Pinker’s deceased mother (Roslyn Wiesenfeld Pinker), to his late friends John Tooby and Donald Symons, and to Daniel Dennett and Daniel Kahneman. The reader who knows Pinker’s career will recognize this as a generational handoff: the cognitive-revolution cohort of 1980s-1990s evolutionary psychology and rationality is past its peak; this book is meant to integrate what that cohort learned with the technical apparatus of game-theoretic epistemics that was developed in parallel and never fully merged with the cognitive-science synthesis.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: ch_01_emperor-elephant-matzo-ball
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Chapter 1 — The Emperor, the Elephant, and the Matzo Ball: What Common Knowledge Is, and Why It Matters
The chapter defines common knowledge via Hans Christian Andersen’s Emperor’s New Clothes: the child’s announcement adds nothing to private knowledge (every onlooker could already see the emperor was naked) but converts private knowledge to common knowledge in one stroke, which “changed their relationship to the emperor, from obsequious deference to ridicule and scorn.” Pinker introduces the three-cartoon visualization: private knowledge (each observer sees, neither sees the other seeing), reciprocal knowledge (each sees through a keyhole, neither knows they have been seen seeing), and common knowledge (each sees the other seeing the event and seeing them seeing it, supporting any number of inferred levels).
The chapter then surveys the framework’s six main claims:

Common knowledge is logically distinct from private knowledge: learning publicly, even when everyone already knows, can change everything.
Common knowledge enables coordination: agents with common knowledge can confidently make complementary choices that private knowledge does not warrant.
Humans are intuitively sensitive to common knowledge — “almost as if we had a sense organ” for the concept.
This sensitivity has empowered Homo sapiens to coordinate behavior across networks (communities, economies, nations); rituals, conventions, and norms are intelligible as solutions to coordination problems; pathologies (fads, panics, bubbles, spirals of silence) are intelligible as common-knowledge failures.
Personal relationships (family, friends, lovers, colleagues) are coordination games whose ratification requires common knowledge.
Because coordination equilibria carry obligations, humans often block common knowledge to escape them — generating rituals of benign hypocrisy, plausible deniability, “catching someone’s drift,” “not going there.”

Pinker disambiguates the technical term common knowledge (Aumann 1976; Lewis 1969) from its colloquial use (“widely-known facts”). The technical literature considered alternatives (mutual knowledge, open knowledge, shared awareness, common ground); the entrenched term is “common knowledge” however misleading. He motivates the term via language itself: words have meaning because each speaker expects every other speaker to interpret them the same way (Diesendruck-Markson three-year-olds taught the word mef assume strangers know it).
The chapter’s Cheryl’s Birthday puzzle (2015 Singaporean Olympiad) is the first worked example of recursive mentalizing: Albert and Bernard each get partial information; their public announcements about what they don’t know let the reader (and each other) deduce the answer (July 16). The puzzle demonstrates that knowledge about knowledge is logically different from mere knowledge, and that humans can deploy this distinction with effort.
Money is the chapter’s main extended example. A piece of paper has value because everyone treats it as valuable and everyone knows that everyone knows that everyone treats it as valuable. Hyperinflation is the breakdown of this iterated structure. Cryptocurrency adds the public-ledger blockchain as a transparent common-knowledge mechanism for the cryptography but not for the speculation: the 2022 Crypto Bowl Super Bowl LVI ads (Matt Damon’s “fortune favors the brave,” Larry David’s anti-FTX cameo) were paid common-knowledge generators of the expectation that other people would invest. FTX collapsed within months.
Apple’s 1984 Macintosh Super Bowl XVIII ad (directed by Ridley Scott) is Pinker’s canonical product-launch example. The political scientist Michael Chwe’s 2001 Rational Ritual showed that Super Bowl ads disproportionately come from products with network externalities (job sites, credit cards, tech) and from social goods (beer, cars, restaurants, movies) where consumption-in-common matters; private-consumption goods (motor oil, breakfast cereal) advertise far less. Chwe controlled for raw audience size in regressions; the common-knowledge effect is real, not just numerical reach.
Political dissent is the chapter’s third extended example. The Soviet pamphleteer joke (a man hands out blank pages: “what is there to write? It’s so obvious!”) and the 2022 Russian arrest of a real woman holding a blank sign exemplify protests that work only because they generate common knowledge of dissent. Pinker cites Erica Chenoweth’s data: nonviolent civil-resistance movements outperformed violent ones (51% vs 25% success rate); the rise of common-knowledge generators (photocopier, fax, internet, social media) accelerated success rates. China’s censorship strategy (King-Pan-Roberts result) targets posts that coordinate action, not posts that criticize.
Justine Sacco’s December 2013 “Going to Africa. Hope I don’t get AIDS. Just kidding. I’m white!” tweet is the chapter’s cancel-culture case study. 170 followers; one snitch retweets; trending #1 on Twitter before her plane lands. Pinker frames this via Jonathan Haidt’s “billion dart guns” metaphor: social-media virality buttons (Like/Share/Retweet, introduced 2009) created common-knowledge punishment infrastructure where individual snipers could cheaply enforce norms. The DeScioli-Kurzban moral-condemnation-as-coalitional-alignment thesis explains why the targets are often innocent: to serve as a coalition focal point, an infraction must be public, observable, and undeniable, which makes intentions and consequences (the bedrocks of moral reasoning) irrelevant.
The chapter closes with the Lakoff-Johnson conceptual metaphor COMMON KNOWLEDGE IS A CONSPICUOUS SIGHT OR SOUND, instantiated by idioms (“the cat is out of the bag,” “it’s on the record,” “you can’t take it back,” “it’s already out there,” “the elephant in the room”). This metaphor structures how speakers without technical vocabulary already think about the framework — confirming Pinker’s thesis that common knowledge is a real cognitive category, even if the terminology is recent.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: ch_02_common-knowledge-and-common-sense
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Chapter 2 — Common Knowledge and Common Sense: Why It’s Hard to Say Goodbye, How to Tell If You Have Spinach in Your Teeth, and Why We Shouldn’t Agree to Disagree
The chapter presents three formal results about common knowledge that violate common sense, each mathematically provable under idealization. Pinker’s thesis is that the results are not “spherical cows” — each illuminates a real feature of human reasoning even when the proof’s idealizations don’t strictly apply.
Result 1 — You can deduce facts about the world from what people don’t know. The Spinach-in-Teeth puzzle (Pinker’s preferred isomorph of the original 1950s “Cheating Wives” puzzle, later sanitized through “Muddy Children,” “Blue-Eyed Islanders,” and other variants). A dinner host announces “at least one of you has spinach in your teeth”; clinks a glass repeatedly; after N clinks, all N spinach-toothed diners simultaneously clean their teeth. The induction works only because the announcement creates common knowledge of the existence of at least one spinach-tooth — private (or even reciprocal) knowledge would not. Pinker also presents the Three Logicians Walk Into a Bar warmup (“everyone wants beer” deduction) and the Purloined Letter literary instance.
Result 2 — No finite number of acknowledgements suffices for coordination. The Electronic Mail Game (Rubinstein 1989) and the Coordinated Attack problem. Two generals on hilltops cannot coordinate an attack via couriers if each courier has a 10% chance of being captured. No matter how many round trips of “I got your message,” “I got your acknowledgement,” “I got your acknowledgement of my acknowledgement”… the second-to-last sender remains uncertain. Pinker quantifies via fighter-pilot illustration: with 10% loss rate, sending a message and acting on it has 90% success; demanding an acknowledgement reduces to 81% success and creates 9% disastrous-attack-by-one-pilot risk; arbitrary numbers of messages cannot reach common knowledge.
The remedy is to weaken common knowledge to common p-belief (Monderer-Samet). For coordination games where miscoordination costs are bearable, common .9-belief or common .95-belief suffices. The pilots’ “roger” convention exists because it puts the commanding officer in the less-vulnerable position. The dial-up modem handshake is the engineering instance of the same logic.
The chapter’s worked illustration is goodbyes: long telephone goodbyes, dinner-party doorknob conversations (“klamke-talk” in Pinker’s Yiddish-grandmother phrasing). Saying goodbye risks asymmetry — the leaver implies “I’m done with you” if the relationship was ambiguously communal; common-knowledge-generators (a wedding ceremony, a contract) are needed to ratify the shift cleanly.
Result 3 — Rational agents with shared priors cannot agree to disagree. Aumann’s 1976 Agreement Theorem: “If two people have the same priors, and their posteriors for a given event A are common knowledge, then these posteriors must be equal. This is so even though they may base their posteriors on quite different information.” The proof is three pages of high-school algebra; the result is “not quite obvious” (Aumann’s understatement).
Pinker walks through a literary-prize illustration adapted from his correspondence with Aumann: four finalists differing in age, sex, and nationality; a juror tells two friends different partial information about the winner; once they make their posteriors common knowledge, agreement is forced. The Geanakoplos-Polemarchakis “We Can’t Disagree Forever” extension (1982) shows that the convergence trajectory is a random walk — each rational update should leave no predictable direction, lest the predictability itself imply unrealized information.
The implications are sharp. Speculative trade is irrational under shared priors and common-knowledge prices: each side believes the price will move in a different direction, but if either side’s reason for moving were sound, the price would already have moved. Pinker connects this to standard low-cost-index-fund advice: any actionable signal you have heard is already common knowledge in markets and already priced. Sports betting and stock-tip trading require at least one irrational party.
The Cowen-Hanson defense of the shared-prior assumption: priors are yesterday’s posteriors; “the world doesn’t care about your melanin or genitals or DNA”; rational agents reason from the viewpoint of eternity behind a veil of ignorance about which body they are incarnated as. Cowen and Hanson conclude that most disagreements are dishonest (Trivers’s self-deception-deceives-others theory) — people adopt self-serving priors about their own competence and rectitude that they would condemn if anyone else did so.
Pinker connects the Aumann ideal to the active open-mindedness norm advocated by the rationality community / Bayesians / forecasters: confidence ranges, steel-manning, adversarial collaborations, betting on predictions (“a bet is a tax on bullshit,” Tabarrok). The chapter closes with the Lakoff-Johnson ARGUMENT IS WAR metaphor — Pinker had once thought their alternative ARGUMENT IS DANCE was strained, but Aumann convinces him: rational argument should be more like a dance than a war, the disputants weaving and twisting toward consensus.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: ch_03_fun-and-games
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Chapter 3 — Fun and Games: The Stag Hunt, the Battle of the Sexes, Hawks and Doves, and Other Coordination Games
Pinker’s central methodological move: coordination games, not the Prisoner’s Dilemma, are the primary structure underlying human social behavior. The chapter introduces five canonical coordination games and shows that each is a different distillation of how iterated knowledge mediates agent choice.
Rendezvous — two friends agree to meet for coffee; cell phones die; both prefer either of two cafés as long as they end up together. Two equilibria with identical payoffs; game theory cannot select between them. The chapter cites Schelling 1960’s seminal observation that common salience (a focal point) can resolve coordination games even without communication. Schelling’s classic example: a separated couple in New York would converge on the Grand Central clock at noon, not because of any logical necessity but because the focal point is mutually expected to be expected.
The Stag Hunt — Rousseau (1755). Two hunters can take down a stag (large reward) only if both bring stag-hunting equipment; either can take a hare (small but certain reward) alone. Two equilibria: stag-stag (best for both) and hare-hare (second-best for both); the dilemma is that uncertainty about the partner’s choice can drive both to defect to the safe equilibrium. Skyrms (The Stag Hunt and the Evolution of Social Structure) treats this as the core evolutionary puzzle of cooperation. Pinker cites the Lamaleran whale-hunters of Indonesia (Alvard-Nolin) as the empirical instance: 8-14 men crew, all roles needed; convention selects which patrilineal-descent groups hunt together. The Coordinated Attack problem of Chapter 2 is a Stag Hunt; bank runs and asset bubbles are Stag Hunts; protests are Stag Hunts (“if enough other protesters show up, all enjoy the stag of regime change; if outnumbered, imprisoned or gunned down”). Movement leaders generate common expectations of success (“we shall overcome”) to convert hare-hunting equilibria into stag-hunting ones.
Battle of the Sexes — both partners prefer either of two equilibria to mismatching, but each has a different favorite (opera vs hockey game). Two equilibria with asymmetric payoffs. The chapter notes that this game underlies real-world bargaining (haggling) and standards-setting (USB-C vs Lightning, the technical standards battle). The “paradoxical tactic” of voluntary loss-of-control (a car salesman who needs the manager’s approval, a buyer who needs the loan officer’s) can force the equilibrium toward one party.
Hawk-Dove (also Chicken) — two teenagers driving toward each other; first to swerve loses face. Two equilibria where players make opposite choices. Mutual hawk play produces catastrophic crash. Maynard Smith’s evolutionary-game-theory naming (Hawk-Dove) honors the species-internal nature of the conflict. The Bourgeois strategy (whoever arrived first plays Hawk, intruder plays Dove) becomes a focal point — and David Hume identified this as the rationale behind the human convention of property. McAdams (legal scholar) argues that legal systems exploit the same focal-point logic: democratic governments cannot enforce most laws via coercion alone; the law’s expressive function (declaring an expectation) creates a focal point that becomes self-enforcing. The 1980s+ no-smoking-in-public-spaces transition is Pinker’s worked example: probably no one was ever arrested under those laws, but once NO SMOKING signs created common knowledge of the new equilibrium, nonsmokers were emboldened to enforce it informally.
The Long Peace and the Territorial Integrity Norm. Pinker uses the chapter’s coordination-game framework to explain the post-1945 decline in interstate war. The territorial-integrity norm — UN members pledge not to wage war except in self-defense or with Security Council approval — is empirically credited (Goldstein, others) with the long peace. As a focal-point convention it works because every existing border becomes the commonly-salient solution to every potential dispute about that border, making compromise and arbitration cheaper than escalation. International Court of Justice success rates and religious-court / arbitral-tribunal track records are exhibits. Notable failures (Russia-Ukraine 2022) do not refute the framework but cost their initiators reputational capital.
Cheap talk vs costly signaling. Pinker distinguishes pure-coordination games (Rendezvous; cheap talk works because interests align) from games with conflict (Battle of the Sexes, Prisoner’s Dilemma; cheap talk is “not worth the paper it’s written on”). The peacock’s tail and the antelope sproing are evolutionary instances of costly signaling; degree certificates are human instances. The chapter closes by re-stating that the chapter’s main thesis — coordination games admit no purely-game-theoretic solution and require some external selection mechanism (common knowledge or its substitute, common salience) — implies that coordination dilemmas, even when analyzed with the hardheaded math of game theory, give pride of place to the messy human preoccupations of culture, history, tradition, symbolism, aesthetics, and casual conversation. The legal scholar Richard McAdams’s observation that “law is not just coercive but expressive” is the chapter’s executive summary.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: ch_04_mind-of-a-mind-reader
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Chapter 4 — Reading the Mind of a Mind Reader: Bystanders, Bank Runs, Beauty Contests
The chapter’s question: how do humans implement common knowledge in a finite skull? Three formal models for representing common knowledge are presented, then tested against empirical cognitive psychology and applied to financial markets and bystander behavior.
Three formal representations.

Iterated/recursive propositions — list “Amy knows X, Brad knows X, Amy knows that Brad knows X…” with infinite tail. The list cannot fit in a finite skull, but the ”…” tail can stand in for the infinite series.
Reflexive/fixed-point representation — “(n): Amy and Brad know X, and Amy and Brad know n” as a self-referential proposition. Mathematically clean but cognitively unintuitive.
Self-evident events — “Amy and Brad experienced a self-evident event that implies X” where a self-evident event (joint attention, public announcement, conspicuous public happening) is by definition known-to-all. Herbert Clark and others argue this is the most plausible psychological implementation.

Empirical cognitive limits. The Kinderman-Dunbar-Bentall study had college students answer questions about embedded mental states (“John thought that Penny knew what Sheila wanted to do” = third-order). Performance is solid up to fourth-order; falls off a cliff at fifth-order. The chapter notes that humans can “chunk” recurring patterns of embedded mental states into single semantic units (bluff, conceal from, deceive, doubt, humor, persuade, suspect) and into longer scripts (affair, scandal, argument); chunked patterns can effectively support more layers without exceeding working-memory.
Pinker’s research team’s experiments. Thomas, DeScioli, Haque, and Pinker (and later De Freitas, Lee, Lindner) ran online studies in which participants imagined being a butcher or baker (Stag Hunt structure) facing different states of knowledge about hot-dog prices.

Private knowledge (only the participant knows): ~20% attempt coordination
Public knowledge (loudspeaker announcement): ~80% attempt coordination
Intermediate orders (second/third-order): ~50% attempt coordination, often committing the “turtles all the way down” fallacy or having the higher-order knowledge collapse into lower-order in working memory

The De Freitas-Pinker follow-up tested whether participants infer that a public event entails any number of embedded knowledge states. They presented an 18-level-embedded sentence about a public car crash; participants overwhelmingly endorsed it as something Edward “has reason to believe.” Self-evidence is the cognitive substrate humans actually use.
Keynesian beauty contests. Keynes 1936 likened stock-market investing to a newspaper beauty contest where readers must pick the prettiest face anticipating what other readers will pick. “We have reached the third degree where we devote our intelligence to anticipating what average opinion expects the average opinion to be. And there are some, I believe, who practise the fourth, fifth and higher degrees.”
Mehta-Starmer-Sugden (replicating Schelling 1960) showed empirical recursive mentalizing: when paired participants must match each other’s choice, they shift from idiosyncratic favorites toward stereotypical responses (rose for flower, red for color, John for boy’s name, London for city, 1 for number). Rosemary Nagel’s “guess two-thirds of the average” experiment found people guess ~36 (one or two layers of recursion), not 0 (full common-knowledge convergence). In real-world newspaper-contest replications about 15% chose 0; the most successful contestants ran little experiments among friends to find the population-specific best response.
Bank runs and asset bubbles. Pinker treats these as Stag Hunts. Two equilibria — keep money in (best for everyone) or withdraw early (second-best); each depositor fears being last to withdraw. Hofstadter’s reverberant doubt names the phenomenon. Banks’ marble columns (and the Pete-Seeger-Weavers song “The Banks Are Made of Marble”) were common-knowledge generators of solvency. FDIC plaques replaced marble in the post-1933 era. FDR’s “the only thing we have to fear is fear itself” is “literally true: the fear of fear itself was the immediate cause of the bank runs.”
The 2023 Silicon Valley Bank collapse is the chapter’s recent case: Twitter-coordinated withdrawals generated common knowledge in hours. Matt Klein’s “more a case of a ‘bank-run by idiots’ than a ‘bank run by idiots’” captures the cascade dynamic. The 2020 toilet-paper hoarding (Wolfers’s analysis) is structurally identical and traces back to a 1973 Johnny Carson monologue joke that was false at the time but self-fulfilling within days; toilet-paper-as-emergency-commodity became a culturally installed focal point.
Meme stocks. GameStop 2021 (Keith Gill’s “Roaring Kitty”); May 2024 leaning-forward cartoon tweet tripled the stock in two days. Pinker’s framework: any conspicuous focal point that brings an asset into mass consciousness can ignite a Keynesian beauty contest, regardless of fundamentals. Closed-end mutual fund example: Caribbean Basin Fund (ticker CUBA) jumped from -10% NAV discount to +70% NAV premium when Obama announced relaxed Cuba relations, despite the fund holding no Cuban assets.
Inflationary spirals, recessions, currency runs. All exhibit the same common-expectation structure. Greenspan: “I’ve learned to mumble with great incoherence… If I seem unduly clear to you, you must have misunderstood what I said.” Alfred Kahn (Carter’s inflation czar, told to avoid the word depression): “We’re in danger of having the worst banana in 45 years”; switched to kumquat when banana producers protested. Central-bank communication is precisely-imprecise common-knowledge management.
Bystander apathy. The 1964 Kitty Genovese case (the 38 witnesses number was largely fabricated; only 6 actually witnessed the attack) inspired the Darley-Latané laboratory studies that found inactive-confederates suppress emergency response 80% to 30%. Diekmann reframed this as the Volunteer’s Dilemma: each bystander prefers someone-else-intervenes > self-intervenes > no-one-intervenes; the optimal mixed strategy depends on payoff ratios and the number of potential volunteers. The Pinker-team experiment manipulated state of knowledge: with private knowledge, volunteer rate is high; with second-order knowledge (you know someone else knows), shirk; third-order, volunteer; fourth-order, shirk; common knowledge produces the textbook bystander effect (more bystanders = less helping).
Joe Biden’s June 2024 dropout. Many of his advisors privately knew of his cognitive decline; voters told pollsters they were worried; but Biden, allies, and the Democratic Party supported his reelection bid as if all was normal. After the June 2024 debate, the percentage doubting his fitness rose only “by a few percentage points,” but the private knowledge became common knowledge, and within four weeks Biden bowed out. Pinker’s freshest illustration of the private-to-common-knowledge phase shift.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.title: ch_05_department-of-social-relations
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/steven.content:
Chapter 5 — The Department of Social Relations: Social Relationships as Coordination Games
The chapter applies the common-knowledge framework to Maimonides’ Ladder of Charity (12th-century Mishneh Torah) and to anthropologist Alan Fiske’s four relational models (Communal Sharing, Authority Ranking, Equality Matching, Market Pricing).
Maimonides’ Ladder. Eight rungs of charity ranked by mutual-knowledge structure:

Lifelong support (loan, partnership, work) so the recipient never asks
Anonymous donor and anonymous recipient (top of the mutual-knowledge rungs)
Donor knows recipient; recipient does not know donor
Recipient knows donor; donor does not know recipient
5–8. Common knowledge (donor-initiated; recipient-initiated; cheerfully-but-too-little; grudgingly)

Eleven-year-old Pinker confronted his Sunday-school teacher about the apparent contradiction: if anonymous giving is so righteous, why is Temple Beth Sholom studded with donor-named pews? The chapter develops this puzzle into a research program with De Freitas, DeScioli, and Thomas.
