Brief biographical sketch surfaces: 35 years old, Harvard MD/PhD anthropology, lives in a church rectory in a poor Boston neighborhood four months a year, the rest of the year doctoring peasants displaced by the Péligre Dam. The opening line of the book — “We met because of a beheading, of all things” — is Farmer’s six-years-later recall.
Kidder takes Farmer to dinner in Boston, sends small donations to PIH over five years, but stays at arm’s length: Farmer “disturbs” him, demands an “extreme definition of doing one’s best.” Chapter ends with Kidder calling Farmer in late 1999 to set up the reporting that becomes the book.
Anchors the book’s organizing tension: Farmer is plainly impressive but his ethic is hard to share; Kidder will spend the rest of the book working out why.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_04_chapter-2
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 2 — The Brigham (December 1999)
Kidder spends a day shadowing Farmer at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, four floors down in radiology. Farmer is now 40, attending physician on the Brigham’s senior staff, professor at Harvard Medical School, head of the Brigham’s HIV service when on rotation. Six cases that day; the focal one is “Joe” — HIV-positive, alcoholic, IV cocaine user, possible TB. Farmer spends 30+ minutes sitting on Joe’s bed, treating the case with the same patience he uses in Cange. He concludes pneumonia, not TB. When Joe asks for a place to live where he can drink a six-pack, Farmer breaks the social work rule and finds him a shelter — and on Christmas brings him a six-pack of beer disguised in wrapping paper.
A janitor calls Farmer “a fuckin’ saint.” Farmer’s reply, prepared earlier: “I don’t care how often people say, ‘You’re a saint.’ It’s not that I mind it. It’s that it’s inaccurate.” But then: “People call me a saint and I think, I have to work harder. Because a saint would be a great thing to be.” Kidder marks this as the moment he realized Farmer had ambitions he hadn’t fathomed.
Farmer’s book Infections and Inequalities (which Kidder reads) makes the same arguments as the Brigham doctor but “shouting on every page.” Email at chapter end: “But that is not my oeuvre. To see my oeuvre you have to come to Haiti.” Sets up the trip that anchors the rest of the book.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_05_chapter-3
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 3 — Zanmi Lasante (January 2000)
Kidder’s first arrival at Cange. The 35-mile drive from Port-au-Prince takes three hours up the wreck-strewn National Highway 3. At the top of a steep incline, headlights pick out the wall and gate of Zanmi Lasante (“Partners In Health” in Creole) — a walled medical citadel on a mountainside in the central plateau, the poorest part of the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere.
Inventory of the complex: ambulatory clinic, women’s clinic, general hospital, Anglican church, school, kitchen feeding ~2,000 daily, brand-new TB treatment building, two laboratories, running water, generator. Tile floors, white walls, Haitian paintings. About 100,000 in the catchment area, 70 community health workers; ~1 million peasants relied on the place.
Health metrics under Zanmi Lasante: HIV mother-to-baby transmission cut to 4% (half the contemporary U.S. rate); no TB death since 1988; vaccinated all children; reduced malnutrition and infant mortality. Cost: ~150-200 to cure uncomplicated TB (vs. 15,000-20,000 in the U.S.). 1999 budget: 1.5 million treating ~175,000 patients (Kidder's local Massachusetts hospital: 60M for the same number).
Farmer’s daily rhythm: early-dawn courtyard rounds, e-mail at the satellite phone, then office hours where 30-40 patients wait in the hall. The “user fee” rule is officially 80 Haitian cents but is “subverted” — everyone pays except women, children, the destitute, the seriously ill (i.e., almost everyone). Farmer’s rule: no one is turned away.
Domestic life: small ti kay across the road, 4-hour nights, two million miles flown, family in Paris (wife Didi finishing anthropology degree, daughter Catherine). MacArthur “genius grant” of $220,000 (1993) donated entirely to PIH’s Institute for Health and Social Justice. Bookkeeper: “you are the hardest-workin’ broke man I know.”
Cases: gangrene from 15-day-old wound; “Lazarus” recovering from AIDS+TB; sickle-cell crisis; “Pott’s disease” (TB of the spine, untreated, irreversible) on a woman bent at 90°. The “sorcery consult” — Farmer reconciling a mother who believes one son “sold” the other to maji. Ti Ofa, AIDS patient with five-drug bottle of indinavir; Farmer is treating impoverished Haitians with antiretrovirals when “almost no one in any poor country” is. The phrase comma — Farmer’s verbal placeholder for “asshole,” directed only at third parties comfortable with the global distribution of money and medicine.
Closes with the late-evening spinal tap on a 13-year-old girl; the girl cries “It hurts, I’m hungry” — Farmer narrates Haiti once more: “Only in Haiti would a child cry out that she’s hungry during a spinal tap.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_06_chapter-4
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 4 — The hike to Morne Michel (the noncompliance study)
Kidder follows Farmer on a five-hour round-trip hike to Morne Michel, the most distant village in Zanmi Lasante’s catchment, to find one TB patient who missed his monthly appointment.
Embedded inside the chapter is the chapter’s analytical core: the late-1980s comparative study Farmer ran when a TB patient died in his absence in 1988. He selected two groups of TB patients. Both got free treatment. One group additionally received community-health-worker visits, monthly cash stipends (~$5 USD) for food, child care, and transport. Result: the medicine-only group had a 48% cure rate; the medicine + cash + community-health-worker group had 100%. Belief in sorcery was equally distributed across both groups and made no difference. The line that crystallized it for Farmer came from an elderly female patient who first told him she didn’t believe in sorcery, then a year later said she did: “Cheri, eske-w pa ka konprann bagay ki pa senp?” — “Honey, are you incapable of complexity?”
Operational consequence: every TB patient now gets directly observed therapy + monthly cash stipend + community health worker. Twelve years and zero deaths since. Farmer’s slogan: “The only noncompliant people are physicians. If the patient doesn’t get better, it’s your own fault. Fix it.”
The Péligre Dam appears in this chapter as Farmer’s “favorite case study” — built mid-1950s by Brown & Root of Texas with U.S. Export-Import Bank funding under a U.S.-supported dictator, ostensibly for irrigation and power but actually serving downstream agribusiness and Port-au-Prince elites. Drowned the central plateau farmland; the patients of Cange are descendants of the “water refugees.” Farmer’s argument: to understand Haiti, Russia, Cuba, identity politics — “you have to be on top of this hill” looking down at the impounded waters.
Anti-cost-effectiveness rhetoric: “We can spend sixty-eight thousand dollars per TB patient in New York City, but if you start giving watches or radios to patients here, suddenly the international health community jumps on you for creating nonsustainable projects.”
Farmer’s reply when Kidder asks why he hikes for a single noncompliant patient: a sweet smile, then “Fuck you.” Then the formal version: “The objective is to inculcate in the doctors and nurses the spirit to dedicate themselves to the patients.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_07_chapter-5
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 5 — The Blue Bird Inn and the Lady Gin (Farmer’s childhood)
Origins. Born 1959 in North Adams, Massachusetts. Father — Paul Sr., “the Warden” / “Elbows” — moved family to Birmingham, Alabama (1966) seeking sales work, then to Brooksville, Florida (1971). Bought at auction a converted bus — the Blue Bird Inn (originally a mobile TB clinic, hence the X-ray-machine turret on the roof). The family of eight lived in this bus in a Florida campground for five years.
Then the Lady Gin — a 50-foot Liberty launch the Warden bought as an empty hull and refitted. The family moved aboard at Jenkins Creek bayou. Cooking with charcoal, washing in brackish water, cockroaches in the bilge, drinking water siphoned from convenience-store spigots. Mother Ginny worked Winn-Dixie cash register; later got her bachelor’s at Smith.
Childhood inputs that mattered: Tolkien’s Lord of the Rings at age 11 (he kept rereading; later said “what could be more religious than Lord of the Rings or War and Peace?”). Aquarium in the bus; herpetology club; gifted-and-talented class; Latin names for everything; played tennis and track at Hernando High; class president; full scholarship to Duke.
At Duke he encountered wealth (preppy classmates, fraternity social-director phase), then walked away from it: quit the fraternity over the all-white membership, joined migrant-labor-camp organizing with Belgian nun Julianna DeWolf, met the first Haitians of his life among migrant workers in North Carolina tobacco country. His father’s instruction picking citrus: “Yeah? I’ll give you white people.”
Encountered Rudolf Virchow at Duke — the 19th-century German physician-anthropologist-politician who declared “medicine is a social science, and politics is nothing but medicine on a large scale.” Farmer’s favorite Virchow line: “The physicians are the natural attorneys of the poor, and the social problems should largely be solved by them.” Virchow becomes the model.
Liberation theology surfaces (1980, after Archbishop Romero’s assassination); the Latin American bishops’ “preferential option for the poor” hits him hard. Curiosity, not just outrage, drives him toward Haiti. Wins a Duke prize for an essay on Haitian artists, uses the $1,000 to fly to Haiti in spring 1983.
Father dies of heart attack 1984 during a pickup basketball game, age 49 — soon after Paul accepted at Harvard Medical School. Paul finds the Warden’s letter saying “I just want you to know how proud I am” and breaks down in the front seat of the derelict bus.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_08_chapter-6
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 6 — Duke, Virchow, and arrival in Haiti (1983)
Duke years. Photographic memory for friends; legions of female friends; food fights and Sound of Music sing-alongs while studying. Summer in Paris with Franco-American family as au pair; took the last course Claude Lévi-Strauss ever taught (carried to the stage). Read fluent French; senior honors thesis on “gender inequality and depression” under medical anthropologists.
Adopts Virchow as his model — the German physician’s combination of pathology, social medicine, archaeology, politics, public health, and “medicine on a large scale.” Virchow’s epidemiological law: “If disease is an expression of individual life under unfavorable conditions, then epidemics must be indicative of mass disturbances of mass life.” Virchow had been fired by the German government for his Upper Silesia report blaming famine fever on “absentee landlordism” rather than the louse vector science would later confirm.
Liberation theology — Latin American bishops’ “preferential option for the poor,” the late-1960s declaration that the poverty of the masses is “institutionalized sin.” Farmer reads about Romero’s assassination, attends the Duke Chapel vigil. The “church ladies” — radical Catholic nuns working with United Farm Workers in North Carolina — impress him more than the academics; “they were the ones standing up to the growers in their sensible nun shoes.”
Visits Krome Detention Center in Florida; protests U.S. policy of accepting Cuban refugees but deporting Haitian ones. Reads Haitian history obsessively — Arawak extermination, French colonial slave economy (one-third of every shipment dead within three years), the 1791 slave revolt, 1804 independence as the world’s first black republic. Calls Haitians “the shafted of the shafted” and decides to spend a year there before medical school.
Lands in Port-au-Prince spring 1983 — François Duvalier Airport, Baby Doc still in power, tontons macoutes in dark glasses. Visits the Hôpital Albert Schweitzer in Deschapelles (Mellon family’s hospital) but recoils — staffed by white expatriates, not training Haitians. Heads back to Port-au-Prince “deflated.” Joins Eye Care Haiti, a small charity that runs mobile outreach clinics, and takes the truck out to its base in Mirebalais.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_09_chapter-7
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 7 — Meeting Ophelia (Mirebalais, 1983)
Ophelia Dahl, daughter of writer Roald Dahl and actress Patricia Neal, arrives in Haiti at 18 as a volunteer for Eye Care Haiti. She has come at her father’s prompting; she had to consult an atlas to find Haiti before flying. After a frustrating attempt to call home, she returns to the Mirebalais Eye Care house in the rain to find a “pale and rangy fellow” — Paul Farmer, 23, just arrived. They talk past 3 a.m.
Over the following weeks, Farmer narrates Haiti for her: explains why the tonton macoute national chief (Madame Max Adolphe, formerly warden of Fort Dimanche, “Buchenwald”) owns the land they’re living on; identifies the clownish “Petit Pierre” Ophelia met at the Hôpital Oloffson as a real Duvalierist informant who served as Graham Greene’s model in The Comedians. They drive past a fatal tap-tap accident on Morne Kabrit; the dead “mango lady” stretched on her bier of fruit becomes the subject of one of Farmer’s poems and the chapter’s organizing image — not every bad thing that happens is an accident.
Farmer’s developing analytical position: anthropology concerns meaning, not measurement; the mango lady’s death has multiple causes — bad road, overloaded tap-tap, exhausted shocks, the desperation of a peasant woman who had to make a sale. The proximate causes go up to the misrule of the Duvaliers and U.S. aid that finances Baby Doc rather than roads.
Years later — opening epigraph of the chapter — Ophelia writes Paul a letter explaining she cannot marry him. The qualities that drew her to him (unswerving commitment to the poor, limitless schedule, massive compassion) are also the qualities that would force her to subordinate her own emotional needs to his work. She remains his closest collaborator and PIH co-founder; she becomes the organization’s chief financial conscience.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_10_chapter-8
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 8 — Cange and Léogâne (1983-1984)
First sight of Cange in May 1983: the squatter settlement of “water refugees” displaced by the Péligre Dam, half a mile up the road from the reservoir. Banana-bark roofs patched with rags; “the absence of tin, in Cange, screamed, ‘Misery.‘” Farmer rides in with the Haitian Anglican priest Fritz Lafontant. Sleeps on the floor of the schoolroom on army blankets.
Tours other situations — comes down with dysentery, recovers, attends Voodoo ceremonies, talks to peasants, volunteers at the Hôpital St. Croix in Léogâne. There he encounters the founding moment of his life’s work: a young pregnant woman in a malaria coma, in respiratory distress, needing a transfusion. There is no blood. The hospital requires payment up front. Farmer scrapes together $15; the sister cannot afford both transport and the blood. The woman and her unborn baby die. The sister, sobbing, repeats: tout moun se moun — “we are all human beings.” This phrase becomes the answer Farmer was already looking for to a question another American doctor had triggered earlier that day: when the doctor had said he could leave Haiti behind because “I’m an American, and I’m going home,” Farmer had replied “Right. Me, too” and known instantly that he could not.
Farmer raises a few thousand dollars from family and Duke friends to buy the hospital its own blood-banking equipment, then learns the hospital will charge patients to use it. Decides on the road back to the central plateau: “I’m going to build my own fucking hospital. And there’ll be none of that there, thank you.”
Goes to work at Père Lafontant’s small clinic in Mirebalais; finds it grim — perfunctory exams, “filthy corncob-stoppered bottles” filled with cough medicine and vitamins for pay. With Lafontant’s blessing, focuses on Cange: starts a hand-tabulated health census of Cange and two neighboring villages, which confirms that infant and juvenile mortality are “horrific” and that maternal death is a structural cause of cascading family catastrophe.
Encounter with a local Haitian woman re: move san, lèt gate (a syndrome where shock turns blood and milk to poison) crystallizes the anthropology-medicine fusion: ethnographic observation alone is “impotent” in the face of “everyday problems of adequate nutrition, clean water, and illness prevention.” The woman tells him: “Surely you are collecting these leaves in order to better understand their power and improve their efficacy.” The “anthropologist within” essay follows.
Enters Harvard Medical School fall 1984 at age 24. Skips most lectures, returns to Haiti, returns to Boston for lab practicums and exams. Classmates nickname him “Paul Foreigner.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_11_chapter-9
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 9 — Building Zanmi Lasante; meeting Tom White (1985-1986)
The Harvard-Haiti commute begins to forge a religious orientation. Farmer wears a wooden cross outside his shirt. He has “faith” — also faith in penicillin, rifampin, isoniazid, the fluoroquinolones, in bench science, in HIV as the cause of AIDS, in the rich oppressing the poor.
Ophelia returns summer 1985. They build their relationship through flash-card medical study sessions, hikes to villages where Farmer recites Latin plant names, meals of dubious fifth-food-group items presented by hosts. Ophelia “gives herself” to him on a Sunday afternoon in Père Lafontant’s empty rectory while everyone else is at church.
Operational construction of Zanmi Lasante. Farmer expands the health census using a manual from rural India. Ophelia walks the gullies and mountainsides counting populations. Drinking water solved by a Haitian-American engineering team from the Episcopal Diocese of Upper South Carolina who pipe a sparkling underground river up to communal spigots in Cange — infant deaths begin dropping immediately. Farmer rejects “appropriate technology” doctrine: “Do you know what appropriate technology means? It means good things for rich people and shit for the poor” (Lafontant’s growl). The first microscope in Cange is a real one — stolen from Harvard Medical School. “Redistributive justice. We were just helping them not go to hell.”
Defining “first line of defenses”: vaccinations, water/sanitation, community health workers trained to recognize TB, malaria, typhoid; women’s health and family planning. Lafontant’s school (built late 1970s, expanded early 1980s with South Carolina money) becomes the moral and operational anchor: “If we had known how to write, perhaps we wouldn’t be in this situation now.”
Tom White enters. Anonymous donor for the Cange bread oven (1984); later identified as a 60-something Boston construction company owner ($1B-class, the largest in Boston) — wartime aide to General Maxwell Taylor, parachuted into Normandy and Holland, became a generous Catholic philanthropist after divorcing and remarrying. Farmer meets him at the airport in plaid polyester golf pants. They argue Reagan, then guilt — White says guilt is useless; Farmer endorses guilt as motivation for the rich. White begins funding Cange substantially. When Farmer reaches his credit card limit and admits he signed his check over to an AIDS patient about to be evicted, White tosses three hundred-dollar bills onto his lap saying “for God’s sakes, eat.” White also asks if he could chuck it all and become a missionary; Farmer says “in your particular case, that would be a sin.” The compact: White’s money, Farmer’s work.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_12_chapter-10
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 10 — Founding PIH; meeting Jim Kim; the broken leg (1986-1988)
Late 1985-1986: the muzzle falls off (baboukèt la tonbe) after Baby Doc flees. Farmer and Ophelia get caught in a Port-au-Prince kouri — a stampede of demonstrators chased by Haitian army trucks with mounted guns. They open the car doors to wounded; once safe, Farmer drives back into the trouble to ferry more out. “It was very important to Paul to witness things.” The smell of burning tires becomes Ophelia’s permanent association with political violence.
1987: Partners In Health is founded. Tom White hires the lawyer, draws up the papers, creates the Boston public charity (PIH) and the sister organization in Haiti (Zanmi Lasante), and seeds it with $1 million. The Boston office is a one-room shop above a seafood restaurant in Cambridge.
Jim Yong Kim joins soon after, recruited via a series of long Boston conversations with Farmer parallel to Ophelia’s Port-au-Prince talks. Korean American, raised in Muscatine, Iowa, Harvard medical and anthropology student. The early PIH culture, defined nightly over closing-time restaurant tables: rejection of “political correctness” (“a self-centered activity”); rejection of cultural-barriers excuses (“There’s nothing like a cure for a disease to change people’s cultural values”); rejection of the radicals’ Guatemalan-peasant clothing aesthetic (“The poor don’t want you to look like them. They want you to dress in a suit and go get them food and water. Comma.”); rejection of the dependency critique against direct service (“They were dying like smelt”). Operative concepts coined here: pragmatic solidarity (sending resources down “the steep gradient of inequality”); AMC (“areas of moral clarity”); WL (white liberals — useful but underwilling to sacrifice).
Decision to build a school in Kay Epin (“House of Pines”), funded by Roald Dahl with £3,000.
September 1988: hurrying around Cambridge running last-minute errands before flying to Haiti for the start of the school construction, Farmer steps off a curb and is hit by a car. Knee shattered. Spends weeks at Massachusetts General Hospital, then returns to Ophelia’s apartment in a giant cast — and to recovery in Cange in a wheelchair. The TB-treatment study (chapter 4) is launched while his leg mends.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_13_chapter-11
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 11 — Aristide, the 1990 election, the 1991 coup
Late 1980s political context: Haitian army rule 1986-1990, with U.S. assistance Farmer documents through declassified material. Dechoukaj — uprooting of Duvalierist symbols — meets army violence; the 1987 election massacre at polling places aborts what would have been Haiti’s first democratic vote.
Farmer hears Jean-Bertrand Aristide preach at St. Jean Bosco in Port-au-Prince (1986), recognizes the ti legliz liberation-theology church he had been looking for, joins the crowd to introduce himself afterward. They become friends — Aristide survives multiple assassination attempts and the firebombing of his church (arranged by the mayor of Port-au-Prince).
1989 hilltop scene above Cange: Farmer, who rarely writes in Haiti because doctoring matters more, climbs alone to write his Ph.D. thesis. AIDS and Accusation will document the “geography of blame” that scapegoated Haiti as the source of HIV (the CDC’s “4-H” risk-group framing — homosexuals, hemophiliacs, heroin users, Haitians) and use epidemiological data to argue the disease almost certainly came from North America to Haiti, plausibly via American sex tourists in Port-au-Prince’s Carrefour district. Looks down at Cange’s transformation: 107 → 178 households, tin roofs replacing banana fronds, Père Lafontant’s communal latrines almost eradicating typhoid, the school and clinic visible.
1990: Farmer receives MD and Ph.D. simultaneously; thesis wins a prize, university press picks it up. He and Jim Kim begin a split residency at the Brigham — Farmer formally permitted to spend half his time in Cange.
The Aristide election (December 1990). Farmer in Port-au-Prince election day, with Père Lafontant. 67% for Aristide; 33% across the other 12 candidates. Aristide promises “dignified poverty” and a Haitian proverb: “The rocks in the water are going to find out how the rocks in the sun feel.” Farmer’s journal: “Perhaps this is a singular chance to change Haiti.”
29 September 1991: the coup. Farmer is at Logan Airport en route to Cange for a meeting about a new Cange hospital. The Haitian cabbie tells him “Dr. Polo, there’s trouble down there.” Farmer dismisses it: “This government has the most massive popular support of any in the world.” The chapter ends just before he learns otherwise.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_14_chapter-12
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 12 — The junta years; The Uses of Haiti (1991-1994)
After the Cédras coup, Farmer continues edgy transit between Cange and Boston. Refuses to take down the Aristide kòk kalite iron sculpture in his clinic room. Refuses to hide his Che Guevara and Castro books. Asks Tom White for $10,000 cash to smuggle in for the underground pacifist resistance; Jim Kim — driving with him from Cape Cod — pleads “If you get yourself killed, Pel, I’m going to kill you.” Farmer screams “What the fuck do you want me to do!” and smuggles the money in.
Sleeps in his clothes with shoes on. Plans to escape into the reforested hillside outside his window if soldiers come for him. A lone soldier enters Zanmi Lasante carrying a gun; Farmer confronts him at the courtyard gate. The soldier: “Who the fuck are you to tell me what I can do?” Farmer: “I’m the person who’s going to take care of you when you get sick.” The crowd’s audible “Ket” (“oh shit”) makes Farmer realize he has misjudged the situation, but the answer holds — Zanmi Lasante is the only good medical facility in the central plateau, useful even to soldiers and their families. This is Farmer’s structural protection from being “banished or worse.”
Three close friends murdered. Receives the MacArthur “genius grant” (1993) — flies to Chicago, immediately retreats to his hotel room and watches the news from Haiti on TV. Donates the entire $220,000 to PIH for the new research arm — the Institute for Health and Social Justice.
Quebec City book retreat. Ophelia gives him money; he checks into a Quebec City hotel and writes 220 pages in 10 days — the draft of The Uses of Haiti. The book is the angriest and most political of his works. Reconstructed from a Haitian peasant’s perspective: U.S. backed the French against the 1790s revolution; refused to recognize Haiti during American slavery; the U.S. occupation reconstituted the modern Haitian army; Fort Benning’s School of the Americas trained the head of the junta’s death squads (the same death squads that murdered Chouchou, the Haitian peasant in AIDS and Accusation); CIA assets work as junta henchmen; Washington publicly deplores the coup while denouncing Aristide and maintaining a leaky embargo. Heroes who don’t look fine in the book: French revolutionaries, Woodrow Wilson, FDR (who claimed to have written the 1918 Haitian Constitution), Frederick Douglass (eagerly served as American ambassador), Mother Teresa (who “gushed” over Baby Doc’s wife Michele).
Ends with anticipation that the Clinton administration will send troops to restore Aristide — but with conditions, including “structural economic adjustment.” Sets up Farmer’s hostility to the IMF/World Bank framework that recurs throughout the rest of the book.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_15_chapter-13
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 13 — The great epi divide and MDR-TB
Short conceptual chapter introducing the “great epi divide” — Farmer’s own coinage — for the partition of humanity between populations who die in their seventies of aging-body diseases and populations who die ten to forty years earlier of violence, hunger, and infectious disease that medicine knows how to treat. The line runs through countries (most of Haiti is on the wrong side; bits of the hills above Port-au-Prince are not) and through cities (Mission Hill next to the Brigham has higher infant mortality than Cuba; 1990 Harlem death rates for males 5-65 exceeded Bangladesh).
TB as the canonical epi-divide disease. First-line drugs cure virtually every standard case for 150-200 over 6-8 months. TB had all but vanished from the rich world by 2000 but still killed ~2 million adults a year worldwide, second only to AIDS among infectious causes; the two share “a noxious synergy” because each makes the other active. Pharmaceutical companies and rich governments had abandoned TB R&D — newest drug 25 years old, antique diagnostic tools, no fully effective vaccine campaign. About one-third of humanity carries TB bacilli; ~10% activate; malnutrition and HIV greatly raise the activation rate.
Multi-drug-resistant TB (MDR). Because a person with active TB harbors hundreds of millions of bacteria, some are mutants impervious to any single drug. Inadequate treatment — wrong drug, too few drugs, too short a course — kills the susceptible bacilli and selects for the resistant mutants. MDR is defined by resistance to at least the two most powerful first-line drugs. It tends to arise where wealth and poverty mingle (some treatment but not enough), not where treatment is wholly absent.
By the mid-1990s Farmer has handled several MDR cases in Cange — the first one, during the junta, died because the drugs weren’t available. He has assembled the resources to fight it at Zanmi Lasante and is curing most sporadic cases when, in 1995, MDR claims a close friend in a shantytown on the outskirts of Lima, Peru. Pivot to Peru.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_16_chapter-14
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 14 — Carabayllo and Father Jack (1994-1995)
Father Jack Roussin — beefy Boston priest, “a character,” former pastor of St. Mary of the Angels in Roxbury where Farmer had boarded as a medical student — moves in the early 1990s to Carabayllo, a slum on the outskirts of Lima, Peru. On visits back to Boston he keeps urging PIH to start a project there.
Jim Kim — for eight years Paul’s “second in command” or PIH’s bayakou (Creole for excrement-collector), running grant proposals and chasing medicines — wants to do more. Farmer is reluctant but consents; Tom White puts up 30,000 of the initial 60,000. Jim envisions a Spanish-language version of Zanmi Lasante: Socios en Salud (Partners In Health), built around community health workers.
Pharmacy bombed. Socios opens a pharmacy next to Father Jack’s church; on midnight New Year’s Eve, while Jack is saying Mass, Shining Path guerrillas blow it up — they object to “crumbs for the poor” as palliatives that suppress revolutionary fervor. The pharmacy is rebuilt elsewhere. Farmer’s coaching for Jim becomes the chapter’s recurring rhythm: “Remember, serving the poor in Carabayllo is more important than soothing your own ego. It’s called eating shit for the poor.” Whatever Jim reports as a catastrophe, Farmer recalls happening “three times in Cange.”
Farmer conducts a health census of the slum. Asks the Socios project director (Jaime Bayona, a Peruvian public-health graduate) whether MDR-TB is a problem. Jaime checks records, reports nothing — the country is universally praised by WHO for its model TB program (DOTS — directly observed treatment short-course). Farmer concedes: “The one thing we don’t need to do here is TB.”
Father Jack’s death. May 1995, Jack falls ill in Lima, flies to Boston, Jim Kim drives him to the Brigham. Diagnosed with TB; put on standard four-drug regimen; dies a month into therapy. The Massachusetts State Lab culture (returned a day or two after his death) shows the bacilli are resistant to all four first-line drugs Jack received — and to the fifth.
Since Jack had never previously been treated for TB, he had to have caught the five-drug-resistant strain from someone else, almost certainly in Carabayllo. MDR is therefore in the Lima slums in a way the WHO model program does not see. Jaime begins reading patient records upside down at Peruvian government clinics — discovers Señora Brigida (twice mistreated, drug-resistant strain, son already dead of TB she infected him with) and dozens of similar cases. Pivots PIH from “we don’t need to do TB here” into a multi-year confrontation with WHO’s standardized TB control orthodoxy.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_17_chapter-15
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 15 — The ten patients (1996)
Kidder’s first arrival at Carabayllo at night. Lima’s northern outskirts spread up steep gray-brown hills with no soil, lit by absurdly oversized highway-style pylons. People migrated from the Andes seeking electricity, water, schools, jobs, and distance from the Shining Path war.
Jaime Bayona has identified ten Carabayllanos with probable MDR-TB. Their sputum samples are sent to the Massachusetts State Lab in Farmer’s suitcase, labeled “Paul Farmer, TB Commissioner.” Results: most are resistant not just to the two strongest drugs but to all five first-line antibiotics, just like Father Jack.
Farmer flies in to examine the ten on a wooden bench at the El Progreso clinic next to Jack’s former church. As he reads their records — Jaime translating, since Farmer can’t yet speak Spanish — the central diagnostic insight of the Peru chapters arrives: these patients had not interrupted treatment. They had completed DOTS strictly under direct observation, then been retreated under the WHO-prescribed retreatment regimen (the same drugs plus one). They had emerged with four- and five-drug resistance.
The biology is elementary. The WHO retreatment formula — derived from 20-year-old African trials in which most failures were noncompliance — selects further resistance when the patient was already mono- or two-drug-resistant. Farmer chooses to call this process “amplification” rather than “recruitment of further resistance” because the term sounds worse. The “eureka moment” has “a bad aftertaste this time.”
The framing turn: WHO’s official guidance contained the line “In settings of resource constraint, it is necessary for rational resource allocation to prioritise TB treatment categories according to the cost-effectiveness of treatment of each category” — meaning that in poor countries, MDR-TB patients should be allowed to die because effective treatment is too expensive. Meanwhile a 1980s outbreak in New York City prisons and homeless shelters had cost American agencies ~1 billion. Peru, paying >1 billion/year in debt service to U.S. banks and international lenders, had been told by international experts that MDR was too expensive to treat.
The chapter makes the book’s central comparative claim explicit: cost-effectiveness analysis is not used to evaluate MDR treatment in absolute terms; it is used to ratify a status quo where the same intervention is “cost-effective” in New York and “too expensive” in Lima.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_18_chapter-16
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 16 — Médicos aventureros (1996-1997)
Hard counsel from Michael Iseman (world’s foremost MDR-TB clinical authority, National Jewish in Denver): even in 1993 his cure rate was ~60%, costs running as high as $250,000 per case, two years of weak side-effect-laden second-line drugs (hypothyroidism, psychosis, intramuscular injections, rare deaths). Carabayllo will be harder, if cheaper.
Jim’s framing reason to take it on regardless: “Forgive me for saying this, but the great thing about TB is that it’s airborne.” A truly threatening MDR variant cannot stay confined to slums; the project can have global reach. Paul’s reply: “Okay. But let’s try ten patients first.”
August 1996 treatment begins. Crew: Jaime, a brilliant epidemiologist (Meche Becerra), two female Harvard medical students (Sonya Shin and Jen Furin) sleeping above the Father Jack Roussin Center. Daily e-mail with Farmer; Farmer designs each patient’s regimen.
Political resistance. The Peruvian TB authorities don’t want to hear that their model program has a flaw. One physician calls them médicos aventureros — “adventuring doctors.” Another tells Jaime that no gringo can know about TB because there is no TB in the United States. Neither Paul nor Jim has a Peruvian license; the TB director threatens expulsion (intercession by a nun on Jaime’s account stays the order). Patients can only be transferred to Socios after they have completed standard treatment and the WHO retreatment regimen — i.e., after their drug resistance has been amplified once more.
David Carbajal dies. Sonya Shin finds a probable MDR victim, begs the authorities to allow earlier treatment, is refused. She watches him die and helps shave him for the funeral. The parents tell her they understand it is “a problem in the system” — the system can’t admit a bigger problem by allowing exceptions.
Jaime’s structural reading of the Peruvian TB authorities’ position: their TB program had been won by 1991 grassroots protests including nuns and priests; their leaders had joined the demonstrations; if Socios sets a new standard for MDR, they would have to meet it nationally; they don’t have the money unless they cannibalize DOTS, which would re-create the conditions that produced MDR in the first place. They don’t have Paul’s freedom of action.
The Chicago speech (February 1997). Farmer is invited to give a TB talk at the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease meeting. WHO TB-division officials and the global TB tribe (“TB” — they call themselves) will attend. Farmer rewrites his “wimpy” prepared speech a few days before. Delivers an itemized list of “myths and mystifications about MDR-TB” — directly attacking quoted WHO statements about cost-effectiveness, about DOTS alone stopping MDR, about MDR being less virulent than regular TB. The moderator (Ken Castro of CDC) calls the talk “provocative.” Farmer turns back at the lectern: “Excuse me, Ken, but why do you qualify my talk as provocative? I just said we should treat sick people, if we have the technology.” A rumor reaches Jaime in Lima a few days later: someone has called Peru’s national TB director and reported that “Paul Farmer says you’re killing patients.” Higher authorities now have noticed.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_19_chapter-17
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 17 — Hepatitis A; Christian’s recovery; the doctor’s daughter
Farmer marries Didi Bertrand in Cange in 1996. About 4,000 attend; Jim Kim and a Duke friend best men; Père Lafontant and three priests preside. Daughter Catherine born 1998.
PIH cash crunch from Peru. Drug costs run 15,000-20,000 per patient; ~50 patients in treatment; average age 29; cure rates already promising. PIH has spent a million dollars borrowed-from-Boston and Tom White’s reserves. Howard Hiatt (eminent Brigham professor, former dean of Harvard School of Public Health) discovers Paul and Jim have been borrowing $92,000 in second-line drugs from the Brigham pharmacy with sweet-talked permission. Tom White writes the check, with a note that the hospital should be more generous.
Farmer’s hepatitis A. Travel schedule: Cange → Port-au-Prince airport → Miami → Lima → Carabayllo → Lima → Miami → Port-au-Prince → Cange — 22 of 48 hours airborne, more if delays. Symptoms hit during the Chicago speech in February 1997. Kidder catalogs the long denial — Farmer suspects MDR (“I’ve exposed all my patients to it”), takes a clandestine X-ray that comes back normal, refuses to consult anyone in Boston, finally diagnoses hepatitis A on his last morning of Brigham service when coffee nauseates him and he sees his urine is dark. Probably from ceviche in Lima. His liver function tests are so high the machine has to dilute the sample.
Recovery in the Brigham; Jim and other doctors briefly worry he might need a transplant. Issues squeaky-voiced drug-procurement orders to PIH from his hospital bed. Ophelia sends him and Didi to a hotel in southern France — his first real vacation.
Christian. Earlier, Jaime had called Socios about a 22-pound 3-year-old wasting away in the Children’s Hospital. Jen Furin had taken the case on. Farmer designed an empiric regimen: high-dose ethambutol plus four second-line drugs including a fluoroquinolone — explicitly against received pediatric “wisdom” (the no-fluoroquinolones rule rests on cartilage damage in immature beagle pups; the no-high-dose-ethambutol rule rests on color-vision loss kids can’t report). “It was a matter of merely applying infectious disease knowledge.” On Kidder’s hospital visit, Christian — now chubby — runs across the corridor on stubby legs. The mother in the Mickey Mouse T-shirt approaches Farmer afterward in the parking lot to thank him. Farmer pursues lips: “For me, it is a privilege.”
The doctor’s daughter. Same day. A Peruvian TB doctor’s own daughter is being kept on the WHO retreatment regimen (all five first-line drugs) despite a Massachusetts State Lab culture showing R-resistance to every one of them. The father has known for months but didn’t dare violate las normas. Farmer plays a “charade” of calling the diagnosis fresh, recommending second-line therapy as “my prejudice” so the assembled doctors can adopt it without losing face. The girl recovers. Walking out, Farmer to Kidder: “What’s the matter with you people? They don’t want to believe in MDR. The delicate thing is, you want to make progress with them. Insult them and forget it.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_20_chapter-18
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 18 — DOTS-plus and the Goldfarb confrontation (April 1998)
Howard Hiatt convenes a special meeting at the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in Boston to present early Carabayllo results: of the first 53 patients treated, >85% cured. Their patients are younger and have fewer comorbidities than Iseman’s at National Jewish, but the cure rate is still extraordinary.
Top TB experts attend, including Arata Kochi, head of the WHO TB program — and a former student of Hiatt’s at the Harvard School of Public Health. Ahead of the meeting Kochi has decided to head off the bad publicity Farmer has generated. His staff coins a new term: DOTS-plus, a strategy that adds MDR treatment in settings of significant drug resistance. Kochi uses the term in his opening remarks. Farmer and Kim get the doctrinal opening they came for before the meeting begins. Years later Kochi explains it in spare English: “DOTS-plus. The world is changing. We have to change, too. If you cannot beat them, join them.” And: “Then, to some extent, we can control them.”
The Goldfarb confrontation. Russian émigré microbiologist Alex Goldfarb, working for the Soros Foundation on Russia’s TB epidemic, raises the utilitarian objection bluntly: he has 6 million; with 3 million he can implement DOTS for 5,000 Russian prison inmates and cure ~4,500; with the other 3 million he can either treat the 500 MDR cases who will die anyway or treat another 5,000 ordinary TB cases. "My choice is not involved in the human rights of five hundred people, but five hundred people versus five thousand people." If he disclosed spending 6,000 per MDR case to the Russian public when tens of thousands die nearby, “they will tell me that I am building a golden palace for a selected few.” This is the cost-effectiveness argument PIH cannot dismiss — and the chapter is honest that they will need a real answer.
Kim’s speech. Next day, Jim opens with a reframe that becomes a recurring PIH frame: every speaker wants to know why a small charity has taken on something so costly. The answer is not local prudence but global ambition — the dream of a “TB All-Star Weekend” where the relevant authorities would expand resources rather than ration them. He quotes Margaret Mead: “Never underestimate the ability of a small group of committed individuals to change the world. Indeed, they are the only ones who ever have.”
The chapter sets up the next move: with DOTS-plus established as discussable, the binding constraint becomes the price of second-line drugs. That is Jim’s project for the next two years.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_21_chapter-19
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 19 — Driving down the price (1998-2000)
Cost-effectiveness analysis has become the gatekeeping discipline of international health: imported from engineering, war, and medicine; deployed by big donors as a test you have to pass. Farmer and Kim’s challenge is partly factual (WHO’s “ineffective” finding is based on no real trial; PIH’s >85% cure rate refutes it) and partly economic — no one has tried to lower the actual binding cost, the second-line drugs.
Kim’s “big-shot strategy.” Make the assertion that prices can fall 90-95%, then figure out how. He discovers in Geneva that no one at WHO knows the patents on all but one class of second-line antibiotics expired years ago. He is born in South Korea, raised in Muscatine, Iowa; valedictorian, class president, football QB; transfers from Iowa to Brown; runs the Third World Center; later embarrassed by his own racial-identity politics phase (“I wanted to learn Korean, be down with my people, be an authorized third world person, so I could say shit”). His Ph.D. fieldwork on the Korean pharmaceutical industry will turn out to be useful background.
The price-fixing diagnosis. Capreomycin sells in Peru for 21/vial (Lilly), in Boston for 29.90, in Paris for $8.80 — but PIH cannot buy Paris stock, because (per the Paris drug agent on the phone) “there’s a global shortage” caused by “an emergency in Peru.” Differential pricing is standard. Hiatt: “Looks like price gouging to me.”
Kim’s logician’s-conundrum chain. To lower prices you need a lot of TB projects using the drugs; for that you need lower prices; for that you need generic manufacturers involved; for that you need WHO to put second-line drugs on its essential drugs list; but rarely-used drugs aren’t essential. He starts pushing the WHO list lobby. The IDA (International Dispensary Association, Dutch nonprofit) and Doctors Without Borders partner with PIH on generic manufacturers. Guido Bakker (IDA): “IDA is going to do everything we can to lower prices, by exploring generic manufacturers.”
The Green Light Committee. To break the “if drugs become cheap, careless places will breed resistance” objection, Kim’s PIH man at WHO finds a precedent — the meningococcal vaccine control committee — and they create the Green Light Committee, a single distribution gatekeeper that demands proof of a sound underlying DOTS program before granting low-priced second-line drugs.
Outcomes. By 2000: drugs to treat a four-drug-resistant case fall from 15,000 to 1,500 — a 90% drop on average; capreomycin is 98 cents/vial (-97%). Eli Lilly grants donations and global price reductions. WHO’s Green Light Committee operates. Guido Bakker: “Eighty-five percent of it was Jim.”
The Salzburg pizza dinner. Jim quits his ID fellowship at the Brigham, signals his interest in policy work over clinical practice. Confesses he wants to make international health policy and feels ashamed about it. Paul: “Well then, do it.” “But didn’t we always say that people who go into policy make a preferential option for their own ideas? For their own sorry asses?” Paul: “Yeah, but, Jim, we trust you with power. We know you won’t betray the poor.”
The post-Tom plan. Ophelia, after years hoarding 1M into a PIH endowment, has spent it all on Peru. They draft a "disassembly strategy" — shrinking PIH to a Cange-only charity. Jim's alternative: ask the Gates Foundation for 45M. Paul: $2-4M, max. Jim, borrowing Paul’s debate gambit: “On what data exactly do you base that statement?”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_22_chapter-20
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 20 — A light month for travel (early 2000)
Howard Hiatt’s framing for the chapter: “Paul and Jim mobilized the world to accept drug-resistant TB as a soluble problem.” He urges Farmer to step out of one-on-one Cange clinical work and become a global executive on TB, AIDS, and malaria — but Farmer refuses. His self-described priorities: patients first, prisoners second, students third.
The chapter follows Farmer through what he calls “a light month for travel” — Cange to South Carolina (church group fundraising) to Cuba (AIDS conference) to Paris (transit) to Moscow (TB) — all funded by a combination of “capitalists, commies, and Jesus Christers.”
The truck out of Cange. Stops at the Croix des Bouquets jail to facilitate a “prison extraction” for the son of a peasant farmer from Kay Epin held on suspicion of murder. Farmer puts a hand on the desk sergeant’s shoulder, talks his way past, gets the father to the cell, talks to the son about the lawyer he has hired. Outside the jail, the truck won’t start; the Cangeois passengers and Kidder push.
E-mail. Farmer gets ~75 messages a day in 2000 (will be 200/day by year-end). Sample reply on the pathophysiology of meningitis-induced hearing loss to a med student: “it’s anatomy and pus. it’s always anatomy and pus.” Greeting from a Zanmi Lasante staffer after a 36-hour absence: “We miss you as the dry, cracked earth misses the rain.” Farmer: “Haitians, man. They’re totally over the top. My kind of people.”
Matthew 25. “When I was hungry, you fed me… Inasmuch as you did it not, you’re screwed.” This becomes the chapter’s organizing scripture. Farmer treats the Gospel passage as the enforceable specification of “preferential option for the poor.”
Miami. Layover at the Admirals’ Club becomes a “Miami day plus” — haircut from his Cuban barber, hot shower, copy of People magazine (“the Journal of Popular Studies”), red wine in a soft chair. Watches Haitians who have never flown before stop at the head of the escalator and try to run to match its speed: “The more ruffles, the more stumbles.” He had once gone to airport administration to ask them to fix this.
Self-disclosure. Farmer to Kidder, en route: “The problem is, if I don’t work this hard, someone will die who doesn’t have to. That sounds megalomaniacal. I wouldn’t have said that to you before I’d taken you to Haiti and you had seen that it was manifestly true.” Ophelia’s gloss on the personality: a need for frenzied activity verging on desperation, towering self-confidence combined with hunger for affirmation, immunity to despair, never depressed: “I’ve never known despair and I don’t think I ever will.” Farmer: “I may be a more sunny, cheerful person than you. No one believes that I’m cheerful because of what I say and write, but I only say and write those things because they’re true.”
The chapter is the book’s clearest extended portrait of how Farmer actually works on a daily timescale: the prison stop, the patients-first rule, the e-mail volume, the airport hub strategy, the Matthew 25 framework.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_23_chapter-21
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 21 — Cuba (early 2000)
Farmer’s relief at landing in Havana: “Look! Only ninety miles from Haiti and look! Trees! Crops!” He admires Cuban medicine on health-statistics grounds, not ideological grounds. Cuban life expectancy is approximately U.S.-equivalent. Cuba (despite the U.S. embargo, despite losing Soviet patronage) controls dengue, typhoid, TB, and AIGS where Haiti does not; doctors per capita 2x the U.S.; per WHO, the world’s most equitably distributed medicine. ~500 Cuban doctors are working gratis in Haiti.
Reframe to Harvard friends who held up Scandinavia as the model: “They were talking about managing wealth. He was talking about managing poverty. Haiti was a bad example of how to do that. Cuba was a good one.”
Farmer’s relationship to ideology — important paragraph for the book’s intellectual frame: he reads liberation theology and Marxism but rejects the orthodoxy of both (“It’s an ology, after all. And all ologies fail us at some point. At a point, I suspect, not very far from where the Haitian poor live out their dangerous lives”). The El Salvador / Guatemala / Haiti dilemma he names: pushing the destitute to claim what’s theirs by right, when the odds are “machetes versus Uzis, donkeys versus tanks,” gets them killed. “We know the answer to that question, because we are digging up their bodies in Guatemala.”
Cuba fundraising and recruitment. Two practical wins on the trip. (1) Lobbies UNAIDS Caribbean lead Peggy McAvoy over multiple days, signs Infections and Inequalities “with high hopes for your help in Haiti,” asks at the cocktail party “Can I give you a kiss? Can I give you two?” Wins the request for a written proposal. (2) Through Jorge Pérez secures private meeting with José Miyar Barruecos (Cuban Council of State secretary, MD); asks “Can I send you two students this year?” Answer: “Por supuesto.” Two Cange youths will go to Cuba’s Latin American medical school. (3) Approaches Luc Montagnier and the French ambassador with a “new triangle” pitch — Cuban doctors + French money in Haiti, playing on the slave-trade triangular-trade reference; Montagnier accepts an invitation to Cange.
Farmer’s two scheduled conference talks: one for clinicians on HIV/TB coinfection, one titled in his own naming as “why life sucks.” Kidder gets a small lesson in supplicant tactics — assume each polite promise is real and obtain as many as possible to maximize the chance one is. Follow up to produce shame if needed.
Closes with Farmer’s confession to Kidder he is taking sleeping pills and looking forward to the flight; chapter sets up the Paris stopover that follows.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_24_chapter-22
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 22 — Paris (Catherine’s second birthday)
Brief stopover. Kidder is sleeping-pill-fogged. Farmer’s wife Didi has been studying the records French slavers kept of their West African commerce — the city’s beauty has accordingly soured for both of them. From the cab through the periphery’s high-rises, Farmer mutters about how much could be done in Haiti with the money the first world spends on pet grooming.
The Paris apartment (three small rooms, borrowed from a Duke friend). Catherine, age almost-2, plays with stuffed animals while Farmer watches from the sofa. Didi calls from the kitchen asking when he leaves for Moscow. Tomorrow, he says. From the kitchen comes the sound of something dropping and a deep-throated exclamation. Farmer covers his mouth with both hands. Kidder marks this as “the first time I’d seen him at a loss for words or action.”
Critique-window: Farmer’s friends increasingly criticize him for not spending more time with Didi and Catherine. Some who criticize seem oddly animated about it — “Can you imagine what it’s like being married to him?” Kim’s gloss: “Paul has a gift for making people feel guilty.” Kidder reads the criticism partly as moral envy at finding “what looked like a chink in his moral armor.”
Embedded confession from Cange: a month after Catherine was born, an eclamptic woman came to Zanmi Lasante. Treatment failed; the full-term baby was stillborn; Farmer had to leave the room weeping. He reflects: “I thought I was the king of empathy for these poor kids, but if I was the king of empathy, why this big shift because of my daughter? It was a failure of empathy, the inability to love other children as much as yours. The thing is, everybody understands that, encourages that, praises you for it. But the hard thing is the other.” Asked how he answers people who say his ambition to love every child equally is hubristic: “All the great religious traditions of the world say, Love thy neighbor as thyself. My answer is, I’m sorry, I can’t, but I’m gonna keep on trying, comma.”
The two photographs Farmer carries on this trip: Catherine, and a Haitian child of about the same age in the throes of kwashiorkor. The Haitian child is his patient, not an abstraction. Kidder: “the worst kind of exile wouldn’t be geographical. It would be something like excommunication” — Farmer’s network of close ties is large, and almost no one slips out of it.
Catherine’s birthday party: a mechanical bird Farmer bought in the Miami airport (almost made them miss the flight). Guests include the French family Farmer had au-paired for in 1980 (now PIH fundraisers), Haitian friends, a Burkina Faso family. “PIH headquarters wasn’t Boston or even Haiti but wherever PIH-ers happened to be.” Closes with Farmer asking his mother in Florida (1 a.m. her time) for a Paris wake-up call; Didi smiles. “I just think it’s so cool that at forty he still does that. I’d miss it if he didn’t.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_25_chapter-23
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 23 — Moscow and the Russian prisons
Russia is now the largest TB project Farmer is engaged with. Origins: Howard Hiatt sent him to George Soros’s Open Society Institute looking for sustaining money for Peru. OSI declined but mentioned its $13M in DOTS-only TB pilot projects in Russia. Farmer wrote a courtly two-page letter explaining why DOTS-only would fail in Russia (post-Soviet collapse → uncompleted therapies + overcrowded prisons + rampant resistance). Soros yelled at his Russian TB program director Alex Goldfarb on the phone, then asked Farmer to fix the projects.
Farmer toured Siberian prisons with Goldfarb and Soros advisers. Goldfarb had earlier called Farmer “the evil enemy from the north.” They came back as friends (after Goldfarb asked Farmer’s fee and Farmer answered “Alex, you idiot, what’s my fee? I charge a lot for prisoners, POWs, and the destitute sick. And I really ramp it up for refugees”). The Russian prison TB scene: incidence 40-50x civilian rates, majority of inmates resistant to at least one drug, ~⅓ in some prisons fully MDR. TB was the leading cause of death in the prisons, with many prisoners released back into civilian society still sick and infectious.
International response had been puny. Doctors Without Borders was stuck in DOTS-only orthodoxy in Prison Colony 33 in Kemerovo (46% cure rate). The CDC in Ivanovo had knowingly treated MDR patients with drugs they were resistant to and cured 5%. Farmer called these “managerial successes, clinical failures.”
The World Bank loan and the Tomsk fight. Hillary Clinton (per Soros’s request) prevailed on the World Bank to set up a “mission to Moscow” — economists, epidemiologists, public health experts working out the loan terms for a TB program loan to Russia. PIH’s whole crew labored on a 177-page Soros-commissioned report (115 pages of appendices, 976 references) covering MDR in Russia, Azerbaijan, Peru, South Africa. WHO contributed an introduction. Farmer served as the chief but unpaid consultant on TB in Russian prisons for the World Bank’s mission, refusing pay because he disapproved of Bank policies (Soros covered his expenses).
Kidder’s Moscow visit. The grim-faced customs officer (“Next time fill out the English form”); Farmer’s gentle gloss “she’s an employee of a defeated superpower.” Visit to Matrosskaya Tishina — Moscow’s central prison. Inmates with gray faces, frostbite-crooked noses; AIDS cells; a uniform-clad prison medical staff who themselves deplore conditions. Most of the actual diplomatic argument with Russian authorities is offstage in the chapter, but Farmer’s central argument lands: a “TB nightmare” too large and too cross-border to bracket the way Haiti can be bracketed; this is the venue where the cost-effectiveness rule meets the geographical fact that Russia borders 12 countries, including some of the wealthiest.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_26_chapter-24
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 24 — The Gates grant; “If Paul is the model, we’re golden”
July 2000: the Gates Foundation grants PIH and a coalition of partners $45 million to wipe out MDR-TB in Peru — virtually everything Jim asked for. William Foege (Gates science adviser) extracts coalition cooperation by telling all the warring TB factions that there will be only one Gates grant; in two hours they make peace. Jim borrows the playbook, including former adversaries (WHO TB branch) as partners. Money flows through Harvard Medical School; PIH runs the actual treatment.
The plan: 5 years, 2,000 chronic MDR patients, ≥80% cure. Convert a community project into a national one. “Scaling-up” risk acknowledged. Boston Globe runs front-page coverage; Farmer worries old donors will think PIH no longer needs their money. He develops the “unusual alliances” stump speech showing slides of Castro + Pope + Gates + Britney Spears, and ends each fundraising appearance: “you are not dismissed.”
The constraint Gates does not solve. Big foundations finance well-publicized disease campaigns, not comprehensive health systems. Tom White’s dwindling fortune still pays Cange’s bills. Farmer expands AIDS treatment in Cange to ~250 antiretroviral patients — grafting it onto Zanmi Lasante’s directly observed therapy + monthly stipend infrastructure. Many revivals; orphanings prevented. UNAIDS rejects his application on “sustainability criteria” (the drugs are too expensive for Haitians to ever afford themselves); when he goes to drug companies for donations they tell him to apply to the same agencies that called his program nonsustainable. Soros’s Haitian-branch helps; Tom White makes a special gift; PIH sells its Cambridge headquarters to fund AIDS drugs.
Harvard Medical School adopts PIH and renames it the Program in Infectious Disease and Social Change. The Brigham later launches its own Division of Social Medicine and Health Inequalities. PIH’s Boston headquarters moves to brick buildings on Huntington Avenue. Ophelia tries to “normalize” the experience of working as a PIH-er — children, 5pm leave, vacations.
The wall sign. A taped paper in a new employee’s office reads “If Paul is the model, we’re golden” — but lift the strip and the original Jim Kim quote is “If Paul is the model, we’re fucked.” Kim’s frame: PIH should not encourage imitation. “Paul has created technical solutions to help the rest of us get to decency, a road map to decency that we can all follow without trying to imitate him. Paul is a model OF what should be done. He’s not a model FOR how it has to be done.” If the poor have to wait for more Paul Farmers to arrive, “they are totally fucked.”
The chapter ends with Farmer answering an emailed student who said he believed in Paul’s cause but couldn’t do what Paul did: “I didn’t say you should do what I do. I just said these things should be done.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_27_chapter-25
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 25 — The boy John
The most narrative-dense and emotionally costly chapter in the book. John, a boy of about 11-12 from Hinche, brought by his mother to Zanmi Lasante in August 2000 with hard swellings in his neck. His mother and he are the only surviving members of their immediate family — his father and three siblings have all died. Asked their cause of death: “Haiti. They died of Haiti” (Farmer adapts a line from Greene’s The Comedians). Farmer suspects cancer because the swellings are too hard for scrofula and the white-cell ratio is wrong.
The diagnostic and transport choreography. Diagnosis that takes hours in Boston takes weeks across this distance. Serena Koenig (PIH-affiliated young Brigham doctor) lines up a Mass General oncologist who agrees to read the biopsy free. A Haitian surgeon agrees to come to Cange for several thousand dollars; the rains are heavy; it takes 12 hours to fetch him; biopsy completed at dawn. Farmer flies the samples to Boston in formaldehyde (Cange has no frozen-section equipment), which delays the diagnosis from one to four days. Result: nasopharyngeal carcinoma — <1% of childhood malignancies, but 60-70% curable if caught early.
The decision. Farmer initially thinks they could administer chemotherapy in Cange. A Mass General oncologist warns Serena: “Serena, if you want to kill this child, there are less painful ways to do it.” Only a handful of U.S. hospitals are equipped for proper treatment. Serena spends three weeks of begging; Mass General agrees to take the case for free. Serena fabricates John’s parents’ first names (“Jean Paul and Yolande”) for the consulate visa application — they don’t know the real names. Carole Smarth (Haitian American resident, fluent Creole) accompanies Serena to fetch John.
Serena calls Farmer (in Europe at a Soros-funded scientific meeting): under what circumstances would they not bring John? Farmer: “No circumstances. It’s his only chance. Tell anyone who asks: his mother brought him to us, and we’re doing everything we can to help him.”
The medevac and the death. When Serena and Carole arrive in Hinche, John is far worse than expected — emaciated; the cancer has metastasized. They fly him to Boston. The medevac flight costs ~20,000. John dies in Boston shortly after arrival; the Mass General team had already warned the cancer was now in his vertebrae and the cure rate had collapsed. Total cost to PIH for this case: ~20,000 in direct costs + the Mass General bill.
The internal critique. A relatively new PIH-er afterward says to Kidder she cannot help thinking about all the things they could have done with that $20,000. Kidder later relays the comment to Farmer in chapter 26 (the Casse hike), where Farmer’s full answer — including “the long defeat” — emerges. Within chapter 25 itself, the chapter is pure narrative: the boy, the mother, the misnamed parents on the visa, the airline first-class ticket Farmer refused to allow to be bought (insisted on cashing in his own frequent-flyer miles instead), the failure.
The chapter is the book’s hardest case for Farmer’s method: maximum effort, maximum expense, maximum failure — and Farmer’s framework still says “Yes, do it again.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_28_chapter-26
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Chapter 26 — The hike to Casse and “the long defeat”
December (~2 months after John’s death). Kidder returns to Cange. E-mail volume now ~200/day. Farmer: “Something’s gotta give. But, as has been noted, I’m not burning out. And I’m not jaded either.”
Ti Jean — Zanmi Lasante’s chief handyman, Farmer’s “chief of staff” and main local male confidant — gives Farmer his cosmology gloss: “You go everywhere, but this is your base. Your nest is Haiti.”
The chapter’s set-piece: an 11-hour round-trip hike to Casse to visit Alcante (a 13-year-old former scrofula patient cured of TB) and his TB-laden family. The hike is longer than the one to Morne Michel. Kidder runs out of water; Farmer feeds him oranges and Cokes. Along the way they encounter “the works of PIH” — schools, scattered patients calling out “Hi, my Doc”; a girl with severe burn scarring whose mouth will be pulled permanently open without plastic surgery (a bwat).
The “long defeat” exchange. Walking, Kidder relays the new PIH-er’s comment about the $20,000 spent on John. Farmer’s full answer:

“I have fought my whole life a long defeat. How about that? How about if I said, That’s all it adds up to is defeat? I have fought the long defeat and brought other people on to fight the long defeat, and I’m not going to stop because we keep losing. Now I actually think sometimes we may win. I don’t dislike victory… You know, people from our background — like you, like most PIH-ers, like me — we’re used to being on a victory team, and actually what we’re really trying to do in PIH is to make common cause with the losers. Those are two very different things. We want to be on the winning team, but at the risk of turning our backs on the losers, no, it’s not worth it. So you fight the long defeat.”

Asked his answer to the cost-of-treatment objection, Farmer redirects: “What about a doctor’s salary? My salary is five times what John’s airplane ride cost. And I’m twenty-nine or thirty-some years old…. If you say, Well, I just think how much could have been done with twenty thousand dollars, you sound thoughtful, sensible. However, if you were to point out, But a young attending physician makes one hundred thousand dollars… that just makes you sound like an asshole. Same world, same numbers, same figures, same currency.”
He frames the position as a refusal of triage by neglect: “Before you turn your back on someone like John you have to be really really sure… Every patient is a sign. Every patient is a test.”
Alcante’s family. Wattle-and-daub hut about 10x20 feet housing 10 souls. Several family members had TB; only the father’s was sputum-positive (the only “epidemiologically significant” case under DOTS, even though the others’ extrapulmonary disease can kill). “It’s fucking unfair.” Plan: a new house with concrete floor and metal roof, nutrition support, school tuition for the kids — the distal intervention model: cure the disease, then change the conditions that produced it.
Kidder’s authorial summing-up. Hiatt’s wealthy friend balks at PIH because “no one could reproduce” Farmer’s work. Standard objections: hiking 7 hours for two patients is inefficient; few people will follow this example. Kidder’s reply (channeling Farmer): if you say 7 hours is too long for two families’ lives, you are saying their lives matter less, “and the idea that some lives matter less is the root of all that’s wrong with the world.” Kim’s variant: “If you focus on individual patients, you can’t get sloppy.”
Closes with the night walk back to Cange — Ti Jean’s instructions on responding to night demons (“I am who you are. I do what you do”) and Farmer’s recognition that ~75% of Voodoo ceremonies are healing rituals, “this simple fact has eluded all the many commentaries on Voodoo.” The three of them sharing a candy bar under Orion’s belt; drums in the valley below Kidder now hears as healing rituals rather than menacing sounds — “like so many hearts beating through a single stethoscope.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: ch_29_afterword
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Afterword (June 2002 update)
June 2002: WHO adopts new MDR-TB guidelines virtually identical to PIH’s Carabayllo protocols. Jim Kim from Geneva: “The world changed yesterday.” Second-line antibiotic prices continue to fall; Green Light Committee distributes drugs to Peru (~1,000 cured or in treatment), Tomsk (~250). The Russian Ministry of Health agrees to a $150M World Bank TB loan terms.
Twin AIDS-and-TB pandemics rage on; mathematical models predict 100M HIV infections by 2010. Some U.S. government voices still argue AIDS can’t be treated in poor countries — but the position is fading. Antiretroviral prices fall faster than second-line TB drug prices. Kim is named senior adviser to a new WHO director-general in 2003. Cange becomes a destination for global health policy makers and U.S. politicians.
Expansion of Zanmi Lasante throughout the central plateau. Global Fund money is delayed (as such monies often are); Farmer chooses not to wait. Summer 2002 expansion begins. PIH borrows $2M from a Boston commercial bank; Tom White guarantees the loan and pays off part; the highest-paid PIH employees cover interest. Three towns get “beefed up” facilities. Lascahobas (Serena Koenig’s team) — a wretched private hospital and an empty public clinic with no drugs and 1pm-closing — is transformed in a month: generator, lab, full medicine, all-day staff, 200-300 daily patients. The passenger truck from Lascahobas to Cange stops running for lack of riders.
Late 2002: a Cangeois petition (drafted with Ti Fifi’s help) wins electricity from the Péligre dam to Cange for a few hours a day, ~20 years after the dam drowned the farmland of Cange’s water refugees. Red Cross announces transfusion post at Zanmi Lasante — a blood bank that patients won’t have to pay for, finally answering the 1983 Léogâne moment that founded Farmer’s life work. Farmer to Kidder: “No more weeping over blood.”
PIH staff at Cange: ~200 community health workers, ~12 nurses, 12 doctors (including a Cuban surgeon and a Cuban pediatrician — the Cuba-Council-of-State pipeline working). Treating >3,000 HIV patients, 350 on antiretrovirals. First open-heart surgeries performed at Cange (Brigham + South Carolina teams). Kidder: “I felt tempted to ask Farmer if this was appropriate technology — not to hear the answer, just to hear him say it.”
The afterword’s force comes from its calendar coincidence: the WHO doctrine shift (the Carabayllo argument at scale) and the Cange electrification (the Péligre dam injustice partially redressed) both arrive in the same season, almost two decades after the moments that generated them. The book closes on the proposition that the long defeat is, locally, also winnable.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: Tracy Kidder Mountains Beyond Mountains — Chapter Deep Dives
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Tracy Kidder Mountains Beyond Mountains — Chapter Deep Dives
27 chapters

Ch.3 — How they met (Mirebalais, December 1994)
Kidder, embedded with U.S. Army Special Forces during the post-coup intervention, meets Paul Farmer outside a small army outpost in Mirebalais.
Ch.4 — The Brigham (December 1999)
Kidder spends a day shadowing Farmer at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, four floors down in radiology.
Ch.5 — Zanmi Lasante (January 2000)
The 35-mile drive from Port-au-Prince takes three hours up the wreck-strewn National Highway 3. At the top of a steep incline, headlights pick out the wall and gate of Zanmi Lasante (“Partners In Health” in Creole) — a walled medical citad…
Ch.6 — The hike to Morne Michel (the noncompliance study)
Kidder follows Farmer on a five-hour round-trip hike to Morne Michel, the most distant village in Zanmi Lasante’s catchment, to find one TB patient who missed his monthly appointment.
Ch.7 — The Blue Bird Inn and the Lady Gin (Farmer’s childhood)
Born 1959 in North Adams, Massachusetts. Father — Paul Sr., “the Warden” / “Elbows” — moved family to Birmingham, Alabama (1966) seeking sales work, then to Brooksville, Florida (1971).
Ch.8 — Duke, Virchow, and arrival in Haiti (1983)
Photographic memory for friends; legions of female friends; food fights and Sound of Music sing-alongs while studying.
Ch.9 — Meeting Ophelia (Mirebalais, 1983)
Ophelia Dahl, daughter of writer Roald Dahl and actress Patricia Neal, arrives in Haiti at 18 as a volunteer for Eye Care Haiti.
Ch.10 — Cange and Léogâne (1983-1984)
the squatter settlement of “water refugees” displaced by the Péligre Dam, half a mile up the road from the reservoir.
Ch.11 — Building Zanmi Lasante; meeting Tom White (1985-1986)
The Harvard-Haiti commute begins to forge a religious orientation.
Ch.12 — Founding PIH; meeting Jim Kim; the broken leg (1986-1988)
the muzzle falls off (baboukèt la tonbe) after Baby Doc flees.
Ch.13 — Aristide, the 1990 election, the 1991 coup
Haitian army rule 1986-1990, with U.S. assistance Farmer documents through declassified material.
Ch.14 — The junta years; The Uses of Haiti (1991-1994)
After the Cédras coup, Farmer continues edgy transit between Cange and Boston.
Ch.15 — The great epi divide and MDR-TB
Short conceptual chapter introducing the “great epi divide” — Farmer’s own coinage — for the partition of humanity between populations who die in their seventies of aging-body diseases and populations who die ten to forty years earlier of…
Ch.16 — Carabayllo and Father Jack (1994-1995)
Father Jack Roussin — beefy Boston priest, “a character,” former pastor of St.
Ch.17 — The ten patients (1996)
Kidder’s first arrival at Carabayllo at night. Lima’s northern outskirts spread up steep gray-brown hills with no soil, lit by absurdly oversized highway-style pylons.
Ch.18 — Médicos aventureros (1996-1997)
Hard counsel from Michael Iseman (world’s foremost MDR-TB clinical authority, National Jewish in Denver): even in 1993 his cure rate was ~60%, costs running as high as $250,000 per case, two years of weak side-effect-laden second-line drug…
Ch.19 — Hepatitis A; Christian’s recovery; the doctor’s daughter
Farmer marries Didi Bertrand in Cange in 1996. About 4,000 attend; Jim Kim and a Duke friend best men; Père Lafontant and three priests preside.
Ch.20 — DOTS-plus and the Goldfarb confrontation (April 1998)
Howard Hiatt convenes a special meeting at the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in Boston to present early Carabayllo results: of the first 53 patients treated, >85% cured.
Ch.21 — Driving down the price (1998-2000)
Cost-effectiveness analysis has become the gatekeeping discipline of international health: imported from engineering, war, and medicine; deployed by big donors as a test you have to pass.
Ch.22 — A light month for travel (early 2000)
“Paul and Jim mobilized the world to accept drug-resistant TB as a soluble problem.” He urges Farmer to step out of one-on-one Cange clinical work and become a global executive on TB, AIDS, and malaria — but Farmer refuses.
Ch.23 — Cuba (early 2000)
“Look! Only ninety miles from Haiti and look! Trees! Crops!” He admires Cuban medicine on health-statistics grounds, not ideological grounds.
Ch.24 — Paris (Catherine’s second birthday)
Kidder is sleeping-pill-fogged. Farmer’s wife Didi has been studying the records French slavers kept of their West African commerce — the city’s beauty has accordingly soured for both of them.
Ch.25 — Moscow and the Russian prisons
Russia is now the largest TB project Farmer is engaged with.
Ch.26 — The Gates grant; “If Paul is the model, we’re golden”
the Gates Foundation grants PIH and a coalition of partners $45 million to wipe out MDR-TB in Peru — virtually everything Jim asked for.
Ch.27 — The boy John
The most narrative-dense and emotionally costly chapter in the book.
Ch.28 — The hike to Casse and “the long defeat”
December (~2 months after John’s death). Kidder returns to Cange.
Ch.29 — Afterword (June 2002 update)
WHO adopts new MDR-TB guidelines virtually identical to PIH’s Carabayllo protocols.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: Front matter (copyright, contents, acclaim)
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Front matter
Three pages of EPUB front matter (copyright, table of contents, acclaim quotes). Lists the 16 numbered chapters plus prologue and epilogue. No substantive content; collapsed.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: Prologue — A Good Man in a Storm
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Prologue — A Good Man in a Storm
Kidder opens not in a basement lab but on a 35-foot sloop in a north-easterly gale en route from Portland, Maine, to New York. Six men are aboard: an aging owner-captain, a psychologist, a physician, a professor, the narrator’s host, and a thin, watch-capped stranger named Tom West, age 40. While the rest of the crew is huddled, seasick, and “half-autistic” with motion-stress, West is in continual motion — taking the helm, swapping sails on the foredeck, reading charts under a swinging lantern, refusing to admit nausea, sleeping only a few hours over four nights, swimming alongside the boat on day three.
