He spots unlit channel markers in the dark and brings the boat in safely. He utters his low-throated “ghost-story” laugh at small wonders of weather. Asked what he does for a living he says “I build computers” but is otherwise opaque about his work. The captain’s later verdict is the chapter’s title and Kidder’s organizing image: West is “a good man in a storm.” The prologue establishes the central character archetype — the obsessive-competent who runs toward crisis, finds it interesting, and treats sleep deprivation as recreation — that the rest of the book will trace into the basement of Westborough.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 1 — How to Make a Lot of Money
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
1 — How to Make a Lot of Money
Kidder establishes the corporate setting. Data General Corporation, headquartered in Westborough, Massachusetts (Building 14A/B, “Webo”), is by 1979 the third-largest minicomputer maker after DEC, with $507.5M revenue and ~70,700 cumulative computers shipped since founding in 1968 — having grown ~30-40% annually for a decade. The lobby contains a glass case displaying the original NOVA, with a CRT cycling through ten years of financial graphs (cumulative shipments, net sales, profit margins).
History: postwar transistor (Bell Labs Nobel) → integrated circuit chips → minicomputer market that IBM ignored, leaving room for DEC’s PDP-8 (1965, designed by Edson de Castro). In 1968 de Castro and two other DEC engineers seceded — disputed origins; DEC’s official history “expunged de Castro” — and founded Data General with $800K, in a former beauty parlor in Hudson, Massachusetts. The NOVA’s design advantage was packaging: especially large printed-circuit boards reducing hardware count, plus latest chips. First director of marketing Allen Kluchman engineered an aggressive image (the famous full-page de Castro ad: “we intend to make a lot of money”; the unpublished “They Say IBM’s Entry Into Minicomputers Will Legitimize the Market. The Bastards Say, Welcome”).
Founders’ “Fuck You Theory” of negotiation: Herb Richman recounts that their lawyer made each founder sell stock to “take down a million bucks” so they could negotiate without fear of losing everything. Trade press calls Data General “the Darth Vader of the computer industry”; Fortune in 1979 calls them “the upstarts” and DEC “the gentlemen.” Earlier (~early ’70s) competitor Keronix accused Data General of arson; courts dismissed but Wall Street suspended trading; some employees still privately believed “someone connected with the company had something to do with that fire.”
Structural risk: a fast-growing computer company can asphyxiate on its own success — demand outruns production, customers go elsewhere. Data General got “one leg caught in this trap” around 1973. The other risk: falling behind in the next CPU generation. By late 1978 Data General has not yet produced a 32-bit supermini to rival DEC’s VAX 11/780. The chapter ends with a businessman’s metaphor of computer competition as downhill ski racing — staying “right on that edge beside disaster” — and the line that frames the book: “What Tom West and his people are doing is a great act of recovery.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 2 — The Wars
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
2 — The Wars
The chapter introduces Tom West as Eclipse Group leader and traces the internal politics that produced the “Eagle” project. West, age 40, drives a red Saab; gestures with his hands; characteristically vague (“you got the feeling West expected you to be on his secret wavelength”).
The technical context: a new product class has emerged — the 32-bit supermini, exemplified by DEC’s VAX 11/780 (~$100K). Data General has fallen behind. The 16-bit minicomputer (NOVA, Eclipse) can address only ~65,000 storage compartments; a 32-bit machine can directly address ~4.3 billion. The market for 32-bit superminis is projected at billions by mid-1980s.
To estimate the threat, West makes a clandestine visit to a customer site to physically inspect a VAX. Posing as someone with permission, he opens the CPU cabinet (twenty-seven printed-circuit boards), counts chips, and concludes the machine costs ~$22,500 to manufacture. He calls the visit “G-Two” intelligence (not “knockoff copy work” / reverse engineering). His judgment: VAX is too complicated, embodies DEC’s bureaucracy. “With VAX, DEC was trying to minimize the risk. We’re trying to maximize the win, and make Eagle go as fast as a raped ape.”
History of “the wars” inside Westborough:

~1975: original Eclipse Group leader leaves to start FHP (Fountainhead Project) — a grand 32-bit machine, ambitious, working from an apartment (suite “007”).
1976: in Massachusetts election year, Data General opens Research Triangle Park facility in North Carolina. FHP project transferred south; some engineers refuse to move. Boston Globe quotes de Castro praising NC’s “can-do attitude” relative to Westborough; “morale hit an all-time low.”
Stay-behind engineers under West design EGO — initials one step back from FHP, like HAL/IBM in 2001. EGO uses a “mode bit”: a 16-bit Eclipse with a switch to become a 32-bit machine. Two months from idea to spec.
“Big shoot-out at HoJo’s”: EGO loses to North Carolina’s FHP at September 1977 meeting with de Castro. EGO’s five engineers were trying to “kill North Carolina.”
“Off-the-wall periods” follow; engineers play Adventure; West makes “speeches of rising and falling expectations”; he creates Project Victor (faster 16-bit) which he calls “a canard.”
After EGO is killed twice, de Castro tells West: “Do something to extend the addressing capability of Eclipses, but don’t use a mode bit.”

West’s reframing: a fully Eclipse-compatible 32-bit machine, built on top of the Eclipse instruction set rather than as a clean-slate design. Carl Alsing names it Eagle (note: “you can’t say ‘Eagle’ without it sounding as if you were saying ‘EGO’”). West’s PR strategy is two-faced: externally low-key it as “insurance” if FHP slips; internally promote it as “the answer to VAX.” He persuades the VPs of engineering and software with a deliberate two-option pitch where Eagle is the obvious win.
Some engineers call Eagle “a wart on a wart on a wart,” “a bag on the side of the Eclipse,” or worst of all, “a kludge.” West’s recruiting pitch: “we’re really gonna build this fucker and it’s gonna be fast as greased lightning… we’re gonna do it by April.” That was less than a year away.
Promise to de Castro: one year. “We had to do it in a year to have any chance.” West summarizes: “We’re building what I thought we could get away with.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 3 — Building a Team
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
3 — Building a Team
The chapter is a tour of the Westborough basement and an account of how the Eagle team was hired. The basement layout — fluorescent-lit cubicles 5.5 feet tall, no doors, plants poking up “like periscopes” above partitions — is described as a deliberately temporary arrangement that “keeps up the basic level of insecurity.” Industry argot is a small foreign language: ECO (engineering change order), “give me a core dump,” “stack overflow,” “his mind is only one stack deep.” Engineers hang framed Marketing photographs of computers they shipped on their walls — “physicians hang diplomas, fishermen mount their biggest catch.”
West’s biography (gathered partly from Carl Alsing): Amherst College physics; Smithsonian Institution (digital clocks, world travel — including yelling “Massachusetts! Massachusetts!” into the dark in Mozambique); RCA self-taught computer engineering; arrived at Data General in 1974. Early Eclipse work: a “great debugger.” Hosts annual pig roasts. Took the Eclipse Group leadership when the founder left for FHP — closed his door for seven weeks to design the IOP after being told it was out of the question. “The day Tom went into his office to do the IOP was the day he started getting tough… the day when he started to care.”
Rosemarie Seale, the Eclipse Group’s secretary: hired off a Data General help-wanted ad (“ARE YOU BORED?”), arrived to a single filing cabinet containing only toilet paper. Becomes the team’s institutional ballast — handles mail, paychecks, fights bureaucratic battles, “trains all the team’s newcomers to tie their shoes.”
Hiring the kids. The team has ~12 experienced engineers; West and Alsing decide to hire ~12 new engineers fresh out of grad school. Inspiration: a videotape of Seymour Cray (Cray Research, Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin) saying he likes to hire inexperienced engineers because “they do not usually know what’s supposed to be impossible.” Plus: cheaper, and disguises Eagle’s real intentions. Smiling, West allowed they might be hiring “their own assassins.”
Group structure:

West (boss)
Steve Wallach (architect / “adjutant”)
Two main lieutenants: Ed Rasala (hardware → “Hardy Boys”) and Carl Alsing (microcode → “Microkids”)
Sublieutenants under each (Ken Holberger under Rasala, Chuck Holland under Alsing)
Total ~30 people

Recruit experience: Hardy Boy Dave Epstein walks into West’s office: “Hi, I’m Dave”; West “just sat there and stared at me.” Microkids housed four-to-an-office in “the Micropit.” Recruits told: “Don’t even mention the name Eagle outside the group.”
Hours, pay, hiring filter:

Newcomer ~20K/year, veteran ~30K, no overtime pay, stock options as a “mere sweetener.”
Microkid Betty Shanahan (the team’s lone female engineer): “You can end up staying all night… my husband complained that the last three times he’s had to do the laundry.” Jon Blau: “I’ve had difficulty forming sentences lately.”
Reject: a candidate who listed “family life” as his main avocation. “He seems to be saying he doesn’t want to sign up.” Grades had to be excellent.

The signing-up ritual. By signing up, the recruit agrees to do whatever is necessary. Alsing’s interview (the chapter’s most-cited passage):

Alsing: “What do you want to do?”
(Recruit must respond with technical fire-in-the-eyes.)
Alsing: “We’re building this machine that’s way out in front in technology…”
Alsing: “It’s gonna be tough. If we hired you, you’d be working with a bunch of cynics and egotists…”
Recruit: “That doesn’t scare me.”
Alsing: “We can only let in the best of this year’s graduates. We’ve already let in some awfully fast people. We’ll have to let you know.”
Then they let him in.

Alsing’s verdict: “It was kind of like recruiting for a suicide mission. You’re gonna die, but you’re gonna die in glory.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 4 — Wallach's Golden Moment
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
4 — Wallach’s Golden Moment
A character study of Steve Wallach, the Eagle architect, and a chapter on the architectural design itself. Wallach grew up in Brooklyn (father was a hot-metal compositor); Stuyvesant High; Brooklyn Polytechnic; UPenn MS in EE; Honeywell, then Raytheon (Navy avionics digital computer — built but never deployed); FHP at Data General (worked two years, machine moved south); EGO (designed and killed); Victor (designed and died gradually). By the time Eagle starts, Wallach has put a decade into five computers; only one has shipped, and the customer didn’t buy it.
Wallach’s initial response to West’s offer to architect Eagle: “Fuck that! I’m not puttin’ a bag on the side of the Eclipse.” He goes home for two weeks, returns angry. After many long conversations, West tells him: “Either you do this or your job description is inoperative.” Wallach goes to de Castro:

Wallach: “What the fuck do you want?”
de Castro: “I want a thirty-two-bit Eclipse.”
Wallach: “If we do this, you won’t cancel it on us?”
de Castro: “That’s what I want, a thirty-two-bit Eclipse and no mode bit.”

Wallach signs up: “Okay, Tom, one more time.”
The architectural problem. Eagle must (1) be fully Eclipse-compatible (preserve the entire 16-bit instruction set so all existing customer software runs), (2) extend logical address space from 16 bits / ~65K compartments to 32 bits / ~4.3 billion, (3) provide memory protection for time-shared use, (4) NOT use a mode bit. Wallach starts with memory management.
The golden moment. A 32-bit address has eight possible values for its first three bits. Wallach designs a “ring” protection system inspired by the MULTICS work at MIT (and that DEC had used in VAX — separately from address). Wallach’s innovation: fold ring number into the address itself by using the first three bits to encode both segment number and ring number simultaneously. Eight rings, eight segments; ring number = segment number = first three address bits. Cheap, simple, hardware-efficient. He had been told the seed of this idea years before by an engineer at a conference.
Alsing’s verdict: “Rings have been around. They’re old hat. What makes Wallach a good Data General engineer is that he came up with a really elegant subset of those ideas — simple, sweet, cheap, efficient, clean.”
Constraints fight. Wallach was forbidden mode bits. The full Eclipse 16-bit instruction set (“the wart on a wart”) had to be retained. He could not match VAX’s “super” instruction set. He even tried to slip in a disguised mode bit; West caught him: “We’re not gonna do that.”
Workaround for sneaking in non-Eclipse-like new instructions: Wallach took ideas to System Software, had them write a memo back requesting the new instruction “so that the idea would be perceived as coming from them, just in case we ever got called on it.” Wallach’s verdict: “Anytime you do anything on the sly, it’s always more interesting than if you do it up front.”
Wallach wrote the architecture spec (“my book”) seven times. ~200 pages. Each chapter opens with an epigraph he found from Hugo, Nietzsche, Shakespeare, T.S. Eliot, Santayana, Tolkien, FDR — twenty hours in the Framingham Public Library. The Macbeth epigraph for the instruction-set chapter:
“We still have judgement here; that we but teach Bloody Instructions, which, being taught, return To plague the inventor.”
The chapter ends with Wallach’s reflection on insight: “Hey, no one knows how that works. I will be constantly chugging away in my mind, making an exhaustive search of my data bank.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 5 — Midnight Programmer
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
5 — Midnight Programmer
A character study of Carl Alsing (microcode lieutenant) and a layered explanation of how a computer actually computes — high-level language → assembly → microcode → gates and electrons.
Kidder is sitting with Alsing at midnight in Westborough, playing the text-adventure game Adventure (Colossal Cave) on the team’s Eclipse computer Trixie. Alsing’s chuckle at Kidder’s flailing in the maze (“YOU ARE IN A MAZE OF TWISTY LITTLE PASSAGES, ALL DIFFERENT”) is the chapter’s atmospheric center. The Microkids have programmed Trixie with personality — typing WHO returns CARL, WHERE returns IN THE ROAD WHERE ELSE!, WHY returns BECAUSE WE LIKE TO CARL.
Alsing’s biography. Family moved to Evansville, Indiana, when he was eight (“I was smaller, paler, weaker… on the bottom of the pile”); coped by taking apart the family telephone. UMass undergrad — flunked everything except the digital-circuits course where he met Boolean algebra (“Alsing’s world was never the same after that”). Discovered nighttime access to a university IBM computer; “I was a midnight programmer.” A few of his cohort lost girlfriends and grades to the addiction. Alsing dropped out, returned, became straight-A. Joined DEC, then Data General (badge #150 — “the lower the number, the longer your service”).
The four-layer stairway into a computer:

High-level language (BASIC, FORTRAN) — pidgin-English-like.
Interpreter translates high-level into assembly language: the ~200 basic operations the machine can execute (ADD, Skip On Equal).
Microcode — for each assembly instruction there is a microprogram of ~3 microinstructions on average. Each Eagle microinstruction is 75 bits, divided into fields, each field signaling a different chunk of the hardware. A simple / (divide) becomes ~10 assembly instructions → ~30 microinstructions → ~2,250 bits of signal.
Gates — transistors arranged so that high voltage = 1, low = 0; AND gates, NAND gates, OR gates — Boolean algebra in metal. The ”/” causes hundreds of gates to open and close in choreographed sequence in nanoseconds.

Why microcode matters: it makes the machine flexible. Eagle’s microcode lives on a floppy disk loaded each boot — fixes can ship as new disks, not new boards. Some computers (notably Seymour Cray’s) remain hard-wired — assembly goes directly to circuits.
Alsing’s working style: legendary procrastination followed by burst output. Eclipse microcode (195 assembly instructions encoded in ~390 microinstructions): Alsing went to the Boston Public Library with manuals and wrote most of it in two weeks (West says two days and nights). Eagle code: he asked his wife to keep three sons off “the microporch” and finished a new Eclipse’s code in two weeks the summer before Eagle began.
Alsing on his craft: “Writing microcode is like nothing else in my life… I get into a mental state where I’m a microcode-writing machine. It’s like being in Adventure. Adventure’s a completely bogus world, but when you’re there, you’re there. You have a hundred L-shaped blocks to build a building… you’re like a kid on a jungle gym.”
Alsing’s role on Eagle. By 35 he is “very elderly within the group.” He runs the Microteam from a distance — chooses members, trains them, mediates, but doesn’t write code himself (“I could not generate the excitement I used to feel about gates and bits”). He’s the social director: organizes Tube Wars (Microkids hide each other’s files), the Honorary Microcoder Awards, weekly meetings (“Alsing’s weekly No-Op”). He talks to West about whether the project is “real.”
The chapter’s broader observation: software/hardware engineers in their 30s often face a “long-term tiredness.” The most common form of advancement is to become a manager. Alsing has detached from coding because he had to: he could not have written all of Eagle’s code himself, so he wrote none.
Alsing on West: “West’s not a technical genius. He’s perfect for making it all work. He’s gotta move forward. He doesn’t put off the tough problem, the way I do. He’s fearless, he’s a great politician, he’s arbitrary, sometimes he’s ruthless… West is interesting. He’s the main reason why I do what I do.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 6 — Flying Upside Down
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
6 — Flying Upside Down
The chapter formalizes “the rules” of the Eagle game and walks through the design phase (summer 1978 to early 1979).
The rules of the Westborough game (per Kidder, confirmed by Rasala/Carman/West):

Compete for resources. Eagle and FHP are run by different VPs; “competition is fostered” by de Castro to surface bad ideas before they reach customers. Carman calls Data General competition “Sunday school” compared to IBM but acknowledges it’s deliberate.
Promise a nearly impossible schedule. West calls this “what’s-the-earliest-date-by-which-you-can’t-prove-you-won’t-be-finished” scheduling. Eagle: one year.
Sign up. Implicit promise of overtime, weekends, marriage strain, in exchange for the right to do the work.
Reward the winners. Stock options were strongly suggested but never explicitly promised. The real reward is “pinball” — winning means you get to play again, build the next machine.
(Alsing’s footnote.) “One never explicitly plays by these rules.”

The lieutenants’ frame. West treats Eagle externally as “insurance” against FHP slipping, internally as the “answer to VAX.” Carl Carman (VP of engineering) makes it policy that team members can come and go without retribution, hoping flexibility serves as an “escape valve” for pressure. Mushroom management: “put ‘em in the dark, feed ‘em shit, and watch ‘em grow.”
The recruit experience under pressure. Microkid Jon Blau is studying Booth’s algorithm for multiplication when called to a meeting where the brass announce that Eagle is late and must ship by April. Blau goes back to his desk: “Practically the next time you look up, it’s midnight… ‘This is life. Accomplishment.’ Tomorrow you’ll have to get to work on an instruction called FFAS.” Hardy Boy Dave Epstein quotes a Micro-sequencer schedule of two months → bargained to six weeks → bragged down to four (“Now, back in his cubicle, Epstein has just realized, ‘I just signed up to do it in four weeks.’”).
Some recruits balk. Hardy Boy Josh Rosen: “There’s no grand design. People are just reaching out in the dark, touching hands… The whole management structure — anyone in Harvard Business School would have barfed.”
Flying upside down. West’s metaphor (originally from a friend Bernie, an electrician who flew his small airplane inverted over West’s farm). In Eagle terms: assume software resources will be there; assume kids fresh out of college can build a major CPU; gamble on a brand-new chip type called PALs (programmable array logic) sole-sourced from a small vendor when conventional wisdom requires at least two suppliers. West’s design rules:

Use as little silicon as possible (a few thousand dollars of chips).
Far fewer boards than VAX’s 27 (target: 7 for the CPU).
Faster than VAX by Whetstone benchmarks.
Compatible with all existing Data General peripherals and Eclipse software.
“No bells and whistles.”
“Not Everything Worth Doing Is Worth Doing Well.” (West’s Magic Marker board.)

Design management. West reviews all designs personally, often with terse “It’s right” / “It’s wrong” / “No, there isn’t time.” But he loosens control over how the team self-organizes. No charts, no organizational tables; “webs of voluntary, mutual responsibility, the product of many signings-up.” A skeptic might think it chaos.
The design takes about six months (late summer 1978 to new year 1979).
Walking an instruction through the engine. Microkid Jon Blau gives Kidder a several-hour informal tour of Eagle’s logical structure. The named subsystems: IOC (Input/Output Control), IP (Instruction Processor — accelerator that prefetches and decodes), ATU (Address Translation Unit — keeps memory map), Sys Cache (System Cache), Microsequencer (issues microinstructions), CC (Console Control board), and a microNova that acts as Eagle’s “therapist” running diagnostics. Following an assembly instruction WSEQ (Skip On Equal) requires three microinstructions executed at one clock tick (220 nanoseconds) each, with parallel signals fanning out to multiple boards. Blau’s working metaphor: “the machine is a sensate thing that asks questions, looks up answers, sends and receives messages.”
A pathological case: an “infinite page fault” — if instructions for the page-fault recovery program are themselves missing from memory, “the machine will fall down an endless series of mirrors.” The CC board and microNova exist partly to detect and halt this.
The chapter ends with West, once driving home: “I can’t talk about the machine. I’ve gotta keep life and computers separate, or else I’m gonna go mad.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 7 — La Machine
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
7 — La Machine
Debugging begins (early 1979) with two prototype Eagles named Coke and Gollum (originally Coke and Pepsi; Holberger demanded Gollum after Tolkien). They sit in a yellow-cinder-block restricted-area lab — wire-wrapped boards exposed, fans roaring, blue and red wires snaking between boards, microNovas stacked atop each prototype, logic analyzers on wheeled carts looking “like surgical gear.” Each clock tick is 220 nanoseconds.
West discovers he doesn’t know how to debug Eagle. The new accelerators (IP, Sys Cache) require many parts to be working before debugging can really begin. Schedules slip “a week a week.” West throws the household water pump across his basement after a minor setback; goes to bed at midday on a Sunday; bans laughter from cubicles outside his office; takes a day off to look at sailboats. He starts using a new word — trust — and decides to stay out of the lab so as not to undermine Rasala. He goes once on a Sunday morning to sit alone in front of a prototype, then never again.
Trust is the chapter’s transition. Alsing’s running commentary: “This week Tom finally gripped the arms of his chair and decided to trust Rasala.”
Ed Rasala (hardware lieutenant). Polish-American Brooklyn upbringing; Rensselaer Polytechnic; Raytheon doing routine assignments until one harder problem awoke him; came to Data General on a whim from a help-wanted ad. Was had into building the first Eclipse. West groomed him as a “mechanic” — one who takes ideas of brighter engineers and makes them work. Led the M/600 (the largest 16-bit Eclipse) before Eagle. Drives himself with self-help books on understanding his boss, regular night-school programming classes despite 10-12 hour workdays, and a one-line self-description: “I’m not gonna go out and invent anything. But making it work is fun. I’m a good designer, I think, and I’m a better debugger.”
Rasala on technical roles: “I realize now that Josh wasn’t as comfortable with the ALU as I was.” Rasala “leads by example” — works both shifts, enforces a “Saturday update” rule for the boards (so each prototype reflects the same fixes). Wants Hardy Boys to be “Smart, opinionated and nonsensitive.”
The engineer’s binary worldview, Kidder observes: “in this world, if you produce right results, your colleagues must accept you. It’s an exciting environment to contemplate; you can change the way people think if you can provide the right reason.” But the EGO wars showed two engineers can argue narrow technical issues forever without resolution.
The lab’s debugging cycle. Engineering change orders (ECOs) document fixes; whichever board gets fixed first, the team writes up an ECO so the same fix gets applied to the other prototype. Updating boards (unwrapping wires, checking with ohmmeters, rewinding) is hated work. A tiny stray wire fragment lodged in the wrong place causes “flakeys” — failures that may take days to find. “Just stuff you never account for in a schedule.”
A schedule game. North Carolina’s FHP, Carman tells West early in 1979, is now slipping by a huge margin — much more than Eagle. The internal competition has “essentially ended.” Eagle has become a corporate necessity. West sits in his office in a wild state, bitter monologue: “Carman says the company’s in a lot of trouble if it’s not there by April. Suppose I quit?… Now I gotta get way out on the edge, full of anxiety about the company falling into a revenue hole if it’s not there by April — ten thousand jobs on the line — and I gotta pretend everything’s fine.”
The team’s vocabulary of fear (Alsing’s taxonomy):

The big mistake — fundamental design flaw discovered late, requiring redesign.
The flakey fear — machine works in the lab but won’t be reliable or buildable in volume.
The bogeyman fear — “just something dark and nameless that the machine just won’t ever work.” West: “It’s the infinite page fault you didn’t anticipate. The bogeyman is the space your mind can’t comprehend.”

Late in the chapter, Rasala internalizes “la machine”:

“Ahhhh, la machine.”
Duel (the Spielberg TV movie) is his image — a faceless trailer truck threatening to drive the hero off the road.
His five-year-old son: “I hope your machine breaks, Daddy.”
Rasala wakes up nights wondering if a prototype has stopped overnight running its diagnostic test.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 8 — The Wonderful Micromachines
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
8 — The Wonderful Micromachines
A study of the Microteam at work, organized around two figures (sublieutenant Chuck Holland and prodigy programmer Neal Firth) and two tools (UINST and the simulator).
The Microteam has its own micro-vocabulary: the Micropit (their four-person office), the microbus (a member’s van), the outdoor microlounge (a stone wall behind the building, in view of the security camera, used for Friday afternoon hangouts when West holds his managers’ meeting). Sample microlounge dialogue: “We have to do this project on the fly.” / “Yeah, we’re all flying.” / “Maybe the electrons aren’t in the computer at all. They just turn on the lights.”
Chuck Holland (sublieutenant). Hired by Alsing largely because Holland in his interview described a sculpture he was building — a five-foot rectangular cage of steel rods, with a single hidden track on which steel balls roll, dropping from one section to another, the geometry creating the illusion of multiple parallel paths. Months of taking it apart and reassembling. Alsing: “It was my clue that he could make something intricate work.”
Holland’s role: organize the microcode. Each of Eagle’s 75-bit microinstructions is divided into fields; each field’s bit-pattern is a “microverb.” Holland and Ken Holberger build the entire microverb dictionary, define their interactions (one verb can override another, or mean different things to different boards), and codify rules of grammar to prevent code-hardware contradictions. The reference document is UINST (“U” for micro, INST for instruction set) — the Microteam’s “bible,” which the Hardy Boys call “a Sears, Roebuck catalogue” or “the Microteam’s wishbook.” UINST is a battlefield: changes weekly, each side trying to push functions onto the other side’s silicon or code.
The simulator. Alsing’s long-running argument with West: he wants a software simulator that mimics Eagle inside Trixie (the team’s existing Eclipse), so microcode can be debugged separately from hardware. Without one, you can’t tell if a failure is hardware bug, microcode bug, or diagnostic-program bug. West has always said no — too long to write. This time Alsing insists.
Two candidate writers:

Dave Peck (DG employee #257; came over from Software; raucous laugh; “the fastest in the East” but takes longer to talk himself into writing a program than to write it).
Neal Firth (22; degrees in CS and EE; near-perfect academic record; one of the very first Microkid recruits).

Alsing’s ploy: he tells Firth a deliberately oversimplified picture of writing a simulator, with friendly enthusiasm. Asks how long it would take. Firth: “Six weeks or two months?” Alsing: “Oh, good.” Then Alsing tells Peck (Firth’s nominal manager) to write a “quick-and-dirty” simulator while Firth works on a “bigger one.” A friendly competition.
Outcome: Peck delivers in six weeks (used by one Microkid for a while). Firth delivers a full simulator at 2.5 months, refines it for two more — a paper Eagle. Without it, “the lab might have looked like a crowded car on a commuter train” with everyone bumping for prototype access. The Microteam tests its code at desk terminals using Trixie + the simulator; can stop microprograms anywhere, examine state, replay traces. They could see what was wrong “in an instant.”
Why it worked. Firth had to write a program for every microverb, then shuffle their order — in the real Eagle, all microverbs in one microinstruction execute in parallel between two clock ticks; in the simulator, they execute serially, one after another, and order matters because verbs can cancel each other. Firth: “I was able to do it because I had no idea of what was going on. Usually it was: ‘We gotta have this feature in the simulator by tomorrow or poor old Jon Blau won’t be able to do a thing.‘”
Firth: “I like to work around ‘why.’ I prefer not to know the established limits and what other people think, when I start a project.” On code: “I can write two hundred to three hundred lines of code in my mind, but I had a hard time remembering my own phone number.”
Alsing’s home-disabled-TV story. He sabotaged all the family TVs, telling his teenaged sons they could watch Charlie’s Angels if they fixed them. They never did fix them, but spent pleasant Sunday mornings working on them with him. (Alsing: when he approves of a show, “as if by magic” one set will start working.)
The chapter’s argument. Coordination between the Microteam and Hardy Boys (UINST as battleground), control distributed deeply (West → Alsing → Holland → individual microcoder), and the simulator as a force multiplier are why a 30-person team built a major CPU in roughly the right time frame.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 9 — A Workshop
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
9 — A Workshop
A character study of West outside the office, organized around his 1780 farmhouse and basement workshop. West drives 20 minutes from Westborough to a country lane; the farmhouse has an ell, a barn, a second barn behind that, a tall wooden silo. He has spent years restoring it himself. His wife: “Tom likes to do things ‘right’ — and I mean quotes around ‘right.‘” The basement workshop is the central image — a stone-walled craft space with a lathe, shaper, radial-arm saw, band saw, drill press, sanding machine, two grinding wheels with goggles, an old belt-driven table saw “in immaculate condition,” a woodworking bench, hammers “practically every kind ever invented right in its place.” Storeroom labeled jars: “Special Car Tools,” “Telephone Stuff,” “Antenna Stuff,” “Brushes,” “Good Brushes,” “Rockets,” “More Rockets.” Tacked-up aphorisms: “The appreciation of pleasing decay is an important one because it is so often neglected.”
The contrast Kidder draws: the workshop is meticulously hand-crafted, every tool dusted and labeled and put away in the proper drawer. The Magic Marker board at work reads “Not Everything Worth Doing Is Worth Doing Well.” West uses the same word “right” both ways — at home, right means craft perfection; at work, right means commercially correct.
Rosemarie Seale’s question, early in the project: “Is it going to be a good machine?” West: “Yes, Rosemarie. It’s going to be good.”
West’s biography (more layers than the recruits know).

Father a senior AT&T executive; family moved often. West rebuilt cars and a sailboat as a boy in Lincoln, Nebraska, then Illinois, then Oklahoma City, then Martha’s Vineyard.
Amherst College: he became “the first officially branded underachiever” under a Calvinist program of expelling smart students who weren’t producing. Spent his year of exile in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in the very early 1960s, playing guitar in coffeehouses, knowing some of the eventually famous folksingers.
Returned to Amherst, decided to become an engineer (“People were leaving Harvard and becoming masons. As for myself, I decided to become an engineer”). Wanted to work on the space program but the interesting jobs were taken; took a Smithsonian Institution job building digital clocks for satellite tracking stations, traveled the world, was briefly jailed in a Colombian border town that mistook the clock for a weapon.
Quit after seven years, needed a draft-deferring job, taught himself computers from library books over six weeks (“dumb jobs don’t work — you come home too tired to do anything”), talked his way into RCA. RCA lost a fortune competing with IBM’s 360; got out of computers.
Came to Data General in 1974. Built first Eclipse with de Castro showing up in the lab eating Fudgsicles. De Castro: “Got that fucking pig working yet?” West: psychologically aroused — “No. But I will.”

West on motivation. With Rosemarie he reflects: “There’s a big high in here somewhere for me that I don’t fully understand. Some of it’s a raw power-trip… The reason why I work is because I win… What makes it all possible is doing this and putting money on the bottom line and not having to go all the way with the capitalist system… What makes it all possible is the kids.”
West on his own past machines: “If you start getting interested in the last one, then you’re dead. The old things, I can’t bear to look at them. They’re clumsy. I can’t believe we were that dumb.” On the rapidity of obsolescence: “You spend all this time designing one machine and it’s only a hot box for two years, and it has all the useful life of a washing machine.” One winter night: “Computers are irrelevant.”
But the fixing remains compelling. Kidder’s wife mentions that their son’s record player is broken; West: “Where is it? I’ll take it with me. I can fix anything.” Eagle’s complexity is “something special… build something larger than myself.”
The chapter ends with Kidder lying in West’s guest bedroom hearing West playing guitar in the living room — “The Banks of the O-hi-o” and the like. “Those are seductive ballads. If you listen to them long enough, you can start believing that your way in life is strewn with possibilities.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 10 — The Case of the Missing NAND Gate
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
10 — The Case of the Missing NAND Gate
The longest and most procedurally detailed chapter — a single multi-day debugging case that crystallizes the team’s craft. Holberger, Veres, and Guyer chase a “time-bomb” failure in Eclipse 21 (a diagnostic program); the resolution is one missing NAND gate (eight cents wholesale).
Setting (mid-May 1979). Both prototypes (Coke, Gollum) ran the diagnostic Eclipse 21 overnight: 921 passes, 30 failures each. Failure-rate is too low to be noise but too rare to easily isolate. Symptom: a “Jump-to-Subroutine and Return” (JSR) sequence executes correctly most of the time, but occasionally returns to the wrong instruction.
The accelerator architecture, briefly. Eagle’s memory system has three layers — IP cache (smallest, fastest), Sys Cache (larger), Main Memory (slowest). Each level should hold an exact copy of any block also held in faster levels. The accelerators are forever evicting blocks and bringing new ones; if their housekeeping desyncs and the IP holds an instruction block that looks like it matches Sys Cache but is actually different, “there’s a time bomb set inside” the machine that will fire many cycles later, far from where the inconsistency arose. This is “the worst sort of problem.”
The hunt:

Holberger and Veres put a logic-analyzer trace on Gollum, see a JSR-and-Return where the machine jumped to the right address but executed the wrong instruction. Implicates the memory system, especially IP and Sys Cache.
Look at I-cache: it has the wrong instruction at the right address.
Two possible culprits — IP itself or Sys Cache (which is supposed to invalidate stale IP cache lines).

Veres picks up after Guyer’s overnight shift. Veres tries a forward-search rather than backward: he runs the diagnostic up to the fourth pass, has Gollum stop at every iteration of the failing subtest, and dumps the analyzer + console state. A floor-length spool of computer paper accumulates. Holberger arrives to find Veres sitting in the chaos, scholarly: “I found it.”
Resolution. At iteration 122 the I-cache holds a block with tag 21. At iteration 151 the Sys Cache instructs the IP to swap tag 21 for tag 45. At iteration 158 the I-cache still has tag 21 — meaning the IP disobeyed the invalidation order. The Sys Cache is innocent. The IP — Veres’s own board — is guilty.
The fix is “almost trivial”: within the IP, the signal from Sys Cache to “throw away tag 21” was being overridden by another signal arriving at almost the same time. The repair is one extra NAND gate (Boolean “not-and”), eight cents wholesale, that delays the second signal by enough nanoseconds to let the IP finish the eviction. Holberger names the new signal “NOT YET”: “Schematics he’s seen from other companies use formal, technical names for signals. The Eclipse Group, by contrast, looks for something simple that fits.”
The aftermath. They install the NAND gate; Eclipse 21 runs ten passes; they re-run the rest of the suite; another diagnostic fails. Lunch (Holberger picks at his food). On return they realize the IP is still on the extender (a debugging frame outside the main chassis); reseating fixes the new failure. Gollum now passes all basic Eclipse diagnostics including 21.
The chapter’s craft observations:

Veres’s morning shower: “Showers are kinda boring things, all things considered” — the new approach (forward-search) comes to him there.
“Time in a computer is an interesting concept.” Rasala says he can see twelve nanoseconds when working at the analyzer “wide” but loses track of what one means when away.
Surgery analogy: Rasala holds up tweezers with a tiny strand of stripped wire — drop it on the wrong pin and you get flakeys for days. Kidder: “It’s like surgery.” Rasala: “Most problems we create are repairable. Most surgery isn’t.”
A board can fail on the extender (debugging frame) and work in place. Standard practice but not always obvious.
“Some problems are easy to find and hard to fix; some are hard to find and easy to fix; some go both ways.”

The chapter’s emotional thermometer: this is the high point of the team’s craft confidence — they have learned to chase a time-bomb through millions of clock ticks and isolate it to a single missing logic gate. There is no celebration: “Plenty of diagnostics stand before them. Much trickier ones, in fact.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 11 — Shorter Than a Season
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
11 — Shorter Than a Season
A short chapter on burnout, illustrated through Hardy Boy Josh Rosen — one of the team’s most credentialed engineers (designed the ALU board; “I was the star at Special Systems,” Rosen says of his prior post inside Data General).
Rosen joined the team mid-1978. Designed the ALU but felt forced to start before the architecture was complete; in August wanted to redesign with different chips; Rasala said no, “put a Band-Aid fix on it.” In December his design used too many chips; West assigned another engineer to examine it (a tacit censure). Rosen’s annual review was the first unflattering one of his career.
Rosen’s frame:

Came from a high-autonomy Special Systems environment (“I was free to pursue pure technical excellence”). Found Eclipse Group “Mushroom management” intolerable: “I felt I had no more rights than an oscilloscope.”
Rasala enforced haste; Rosen wanted to redesign to get it right; “We can’t think about that,” Rasala kept snapping.
“I’m not much of a team player, I guess… I have a sort of very antiathletic point of view. That’s the sort of thing nice Jewish boys don’t do.”
West “literally never said hello” to him after hiring; communication only through Rasala, “a pretty narrow filter.”

Burnout becomes Rosen’s diagnosis: at 24, after six years of 60-80 hour weeks (started even at Special Systems, where Personnel had told him “we’ll remind you to take vacations” and never did), he realizes “I have no social life. Nothing.” He suspects Rasala and West are also burning out. “All of a sudden I just didn’t care. It was, all of a sudden, a job.”
The chapter’s titular note. Rosen takes Carman’s “escape valve” privilege seriously now, leaving notes on his terminal when he disappears. One day he leaves: “I’m going to a commune in Vermont and will deal with no unit of time shorter than a season.”
Surrounding observations:

Engineers were dropping out for many reasons throughout the project: kludge-aversion, pecking-order disappointment, peer pressure (“If I screw up this, then I’ll be the only one”). The team is self-selecting harder.
Rosen does keep working through winter and spring — peering into Coke with logic analyzers, repairing his ALU’s bugs creditably.
He had once visited “a very liberal arts college” in Vermont, walked into a geodesic-dome doorframe at the sight of a topless young woman; the memory recurs.
The chapter’s dread image: Rosen frozen in front of an analyzer trace, knuckles in his teeth, looking like “a painting of a nightmare by Goya.”

Rosen quits not long after — Jon Blau will inherit the ALU debugging in chapter 14.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 12 — Pinball
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
12 — Pinball
The chapter introduces the book’s most-quoted concept — pinball — and lays out the team’s complaints about resources, recognition, and West’s distance.
The basement environment has degraded. The lab’s cooling system fails, temperatures hit ~90°F, Holberger props the door open (“So we can get the hot breeze from the hallway”); Carman kicks it shut on a security visit; the Hardy Boys walk out, West “went into forest-fire mode,” Maintenance finally repairs the cooling. Trixie is shared, the Microteam can’t have a second computer. Bernstein’s group has two computers; the Eclipse Group has two prototypes plus a shared Eclipse (Woodstock). Holberger sometimes broadcasts a fake EMERGENCY WARNING MESSAGE to free up Woodstock so he can reprogram a PAL.
Material complaints. The Eclipse Group has built four Eclipse models and “we haven’t even got one for our own use in the lab.” The Microteam ate a battle just to get Trixie. Mini News (DG’s in-house paper) brags that R&D spending is high — “Hey, Tom, where’s it all going?” Holberger asks. (Suspect: North Carolina.) Personal business cards are denied; West says no. Apocryphal quote: “An analyzer costs ten thousand dollars. Overtime for engineers is free.” Dave Peck pleads for a return trip to DG’s California semiconductor facility for a near-impossible job; West refuses: “I’m not gonna send Peck out there for another vacation on company time.”
Peck’s small revolt. He hangs a Lord of the Rings poster next to Woodstock; labels the Hobbits “Microkids,” the skinny treacherous Gollum “Tom West.” Younger members move it to a hidden corner.
Many on the team blame West for the small frustrations. Why are some managers effective at getting resources and Tom isn’t? “He’ll look off in another direction as he walks by, and you never see him smile.” One Hardy Boy: “West may be acting as a real good buffer between us and the rest of the company. Or maybe he’s not doing anything.”
Alsing’s interpretation, which is also the chapter’s payoff.
Alsing: “When this is all over, there are gonna be thirty inventors of the Eagle machine. Tom’s letting them believe that they invented it. It’s cheaper than money.”
West has said: “There’s thirty guys out there who think it’s their machine. I don’t want that tampered with. It’s very useful to me right now.” Another time: “Some of the kids don’t have a notion that there’s a company behind all of this. It could be the CIA funding this. It could be a psychological test.”
Sealing the team. The team is sealed off — recruits told never to mention Eagle outside the group; bureaucratic problems never reach them; Rosemarie absorbs administrative friction. West refuses to pass on criticism in either direction. Alsing and Rasala close West’s office door to ask him for more space and equipment; West usually refuses. Alsing’s read: “He doesn’t want to fight for petty wins when there’s a bigger game in town.” Rasala’s read: same.
Pinball. The bigger game has a name. West coined it: “You win one game, you get to play another. You win with this machine, you get to build the next.” Stock options didn’t matter much; pinball is what counted. Holberger: “I will do this, I want to do it. I recognize from the beginning it’s gonna be a tough job. I’ll have to work hard, and if we do a good job, we get to do it again.”
Rosemarie’s verdict (kept private until later, then poured out):

“Maybe the guys thought that project was a gift from upstairs, but there’s no doubt in my mind — it wouldn’t have happened if he hadn’t been there… nobody would have had the chance to do what we wanted to do.”
“He had a twinkle in his eye! You can’t be scared of someone with a twinkle in his eye who allows you to do things.”
“He kept it inside him… he allowed all the complaints to be on himself. I think it was deliberate. My opinion is he wanted them to have someone to lay it all on… ‘You’re the daddy.‘”

Late in the chapter, more concrete operational tasks arrive: design the AC plug; ensure Eagle fits in a freight elevator (Rasala once had to disassemble an M/600 in a London parking lot for that reason); choose between a key and a button for power-on; manage Software’s involvement; prepare for the June Product Board where West will formally present Eagle to de Castro.
PAL crisis. West gambled on PAL chips from a single supplier. The supplier is now near bankruptcy; the team is rationing PALs to repair prototypes; thousands more will be needed for mass-production. “We could lose the whole thing right there.” Younger team members aren’t told.
End-of-chapter image: West at home on his beige couch, smoking, sketching team members from memory — knew their hobbies, strengths, weaknesses, even those he never greeted. “The postpartum depression on this project is gonna be phenomenal. These guys don’t realize how dependent they are on that thing to create their identities. That’s why we gotta get the new things in place.” West has already designed about half a dozen successor machines and assigned each to suitable team members.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 13 — Going to the Fair
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
13 — Going to the Fair
The team rides a chartered bus to the National Computer Conference (NCC) in New York City — an interlude that puts the Eagle project in a wider industry context. West refuses to come and stays back at Westborough preparing for the upcoming Product Board. Most of the team turn up in jackets and ties.
At DEC’s booth Wallach kneels in front of a VAX 11/780 and starts to open the smoked-Plexiglas door behind which the CPU sits; a DEC saleswoman sees the team’s badges (“Data General, Engineer”), makes a face, shoos them away. They go laughing to the Data General booth — DG’s signpost is the tallest in the hall, taller even than IBM’s. (“If the trend continued, someday Data General would have to set up its booth outdoors.“)
DG’s catchy attraction this year: Dr. Gideon Ariel, a sports-medicine practitioner using an Eclipse to digitize Olympic athletes’ jogging form for NBC’s Today show. Alsing whispers, partly true: “We gave him an Eclipse with only two-K of memory and no peripherals.”
Rasala leans against the M/600 he built; Alsing pretends to be a confused customer (“What’s this switch for?”); Holberger: “It works. But it’s not useful for anything.”
Wallach’s tour. He sniffs at displays — a snort = kludge, a shrug = ordinary, a judicious nod = “evidence that some people knew what they were doing.” IBM’s booth is real oak, no flashy displays, white-shirted attendants — IBM has three years’ back-orders on the new 4300 line and doesn’t need to sell. Sperry Univac with a slide show; Burroughs with trumpet fanfares and dishwasher-shaped cabinets; National Cash Register with twin blonde models (“the bipolar blondes”). Wallach gauges the 32-bit supermini competition Eagle will face: VAX orders alone are approaching a thousand units, ~half a billion dollars.
The smaller booths along the walls are pin-compatible memory makers, software houses, OEMs, graphics outfits (“computers were cranking out many sorts of pie charts”), tape drives, modems, bubble memory. “A great deal of the overall industry, it seemed, consisted of computer companies taking in each other’s wash.”
Names: Itty Bitty Machines, Parasitic Engineering. Centronics, Nortronics, Key Tronic, Tektronix, General Robotics, Northern Telecom, Infoton, Centurion (with a Roman-soldier costume), Colorgraphics, Summagraphics, Altergo, C. Itoh, Ball (“Aren’t they the mason jar people?” “Yeah, but they also make disk drives”), Datum, Data Pro, Data I/O, Tri Data, Epic Data, Facit Data, Control Data, Decision Data, Data General, Data Specialties, Itek, Pertec, Mostek, Wavetek, Intertek, Ramtek.
The reflective core of the chapter. Kidder pulls back to consider the social effects of the computer revolution.

Norbert Wiener (1947) coined cybernetics and warned that “the average human being of mediocre attainments or less” might end up having “nothing to sell.” Some boosters quote him to ridicule the prediction; Wiener actually meant it as a plea for humane control.
Revolution is the wrong word: in the 1970s computers had often “served as a prop to the status quo,” extending executives’ reach as “handy greed-extenders,” not redistributing power.
Daniel Bell argued in The Coming of Post-Industrial Society that 19th-century inventions like the railroad changed individual lives more than computers have. Tom West echoes: “Let’s talk about bulldozers. Bulldozers have had a hell of a lot bigger effect on people’s lives.”
One unnamed reporter’s summary: “Everything is quantified. Whether it’s the technology or the way people use it, it has an insidious ability to reduce things to less than human dimensions.”
Jacques Ellul: technology operates by its own laws, alterable by no human action except complete abandonment of technique. (Kidder thinks this is too pessimistic.)
~40% of commercial computer applications, by one estimate cited, have proved uneconomical: the job costs more after computerization than before. The PR slogan (“we’re not in competition with each other; we’re in competition with labor”) isn’t always true.
Kidder’s own line: computers are used “in ways that are salutary, in ways that are dangerous, banal and cruel, and in ways that seem harmless if a little silly. But what fun making them can be!”

The team’s frame on social use. They mostly profess not to care how computers are used. Alsing: “I don’t even know how much an Eclipse M/600 costs.” But not everyone holds it consistently. Chuck Holland: “I could have worked for a company that makes machines directly for the military, and for more money. But I’m not gonna design anything that directly bombs someone.” Eagle is, by plan, a general-purpose computer — Data General will ship blueprints to an OEM that will “ruggedize” Eagle for the military. “A dissenter could indeed refuse to do work that might end up in the hands of soldiers: that would mean, in effect, not being a computer engineer.”
Jon Blau worries openly. He once asked de Castro at a “cocktails with the Captain” event whether DG did business with apartheid South Africa; de Castro: not at the moment, but “Data General wasn’t necessarily guided by politics.” Blau: “For every bad use of a computer, I can think of a good one.”
The chapter ends on the bus ride home — Honorary Microcoder Award given to Holberger, beer handed back from seat to seat, Alsing standing in the aisle riffing on Times Square massage parlors. The team is “free for a little while on a summer’s night… for the moment unbound from their machine.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 14 — The Last Crunch
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
14 — The Last Crunch
The chapter covers August through early October 1979 — the final crunch through the slowdown, the false starts on Adventure, and Eagle’s transition to a working computer.
The April → May → June → September deadline cascade. West has named a new deadline at each slip; Rasala has drawn a corresponding new debugging schedule. By August, “Our credibility, I think, is running out.” Rasala stops making new promises but believes they have to finish by end of September.
Premature celebrations. The team starts inventing awards at every milestone:

Honorary Microcoder Awards (Microteam-instituted).
PAL Awards (Hardy-Boy reply): a framed citation with an empty PAL chip socket glued to the center.
Under Extraordinary Pressure Awards (Holland): for Neal Firth (“who gave us a computer before the hardware guys did”), Betty Shanahan (“for putting up with a bunch of creepy guys”).
All-Nighter Award: Jim Guyer, citation under the plastic of an insulated coffee cup.
Eagle Awards (Eclipse Appreciation and Gratitude for Lonely Evenings): for the wives. Penny Rasala’s: she “endured many lonely hours… and on many occasions wondered what was the advantage of Ed being boss if he had to work 2 shifts.”

Alsing’s joke: “We congratulated ourselves on finishing Eagle and then we went back and finished it.”
Late summer slump. The Hardy Boys revert to single shifts. Bugs are now harder, less interesting; “this is the grind part.” Rasala spends time with Jon Blau (replacing the departed Rosen on the ALU). Blau is keeping “Alsing hours” (1 PM to whenever) which disrupts shared-machine scheduling. Rasala speaks of Rosen’s loss as a personal failure: “I failed… If only I’d had more time.”
Whetstones. The Whetstone benchmark is a popular measure of floating-point performance. West had hoped Eagle would beat VAX. Early benchmarks on an unfinished prototype show Eagle is no faster than VAX in single precision. Rasala: “It’s discouraging.”
Rasala enters the lab. “But it was time for a change.” Rasala chooses Guyer as his lab partner and works a regular shift. He’s not as fluent in Eagle’s hardware as the others (“the others had come to know it as well as you do the rooms of your childhood home”). Eventually he tries the heat gun on a chip he suspects of overheating — and melts the socket. The team teases him for days at the Cain Ridge Saloon. (“Meltdown!” “We need more fire extinguishers in the lab, Ed!“) Rasala in mock trepidation. The chapter’s emotional inflection: this is where the team’s mood lifts again. “Under his influence, they had returned.”
The carpenters arrive. The long-promised office remodel. Walls come down. “The veneer of equality was gone, and with it perhaps some of what had made the Eclipse Group seem unusual.” The new cubicles are sized by seniority — the pecking order made visible “in steel partitions.” More phrases like “peons” and “someone at my level” appear.
Holberger’s discovery. Holberger finds a paycheck stub from one of the Portsmouth technicians who came down to help debug. The technicians get paid for overtime; engineers do not. The technicians are taking home more than twice what Holberger does. He takes the stub to Rasala; together they burn it so the team won’t see. Holberger laughs: “I don’t work for money.”
The last big push. Saturday Sept 15 onward. Rasala: “We’re gonna work round the clock, Saturday, Sunday. We’re gonna do it all, and bathe in glory, guys.”
A bug appears on Gollum running an interrupt diagnostic at the page boundary. Stymied for a day. Sunday morning Guyer sees it: Coke had two boards of Main Memory, Gollum only one; the diagnostic crossed a memory-block boundary that Gollum’s first board did not contain. “Gollum fell off the end of the world.” They had been thinking in Eclipse’s numbering rather than Eagle’s. They install a second board; the interrupt works. “It’s kinda embarrassing,” says Guyer. West, chewing a toothpick, scowls: Rasala should have known better.
The first attempt at Adventure (Sept 21). Rasala has decreed that no machine ships until it can play Adventure — because the M/600 had a bug that crashed Adventure that wasn’t caught until customers got it. The team gathers around Gallifrey (one of two new prototypes named for the home planet/time machine of Doctor Who, joining Coke and Gollum). Rasala types. Console: FATAL ERROR. Rerun. FATAL ERROR. Adventure does not run that night.
West threatens to take the lab. He calls for Rasala: “I want to go into the lab.” Rasala: “Gimme a few more days.” Sept 25: “As of this morning, Eagle ran Multiprogramming twelve hours overnight without failing.” Holberger, retrospectively: “I know how West felt, but he couldn’t have done a thing.” West himself: “It wasn’t an empty threat. The game, of course, though, is that when I say I’m gonna go in there, they haul ass, because they assume it’s gonna be some kind of trivial, dumb thing.”
Oct 4: Adventure runs on Gallifrey. Holberger is at the controls, plays as a novice (“didn’t even meet the pirate or garner a treasure”), shuts it down. Whetstones run again with a near-fully-functional machine: Eagle is ~10% faster than VAX at single precision, ~2x the fastest Eclipse. West’s commandment satisfied.
Oct 6: a residual flakey. Carl Carman on a routine lab visit picks up the ALU board (sitting on its extender), grasps the edges, shakes it. Gallifrey fails. They have just located the problem. The team replaces all the chip sockets in the center of the ALU; the flakey is gone. Holberger: “Carman did it. He got it to fail by beating it up.”
Oct 8: Gallifrey is rolled on a dolly down the hall to the Software Department.
End-of-chapter mood. Rasala had said in January they would open champagne at this milestone but doesn’t feel like it now. He is more tired than he has ever been. “False rumors were running around to the effect that West was on his way out.” West gets a haircut “short like a soldier’s” and looks plucked. He smiles: “The rumors of my death are greatly exaggerated.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 15 — Canards
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
15 — Canards
The chapter is the book’s interpretive coda — the question of who actually invented Eagle, framed against the labor-and-craft argument that closes the book.
Aftermath. The PAL crisis was real but resolved; Eagle’s announcement was put off until spring 1980. The delay turned out to help: more software, more diagnostics, more refinement. By the time Eagle shipped, “you could switch boards among Eagles without worry.”
A late evil bug. Holberger fixes it by adding a single wire to a circuit, unable to explain why the fix works. “But, truly, the Hardy Boys had arrived at the state in which they could feel what was wrong with their machine.”
Commercial outcome. By early 1981, rumor: orders for Eagles ~10% of all new Data General orders. The product line is rejuvenated; Data General would have missed the supermini market without Eagle (North Carolina’s FHP still hadn’t shipped by spring 1981).
Who invented Eagle?
The chapter polls the team:

De Castro is described variously as “the Captain,” “God,” “the Man in the corner office.” West: “De Castro does this crazy, apparently bungled stuff, but after a while you see this incredible order.” West argues de Castro’s “no mode bit” was a succinct description of the perfect machine. “I think we all have that feeling about de Castro,” another team member says, only partly joking.
A skeptical veteran: “De Castro isn’t that good. He’s lucky and he’s smart, but most importantly, he has people around him like West, who pull his ass out of a fire and then attribute it all to him.”
De Castro himself, interviewed by Kidder: smiles that some members of the team felt neglected, says “that’s frequently the case.” On whether the team’s entrepreneurial feeling was fostered: “I think that if you try to foster that attitude, you will be unsuccessful… we try to provide an environment where those things oughta happen.”

The Cain Ridge Saloon argument. Hardy Boys reminisce. Guyer: “We didn’t get our commitment to this project from de Castro or Carman or West. We got it from within ourselves.” Holberger laughing: “Their idea was piped into our minds!” Guyer: “The company didn’t ask for this machine. We gave it to them. We created that design.” Then Rasala, quietly: “West created that design.” Holberger: “You mean West created the excitement.” Rasala, flat: “No. The machine.” Conversation turns elsewhere.
Ruskin’s Gothic. The chapter’s literary frame. John Ruskin, in The Nature of Gothic, decries the industrial age’s tendency to fragment work into tasks fit only for slave labor. The cathedrals of Europe were built by free labor freely given — “temples to God.” Kidder: “That’s what West and his team of engineers were looking for, I think… They themselves liked to say they didn’t work on their machine for money.” Job-satisfaction studies cited at the time list engineer complaints — declining technical challenge, misutilization, limited freedom of action, tight control of working patterns. “No one who made it through the Eagle project could in fairness have raised such objections.”
Guyer’s articulation: “Look, I don’t have to get official recognition for anything I do. Ninety-eight percent of the thrill comes from knowing that the thing you designed works, and works almost the way you expected it would. If that happens, part of you is in that machine.”
Rosemarie’s verdict: “He set up the opportunity and he didn’t stand in anyone’s way… I would do it again. I would be very grateful to do it again. I think I would take a cut in pay to do it again.”
Kidder’s thesis. “But to at least some engineers, at the outset, Eagle appeared to be a fairly uninteresting computer to build. Yet more than two dozen people worked on it overtime, without any real hope of material rewards, for a year and a half; and afterward most of them felt glad. That happened largely because West and the other managers gave them enough freedom to invent, while at the same time guiding them toward success.”
West’s role recharacterized. He helped transform a dispute into “a virtual War of the Roses.” He created “brushfires” and got the staff charged up about putting them out. He welcomed a journalist (Kidder) — “how it did delight him when one of the so-called kids remarked to me, ‘What we’re doing must be important, if there’s a writer covering it.‘”
Alsing on the secret of West’s grip: “West took a bag on the side of the Eclipse and made it the most exciting project in the company, the most exciting thing in our lives for a year and a half. West never bored us.”
Kidder on West himself. The Eagle let him reconcile two opposite ambitions: “He was back in Cambridge, as it were, singing folk songs, while at the same time putting money on Data General’s bottom line. He could be, for a little while, a balladeer of computers.”
Inventory of artifacts produced: 4,096 lines of microcode (~8 inches thick), thousands of lines of diagnostic code, 200,000+ lines of system software, several hundred pages of flow charts, ~240 pages of schematics, hundreds of debugging ECOs, 20 hours of marketing videotape, two functioning prototypes plus orders for many more. “All this, at last, was no canard.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: 16 — Dinosaurs
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
16 — Dinosaurs
The closing chapter is about West’s exit from the Eclipse Group and the team’s dispersal. The frame: the Eclipse Group as a wild-West gunslinger crew that the town can no longer accommodate after the cleanup is done.
Hidden labor surfaces. After the announcement, Jon Blau finds in the documentation an unfamiliar cable name. Holberger tells him: “That looks like a Tom West special.” Blau realizes for the first time how many other groups had been brought in to design and fabricate small but critical pieces — and that “It had to have been West” who anticipated and arranged each. He couldn’t have done it himself: “you’d need intimate knowledge not only of the CPU but also of the company’s entire product line.” West had “secretive as a mother cat about the location of her kittens” masked most of his activities, including his worrying.
West’s wear. He realizes after his sailboat diesel breaks down off Cape Cod (he eventually gets it running, but says afterward “I had never worked on a diesel engine before, and I was kinda pissed. I didn’t think I could do it”) that he is tired of playing the hero with mechanical things. He keeps losing weight. He starts taking his oldest daughter on Sunday-evening bike rides, reasserting a tradition his father had with him. He says: “That’s the bear trap, the greatest vice. Your job. You can justify just about any behavior with it. Maybe that’s why you do it, so you don’t have to deal with all those other problems.”
Holberger’s gunslinger analogy (a year later, in a barroom): “A town hires a gunslinger to clean it up, but when he’s taken care of their problem, he’s still a gunslinger and sooner or later the respectable citizens are going to run him out of town.” Alsing: “Of course! That’s a classic American story.”
The environment around them changes. New executives are hired to fill management gaps, from outside companies; they don’t know the Eclipse Group’s odd unspoken rules. New rules: a property pass for taking home used packing boxes. West stuck in the parking-lot traffic: “I used to be able to park at the front door of this company.”
Rasala: “The real fun — the way you get an Eagle out the door — is to get the guys to invent it… Once we’ve got that, okay, baby, we’re gonna do a hell of a job. And I think that’s what West is fighting for.” Rasala observes the battle “with mounting anxiety and then with resignation.”
End-of-September incident. At a meeting attended by outside bosses, West publicly criticizes Rasala for a small mistake — to disprove the allegation that he never criticizes his own group. Afterward West takes Rasala aside, apologizes, says he is being accused of criticizing only outsiders. Rasala feels West is “growing rather desperate, and it made him sad.”
Early November. West calls the team together: he is leaving for “the upstairs of Westborough” — a marketing job that will take him often to Japan. Rasala, Wallach, and Alsing will run the group. He has lined up new projects. “The fundamentals are right.” Some smile broadly. Many young engineers feel indifference. West loyalists — to them “the earth had moved.”
The clock ceremony. Mid-November West is on a business trip; Rosemarie cleans out his office. The last item: West’s clock in the oak case. A technician wheels it on a cart. Alsing offers to hold it steady. Rasala and Blau join the procession. They go upstairs, get lost, ask “some stranger in a suit” for directions. West’s new office is narrow and windowless, like the old one. They put the clock on the floor. “It’s our three-o’clock Friday meeting,” says Rasala. Going back downstairs Alsing has the feeling he had just attended a funeral.
West’s own withdrawal. “I feel awful withdrawal symptoms. I wake up at three A.M., sweating, worried and so on. It’s a real problem becoming just an everyday Joe.” Then he gets up — “It’s really tempting for me to look back on Eagle and bask in it now. Next question you gotta ask yourself — is that a trap? Ahhhhhhhhnd, the answer is: Yeah, probably.” Books about the Orient stacked on his coffee table. He’s going to teach engineers at the Japanese minicomputer firm Data General partly acquired how to build DG computers. “Japan! The Orient! Man, I could really get into building machines in Japan!”
The team disperses.

Josh Rosen joins another computer company; defines architecture for another 32-bit machine; eight-hour days, five-day weeks; “happy at last.”
Dave Peck quits, learns he is entitled at age 65 to a $53/month pension.
Steve Wallach gives the talk he had once feared, presenting Eagle’s architecture to a society of computer professionals; they applaud — “the ultimate reward.” Then leaves the Eclipse Group, then leaves Data General.
Carl Alsing resigns from Data General, takes a higher-paying job in California — “That wasn’t why I left.” Alsing and Wallach both felt unappreciated; Alsing in the project’s aftermath had “most of his former responsibilities taken away.” “I feel that I am free to go.”
Carl Carman (VP of engineering) leaves the company.
Ed Rasala leaves Data General last among the senior managers, joins Alsing in California.

Data General’s downturn. Disappointing financial reports begin to arrive. Stock plunges, rises, falls again. Business Week blames de Castro’s management style. The product line had grown stale; without Eagle “Data General’s present troubles would have looked far worse than they did.” Many vice presidents leave during this period.
Eclipse Group disbanded in fall 1980. Pinball turned out to be partly a lie — the team was broken up, not allowed to play another game together. Some old hands mourned, others said it was inevitable.
Bitterness wasn’t general or enduring. Many got promotions, business cards, “a few free trips, and, though they were a very long time in coming, stock options.” Many got to work on the successor projects West had concocted before leaving.
West’s final reflection: “Yeah, it’s all blown apart, but the ethic’s still in place. In some sense spreading that around may be beneficial.” And: “It was a summer romance. But that’s all right. Summer romances are some of the best things that ever happen.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: Epilogue
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Epilogue
A short coda. Before the team formally disbanded, the Eclipse Group met to determine which engineers had contributed to Eagle’s patentable features. The meetings were painful: bickering, harsh words, even a question raised about whether Alsing’s name (or West’s) should appear on any patents. Ironically the meetings illustrated that Eagle was a true collective effort — they themselves couldn’t agree on credit. “The team was losing its glue. ‘It has no function anymore. It’s like an afterbirth,’ said one old hand.”
Days after the last patent meeting, North Carolina’s leader sent telegrams of congratulations to Wallach, Alsing, Rasala, and West. “That was a classy gesture, all agreed.” The next day Eagle finally went out the company’s door.
April 29, 1980. The Roosevelt Hotel, New York City. Eagle is announced “to the world.” 128 terminals hooked to one Eagle (the boards from Gollum). The machine crashes during the demo; engineers fix it so deftly only they notice. About a dozen team members attend in new suits. Marketing has rechristened the machine the Eclipse MV/8000. Reporters are surprisingly numerous; the next day the announcement is in the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times financial pages.
The presenters from Marketing had nothing to do with making it. Alsing: “After Marketing gets through, you go home and say to yourself, ‘Wow! Did I do that?‘” People who had not been around when Eagle was conceived are described in the press release as having had responsibility for it.
The engineers stick together at the formal lunch like young men at a dance, a small confusion at their table about whether to take the salad on the left or the right.
West attends but doesn’t sit with the team. He talks easily and pleasantly with members during the day. He wears a brown conservatively tailored suit. At the door, asked his title, he says: “‘Business Development.‘” A reporter at the cocktail party: “You seem to know something about this machine. What did you have to do with it?” West mumbles, waves his hand, changes the subject. Alsing overhears, takes the reporter aside: “That guy was the leader of the whole thing.”
Walking to Penn Station with Kidder afterward, West’s mood lifts. “It’s just a computer. It’s really a small thing in the world, you know,” Kidder says. West smiles softly: “I know it.” None of it had come out the way he imagined, but it was over and he was glad.
The next day in New York, the regional sales manager addresses the DG sales force on the new product. “What motivates people?” he asks. “Ego and the money to buy things that they and their families want.”
Closing line: “It was a different game now. Clearly, the machine no longer belonged to its makers.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.title: Tracy Kidder The Soul Of A New Machine — Chapter Deep Dives
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/tracy-.content:
Tracy Kidder The Soul Of A New Machine — Chapter Deep Dives
20 chapters

Ch.1 — Front matter (copyright, contents, acclaim)
Three pages of EPUB front matter (copyright, table of contents, acclaim quotes).
Ch.2 — Prologue — A Good Man in a Storm
Kidder opens not in a basement lab but on a 35-foot sloop in a north-easterly gale en route from Portland, Maine, to New York.
Ch.3 — 1 — How to Make a Lot of Money
Data General Corporation, headquartered in Westborough, Massachusetts (Building 14A/B, “Webo”), is by 1979 the third-largest minicomputer maker after DEC, with $507.5M revenue and ~70,700 cumulative computers shipped since founding in 1968…
Ch.4 — 2 — The Wars
The chapter introduces Tom West as Eclipse Group leader and traces the internal politics that produced the “Eagle” project.
Ch.5 — 3 — Building a Team
The chapter is a tour of the Westborough basement and an account of how the Eagle team was hired.
Ch.6 — 4 — Wallach’s Golden Moment
A character study of Steve Wallach, the Eagle architect, and a chapter on the architectural design itself.
Ch.7 — 5 — Midnight Programmer
A character study of Carl Alsing (microcode lieutenant) and a layered explanation of how a computer actually computes — high-level language → assembly → microcode → gates and electrons.
Ch.8 — 6 — Flying Upside Down
The chapter formalizes “the rules” of the Eagle game and walks through the design phase (summer 1978 to early 1979).
Ch.9 — 7 — La Machine
Debugging begins (early 1979) with two prototype Eagles named Coke and Gollum (originally Coke and Pepsi; Holberger demanded Gollum after Tolkien).
Ch.10 — 8 — The Wonderful Micromachines
A study of the Microteam at work, organized around two figures (sublieutenant Chuck Holland and prodigy programmer Neal Firth) and two tools (UINST and the simulator).
Ch.11 — 9 — A Workshop
A character study of West outside the office, organized around his 1780 farmhouse and basement workshop.
Ch.12 — 10 — The Case of the Missing NAND Gate
The longest and most procedurally detailed chapter — a single multi-day debugging case that crystallizes the team’s craft.
Ch.13 — 11 — Shorter Than a Season
A short chapter on burnout, illustrated through Hardy Boy Josh Rosen — one of the team’s most credentialed engineers (designed the ALU board; “I was the star at Special Systems,” Rosen says of his prior post inside Data General).
Ch.14 — 12 — Pinball
The chapter introduces the book’s most-quoted concept — pinball — and lays out the team’s complaints about resources, recognition, and West’s distance.
Ch.15 — 13 — Going to the Fair
The team rides a chartered bus to the National Computer Conference (NCC) in New York City — an interlude that puts the Eagle project in a wider industry context.
Ch.16 — 14 — The Last Crunch
The chapter covers August through early October 1979 — the final crunch through the slowdown, the false starts on Adventure, and Eagle’s transition to a working computer.
Ch.17 — 15 — Canards
The chapter is the book’s interpretive coda — the question of who actually invented Eagle, framed against the labor-and-craft argument that closes the book.
Ch.18 — 16 — Dinosaurs
The closing chapter is about West’s exit from the Eclipse Group and the team’s dispersal.
Ch.19 — Epilogue
Before the team formally disbanded, the Eclipse Group met to determine which engineers had contributed to Eagle’s patentable features.
