06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Introduction
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Introduction
Spine

A 2013 Buddhist-temple-keeper named Hatsumi told Morimoto that there was a “nuclear ghost” (houshanō obake) in Minamisōma, the city ten-to-thirty-four km north of TEPCO Fukushima Dai-ichi (1F), and the rest of the book is a sustained, post-hoc reading of what she meant.
The author chose to call the disaster the “TEPCO accident” rather than “the Fukushima nuclear disaster” so the agent (Tokyo Electric, generating power for the capital) is named and Fukushima itself is decentered as the scene of harm.
Morimoto came to fieldwork in July 2013 with a Geiger counter, expecting to find a population in denial in the radiation-centered narrative familiar from Hiroshima/Nagasaki/Chornobyl/Hanford. He was wrong: residents resisted the biological-citizenship mode (Petryna 2013) and refused to weaponize their irradiated bodies against state and TEPCO.
The book’s central conceptual move is to suspend the “radiation-centered” narrative in favor of an ethnography of atomic livelihoods — how people kept living, dying, farming, praying, and burying ancestors in coastal Fukushima despite chronic low-dose contamination.
The methodological vocabulary borrows from the Buddhist concept of en (縁), an indirect cause / hidden condition for interconnection, and treats ethnography as following invisible threads of chance encounter rather than searching for “the victim” (higaisha) or “the exposed” (hibakusha).
Morimoto names the dominant epistemic regime he resists as half-life politics — a technosensory politics that foregrounds the presence/absence of radiation in environment and its potential biological harm above all else (quality of life, cultural continuity, intergenerational succession, biodiversity).
He frames residents’ postfallout livelihoods as “atomic” in two senses: (i) objectively, they live in a more contaminated environment, and (ii) sociologically, the accident has individualized, isolated, alienated them from each other (following Ui Jun [1971] 2006 on environmental disaster as discrimination).
The book’s ethics rule: residents do not need outsiders to translate them into a “suffering slot” (Robbins 2013); damage-centered research (Tuck 2009) is harmful; the analytical question is not what the ghost is but what its message is.

Key claims

Most TEPCO accident debris released ~one-tenth of Chornobyl’s 5,300 PBq (Onda et al. 2020); Minamisōma residents’ average exposure was ~0.1–0.2 mSv internal and <2 mSv external (Tsubokura et al. 2015) — medically negligible.
The primary postfallout health damages were secondary (diabetes, cardiovascular issues, obesity, mental health, suicides, alcoholism), not radiation-driven cancers — except a debated thyroid-cancer cluster.
Gray zone (借用ed from Kishō Kurokawa 1977’s The Culture of Gray) names the perspectival, contextual, in-between condition of postfallout Minamisōma where binarisms (safe/unsafe, contaminated/clean, victim/non-victim) fail to fit residents’ experience.
Three audiences are implicit: anti-nuclear activists who want Fukushima to remain dangerous; pro-nuclear normalizers who want the accident behind them; and residents who want neither.
Throughout, Morimoto borrows epigraphs and analytical phrases from Haruki Murakami to mark the gray-zone, surreal, ineffable register of postfallout experience.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

“Once the ghost reveals itself to you or is revealed through others’ determination, there’s no turning back” — Hatsumi’s warning, the book’s epistemological hinge (Intro).
Hatsumi’s anger at the foreign film director who wanted local residents visibly furious for the camera — Morimoto’s first lesson in extractive disaster-ethnography failure (Intro).

Cross-link hooks

Half-Life Politics → atomic concept (Morimoto coinage)
Atomic Livelihood → atomic concept
Gray Zone (Kurokawa) → conceptual borrow worth tracking
Damage-Centered Research (Tuck 2009) — analytical anti-pattern Morimoto refuses

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Naming the Nuclear Ghosts
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Chapter 1 — Naming the Nuclear Ghosts
Spine

Two competing “nuclear ghost” concepts are in circulation: Masahiro Ono’s (Imperial College immunologist, 2015 Yahoo! Japan News essays) and Hatsumi’s.
Ono’s nuclear ghost is radiophobia — irrational fear of low-dose radiation that “paralyzes democracy” and prevents productive social-contract negotiation. His prescription: name the ghost to dispel it; science can’t be the sole authority but it should remain the rational baseline. Morimoto reads this as a sophisticated version of half-life politics.
Hatsumi’s nuclear ghost is the demoralizing effect of the radiation-centered discourse itself — it renders contamination hypervisible while leaving residents’ lives in monochrome gray. Naming it does not dispel it; living through it is the only response.
Morimoto travels Route 6 (Rokkoku) — the coastal highway running north-south through Minamisōma — as a methodological device. Walking across it marked him to locals (Sachiko) as an outsider; locals drive, never walk. This becomes the book’s recurring “drive through Minamisōma” structure.
Geographic-administrative breakdown: the city consolidated three former municipalities (Kashima town, Haramachi city, Odaka town) in 2006; the 2011 evacuation orders fell roughly along those old-municipality lines (Kashima ~30 km, Haramachi ~20 km, Odaka <20 km). The Merger Policy was contested and the district-level identities are stronger than the city-level identity.

Key claims

Tōhoku as “deep north” — Michinoku, Isabella Bird’s Unbeaten Tracks in Japan (1880) — has a long pre-3.11 cultural history of being the periphery to be civilized; the TEPCO accident layered radiological peripheralization onto this older marginality.
Minamisōma was the only municipality in coastal Fukushima that fell under all three evacuation zones (20 km / 30 km / specially designated areas) AND had territory outside the 30 km zone (most of Kashima district), AND did not enforce total evacuation (Mayor Sakurai’s decision).
~57,600 people lived in Minamisōma at start of 2022; >6,600 back in former evacuation zone <20 km from 1F. >37% of residents were >65 years old; ~50% in former evacuation zone.
The evacuation cut infrastructure (Joban train line, Route 6) and produced a “two Minamisōma” perception: the contaminated space on outside maps vs. the place where people lived despite contamination.
Denial of coevalness (Fabian 1983) frames the methodological problem: outsiders treat the residents as “the Other” stuck in the past disaster, requiring a translator (researcher); Morimoto refuses that role.
Hatsumi’s instruction “you will know what I mean when you learn about Minamisōma” reframes nuclear-ghost knowledge as situated, place-based, requiring participant observation rather than theoretical mastery.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

“We are not in a contaminated community, but a divided community!” — an Odaka evacuee living in Kashima kasetsu unit, the line that gives the chapter its analytical thrust. (ch. 1)
“Walls cannot stop particles from traveling to Kashima” — Kashima resident’s bitter joke about the state’s evacuation-zone borders. (ch. 1)

Cross-link hooks

Sacrifice Zone Chronotope — peripheralization of Tōhoku → Hamadōri → Minamisōma → Odaka traces the temporal-spatial nesting
Public Anthropology Method — Morimoto’s refusal of “urgent ethnography” (Slater 2013) and damage-centered research
Denial of Coevalness (Fabian) — analytical concept Morimoto deploys

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Spirited Away
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Chapter 2 — Spirited Away
Spine

The chapter follows Naoko, a woman in her late 70s in 2013, an Odaka evacuee living in kariage (state-leased) housing in Kashima with her grandson Toru, son Tengo, and Tengo’s wife.
Naoko’s family compound is c. 25 km north of 1F; her predisaster life was farming, miso-making, attending the family Buddhist altar and grave on the property.
Morimoto met Naoko through the same German film director who had introduced Hatsumi; the en (chance encounter) thread is explicit.
Naoko’s interpretive struggle: she sees evacuees in kasetsu (state-built temporary housing) as having “become greedy” — accepting too many giveaways, gambling away compensation at pachinko parlors. She refuses to participate. This is not a moral judgment but a defense of her dignity (songen) against the secondary-victimization of disaster aid.
Tengo’s choice to refuse compensation initially is a parallel move — he commutes 2+ hours to the same company (relocated to Miyagi to escape “Fukushima” address) to maintain identity as a worker rather than a compensated victim.

Key claims

Distance signaling: Naoko’s family is in kariage housing rather than kasetsu; kariage gave more privacy and less public visibility but locked them out of giveaways/community supports that flowed only to kasetsu. Legal confidentiality of kariage addresses made kariage evacuees invisible to relief organizations.
Generational tension over radiation tolerance: Naoko, near 80, decides she’s too old to worry about low-dose radiation risk. Toru, in his early 20s, has decades of latency to absorb the same dose. The household cannot reach a single answer; Naoko stays silent (“purse my lips tight, remain silent, wait for the state’s decision in my favor”).
The ghost-town inversion: Eiji Oguma (2013) wrote “nobody dies in a ghost town”; Morimoto met “many people who wanted to die nowhere else but in this ghost town” — the desire to die at home is the central counter-argument to the evacuation-as-protection logic.
Naoko’s small garden plot in front of her kariage (built 2015 with extra-potash soil to reduce cesium uptake) is the chapter’s emblem: simultaneously an act of returning agency, a concession that displacement will continue, and a learned-from-other-farmers technical workaround.
The state communicated only the technical 1 mSv/y target (ICRP 2007 recommendation) and offered no plain-language guidance about what livability meant — leaving each household to negotiate the radiological judgment privately, eroding collective deliberation.
The chapter’s title (Wakamatsu’s poem epigraph) names the disappearance: many residents described long-term evacuation as feeling “spirited away” — physically, socially, and from one’s own future.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

Naoko: “I would have felt so much better if we were told early on that we would not be able to go back. Then we could have thought about our future more realistically.” (ch. 2) The harm of false hope under state-managed delay.
Tengo: “I work and I can live without any compensation.” His refusal of compensation as identity preservation against the public imagination of Odaka residents as compensation-dependent. (ch. 2)

Cross-link hooks

Atomic Livelihood (Gray Zone) — Naoko’s kariage garden is the cleanest microcosm
Sacrifice Zone Chronotope — Odaka as inaccessible-from-Kashima despite 15 km separation

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Kaleidoscopic Harm
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Chapter 3 — Kaleidoscopic Harm
Spine

The chapter catalogs the “stupid lines” drawn on the evacuation maps — the chronology by which the state shifted boundaries between March 11 and 2012, and the residents’ bitter epistemic conclusion that physical distance from 1F (not contamination level) was the operative variable.
Hatsumi (Haramachi resident) discovers in 2012 that her old Kashima friend has cut contact: Hatsumi gets compensation; Kashima residents do not. The compensation policy has dissolved an old friendship.
An anecdote: a Kashima resident’s house was relocated out of the 30 km zone after the state moved the accident center from the outer plant boundary to the four-reactor centroid (between units 2 and 3). He lost ~11 months of psychological-damage compensation — an arbitrary cartographic adjustment with hard economic consequences.
The chapter introduces fūhyō higai (rumor-related harm) — economic loss from consumer/trader avoidance of Fukushima foodstuffs, formally compensable under the 2011 Dispute Reconciliation Committee guidelines as “actual harm” if the consumer concern is “reasonable from the perspective of an average ordinary person.”
The 1954 Lucky Dragon Incident (US H-bomb test contaminating tuna in Japanese fishing market) is the legal-historical origin of the fūhyō concept — the 1956 kansetsu songai (indirect damage) doctrine.

Key claims

The Japanese state set food-radiation limits (100 Bq/kg cesium combined for general foodstuffs from April 2012) ~10× stricter than the international Codex Alimentarius (1,000 Bq/kg) and US (1,200 Bq/kg). In 2013 Fukushima Prefecture tested 11,006,534 bags of rice; 28 (0.0003%) failed.
Anzen vs anshin: the technoscientific safety standard (anzen) does not equate to the consumers’ subjective sense of safety (anshin). Sternsdorff-Cisterna (2015): “safety is more than laboratory tests; safety is also a social relationship.”
Local vernacular of contamination — takai (high), hikui (low), koi (thick) — carried affective weight (mushrooms felt “thicker” than rice) that becquerels and sieverts could not capture. Residents translated science back into experience.
Saeki: feeling disposable to the state was more dreadful than fear of radiation. “Kimin” (abandoned people, Wakamatsu) names the political condition of the not-quite-victim.
The “rumour” framework reframes consumer-producer relations: pre-data avoidance was “rational” (no information); post-data avoidance is “irrational” (rumour-based). Miura argues this conflict serves only the state and TEPCO by displacing accountability from them to the consumer-producer dyad.
Erikson (1991, 1994) on radiological emergencies as “plotless” — they violate the rules of plot, the all-clear never sounds. The chapter’s closing reframes “kaleidoscopic harm” not as a snapshot but as a process whose harm typology shifts over time.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

A Kashima resident: “I am harmed not only by the accident but also by those idiots who think drawing stupid lines on the map means nothing.” (ch. 3) The political-cartography critique in vernacular form.
Miura (Shinchi rice farmer, 2015 book title): Fukushima Rice Is Safe but I Am Fine If You Do Not Want to Eat It. The producer’s solidarity with consumer fear, against the scientific-paternalist wedge.

Cross-link hooks

Half-Life Politics — the cartographic-administrative variant of half-life politics
Sacrifice Zone Chronotope — zone-redrawing as bureaucratic violence
Anzen vs Anshin (Sternsdorff-Cisterna) — secondary concept worth tracking

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: The Compensation Game
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Chapter 4 — The Compensation Game
Spine

A “second-person ethnography” — the chapter addresses the reader as “imagine you are a resident of Minamisōma” and walks through the decision-tree of compensation eligibility, residence choice, and silence/voice.
Hiroshi Kainuma’s analytical frame — postfallout Fukushima as katarinikui (hard to tell) and ikinikui (hard to live) — names the dual epistemic-existential strain.
The compensation guideline numerics: psychological-harm compensation (hinanseikatsu touni yoru seishinteki songai baishō) was 100,000 yen/person/month; for a Haramachi 4-person evacuee family, the total was ~33.6 million yen ($250K) over 84 months. This created visible economic disparities across district lines.
Galtung-Farmer “structural violence” is named explicitly as the analytical frame for the felt harm: residents could neither consent nor refuse to the situation; “everything was already decided” (the stupid lines), and they were left only the choice to be quiet or leave (and to where?).
The reopening logic is reverse-engineered: each removal of an evacuation line means (a) the area meets the negotiated-down dose target (initially 1 mSv/y aspirational, then 20 mSv/y operational from Nov 2013), and (b) compensation will end ~1 year later. Reopening is therefore both progress and termination of the support pipeline.

Key claims

The state’s April 2011 primary guidelines on the “scope of nuclear damage” never define “the victim” — they define those qualified for compensation. Victimhood is administratively constructed, not biographically tracked.
Reopening produced conflict among residents and within households: those committed to return wanted reopening; those who’d given up and started new lives wanted continued compensation. Decisions split families.
The November 2013 state declaration that the ICRP 1 mSv/y standard was “aspirational” rather than the reopening criterion — replaced operationally by 20 mSv/y — is the explicit policy moment when half-life politics shifted from health-protection to reopening-feasibility.
The compensation policy operationalizes residents’ multiple statuses: “natural disaster victim → nuclear accident victim → exposed person (hibakusha) → experimental subject (hikensha)” — the chapter argues these are sequential roles assigned, not biographically self-chosen.
The “compensation economy” produces an inverse incentive: the longer evacuation lasts, the more compensation flows; the earlier the reopening, the faster the cutoff. This structurally pits some residents (who want to die at home) against others (who want continued support).
Saeki’s silence rule: in Minamisōma, “the smart thing to do is to be quiet and keep things to yourself” — voicing concern about radiation invites accusation of being stuck in the past or envious of compensation; voicing acceptance invites accusation of indifference to suffering. Either utterance loses.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

“It is called the ‘Fukushima nuclear disaster.’ With the name, no one takes any accountability for the fallout aside from us who have to live with the name.” — Tengo (also returns in ch. 9). The naming-as-displacement-of-blame argument.
Beck (1987): in a contradiction between survival and danger-perception, “everyday and political rigidifications and fanaticizations proliferate” — both the deniers and the catastrophists are a postfallout pathology, not a position.

Cross-link hooks

Half-Life Politics — the compensation-economy variant
Atomic Livelihood — what survives the compensation game
Structural Violence (Galtung 1969 / Farmer 1996) — analytical concept Morimoto uses

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Radioactive Mosquitos and the Science of Half-Lives
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Chapter 5 — Radioactive Mosquitos and the Science of Half-Lives
Spine

The chapter centers on Dr. Masaharu Tsubokura (hematologist, then U. Tokyo, later Fukushima University) — who arrived in Minamisōma April 2011, set up the first Whole Body Counter (WBC) internal-exposure monitoring at the city hospital in July 2011, and ran the radio program I, Tsubokura, Will Answer Your Concerns on Hibari FM (2012–2013).
Episode 6 (summer 2012): a listener asks whether mosquitos breeding in radiation-concentrated puddles transfer cesium intravenously when they bite. Tsubokura nervously laughs but answers — and Morimoto reads the question as the listener’s attempt to translate science back into mundane experience.
The chapter contrasts Tsubokura’s locally-grounded, lifestyle-oriented risk communication with Columbia Mailman School’s 2019 RSO training Morimoto attended, which presented Fukushima as a “failure of risk communication” — radiophobia, “all we need to know is ALARA.”
The Columbia instructors quote David Ropeik’s March 21, 2011 Scientific American blog: “the peril is not just the radiation. It’s people’s fears of radiation. Whether those fears are consistent with the evidence of the actual physical risk (they aren’t) doesn’t matter.” Morimoto reads this as the canonical ghostbusting position Tsubokura’s work refused.
ALARA’s Reference Man (an “average white male”) is the standard subject of dose calculation; Cram (2015) is the genealogy. Morimoto cites this to show how the universal subject of radiation safety encodes a specific-bodied default.

Key claims

Tsubokura’s WBC data on Minamisōma residents (≥10,000 measurements by 2012) showed average internal exposure of 0.1–0.2 mSv and external <2 mSv — medically negligible. The data supported residents’ continued residence, but also was instrumentalized by anti-Tsubokura readers as “pro-TEPCO” or “promoting the safety myth (anzen shinwa).”
Every risk communication risks hurting someone: Tsubokura’s booklet for mothers who stayed implicitly labeled mothers who left as irrational. The booklet’s collaborators (local women’s group, the Veteran Mothers’ Society, 2014) negotiated language carefully to avoid the ghostbusting tone.
The thyroid-cancer debate: ~287 cases among Fukushima youth as of June 2022. Medical community frames as screening bias (better detection, earlier than Chornobyl latency); residents experience as accident-caused. The case exemplifies how scientific reasoning can invalidate subjective experience under disaster.
Sae Ochi’s frame: residents talk about “life instead of science” — the radiological-protection experts cannot deliver “life communication.” Risk communication should be done not by physicians but by social workers, counselors, community leaders.
The lessons learned by Tsubokura — consistency of data and stance, taking responsibility for changing facts — are explicitly presented as critique of the inconsistent state and expert positions (shifting “permissible” thresholds; deferring assessment to individual residents).
Beck’s individualization of risk is reread by Morimoto: in postfallout Fukushima, what is individualized is not the risk itself but its perception — the state and experts atomize the residents into solitary judgers of the same external phenomenon.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

Hatsumi: “It is unfortunate that Japan has come to offer, yet again, the data for hibaku. It is the capital of radiation exposure research.” — the Hiroshima-Nagasaki-Fukushima continuity as enrollment-as-experimental-body. (ch. 5)
Tsubokura’s later reflection: “Many people inside and outside often accuse me of being a pronuclear doctor working for TEPCO… as a scientist, what I tell people based on the data is this: there is almost no significant radiological risk from the accident for people around the evacuation zones.” (ch. 5, paraphrased)

Cross-link hooks

Half-Life Politics — Morimoto’s named framework receives full theoretical treatment here
Public Anthropology Method — Tsubokura’s locally-grounded, dialogic style as exemplar
ALARA / Reference Man — universal-subject critique

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Between Fūhyō and Fūka
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Chapter 6 — Between Fūhyō and Fūka
Spine

The chapter contrasts two “winds”: fūhyō (rumor → reputational harm via outsiders’ over-attention) and fūka (weathering → forgetting via outsiders’ under-attention). Coastal Fukushima residents must navigate between both.
Morimoto recounts a May 2015 visit to Fukushima Dai-ichi (1F) — TEPCO had loosened its visitor policy by end of 2014 to signal stabilization. The chapter uses the tour as a method to expose how 1F became a site of public anthropology against TEPCO’s prior closed-door policy.
The chapter traces TEPCO’s first nuclear plant plan from the 1950s and the postwar decision to bring 1F to the depopulating Hamadōri region as economic revitalization. The 1955 origin (TEPCO’s nuclear-research department founded that year, the same year as Hiroshima’s 10th anniversary) is the historical hinge.
The chapter introduces trust in symbiosis and mutual prosperity (kyōzon kyōei) as the local-political vocabulary of the original 1F siting deal; the accident broke that frame and the postfallout reconstruction is still searching for its successor.
The ephemera-of-loss middle section traces small material-cultural losses (Futaba town museum’s evacuated rooms; a TEPCO history book; a memorial tablet for cows) that radiation-centered narratives never index.

Key claims

The state and TEPCO’s public-relations strategy oscillated between two failure modes: in 2011–2013, opacity that residents read as deceit; from 2014, “openness” (1F tours, Fukushima Innovation Coast Framework) that residents read as normalization-by-tourism.
Surviving Ground Zero: the chapter documents specific evacuated towns (Futaba, Ōkuma) that hosted 1F; their political-economic dependence on TEPCO before 3.11 is structurally different from Minamisōma’s relationship to TEPCO (“Minamisōma has never depended directly on the nuclear power plant; what we have received from TEPCO is nothing but lopsided harm” — Mayor Sakurai, returns from intro).
Postwar nuclear-Japan history is asymmetric: the bombs (1945) were the perpetrating West; the plants (1955–) were the “peaceful atom” of Japanese national-revitalization. The Hamadōri siting recapitulates the colonial geography of central-Japan-vs-periphery (Akasaka 2014).
The chapter uses fūka (weathering) to name the forgetting work — that the rest of Japan and the world will simply move on, while residents remain. The 11th anniversary in 2022 was less covered than the 10th in 2021.
The 1F tour exposed the contradiction between containment progress and ongoing contamination: contaminated water continues to be released; spent fuel removal continues; the decommissioning is projected to take 30–40 more years (TEPCO’s 2022 estimate).
The chapter argues postfallout reconstruction must contend with a double obligation: to the dead (memorialization, intergenerational transmission) and to the as-yet-unexposed (preventing future siting). The “trust in symbiosis” frame served only the first generation of plant workers.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

A Minamisōma resident: “Fukushima Prefecture lost 1,614 people from the tsunami; Minamisōma alone lost 636. The TEPCO accident made the searching for missing family more traumatic for those who had to give up.” — the layered loss the radiation-centered narrative obscures. (ch. 1, returns in ch. 6)

Cross-link hooks

Sacrifice Zone Chronotope — the 1955→1971→2011→2065 timescale of the Hamadōri sacrifice
Half-Life Politics — applied to memorialization and forgetting
Public Anthropology Method — the 1F-as-tour-site as ethnographic terrain

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Frecon Baggu and the Archive of (Half-)Lives
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Chapter 7 — Frecon Baggu and the Archive of (Half-)Lives
Spine

Frecon baggu are 1-ton flexible polyethylene “flexible-container” bags that the state-led decontamination project filled with topsoil, leaves, twigs, sludge, and personal items removed from properties. From early 2015 onward, hundreds of thousands of them accumulated in Minamisōma.
The chapter follows Saeki’s parents’ inspection day in central Odaka, early 2015 — pink ribbons mark items to keep, yellow ribbons mark items to remove. Saeki acts as proxy for her parents (who evacuated outside Fukushima) and bargains item-by-item over the phone.
The state’s 2011 Act on Special Measures defines “waste” as “refuse, bulky refuse, burnt residue, sludge, excreta, waste oil, waste acid, waste alkali, carcasses, and other filthy and unnecessary matter” — without specifying who decides what is filthy and unnecessary. The vagueness is the chapter’s analytical hinge.
The decontamination paradigm’s logic: all material objects in a contaminated zone are equally contaminated and subject to removal (Beck 1999’s egalitarianism of modern risks, applied to objects). Residents’ personal-memory weight is invisible to the technoscientific frame.
The Ministry of the Environment’s goal: 1 mSv/y or 0.23 μSv/h within a locale is the operational target — but Saeki’s parents’ property already met it before decontamination. Saeki’s question: what’s decontamination for?

Key claims

Decontamination as ritual: Saeki’s interpretation — “getting your place decontaminated is kind of like a ritual… makes the place look more habitable.” The radiation-reduction framing covers what is, in practice, a return-readiness ritual that lowers anxiety more than dose.
By March 2017 the state had decontaminated 61 km² in Minamisōma alone, including 4,500 households, 17 km² of farmland, 13 km² of forests, 2.7 km² of road — producing 965,000 m³ of decontaminated waste in 22 temporary storage sites. Total national decontamination + interim-storage budget exceeded $40 billion.
Reverse tillage (hanten kou) — flipping topsoil and burying it in lower layers rather than removing — was a state concession to farmers’ attachment to soil. It reduces waste-generation and shields radiation while preserving the farmer-soil tie.
The chapter introduces “white space” (hakuchi) — bureaucratic jargon for areas excluded from the reconstruction plan. Decontamination signals the state thinks an area has use-value; white space is the un-cared-for.
Naoko’s losses are layered: family land → soil (cesium-bound topsoil bagged) → persimmon tree → house (demolished as “decontamination” 2016) → calendar from March 2011 left hanging in evacuated bedroom → kimono from her wedding 60 years prior. The chapter’s lesson: decontamination is not just remediation but biographical erasure.
The “temporary temporary storage” (kari kari okiba) is local bitter humor naming the indefinite deferral of the waste’s final disposition; the state has promised to move all decontaminated waste out of Fukushima by 2045 (30 years after first bags arrived) but has no host-prefecture agreement.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

Naoko, holding her wedding kimono from 60 years ago: “It was the first and last good kimono I got from my parents.” She refolds it and returns it to the dresser. The book’s clearest single moment of the noncontaminable-personal-archive against half-life politics. (ch. 7)
Naoko: “When I see my soil removed and stuffed in those bags, I feel like my history has been stolen from me.” Soil as intergenerational patrimony, not just substrate. (ch. 7)
Naoko: “Those bags are not going to kill me, but believing that those bags could kill me at my temporary house would.” The radiological-vs-existential calculus (ch. 8 in original, ranged into the frecon baggu arc).

Cross-link hooks

Atomic Livelihood — the everyday-archive that survives decontamination
Half-Life Politics — the decontamination variant
Sacrifice Zone Chronotope — the 2045 promise as nesting deferral

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: In Search of the Invisible
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Chapter 8 — In Search of the Invisible
Spine

Opens with summer 2018, Naoko’s warehouse: an ossified animal bone of unidentified origin (rabbit? civet?) inside the locked building, traces of struggle. Naoko sweeps the remains and prays at the family altar. Radiation is not the only invisible thing in Minamisōma.
The chapter centers on Nishiyama, chief priest at Hiwashi Shrine in Odaka — c. 650 years old, on a hill 30m above sea level, enshrining a war god (and gods of fertility, sericulture). The 2011 tsunami stopped less than 2 km inland, near Hiwashi.
Nishiyama’s analysis: ancestors emplaced shrines on high ground because they understood tsunami reach; the shrine’s tall trees, however, also concentrated atmospheric cesium. The same architecture is tsunami-resilient and radiation-vulnerable.
Hatsumi’s offhand remark in early 2016: “I have not seen any snakes since 3.11.” This becomes a thread that returns in ch. 9 (Hinton’s snakes-as-radiotracers research).
The chapter visits Namie, the radioactive ghost town about 10 km southeast of Hiwashi: ~21,000 evacuated; >440 evacuation-related deaths since 2011; ~80% of town in highly contaminated exclusion zone as of 2021. The eastern Tsushima region had >200 μSv/h zones; March 13, 2011 readings >1,200 μSv/h were not communicated to residents who had evacuated into Tsushima from areas closer to 1F.

Key claims

The chapter’s shrine-vs-temple division: Buddhism handles endings (funerals, the deceased), Shintoism handles beginnings (planting, building, blessings). Hatsumi’s temple was overwhelmed by muen botoke (unidentified tsunami remains, ~570 cremains housed there); Nishiyama’s shrine prepared to bless the returning households.
Helen Hardacre’s frame: Japanese religiosity is “closely linked to the family and to tradition, emphasizing the things that people do, rather than their strict adherence to a set of doctrines.” Naoko prays for the unknown dead animal not from doctrinal obligation but from the local ethics of en with all beings.
Namie as “late industrialism” (Kim Fortun 2012): both the infrastructure and the paradigm that produced it are exhausted; nuclear technology, in its meltdown rather than its operation, achieved its propaganda goal of “going green” — by purging humans from the built environment.
The “radioactive persimmon hunt”: Morimoto picks a kg of persimmons from a Namie tree where a wild boar was eating; the test result shows ~1,600 Bq/kg cesium combined (16× the 100 Bq/kg standard). Tengo discourages Naoko from eating her Odaka persimmons.
Persimmon migration history: 18th-century Tenmei Famine reduced Sōma domain population from ~89,000 to ~32,000; Hokuriku migrants (Toyama / Kanazawa, brought by Shin Buddhist temples, 1,800+ households by 1845, ~3,000 by 1871) carried persimmon sticks (kept moist in daikon radish) on the 500-km hike. Persimmons are not just fruit; they are the plant-historical archive of migration, discrimination, and reconstruction.
The chapter argues for a multi-invisible ontology: ghosts, gods, en, ancestors, supernatural beings, and radiation are all invisible. Privileging only radiation as “the invisible to be made visible” enacts a Western/biomedical hierarchy that ignores how local cosmology already handled invisibility.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

Nishiyama: “Science is great unless we foolishly come to believe nature is controllable. Science that does not pay any respect to the power of nature is a human disaster (jinsai).” (ch. 8)
Nishiyama: “Either TEPCO or not, disaster recovery requires people, who have gone missing in this region. The divine spirits would not discriminate against anyone who would pay proper respect.” — the priest’s pragmatic recruitment of TEPCO volunteers to clean Hiwashi grounds (2014). (ch. 8)
Hatsumi: “Nature is powerful and scary. Because we are always inferior to nature, we must pretend as if we own it. Because we pretend it so much, we forget that we cannot own nature.” — Namie as the antidote to anthropocentrism. (ch. 8)

Cross-link hooks

Atomic Livelihood — the supernatural-spiritual layer of livelihood
Sacrifice Zone Chronotope — the 18th-c. famine → migration → 1955 plant → 2011 fallout sequence
Multispecies Ethnography — pivotal for ch. 9

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: A Wild Boar Chase
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Chapter 9 — A Wild Boar Chase
Spine

“Contrary to what outsiders fixate on about Fukushima, the practical obstacle of living here is the wildlife, not radiation” — Tengo, returning to Odaka 2019. The chapter is the multispecies-ecology argument.
Boar populations in Minamisōma jumped from 39 captured (2011) to 1,300 (2014) to >1,700 (2016). Across Fukushima Prefecture, captured boars: ~3,000 (2011) to ~20,000 (2017). Agricultural damage rose from 500K to 1M.
April 2016, Sōma city built a $1.6M wildlife incinerator (Miyamoto company, also makes human crematoriums) to handle culled boars at 800°C, 120 kg/load, with HEPA-bagged ash separated from household waste. Minamisōma followed in April 2019.
TEPCO 2018 “decontamination-support initiative” includes drones with ultrasonic emitters (4–50 kHz) by EAMS Robotics to chase boars away from evacuation-zone properties. Morimoto, invited as a “boar expert” to TEPCO’s Tomioka headquarters, asks: “where are the chased boars going?” — the room goes silent.
Thomas Hinton (radioecologist, Fukushima University) studies boars and snakes as radiotracers — his collared boars wear GPS + dosimeter; his snakes (after Hatsumi’s earlier “no snakes since 3.11” remark) become a localized indicator due to their soil-bound habitat and carnivory. Hinton’s 2021 Cunningham et al. paper concludes wildlife shows “resilience to chronic LD-LDR exposures.”

Key claims

Wild boars as surrogate body: Tengo’s “drunken theory” — boars are eerier than monkeys because humans used to eat boars; they share the local food chain and can transfer radioisotopes intravenously to humans via consumption. The state-imposed November 2011 ban on boar-meat consumption broke this en and turned boars from food into vermin (yūgai chōjyū).
Decontamination produces nuclear waste: incinerated boar ash measured >135,000 Bq/kg in Minamisōma (2021) — 1,350× the 100 Bq/kg food-safety standard. By killing boars to keep humans safe, the state-resident-hunter chain produces new concentrated radiological waste from organisms that were merely consuming the contaminated environment.
The TEPCO drone chase fails the ecological-systems test: boars chased from Namie or Tomioka relocate northward and become Sōma’s, Minamisōma’s, or Date’s problem. Local-municipal containment cannot solve a regional-ecological process. The half-life politics’ anthropocentric frame breaks at the ecosystem boundary.
Yowai tsunagari (weak connections, Hiroki Azuma 2014) is Morimoto’s methodological resource — the unsystematic, surreal, en-based connections (boar-persimmon-Naoko-Hatsumi-snake-Tengo-Hinton) that ethnography surfaces against the strong-connection narrative (Fukushima = contamination).
Hinton’s critique (2004 article): “the fact that humans are among the most sensitive mammals, and therefore the most sensitive species, has led, in part, to the dogma that if we protect humans, then other biota are protected as well.” Anthropocentrism is built into ICRP radiation-safety standards.
Tengo’s framing argument: “It is called the ‘Fukushima nuclear disaster.’ With the name, no one takes any accountability for the fallout aside from us who have to live with the name” — TEPCO operated 1F since the 1970s to supply Tokyo exclusively (Akasaka & Oguma 2012; Iwamoto 1994). The TEPCO accident is radioactive colonialism (Brugge et al. 2006 on Navajo uranium parallel). The chapter ends framing the nuclear ghost as the message of this colonial geography.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

Gotanda (Sōma boar-cremator, retired fisherman, ~60s): “The fact that they are contaminated, captured, killed, and burnt like this with no mercy now is not their fault but the fault of us humans.” The clearest articulation of anthropogenic guilt in the book. (ch. 9)
Tengo: “Radioactive materials are everywhere, and we are always already contaminated regardless of what we sacrifice or destroy to try distancing ourselves from them.” (ch. 9)
Naoko: the TEPCO accident was “an ultimate denier of my livelihood.” (ch. 9)

Cross-link hooks

Atomic Livelihood — extended to multispecies frame
Sacrifice Zone Chronotope — radioactive colonialism explicitly named
Public Anthropology Method — the Fukushima-University-radioecology vs TEPCO-drone-engineering vs ethnographer-of-en triangulation

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Epilogue — The Age of Decommissioning
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Epilogue — The Age of Decommissioning (Hairo no Jidai)
Spine

Hairo no jidai — “the age of decommissioning” — names the projected 30-to-40-year horizon (TEPCO’s 2022 estimate) for cleaning up 1F. The epilogue treats this temporal horizon as the actual political-temporal frame for thinking about Fukushima, replacing the spectacular event-frame.
The Fukushima Robot Test Field (RTF) in Minamisōma + Namie — partially opened 2018, fully opened March 2020 — is the state’s “Society 5.0” / Innovation Coast Framework bet on robotics for disaster response, decommissioning, and elder care. Saeki: “Maybe the future is we elders become cyborgs ourselves to join the cleanup.”
March 16, 2022 (5 days after 11th anniversary): magnitude 7.4 + 6.1 earthquakes off Fukushima coast, 20cm tsunami warning, weeks-long power/water loss in Kashima district. Saeki: “I am not sure how the broken TEPCO reactors could still stand!”
109 earthquakes >M5.0 since 3.11 (as of 2022). Each tests structural fatigue at 1F.
Russian invasion of Ukraine (2022) + climate-change pressure repositions nuclear power as “cleaner” energy — the same rationale that brought 1F to Hamadōri in the 1970s. The selective forgetting is the epilogue’s political-historical pivot.

Key claims

Stopping nuclear-energy production does not eliminate decommissioning labor: failed structures must be cleaned up; bodies will be exposed; land will be sacrificed for waste storage. Nuclear power is a “social technology that produces and reproduces a community of the exposable.”
The 2021 Ministry of Environment survey of 4,200 citizens: >45% of non-Fukushima residents believe in adverse intergenerational hereditary consequences of the TEPCO accident, vs. ~27% of Fukushima residents. Despite improving science, the trust gap is widening — half-life politics has not delivered the promised reassurance.
The age-of-decommissioning ethic Morimoto offers: remember and not be complicit; accept that the accident’s effects will remain spatially-temporally dislocated and shapeshifting; refuse to externalize the problem (“not somebody else’s problem… our collective problem”).
Saikan and the future past (epilogue’s closing section): the residents who chose to live and die at home are the seed-planters of the better future — not despite their contamination but with it.
The 2022 Minamisōma population (~57,600) lives “against the odds and despite the hypervisualized risk of exposure.” Morimoto’s choice of “against the odds” rather than “in denial” or “in danger” is a final taxonomic move against half-life politics.
284 newborns in 2021 vs 579 in 2010 — the demographic stake. The age-of-decommissioning will be carried on aging shoulders with replacement-rate-collapsed succession.

Standout passages (paraphrased)

Hatsumi (epigraph): “Think about it. Isn’t it weird that we met? There must be some supernatural cause, don’t you think?” — the en-based explanation of the encounter that produced the book. (epilogue)
“It [the TEPCO accident] requires a cycle of people and land to be exposed to protect others. Nuclear power is a social technology that produces and reproduces a community of the exposable.” (epilogue)

Cross-link hooks

Atomic Livelihood — closing reaffirmation
Sacrifice Zone Chronotope — explicit 2065-projection
Public Anthropology Method — the political ethic Morimoto builds toward

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: ch_07_preface-1934
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Preface to the First Edition (1934)
Spine

Working scientists begin from an organised structure of accepted theory and a generally-accepted problem situation; philosophers begin from “a heap of ruins” without a shared problem situation.
Despite the disorder, genuine philosophical problems about things (not words) exist; rejecting the problem-situation pessimism is the precondition of doing philosophy.
The book is offered as a fresh start that does not accept any of the “existing creeds” of philosophical method.

Compressed prose
The 1934 Preface is short and rhetorical. Popper opens by quoting Schlick’s 1930 worry that philosophy may never reach a genuine problem, then opposes it with Kant’s countering 1786 conviction that long-running philosophical disputes are about things, not mere words. Popper’s own position is the Kantian one: philosophical problems are real, philosophy can pose them, and the appearance of philosophical chaos reflects the absence of a shared problem situation rather than the absence of problems. The preface ends with an Acton quotation tying the philosophy of science to the historical-and-logical study of how error is detected. Vienna, autumn 1934.
Why this preface matters for the book
The preface frames the polemical stance Popper takes throughout: linguistic-philosophy and Vienna-Circle positivism both deny the existence of substantive philosophical problems; Popper insists that the demarcation problem and the induction problem are substantive, not pseudo-problems. The preface is two pages but signals the entire methodological orientation.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: ch_08_preface-1959
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Preface to the First English Edition (1959)
Spine

Targets linguistic-analysis philosophy of the 1950s (the “two main schools”: the language-of-science model-builders and the ordinary-language analysts).
Thesis 1: there is no method peculiar to philosophy. Philosophers may use any method consistent with rational discussion.
Thesis 2: the central problem of epistemology has always been the growth of knowledge, best studied as the growth of scientific knowledge.
The “one method of all rational discussion” is stating a problem clearly and trying to overthrow proposed solutions. Popper italicises rational discussion and critically to underline the equation of the rational and the critical attitude.
All three approaches Popper distinguishes (ordinary-language, language-of-science model-construction, analysis of scientific knowledge) miss the growth of knowledge problem unless they take the third route — but even the third route should not become a specialism that loses sight of “the riddle of the world”.

Compressed prose
Written in spring 1958 from Penn, Buckinghamshire, the 1959 Preface is Popper’s update of his 1934 stance to engage the language-analysis dominance of post-war Anglophone philosophy. Linguistic analysts hold that there are no genuine philosophical problems or that those problems are problems of word-usage; Popper insists that there is at least one (the cosmological problem of understanding the world including ourselves), and that this problem dwarfs the methodological-cleanliness obsessions of the language analysts.
He divides language analysts into two groups: those who construct artificial model languages of science (whose constructions, Popper notes, lack means to express identity, arithmetic, or measurable properties; they are “essentially poorer than ordinary languages”), and those who analyse ordinary language. Both miss the growth of knowledge problem, which is the pre-eminent problem of epistemology from Plato to Russell.
Popper then introduces a third group — those who analyse scientific problems, theories, and procedures as their philosophical method, taking historical episodes (Newton, Maxwell, Einstein) as material. This group, Popper argues, is doing the right kind of philosophy of science: rather than constructing miniature model languages, it analyses the discussions through which actual scientific theories were accepted or rejected, “as if through a microscope”.
He warns against treating philosophy of science as a specialism for its own sake. The riddle of the world and of man’s knowledge of that world are what justify both science and philosophy; specialised methodology that loses sight of these riddles risks becoming “an obscurantist faith in the expert’s special skill”. The Preface concludes with a defence of rational philosophy against the post-rationalist mood Popper sees in mid-century Anglophone academic culture.
Why this preface matters for the book
The 1959 Preface is the pedagogical introduction to the Logic. Where the 1934 Preface is rhetorical, the 1959 Preface is doctrinal: it states the two theses (no philosophical method, growth-of-knowledge as central problem) that organise the entire book; it establishes the explicit equation of rationality with critical attitude; and it explains why Popper takes the Logic to belong to the third (scientific-discussion-analysing) tradition rather than to either branch of language analysis. Read the 1959 Preface together with sec. 11 (methodological rules as conventions) and sec. 85 (the path of science) for a near-complete summary of Popper’s position.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: ch_09_part-i
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Part I — Introduction to the Logic of Science (chs. 1-2, sec. 1-11)
Spine
Two short chapters that state the entire programme. Chapter 1 frames the problem (induction is invalid; demarcation is unsolved by the verifiability criterion; falsifiability is proposed); chapter 2 frames the methodology (rules of the game of empirical science as conventions designed to keep falsifiability operative).
Chapter 1: A Survey of Some Fundamental Problems (sec. 1-8)

Sec. 1, The Problem of Induction. Inductive logic cannot be the logic of empirical science. Hume showed inductive arguments are not deductively valid. Reichenbach’s reply (a synthetic principle of induction assigns probabilities to scientific theories) only reproduces the original problem at a level lower (any synthetic principle either generates an infinite regress or is dogmatically a priori).
Sec. 2, Elimination of Psychologism. The act of conceiving a hypothesis is psychological and outside the scope of the logic of knowledge. Popper sharply separates quid juris (justification, which the logic of discovery treats) from quid facti (the empirical psychology of having ideas, which it does not). Einstein cited approvingly: “There is no logical path leading to these laws.”
Sec. 3, Deductive Testing of Theories. The four channels of testing: internal consistency check, logical-form check, comparison with other theories, empirical test of derived predictions. The empirical test deduces singular predictions from the hypothesis; if one is observed false, the hypothesis is refuted (modus tollens). A verified prediction does not establish the hypothesis as true or as probable; it only fails to falsify it.
Sec. 4, The Problem of Demarcation. The objection: rejecting induction removes the boundary between empirical science and metaphysics. Popper’s reply: yes, and that is why a new criterion of demarcation is needed. The Vienna-Circle verifiability criterion conflates demarcation with meaning; consistently applied, it would expel scientific laws (which are also non-verifiable) along with metaphysics. Popper presents his criterion as a convention to be evaluated on fertility, not as a discovered fact.
Sec. 5, Experience as a Method. Empirical science is distinguished from logically-similar systems not by logical form alone but by the deductive method of testing. “Experience” on this view is a method, not a body of data.
Sec. 6, Falsifiability as a Criterion of Demarcation. The signature thesis: falsifiability replaces verifiability. Universal statements are not derivable from singular ones but can be contradicted by them; therefore the asymmetry between verification and falsification follows from the logical form of universal statements. A scientific system is one that can be refuted by experience. Popper’s parenthetical disclaimer (footnote *3, p. 18): “Falsifiability separates two kinds of perfectly meaningful statements: the falsifiable and the non-falsifiable. It draws a line inside meaningful language, not around it.” A standard objection — falsification can always be evaded by ad hoc auxiliary hypotheses — is acknowledged and answered methodologically (the empirical method, by convention, prohibits these moves).
Sec. 7, The Problem of the ‘Empirical Basis’. If theories are tested by deducing singular statements that observation may refute, what makes the singular basic statements themselves empirical? Popper introduces the term “basic statement” (replacing “protocol sentence”) and signals the discussion in sec. 25-30.
Sec. 8, Scientific Objectivity and Subjective Conviction. Objectivity = inter-subjective testability. Popper aligns with Kant’s quid juris sense of objectivity (a justification is objective if anyone can examine it) and rejects subjective-conviction-as-justification. Repeatability and reproducibility of experimental effects are the operational form of inter-subjective testability (“occult effects” — irreproducible — fall outside science by methodological rule).

Chapter 2: On the Problem of a Theory of Scientific Method (sec. 9-11)

Sec. 9, Why Methodological Decisions are Indispensable. The positivist treats methodology as either logic or empirical psychology of scientists; Popper rejects both. Methodological decisions are constitutive of empirical science: without rules that prohibit dogmatic defence of theories, “no conclusive disproof of a theory can ever be produced” (because one can always reject the experimental data or invoke auxiliary hypotheses).
Sec. 10, The Naturalistic Approach to the Theory of Method. Methodology is not an empirical science (a study of how scientists actually behave). What counts as “science” or as “scientist” is itself a matter of convention.
Sec. 11, Methodological Rules as Conventions. Rules of method are “the rules of the game of empirical science”. Two examples: (1) the game is in principle without end — anyone who declares his theory finally verified retires from the game; (2) a hypothesis that has proved its mettle may not be dropped without “good reason” (such as replacement by a better-testable theory or falsification of one of its consequences). The supreme rule: “the other rules of scientific procedure must be designed in such a way that they do not protect any statement in science against falsification” (p. 32, paraphrased). The methodological apparatus thus exists to keep the falsifiability criterion operative against conventionalist-evasion attacks.

Why Part I matters for the book
Part I is the high-leverage portion of the book — sixty pages that state the entire programme. Sections 1, 4, and 6 of Chapter 1 are the irreducible core (induction-is-invalid, demarcation-needs-a-new-criterion, falsifiability-is-the-criterion). Section 11 of Chapter 2 supplies the methodological apparatus (rules-of-the-game, the supreme rule against conventionalist evasion) that prevents the falsifiability criterion from being trivialised by ad hoc rescues. A reader with time only for sixty pages of Popper should read these.
Open questions raised in Part I

The empirical basis problem (sec. 7) — what makes a basic statement empirical? — is acknowledged but deferred to sec. 25-30.
The conventionalist objection (sec. 4 and sec. 6) — falsification can always be evaded — is answered by methodological prohibition (sec. 11) but the prohibition is a desideratum not a procedure. This is the Duhem-Quine gap that Lakatos’s research-programmes framework later tries to fill.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: ch_10_part-ii
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Part II — Some Structural Components of a Theory of Experience (chs. 3-10, sec. 12-85)
Spine
Eight chapters of formal-and-applied apparatus that operationalises the Part I programme. Chapters 3-7 build the formal layer (theories, falsifiability, basic statements, degrees of testability, simplicity); chapters 8-9 handle probability and quantum theory; chapter 10 closes the book with corroboration and “The Path of Science”. Popper’s case is not made by his rhetoric — it is made here.
Chapter 3, Theories (sec. 12-18)
Causal explanation = deducing a singular statement from a universal law plus initial conditions (the thread-and-weight example, sec. 12, p. 38). Popper avoids “the principle of causality” because it is unfalsifiable (sec. 12, p. 39). Strict universality (an “all-statement” about any place and time) is distinguished from numerical universality (a statement equivalent to a finite conjunction of singular statements; sec. 13). Universal vs. individual concepts (sec. 14); strictly universal vs. existential statements (sec. 15); theoretical systems as deductive closures (sec. 16); axiom-system interpretation (sec. 17); levels of universality and modus tollens (sec. 18).
Chapter 4, Falsifiability (sec. 19-24)
The conventionalist objection (Poincaré, Duhem) — a theory can always be rescued — is the central foil (sec. 19). Popper’s reply is methodological: the empirical method, as a convention, prohibits these rescues (sec. 20). The logical investigation of falsifiability (sec. 21) defines falsifiability as a property of a system of theory plus initial conditions: a system is falsifiable iff it forbids some logically possible singular statement. Falsifiability (a logical property of a statement) is sharply distinguished from falsification (a methodological act of refutation; sec. 22). Occurrences vs. events as the building blocks of falsifying basic statements (sec. 23). The internal consistency of the falsifiability criterion (sec. 24).
Chapter 5, The Problem of the Empirical Basis (sec. 25-30)
The Vienna Circle’s protocol sentences (Carnap, Neurath) treated as foundational singular statements. Popper rejects (sec. 25-27): perceptual experiences cannot logically justify statements; only statements can justify statements. Basic statements (sec. 28) are accepted by convention under the inter-subjective-testability rule. Fries’ trilemma (dogma vs. infinite regress vs. psychologism) is dissolved by accepting that tests do not bottom out in certainty but in conventionally-accepted singular statements that could in principle be tested further (sec. 29). Theory and experiment are mutually entangled — observation is theory-laden (sec. 30).
Chapter 6, Degrees of Testability (sec. 31-40)
The book’s most technical body chapter, and the source of the formal layer that distinguishes Popper from a generalised methodological-virtue advocate. Sec. 31-32: the programme — make falsifiability comparable. Sec. 33-34: the subclass relation between potential-falsifier classes — theory A is more falsifiable than theory B iff A’s class of forbidden statements properly includes B’s. Sec. 35: empirical content = the class of forbidden statements. Sec. 36: levels of universality (a strictly more general theory is more falsifiable) and degrees of precision (a more precise theory is more falsifiable). Sec. 37-40: logical ranges, dimension of a theory, set-of-curves dimension reduction. The complement of empirical content is logical probability — so high empirical content means low logical probability. The inductivist’s preference for “probable” theories is therefore inverted: the less probable a theory is, the more it says about the world.
Chapter 7, Simplicity (sec. 41-46)
Simplicity is reduced to degree of falsifiability. A “simpler” theory is one that forbids more, has higher empirical content, has lower logical probability. The aesthetic and pragmatic notions of simplicity (sec. 41) are rejected as conflating the empirical-content meaning with subjective preferences. Geometrical shape and functional form (sec. 44), the simplicity of Euclidean geometry (sec. 45), and conventionalism’s appeal to simplicity as an aesthetic preference (sec. 46) are addressed.
Chapter 8, Probability (sec. 47-72)
The longest chapter. Subjective vs. objective interpretations (sec. 48). The fundamental problem of the theory of chance (sec. 49) — how to ground probability statements in the world. Von Mises’ frequency theory (sec. 50). Popper’s own axiomatisation building on relative frequency in finite classes (sec. 52-56). Bernoulli’s theorem (sec. 60-63). The decidability of probability statements (sec. 65). The theory of range (sec. 72) generalising frequency. Mostly essential only for philosophy-of-probability specialists, but the technical machinery feeds directly into sec. 80 (probability of hypotheses) and into the new appendices *iv-*v on the formal calculus of probability.
Chapter 9, Some Observations on Quantum Theory (sec. 73-78)
Heisenberg’s programme (sec. 73). The statistical interpretation of quantum theory (sec. 74). Popper’s statistical re-interpretation of the uncertainty formulae (sec. 75) — the uncertainty relations are scatter relations about ensembles, not in-principle limits to single-system measurement. An attempt to eliminate metaphysical elements by inverting Heisenberg’s programme (sec. 76). Decisive experiments — experiments designed to choose between competing theories — proposed (sec. 77). Indeterminist metaphysics distinguished from indeterminist physics (sec. 78).
Chapter 10, Corroboration, or How a Theory Stands up to Tests (sec. 79-85)
The destination chapter. Sec. 79 (“Concerning the So-Called Verification of Hypotheses”) rejects the verification idea: theories are not made true by past predictive successes; they are made corroborated (provisionally trusted in proportion to severity-of-tests-passed). Sec. 80 is the technical core: probability-of-hypotheses is shown not to be reducible to probability-of-events (Reichenbach’s truth-frequency proposal fails; the construction either gives universal laws probability zero or makes their probability insensitive to falsification). Sec. 81 extends the criticism to inductive logic generally. Sec. 82 (“The Positive Theory of Corroboration”) builds the alternative: a theory’s degree of corroboration is a non-probabilistic report of severity-of-tests-passed, updated over time. Sec. 83 connects corroborability, testability, and logical probability — high corroborability requires high empirical content requires low logical probability. Sec. 84 distinguishes “true” from “corroborated”. Sec. 85 (“The Path of Science”) closes the book: science is quasi-inductive (it ascends from theories of lower universality to theories of higher universality, each new layer containing the corroborated portion of the old as a limiting case); science does not converge on truth and never claims to. “We do not know: we can only guess” (p. 278). The 1972 Addendum at the end of sec. 85 adds verisimilitude (truth-likeness) as the regulative ideal that corroboration tracks but does not measure.
Why Part II matters for the book
Part II contains the formal-technical-applied apparatus that distinguishes Popper from a methodological exhortation. Without it, falsifiability is a slogan; with it, falsifiability is a comparable, formally-defined property linked to empirical content, logical probability, simplicity, and (via sec. 80 and Apps. *vii-*ix) a non-probabilistic alternative to truth-frequency.
The chapters with the highest leverage:

Chapter 4 (sec. 19-24) — the formal investigation of falsifiability and the methodological reply to conventionalism.
Chapter 5 (sec. 25-30) — basic statements as conventions; the protocol-sentence dispute resolved.
Chapter 6 (sec. 31-40) — the comparison machinery (subclass relation, empirical content, dimension).
Chapter 10 (sec. 79-85) — corroboration and the path of science.

A reader with time for one chapter of Part II should read Chapter 10. With time for two, add Chapter 6. With time for three, add Chapter 4. Chapters 8 and 9 are essential only for philosophy-of-probability and quantum-foundations specialists.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: ch_19_app-i-induction-demarcation
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
New Appendix *i — Two Notes on Induction and Demarcation, 1933-1934
Spine
Two short pre-publication pieces that contain the cleanest statement of Popper’s programme.

The 1933 letter to Erkenntnis (originally Annalen der Philosophie 11, no. 4-6, pp. 426 f.), written before Logik der Forschung (which was cut from a much longer manuscript) appeared.
A 1934 contribution to a discussion of Reichenbach’s paper at a Prague philosophical conference (published in Erkenntnis 5, 1935, p. 170 ff.).

Compressed prose
The 1933 letter, “A criterion of the empirical character of theoretical systems”
Popper introduces the letter to correct a Vienna-Circle misreading: he is not proposing falsifiability as a criterion of meaning. He is proposing it as a criterion of demarcation — the line between empirical-scientific systems and metaphysical systems, both of which are meaningful.
(1) Preliminary Question: Hume’s problem of induction. Schlick (under Wittgenstein’s influence) tried to resolve it by saying natural laws are not statements but “rules for the transformation of statements”. Popper objects that this only verbal-dissolves the problem and shares an unfounded assumption with apriorism and conventionalism: that all genuine statements must be both verifiable and falsifiable. Drop that assumption and natural laws can be treated as unilaterally falsifiable genuine statements.
(2) Main Problem: Demarcation. Wittgenstein’s solution (every meaningful proposition is a truth-function of atomic propositions reducible to singular observation statements) annihilates not only metaphysics but science along with it (since natural laws are no more reducible to observation statements than metaphysics is). Popper’s alternative: adopt one-sided/asymmetrical/unilateral decidability (i.e., falsifiability) as the criterion of demarcation. Meaningful statements split into the falsifiable (empirical-scientific) and the non-falsifiable (metaphysics, mathematics, logic). The line is drawn inside meaningful language, not around it.
The letter contains the cleanest formulation of the programme: In so far as a scientific statement speaks about reality, it must be falsifiable; and in so far as it is not falsifiable, it does not speak about reality. Popper notes the formal analogy: non-contradictoriness is to all science what falsifiability is to empirical science — both pick out a proper sub-set of all logically possible statements.
The 1934 Prague discussion of Reichenbach
A theory of induction is superfluous and impossible: any inductive theory either generates an infinite regress or operates with an unfalsifiable a priori principle. Reichenbach’s distinction between a procedure of finding and a procedure of justifying a hypothesis is accepted; the procedure of finding is psychological and outside the logic of science. The procedure of justifying does not require induction — it requires deductive testing. The best we can say of a hypothesis is that it has shown its worth and has been more successful than other hypotheses, never that it is true or probable.
Popper criticises Reichenbach’s attempt to extend frequency-probability to “probability of hypotheses”. Hypotheses cannot be satisfactorily interpreted as sequences of statements; even if they could, the truth-frequency interpretation gives a hypothesis falsified every second result the probability 1/2 instead of 0. An alternative interpretation (a hypothesis as an element in a sequence of hypotheses, with a falsity-frequency) cannot satisfy the basic demand that a falsifying observation should produce a marked decrease in the probability of the hypothesis.
The conclusion: science is not a body of knowledge but “a system of guesses or anticipations which in principle cannot be justified, but with which we work as long as they stand up to tests”.
Why Appendix *i matters for the book
The appendix is the cleanest existing six-page summary of the entire Popper programme, written before the formal apparatus was added. For a reader who has finished the body and wants to re-read the central thesis without the formal machinery, this is the document. For a reader new to Popper, the 1933 letter is a better entry-point than Chapter 1 of the Logic: it states the demarcation-not-meaning point with maximal clarity in two pages.
The appendix also documents that Popper’s central ideas were in place by 1933 — predating most of his published exchanges with the Vienna Circle and pre-empting the misreadings (especially the conflation of falsifiability-of-demarcation with falsifiability-of-meaning) that would dog him through the rest of his career.
