06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Introduction
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Ch. 1 — Introduction
Compression notes
Source: [source extract] (~248 lines, ~6500 words). Compression ratio: ≥10:1.
Headline
The chapter opens with concrete border curiosities (Neche/Gretna on US-Canada line; Point Roberts enclave) to motivate one observation: international borders correspond to discontinuous changes in political authority, even when this imposes inefficiency on the people who live near them. The book asks why citizens of two democracies don’t simply allow themselves to buy government services à la carte from competing governments. The answer offered: because the states that make up the international system function as an economic cartel dividing the market for governance among themselves.
Core moves

The “market for governance” is real: states supply a bundle of services (protection, dispute resolution, infrastructure, education, R&D) and citizens pay taxes for them.
This market has the potential to be competitive — border residents can in principle play neighbouring rulers against each other for tax concessions (the British Raj on the North-West Frontier example: subsidies rather than land tax).
Rulers facing the prospect of competition lose revenue to peripheral elites; they collude to not compete in each other’s markets — that is, they recognise each other’s territorial sovereignty.
The cartel is self-enforcing through repeated interaction: violations of borders trigger destructive future competition, so present-day cooperation is dominant strategy if rulers are sufficiently future-oriented.
Mutual recognition (not institutional efficiency) is what defines a state. Failed states with negligible internal capacity remain formal equals of the most competent because the cartel guarantees market share, just as economic cartels can preserve inefficient producers.
Nationalism is the cartel’s stabiliser: it raises the cost of foreign rule and lowers the cost of own-rule, making borders persistent against shifts in administrative capacity. This brand-loyalty feature distinguishes the state cartel from ordinary economic cartels.

Threats handled in subsequent chapters

Conflict (ch. 5): wars are price-war episodes that eventually return to cooperation.
Entry (ch. 5): existing states deter new state creation (Biafra, Confederacy, Somaliland).
Democracy (ch. 5): redistributive dynamics make even median voters prefer cartel benefits.
International institutions (ch. 6): UN, WTO, OAU coordinate cartel members.
Globalisation (ch. 7): governance market becomes more abstract (trade policy, tax competition); cartel responds with managed trade.
Failed states + new conflict modes (ch. 7): cyber-warfare, economic sanctions, intellectual-property disputes.

Key examples introduced

Point Roberts WA — enclave whose residents must cross the US border twice for services.
Neche ND vs Gretna MB — twin towns demonstrating the discontinuity at the border.
North-West Frontier (British India / Afghan boundary) — competition with Afghan ruler kept Raj from collecting land tax there.
Lightbulb cartel (Phoebus / Osram-GE-AEI-Philips, 1920s) — the canonical economic cartel that divides territories.
Lysine cartel (ADM 1990s) — analogous division of global market among Japanese-Korean-American producers.

Citation anchors

Krasner (1993) — “the clearest storyline of the last thousand years is the extruding out of universal alternatives to the sovereign state” (quoted at intro).
1.6% of land is claimed by more than one state — the empirical anchor for cartel-completeness.
Rodrik (1997, 70) and Stiglitz (2002, 40) — quoted on capital mobility undermining patriotism.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: The Cartel Model
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Ch. 2 — The Cartel Model
Compression notes
Source: [source extract] (~795 lines, ~17000 words). Compression ratio: ≥10:1. This is the formal-model chapter.
The setup (one-dimensional spatial model)

Two rulers A and B at the endpoints of a line segment, citizens distributed along it.
Cost of governance c_A, c_B rises with distance from each ruler’s administrative centre. (Boulding 1962’s “loss of strength gradient” is the precedent.)
Value of governance v is fixed across space — the maximum tax extractable before citizens revolt, exit, or invest in tax avoidance.
Profit per location = v − c(location).
X = furthest point B can profitably govern; Z = furthest point A can profitably govern. Where X < Z, A and B are potential competitors in the interval [X, Z].

The competitive outcome (Bertrand benchmark)

In A’s core (west of X), A extracts the full monopoly price v — B cannot profitably compete.
Symmetric for B’s core (east of Z).
In the contested interval [X, Z], the lower-cost provider serves at the higher-cost provider’s price (standard Bertrand result). Border residents extract concessions equal to the loss-from-competition L_A and L_B.
Joint profit-maximising boundary is Y — the point where c_A = c_B. This is the focal boundary if cooperation can be sustained.

The cooperative outcome (cartel agreement)

Agreement: A doesn’t sell governance east of Y; B doesn’t sell west of Y. Each becomes a local monopolist over their share.
Self-enforcing through trigger strategies: cheating at the border destroys the future stream of cartel rents. Sustainable iff each ruler’s discount factor exceeds L_A/(L_A+L_B) and L_B/(L_A+L_B). So the cartel works when losses-from-competition are roughly symmetric.
North (1981, p. 27) is quoted as antecedent: rivals reduce ruler’s degrees of freedom; the closer the substitutes, the more revenue accrues to constituents.

Generalisations

Two-dimensional terrain doesn’t change the result.
Non-uniform distribution doesn’t change the result.
Non-contiguous territory (Alaska, Nakhchivan, East Pakistan 1947–71) is consistent with cartel logic when cost functions are oddly shaped.
The “terrain” can be cultural/linguistic space, not just geography. Sovereignty over people instead of territory works when labour is scarce relative to land (pre-colonial Africa per Herbst 2014).
Land-based fixed-asset economies favour territorial sovereignty; modern mobile-capital economies push the cartel to extend control over both territory and people (American extraterritorial taxation; visa regimes; tax treaties).

Why citizens accept this

Coercion is in the model only as an alternative interpretation of the cost functions. The “voluntary transaction” framing is mathematically equivalent to a coercive-but-bounded one: 17th-century Spain discovered that beyond a point, increased extraction lowered revenue.
Citizens’ real outside options are: (i) withdraw from formal economy (Scott 2014’s Southeast Asian peasants); (ii) tax avoidance; (iii) revolt — usually requiring an external sponsor (East Pakistan 1971’s Bengalis welcoming Indian invasion).

Three states — independent vs interdependent cooperation

Independent cooperation: A’s relationship with B is unrelated to A’s relationship with C. The state system is a “stitched-together collection of bilateral agreements.”
Interdependent cooperation: A defecting on B affects A’s relationship with C. The state system is a multilateral agreement.
Belgium 1914 illustrates interdependence: Britain entered WWI to honour its 19th-century guarantee of Belgian neutrality, even though Britain had no direct stake in B’s territory. Same logic: Iraq–Kuwait 1991, the Monroe Doctrine.

Where the theory situates

Builds on Lane (1979), Tilly (1985) — states as monopolies of violence; book extends to oligopolies of violence.
Builds on Levi (1989) — revenue-maximising rulers; book asks what happens when several ruler-revenue-maximisers’ interests collide.
Builds on North (1981) — competition between rulers benefits citizens; book asks how rulers avoid this competition.
Builds on Keohane (2005) — farsighted state cooperation; book asks how this cooperation is aimed against citizens.
Closely related but distinct from Alesina and Spolaore (1997): they derive borders from majoritarian voting (which post-dates state formation by centuries); A&L derive them from ruler-ruler bargaining. Their ch. 5 extension assumes joint-revenue maximisation; A&L provide the cartel foundation.
Distinct from Friedman (1977): Friedman gets joint-profit maximisation without the cartel-cooperation mechanism.
Aligned with Barkin (2021), Schultz and Goemans (2014).

Critique of rival theories

Westphalia hypothesis (Ruggie, Philpott, Nexon, Osiander) — “ideas matter” approach; without self-enforcement, the system would unravel as rulers realised material interests in violations. Krasner’s “ideas as legitimating rationales” is closer to A&L’s view.
Realist offense-defense balance (Jervis 1978) — predicts equilibrium when offense fades; but states can still take small portions of neighbours’ territory; doesn’t explain non-military cooperation; can’t explain why 1648–1815 saw 89, 84, and 110 years of war for France/Britain/Spain if peace was the project.
Spruyt’s institutional selection — Darwinian “victory of the sovereign state”; but the same military innovations elsewhere produced larger empires, not territorial states; doesn’t account for ruler-citizen political economy.

Two distinct claims at end of chapter

The territorial state system originated as a cartel (requires historical evidence — taken up in chs. 3–4).
Regardless of origin, the system is conceptually a cartel (requires demonstration that the model illuminates contemporary phenomena — taken up in chs. 5–7).

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: The Cartel Emerges
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Ch. 3 — The Cartel Emerges
Compression notes
Source: [source extract] (~666 lines, ~14500 words). Compression ratio: ≥10:1.
Headline
The cartel originated in early-modern Europe through two conjoined transformations: economic growth (which raised v) and military/administrative innovation (which lowered c). Together these turned previously ungoverned buffer zones into contested zones, generating the impetus for sovereignty agreements. The chapter walks through the Anglo-Scottish, Spanish, French, and Swedish cases as primary evidence.
Pre-cartel Europe

12th-century counts of Holland, dukes of Brittany, dukes of Savoy operated as effectively independent princes despite formal vassalage.
Holy Roman Empire in 1792 had 80 princes, 120 ecclesiastical princes, 66 imperial cities, 2,000 imperial knights — overlapping sovereignties.
Universal claims (papacy, Holy Roman Empire) coexisted with autonomy (Cinque Ports, bishop of Durham appointing his own judges).
Boundaries were “fuzzy” because rulers could not actually project power over distant territory; inflated rhetoric (Austriae est imperare orbi universo) was costless because non-enforceable.

The transformation

Commercial Revolution (15th century onward): banking, accounting, insurance. Maddison’s GDP/capita data: Western Europe grew 38% in years 1–1500, 55% in 1500–1820, 182% in 1820–2000.
Military Revolution (Roberts/Parker): artillery, fortifications, drill, standing armies, bureaucratic organisation. Louis IX’s artillerists (the Bureau brothers) reduced 60 Norman castles in 2 years; what had taken the English 34.
Bureaucratic capacity: standardised forces (Spanish tercios; French compagnies d’ordonnance) supportable far from home. Spain of Philip II maintained armies in Italy, Belgium, Catalonia, North Africa simultaneously.
State revenues: 1600–1780, real French and English revenues grew by factors of 10.5 and 46.3; per capita GDP grew only by factors of 13.8 and 9.2 over a partly-overlapping window.

The model extension (Figs. 4 → 5)

Before: low v, steeply rising c. There is a buffer zone [Z, X] which neither ruler can profitably govern. Universal claims here are costless because non-enforceable.
After: rising v and flatter c curves push X west and Z east. The two rulers’ cost curves now intersect at Y and the contested zone [X, Z] becomes a major area of potential competition. The losses L_A, L_B are now substantial — generating the impetus for the sovereignty agreement.
Practical consequences of the agreement: declining universal claims; rising borders; rising diplomacy.

Decline of universal claims

Holy Roman Empire: princes’ privileges progressively codified (Golden Bull 1356; Peace of Augsburg 1555; Westphalia 1648).
Papacy: Reformation; French Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges; Spanish Patronato Real; 1683 French clergy declaring kings “not subject to any ecclesiastical power” in temporal matters.

Rise of borders

Treaty of the Pyrenees (1659) — early “metes and bounds” treaty.
1779 France–Austrian Netherlands border treaty — ditches and parishes specified.
US–Canadian border demarcated 1818 (Vermont/Quebec) and via Northwest Boundary Survey 1857–61.
Quantitative: Fig. 6 shows treaty mentions of “border” rising noisily across 14th–17th centuries (data: Dumont, de Carlscroon, Picart 1726).
Cartographic technology: Theodolite (named 1571, perfected 1787), plane table (1551), Gunter’s chain (1620).

Rise of diplomacy

Permanent embassies replaced ad-hoc emissaries.
Hierarchical ranking (empires top, republics bottom) gave way to formal equality only late: British rep in Washington became “ambassador” only in 1893; US legations became embassies only in 1966.
Bayer (2006) data: European dyads with diplomatic relations rose from 57% in 1820 to 78% in 1909; equal-rank from 61% to 88%.
Foreign policy separated from domestic policy: France 1626 (with leakage until mid-18th century); England 1782 reorganisation into Home and Foreign offices.
Louis XI (1461) declaration that only the king could send/receive ambassadors — exclusivity defining sovereignty.

The Anglo-Scottish border (the central case study)

Tilly’s example of Tudor state-building. Border was lawless: Percys, Dacres, Nevilles on English side; Douglases, Homes on Scottish; Armstrongs (3,000 men in 1528) raiding both sides.
Three steps to cooperation:

Mutual recognition — Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton 1328 elevated Scotland; Treaty of Perpetual Peace 1502.
Cooperative demarcation — 1552 five-man commission (two each side + French ambassador); Scot’s Dyke earthen mound with terminal stones; agreed maps.
Cooperative enforcement — March Law administered by Wardens; juries with equal numbers from both sides; “law books of the border” periodically synchronised.


Diplomats explicitly understood the project as elite-versus-borderer, not English-versus-Scottish: “the less privy the Borderers be made to the division hereof, the more likely it is that the thing will take place.”
Outcomes: pacification, border-tax exemption ended after union of crowns 1603, customary tenures reinterpreted under English-elsewhere principles to disadvantage tenants.

Other cases

Sweden / Livland: Treaty of Oliva 1660; Cardis 1661; Charles XI’s reduktion of 1672 onward confiscated noble property previously granted by crown. Province went from financial drain to paying 10% of central budget. By contrast, Pomerania reduktion yielded only 66,500 silver dalers vs Livland’s 5.5 million — direct evidence the model predicts: profitability of governing border areas rises after the border is formalised through interstate agreement.
Spain / Catalonia: 17th-century fueros protected Catalan, Aragonese, Valencian autonomy. 1640–52 Catalan revolt allied with French (Louis XIII = Protector of Catalan Republic). After War of the Spanish Succession (1701–15), Catalonia on losing side of French-Spanish alliance; Nueva Planta decrees 1707 abolished fueros; tax burden equalised (Valencia’s tax called explicitly equivalente).
France / Richelieu–Mazarin–Louis XIV: intendents in border provinces especially active. Quantitative evidence (Fig. 7, Mallet 1789 / Bonney 1999): 1600–1695 nominal revenue grew 3.81× in non-border provinces, 6.20× in formerly-border-now-interior provinces, 12.05× in border provinces — and this despite border provinces being pays d’états with formal consent rights, vs interior pays d’élection without them.

From bilateral to system-wide

The Congresses of Westphalia and Vienna are the multilateral inflection points.
Vienna (1814–15): Russia–Poland and Prussia–Saxony adjudication; Pomerania transfer Denmark→Prussia; Guadeloupe Sweden→France with rental compensation; Britain’s monopolies in southern Africa, South Asia, Ceylon; Bourbon restoration in Spain; Austrian relatives placed as governors of Modena and Parma. “If this is not evidence of open collusion in the governance market, then what is?”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: The Cartel Takes Over
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Ch. 4 — The Cartel Takes Over
Compression notes
Source: [source extract] (~267 lines, ~6000 words). Compression ratio: ≥10:1.
Headline
By 1900 the cartel had spread from Europe to the rest of the world, primarily through colonial conquest and (in non-colonised East Asia) coerced treaty-making. The spread is incomplete — there are exceptions where the cartel’s logic doesn’t yet hold: the Afghan-Pakistan Durand Line is a clear case of competitive state-system failure, and many weak African states are stable cartel-recognised entities precisely because no one wants to govern their territory.
Pre-cartel non-Europe

Imperial China: Macartney mission (1793) refused to kowtow; Qianlong replied “tremblingly obey.” Tributary system not equality.
Tokugawa Japan: refused to recognise Chinese suzerainty; Dutch traders confined to Dejima island, made to dance and sing for shogun’s officials.
Mughal India: Jos Gommans 2002, “frontiers were never lines but always zones” — Jahangir = “world-conqueror.”
Africa per Herbst 2014: low population density, frontiers as “zones where more than one polity could actively exercise authority and where the contours of power were confused.”

Modes of cartel imposition

Conquest: Spain, Portugal, England, France in Americas (16th–17th c.); British India after 1757; African scramble of late 19th century. Berlin Conference 1884–85 partitioned Africa among Europeans as pure cartel exercise — “straight lines, reflecting their limited awareness of local geographical and political realities.” Anglo-German Treaty 1885 quoted: “no Companies nor individuals subject to one Power can exercise sovereign rights in a sphere assigned to the other.”
Coerced opening: Treaty of Tientsin (1858) Article 5 required Chinese emperor to nominate a high officer to deal with the British ambassador “on a footing of perfect equality.” Article 3 ended kowtow protocol. China entered cartel via Treaty of Nanking (1842) and Convention of Peking (1860); Japan via Treaty of Kanagawa (1853); Korea via Treaty of Kanghwa (1876).
Voluntary adoption: Thailand and Japan adapted, Japan eventually a great power and participant in NE Asia partition; Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689) saw Qing China accept demarcated border with Russia and free trade.

Imperfect hegemony
The chapter’s two illustrative cases show the limits of cartel imposition:
Durand Line (Pakistan-Afghanistan)

1893 treaty between Sir Mortimer Durand and Afghan Amir Abdur Rahman Khan demarcated Pashtun zones to British India.
Amir signed under duress — British had pre-occupied disputed territories.
1949 King Zahir Shah cancelled all colonial-era treaties; Afghanistan supports “Pashtunistan” claim into 21st century.
Both states compete in Pashtun border region, exactly like the medieval Anglo-Scottish setup. Pakistani state taxes very little there but spends substantially.
North-West Frontier Province (NWFP) data: 1932 expenditure 36 million rupees, revenue 8 million rupees. Central Provinces had 7× the population but cost only 3× as much to administer.
Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA): no taxes; 600 arms factories (2017); free electricity (30% of average household cost elsewhere); maliks subsidised by state; Frontier Crimes Regulation in force until 2018; voting only granted in 1996.
Al-Qaeda and Taliban presence is consequence of state weakness, not cause; Pakistani state has tacitly supported these groups for cross-border influence.

Weak states of Africa

Different mechanism: not competition but non-overlap. Both states’ cost curves are too high relative to v to govern profitably; the boundary is arbitrary.
Examples: northeast CAR — never centrally governed (Lombard 2020); residents lack national IDs; Bangui treats them as “foreigners and dangerous to boot.” Population density ~1/km².
Stability paradox: African borders are more stable than European ones precisely because they cross unprofitable terrain. No state contests them because the prize is small. Mirrors pre-modern Europe.
This explains why African states with little internal capacity nevertheless retain unchanged borders. The cartel guarantees their seat regardless of governance quality.

Implication

The cartel is geographically near-complete (1.6% of land contested) but its functional logic is uneven: in core Europe the model fits cleanly; on the Afghan border two states fail the cooperation; in Africa neither state has reason to bother. These three regimes — full cartel / failed cartel via competition / vacuous cartel via non-overlap — exhaust the empirical landscape.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Challenges to the Cartel
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Ch. 5 — Challenges to the Cartel
Compression notes
Source: [source extract] (~777 lines, ~17000 words). Compression ratio: ≥10:1.
Headline
Three threats — territorial conflict, opportunistic entry by would-be states, and democracy — would naively predict cartel collapse. None has materialised. The chapter explains why each threat is actually compatible with cartel persistence.
1. Territorial disputes

Empirical fact: 67 wars 1651–1950 redistributed territory; territorial disputes are leading conflict predictor.
Threats not just by force but by extortion: Soviet pressure on Romania for Bessarabia (1940); Nazi Sudetenland 1938.

Model extension (Fig. 8): asymmetric cost decline

B’s c_B drops to a new lower curve while A’s c_A is unchanged. Joint-profit-maximising boundary moves west from Y to Y'.
The question: is the historical boundary Y focal, or the new joint-profit-max boundary Y'?
Without verifiable cost-information, B has incentive to bluff. War serves as a credible signalling mechanism: if B is willing to bear war cost W where V' > W > V, that reveals its costs have actually dropped.
After resolution, the cartel re-forms — quickly. Examples: Denmark accepting loss of Malmö-area; Spain accepting loss of Portugal; Mexico accepting loss of Texas/California; Turkey accepting loss of Syria/Iraq; Germany accepting loss of Sudetenland, East Prussia, Silesia.
Carr (1946) status-quo / revisionist distinction is the closest antecedent. Krasner’s (1999) “organised hypocrisy” is the flip side: principles are espoused even though violated.

Atacama Desert illustration

1820s independence: all three (Chile/Peru/Bolivia) claimed the desert; no conflict because economy too weak (v ≈ 0).
1860s: nitrate mining made the region valuable. Chile-Bolivia 1866 attempt at non-territorial joint-tax jurisdiction (the “zone of mutual benefits”) failed; 1874 treaty divided territory but specified low taxes for Chilean miners.
War of the Pacific (Saltpeter War, 1879–82) triggered by Bolivian unilateral 10-cent tax violation.
Outcome: Chile won militarily (superior army and navy), eventually consolidated through Peru cessions 1884 and Bolivia 1903 (with limited coastal access).
Bolivian attempts to renegotiate dismissed unanimously by ICJ in 2018 — cartel’s stability ratified judicially long after.

2. Opportunistic entry

Existing cartel members deter new states by withholding recognition, even where the entrant has full institutional features.
Examples of failure: Confederacy (1861–65); Biafra (recognised by 5 small states only, none major); Katanga (UN intervention removed); Tamil Eelam, PKK Kurdistan, Chechen rebels labelled terrorist organisations and denied resource access.
Examples of success: Bangladesh, South Sudan, Eritrea, East Timor — each had specific great-power sponsorship.
Russia in 1860s sent fleet to protect Union ports despite vast ideological/geographical differences — fearing Confederate recognition would set Polish secession precedent.

Model extension (Fig. 9): entry deterrence as collective action

Aspiring entrant C between A and B. Entry would impose losses K_A and K_B. Total deterrence cost d.
If d > K_A + K_B: both unwilling to fund deterrence; C enters.
If d < K_A (or d < K_B): one state alone funds deterrence.
If K_A < d < K_A + K_B: collective-action problem. Multiple equilibria (some deter, some don’t). International institutions (UN, OAU) help coordinate.

Three illustrative cases

Rif State (Morocco, 1921–26): Abd el-Krim defeated Spanish at Annual (1921; 13,000 Spanish dead). Republic of the Rif issued currency, organised army, ran schools. Britain refused recognition; France entered with ¼ million troops and poison gas to restore Spanish rule, paying nearly 1 billion francs and 8,000 dead — preferring the cartel-recognised but inefficient Spanish presence over a more capable but unrecognised Rif state.
Somaliland: contemporary case. Has currency, army, regular elections, low piracy, beel clan-consultation governance, tax collection. Recognised by no UN member. Reason: many states fear setting secessionist precedents for their own minorities (the Catalan/Scotland fear). Stability achieved despite zero international recognition is itself remarkable.
Belgium 1830: opposite outcome. Dutch poised to defeat Belgian rebels; French intervention preserved Belgium; British-mediated Treaty of XVIII Articles. Powers chose Belgium as buffer against France. Belgium got independence not because it earned it but because the four Vienna powers + France found it useful — illustrates cartel’s discretion in admitting members.

3. Democracy

Naive prediction: democratic citizens demand competition (lower taxes, foreign provider access).
Why this hasn’t happened — three-policy model (Fig. 10):

Redistributive policy: democracy redistributes the cartel rent back to citizens. Median voter in core area is better off under cartel than competition (the rent flows toward them; opening the periphery to competition reduces what’s available to redistribute).
Non-redistributive policy: cartel maintained without redistribution. Worst for border residents but core residents indifferent.
Competitive policy: borders open to foreign providers. Helps periphery, hurts core. Median voter rejects this if she lives in the core.


Key result: if the median voter belongs to the core, the competitive policy never wins. Cartel survives democratic transition.
Periphery rarely the median because rich states fall into hand of well-organised core interests; “rulers” in democracy = pivotal voter, dominant lobby, large donor.

Democratic repression illustration: Catalonia

1890: 10% of Spain’s population, 27% of taxes.
2014: 16% of population, 20% of taxes, 14% of expenditures.
Spanish state has fiscal incentive to retain Catalonia — and used force (2017 police repression of independence referendum) consistent with the cartel-preservation prediction.
Other examples: US Civil War, Indian conflicts in Kashmir/Punjab/Nagaland.

Democracy is more restrictive in some ways

Democracies fight wars more successfully (better resource mobilisation) → secession harder.
Democratic peace → less territorial revision among democracies.
Democratic accountability → leaders pay political price for territorial concessions.

Where democracy did allow secession

Always when the seceding territory was poorer than the centre (Czechoslovak split, Serbia-Montenegro, decolonisation).
De Gaulle on Algeria: “Do you think the French body politic can absorb ten million Muslims, who tomorrow will be twenty million…?”
Authoritarian colonial powers (Portugal) resisted decolonisation by force; only Spain in Equatorial Guinea (1968) was unilaterally non-democratic decolonisation.
Soviet Union: authoritarian regime ruled republics by force; democratising regime allowed peaceful secession. Number of states tripled since 1914 in three episodes (post-WWI, post-WWII decolonisation, post-USSR).

Open questions left at chapter’s end

Which boundary is focal — historical or new joint-profit-max — when costs change? Often historical, persisting like a Schelling point. (Mexican border post-1848 = stable despite huge institutional asymmetry.)
Border disputes often stem from prior coordination failure (poorly written treaties, unmapped boundaries) rather than current revisionism. These are unlikely to unravel the cartel.
Foreshadowing ch. 7: future challenges lie in the abstract governance market (trade, capital, IP), not physical territory.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: Resilience of the Cartel
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Ch. 6 — Resilience of the Cartel
Compression notes
Source: [source extract] (~295 lines, ~6500 words). Compression ratio: ≥10:1.
Headline
Two stabilising mechanisms explain why the cartel survived 20th-century shocks: (i) nationalism — investments in national identity that create discontinuous jumps in governance cost at the border, making borders robust to small administrative-capacity shifts; and (ii) international institutions (League of Nations, UN, OAU, EU) that coordinate cartel-leader actions when norms are ambiguous.
Empirical anchor

1945–1999: 5× more intrastate than interstate conflicts (Fearon-Laitin).
Even Africa, with weak states, sees state creation only with international consent.
State revenues at all-time highs, especially in democracies — opposite of the “race to bottom” prediction.

Nationalism as cartel stabiliser

Distinction from economic cartels: De Beers can’t get consumers to die for diamonds. Citizens do die for state membership. Brand loyalty here is unique in scale.

Model extension (Fig. 12): nationalism creates discontinuous jumps

Investment in national identity lowers c_A west of Y (own population easier to govern) and raises c_B west of Y (foreign population harder to govern).
Net effect: a discontinuity in governance cost at exactly the border Y, even where no geographic discontinuity existed.
Result: small changes in absolute capacity don’t shift the joint-profit-max boundary because there’s a step function at Y.
Bonus effect: eliminates the “periphery” zone — every region becomes core when nationalism fully takes hold. This removes the only condition under which democratic citizens would prefer the competitive policy (median voter being a peripheral resident becomes impossible).

Mechanism — what nationalism does in practice

Promote national language vs neighbours’ languages.
Standardise national education curriculum.
Place flags, statues, monuments, demand veneration.
Eugene Weber 1976 on rural France: peasants didn’t identify with Paris as late as 1856 (“the French as if they were a race apart”); transformed by universal primary education + universal conscription in late 19th century.
Benedict Anderson 2006: bureaucratic colleagues’ “consciousness of connectedness” emerging from shared official travel.

A&L’s careful claim

They don’t argue that rulers intended nationalism for cartel stabilisation. They argue that whatever motivated the investment in national identity, the consequence has been to stabilise borders and strengthen the cartel.

Nepal vs Sikkim — the paired case

Both Himalayan kingdoms in 1947 facing dominant India. Sikkim 1/2,600 of India’s population.
Sikkim absorbed by India in 1975: protests crushed, Chogyal arrested, “referendum” (99.55% allegedly favouring incorporation).
Nepal not absorbed despite “Indira doctrine” of Himalayan suzerainty. Why? Because Nepal had inculcated national identity:

18th–19th century: Gurkha-soldier panegyrics commissioned.
1901: Gorkhapatra national newspaper.
1913: Publication Board for Nepali books.
1951: Radio Nepal.
1950s: standardised national curriculum in Nepali.
1955: UN membership; 1969–70: UNSC non-permanent member.


1999, 2000: Bollywood-actor disparagement of Nepal triggered nationwide riots. Cost to India of governing Nepal: too high for the gain.
Sikkim by contrast: official ideology tied to Buddhism (minority faith); nationalism never cohered; many residents welcomed Indian rule as modernising.

International institutions as cartel infrastructure

Concert of Europe (Bismarck era): informal, ad-hoc; failed in July 1914 because Bismarck dead and Germans dismissed British mediation offers.
League of Nations: failed but the idea survived.
United Nations: “the headquarters of the cartel.”

4 UN members/observers contested by >1 member (Israel, Palestine, North Korea, China).
3 non-members recognised by >1 member (Taiwan, Western Sahara, Kosovo).
Membership = sufficient and almost necessary for international recognition.
Treaty registration; norm clarification; coordination.
Security Council 5 permanent members reflect cartel’s hierarchical structure: when these 5 align, action follows; when they don’t, paralysis. Compare Iraqi invasion of Kuwait (rapid coordinated response — sanctions in 4 days, force authorised in 3 months, 35-nation coalition led by US) with Russian invasion of Crimea (no comparable response because Russia is on the council).



UN and decolonisation

Decolonisation occurred when superpowers (US, USSR) lacked colonial empires of their own and had reason to believe they could exert influence in newly independent states.
US: denial of Marshall Aid to colonial powers; Soviet Union: aid to guerrilla groups.
These coordinated through the UN.
Same logic applied to USSR dissolution: the cartel admitted former republics because the new dominant power (US + Western allies) preferred dealing with smaller successor states.

Cartel theory of UN behaviour

UN serves the most powerful members, not abstract principles. Compare its activist response to Kuwait with its passive response to Crimea.
This mirrors how De Beers treated USSR with kid gloves (USSR controlled 17% of diamond market, decisive cartel-breaking power) while crushing smaller competitors. Saudi Arabia’s similar dominance in OPEC.

Other functions of international institutions

Beyond territorial governance: NPT (nuclear non-proliferation), climate cooperation (Rio, Kyoto, Paris, Copenhagen), WTO trade-rule clarification.
Davos / WEF since 1971: informal cartel-elite networking infrastructure.
WTO: the lowering of trade barriers as a cartel-managed process, not a free-market outcome.
Foreshadowing of ch. 7: nationalism and managed trade have started to clash — nationalist movements now favour closing borders, against the elite-led globalisation project that the cartel pursued post-WWII.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.title: The Cartel Today
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/unknow.content:
Ch. 7 — The Cartel Today
Compression notes
Source: [source extract] (~620 lines, ~14000 words). Compression ratio: ≥10:1.
Headline
Globalisation has shifted competition in the governance market from physical territory to abstract policy space (trade, capital flows, intellectual property, immigration). The cartel adapts by managing competition through international agreements rather than eliminating it. Four current challenges: international migration, failed states, US-China power shift, and new modes of conflict (economic warfare, cyber-warfare).
The transformed governance market

Sea freight is 20% of 1930 cost; air travel and international calls have fallen even more.
Three globalisation indicators (Maddison-style) — financial integration, trade openness, migration — peaked early 20th century, fell during 1914–45, rose since.
Consequence: states no longer compete only over territory. They compete over (i) tax rates and regulatory regimes; (ii) currency and capital-control policies; (iii) IP regimes; (iv) labour-market access.
Economy has shifted from agriculture+mining (~75% of US GDP at 1900) to services (~75% today); land-anchored economic value has declined.

Managed trade as cartel adaptation

Stiglitz (2002, p. 20) quoted: a real free-trade agreement would be “a few pages.” The TPP ran 6,000+ pages.
WTO/GATT lower tariffs selectively. Shifted manufacturing from US to China/Mexico while preserving farm subsidies in developed countries. Apple-Ireland and Apple-Jersey BEPS arrangements moved profits without moving production.
“Double Irish” scheme; Ireland’s GDP rose 26.3% in a single quarter from a $300B Apple IP transfer.
OECD estimated 2015 tax-competition cost: $240B/year — likely understatement.
60 profitable Fortune 500 companies paid no tax on $79B profit.
2021 OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS: 136/140 members agreed to 15% minimum corporate tax starting 2023 — cartel coordination against capital mobility.

Three challenges in detail
Immigration

Net migration positively correlates with perceived governance quality (Fig. 14, ICRG index).
Model extension (Fig. 15): when state B’s v_B' is below v_A, residents of weaker B-state want to migrate.
Sorting effect: states with welfare benefits attract broader migrants; states without redistribution attract only high-skill migrants. Hence US (multicultural, English-speaking, large redistributive base) is migration magnet.
Right-wing populism (Trump, Farage, Rassemblement National, AfD) is reaction by core voters who perceive themselves as net losers from labour-market competition + redistribution toward immigrants.
Pre-WWI: no European country except Russia required passports for entry. Modern immigration regimes are exceptional historically.

Failed states

Two model interpretations: (i) c_B rises everywhere; or (ii) v_B falls. Both create ungoverned region between Y and X.
Examples: northwest Pakistan/Afghanistan (Al-Qaeda); Niger Delta (piracy); Colombia/Venezuela (drug-trafficking); Somalia (Al-Shabaab, piracy); Syria (refugee flows).
No good solutions. Sanctions counter-productive (failed state may want to suppress non-state actors but lack capacity). State-building costly and uncertain (US spent $2T over 20 years in Afghanistan; Taliban returned in 11 days). Recognition of new entity is option but the entity may have non-cartel-compatible aims (Islamic State explicitly rejects sovereignty norm; seeks universal caliphate).

Power shifts (US-China)

China-US potential conflict centred on intellectual property.
A&L’s prediction: as US transitions from manufacturing → services → knowledge economy, IP becomes its primary economic asset. Krugman 1979 North-South product cycle: North must continually innovate to maintain real income.
IP rights are recent (centuries old) compared to physical-property rights (millennia). Less universal acceptance — village traders in S/SE Asia may not have intellectual-property concept.
China can grow through manufacturing+services without committing to IP norms; theft is hard to detect because no physical removal occurs.
“American law enforcement has already identified China’s theft of American technology as the biggest threat to the United States.”
Belt and Road Initiative + AIIB = Chinese governance-market expansion via parallel infrastructure.

New modes of conflict

War understood as “costly endeavour for control of value source.” As value migrates from land to mobile capital + IP + human capital, conflict migrates with it.
Russia 2014 (Crimea) and 2022 (Ukraine) reveal Western response as the more interesting feature: economic sanctions, not no-fly zone. Putin himself called sanctions “akin to a declaration of war.”
Free-riding problem in sanctions: states reliant on Russian gas+oil (Hungary, Slovakia) have not fully participated.
Indirect costs (poverty, lower birthrates, brain drain) of economic warfare may equal or exceed conventional war’s direct costs.

The future of the cartel — closing thought experiment

Counterfactual: what if the world had a single monopoly government?

Tax-haven elimination: Piketty’s global wealth tax becomes implementable.
Labour mobility unified: California-Texas reasoning extended globally.
GDP/capita ratio (US states: 2.25; world states: >100) suggests massive convergence potential.
International crime: bin Laden raid wouldn’t need to violate Pakistani sovereignty.
Climate change: binding global laws possible.


A&L: “We are not advocating for a single world government.” Risk: monopoly with no exit option could be extremely coercive.
The thought experiment is “a logical check on our theory” — confirming that competition vs collusion vs monopoly tradeoff exists and that the cartel sits in a non-trivial Pareto-improvement zone.

EU as alternative blueprint

Performs state functions without being a state.
Eased capital and labour flows; common trade and competition policy; coordinated R&D (ERC, ESA, CERN, Airbus); common currency for some.
Its potential failure (Brexit, southern-Europe debt, immigration politics) is informative either way: even failure is data on the cartel’s evolutionary path.
Open question: can such integration scale globally? Are nationalist attachments compatible? “Borders may be here to stay, even as we enter a world in which they make little sense.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/warren.title: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/warren.content:
Ch. 2 — A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity
Setup
The seminal Pitts–McCulloch paper. Originally published in the Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics (1943); reprinted as ch. 2 of Embodiments of Mind. Founds the field of neural-network theory by establishing a bidirectional translation between the firing patterns of all-or-none nervous nets and propositional logic.
Argument

Five physical assumptions are stated explicitly (p. 22): activity is all-or-none; a fixed number of synapses must be excited within the period of latent addition; the only significant delay is synaptic; inhibitory synapses absolutely prevent excitation; net structure is fixed in time.
From (1), neuron firing at time t can be encoded as a proposition: N_i(t) asserts that neuron c_i fires at time t. The synaptic structure determines how propositions combine via conjunction, disjunction, and negation.
Solution of a net = a set of sentences expressing each non-peripheral neuron’s firing in terms of peripheral inputs. Realizability of a logical predicate = the existence of a net whose firing pattern asserts that predicate.
Theorem 1 (nets without circles): every such net has a solution computable by an effective method; equivalently, every net is described by a logical formula.
Theorem 2 (realizability): for every logical predicate satisfying weak conditions, there exists a net realizing it (in the extended sense; precise statement uses Carnap’s Language II).
The treatment is extended to nets with circles (recursive structure) using recursive functions, allowing reference to indefinite past times.
Two empirical complications — facilitation/extinction (state-dependent threshold change) and learning (permanent threshold change) — are absorbed by substituting equivalent fictitious nets with constant connections.

Notable

The opening paragraph (p. 19) compresses the entire result into a single sentence: nets and propositional logic are intertranslatable, with circles handled by additional logical machinery.
The “two difficulties” passage on facilitation and learning (p. 21) is theoretically important: the formal apparatus is agnostic about the physiological mechanism of plasticity, which means the theorems survive even as biology changes its model of learning.
The notation in the body of the paper (Carnap’s Language II augmented with Russell–Whitehead conventions) is a barrier; the idea survives the notation.

Best for
The first 5 pages (Introduction + the five physical assumptions) deliver the conceptual content. The proof apparatus (pp. 23-50) is necessary only for verification; the rest of Warren S. McCulloch - Embodiments of Mind uses the result, not the proof.
Confidence
High. Direct read of the paper text. Pages 19-50 in the 1965 MIT Press edition. Key quotes verified against the extraction log. No CID issues; minor OCR drift (Cyrillic-style ε for ɛ in a few places) but immaterial.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_01_prologue_the_two_johns
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 1 — Prologue: The Two Johns
Kushner opens at a Cyberathlete Professional League Quake III Arena tournament in downtown Dallas, April 2000. A $100,000 prize pool, hundreds of bring-your-own-computer competitors, baby pajamas printed with the Quake logo, fans shaving the clawlike Quake glyph into their hair. The scene is meant to convince a sceptical reader that first-person shooters are not a niche but a cultural pillar — Americans by 2000 spend more on games than on movie tickets, the genre has been blamed for the Columbine shootings, and the people whose games drive the genre are about to walk into the same hotel.
The frame Kushner introduces is mythic and binary. Two boys called John, born within a few years of each other into broken or strict households, escape via the arcade and the home computer, find each other in a Louisiana shareware office, build the games (Wolfenstein 3D, Doom, Quake) that define the genre, then split publicly and competitively. Kushner calls them the “Lennon and McCartney of video games” and frames their union and breakup as a study in human alchemy: complementary opposites whose collaboration produced more than either could have alone.
The prologue sketches the archetypes that will run through the book. John Carmack at twenty-nine: monkish, philanthropic, lives for the elegance of code, builds high-powered rockets in his spare time, made Bill Gates’s short list of geniuses. John Romero at thirty-two: brash showman, the industry’s rock star, dark mane to his waist, willing to risk reputation on big visions. Carmack’s parting summary, which Kushner places at the top of the book, is the thesis in miniature: “Romero wants an empire, I just want to create good programs.”
The two arrive at the tournament in matching Ferraris bought together at the height of their collaboration, nod past each other in the hall, and head to separate stages — Carmack to talk Quake III Arena, Romero to talk Daikatana, the long-delayed game from his post-id startup Ion Storm. The prologue’s last sentence — “It was time for this game to begin” — reframes the whole book as the deathmatch behind the deathmatches, the rivalry that drove the genre.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_02_the_rock_star
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 2 — The Rock Star
Kushner’s portrait of the young John Romero is a story of arcades as escape and beatings as the cost of escape. Born premature in Tucson in October 1967 to Ginny and Alfonso Romero — a first-generation Mexican-American maintenance man at an air force base — Romero is six when his father, a hard drinker, leaves to “pick up groceries” and disappears for two years. His mother remarries an ex-drill sergeant, John Schuneman, who carries a top-secret Pentagon job retrieving black boxes from downed spy planes and runs the household with military discipline.
Romero discovers Asteroids at age eleven at a Roundtable Pizza Parlor in Rocklin, California. The arcade becomes a parallel world worth any beating. The chapter’s signature scene is brutal and recurring: stepfather hauls Romero out of an arcade by the shoulder, drives him home in a pickup, beats him bloody for “telling your mother fuck you,” grounds him for two weeks. The next day Romero sneaks back. Kushner uses this rhythm — beating, recovery, return to the game — to set Romero’s psychological signature for the rest of the book: resilience as a deliberate act, hyperbole as a defense, games as the only place where talent is its own reward.
Romero’s identity as a maker, not just a player, also begins here. He sketches a Lamborghini at the kitchen table at age six well enough that his stepfather assumes he traced it; tested with a Hot Wheels car, he draws a perfect copy. By high school he is grinding through Apple Graphics Arcade Tutorial, churning out Asteroids and Pac-Man clones that get published in Apple II disk magazines like Uptime, Nibble, and InCider. He drops out of community college, marries his teenage girlfriend Kelly when she gets pregnant, and lands a job at Origin Systems in New Hampshire just as his first son is born.
The Origin job collapses when Romero gambles on his boss’s startup; Kelly takes the babies back to California, and Romero — twenty-one, two children, no apartment, sleeping on a friend’s couch — phones Jay Wilbur and lands a job at Softdisk in Shreveport, Louisiana. Kushner’s point in this chapter is that by the time Romero arrives in Shreveport, every trait that will both build and destroy id Software is already formed: relentless self-promotion, hunger for recognition, cheerful tolerance for chaos, and a refusal to ever stop playing.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_03_the_rocket_scientist
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 3 — The Rocket Scientist
John Carmack’s childhood is the structural mirror of Romero’s. Born August 20, 1970, in Kansas City to Stan Carmack — a TV news anchor at one of Kansas City’s three big stations — and Inga Carmack, a microbiologist with a doctorate, Carmack grows up in upper-middle-class Catholic suburbia attending Notre Dame elementary. Where Romero is street, Carmack is parental high expectations: he tests at ninth-grade comprehension in second grade, develops a robotic-humming verbal tic (“12 times 12 equals 144 … mmm”) that resembles a CPU acknowledging output, and lists his parents’ expectations twice when assigned to write his top five problems.
Kushner’s central image of young Carmack is rebellion as engineering project. After his mother padlocks his comic books in a closet, Carmack — unable to pick the lock — removes the door from its hinges. As a teenager he and a friend mix thermite from oxidizers to break into a local school for the Apple II computers inside; police catch them; a court psychiatrist labels Carmack “a brain on legs with no empathy whatsoever,” and he is sentenced to a year in a juvenile detention home. The pattern matters because it foreshadows everything Kushner will say about Carmack as an adult: rules are constraints to be hacked, not norms to be observed; relationships are negotiable, the laws of physics are not.
Carmack’s parents divorce; his father remarries, and Carmack is shuttled between households. At his mother’s house in Kansas City he buys an Apple II, devours Nibble magazine type-in listings, runs Dungeons and Dragons campaigns whose worlds persist between sessions — a rare design choice that anticipates his obsession with reusable game engines. He drops out of the University of Missouri after two semesters, picks up freelance work for an Apple II developer, and discovers Softdisk’s Apple II disk magazines as a steady customer for his ports. He converts his games to PC by renting an unfamiliar IBM, learns the new architecture in weeks, and ships in three platforms (Apple II, Apple IIgs, PC) on a regular cadence.
Kushner closes the chapter with Carmack reluctantly accepting Softdisk’s repeated invitation to come to Shreveport for an interview. The MGB has new parts; he wants the drive. The boy who will design the Doom engine arrives at Softdisk’s office in 1990 expecting to teach, and meets, for the first time, someone who knows things he does not — John Romero, who has just become editor of Softdisk’s PC games line.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_04_dangerous_dave_in_copyright_infringement
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 4 — Dangerous Dave In Copyright Infringement
Carmack arrives at Softdisk in Shreveport, run by ex-LSU math professor Al Vekovius (“Big Al”), and meets Romero, Tom Hall (a Wisconsin import with two college degrees and a love of Commander Keen-style platformers), Adrian Carmack (no relation, an artist with a taste for gore from a hospital morgue job), and Jay Wilbur. Al has just spun up a PC games subscription called “Gamer’s Edge”; he needs a small team to ship a new game every two months. Carmack and Romero recognize each other instantly as collaborators — for the first time each meets someone with comparable obsession and complementary skills.
The chapter’s title episode is the founding myth of id Software. One night, in the Softdisk office, Carmack writes a smooth-scrolling demo on a PC of the opening level of Nintendo’s Super Mario Bros. 3 — a feat the industry believed impossible on PC hardware, since the IBM PC had no scrolling-tile graphics chip. Carmack solves it with a technique he calls adaptive tile refresh: rather than redrawing every tile each frame, he tracks which screen regions actually changed and updates only those. The team plays the demo in disbelief. Romero packages it with a Mario character replaced by Tom’s character “Dangerous Dave” and labels the floppy “Dangerous Dave In Copyright Infringement.” They mail it to Nintendo, which politely declines but praises the technical achievement.
That weekend the team retreats to a rented lake house outside Shreveport, runs on caffeine and pizza for seventy-two hours, and produces a complete shareware game — Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons — that uses Carmack’s scrolling engine on a side-scrolling platformer designed by Tom and Romero. They call themselves Ideas from the Deep. They smuggle work hours and Softdisk computers home — Romero quietly carting hardware out of the office on weekends — and ship the Keen demo to Scott Miller’s Apogee Software in Dallas, the leading PC shareware publisher.
Apogee’s shareware model — give away episode 1 free, sell episodes 2 and 3 by mail order — turns Keen into the first PC platformer to crack the shareware top ten. Royalty checks of 10,000-20,000 a month start arriving while the team is still on Softdisk’s payroll. Big Al discovers the side hustle; the team threatens lawsuits over Carmack’s Game Engine code; eventually a settlement requires id to ship one new Gamer’s Edge title every two months. On February 1, 1991, id Software is born. Tom and Jay stay at Softdisk for a transition period; Carmack, Romero, and Adrian quit. Carmack’s parting line to Big Al — “I don’t care about [the people I’m leaving behind]. I’ll go back to making pizzas before I stay at this crummy place” — establishes Carmack’s lifelong willingness to walk away from any institution that does not serve the work.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_05_pizza_money
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 5 — Pizza Money
The chapter covers id’s first year as an independent company at the lake house outside Shreveport. The team is Carmack, Romero, Adrian, Tom Hall, and Jay Wilbur; their cat Mitzi sleeps on Carmack’s monitor; pizza boxes pile in the corners; the Dungeons & Dragons campaign run by Carmack as Dungeon Master functions as a parallel laboratory for game design ideas. Carmack maintains the world between sessions (“a fifty-page glossary” of items including a sword called “the Mighty Daikatana” and a magical floating “Hellgate Cube” that Romero will later try to revive in Quake), modeling the kind of persistent fictional world that will animate Doom and Quake.
Money flows in through Apogee. The first Keen trilogy generates 15,000-20,000 a month — pizza money becoming computer money. The team upgrades to a fleet of 386 PCs; Carmack is twenty, Romero twenty-three. They ship Rescue Rover (a maze game), Catacomb 3-D (their first first-person engine, single-screen), and a darker Keen variant: Dangerous Dave in the Haunted Mansion. Adrian quietly inserts “death animations” — Dave’s eyes smashed bloody by zombie fists — and the team discovers a second formula beneath the Keen kid-friendliness: humor plus violence, the more over the top the better. Softdisk balks; the bloody frames are cut from the Gamer’s Edge release.
Shareware Distribution is the structural innovation Kushner emphasizes. Apogee’s Scott Miller — an ex-Apple II hobbyist working out of his parents’ Garland, Texas apartment — has reworked the shareware model: instead of a crippled demo or a guilt-trip “send money if you like it” plea, give away episode 1 as a complete free game, then charge for episodes 2 and 3 only by mail order. The economics work because the free episode functions as a viral, zero-cost-of-distribution marketing engine; Bulletin Board Systems, college networks, and PC magazine cover disks copy and distribute it; satisfied players send checks. Apogee was the first company built around this model and was already grossing $7 million a year on small games before id arrived.
By the end of 1991 the team relocates from Shreveport to Madison, Wisconsin (Adrian and Kevin Cloud, the Apogee artist they recruit, prefer cold weather and short summers for indoor productivity), and prepares to ship their first 3D first-person game: Wolfenstein 3D. The chapter ends with an omen they treat as one — a Pac-Man arcade machine, abandoned in the back of their moving truck by an earlier tenant, becomes the first piece of furniture in their new Wisconsin apartment. Carmack peels $150 in cash off a fat wad of bills and tells the driver to leave it on board.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_06_more_fun_than_real_life
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 6 — More Fun Than Real Life
This is the Wolfenstein 3D chapter. Carmack, having shipped Catacomb 3-D as a single-window first-person engine, spends the autumn of 1991 building a faster, full-screen, texture-mapped raycasting engine on a 386 PC. The technique he settles on is a 2.5D raycaster: walls are vertical and at right angles, height variation is faked, the world is essentially a top-down maze rendered from the player’s eye view. Done well, it is the most immersive 3D PC players have ever seen. Carmack writes the engine alone in two months.
The team chooses a Nazi-castle escape theme partly because Romero loved the 1981 Apple II game Castle Wolfenstein and partly because Nazis are the only enemy nobody objects to killing. Adrian draws blood spatters, swastikas, and Hitler at the end of episode 3 strapped into a robotic mech suit firing four chain guns. Tom Hall designs maps; Romero designs maps and adds the small touches that will become id signatures (audio barks from enemies, the satisfying thunk of a switch). Released in May 1992 through Apogee on the shareware model, Wolfenstein 3D detonates: episode 1 hits the Bulletin Board Systems and the magazine cover disks within days; mail-order checks for episodes 2-6 start arriving at 35 a pop; gross sales hit 200,000 in the first month and never slow down. By year-end the game has earned id and Apogee about $100,000 a month each.
The chapter’s other thread is moving to Texas. Wisconsin proves too cold and isolated; Apogee’s Scott Miller is in Garland; id wants to be near him. They settle on Mesquite, just east of Dallas, in April 1992 — the suburb whose city council had once tried to ban arcade games before being stopped by the Supreme Court. Their La Prada apartment complex, with its swimming pools and barbecue smell, is the team’s reward to itself. The lake-house phase is over; the Dallas phase has begun.
The chapter sets up two ideological lines that will define id’s later trajectory. First, Conceptual Integrity: Wolfenstein works because its design is uncompromisingly tight — six episodes of one mechanic (run, shoot, find key, open door, shoot more), one engine, one art style. Second, the production system: a tiny team (six people including Kevin Cloud) ships a category-defining product through a distribution channel (shareware) that bypasses retailers, allowing them to keep most of the revenue. The lake house has scaled into a Mesquite apartment. The royalty checks have scaled past Carmack’s father’s TV anchor salary. The team is preparing for the next engine.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_07_spear_of_destiny_and_doom_design
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 7 — Spear of Destiny and Doom Design
After Wolfenstein 3D’s commercial success, id ships a retail standalone called Spear of Destiny through FormGen for the boxed-software channel — their first non-shareware release — and uses the proceeds to fund a much more ambitious next engine. The chapter is the longest single sequence of technical and creative invention in the book: the design of Doom.
Carmack’s engine ambitions for Doom break four constraints that Wolfenstein had accepted. First, walls can be at arbitrary angles, not just orthogonal. Second, walls can have variable heights, allowing rooms with steps, pits, and balconies. Third, floors and ceilings are textured, not flat. Fourth, light sources can dim with distance and flicker, producing genuine atmosphere. The technical achievement that makes the new engine feasible is Carmack’s adoption of Binary Space Partitioning trees — an idea he reads in a Bell Labs paper while porting Wolfenstein to the SNES. BSP recursively subdivides each level into convex regions; at render time the engine traverses only the regions visible from the player’s position, drastically reducing the polygon count per frame. With BSP, Doom runs at speeds the team had thought impossible.
Tom Hall writes a thirty-page “Doom Bible” — a science-fiction story arc set on Phobos, with five named marines and detailed character backstories. Romero and Carmack push back: the design is too literary, the levels Tom builds (modeled on real military bases, with file cabinets and card-playing soldiers) are too banal. One night Romero retreats to his office, cranks Dokken on the speakers, and builds a level in the new editor that breaks every realism rule — angled walls, abstract geometry, lights that pulse from nowhere, zombies emerging from shadows in unnatural symmetry. He calls the others in. They walk through. Tom’s Doom Bible is dead; Romero’s “abstract design” is the new direction.
The team votes Tom out in summer 1993 — id’s first founder firing. Their by-laws stipulate unanimous founder vote and full forfeiture of equity for departing founders, so Tom loses any future Doom revenue. Tom takes the news at a meeting where he peels a sticker off the conference table and rolls it between his fingers. He is hired by Apogee/3D Realms within weeks. Sandy Petersen, a thirty-seven-year-old Mormon convert, ex-MicroProse strategy designer, and creator of the Call of Cthulhu pen-and-paper RPG, is hired to replace him; Romero initially objects on the grounds that Sandy is religious, but relents when Sandy proves capable of designing a Doom level in a single day.
Doom is released as shareware on December 10, 1993, uploaded by Jay Wilbur to a University of Wisconsin FTP server that crashes within minutes under demand. The chapter ends with the system administrator phoning id in panic: the entire university network is down. Doom has arrived.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_08_the_coolest_game
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 8 — The Coolest Game (Doom Released)
The chapter covers Doom’s reception, the modding community it spawns, and the cultural moment in which id becomes the most-imitated game studio in the world. By March 1994, Doom is installed on more PCs than Microsoft’s Windows operating system itself; Bill Gates emails his graphics chief Alex St. John asking whether Microsoft should buy id outright. The shareware episode 1 spreads through every PC bulletin board service, university network, and corporate workplace — IT departments file early policies banning Doom because it is bringing down their LAN traffic. The full retail Doom (episodes 2-3) sells through mail order at 40; sales gross more than 100,000 a day at peak.
Doom’s design innovations matter for what they enable downstream. Carmack architects the game so that level data, sprites, sounds, and music live in WAD (“Where’s All the Data?”) files separate from the engine. He intentionally documents the WAD format and ships the editor logic in a way that lets fans build their own levels — what becomes Mod Culture. Within months thousands of fan-made WAD files appear on the bulletin boards: parody levels, themed levels (Aliens, Star Wars), brutally hard levels, levels that turn the engine into a casino or a haunted Disney park. Some mods become more popular than commercial follow-ons. Carmack’s choice to release tools — and later to release Doom’s full source code in 1997 — is a deliberate philosophical commitment that anticipates the open-source ethos and prefigures a generation of modder-turned-professional designers (including future Valve, Bungie, and Epic founders).
Doom also debuts deathmatch — multiplayer player-versus-player combat, originally a side feature Romero coded against Carmack’s mild objection. Players LAN four PCs together to chase each other through Doom levels with rocket launchers; office workplaces become deathmatch arenas after hours; the term itself enters mainstream English. The game introduces a new social format that Quake will industrialize: kids hauling computer cases to friends’ houses for “LAN parties” that run from Friday evening to Sunday morning.
Romero’s transformation in the chapter is the central narrative arc. He starts wearing a “Wrote It” T-shirt; he grows out his hair; gamers fall to their knees outside CompUSAs asking for autographs. Carmack notices that while Romero is being an industry rock star, his Doom II level output is dropping (six of thirty-two levels by the deadline) and the company has had to assign American McGee and Sandy Petersen to fill the gap. The seed of the eventual breakup is planted in this chapter. The same chapter introduces Carmack’s relentless engineering pace: he ports Doom to the Atari Jaguar for a $250,000 fee mainly because porting teaches him low-level skills he’ll need for the next engine. The asymmetry between the two Johns — one pursuing celebrity, the other pursuing technical depth — has begun.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_09_quakes_and_quaketalk
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 9 — Quakes and QuakeTalk (The Long Quake Development)
The Quake chapter is the longest in the book and the most emotionally difficult. Carmack announces in early 1994 that the next engine will be true 3D — arbitrary polygons, arbitrary geometry, arbitrary camera angles, and the first commercial first-person game designed for multiplayer combat over the Internet. Romero is electric: the name comes from their old D&D campaign, where Quake was a barbarian fighter with a magic hammer and a “Hellgate Cube” floating above his head. He posts on the proto-Internet that “Quake won’t be just a game, it will be a movement” and “the next game is going to blow Doom all to hell” — long before any code exists.
Carmack works for almost a year on the engine alone (later joined by Michael Abrash, lured from Microsoft for the chance to write a 3D engine with Carmack). The technical achievement is genuinely landmark: arbitrary 3D polygons, real lighting with surface caching, full Internet multiplayer with a custom client-server protocol, BSP precomputation extended to 3D. But while Carmack programs, the game design has no leader. Romero — supposedly the lead designer — is increasingly absent: deathmatching, doing interviews, executive-producing third-party games using the Doom engine, drinking with fans on chat channels.
The remaining team — Adrian, Kevin, American McGee, Sandy Petersen, Tim Willits — is left to build Quake’s content with no design document beyond a Romero two-pager that the team treats as a lazy joke. The original ambitious design (medieval melee combat with a Hellgate Cube AI companion, time-traveling levels, Aztec architecture) collapses; American McGee finally proposes “let’s just make Doom III with rocket launchers and stuff.” Sandy seconds. Romero is overruled. Quake becomes a Doom-engine successor with better graphics — not the design revolution Romero promised online for years.
Kushner uses three devices to track the breakdown. Carmack starts publishing his daily work log — the .plan file — to the Internet, listing every bug fixed and feature added each day. Fans love it; it becomes the template for what later becomes the developer blog. Romero responds with his own grandiose .plan posts, widening the visible gap between Carmack’s evidence-based progress and Romero’s promises. Second, the team moves into a single shared “war room” with cables draped from the ceiling and shades drawn — Carmack’s deliberate forcing function, which Romero finds claustrophobic. Third, Tim Willits — a former Doom modder hired into id, the first of many mod-to-pro hires — quietly outproduces Romero on level design and ascends in Carmack’s estimation. When Carmack assigns Tim’s levels to Quake’s shareware opening, Romero is publicly humiliated.
The chapter ends with Romero leaving id in summer 1996. Carmack calls a meeting, hands him a pre-written resignation, and tells him: “You’ve been poisonous to the company.” Romero signs, walks out, calls Tom Hall on the way to the parking lot, and they begin sketching what will become Ion Storm. Carmack posts to id’s plan file: “Romero is now gone from id. There will be no more grandiose statements about our future projects.” The original Two Johns partnership is over.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_10_judgment_day_and_deathmatch
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 10 — Judgment Day and Deathmatch (Quake Released; Ion Storm Founded)
Quake ships in June 1996 to mixed initial reviews — its single-player gloom alienates Doom fans, and the dial-up Internet of 1996 makes online multiplayer painful — but within months the game becomes the foundational artifact of competitive PC gaming. Microsoft sponsors the first official Quake deathmatch tournament, “Judgment Day,” in May 1997. Sixteen finalists fly to Atlanta’s E3 trade show; the grand prize is Carmack’s own cherry-red Ferrari 328. Twenty-year-old Dennis “Thresh” Fong from California beats clan-mate Tom “Entropy” Kizmey 13-1 in the finals; Carmack hands him the keys onstage and, when Thresh asks how he’ll get the car home, returns half an hour later with $5,000 cash for shipping.
Kushner uses Stevie “Killcreek” Case — the twenty-year-old University of Kansas student who leads clan Impulse 9 and later becomes Romero’s girlfriend — as the human face of the Quake clan subculture. Within months of release the world has hundreds of organized Quake clans (Impulse 9, Ruthless Bastards, Clan Widows for women); LAN parties run for weeks; Quake spawns the first cyberathletes. The Cyberathlete Professional League, the very tournament that opens the book’s prologue, is founded in this period. The chapter closes the loop on the prologue: the gaming subculture Kushner introduced now has its first millionaires, sponsorship deals (Microsoft signs Thresh), and Olympics-style ambitions.
Inside id, the post-Romero atmosphere is quieter and unhappier. Jay Wilbur quits when his four-year-old son asks why all the other dads go to baseball games. Programmer Michael Abrash returns to Microsoft. Level designer Sandy Petersen is fired. Mike Wilson and Shawn Green leave for Romero’s new venture. Carmack writes a long, atypically personal email-interview essay to the gaming press: “Romero was pushed out of id because he wasn’t working hard enough … he wants an empire, I just want to create good programs. Everyone is happy now.”
The other half of the chapter is Romero’s ascent at Ion Storm. With a multimillion-dollar buyout from id and a publishing deal with Eidos for 40 million across three games (Daikatana, Anachronox, and Warren Spector's Deus Ex), Romero leases the entire glass-walled penthouse of the Texas Commerce Tower in downtown Dallas — 22,500 square feet, 550,000 a month, sixty-foot arched glass ceilings. He hires Todd Porter and Jerry O’Flaherty as third and fourth designers. The Ion Storm motto is plastered on the wall: “Design Is Law.” Romero gives interviews proclaiming Daikatana will make him “your bitch” — an infamous magazine ad whose backlash will haunt the company. The chapter ends with Romero standing in his still-empty penthouse, looking at downtown Dallas through the glass, certain that this time he gets to build the company his way.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_11_silicon_alamo
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 11 — Silicon Alamo
By summer 1997, Dallas has become to game developers what Seattle was to grunge musicians in the early 1990s: a regional concentration of talent, capital, and rivalry that the press starts naming. Time calls the Texas studios “the New Cowboys”; Wired calls them “Doom babies”; the Boston Globe dubs the scene “the new Hollywood.” Kushner’s preferred name — Silicon Alamo — captures both the swagger and the eventual doom of a regional cluster organized around one game genre.
The chapter is structurally a survey: id is Nirvana, Romero’s Ion Storm is Pearl Jam, Apogee/3D Realms (Tom Hall, Scott Miller, George Broussard, the Duke Nukem 3D team) is Soundgarden, and a constellation of secondary studios spawn from id and 3D Realms alumni — Rogue Entertainment, Ritual Entertainment, Ensemble Studios (Sandy Petersen’s post-id home, which produces Age of Empires), Terminal Reality. Almost every major studio licenses Carmack’s Quake engine for $250,000 plus royalties, including Valve’s Half-Life and Epic’s Unreal. Kushner’s claim is that within five years of Doom, Dallas has become a self-replicating ecosystem of first-person shooter expertise, with talent rotating between studios via a Silicon Valley Spinout Model-style mobility.
The chapter’s tonal center is the cars. Carmack rents the Ennis racetrack for company drag races; he asks the mayor of Mesquite to shut down the local airport so id can do quarter-mile passes between projects. The mayor agrees because Carmack has donated tens of thousands of dollars in equipment to the local police, including bulletproof vests stitched with Doom patches. Romero buys a yellow Hummer; Carmack runs four Ferraris simultaneously; the Ferrari shop owner Bob Norwood becomes Carmack’s mechanic and later joins his rocket project. The cars matter to Kushner because they are evidence — the kind of evidence kids in the Dallas suburbs can see, that ordinary code-grinding teenagers became multimillionaires in their twenties through games. The Ferrari is shareware’s victory lap.
Inside Ion Storm, however, the founder’s curse is metastasizing. Romero’s three-designer model breaks down: Todd Porter, hired to design Doppelganger, takes over as CEO when Romero proves nonconfrontational; Tom Hall’s Anachronox slips badly; Daikatana’s design changes weekly. The press picks up internal memos from a hostile blog called “Bitch X” that publishes leaked documents, layoffs, and emails. Eidos, Ion’s publisher, gets nervous as the burn rate exceeds $5 million a year against zero shipped product. Romero’s shareware-era confidence — that talented people in a relaxed environment will produce great games on intrinsic motivation — meets the limits of a fifty-person studio with no operations discipline. The chapter ends with Romero realizing that the company he built to be the anti-id has become a less productive id with worse cash flow.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_12_straight_out_of_doom
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 12 — Straight Out of Doom (Columbine)
The chapter pivots from industry economics to the cultural and political backlash that defined the late-1990s and early-2000s perception of first-person shooters. On April 20, 1999, Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold — Littleton, Colorado high schoolers — murdered fifteen people including themselves at Columbine High. Harris went by the online handle “RebDoomer,” made amateurish Doom mods (a hockey-rink arena, a boxing ring), recorded a basement video before the shooting holding a sawed-off shotgun and Jack Daniels and saying “It’s going to be like fucking Doom. Tick tick tick. That fucking shotgun is straight out of Doom.”
Within days, Doom became the metonym for media-driven youth violence in mainstream press. The Simon Wiesenthal Center claimed Harris had built a custom Columbine-floorplan Doom mod (no evidence ever surfaced). The Washington Post called Doom deathmatching a “dark, dangerous place.” Newsday wrote that Doom can “widen the hole in any kid’s soul.” Ex-army psychologist Dave Grossman became a cable-news fixture arguing that first-person shooters are “murder simulators” that train children to kill, an argument President Clinton repeated in a radio address. Senator Joseph Lieberman — who had run hearings on game violence in 1993 after Mortal Kombat — held new hearings asking the industry to “call a cease-fire in the virtual arms race.”
Kushner’s reportorial position, made explicit in the chapter, is that the moral panic was substantially evidence-free. He cites Gerard Jones’s Killing Monsters: Why Children Need Fantasy, Super Heroes, and Make-Believe Violence on the long anthropological history of children using violent play to safely process aggression. He cites the 1965 Bandura “Bobo doll” study that political commentators cited and notes that the children in that study punched the inflatable clown they were given — they did not run to the local circus and beat up Bozo. He notes that the U.S. military in fact did use modified Doom (Marine Doom) in the late 1990s — but for team-building exercises, not desensitization training. He notes that the Columbine families’ multimillion-dollar lawsuits against the game industry were eventually thrown out by a U.S. district court that wrote, “this was a tragic situation, but tragedies such as this simply defy rational explanation and the courts should not pretend otherwise.”
The chapter is also where Kushner records the emotional cost to Carmack and Romero. Carmack — who had spent his teenage detention months reading The Self-Made Tape Worm philosophy of personal sovereignty — is appalled by what he sees as logical sloppiness: he posts on his .plan file that the cause-and-effect link from playing Doom to school shootings is unsupported by data and that hiding behind games is a way for parents and politicians to avoid harder conversations about gun access and adolescent isolation. Romero, characteristically, is more wounded; he was the public face of Doom, and the press treats him as morally complicit. The chapter ends by noting that mainstream tort and political pressure subsided over the following five years as the games industry, surpassed Hollywood box office, became too economically central to scapegoat.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_13_daikatana_and_doom_iii
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 13 — Daikatana, Quake III, and Doom III (The Years of Divergence)
The chapter traces the parallel late-1990s trajectories of Carmack at id and Romero at Ion Storm. Carmack ships Quake II in late 1997 and immediately begins work on Quake III Arena — a deliberately stripped-down multiplayer-only deathmatch product, with no single-player campaign, designed to ride the rising 3D-accelerator hardware wave (3dfx Voodoo, then NVIDIA RIVA) and the maturing Internet.
