Mokyr defends the Cortesian-army principle: progress depends on a small elite of contributors (“a relatively small elite, even if we take into account the majority of experimenters, philosophers, would-be inventors, and thoughtful mechanics whom history has not recorded”). Average human capital matters for the deployment of techniques, not for their invention. This is empirically consistent with the observation that the most literate countries in early-nineteenth-century Europe (Scandinavia, the Netherlands, Prussia) were not the first to industrialize — Britain’s lead came from elite networks of inventors and their middle-class patrons, not from mass schooling. The implication for modern policy is that R&D-promoting institutions should target the right tail of talent rather than treat human capital as a uniform stock to be expanded by the school year.
The chapter closes with appropriate skepticism. Mokyr does not claim that the Western trajectory was inevitable, nor that it is irreversible. The growth of useful knowledge has substantial autonomy — Hume’s observation that “you will never want booksellers while there are buyers of books, but there may frequently be readers where there are no authors” captures the Mokyr point that supply-side dynamics matter as much as demand-side inducement. Nor does Mokyr claim that more useful knowledge automatically improves human life — Athena gave Cecrops the olive but also gave Troy the wooden horse. The framework explains how the West got rich; it does not promise that the same mechanism will deliver wisdom or virtue.
Important examples

The cross-country distribution of nuclear-energy adoption (France 75%, Belgium 56%, Netherlands 4%) as evidence that aggregator-rule differences swamp pure economic factors.
Khan and Sokoloff’s research showing the American patent system was unusually market-friendly, accessible, and democratic.
The Netherlands and Switzerland abolishing their patent systems in the late nineteenth century without obvious harm — small-country free-riding on the global \Omega pool.
German chemical-industry training producing the world’s chemists (Caro, Hofmann, Liebig’s students), with national chemistry communities cross-pollinating across the West.
Wester sugar refinery (Amsterdam) by 1880 routinely flying European experts in by train — vivid case of access-cost collapse.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_01_optimistic_skeptic
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 1 — An Optimistic Skeptic
Tetlock opens by juxtaposing two forecasters: Tom Friedman, the celebrity New York Times columnist whose forecasts are ubiquitous but never scored, and Bill Flack, an obscure retiree from Kearney, Nebraska whose hundreds of geopolitical predictions have been independently dated, recorded, and graded. Flack is a “superforecaster”; about 2% of the thousands of volunteers in Tetlock’s tournaments earn that label by sustained accuracy. The book’s task is to explain why, and to argue that this skill is cultivated rather than innate.
Tetlock revisits his own famous “dart-throwing chimpanzee” punch line from the EPJ research (1984–2004) and pushes back against the way it has been distorted. The actual finding was narrower: average expert accuracy decayed toward chance only at three- to five-year horizons, and a sub-group of more pragmatic thinkers reliably beat the chimp. The result was misread as nihilism about all expertise.
He then stakes out the “optimistic skeptic” stance with two illustrations. The Mohamed Bouazizi self-immolation that triggered the Arab Spring shows Lorenz-style nonlinear, butterfly-effect limits on long-range political forecasting (the “Lorenzian cloud”). But the morning routine of a Kansas City actuary shows how much of life is “clocklike” and reliably predictable — traffic, sunrise, electricity demand, mortality. Predictability is therefore domain-, horizon-, and condition-dependent, not a global property of reality.
The chapter introduces the Good Judgment Project and the IARPA tournament (2011–2015). GJP recruited ~3,200 volunteers in year 1, eventually generating over a million forecasts on ~500 questions; it beat the official control group by 60% in year 1, 78% in year 2, and outperformed academic competitors and intelligence-community analysts with classified access. Two headline conclusions: (1) foresight is real and measurable on horizons of 3–18 months, and (2) the difference between superforecasters and the rest is how they think, not who they are or what they know. A simple one-hour training tutorial improved accuracy by ~10%.
Closing on a David Ferrucci interview, Tetlock argues the future of forecasting is human-machine “freestyle,” not pure algorithmic replacement, and that the guru-versus-guru pundit model is what will become obsolete first.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_02_illusions_of_knowledge
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 2 — Illusions of Knowledge
Tetlock uses the story of Archie Cochrane — the British physician later credited with founding evidence-based medicine — to expose how even sophisticated experts substitute intuitive certainty for evidence. In 1956 a renowned specialist, without waiting for the pathologist’s report, told Cochrane he had terminal cancer and removed his pectoralis minor. He didn’t have cancer at all. Cochrane, who would soon make a career of attacking medical “God complex” thinking, meekly accepted the verdict. The two riddles — why the specialist didn’t wait, and why Cochrane didn’t push back — frame the chapter.
The historical backdrop is medicine’s millennia-long stagnation under what Richard Feynman would later call “cargo cult science.” From Galen to George Washington’s bleeders, physicians treated each outcome as confirming evidence for theories that had never been tested. James Lind’s 1747 scurvy trial was a near-miss; only after Austin Bradford Hill’s twentieth-century work did randomized controlled trials displace authority-based judgment.
The cognitive machinery responsible is dual-process: System 1 (fast, automatic, pattern-matching) versus System 2 (slow, effortful, deliberative). Tetlock illustrates with the bat-and-ball problem (most answer “10 cents,” the wrong System-1 answer). Kahneman’s “WYSIATI” — what you see is all there is — captures System 1’s structural insensitivity to evidence quality: it treats whatever is at hand as sufficient. Confabulation (Gazzaniga’s split-brain shovel/chicken-claw experiment) shows we generate plausible explanations regardless of whether we actually know.
The post-Oslo-bombing rush to blame Islamists illustrates confirmation bias: a plausible hypothesis becomes The Truth without serious tests for falsification. Cochrane’s own collapse is explained by attribute substitution (“bait and switch”): rather than answer “do I have cancer?” he answered the easier “is this the sort of person who should know?”
Tetlock then refuses the blink-vs-think dichotomy. Klein’s research on firefighter intuitions and Kahneman’s research on heuristic failures are reconciled: intuition is reliable when there are valid, learnable cues (firefighting, chess, infant infection), unreliable when there are not (stock-picking). The chapter closes by drawing a parallel: twenty-first-century forecasting today resembles nineteenth-century medicine — confident, untested, expensive, and roughly as accurate as elixirs from a wagon. The cure, again, is a tablespoon of doubt.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_03_keeping_score
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 3 — Keeping Score
If forecasting is to be improved, accuracy must be measured — and measurement turns out to be deceptively hard. Tetlock dissects two famous “wrong” forecasts to show why. Steve Ballmer’s 2007 prediction that the iPhone would get no “significant market share” sounds laughable until you read the full passage and realize he was talking about share of the global mobile phone market (where Apple did stay around 6%), and never defined “significant.” The 2010 open letter to Ben Bernanke signed by Niall Ferguson and others warned that quantitative easing would risk “currency debasement and inflation” — but it gave no time frame and used the word “risk,” so no outcome can definitively falsify it.
The chapter then walks through the conceptual machinery needed for scorable forecasting: clearly defined terms, explicit time frames, and numerical probabilities. Sherman Kent (CIA Office of National Estimates) discovered in the late 1940s that colleagues writing “serious possibility” silently meant anything from 20-to-80 against to 80-to-20 in favor. He proposed a numerical translation chart — “probable” = 75% ± 12%, etc. — but the intelligence community resisted. Two reasons recur: aesthetic discomfort with sounding “like a bookie” (Kent: “I’d rather be a bookie than a goddamn poet”), and the political safety of vague language under the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy, in which a 70%-rain forecast is judged “wrong” if it doesn’t rain. Vague verbiage gives forecasters retroactive cover; numbers expose them.
To judge probabilistic forecasts at all, you need many of them. Tetlock introduces calibration (a forecaster claiming “70%” should see those events occur 70% of the time) and resolution (the willingness to commit to high or low probabilities rather than hedging at 50%). Glenn Brier’s 1950 scoring rule combines both: lower is better, 0 is perfect, 0.5 is the chimp.
The chapter then presents EPJ — Tetlock’s twenty-year (1984–2004) study of 284 experts producing ~28,000 forecasts. The headline result is the chimp punch line, but the more important finding is that two statistically distinct sub-populations exist. Drawing on Isaiah Berlin’s essay on Archilochus, Tetlock labels them hedgehogs (one Big Idea, ideologically coherent, confident, “moreover”-style speech) and foxes (eclectic, “however”-style speech, comfortable with maybes). Foxes outperformed hedgehogs on both calibration and resolution; hedgehogs were worse in their own specialties because the green-tinted glasses of their Big Idea distorted everything they saw. Larry Kudlow’s denials of recession through 2008 illustrate the failure mode. The chapter closes with Galton’s ox, “wisdom of the crowd,” and the dragonfly-eye metaphor: foxes succeed because they aggregate perspectives within a single mind.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_04_superforecasters
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 4 — Superforecasters
The chapter opens with the October 2002 National Intelligence Estimate that judged Iraq had active WMD programs — one of the worst intelligence failures in modern history. Tetlock leans on Robert Jervis’s analysis (in Why Intelligence Fails) to make a key distinction: the IC’s conclusion was reasonable given what was known at the time, but it was wrong, and the deeper failure was epistemic — the IC stated “Iraq has…” with no probability hedge, never red-teamed the claim, and “did not even consider as a possibility” that Saddam had ended his programs. The lesson is the process-vs-outcome paradox: a wrong-but-reasonable judgment is different from an unreasonable one, and a right-but-unjustified one is different from a justified one. Good poker players, investors, and intelligence analysts must keep them apart.
The shock of the WMD failure made IARPA possible. In 2006 it was created on the DARPA model; in 2008 the IC commissioned a National Research Council report (chaired by Baruch Fischhoff, including Tetlock) that called for evidence-based testing of analytical methods. IARPA then ran a four-year tournament (2011–2015) requiring competing teams to forecast Goldilocks-zone questions on the same problems daily, with margins to beat the unweighted control group of 20% (year 1) rising to 50% (year 4).
Tetlock then introduces three forecasters. Doug Lorch — retired IBM programmer, Santa Barbara, no special expertise — produced ~1,000 forecasts in year 1 with a Brier of 0.22 (5th of 2,800), then 0.14 in year 2 (best of 2,800), beating the extremizing algorithm and the prediction market. He was paid in $250 Amazon gift certificates. Bill Flack and 58 others joined him as the first-class superforecasters. Across all four years, superforecasters’ three-hundred-day forecasts beat regular forecasters’ one-hundred-day forecasts.
The chapter then preempts the obvious skeptical objection: with 2,800 coin-flippers, some will look superhuman by chance alone. Tetlock applies regression to the mean as the test. If skill is real, top-cohort scores in year t should persist into year t+1; if luck dominates, they will collapse. Roughly 70% of superforecasters retained the label year-on-year (correlation ≈ 0.65, modestly above father–son heights at 0.5). The probability of that pattern arising from coin-flippers is about 1 in 100 million. Some of the persistence is artifact (being told you’re “super” and grouped with peers boosts performance), but the bulk is skill. The Washington Post’s David Ignatius reported a leak that superforecasters beat IC analysts with classified access by ~30%. The remaining puzzle — why these particular people are so good — sets up chapters 5–9.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_05_supersmart
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 5 — Supersmart?
If superforecasters were just very smart, very informed people, the rest of us would have no path forward. Tetlock tests the hypothesis with Barbara Mellers’s psychometric battery: fluid intelligence (Raven-style spatial puzzles) and crystallized intelligence (knowledge questions). Volunteers as a whole scored above the U.S. mean (~70th percentile). Superforecasters scored higher still (~80th percentile). But the big jump is from the public to the volunteer pool, not from volunteers to superforecasters. Most superforecasters are well above average, but well short of “genius” (top 1%). Sandy Sillman, the chapter’s opener — Brown/MIT/Harvard, PhD in applied physics, six languages — is an extreme; the modal superforecaster is an attentive NYT reader with quantitative comfort. The McNamara-on-Vietnam example reinforces that raw intelligence without analytic discipline produces overconfidence.
What matters more, the chapter argues, is how the available cognitive horsepower is used. Tetlock walks through the five-step procedure that recurs across superforecasters’ work:


Fermi-ize: decompose intractable questions into knowable and unknowable sub-components. Tetlock uses Daniel Levitin’s piano-tuners-in-Chicago classroom: starting with population, piano-ownership rate, tuning frequency, and tuner work-hours, you can converge on ~63 — close to the actual yellow-pages count. Sandy Sillman calls this “part of my natural way of thinking.”


Take the outside view first. Faced with the IARPA question on whether French or Swiss inquiries would find polonium in Yasser Arafat’s remains, Bill Flack didn’t dive into Israeli-Palestinian politics. He first researched whether polonium could even be detected in remains years post-mortem, then enumerated all pathways by which contamination could occur (Israel, Palestinian rivals, post-mortem framing). The Renzetti family pet question is the canonical illustration: 62% of US households own pets is the right starting anchor; 73% for single-family detached homes is a refinement; biographical details should adjust the prior, not replace it. Anchoring research shows you must start with the outside view because we underadjust from initial anchors.


Inside view: investigate hypotheses methodically — what would have to be true? Do the research with target.


Synthesize outside and inside. David Rogg’s Charlie-Hebdo question is exemplary: base rate of attacks (1.2/year), updated for ISIS surge (1.5), updated for post-attack security (1.8), pro-rated to 69 days = 34%.


Seek other perspectives. Get teammate critique, do “the crowd within” by waiting and re-estimating, or even just re-word the question (“will the visa be denied?”) to defuse confirmation bias.


The chapter introduces Jonathan Baron’s Active Open-Mindedness (AOM) scale — agreement with statements like “people should consider evidence against their beliefs” and disagreement with “changing your mind is a sign of weakness.” Superforecasters score high. The slogan: beliefs are hypotheses to be tested, not treasures to be protected.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_06_superquants
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 6 — Superquants?
Superforecasters are uniformly numerate — most pass basic numeracy tests easily and many have backgrounds in math, science, or programming (Lionel Levine, the chapter’s opener, is a Cornell math professor). But Tetlock argues the value of numeracy is not that it lets superforecasters deploy esoteric models. Levine takes pride in not using formal math; Bill Flack will occasionally build a Monte Carlo for currency questions, but most superforecaster forecasts are “the product of careful thought and nuanced judgment.” What numeracy buys is probabilistic thinking — the ability to populate a fine-grained “maybe” dial.
The chapter contrasts the fictional Leon Panetta in Zero Dark Thirty (frustrated by varying confidence estimates from his analysts; impressed by Maya’s “100%, he’s there”) with the real Leon Panetta (welcomed the diversity, “nothing is one hundred percent”) and Barack Obama as Mark Bowden reported him in The Finish: faced with a CIA spread of 30%–95% on whether bin Laden was in the Abbottabad compound, Obama said “this is fifty-fifty…a flip of the coin.” Tetlock unpacks several possible meanings; the most charitable is that Obama meant “I’d act on any reasonable probability.” The least charitable is the three-setting mental dial — yes / no / maybe — onto which probability collapses. Amos Tversky once joked that “most people only have three settings.” The chapter argues this is the universal default: a Stone-Age heuristic well-suited to lion-versus-no-lion decisions, badly suited to modern probability.
Two costs of the three-setting dial: (1) people equate confidence with competence and treat probabilistic forecasters as ignorant or weak (research on financial advisors); (2) we exaggerate the certainty of high-probability claims — 80% gets read as “this will happen” — as Robert Rubin had to “pound the table” to correct in his Treasury years.
Probabilistic thinking, by contrast, treats certainty as illusory (“nothing is chiseled in granite”). It distinguishes epistemic uncertainty (in principle knowable; clocklike) from aleatory uncertainty (irreducibly random; cloudlike). Superforecasters who sense aleatory dominance keep their estimates inside 35–65% and move tentatively. They are also strikingly granular: about a third of their forecasts use single-percentage-point precision (3% rather than 5%). Mellers showed this granularity is not bafflegab — rounding superforecasters’ forecasts to the nearest 5% measurably degraded their Brier scores; rounding regular forecasters to 20% buckets did not.
The chapter closes with a controversial claim: superforecasters are notably less likely to endorse “fate” or “everything happens for a reason” beliefs. On a 9-point fate-vs-randomness scale, they sit firmly on the rejection-of-fate side, and individual fate-belief correlates negatively with Brier accuracy. Probabilistic thinking and divine-order thinking are like oil and water; embracing meaning may be psychologically beneficial but appears costly to forecasting accuracy.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_07_supernewsjunkies
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 7 — Supernewsjunkies?
This chapter is about belief updating. Superforecasters update much more frequently than regulars — Devyn Duffy made 2,271 forecasts on 140 questions in season 3, more than 16 per question — but Tetlock pre-empts the dismissal that they are simply news-watchers with no real edge. Their initial forecasts were already 50% more accurate than regulars’. Updating amplifies the edge but does not create it.
The Charybdis-and-Scylla framing organizes the chapter: forecasters can fail by underreaction (sticking to a prior in the face of diagnostic news) or overreaction (lurching wildly on a single new datapoint). Both shrink accuracy.
Three updating examples: (1) Bill Flack on Arafat-polonium — when the Swiss team announced an unexplained delay, Flack inferred (correctly) that they had detected polonium and were testing for the lead-decay alternative; he raised from 60% to 65%, while a parallel prediction market sat near 4%; the Swiss test was positive. (2) Bill Flack on Shinzo Abe and the Yasukuni Shrine — Flack underreacted to a leaked statement that Abe would visit, because he had unconsciously substituted “would I, as PM, visit?” for “will Abe visit?” Abe visited. (3) Doug Lorch on Arctic sea ice — Lorch overreacted, swinging from 55% to 95% on a one-month-old report from the Sea Ice Prediction Network; the trend reversed and his Brier score suffered.
Tetlock then explains underreaction as belief perseverance, illustrated with Earl Warren and the World War II internment of 112,000 Japanese-Americans. General John DeWitt’s 1942 line — “the very fact that no sabotage has taken place to date is a disturbing and confirming indication that such action will be taken” — is the extreme case: any new evidence is reinterpreted to preserve the prior. Tetlock’s metaphor is Jenga: when a belief sits at the apex of the cognitive tower, it is cheap to revise; when it sits near the base (Dan Kahan’s research on identity-protective cognition; views on gun control or climate change), revising it threatens the whole structure. Superforecasters’ relative lack of professional or ideological investment in any single forecast is therefore a comparative advantage.
Overreaction is illustrated by Burton Malkiel’s data: U.S. households trading stocks most frequently in the 1990s underperformed buy-and-hold by 6.5 points annually, because each new datapoint felt diagnostic when it was noise.
The chapter then introduces Tim Minto (Vancouver software engineer, season-3 winner with Brier 0.15). Minto updated 34 times on a single Syrian refugees question, with average update size of 3.5%. Many small updates is the pattern. Tetlock derives this from Bayes’ theorem (P(H|D)/P(¬H|D) = P(D|H)/P(D|¬H) · P(H)/P(¬H)) but emphasizes that superforecasters are “Bayesian without using Bayes”: they have internalized the idea of moving in proportion to evidence weight without doing the algebra. Ulfelder’s analysis of the Hagel confirmation question (96% prior, dropped only to 83% after the bad hearing) illustrates Bayesian discipline against media panic. The chapter closes with Doug Lorch’s Arctic-sea-ice course-correction (55% → 95% → 55% → 15% as the underlying report failed): rules of thumb sometimes need to be broken outright. Orwell’s sixth rule of language applies — break any of these rules sooner than saying anything outright barbarous.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_08_perpetual_beta
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 8 — Perpetual Beta
The chapter argues that the deepest predictor of superforecasting status is not intelligence, numeracy, or open-mindedness considered statically, but a disposition toward continuous self-improvement — what Tetlock, borrowing from software, calls being in perpetual beta.
Mary Simpson, an economist who missed the 2008 crisis despite being well-positioned to see it, opens the chapter; the experience of failing where she “should have done better” pushed her into the GJP. Carol Dweck’s distinction between fixed mindset (“I’m bad at math, always will be”) and growth mindset (“abilities can be cultivated”) is the key contrast. Dweck’s brain-scan studies show fixed-mindset subjects tune out information that could improve their answer; growth-mindset subjects engage with it. Keynes is the canonical exemplar: his investment record (multiple near-wipeouts followed by reinvention as a value investor before Graham coined the term) embodied “try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again.”
Tetlock then unpacks what informed practice requires:

Try: Polanyi’s bicycle-physics example shows tacit knowledge can’t be transferred by reading. You must forecast to learn forecasting.
Fail with feedback: Don Moore’s research on police lie-detection shows experience without clear, prompt feedback yields confidence-without-skill. Meteorologists and bridge players are well-calibrated because they get clean, fast feedback. Two structural barriers to feedback: vague language (the Forer effect — generic personality statements feel personally accurate; vague forecasts feel personally vindicated) and time lag (creating space for hindsight bias). Tetlock’s own 1988 elicitations from Soviet experts: when re-asked in 1992–93 to recall their pre-1991 estimates of Communist-Party survival, experts on average remembered numbers 31 percentage points higher than what they had actually said. One expert who had said 20% recalled 70%.
Analyze and adjust: Devyn Duffy’s postmortems for his team after the polonium loss are exemplary; Jean-Pierre Beugoms started writing detailed comments on his forecasts because old ones were too sparse to support self-critique. Successful counterfactual reasoning is asymmetric — most experts in EPJ welcomed “I was almost right” what-ifs but rejected “I was almost wrong” ones; Devyn was unusual in saying “we lucked out.”
Grit: Angela Duckworth’s term for sustained passion-and-perseverance toward long-term goals. The chapter highlights two non-superforecasters who exemplify it: Elizabeth Sloane forecasting through brain-cancer treatment to “re-grow her synapses,” and Anne Kilkenny, the Alaska housewife who fact-checked the UN’s Central African Republic refugee data in French and finished all 150 questions for an inert team.

Tetlock closes with a composite portrait of the modal superforecaster organized in three layers — philosophic (cautious, humble, nondeterministic), cognitive (actively open-minded, intelligent with high need for cognition, reflective, numerate, pragmatic, analytical, dragonfly-eyed, probabilistic, thoughtful updater, intuitive psychologist), and work-ethic (growth-mindset, gritty). Crucially, perpetual beta is roughly three times as predictive of rising into the superforecaster ranks as intelligence. Superforecasting is, paraphrasing Edison, 75% perspiration and 25% inspiration.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_09_superteams
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 9 — Superteams
The chapter opens with the contrast between two Kennedy-administration decisions: the Bay of Pigs (1961), an obvious failure of group judgment, and the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962), where roughly the same advisers reached vastly better decisions. Irving Janis’s Victims of Groupthink (1972) gave the failure mode its name: cohesive groups protect esprit de corps by suppressing critical examination. After the Bay of Pigs, JFK redesigned the deliberative process — RFK and Sorensen as “intellectual watchdogs” charged with relentless devil’s-advocacy, hierarchy suspended, Kennedy himself sometimes leaving the room so deference wouldn’t channel discussion. The same group, restructured, considered ten alternatives by end of day one.
Tetlock then describes the GJP team experiment. In year 1, several hundred forecasters were randomly assigned to work alone or on online teams (no face-to-face contact, communicating by forum/email/Skype). Teams got a primer: cooperate but not deferentially, practice constructive confrontation (Andy Grove’s term) and precision questioning (Matthies and Worline) — a counter-Bay-of-Pigs dialogue is sketched (“how far is the Bay of Pigs from the Escambray Mountains?” — eighty miles of swamp). Result: teams beat individuals by 23%.
In year 2, the project deliberately put superforecasters together in superteams. Risks were obvious — labeled superiority can feed CEO-disease overconfidence. But superteams worked. Tetlock describes the social work involved: Elaine Rich was initially intimidated and stayed quiet; Marty Rosenthal “led from behind” with conference calls; people learned to invite explicit pushback (“I want push-back if you see something I don’t”). Adam Grant’s distinction between givers, matchers, and takers explains the cultural dynamic: givers like Marty, Doug Lorch (sharing his diversified-news-source program), and Tim Minto (sharing automatic-update tools) shifted others’ behavior in pro-social directions, and the giver-rich teams won.
The headline result: superforecasters placed on superteams in year 2 became 50% more accurate than they had been alone. The pattern repeated in year 3.
Tetlock then runs the superteams against prediction markets (Inkling, Lumenogic). Conventional wisdom (efficient-market intuition) predicts markets win. They didn’t. Teams of regulars beat the wisdom of the crowd by ~10%; prediction markets beat regular teams by ~20%; superteams beat prediction markets by 15%–30%. Tetlock concedes the markets may have lacked liquidity, but the result is striking. He attributes it to active open-mindedness as a group-level emergent property — not the sum of members’ individual AOM scores, but a function of communication patterns and shared purpose (Amy Edmondson’s “psychologically safe” surgical teams). Linguistic marker: “our” more than “my.”
The chapter closes by reconnecting to Scott Page’s slogan “diversity trumps ability.” The extremizing algorithm that wins regular-forecaster pools depends on diversity of information — superteams that share too well leave less room for it. The picture is not “diversity vs ability” but tuning the mix.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_10_leaders_dilemma
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 10 — The Leader’s Dilemma
The apparent contradiction: leaders must convey confidence, decisiveness, and vision; superforecasters cultivate doubt, slow self-criticism, willingness to revise, and intellectual humility. How can a single person be both?
Tetlock’s resolution leans on Auftragstaktik — “mission command” — articulated by Helmuth von Moltke in nineteenth-century Prussia, refined by the Wehrmacht command manual, and adopted by the U.S. military as official doctrine in 1982. Three features matter:

Nothing is certain. “No plan of operations extends with certainty beyond the first encounter with the enemy’s main strength” (popularly: “no plan survives contact with the enemy”). German war-academy training privileged critical thinking, including criticism of senior officers; Tetlock tells the story of Frederick the Great and Seydlitz at Zorndorf (“Tell the King that after the battle my head is at his disposal, but meanwhile I will make use of it”) to show that disagreement was institutionally sanctioned.
Decisive implementation once a course is chosen. The Wehrmacht manual: “If one wishes to attack, then one must do so with resoluteness…only strength and confidence carry the units with them.” Officers separate the deliberation phase (uncertain, plural, complex) from the execution phase (resolute, calm, confidence-instilling).
Decentralized decision-making. Subordinates are told what to achieve, not how. Captain takes the town; the means is up to him given local conditions. The 1940 Eben Emael assault — where the lieutenant in command landed in the wrong country and a sergeant ran the operation until he arrived — illustrates the resilience of trained-for-improvisation units.

The contrast is the inter-war U.S. Army that disciplined a young Eisenhower for publishing a forward-looking article on tank tactics. After WWII, it took the IDF, the Soviet quantitative threat, and study of Wehrmacht and Israeli practice to push the U.S. military toward adopting mission command. David Petraeus is Tetlock’s exemplar: PhD from Princeton, push-people-out-of-their-comfort-zone training exercises, “thunder run” into Baghdad, and the Mosul counter-insurgency improvised on his own initiative as 101st Airborne commander.
Tetlock argues the same logic governs Bezos’s “Have backbone; disagree and commit,” 3M’s R&D under William Coyne (“we let our people know what we want them to accomplish… [but] do not tell them how”), and the Walmart leadership academy designed by Damian McKinney (a former British Royal Marine).
The chapter resolves the humility paradox with Annie Duke’s distinction: superforecasting requires intellectual humility (reality is complex, my model is partial, I will be wrong) — not personal self-doubt (I am incompetent or unworthy). Lincoln’s “as God gives us to see the right” is the structural template: fierce conviction paired with acknowledgment that vision is limited. The postscript explains the choice of the Wehrmacht as exemplar: forecasters who can’t separate moral judgments from competence judgments will routinely underestimate effective adversaries.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_11_really_so_super
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 11 — Are They Really So Super?
This chapter addresses the two strongest critiques of the superforecasting program — Daniel Kahneman’s worry that biases are intractable, and Nassim Taleb’s worry that what matters most can’t be forecast at all.
Kahneman’s challenge: are superforecasters different kinds of people, or people doing different things? Tetlock answers “a bit of both,” but argues that the System-2 self-monitoring superforecasters perform is exhausting; eventually intuitive System 1 wins. The chapter’s centerpiece is an adversarial collaboration between Kahneman and Mellers on scope insensitivity. Kahneman’s classic Toronto-lakes finding (people will pay ~10 to clean either *a few* lakes or *all 250,000* lakes in Ontario; ~80 to save 2,000, 20,000, or 200,000 migratory birds) is reframed as a forecasting test. Random subgroups of superforecasters and regulars were asked, “How likely is the Assad regime to fall in 3 months?” or “in 6 months?” Regulars showed near-zero scope sensitivity (40% vs 41%). Superforecasters were sensitive (15% vs 24%) — not perfectly so, but enough to surprise Kahneman. Tetlock’s interpretation: the System-2 corrections (taking the outside view, mentally varying the time frame, etc.) practiced enough times can become System 1 — analogous to a golfer’s swing checklist eventually becoming automatic.
Taleb’s challenge: history is dominated by black swans — high-impact, low-probability events outside the bell curve. If so, IARPA’s tournament tests the wrong skill. Tetlock concedes part of the case but distinguishes the strict (literally-inconceivable-before-it-happens) definition from the modest (highly improbable consequential event) one. Many things called black swans — 9/11, World War I — were not unimaginable; they had been imagined and warned about. Tetlock argues:

The world is partly clocklike too — incrementalist history (life expectancy, 1–2% global GDP growth) matters and is forecastable.
Black-swan events gain their black-swan character from the consequences that follow over weeks, months, years — and those consequences depend on follow-on decisions that are tractable (will the U.S. demand bin Laden’s extradition? will the Taliban refuse?). Question clustering can chip away at the larger pattern.
Taleb-style “fat-tailed” distributions (height vs wealth) imply that a 1914 policymaker who underestimated the right-tail risk of war casualties (assuming a normal distribution centered on ~100,000) would have dismissed a forecast of 60M deaths as crackpot, when fat-tailed reasoning would have taken it seriously enough to act.
Kahneman’s counterfactual on Hitler/Stalin/Mao zygotes (each had a 50% chance of being female; 87.5% chance at least one would have been) drives home that history is “but one that emerged, quasi-randomly, from a vast population of once-possible worlds.”

Tetlock, Kahneman, and Taleb agree there is no evidence anyone can usefully forecast geopolitics ten years out. They disagree on whether shorter-horizon, well-calibrated probabilistic forecasting is therefore worth the effort. Tetlock thinks yes. The chapter ends invoking Eisenhower (“plans are useless, but planning is indispensable”) and Richard Danzig’s prescription: where the horizon defeats forecasting, plan for adaptability and resilience — but plans for adaptability still rest on probability estimates.

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_12_whats_next
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Ch. 12 — What’s Next?
Tetlock opens with Daniel Drezner’s Washington Post piece after the Scottish independence referendum: rather than join the chorus of confident retrospective explanations, Drezner asked a “teachable” question — “what does one do with data points like this to adjust one’s worldview?” — and committed publicly to making clear, scorable predictions with explicit confidence intervals going forward. That is the cultural change Tetlock is hoping for.
Whether it happens depends on a competing force: kto-kogo politics (Lenin: “who, whom?”). The chapter concedes that forecasting often serves coalition advancement rather than truth — the Banco Santander Brasil analyst fired for forecasting a left-wing market decline; Dick Morris explicitly admitting his pre-2012 Romney landslide forecast was meant to rally the base; Nate Silver praised by Democrats when he forecast Obama and reviled when he forecast a Republican Senate. If kto-kogo dominates, evidence-based forecasting has no future.
But Tetlock argues by analogy to Ernest Codman, the Boston physician who in 1914 demanded hospitals publish “End Result” outcome statistics. Codman was booted from Massachusetts General, fired from Harvard, cartooned out of his medical society — and ultimately won. Evidence-based medicine, evidence-based policy, evidence-based sports performance (“Moneyball”) all emerged despite hostile incumbent interests. The IARPA tournament is itself evidence: the most kto-kogo-vulnerable institution imaginable (an intelligence community whose forecasts are fodder for partisan blame-games) chose to test itself.
Two specific tools the chapter proposes:


Bayesian question clustering. Big questions (“how does the Korean peninsula turn out?”) can’t be scored. But they decompose into clusters of small scorable ones (will North Korea test a rocket? rebuff diplomatic talks? fire artillery?). Pointillism: a single dot is not a painting; many dots converge on a portrait. Future research aims to operationalize this for “big” questions.


Adversarial collaboration between superforecasters and superquestioners. Tom Friedman’s Iraq column (“Is Iraq the way it is because Saddam is the way he is, or vice versa?”) passes the smack-the-forehead test — it generates the right question for forecasters to attack, even if Friedman himself drew the wrong conclusion. Tetlock argues for a “Tom-Bill symbiosis”: superquestioners produce the question architecture; superforecasters produce the calibrated answers. The Tom-vs-Bill framing of chapter 1 was the book’s “final false dichotomy.”


The chapter closes with the November 2010 letter to Ben Bernanke. Bloomberg in October 2014 contacted the signatories. None said they’d been wrong; some said inflation was just hidden (“on Wall Street”); Niall Ferguson noted the letter said “risk” without a date and was therefore not yet falsified. Tetlock contrasts this with the Kahneman–Klein adversarial collaboration. He proposes that policy adversaries jointly design ex-ante scorable forecast tests (defined inflation metric, defined window, defined threshold). Some will rationalize when they lose. Others will say “I was wrong.” Either way, observers learn. “All we have to do is get serious about keeping score.”

06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.title: ch_13_epilogue
06_Source_Notes/chapter_summaries/z-libr.content:
Epilogue
The book closes with a brief portrait of Bill Flack reacting to a draft of chapter 1. Flack notes that he is technically not a “native Cornhusker” — he was born in Kansas City and moved to Nebraska at age 7 — and asks Tetlock to correct it. Tetlock takes the correction as a small but characteristic display of precision, the trait that runs through superforecasters’ work.
Flack explicitly disavows any claim to deserve a Davos seat — “I’d have to go to Google just to find out who the prime minister of Fanatistan is” — and respectfully gives the Tom-Friedmen-of-the-world credit for in-depth area knowledge he doesn’t have. This is the intellectual humility chapter 10 distinguished from personal self-doubt. Pundits, in Flack’s framing, function “something like lawyers in an adversarial judicial system”: they make the strongest case for one outcome, and the superforecaster aggregates competing cases into a weighted forecast. Tetlock extends Flack’s metaphor with a baseball image: superquestioners pitch the questions; superforecasters bat at them.
Flack also acknowledges that luck plays a real role in any individual forecasting season, and that an overconfident bad call could “shatter” his self-image less than the Brier-score feedback would simply modify his behavior. He expects to keep iterating. The Brier score is the means by which “try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again” remains operative even at the top of the leaderboard.
Tetlock’s final sentence: that disposition — perpetual beta — is “why he is a superforecaster.” The frame closes where the book opened: with a comparison to Tom Friedman that resists the temptation to declare a winner, and that locates the value of superforecasting not in any individual’s verdict but in the disciplined process that sustains accuracy over time.
